en: Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Extensive and Vast, Scroll One, including the Preface.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang;
recorded as annotations to the sūtra by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.

Coming and going are without limit; movement and stillness share a single source. Encompassing all wonders with abundance, it transcends words and thought to emerge far beyond them—is this not the Dharma-realm alone?
It cleaves open the profound and subtle, illuminating the expanse of mind and world, exhausting all principles and perfecting all natures.
The fruition penetrates the cause; vast and profound, it is all-encompassing and complete—this can only be the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* of the Buddha.

Thus, when our World-Honored One first fulfilled the ten bodies and initially attained perfect enlightenment, he employed his vows and practices to encompass all things, merging with empty space as his essential nature.
He is richly endowed with myriad virtues, yet remains as pure as a mote of dust; his wisdom is serene and profound.
The clear waves of the ocean contain all phenomena within their voidness; like the full moon of the luminous nature of emptiness, they suddenly descend upon the hundred rivers.

Without arising from the King of Trees, they array the seven locations throughout the dharma-realm; never deviating from the future limit, they unfold the nine assemblies at the very moment of initial realization.

The profound essence of the vast and expansive is fully exhausted; it envelops the inconceivable ocean-like assemblies. The perfect sound resounds clearly and far-reaching, instantly encompassing the ten lands;
the primary and attendant teachings are layered upon one another, resonating in unison throughout the ten directions.
Although the void is traceless, the constellations of the Dharma-realm shine brilliantly; though the depths are beyond words, the waves of the ocean of teaching are vast and surging.
If the myriad gates flow in secret confluence, it serves as the great source for all scriptures; if the ten thousand virtues converge, it embraces the multitude of sūtras as its retinue.
As for its essential purport: it darkly realizes the true essence within the realm of myriad transformations, and it manifests the marks of virtue at the gate of profound mystery.
Its functions arise in profusion yet remain eternally as they are; its wisdom reflects all things while remaining perpetually still. Thus, truth and delusion intersect...
Penetration means that by means of the ordinary mind one perceives the Buddha-mind. One cultivates both phenomena and principle; relying on fundamental wisdom, one seeks Buddha-wisdom.
When principle accords with the transformations of phenomena, the dependent origination of the one and the many becomes boundless.

When phenomena attain harmony with principle, the myriad differences interpenetrate without obstruction. Thus, the ten bodies are clearly manifest while acting as one another, and the six positions remain undisturbed.
Furthermore, they are gathered; the vast and great immediately enters the space without interval.
Dust motes and hairs contain all within them without exteriority, appearing vividly and simultaneously like mustard seeds within a jar. One and many are unimpeded, comparable to drops in the ocean;

they are equal to a thousand lamps in an empty room, where concealment and manifestation are both perfected, resembling a crescent moon in the autumn sky, reflecting one another in infinite layers. If...
The hanging pearls of the celestial net are perfectly interfused in every thought-moment; the successive dharma-gates are like clouds arising in the vast sky.
The myriad practices unfold in profusion, comparable to flowers blooming upon brocade.

As for that which is so lofty it cannot be looked up to, there are bodhisattvas who have accumulated practices, their gills and scales basking at the Dragon Gate; as for that which is so deep it cannot be fathomed, there are those of supreme virtue.
The Śrāvakas closed their eyes and ears to the sublime assembly; yet with seeing and hearing as the seeds, they transcended the stages of the ten bhūmis despite the eight difficulties.

With understanding and practice embodied, they perfected the fruits of vast eons in a single lifetime. Like the lion’s vigorous leap, the multitudes of the ocean were suddenly realized within the grove;
like the elephant king’s majestic turn, six thousand attained the Way beneath his words. Thus was the Eastern Temple illuminated by wisdom.
Fulfillment does not differ from the initial resolve; though one seeks through various stages, the perfection of causes does not exceed a single pore.

By opening the sutra-scrolls within a single atom, the fruit is realized in every thought-moment; by exhausting the gates of aspiration for all sentient beings, every speck of dust fulfills the practice.
This can truly be called the wondrous teaching of eternity, the grand standard that penetrates all directions, and the ultimate discourse in accordance with the nature of reality.

This is the essential path of the One Vehicle. When one investigates this profound principle and then surveys other sutras, it is like the bright sun adorning the sky, eclipsing the brilliance of all other lights;
or like Mount Sumeru spanning the ocean, surpassing the height of all other peaks.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas sought its secrets in the Dragon Palace, and great sages propagated it in the Eastern Land. Looking back upon this era of the True Dharma, it is still...
The pure radiance remains concealed. How fortunate that, in this age of the Semblance Dharma, I have encountered this profound transformation.
Moreover, having met the Sage Ruler and being able to dwell upon this Sacred Mountain, I exhaust my thoughts upon the subtle essence; how could I not feel joy and exultation?
As for the title *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, it is the collective name for the inexhaustible sūtras. As for "Chapter One: The Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruling Lords," it is...

This is a categorized table of contents for the various sections and meanings of the *Saṃyuktāgama*. "Great" (*da*) signifies its vastness and all-encompassing boundlessness; "square" (*fang*) signifies upholding oneself through the True Dharma (*saddharma*);

"broad" (*guang*) signifies being pervasive in accordance with the essential nature. "Buddha" refers to awakening to this profound mystery; "flower" (*hua*) is a metaphor for the myriad practices of merit;

"ornament" (*yan*) refers to adorning the Dharma to perfect the person; and "sūtra" (*jing*) is a gushing spring from which the Dharma never exhausts, threading together the profound and concentrated sublime meanings.

It encompasses boundless ocean-like assemblies and establishes an eternal standard for all time. Both Buddhas and various kings are equally titled "World Lords," and both the Dharma-gate and its physical support are described as "Sublime Adornments.
By distinguishing categories of meaning to manifest the titles of the chapters, this work stands at the head of all sections as the foremost.
This sutra consists of thirty-nine chapters; since this chapter is established at the beginning, it is called "The Great Square" (Mahāvaipulya).
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Chapter One: The Sublime Array of the World-Ruling Lord.

I take refuge in the Teachers of the Ten Directions throughout the three periods of time, Who are the perfectly luminous guides within every atom of the lands, Whose clouds of great compassion are the virtues of the Dharma-realm, And who are Vairocana, the great ocean of wisdom.
The profound true nature of reality wherein all abide, And the perfect sūtras that flow therefrom—
Within every atom and in every direction, amidst the assemblies of Buddhas, Are Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī,
and all the great bodhisattvas. Now, with the wisdom of a single hair, I wish to measure the emptiness of the boundless realm of phenomena.
May we rely upon the compassionate essence of the Three Jewels as one, May every word accord in secret with the intent of all Buddhas,
And cause the Eye of the Dharma to never be deficient, Throughout the entire realm of sentient beings, like Samantabhadra.
May this supreme merit reach all living beings, So that they may swiftly realize the fruit of Bodhi, eternal bliss.

In explaining the meaning of this scripture, ten general sections are opened: first, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, the classification within the scriptural collections (piṭaka) and teachings;

third, the delimitation of the principles and meanings; fourth, the capacities of the sentient beings to whom the teaching is addressed; fifth, the depth of the essence of the teaching; sixth, the scope and limitations of its fundamental aim.

Section Seven: Categories of Texts; Section Eight: Accounts of Translation and Spiritual Resonance; Section Nine: General Explanation of the Scripture’s Title; Section Ten: Detailed Exposition of the Text’s Meaning.
Regarding the first, the "Causes and Conditions": Now, when sages establish their teachings, there must necessarily be a specific purpose and origin. It is like Mount Sumeru or the vast ocean.
Only a great cause can cause such shaking and swaying. Now, to shake the Tathāgata’s mountain of refined gold-like virtue and to stir his ocean of profound and vast wisdom is no small matter.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "The Tathāgata does not appear nor achieve manifestation through a single cause or a single event;
he appears for the sake of the Great Avataṃsaka. Thus, there is first the cause and subsequently the conditions.
Each [chapter] opens ten meanings to manifest their inexhaustibility. As for the ten meanings: first, because it is the nature of phenomena;
second, to repay past causes; third, to accord with the resonance of sentient beings' capacities; fourth, as the foundation of the teaching; fifth, to manifest the merit of the fruit;
sixth, to clarify the stages and positions; seventh, to explain the sublime practices; eighth, to reveal the true Dharma; ninth, to open up the causal nature.
For the sake of ten benefits hereafter, it is said that this is the nature of things (*dharmatā*). Now, the royal path is broad and level;
its regulations have been the same for a thousand ages. The profound gate of the One Vehicle has been realized by all Buddhas alike.

Therefore, all Buddhas, as the nature of things, constantly turn such an inexhaustible wheel of Dharma throughout infinite worlds, causing all sentient beings to return to their origin and source, reaching the ultimate limit of the unmanifested.

The future limit is without cessation; therefore, in the "Inconceivable" chapter, it is clarified that all Buddhas are able, within a single body, to manifest as many heads as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, with each individual head...
Transforming as many tongues as there are, from each tongue, they produce as many sounds, even down to every letter, word, and meaning, so that each fills the entire Dharma-realm without end.
This means that spatially, one uses the tip of a hair to encompass the Dharma-realm horizontally;
temporally, one uses a single kṣaṇa to exhaustively penetrate the ocean of kalpas vertically. Spatially, it arises instantaneously; temporally, it arises eternally. It does not...
Awaiting other causes, we merely follow what has been seen and heard to speak of the initial formation of the nine distinct assemblies.
Within the inexhaustible, those who possess great compassion have briefly delineated this cycle of transmigration so that seekers may, by investigating it, perceive the boundless Dharma—
just as one perceives the infinite void through a window crack— and realize that at such a time and place, the particular is identical to the inexhaustible, for one place is indeed all places.
Regarding the "occasion": first, because a single moment is all moments. Second, regarding the repayment of past causes: why does the Dharma necessarily evolve in this manner?
Because past causes are profound. Indeed, when the roots are deep, the fruit is lush; when the source is distant, the stream is long.
Since past causes are profound, the arising of the teaching is likewise vast. What is meant by "profound and vast"? Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, was the first to tread upon the mysterious path.
The spirit dwells in wondrous stillness; compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem; and conduct and vows are brought to completion.
Thus, although delusive thoughts are not severed, the nature of emptiness is vast and penetrating; and although the spiritual mirror is not polished, the myriad dharmas are suddenly clarified.
It is through this unobstructed liberation that this wondrous gate is revealed. Although past causes are manifold, they may be briefly summarized as two kinds: first, by the power of great vows.
The "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" states: "The Buddha Vairocana, through the power of his vows, pervades the entire Dharma realm;
within all lands, he constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel. The verse from Tuṣita says: "The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any nirvāṇa."
By the power of his original great vows, he manifests the sovereign Dharma. All the Buddhas in the assemblies empower him, and all declare it to be the power of his vows;

furthermore, there is more than one authentic textual proof for this. Second, it is due to the power of his past practices. That is to say, throughout immeasurable kalpas, he gave rise to practices based on his vows;

once these practices were perfected and the fruit attained, he was then able to expound [the teachings] instantaneously. Thus, the verse of the presiding mountain deity says: "Having cultivated excellence in the past..."

His practices are boundless, and the supernatural powers he has now attained are likewise immeasurable. He has extensively opened up dharma-gates as numerous as motes of dust, causing all sentient beings to deeply awaken and rejoice.

Regarding the third point, "conforming to the resonance of capacities": this means that although [the Buddha's power] is eternally pervasive due to the natural law (*dharmatā*) of past causes, its transmission to others depends entirely upon the resonance of capacities. For if one were to preach the Dharma apart from such resonance, it would serve no purpose. Its...
It is like the bright moon above reflecting in a clear pool below; when the pool is pure, its image appears, and as the conditions respond, the reflection arises.
Thus, a verse from Tuṣita states: "Seeing the Buddha is likewise so; it must rely upon the power of various virtuous deeds. The Buddhas of the ten directions told Guṇakara:
"And by the power of the roots of goodness of this assembly of Bodhisattvas. Vimukticandra said: "This assembly is without..."

"All defilements," "the will and understanding are entirely clear and pure," and so forth—all of these are manifestations of the capacity [of the audience] and the response [of the Buddha]. They extensively reveal the capacity for resonance (*gān*).

As in the section on the capacities to be reached by the fourth teaching, this resonance of capacity extends across both the present and the future. Those who are appropriately matched to the various assemblies are those of the present;
those who hear it now are the capacities of the future. Regarding the phrase "the four are the basis of the teaching," this refers to the fact that they are not the ocean [of the *Avataṃsaka*].
There is no way to flow secretly without a source; there is no way for the end to be sustained without the root.

Desiring to follow the capacities [of beings] and gradually bestow the provisional teachings, one first demonstrates the fundamental Dharma by expounding this sutra all at once. Furthermore, there are two aspects to this: first, to reveal the root of the gradual teachings. As the "Appearance" chapter states:
"Just as when the sun first rises, it first illuminates the high mountains. Second, to encompass the root of the provisional teachings. It is like the sun...

Because at the time of cessation, it again illuminates the high mountain; thus, there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm, and there is nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm.
The Lotus Sutra also says: "As soon as they see my body and hear what I say, they all immediately believe and accept it."

"Entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata" is the fundamental basis of this gradual [teaching]. Next, it says, "excepting those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna," which opens up the gradual path.
Furthermore, it says, "I now also cause them to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom," which means bringing the branches back to the root.
Thus, the Lotus Sutra also points to this sutra as its foundation. (Five: Manifestation)

Regarding the "Virtues of the Fruit" (*phala-guṇa*): this refers to the manifestation of the Buddha’s supreme virtues within this fundamental Dharma, so that all bodhisattvas may have faith in, aspire toward, and realize them.
Just as one who does not recognize precious gems cannot obtain their utility, how could one who does not know these virtues ever look up to them with longing?

Furthermore, there are two kinds of virtues of the fruit: first, the "concordant fruit" (*niṣyanda-phala*), such as the Flower Treasury World-Ocean (*kusumatalagarbhavyūha-lokadhātusamudra*) and so forth; second, the "actual fruit" (*maula-phala*), namely the ten [powers] of the Tathāgata.

The body and so forth—these two being unimpeded constitute the virtues of a Buddha. Furthermore, regarding the unimpeded interpenetration of the environment (*āśraya*) and the embodied being (*adhiṣṭhita*), there are six propositions:

first, the environment appearing within the environment, such as oceans of lands within a single atom; second, the embodied being appearing within the embodied being, such as Buddhas appearing from within a pore;

third, the embodied being appearing within the environment; fourth, the environment appearing within the embodied being; fifth, both the environment and the embodied being appearing within the environment; sixth, [both] appearing within the embodied being.
Within, there is the manifestation of the true basis (*samyak-āśraya*). Its textual expressions are not singular; furthermore, there are four propositions:

first, "only the basis," because the Buddha is the realm (*kṣetra*); second, "only the true," because the realm is the Buddha; third, both; and fourth, their merging. These can be understood through reflection.

Taking up any single door, it encompasses all, as will be explained below. Sixth, regarding the manifestation of the stages and positions (*bhūmi-pada*): this is for the purpose of revealing the Bodhi...
The Bodhisattva practices the causes of Buddhahood; yet, because there are gradations on the single path leading to the fruit, there must be such a thing as "position" (*sthāna*).
Indeed, for a sage, the greatest treasure is said to be position. Without this position, practice cannot reach fulfillment. This [position] is also of two kinds:

first, the gate of sequential arrangement (*paṭalaka-dvāra*), which establishes the distinctions between positions; second, the gate of perfect fusion (*yuganaddha-dvāra*), wherein a single position subsumes all positions. Each and every position...

It is "fulfilled" because one immediately reaches the Buddha-nature. As it says in the *First Stage* (*Prathamabhūmi*): "Within a single stage, all the merits of every stage are subsumed; faith encompasses the ocean of fruition;
at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening. Nevertheless, these two [aspects] are non-obstructive.
The sequential arrangement (*saṃbheda*) is the provisional designation of the teaching, while perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*) is the essential nature, its qualities, and its function.

Since these characteristics are the characteristics of the very nature, sequential arrangement does not obstruct perfect interpenetration. Since this nature is the nature of the very characteristics, perfect interpenetration does not obstruct sequential arrangement.
Because perfect interpenetration does not obstruct sequential arrangement, the one becomes the immeasurable; because sequential arrangement does not obstruct [perfect interpenetration]...

Because they are fused, the immeasurable becomes one. Because the immeasurable becomes one, they are interpenetrating and pervasive. Because the one becomes the immeasurable, they enter into one another in layers upon layers.
Thus, Vasubandhu, through the six aspects of perfect fusion (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa-saṃpuṭita*), expresses this in numerous passages throughout the text.

Seventh is the teaching on the superior practitioner. One who wishes to ascend to the sublime station cannot do so without practice. As it is said: "The gentleman does not worry about lacking a position;
he worries that he himself is not established. Practice is also of two kinds. First, the instantaneous perfection of all practices, because one single practice encompasses all practices.
The *Daśabhūmika-parivarta* states: "One is many, and many are one," and so forth. This is explained in the *Samantabhadra-caryā-parivarta*.
First, the severance of all [defilements] at once; second, the universal accomplishment of all practices.

This refers to the sequential progression (*kramika*), meaning from the essential nature, characteristics, and merits of the Great Bodhicitta up to the practice within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). These two are unimpeded, as explained according to their respective stages.

Eighth, "revealing the true Dharma": to accomplish the stages of practice, one must understand the principles of the Dharma; one cannot realize the reality of things without understanding these principles.
Practice is also not ultimate reality. Thus, a verse from the *Tuṣita* states: "Because they do not understand the true Dharma, the Buddhas appear in the world. This also has two aspects:
first, it reveals the dharma of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle; second, it reveals the dharma of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena.

Both are as explained in the *Yìfēnzhì* (The Delimitation of Meaning). Ninth, regarding the opening of the causal nature: this refers to the aforementioned causes and effects, phenomena and principle, all of which arise from—
The nature of sentient beings exists. If that nature were not gold or jade, it could not be fashioned into precious vessels despite being carved.

This is because sentient beings take the inherent virtues of their nature as their substance and rely upon the ocean of wisdom as their source. However, as appearances change, the substance becomes distinct; as emotions arise, wisdom is obstructed.
Now, by causing them to know that the mind unites with the substance and to realize the fundamental, emotions vanish. Therefore, this sutra is spoken in order to manifest this truth.
Manifestation also has two aspects: first, to reveal it through words so that one may know its existence;

second, to cause one to practice so as to realize and enter into its manifestation, such as the example of a scroll of scripture being revealed from within dust. It is also as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*:
"It is solely for the sake of the one great causal matter that [the Buddha] appears in the world; that is to say, to open, show, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge."
[The Buddha] saw that all sentient beings possess [this potential], and therefore spoke of it as being "only one. Regarding the "ten benefits for the present and future":

since they all equally possess this portion, they will bring vast benefit to the boundless. This also has two types: first, benefiting the present, which refers to those who encounter the Buddha directly;

second, benefiting the future, which refers to those who hear or see [the teaching] now and subsequently resolve their minds [on enlightenment]. As the *Pinfaxingpin* (Chapter on the Nature of Resolve) states: "We Buddhas shall protect and uphold this Dharma."
This shall cause all bodhisattvas in future ages who have not yet heard it to hear it entirely.
This benefit is twofold: first, to cause them to see and hear so that it may become a firm seed; as the *Avataṃsaka* (Chapter on Manifestation) says:
"Just as when a person consumes a small amount of diamond, it is never digested," and so forth. Second, to cause them to initiate practice and achieve realization; as the *Avataṃsaka* further says:
Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas,

practiced the six pāramitās and cultivated various factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma). If they have not heard this Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable great majesty and virtue,
or if, having heard it at some time, they do not believe it, do not understand it, do not accord with it, and do not enter into it, they cannot be called true [bodhisattvas].

Although they are indeed bodhisattvas, because they are unable to give birth into the family of the Tathāgata, if they hear this Dharma, believe and understand it, comply with it, and awaken to its entry,
one should know that such persons are born into the family of the Tathāgata, even penetrating deeply into the immeasurable realm of the Tathāgata.

This is truly because cultivation through effort over many kalpas ultimately results in decay and destruction, whereas the ultimate limit of the essence of the non-active mind is realized in a single thought-moment.
This brings one into accord with the Buddha-family. The "Chapter on Worthy Leaders" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*) states:

"If one were to serve as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields for the duration of an entire eon, yet if one can recite and uphold this chapter, its merit is most supreme, surpassing all those [former acts].

Furthermore, this benefit specifically corresponds to the preceding nine [benefits], thereby constituting ten kinds of benefit; namely, first, by hearing the Dharma, one immediately realizes the eternal.

1. By hearing [the teaching] universally, one achieves the benefit of seeing and hearing. 2. By hearing the fundamental practices and vows, one studies the Buddha and gives rise [to the aspiration]; thus one achieves the benefit of generating the bodhicitta. 3.

By hearing of the responsive resonance between capacity and stimulus, one knows that the Dharma arises from goodness; thus one achieves the benefit of engaging in cultivation. 4. By hearing that [the Dharma] is the foundation, one realizes its meaning is perfect and complete;

thus one achieves the benefit of sudden realization. 5. By hearing of the merit of the fruition, one’s faith, joy, and aspiration become unified; thus one achieves the benefit of extinguishing hindrances. 6. Six.

1. Hearing the stage (*avasthā*): Resolving to realize and enter it, which accomplishes the benefit of encompassing the stage. 2. Hearing practice (*caryā*): Arousing the intention to practice, which accomplishes the benefit of initiating practice. 3. Hearing the Dharma (*dharma*):

Resolving to understand and comprehend it, which accomplishes the benefit of conforming to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). 4. Hearing the cause (*hetu*): Knowing that all things are identical, which accomplishes the benefit of transformation. 5. Hearing the fruit (*phala*): Resolving to attain the ultimate fruition, which accomplishes the benefit of non-retrogression. 6. Hearing the stage: Resolving to realize and enter it, which accomplishes the benefit of encompassing the stage. 7. Hearing practice: Arousing the intention to practice, which accomplishes the benefit of initiating practice. 8. Hearing the Dharma:

Resolving to understand and comprehend it, which accomplishes the benefit of conforming to the nature of reality. 9. Hearing the cause: Knowing that all things are identical, which accomplishes the benefit of transformation. 10. Total possession of the preceding nine: Which accomplishes the benefit of swift realization. Thus, these are the nine causes.
All of these may also serve as present benefits. Each of the preceding gates establishes ten benefits, which can be understood through reflection.
Because of the aforementioned ten meanings, this teaching has arisen. Within the "Chapter on Generating the Resolve," there are ten causes; it says:

"By the spiritual power of the Buddha, by the power of the World-Honored One’s original vows," and so forth. Causes and conditions intermingle, and one may correlate them with the conditions of the assembly.
It is obtained through the mind.

Second, regarding the explanation of the conditions for preaching the sutra: at the beginning of all sutras, the mention of the time, place, person, and so forth, constitutes the *nidāna* (causal origin).
Now, there are ten such conditions: first, based on time; second, based on place; third, based on the principal teacher; fourth, based on samādhi; fifth, based on...
The manifestation of signs: (6) based on the speaker, (7) based on the listener, (8) based on the root of virtue, (9) based on the requester, and (10) based on the bestower of empowerment.
First, regarding the time: when the mind merges with the ultimate Way, then past and present are unified as one.
The Dharma-realm is unborn and fundamentally devoid of temporal divisions. As a verse in the subsequent sutra says: "The Buddhas attain Bodhi; in reality, they do not calculate [time]."

How much more so regarding boundless discourse? How can one contemplate the perfect interfusion of eons! Now, through the time that is timeless, I shall briefly manifest ten layers of temporal distinctions.
First is a single thought-moment; second, the full seven days; third, pervading the three periods of time; fourth, subsuming eons of the same category;
fifth, gathering eons of different categories; sixth, subsuming eons within a thought-moment; seventh, the mutual inclusion of eons and thought-moments; eighth...

In the period of different realms, there are ten [points]: first, the mutual inclusion of these and that; second, subsuming the derivative within the fundamental—meaning that what is not an eon is treated as an eon;

third, constantly expounding this sutra throughout the aforementioned ten periods; fourth, each of these ten types being fully encompassed by any one of them; fifth, when speaking according to time, there is neither beginning nor end;
sixth, speaking of the initial formation and so forth according to what is seen and heard; and the rest are as previously stated regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This is clarified within the middle section. If one relies upon this time, it is utterly distinct from other teachings, yet the time of those other teachings does not transcend this.

Some speak of three, seven, six, or seven [weeks] and so forth, according to what they have seen or heard; this is explained in detail in the *Zhigui* (The Return to the Source). Second, regarding the locus:
when wisdom exhausts the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), both subject and object vanish. It is conventionally said that it "relies on the truth," yet it is not a physical land.

Moreover, since the atoms of the lands enter one another and the defiled and pure realms merge and harmonize, the universal pervasiveness of the perfect teaching makes it difficult to distinguish their respective locations.
Yet, the Truth is not external to phenomena; it does not destroy its basis. Through the timelessness of the ultimate, it pervades all places that are not fixed locations.
Nevertheless, some say this sutra was preached in a defiled land because it was situated in Magadha and other such regions; others say:

It is taught as being situated in a pure land because it resides within the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha). Some say that regarding the "meaning as it truly is," there are two types of bodies and lands that do not have fixed or distinct locations;

rather, they are perceived differently within a single location due to differences in what is seen and heard. Among the three meanings mentioned above, the latter one is closest to our own school’s tenet.

However, regarding the places where this sutra is preached, purity and defilement are unimpeded; the universal and the particular interpenetrate. There are two sets of four propositions for each. First, concerning purity and defilement:

it may be exclusively defiled, or exclusively pure, as in the first two meanings [of the preceding analysis]; or it may be both, because the Sahā world is within the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*);

or it may be merged, because the characteristics of defilement and purity are exhausted, being one with the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Furthermore, it may be exclusively defiled, such as in Magadha...

[The first case is] "both," because the characteristics of both purity and defilement are covered. [The second case is] "only pure," because the ground is vajra-like and the characteristics of defilement have been exhausted.

[The third case is] "both," because concealment and manifestation are without obstruction. [The fourth case is] "neither," because the two characteristics mutually cancel each other out until both are exhausted.

Next, to clarify the two sets of four propositions regarding the interpenetration of the particular and the universal: [the first is] "particular," because it pertains to this single realm; [the second is] "universal," because it encompasses the ten directions.
Or they are both: because this very [realm] is pervasive; or because the two characteristics are entirely extinguished.
Or it is restricted: because this realm subsumes all; or it is universal: because this enters into all. Or it is both: because it subsumes and enters simultaneously; or it is extinguished.

Because forms and their characteristics are exhausted [in mutual sublation], and because a single atom may be used as an analogy for a *kṣetra*, there are likewise four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to be understood.
From the narrow to the broad, ten locations are briefly indicated. First, these seven places and nine assemblies of Jambudvīpa pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
1. As in the "Chapter on Ascending Mount Sumeru," [the light] pervades two cycles of ten billion similar realms within a single world-system;

2. as in the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance," it pervades three types of dissimilar lands, such as those shaped like trees; 3. it pervades the world-systems; 4. it pervades the world-germinal systems (*dhātu*); and 5. it pervades the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpakaraṇḍa*).

Sixth, throughout the oceans of lands in the remaining directions, whether by seed or by land; seventh, throughout the atoms of the six aforementioned types of lands, all of which contain both similar and dissimilar lands;
eighth, throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, where within every single point the size of a hair-tip there are infinitely many oceans of lands;
ninth, like a net of Indra; tenth, as with the other Buddhas. Thus, each of these ten categories individually pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Among these realms, the first nine are precisely the places where Vairocana preaches the Dharma.

However, although the locations for preaching the *Daśabhūmika* and other stages each pervade the entire dharma-realm, even down to the pores and hairs of the body, they do not become confused despite their differing gateways.

If one considers the mutual inclusion of the entire positions of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) and the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), then while they are mutually exclusive in their specific aspects, each individually pervades the dharma-realm.
If one considers how the various stages support one another, then this and that exist mutually, equally pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
each assembly should be understood according to this principle. Regarding the identity of the ten or more Buddhas: since this Buddha is thus, so too are the other Buddhas;
therefore, at the conclusion of each assembly, it is universally stated, "We, all Buddhas, also speak thus. Nevertheless, the presiding Buddhas do not see one another.
The companions do not see one another; it is only when the principal sees the companions and the companions see the principal that they see each other.

If they did not see one another, they would each pervade the entire Dharma-realm individually; because they see one another, they equally pervade the Dharma-realm together, without confusion and without obstruction.

Furthermore, these ten aforementioned locations function collectively as a single dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), wherein the mention of any one part encompasses the whole, for each individual location accords with the Dharma.
Because of their nature, they pervade all these locations simultaneously with each preceding moment; likewise, each individual location is fully endowed with each preceding moment.

This explanation of the scripture is given in terms of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). If, however, one speaks in terms of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*jñāna-saṃbodhi*), [it is as follows].
As for the world of sentient beings, within each and every Buddha-body—down to its limbs, joints, and pores—all infinite and multilayered lands are subsumed;
it is the same for every single Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) and sentient being, and all are places where Vairocana preaches the sutras.
Third, regarding the "Dependent on the Master" (yishu): Now, the True Body (*dharmakāya*) is vast and remote, merging with the *dharmadhātu*.

Its essence encompasses all without exterior, being equal to the myriad transformations; its function exhausts the source without duality, yet when grasped through its traces, it manifests in many ways.

Whether one body or many bodies, the sūtras and śāstras offer divergent explanations. Now, concerning the Buddha of this sūtra: is he the True [Body] or the Responsive [Body]? Is he one or many? If...
Regarding the term "True" (Svabhāva): why is he named Śākyamuni? He dwells in the Sahā world and is seen alike by humans and devas.
If he is called the "Responsive" (Nirmāṇakāya), why is he called Vairocana? He dwells in the Lotus Treasury World and is seen by great bodhisattvas;
they see the Buddha’s Dharmakāya. If he is said to be one, why does he manifest in many places? If he is said to be different, why is it further said that he does not divide his body?

Therefore, the Buddha who preaches this sutra is not the same as the one previously described; he is the inexhaustible cloud-body of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), in which the true and the responsive are fused, and the one and the many are non-obstructive. He is Vairocana because he is Śākyamuni;
he is always here because he is elsewhere; he is far away in other lands because he eternally dwells here; his body is not divided into parts, yet it is not a single unity either.
Simultaneously existing in different locations, yet each body is perfectly complete and fully manifested;
because this cannot be conceived by any bodhisattva, we shall first clarify the ten bodies and subsequently manifest their non-obstruction. Regarding the "ten bodies," there are two meanings. First:
Regarding the condensation of the three worlds into ten types: first, the body of sentient beings; second, the body of the land; third, the body of karmic retribution;
fourth, the body of śrāvakas; fifth, the body of pratyekabuddhas; sixth, the body of bodhisattvas; seventh, the body of the Tathāgata;
eighth, the body of wisdom; ninth, the body of dharma; tenth, the body of empty space. Second, within the Buddha himself, there are naturally ten bodies: first, the body of bodhi...
1. The body of birth; 2. the body of vows; 3. the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); 4. the body sustained by power; 5. the body adorned with the marks and signs of excellence;
6. the body of majestic power; 7. the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*); 8. the body of merit; 9. the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); 10. the body of knowledge.

Their characteristics are extensively revealed as explained in the Eighth Stage (*Aṣṭamabhūmi*) and the Chapter on Transcending the World (*Lokātīta-parivarta*). Regarding what is called "unimpeded," there are briefly ten meanings.

1. Unobstructed pervasion of activity (*kriyā-vyāpti-nirāvaraṇa*). This refers to the fact that throughout the aforementioned realms of thoughts, eons, lands, atoms, and so forth, the Vairocana Buddha manifests clouds of Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-megha*), whose activities are boundless and entirely pervasive. As the Sūtra says:
"Just as one sees the Buddha seated here, so it is in every atom," and such passages occur more than once. 2. Unobstructed pervasion of marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyāpti-nirāvaraṇa*). This refers to...
1. Regarding the distinct functions of the aforementioned [bodies], each encompasses all karmic activities; therefore, there are three. 2. The non-obstruction of quiescence and activity:

because they are accomplished without partiality. 3. The non-obstruction of the basis and its arising: because they manifest instantaneously without thought, through the power of the Ocean Seal Samādhi.

4. The non-obstruction of the real and the responsive: because the responsive is identical to the Dharma, being of one flavor and equality. 5. The non-obstruction of the partial and the complete: each and every body...
7. Non-obstruction of parts: because it possesses the entire body. 8. Non-obstruction of cause and effect: because it does not obstruct the manifestation of causes.

9. Non-obstruction of the environment and the inhabitants: because it does not obstruct the manifestation of the basis [the environment]. 10. Non-obstruction of secret entry: entering the realm of sentient beings like the *tathāgatagarbha*;
although acting as a sentient being, it does not lose its own nature. Thus, the "Appearance Chapter" says: "The Buddha-wisdom secretly enters..."
"The mind of sentient beings. It is also said: "Within the minds of sentient beings, there are Buddhas who have attained perfect enlightenment," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is taught that all sentient beings are gathered within a single pore. The Deva King Skillful Transformation said: "You should contemplate a single pore of the Buddha."
All sentient beings are entirely within it. (10) It is perfectly pervasive and unobstructed. This means that this Buddha-body is simultaneously principle and phenomenon;
simultaneously one and many; simultaneously the basis and the supported; simultaneously the entry and the dharma; simultaneously this and that;
simultaneously sentient and non-sentient; simultaneously deep and vast; simultaneously cause and fruit; and simultaneously the three bodies and the ten bodies—all are identical.
The cloud-like body of the unimpeded Dharma-realm pervades all preceding times and places through these clouds of bodies, constantly preaching the *Avataṃsaka*.
Thus we know that some say the reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) resides in Akaniṣṭha, speaking from the perspective of the inclusion of the reward;

some say the reward-body resides in other pure lands, speaking from the perspective of drawing in and gathering; and some say Śākyamuni sits upon a thousand-petaled lotus, speaking from the perspective of subsuming the two stages.

Some say that the stages are seen only upon ascending; this is spoken in reference to superior capacities. Others divide them into three distinct categories based on essence, characteristics, and function.
Neither of these represents the true meaning of this sutra. Even if one were to distinguish thirty different levels, these would still be explained as a pairing of provisional and ultimate truth.
If one does not integrate the preceding meanings, one also loses the core tenet of the sutra. Regarding the fourth point, relying on samādhi:

movement and stillness belong only to material things; how could this be the case for a Sage? To demonstrate the model for future disciples and to clarify that there is a teaching to be given, one must first contemplate the preceding principles in stillness and receive the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas.
Only after arising from meditative concentration does one speak; such speech is necessarily true and appropriate, and being necessarily true and appropriate, it is so.

Therefore, the minds of those who receive [the teaching] naturally become sincere. Thus, across various assemblies, there is frequent clarification of entering meditative absorption as the occasion for preaching the sutra.
As for those who do not enter, it shall be explained when we reach the relevant passage. All such entries into absorption exhaust the source of the Dharma;

their functional manifestations are inconceivable. Fifth, regarding the manifestation of signs: this means that although the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is tranquil and void, it is devoid of all signs.
The mark of the signless is not obstructed by manifold activity. The manifestations of the teachings are diverse, and their marks do not conform to a single standard.
Sometimes light is emitted and lands are shaken; sometimes there is a rain of flowers and clouds of incense—all these serve as catalysts for the teaching.

Therefore, within the various assemblies, whenever he is about to preach the Dharma, he frequently first emits light to universally manifest the light of wisdom for the sake of reaching sentient beings. Furthermore, there are two types: the first is... [text truncated]
The light that destroys the sequence [of afflictions] increases or diminishes according to the respective stages. Second is the light of universal penetration and non-obstruction;

because each individual ray of light connects and penetrates all things, it emits different manifestations in various locations. In total there are ten lights, each of which has its own symbolic significance, as should be understood from the text itself.

As for the shaking of the earth and so forth, these mostly occur at the conclusion of the discourse and merely serve to celebrate having heard [the teaching], as is the case in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. Although...

This celebrates what precedes it; in its meaning, it also initiates what follows, thus serving as the causal condition for the teaching. Sixth, regarding the person who expounds [the teaching]: the Dharma neither perishes nor arises;
its propagation depends upon people. As the text below states: "If the Buddha-dharma were not expounded by someone, even those with wisdom could not comprehend it.
This present expounder encompasses the three worlds, which, when divided, become five: namely, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas.
Sentient beings and the vessel-world are further expanded into ten categories by adding the three periods of time, atoms, and pores;
this is because both the vessel-world and sentient beings each have their own partial and complete aspects. The "pores" and "atoms" refer specifically to the partial aspect.

Since all the aforementioned explanations encompass the three periods of time, the *Samantabhadra-caryā-prasthāna-parivarta* states: "The Buddha speaks of sentient beings, he speaks of [the vessel-world], and he speaks of lands."
"Thus it is said regarding the three periods of time," and so forth; in detail, they are immeasurable, for within the *Dharmadhātu-parivarta*, the types [of speakers] are not one.

Just as with the *lakṣaṇānuvyañjana* (marks and secondary signs), some are spoken by the Buddha himself, while in other assemblies, many are spoken by bodhisattvas. At the beginning of the *Dharmadhātu-parivarta*, there are those spoken by śrāvakas;
most are spoken by "good friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*) and other bodhisattvas, which is also termed "spoken by sentient beings. [This concerns] the Bodhi tree.

The phrase "and so forth" refers to the explanation of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*); this should be understood according to the relevant passages. As for the person who teaches, the methods employed differ:
they may use vocal sounds, or they may use sublime forms (*rūpa*) and so forth, as analyzed in the section on the essence of the teaching (*deśanātattva*). Seventh, regarding the listener:
When Ziqi spoke of his mourning, Boya stopped playing the strings. If there were no listener, there would ultimately be nothing to express.

Thus, the various assemblies below are briefly categorized into ten types, which shall be clarified in the text. Excluding the assembly of those with the immediate capacity (*tatkālika*), all others are merely conditions.

Regarding the eighth category, "those who rely on the root of virtue": as a river does not dry up because it contains pearls, and a mountain increases its luster because it contains jade, so too within [the practitioner]...
O Guṇamati, how could those outside [this tradition] possibly discuss this? Nevertheless, regarding the speakers of this Dharma, there are briefly two categories.

First, because wisdom is preeminent: the Buddhas of the ten directions addressed Vajradhvaja, saying, "Because of the purity of your wisdom," and they addressed Vajragarbha, saying, "Also because of your superior power of wisdom."
Second, by the power of other practices and vows, the Buddhas of the ten directions address Samantabhadra, saying:
"It is also because of the power of your cultivation of all practices and vows. The Buddhas of the ten directions also address Dharmamati, saying:
"By the power of the roots of goodness you have cultivated, cause him to enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma. Whether it be the roots of goodness that have been inspired, or...
The vows and practices of the Transformation Master all belong to the category of explaining the causes. Regarding the ninth point, which concerns the person who requests [the teaching]:

if one considers his profound compassion, there are instances where he speaks spontaneously without being questioned; yet, if one considers his reverence for the Dharma and respect for the person [of the Teacher], it is necessary that he speak only after a sincere request.

Those with beginner minds have dull consciousness and do not yet understand how to inquire; those of superior wisdom, out of compassion, raise their doubts and offer formal requests. However, there is...
There are two types: first, invitation by speech; second, invitation by mindfulness. Whether such assemblies exist or not shall be analyzed in the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs.
Regarding the tenth [point], which relies on the one who bestows empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*): Now, the Sage does not respond to ordinary requests; he responds to those who possess sincere devotion.

When the mind merges with the ultimate reality, one thereby receives the Buddha’s empowerment. However, if the Buddha were to speak of himself, he would not require such empowerment, as was the case in the ninth assembly. Because...

Some say that it is necessary to add [the empowerment] above; however, in the eighth assembly, because the practice is cultivated in accordance with the Dharma and is no different from what precedes it, there is no addition.
Furthermore, because the two sevens do not enter meditative absorption, there is no addition. In all other cases, the additions are fully present.
The reason for adding them is to manifest that all Buddhas empower [the teaching] together, which is equivalent to speaking together; for when one speaks, all speak. It is also...
The ocean of fruits is revealed as ineffable because the characteristics of the causes can be described.

If that were so, the *anuvyañjanas* (minor marks) would not be "all-encompassing," because they manifest subtly and are difficult to perceive, and because they transcend cause and effect. However, since their designations differ, one should not apply a single standard to all of them.
There are two kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*): first, manifest empowerment, which is complete in the three types of action; second, subtle empowerment, which is...

I instruct Jñānin to explain this: the Dharmadhātu of Universal Radiance possesses no manifestation but has obscurity; all others possess both, because wherever there is manifestation, there must necessarily be obscurity.
The details of the others will be clarified below.

△ Within the second section, "Inclusion by the Pitakas and the Teachings," there are two parts: first, inclusion by the pitakas; second, inclusion by the teachings. Within the former, there are also two:

first, the pitakas; second, the inclusion. Now, for the first, the pitakas: this refers to the three pitakas and the two pitakas. They are collectively termed "pitaka" (basket) because they contain and encompass [the teachings].
The first chapter of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* and the fourth chapter of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* both state: "Those three and those two... [as follows:]... 云 (it is said).
What is meant by "piṭaka" (basket)? The answer is: because of inclusion. That is to say, it includes all meanings that ought to be known;
"inclusion" means containment. Regarding the three piṭakas: first, the Sūtra-piṭaka; second, the Vinaya-piṭaka; third, the Abhidharma-piṭaka.

Concerning the first [the Sūtra-piṭaka], there will first be a definition of its name, followed by a clarification of its characteristics. Now, for the first: it is also called Sūtra, and it is also called...

*Sūtra*. These are all variations of the Sanskrit sound, like the dialects of Chu and Xia. In ancient translations, it was rendered as *qijing* (契經). In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is termed the *Sūtra-piṭaka*.

"Qie" (契) means to accord with principle and accord with the capacities [of sentient beings]; "jing" (經) means to string together, encompass, and transform. Thus, it is a sūtra that accords with principle and fits the capacities.
This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound based on its primary attribute. "Qiejing" (契經) is the *piṭaka*; this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. Furthermore, it is said that the correct translation is...
It is called "sūtra" (line). A line can thread through flowers; a warp-thread can hold the weft. In this region, the term for "line" is not esteemed, so the word "sūtra" is retained. Some say:
"According to the records, in the five regions of India, what is called 'line,' 'matting,' 'warp-thread,' 'rope,' or 'holy teaching' is all termed *sūtra*;
thus, 'sūtra' is precisely the equivalent [of 'scripture']. This was refuted by the ancient masters, who held that 'sūtra' is not the equivalent. Now, let us examine this in detail."
If the single term "four" were applied to all four realities as being in opposition, then it would be refuted by ancient authorities.

If, however, it includes the sense of "conformity," then the sūtra itself belongs to the category of sūtras that oppose [the Abhidharma], and thus should be termed "Śāsanā" (Holy Teaching). Therefore, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the Liang dynasty was translated as "Śāsanā."
That treatise states: "There is Abhidharma that is not the holy teaching (āgama). In order to establish it as the holy teaching, the term 'Sūtra' is added.
When the ancient masters observed that both Confucians and Mohists referred to their own texts as "Jing" (Scriptures), they consequently borrowed that designation "Jing" to name the holy teaching.
Thus, it encompasses both meanings simultaneously, conforming to both traditions by borrowing the meaning to assist the name, and further adding the term "Yi" (Agreement/契).

The term "character" (*akṣara*) serves to distinguish it from the *sīkṣāpada* (precepts) and the *sūtra* (text), which is highly appropriate. Second, regarding the manifestation of its characteristics:

although the four names used in the four regions differ in their literal designations, their essential meaning is similar; therefore, they are all equally called *sūtra*. Furthermore, the holy teaching contains many meanings and possesses the three aforementioned senses.
Thus, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states that the *sūtra* has five meanings: first, it is like a gushing spring; second, it is like a source of production; third...
The first is called "Manifestation. The fourth is called "Plumb Line. The fifth is called "Stringing Garlands. "Gushing Spring" refers to that which flows forth without exhaustion;
"Giving Birth" refers to that which increases and multiplies through successive stages. Their meaning is the same as "Well-Rope," for there is the act of drawing water from it.

"Manifestation" is precisely this because the holy teaching manifests phenomena and principles. "Plumb Line" refers to the calibration of the correct and the deviant; it is also the rope used as a measuring line, capable of—
It maintains the warp; it shares the same seat as the meaning of the sūtras; it forms a garland, being like the thread [that binds flowers].

Because a thread can string together flowers to form a garland, these five meanings mentioned above do not transcend "stringing" and "gathering. Thus, the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* states: "It is able to string and able to gather."

Therefore, it is called a *sūtra*. Because the holy teaching of the Buddha pierces through (*praveśa*) and upholds (*dhāraṇa*) the meanings that ought to be explained for the sake of those beings to be converted, it is termed a *sūtra*.

This may mean that it both pierces through and upholds what is taught and those to be converted; or, it may mean that it pierces through the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and upholds those to be converted.

Furthermore, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, commenting on the term "pervasion" (*saṃdhāna*), states: "It is called 'pervasion' because it is able to pervade by way of the basis (*āśraya*), the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the phenomenon (*dharma*), and the meaning (*artha*).
As for the 'basis,' it refers to the locus upon which one relies; it is that by virtue of which, and for whose sake, something is taught. As for the 'characteristic'..."
This refers to the characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the characteristics of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

"Phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), truths (*satya*), nutriments (*āhāra*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), formless attainments (*ārūpya*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the absence of conflict (*araṇa*), etc.
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to that which accords with the intentional terminology (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*), and so forth. (See *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 25; *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* 20).
Dàtóng (Great Sameness) agrees with this explanation. Other meanings will be clarified in the section on the twelvefold division [of the scriptures]. Second is the Piṇaya-piṭaka (Vinaya Piṭaka).
Its initial name and its subsequent characteristics are also called *vinī* in the middle [sections], which is merely an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term. This is translated as "subduing" (*tiáodú*).
It refers to the refining of the three types of action (*trikarma*) and the suppression of faults and transgressions. Refining pertains to both abstention and performance, whereas suppression...

This clarifies the cessation of evil. It designates the name based on the practice it explicates; that is, the Piṭaka of Discipline (Vinaya). Alternatively, it refers to the Piṭaka as the instrument of expression which possesses the capacity for discipline;

this is an *adhāra-rahasya* (possessive) compound. Such an interpretation occurs within the Sūtra Piṭaka as well. Regarding *vinaya*: *Vinīyate 'nena kleśo vibhavo vā vinayati vā / vinayo vinītir vāpi vinayo vinayatīti vā //* By means of this, afflictions (*kleśa*) are subdued, or one attains liberation (*vibhava*). Or, it is "discipline" (*vinaya*) because it disciplines, or it is "discipline" because it is the act of disciplining. Thus, it is called *vinaya*.

Alternatively, it is translated as "cessation" (*nirodha*). Cessation has three meanings: first, the cessation of unwholesome karma; second, the cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*); and third, the attainment of the fruit of cessation.
Alternatively, it is called *śīla*. In full, it is *śītalā*, which means "cooling. This is because one leaves behind the causes of feverish affliction and attains the fruit of coolness.
It is also called *prātimokṣa*, which means "individual liberation. This refers to the cause.

It receives its name for two reasons: first, it is called "distinct" (*prātimokṣa*) to distinguish it from the paths of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); second, because the seven branches of the two types of karma each prevent wrongdoing, they are called "distinct.

It is also translated as "conducive to liberation" (*prātimokṣa*), which is established based on its result, as it conduces to the two kinds of liberation—conditioned and unconditioned. It is also called "virtuous by nature," as in the case of the ten...

Reciting the Vinaya is also called "upholding the precepts" (*śīla*), because one is truly able to maintain them exactly as they were originally received. Regarding the subsequent explanation of its characteristics:
these are already contained within the aforementioned names, namely the characteristics of restraint (*saṃvara*) and action (*kriyā*), which constitute the *vinaya*.

To explain them separately, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Vasubandhu states that the *vinaya* has four meanings: namely, transgression (*āpatti*), origination (*samutthāna*), purification (*vyutthāna*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).
Therefore, it is as explained extensively in that treatise. Third is the Abhidharma Piṭaka. "Abhi" means "toward" or "confronting";

"dharma" means "phenomenon" (dharma). There are two kinds of dharmas: first, ultimate dharma (*paramārtha-dharma*), which refers to nirvāṇa itself; because it is wholesome and eternal, it is called "ultimate.
Second, dharma-as-characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-dharma*), which encompasses the four noble truths. "Characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) means "nature" or "aspect. Both of these are termed [dharma].
Regarding the characteristics: since phenomena (*dharma*) are twofold, their "counterparts" (*pratipakṣa*) also have two meanings. First is "orientation," meaning being directed toward *nirvāṇa*.

Second is "contemplation," meaning contemplating the four noble truths (*catuḥsatya*) before one. That which is capable of being the counterpart consists of untainted pure wisdom (*anāsrava-śuddha-prajñā*) and its associated mental factors (*caitta*).
Because the names of the two counterparts are distinguished by virtue of being counterparts to a result and counterparts to an object, wisdom is only the counterpart [to the result], and not...
This dharma is not that which is opposed; rather, it is called "Abhidharma" (Dharma of Opposition) because it is the opponent of [other] dharmas.

Therefore, the Abhidharmakośa is specifically termed a treatise on wisdom (*prajñā-śāstra*). It was translated in the past as "Incomparable Dharma" (*Anupama-dharma*), because it characterizes the excellence of wisdom. As the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states:

The Abhidharma has four meanings: namely, "confrontation" (*abhi*), "enumeration" (*sam*), "subjugation" (*vid*), and "pervasion" (*dharmma*). The meaning of "confrontation" is as explained previously.

Regarding "enumeration": for each and every phenomenon (*dharma*), it repeatedly explains and analyzes their etymological definitions, specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Because it possesses immeasurable distinctions. It is called "subduing" (*vāda*) because, by being fully endowed with the locus of discourse and other factors, it is able to overcome the arguments of others.
It is called "penetrating" (*sādhana*) because it is able to thoroughly explain the meaning of the *sūtras*; it is also termed *upadeśa*.

This is called *vāda* (discourse on meaning), which is also termed *mātṛkā*. This means "root-text" (*benmu*); it refers to that which takes the teachings and their meanings as its root and serves as a mother.
It is also called *āśraya* (basis), because the treasury (*piṭaka*) gives rise to understanding, and the treasury serves as the mother of understanding; thus the root is itself the mother.

It is also called *mātikā*, which means "matrix of practice" (*xingmu*), because one accomplishes practice by relying on the treasury, and because it is the mother of practice. However, these three—[the discourse, the matrix, and the basis]—...
Regarding the Pitakas, there are briefly two approaches based on what they expound. First, in terms of their specific nature (*lakṣaṇa*), the Sūtras expound the three trainings:
the Vinaya expounds only the trainings of morality and mind, while the Śāstras expound only the training of wisdom, as stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

Second, in terms of the primary and secondary, among the Three Pitakas, the Sūtras primarily expound concentration (*samādhi*), the Vinaya expounds morality (*śīla*), and the Śāstras expound wisdom (*prajñā*); yet each also secondarily encompasses all three.
Second, the explanation of the two collections (*piṭaka*): first, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

These are designated as the Śrāvaka-piṭaka because they elucidate the principles, practices, and fruits of the śrāvakas through the aforementioned three collections; they are designated as the Bodhisattva-piṭaka because they elucidate the principles, practices, and fruits of the bodhisattvas.
Thus, the fourth chapter of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "These three collections [are distinguished] by way of superior and inferior..."
Due to the distinction between vehicles, there is further the Śrāvaka Piṭaka and the Bodhisattva Piṭaka; the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* follows this same principle.

This is done by combining the two vehicles because their principles and fruits are identical. However, if distinguished according to their teachings and practices, they are opened up into three vehicles.

These are considered the Tripiṭaka, such as the *Puchao jing* and other sūtras. Furthermore, because Pratyekabuddhas generally do not rely on formal teaching and appear in worlds where no Buddha is present—and because when a Buddha does appear in the world, they are subsumed under the Śrāvakas—they are divided only into two categories.
These are the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, or the Half and Full Teachings. Second, regarding what is subsumed: within the Tripiṭaka, this sūtra belongs strictly to...

The *Sūtra* collection subsumes [this teaching], while simultaneously elucidating the other two; this is because the "Ten Treasuries" and other chapters extensively manifest the precepts, whereas the "Chapter on Names" and others clarify the meaning of the treatises.

If one distinguishes the teachings according to their meaning within the *Sūtras*, they are subsumed solely within the Ten Treasuries, for they fully possess the primary and attendant elements and manifest inexhaustibility, as the teaching and its meaning are fused. Among the two collections, it is only the Bodhisattva...

Regarding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka: if one distinguishes between the provisional and the ultimate, it is subsumed under only one portion of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, as the provisional is not included therein.
However, if categorized according to this [comprehensive] inclusion, even the Śrāvakas are subsumed within this sūtra, for it is capable of encompassing immeasurable vehicles.
The distinction between the provisional and the ultimate will be clarified below in the section on the establishment of the teachings.

Having already examined the inclusion within the *piṭakas*, the second point—clarifying the inclusion within the teachings—is now addressed. There are two types of teachings: first, the general characteristics, namely the twelve divisions of the teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), which are also divided into Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
these will be distinguished below in the "Ten Categories" (*Daśadharmaka*) chapter. Second, the various schools, wherein the two types of teachings differ. This shall now be discussed.

A Brief Explanation. Now, the ocean of the teachings is profound and deep; the clouds of the Dharma spread far and wide. The light of wisdom is boundless, and its wondrous discernment is utterly inexhaustible.
By means of words that are wordless, it elucidates principles that transcend speech; by means of transformations that are unchanging, it responds to infinite capacities.
That which is received at the ultimate stage is difficult for ordinary minds to grasp. Now, relying on the power of principle and teaching, I shall briefly open four gates.

First, the convergence and divergence of the general intent; second, the contradictions and harmonies between the ancient and the modern; third, the classification of schools and the establishment of teachings;

fourth, the comprehensive synthesis and reconciliation. Now, for the first: regarding the lineages that propagated and expounded [the Buddha’s word] in the Western Regions and the Eastern Land (China), they either opened up schools and divided the teachings or directly explained the scriptural texts, as each approach contains both merits and defects. For now, we shall not differentiate them.

Regarding "intention" (*abhiprāya*), there are briefly five aspects. First, the principle is fundamentally of a single flavor; though there are diverse paths, they lead to the same destination, and thus it cannot be divided.
Second, a single sound universally responds, and a single rain universally nourishes. Third, the original intention of the Sage was for a single purpose.
Fourth, according to each individual phrase, various understandings differ. Fifth, through various modes of teaching the Dharma, branches and streams are formed.
Therefore, by virtue of these five meanings, it is not to be divided. To divide it would cause the intellect to construct heterodox views, leading to a contest of right and wrong;
thus, non-division is considered the attainment. As for those who do divide the teachings, there are also many reasons:

first, although the principle is of a single flavor, the explanations have varying depths; therefore, one must divide them so that the provisional and the real may be known. Second, regarding the Buddha, although...

1. Although the Buddha’s voice is one, the teachings differ according to the varying capacities of sentient beings; thus, the three original intentions have not yet been fully revealed, as there are differences due to speech adapted to the intentions of others.

2. Words possess both general and specific meanings; this is because they are explained according to what is manifest. 3. Although provisional and ultimate teachings are distinguished, one must skillfully harmonize them with the Buddha’s intent, for there is an opening toward revelation;
furthermore, the King’s cryptic words serve distinct purposes, and those who fail to recognize the provisional and the ultimate will not understand.
To treat the profound as shallow is to lose great benefit; to treat the shallow as profound is to render one's efforts vain.

To adorn the holy teachings so that they become deep and vast is appropriate, for within the various holy teachings there are naturally distinct divisions, and the great Bodhisattvas have likewise opened them up.
For these many reasons, to open [the teachings] results in gaining much while losing little, whereas to close them results in gaining little while losing much.
Much. However, as long as one can empty oneself to seek the fundamental principle (*zong*), it is permissible to divide what is indivisible; how could this deviate from the great purport?
Therefore, I now divide [the text].
*The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle One.
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Fascicle Two.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang;
recorded with annotations to the sūtra by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.
Second, the agreement and divergence between ancient and modern views is divided into two parts: first, an account of this region (China); second, an elucidation of the Western Regions (India).
Regarding the first: although the various schools of exegesis are numerous, I shall briefly describe several traditions, organizing them into five sections.
First is the establishment of the doctrine of a single sound (*ekasvara-dharma*). This refers to the teaching of the Tathāgata throughout his entire career, which does not depart from a single voice.

Regarding this, there are two masters: first, Bodhiruci of the Later Wei dynasty stated that the Tathāgata’s single voice simultaneously responds to ten thousand beings, presenting both the Great and Small Vehicles together.
Second, Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty stated that the Buddha’s single, perfect voice is equal and non-dual, without...
The universal response is uniform, yet the capacities of those who hear it differ; this does not mean that the original sounds of the teaching were inherently presented as either Great or Small.

Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each understand it according to their own capacity. Regarding the two masters mentioned above:
Initially, the Buddha’s voice possesses various distinct qualities; subsequently, these distinctions depend upon the capacities of the listeners.
Each attains a single meaning from the perfect voice, yet this is merely intended to show that, as the foundation of the teaching, there is no differentiation.

The second [approach] establishes two types of teaching, for which there are four schools of thought. First, the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Western Qin established the teachings of the "Half" and the "Full.
That is, the Śrāvaka Piṭaka is the teaching of the half-syllable (bān-zì), while the Bodhisattva Piṭaka is the teaching of the full-syllable (mǎn-zì).

The Dharma Master Huiyuan of the Sui dynasty likewise established this. This is based on textual evidence from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which essentially contrasts the Small Vehicle to reveal the Great Vehicle.

Regarding the intent of the "General Characteristics" (Tongxiang): it does not yet explicitly reveal the provisional and the real within the *Mahāyāna*, nor does it fully encompass both the "Half" and "Full" teachings.

Second, Master Fayuan of the Sui dynasty established the two teachings of Gradual and Sudden. He maintained that regarding those with gradual capacity for awakening, the Great [Vehicle] arises from the Small;

because what is established therein possesses all three vehicles, it is called "Gradual. If, however, one refers to those with sudden capacity, they proceed directly to the Great [Vehicle] without relying on...

The "Small" is termed "Sudden. Although this distinction between the gradual and the sudden is made in reference to the capacities of sentient beings, the teachings expounded do not transcend the categories of the "Half" and the "Full.
During the early Tang dynasty, Master Yin also established two types of teaching:

first, the "Crooked Teaching," referring to the sūtras of Śākyamuni that follow the dispositions of beings to refute attachments according to their various conceptualizations, such as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and others; second, the "Level Teaching."
This refers to the *Vairocana Sūtra*, which is taught with sovereign freedom by pursuing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), such as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Furthermore, these two teachings have briefly four differences: first, a difference in the principal [teacher], meaning that the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Śākyamuni differs from the ten bodies of Vairocana;
second, a difference in location, meaning the tree and grass seat in the Sahā world-system differs from the jewels within the Flower Treasury World-system (*Puṣpasaṃbhava-kṣetra*).
First, they differ in their setting, such as the jewel-adorned thrones and so forth. Second, they differ in their audience;
that is, the teachings spoken for *śrāvakas* and bodhisattvas differ from those spoken exclusively for bodhisattvas at the ultimate stage. Third, they differ in their mode of exposition;

that is, the teachings restricted to a specific location differ from those that pervade the ten directions. This is a judgment based on the pedagogical method (*vinyāsa*). However, although the *Avataṃsaka* does contain [elements of]...
The various sentient beings are each individually tamed; all of this is skillful means that accord with the nature (*dharmatā*).
Although [the teaching of] Nirvana and so forth may speak of a single ultimate, it is either a provisional manifestation of the real or a convergence of differences into unity.

Thus, whether all Tathāgatas speak of it or not, it is called "indirect" (*ku-chü*). If one takes Śākyamuni as the primary subject, then the ten bodies (*daśakāya*) have not yet been revealed. The ten...

When this world-system (*Sahā*) is the primary locus, it must necessarily encompass the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpasaṃcaya*); where the Flower Treasury World is not yet fused with *Sahā*, it is because *Sahā* is the primary locus.

Where the Flower Treasury World is present, it must necessarily fuse with *Sahā*. Briefly stated, there are four points of difference, though in reality there are many more. It is truly as you have judged;
however, within these complexities, the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Dharma have not yet been fully revealed. This was also the view of Liu Qiu, a recluse of the Qi dynasty.
The establishment of the two teachings—gradual and sudden—is as follows: the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is termed the "Sudden Teaching," while all others are termed "Gradual.

Beginning at the Deer Park and ending at the Twin Trees, [the gradual teaching] proceeds from the small to the great. However, this scripture is like the rising sun, which first illuminates the high mountains;
this is the meaning of the "Sudden. That the compassionate dragon sends down rain to illustrate the meaning of the "Gradual" is reasonable in principle.
Gradually, [the teachings] are summarized into five periods, which shall be analyzed below.
Third, regarding the establishment of three types of teaching, there are likewise three schools. First, the various masters of the South and the Central Region collectively establish three teachings.

This refers to adding the teaching of "indeterminate" [sudden] to the previously mentioned gradual and sudden approaches. Since within the gradual approach one first practices the Small Vehicle and subsequently the Great Vehicle, yet the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* teaches [the Great Vehicle] within six years, this difficulty is raised. To preclude this objection, the category of "indeterminate" is established.
