The first school takes practice as its primary tenet (*zong*), explaining the stages of practice so that one may achieve contemplation (*guan*). The eighth school asserts that the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) is the primary tenet;
for whether in the forward or reverse order, regarding both principle and phenomena—even up to the Indra’s Net (*indrājāla*)—all appear simultaneously like the waves of a tranquil ocean.

The ninth is Master Liangtong, who takes the reality of cause and effect as his primary tenet; for he holds that cause and effect constitute the practices and stages to be accomplished, while the reality of principle constitutes the *dharmadhātu* upon which they rely.

The tenth is Master Xianshou, who, because the preceding [masters] were each individually deficient, takes the totality of cause, effect, dependent origination, and the reality of the *dharmadhātu* as his fundamental aim. This means that the two former masters merely...

Regarding the attainment of the Dharma-realm as the basis for reliance: while the second and third masters clarify only dependent origination, and the fifth and sixth clarify only cause and effect, the seventh clarifies only the cultivation of causes and the eighth only the function of the fruit;
since they all mutually lack these elements, Master Xianshou intended to adopt the interpretation of Master Guangtong.

Yet, the term "dharma-dhātu" is added to "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda). This is because Master Guāngtǒng held that cause and effect are themselves dependent origination, and that their ultimate principle is itself the dharma-dhātu;
therefore, he did not differentiate them. Master Xiánshǒu, however, maintained that cause and effect are specific categories within the broader scope of dependent origination.

In reality, this is a specific meaning within the *dharmadhātu*; therefore, the general name is added. This is because the *dharmadhātu* possesses both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*), as well as non-obstruction;
furthermore, it is the function upon the essence of dependent origination. For these reasons, it is added. Second, regarding the presentation of the present interpretation:
based on the latter two masters, there have been some modifications. If one wishes to capture everything concisely through a brief statement, one should say "Dharma" (or *dharma*).

The inconceivable dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu* is the central thesis. If one takes the complete title from the tenth master, adding "inconceivable," this then encompasses the general title as a whole.
In reality, "Great" (*mahā*) refers to the *vaipulya*, while "Dependent Origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) refers to the *vaipulya* itself.
The *dharmadhātu* generally subsumes both of these causes and effects; this is precisely the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*. By examining its general title, one already knows its specific meanings. And...
Terms such as "Dharmadhātu" (the Dharma-realm) may appear in various sūtras, yet they do not explicitly reveal its unique distinction.
Therefore, it is "inconceivable" (*acintya*) that permeates them; thus, the Dharmadhātu and all else are inconceivable, making this the central tenet of the sūtra.
This is why Nāgārjuna pointed to this as the *Acintyasūtra*—it is excellent evidence. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, however, clarifies only the inconceivable liberation of functional activity.

This is merely the meaning of a single portion; it does not yet manifest the inconceivable nature of the interpenetration of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) and so forth, and is therefore not the same [as the present teaching].

If one analyzes the body, essence, purpose, and function according to the title, then "the reality of principle" (li-shi) constitutes the body, while "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) constitutes the function. As for the cause...

The fruit is the thesis (*pakṣa*). Seeking the thesis causes one to proceed toward the reality of the principle. The dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) subsumes the three aforementioned [categories]. Now, to explain the preceding meaning, it is briefly divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the names; second, the manifestation of the meanings. Regarding the first: the names and essences of the dharma-realm are as extensively explained in this chapter;
here, I shall briefly set forth two aspects: first, the phenomenal dharma-realm (*vastu-dharmadhātu*); second, the noumenal dharma-realm (*tattva-dharmadhātu*). These two dharmas are both...
Regarding the section on "Containing and Sustaining the Rules": the two realms differ in their essential natures, yet they are mutually accessible in their functions.
Within the second part, "Clarifying the Meaning," there are four sections. The first is the distinct opening of the *dharmadhātu* to establish cause and effect;
that is, the *dharmadhātu* of Samantabhadra is the cause, and the *dharmadhātu* of Vairocana is the fruit. Thus, cause and effect do not depart from the reality of the *dharmadhātu*. Within this:

The ten matters consist of five pairs, which constitute five cycles of cause and effect: first, the cause and effect of what is to be believed; second, the cause and effect of differentiation; third, the cause and effect of equality;
fourth, the cause and effect of accomplishing practice; and fifth, the cause and effect of realization and entry. These shall be pointed out in the text below.
Furthermore, this cause and effect serve as each other’s fundamental tenets throughout the beginning and end of a single scripture, for they never depart from cause and effect.

Thus, while taking cause and effect as the primary tenet, it does not contradict the *dharmadhātu* upon which it relies. In the second assembly, cause and effect are harmonized and integrated, as they are identical with the *dharmadhātu*.

Within the gateway of the *dharmadhātu*, there are likewise ten matters arranged in five pairs that serve as mutual themes and objectives. First, the pairing of teaching (*śāsana*) and meaning (*artha*):

this means taking the teaching as the theme and revealing the meaning as the objective; or alternatively, taking the meaning as the theme and revealing the teaching as the objective, so that by clarifying the profundity of the meaning, the teaching may be rendered superior.
Second, the pairing of person (*pudgala*) and dharma: this means taking the person as the theme, so as to cause one to know the dharma.

1. As for the goal (*yāna*): the Dharma is presented as the principle (*zong*) so that one may attain the person as the goal. 2. Regarding the correspondence between principle and phenomena: phenomena are presented with the intent to lead toward the principle;

the principle is presented with the intent to harmonize phenomena. 3. Regarding the correspondence between object and wisdom: the observed object is presented so that contemplative wisdom may be established;

the wisdom accomplished through cultivation is presented so that one may realize the identical true object. 4. Regarding cause and effect: [the cause is presented] so that... [the effect may be realized].
"Relative" refers to citing those causes of cultivation so that one may realize the fruit, and citing those supreme fruits so as to encourage the cultivation of the cause.
These five pairs are explained individually as the "purpose" (*tātparya*) of this treatise; these five pairs being mutually identical constitute the "nature" (*svabhāva*) of the treatise.

The aforementioned five cycles of cause and effect do not depart from these five pairs of dharmas, which are precisely the dharma-realm of phenomena and principle. How much more so since cause and effect lack intrinsic nature! When [this is realized],...
Its essence is identical to the True [Dharmadhātu]. Therefore, it takes only the Dharmadhātu as its central tenet, yet this does not contradict cause and effect.
In the third section, the cause and effect of the Dharmadhātu are clearly revealed; there are also ten meanings in five pairs: first, the peerless object. This has two stages:
first, while enmeshed in afflictions (*saṃvṛta*), the intrinsically pure Dharmadhātu serves as the object of faith; second, having emerged from entanglements (*niḥsṛta*), it is supremely pure.
The dharma-realm is the object to be realized. Second, the peerless mind, which also has two meanings:

first, the great bodhicitta, because it is the root of the conduct of Samantabhadra; second, faith, compassion, wisdom, and so forth, because they arise in accordance with that conduct. Third, peerless conduct.
This also has two meanings: first, the practice of differentiation, because each is cultivated separately; second, the practice of Samantabhadra, because one is all.
Fourth, the stage of the peerless: this also has two meanings: first, the stage of sequential arrangement, because realization is distinct through comparison;
second, the stage of perfect fusion, because the realization of one is the realization of all. Fifth, the fruit of the peerless: this also has two meanings: first, cultivation...

The first is the fruit of birth (*utpatti-phala*), for it is only now that it is first accomplished. The second is the fruit of manifesting through cultivation (*bhāvanā-vyañjana-phala*), for it is inherently possessed from the beginning.

Among these five pairs above, the first phrase of each constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the latter phrase constitutes the goal (*prayojana*). Furthermore, among the aforementioned five, the first is the true *dharmadhātu*; the second is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);
and since the second, third, and fourth are all causes of dependent origination while the last is the fruit of dependent origination. — Thus stated by Guǎngtǒng.

Taking these two meanings as the central thesis, there is no contradiction. Regarding the fourth [point], the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) wherein cause and effect are mutually fused and both transcended, such that essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are intermingled in unimpeded freedom, there are likewise ten points.

First, because it is free from characteristics, cause and effect are not different from the dharma-realm; thus, cause and effect are non-cause and non-effect. This takes "characteristics" as the central thesis, while "freedom from characteristics" serves as...

The destination (*gati*). Alternatively, taking the absence of characteristics as the thesis (*pakṣa*), the disappearance of cause and effect is the destination. The following nine [points] should be understood by analogy.
Second, because it is free from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is not distinct from cause and effect; that is, the dharma-realm is not [merely] the dharma-realm.

Third, because it is free from intrinsic nature yet does not obliterate intrinsic nature, the dharma-realm is itself cause and effect. At such a time, the dharma-realm remains perfectly manifest; thus, one takes "not being the dharma-realm" as [the destination].
It is the dharma-dhātu. Fourth, because it is free from characteristics yet its characteristics are indestructible, cause and effect are identical with the dharma-dhātu;

while cause and effect remain distinct in time, they are taken as cause and effect precisely because they are not [inherently] cause and effect. Fifth, because being free from characteristics is no different from being free from nature.
The dharma-realm of cause and effect is simultaneously obliterated and mutually separated, transcending speech and thought.

This is because, through the six aspects of non-destruction, non-difference, and non-obliteration, the dharma-realm of cause and effect both exist and manifest before one, appearing with vivid clarity.

Furthermore, because these five and six aspects of existence and obliteration are again not different, this wondrous Dharma that transcends sight and hearing is nowhere that it does not constantly pervade seeing and hearing. It is absolute.
The profound meaning of this contemplation has never been obstructed by words or thought. This is due to eight reasons:

first, because the nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is fused and indivisible, the cause and effect of the dharma-realm are simultaneously present, fully encompassing the entire dharma-realm without exception.

Ninth, when cause and effect each fully encompass the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), cause and effect follow the dharma-realm, such that each manifests within the other within the context of cause and effect.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva exists within the Buddha, and Samantabhadra exists within the Buddha.

Tenth, because in both the positions of cause and effect, there is nothing among the various differentiated phenomena that is not subsumed within the dharma-realm, every single phenomenon and every single...
Practice. Each stage and each virtue individually and collectively encompasses the inexhaustible within the inexhaustible, like the infinitely layered nets of Indra;
these are the oceans of all dharma-gates. This is called the inexhaustible tenet of the Avataṃsaka. Regarding the four preceding gates: the first is the function of the essence;
the second is the essence of the function; the third is the simultaneous manifestation of both essence and function; the fourth is [the synthesis of] essence and function.
They are fused together. Furthermore, the first [gate] is the causal dependent origination; the second is the ultimate reality of the Dharma-realm;
the third clarifies both simultaneously; and the last is the inconceivable. Since the fourth fuses the preceding three, the four gates are of one principle.

Therefore, it is illumination while negating, and negation while illuminating; it is the simultaneous illumination and simultaneous negation of the single contemplation of perfect clarity. Thus one accords with the essential purport of this school.
△ Seventh, the Section on Categories and Concordances: Having understood that the underlying intent is profound and deep, one may still wonder about the expressive texts.

Regarding the discussion of breadth and narrowness, there are four parts: first, manifesting the primary division; second, revealing the chapters and assemblies; third, clarifying the branches and categories; and fourth, distinguishing the commentaries and exegeses.

Within the first part, concerning the expression of the ocean of nature (*dharmadhātu*), it is constantly and universally taught, exhausting the limits of the *dharmadhātu* and being difficult to measure.
Now, narrowing this vastness, we shall briefly categorize it into ten types. The first is the abbreviated root sūtra, which is the present [text].
The eighty-fascicle version as transmitted [by Xuanzang] and the sixty-fascicle old translation are both abridgments from among the one hundred thousand verses;
they were not translated in their entirety. Second are the "abridged versions" of the sutra, namely the Mahāyāna Piṭaka.
This was compiled by Mañjuśrī and Ānanda Sāgara between the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) and subsequently deposited in the Dragon Palace by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
Nāgārjuna went to the Dragon Palace and saw this Great Inconceivable Sūtra (Mahā-acintya-sūtra), of which there were three versions.
The inferior version consisted of one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters; Nāgārjuna was able to recite it, and it has been transmitted to the world.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refers to this as the "Inconceivable Sūtra" consisting of one hundred thousand verses. In the *Tattvasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* of the Liang dynasty, it is called the "Hundred-Thousand Sūtra. In the West...

The *Yujiji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that this complete version exists in the country of Cakuban (Cakubana). Among the three versions of the original sutra, it is that which was seen there;
it consists of four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses and one thousand two hundred chapters. This is the fourth, the superior version of the original sutra.

That which was seen therein consisted of verses numbering as many as the atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms and chapters numbering as many as the atoms in a single four-continent world-system.
These two preceding versions could not be sustained by the mental power of the people of Jambudvīpa; therefore, they were not transmitted.
The fifth, the *Puyan jing* (Universal Eye Sūtra), was that which was held by Sāgaramegha; it would require ink equal in volume to the great ocean and [writing materials] as large as Mount Sumeru.

I have gathered my brush to write this Universal Eye Dharma Gate: a single gate within one chapter, a single dharma within one gate, a single meaning within one dharma, and a single phrase within one meaning. Not even a small portion can be grasped, let alone the whole.
This is something that can only be sustained by the power of the *dhāraṇī* of Bodhisattvas who have entered the profound Dharma-realm. All the sutras hereafter are likewise [of this nature].
This is not something that can be received by ordinary power. Sixth is the teaching of the same sūtras:
this refers to a single class of worlds shaped like Mount Sumeru, which pervade all of space; even within a space the size of a hair-tip, one may preach with vocal sound without end.
As it says in the "Inconceivable Dharma" chapter: "Just as a single Buddha-body, by means of supernormal powers, expounds such various and distinct teachings."
The wheel [of Dharma] is such that no worldly phenomena can serve as a metaphor for it.
Thus, throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, in every location the size of a single hair-tip, and even within each individual transformation body, it is explained in this same way.
The sounds, words, phrases, and meanings each completely fill the Dharma-realm and so forth. Furthermore, the *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* states: "Within the light, one sees the Buddha..."
It can be said that the Dharma taught by the Buddha is ineffable; even the differentiation of the dharma-gates within each individual *sūtra* is ineffable, and so forth.
This meaning refers simply to the fact that once the Dharma has been taught through a certain type of vocal sound, it cannot be compiled [as a fixed text].
How could those of lower capacities be able to uphold it? Regarding the seven ways of reciting the scriptures—such as the "tree-shaped" world and others—once these have already occurred...
They are diverse. Among those sentient beings, their types of retribution are also distinct. The Tathāgata manifests his body and establishes teachings for them, with various different arrangements.
It is impossible to definitively determine whether they are material or immaterial, verbal or non-verbal, and so forth; thus, their categories are difficult to measure.

8. The Sūtra of the Principal and the Retinue (*maulopakāra-sūtra*). This refers to that which was spoken by Vairocana; although it pervades the entire Dharma-realm, the Buddhas act as both principal and retinue to one another.
For example, when the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) were taught, those who came from the ten directions to bear witness all said, "In my land, this is also being taught," and so forth.

Thus, the preceding seven sūtras all possess both a principal and a retinue. 9. The Sūtra of the Retinue (*parivāra-sūtra*). This refers to other types of faculties (*indriya*) who are unable to hear this [Dharma].
The teaching that penetrates all directions provides instruction according to what is appropriate, causing beings to enter this gate;
because these are all the superior skillful means of this sutra, they are called its "retinue. Therefore, the subsequent sutra states:

"The Universal Eye Sutra has as its retinue as many sutras as there are atoms in a buddha-field," and so forth. Thus, the preceding eight [sūtras] all have their own retinues. This is the *Daśaparipūrṇa-sūtra*.
This means that all these aforementioned versions are integrated into a single, inexhaustible great ocean of sūtras.
Within each assembly, each chapter, each sentence, and each phrase, everything is subsumed without limitation. Therefore, the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" states:
"Vairocana Buddha’s power of vows pervades the entire Dharma-realm; within all lands, he constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel," and so forth.
Therefore, among the seventy-three [sections], this is what is called the "Wheel of Perfect Causes.

Regarding the differences between the assemblies in the second chapter, this reveals the similarities and differences between the present sutra and the Jin translation. The present sutra consists of nine assemblies. Because...

The seventh assembly of the *Jin* (Chinese) translation lacks the "Ten Samādhis" chapter (*Daśadharmaka-parivarta*) at the beginning; because it was reassembled at the Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsvara*), it contains only eight assemblies.
It currently consists of thirty-nine chapters, with six chapters in the first assembly. That [Tibetan] version has only thirty-four, because within its first assembly there are only two chapters:
first, the "Chapter on the Pure Eye of the World" (*Lokanetra-parivarta*), which is the present "Chapter on the Lord of the World" (*Lokendra-parivarta*); second, the "Vairocana... [chapter].

The "Chapter on That" (*Tat-saṃgraha-parivarta*) consists of the five chapters beginning with "Manifesting Signs Now" (*Pratyutpanna-nimitta*). In the first assembly, four chapters are missing, and additionally, the ten *samādhis* are absent;
therefore, there are only thirty-four chapters. The other chapters and assemblies are largely the same, though their titles differ slightly, as shall become evident in the text itself.
Third, regarding the clarification of the categories of branches (*śākhā-vibhāga*), there are two further divisions therein. First, the manifestation of the branch-streams:
within the *Pṛthag-caryā Sūtra-piṭaka*, the one-fascicle *Tuṣita Sūtra* is the "Chapter on Names and Titles"; the one-fascicle *Bodhisattva-mūla-karma Sūtra* is the "Chapter on Pure Conduct";
the one-fascicle *Laghu-daśabhūmika Sūtra* is the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes"; and the four-fascicle *Mahā-daśabhūmika Sūtra* [is likewise].
Furthermore, the *Jianbei Yiqiezhide Jing* (Sūtra on the Gradual Preparation of All-Wisdom Virtues) in four fascicles is the "Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmi*) chapter.

The *Dumujie Pusa Suowen Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi Asked by the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin) in two fascicles is the "Ten Samādhis" (*Daśaniyama*) chapter. The *Wubian Gongde Jing* (Sūtra on Boundless Merit) in one fascicle is the "Life Span" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa*) chapter.

The *Rulai Xingqi Weimi Zang Jing* (Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Nature-Arising Secret Treasury) in two fascicles is the "Manifestation" (*Nirmāṇa*) chapter. The *Duoshi*... [text ends]... is the "Transcending the World" chapter.
The *Sūtra* in six fascicles is the "Chapter on Leaving the World. The *Rāmaka-sūtra* in three fascicles is the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm.
These and others were all extracted from the Great Canon according to the capacities of those who received and upheld them. Second, the categories of derivative works:
namely, the *Cultivation of Compassion Sūtra* in one fascicle, the *Vajramālā Sūtra* in ten fascicles, and the *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa Sūtra* in one fascicle.

These are all of the same genre as the *Avataṃsaka*, yet they do not belong to its primary division (*mūla-bhāga*) or specific recensions (*pṛthak-caryā*). It is possible that some specific recensions have not yet been fully transmitted;

I have not ventured to provide a detailed determination of this. The rest is as clarified in the *Zuǎnlíngjì*. Fourth, regarding the commentaries (*śāstra-vyākhyāna*), I shall briefly cite four examples.

First, once Nāgārjuna obtained the "inferior version" (*hīna-pustaka*), he subsequently composed the *Mahā-acintya-śāstra* (Great Treatise on the Inconceivable), which also consists of one hundred thousand verses (*śloka*).

The records of the Western Regions transmit that this work, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* in sixteen fascicles, is precisely the commentary on the first two of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) from that treatise.
The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* to explain the "Ten Stages" chapter.
During the Wei dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati and Bodhiruci each translated a version of it. [This was] Guangtong...
He submitted a petition requesting that two or three Tripitaka masters collaborate to compile it into a single work consisting of twelve fascicles; this is the version transmitted today.
Third, Liu Qianzhi of the Northern Qi, at Mount Qingliang, was moved by divine inspiration to compose a treatise of six hundred fascicles providing a comprehensive commentary on a single sutra.
Fourth, the monk Lingbian of the Later Wei, atop Mount Wutai, wore this sutra upon his head while performing circumambulations for one year.
He subsequently realized the profound essence [of the teachings] and composed a treatise in one hundred fascicles, which has also been transmitted to the world.
△ The eighth section concerns the transmission, translation, and spiritual resonance, divided into two parts: first, clarifying the dates of the translations;

second, clarifying the signs of spiritual resonance and penetration. Within the first part: this sutra, including its supplementary versions, consists of two complete translations in total, making four versions altogether.

The same. In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas (translated as Jue Xian) from North India translated thirty-six thousand verses from the Sanskrit original at Xie Sikong Temple in Yangzhou, producing fifty fascicles—or sixty fascicles—of the Jin version of the scripture.
The śramaṇa Faye acted as the scribe, while Huiyan and Huiguan [oversaw the work].

Regarding the "Polished Edition": The Sīkōng Temple (Temple of the Minister of Works) mentioned here is the present-day Xingyan Temple in Runzhou. It was so named because it originally arose from the flourishing of the Avataṃsaka (Huayan).

During the first year of the Yonglong era of the Great Tang, the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha (translated into Chinese as Rìzhào, "Sunlight") translated the *Jie fajie pin* (Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm) at the Taiyuan Temple in the Western Capital. Within this [translation], there were omissions in two places.
First, from after Lady Māyā until before Bodhisattva Maitreya, there were ten spiritual friends in the interim,
beginning with Devendrābha. Second, from after Bodhisattva Maitreya until before the spiritual friends as numerous as the atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems,
there was Mañjuśrī extending his hand across one hundred and ten yojanas.

[The Emperor] placed his hand upon the crown of Śāṇakavāsin’s head. Fifteen lines of the sūtra were translated jointly by the Venerable Daocheng, Vinaya Master Lüshi, Dharma Master Bocen, Dharma Master Dashengji, and others.
Dharma Master Fuli polished the prose. This was established according to the sixty-fascicle version.
In the first year of the Zhengsheng era, the Tripiṭaka Master from Khotan, Śikṣānanda (translated as Xixue), at...
At Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital, the old text was retranslated and various omissions were supplemented, resulting in an increase of nine thousand stanzas.
Including the original, the total reached forty-five thousand stanzas, compiled into eighty fascicles as the Tang edition.

This was accomplished by the Tripitaka Master Yijing Da-de, along with Meditation Master Hongjing, Dharma Master Yuance, Dharma Master Shenyi, Dharma Master Fabao, and Xian... [the text here is incomplete].
The Dharma Master Xuanshu and others translated it together, while the Dharma Master Falin composed the prose.

Fourthly, although the previous third version had added several passages, it nonetheless omitted the passage concerning Mañjuśrī placing his hand upon Sudhana’s head as supplemented by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta.
Thus, the Dharma Master Xianshu compared the new and old translations with the Sanskrit original and restored the passage [supplemented by] Jñānagupta.
Supplementary Note: Anxi studied the point of detachment and was thus able to continue the text so that its meaning remained connected.
The essentials of this text shall be analyzed below. What is transmitted here is the fourth version; as for the third version, it had already been circulated previously.
The scriptures currently circulating in the world still contain many omissions; this is the third version. I pray that those of profound learning who notice these deficiencies will supplement them.

Second, regarding the manifestation of spiritual resonance in the transmission [of the teachings]: since the subtle words were translated during the Jin dynasty, the two youths appeared as auspicious omens;

when the ultimate teachings were translated during the Tang dynasty, the sweet dew manifested its blessings. This secret protection is clearly evident, having even been personally honored by the Emperor’s own brush.

When the treatise was completed in the Western Regions, the earth quaked and light streamed forth; when his resolve reached Qingliang, he was moved by a spiritual resonance and attained profound awakening.

As for its transcription, the sutra shone with five colors, its fragrance permeated the four quarters, Cai Xiang’s ink blossomed with brilliance in winter, and auspicious birds carried flowers in their beaks.
When reciting and chanting, he would soar as if treading upon the void; it was as if he were gazing into a mirror.

Whenever he held the śarīra relics, they would spontaneously coincide with the appearance of a divine monk who leaped from the earth, manifesting a golden-hued body; ascending to heaven, he halted the battle array of the asuras.

When practicing contemplation, he entered realization through the "Verse on Non-arising," which filled the sky with its praise. Hearing this, the sea deity sent down a torrential rain, and the celestial youths welcomed him as the Great [Vehicle]...

The waters overflowed. When the teachings were expounded, both the Chinese and Sanskrit harmonized their rhythms; humans and devas alike followed them. When the great flood cut off the flow, divine light entered the halls.
This was truly because the subtlety of a single word encompasses all meanings without omission, and the merit of a single verse can destroy the hells.
Even water used for washing hands and rinsing the mouth can yet rescue living beings; as for reciting, contemplating, and practicing, its merit is equal to that of the Buddha’s omniscience. [Past...]
How fortunate I am to have encountered this sacred text! Its significance is manifest and fully recorded in the biographies and chronicles.
*Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Four.
*Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Five (Entering the First Scripture).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang;
recorded and annotated by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui. △ Ninth:
General Explanation of the Title, divided into two parts. First, explaining the title of the sutra; second, clarifying the name of the chapter. Now, the first part.
The general title of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* encompasses its specific meanings;
within this nameless state that subsumes inconceivable dharma-gates, we have provisionally divided it into ten sections: first, a general explanation of how the title is derived;
second, a comparative analysis of the opening and closing [of the gates]; third, a full manifestation of the categories of meaning; fourth...
A separate explanation of how it acquires its name: Fifth, its unfolding is inexhaustible; Sixth, its rolling up exhausts all characteristics; Seventh, its unfolding and rolling up are unimpeded;
Eighth, it perfectly encompasses all meanings; Ninth, it gathers them back into the one mind; Tenth, it merges them into the equality of sameness.
First, regarding the titles of various sūtras, there are many types. Some are named after persons, while others are named after dharmas.
Among persons, there are distinctions such as those who requested the teaching; among dharmas, there are differences such as the dharma itself or a parable.

Furthermore, they may refer to essence or function, fruit or cause, being sometimes compound and sometimes simple; their categories are thus vast and manifold. The title received by the present sūtra likewise differs in many ways.
First, names are designated based on numerical figures. For example, the first volume of the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty states:
"The hundred thousand sūtras" refers to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, which consists of one hundred thousand verses. Second, names are received based on metaphors.

For instance, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* refer to this sūtra as the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra* (Flower Garland Sūtra), because its myriad practices are intermingled within the principle of dependent origination.

1. Named according to its compilation; 2. Named according to its primary subject matter, as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*’s commentary on the "Entrusting" chapter (*Parīndanā-parivarta*), which designates this sutra as the *Acintya-vimokṣa-sūtra*; 3.
Named according to the manifestation of its Dharma, as in the commentary on the "Entrusting" chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which titles this sutra the *Acintya-vimokṣa-sūtra*;

4. Named according to its thematic function, such as the ten distinct titles found in each of the "Leaving the World" (*Lokānuvartana*) and "Manifestation" (*Saṃdarśana*) chapters. According to the present Sanskrit manuscript, it is called the *Mahāvaipulya*.
*Buddhagandhavyūhasūtra*. This is translated as *The Great Vaipulya Sūtra of the Buddha’s Adornments with Various Flowers*;

here, the characters for "various" (*za*) and "adornments" (*shi*) have been omitted. The three preceding alternative titles are largely general abridgments of the meaning. It consists of two chapters and ten sections.
Because [the previous titles] mostly followed specific meanings and were limited to their respective chapters, the present translator has provided the title in its entirety using six characters.

Thus, it simultaneously designates both the person and the dharma, and presents both the dharma and the metaphor together. It encompasses both the essence and the function, and includes both the fruit and the cause; as such, it exhausts the principle and perfects the meaning, and is therefore placed at the beginning of the sutra.
Second, regarding the analysis of the opening and closing [of the title], there are ten items and five pairs within the seven characters of the title. First, the pair of teaching and meaning:

the single character "Sūtra" (經) refers to the teaching as the means of expression (*abhilāpa*), while the six characters "Mahā-vaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka" refer to the meaning as that which is expressed (*abhidheya*).
Second, within the meaning, the pair of phenomenon and metaphor: "Mahā-vaipulya" is the phenomenon (*dharma*), and "Buddhāvataṃsaka" is the metaphor (*upamā*). Third, within the phenomenon...
The pair of person and dharma refers to the fact that "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Extensiveness) is the unimpeded dharma to be realized, while the Buddha is the person who realizes it;
it is also called the pair of object and wisdom. Within the four aspects of dharma, there is the pair of selection and retention:

the single character "Mahā" (Great) performs the function of selection, while "Vaipulya" (Extensiveness) performs the function of retention. That is to say, it selects the Great as distinct from the Small, the Real as distinct from the Provisional, and the Fruit as distinct from the Cause.
This is also a pair of essence and function. "Great" (*da*) is the essence, for the Great Dharma has no corners. "Vast" (*fang*) is the function;

among the five categories of beings, it borrows the character "flower" (*hua*) from the lower category [of humans] to serve as a metaphor for its cause—thus forming the pair of cause and effect, for the Buddha is the fruit.
Therefore, if one uses only the character "flower," it merely cites a metaphor for the cause. However, if combined with "Flower Adornment" (*Huayan*), then...
This also serves as a metaphor for the four characters above, which shall be clarified below.

Third, regarding the manifestation of the categories of meaning: this refers to the seven characters beginning with "Great" (*mahā-*) and so forth, all of whose meanings are immeasurable; these are briefly explained by means of ten aspects.

First, to clarify the meaning of "Great": first is the greatness of essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*), meaning that whether in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) or functions (*vṛtti*), they are all identical.
Because the true nature is eternal and pervasive, it is the "Great Letter" (*mahā-akṣara*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which is called 'great' is named 'eternal'.
This clarifies that its essence does not undergo change; it is called "great" because it is the most supreme, like the tallest person.

It further states: "The great is its nature of vastness, just like empty space. This clarifies that its essence is all-pervasive. Second is the greatness of characteristics, referring to [the virtues] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Because the inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) are fully possessed without exception, they mutually penetrate one another; being subtle, layered, and so forth, they possess the ten gates of mystery (*daśa-mahā-ausadha-dvāra*), as these are all their characteristics.

This corresponds to the character *fang* (方) in the sutra. *Fang* means "Dharma. It refers to the greatness of the three functions, meaning that their karmic activity is universal, just as the essence is pervasive.
This corresponds to the character *guang* (廣) in the sutra. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Furthermore, 'great' (*da*) means it is able to establish great significance."
This is based on their functional application. Since *nirvāṇa* has no "vastness" (*vaipulya*), and "vastness" is identical to "greatness" (*mahat*), "vastness" is explained by means of "greatness.

Since "extensive teaching" (*vaipulya*) has no "greatness," and "greatness" is conjoined with "vastness," "greatness" is explained by means of "vastness. This sutra possesses both; therefore, they are each assigned accordingly.

The four fruits are "great" because their wisdom (*jñāna*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and the support and supported (*āśraya-ālambana*) all pervade the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); this refers to the character "Buddha" (*buddha*) in the sutra.

1. The greatness of the five causes: that is, generating the bodhicitta and giving rise to understanding, practice, vows, and realization, accomplishing all stages through diligent and tireless effort.

This corresponds to the character *hua* (flower) in the sutra. 2. The greatness of wisdom: that is, with great wisdom as the primary guide, it mobilizes all myriad practices to universally adorn everything without exception.
This corresponds to the character *yan* (adornment) in the sutra. 3. The greatness of the teaching: that is, every single word and phrase...
There is nothing that does not form a connection, pervading all ten directions and the three periods of time in a layer upon layer of inexhaustibility;

such is the character of the Sūtra. Eighth is the greatness of meaning (*artha-mahattva*): the dharmas it expounds exhaustively reach the limits of the Dharma-realm, leaving nothing out, even down to the Indra-net of worlds;
this refers to the six characters of the title. Ninth is the greatness of the object (*viṣaya-mahattva*): by means of the aforementioned dharma-gates, [it encompasses] all infinite multitudes...

It is "born" because it manifests for the sake of transforming realms. It is "great" in ten ways regarding its activity: that is, throughout the three periods of time and across the entire extent of the dharma-realm, it constantly employs this Dharma to benefit sentient beings without rest.
This is like the seven kinds of greatness described in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts.
They are not separate from this. Second, the ten meanings of "direction" (*fang*): "direction" means "dharma.

That is to say, the aforementioned ten "greats" are all termed dharmas—namely, the dharma of essence, the dharma of characteristics, and so forth. Third, the ten meanings of "extensiveness" (*guang*): "extensive" means "many.

Because their functions arise in great abundance and they encompass everything without exception, these preceding ten are all "many"; this clarifies that the one pervades all, which is termed [the meaning of extensiveness].
Its greatness consists in its encompassing all within one. It is called "vast" because it can also reach this [level]. This is an analysis based on the individual characters.
If one explains the two characters "vast" (*vaipulya*) as a compound, there are also ten meanings:

first, the meaning of being a vast basis, meaning that if the teachings are manifold and extensive, they serve as a basis for sentient beings; second, the meaning of vast exposition, meaning that one proclaims the broad and profound Dharma; third...
1. The meaning of extensive destruction: because it destroys all obstacles without exception. 2. The meaning of extensive transcendence:
because there are no phenomena capable of being compared to it. 3. The meaning of extensive remedy: because it fully encompasses boundless remedial dharmas as the means of counteraction.
4. The meaning of extensive inclusion: because it universally includes boundless dharmas of diverse categories. 5. The meaning of extensive virtue: because it fully encompasses...
Second, the sense of "extensive adornment," because it adorns all supreme virtues. Eighth, the sense of "extensive production," because it can produce an immeasurable and vast ocean of fruits.
Ninth, the sense of "extensive transcendence," because it cannot be known by the measurements of mind or consciousness.

Tenth, the sense of "extensive knowledge," because it is fully endowed with the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), destroying the obstacles of false views without remainder. Regarding these ten meanings, the first four correspond to the *Saṃcaya-gāthā*.

The first four meanings are contained within the eleventh chapter [of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha*], while the latter six correspond to the six meanings in the first chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*.

Regarding the "Four Buddhas and Ten Meanings," these are the ten Buddhas: "Great" (*mahā*) refers to the Buddha of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-buddha*); "Square" (*caturaśra*) refers to the Buddha of Original Nature (*prakṛti-buddha*);

"Broad" (*vistīrṇa*) refers to the Buddha of Nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-buddha*) and the Buddha of Accordance with Desire (*yathābhiprāya-buddha*); "Buddha" (*buddha*) refers to the Buddha who has attained Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi-buddha*); and "Flower" (*puṣpa*) refers to the Buddha of Vow (*praṇidhāna-buddha*).
"Buddha" refers to the Buddha of Samādhi; "Yan" (Adornment) refers to the Buddha of Karmic Retribution; and "Jing" (Sūtra) refers to the Buddha of Sustenance.

Collectively, they do not depart from the mind; all seven characters are the Mind-Buddha. The meaning of these ten Buddhas is explained as it is analyzed in the Eighth Stage and the "Detachment from the World" Chapter.
Furthermore, the first chapter of the *Buddhatva-śāstra* states that the Buddha also possesses ten meanings, namely: being endowed with all-knowledge (1).

He possesses all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), is free from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and is able to awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects for himself, as well as to awaken all sentient beings. Because he is like one waking from a dream or a lotus flower opening, he is called a Buddha.
Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi* cited by Paramārtha also contains ten meanings; fearing prolixity, they are not recorded here.
The five flowers and ten meanings are as follows: first, the meaning of containing reality, because it signifies that the dharma-realm contains the virtues of its intrinsic nature;
second, the meaning of radiant purity, because fundamental wisdom is clearly manifest; third, the meaning of subtle excellence, because each and every phenomenon is identical to the dharma-realm.

Fourth is the meaning of "appropriateness," because it accords with the capacities of sentient beings. Fifth is the meaning of "inducing results," because conduct serves as the cause for birth and gives rise to perfect enlightenment.

Sixth is the meaning of "uprightness," because conduct is conjoined with vows and is without deficiency. Seventh is the meaning of "non-defilement," because each and every door of practice is accompanied by samādhi.
Eighth is the meaning of "skillful accomplishment," because the virtues and deeds cultivated are skillfully perfected. Ninth...
The meaning of fragrance: because it sustains all virtues and its sweet scent spreads far and wide. The meaning of blossoming: because all practices flourish and cause the mind to open to awakening.
Now, there are two kinds of flowers: first, the flowers of plants and trees, which metaphorically represent the causes of the myriad practices.

However, these may either coexist with their fruit or not coexist with it. The two types of "adornments for the body" (śarīra-puṣpa), including those made of gold, jade, and so forth, serve as metaphors for the supernormal powers (abhijñā) and the various marks (lakṣaṇa);

these exist only simultaneously with their fruit. Among the ten preceding meanings, one, five, nine, and ten are restricted to flowers of grass and wood, while the remainder apply to both types of flowers.
As for the "six adornments," this refers to the aforementioned ten flowers collectively adorning a single Buddha.

The adornments are not the same; they also consist of ten meanings. Furthermore, the aforementioned ten flowers adorn the preceding ten Buddhas in their respective order, which constitutes these ten meanings.
Thus, the general and the particular are without obstruction. Moreover, there are another ten meanings: first, using the cause as an adornment for the fruit to constitute the person.
This is the Flower Adornment Buddha (Avataṃsaka-buddha). First, the fruit is used to adorn the cause, because the fruit is attained through the cause;

second, the cause is used to adorn the fruit to manifest its excellence, because after the fruit is realized, each and every causal practice becomes boundless; third, the person is used to adorn the Dharma to manifest its function.

1. This means that the Buddha cultivated causes over vast eons precisely to manifest the essence and function of the Dharma. 2. Fourth, one adorns the person with the Dharma to manifest its perfection;

for if one does not attain the essence and function of the Dharma, cause and effect cannot be perfectly sublime. 3. Fifth, one adorns the function with the essence to ensure its universal pervasiveness;
this means that if the function does not accord with the essence, it cannot be all-pervading. 4. Sixth, one adorns the essence with the function.

1. One knows the essence through the fundamental; for were there no great function, the vastness of the essence and its source would not be manifested. 2. Seventh, one knows the wondrous through the adornment of the essence by means of the marks;

that is to say, if the marks possess an essence, they immediately enter into a state of mutual interpenetration. 3. Eighth, one clarifies the profound mystery through the adornment of the marks by means of the essence;
for without the marks, the depth and mystery of the essence would not be revealed. 4. Ninth, the meaning adorns the teaching so that it transcends words and thought.
Because that which is expressed is inconceivable, and because the expressive words are transcendent, the ten causes mutually adorn one another through integration and inclusion.
This is like how there would be no way to exhaustively fathom stillness without wisdom, and no way to deepen illumination without stillness, and so forth.

Furthermore, the mutual adornment discussed above all involves the fourfold logic of mutual support and mutual identity; now, this is further elaborated in terms of the mutual adornment of principle and practice.
Clarification: Regarding the four propositions of mutual support at the initial stage: first, because principle is manifested through cultivation, one uses practice to adorn and expand principle.
Second, because practice is generated from principle, one uses principle to adorn and expand practice. As the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty states:

"There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm, and there is nothing that does not return to realize this Dharma-body. Third, principle and practice are both fused; though non-dual, they appear as two.
Without conduct that flows from the ultimate reality, there is no way to accord with that reality; yet without the reality that gives rise to conduct, it cannot be manifested through conduct.
This is because when the essence merges with conduct, the cause is perfected; when conduct encompasses reality, the fruit is fulfilled. For this reason, it is designated as the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*.
Herein, both principle and conduct are simultaneously transcended; they are two yet non-dual. Because it is the conduct of principle, it is not conduct; because it is the principle of conduct...
Because it is not [conformable to] principle, it is irrational. Thus, both subject and object vanish; it transcends emotion and severs all marks.
It is neither adorned nor unadorned—this is called the *Avataṃsaka*. Its marks consist of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), and its principle and practice encompass them entirely.

This can be seen through reflection. Thus, the dharma and the metaphor illuminate one another, their presence being clearly manifest. Regarding the "seven scriptures and ten meanings," the five meanings of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* have already been seen above.
The *Wén* (Text) states that the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* contains two meanings: first, to thread together what has been taught; second, to sustain those to be converted.

This is identical in meaning to the "garland" (*mālā*) of the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya*. When combined, the term "garland" should be excluded, and when expanded, it constitutes six meanings. It is according to this that the instruction is given.

Furthermore, there are four meanings: first, "constant" (nitya); second, "dharma"; both are explained as previously. Third, the meaning of "sūtra" (*sūtra-artha*), which refers to the path for sentient beings.

Fourth, the meaning of "scripture" (*śāstra-artha*), because it causes one to see and hear the True Dharma. There are also ten meanings in the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*, but fearing prolixity, they are not cited here.

Fourth, regarding the specific explanation of the names: the names are first established and then explained. First, as for the name "Great" (*mahā*): it receives its name according to its essential nature.
"Constant" (*nitya*) means that vertically there is no beginning; "pervasive" (*vyāpin*) means that horizontally it encompasses all without exception. As for "Square" (*caturaśra*)...

It is named according to its dharma; "guiding" (*vini*) and "sustaining" (*śasana*) constitute its meaning. It sustains both essence and characteristic, for it guides sentient beings toward understanding.

"Extensive" (*vaipulya*) is named according to its function; "encompassing" and "vast" constitute its meaning. To encompass is to contain widely; to be vast is to pervade extensively. "Buddha" is named according to the person;
"awakening" (*budh*) and "illumination" (*jñāna*) constitute its meaning. Illumination clarifies the profound depths of the myriad dharmas; awakening is the realization of them.

The tenth [point], "Merging into Equality," is intended for those who have not yet realized it, so as to cause them to realize their own mind.

If one knows that all objects encountered are mind, only then does one realize the nature of the mind. Thus, the *Brahmacarya-parivarta* states: "To know all phenomena is to know the self-nature of the mind."
One achieves the body of wisdom and does not rely on others for awakening. Yet, those who study the Dharma today mostly abandon the internal while seeking the external;

Once the mind and its objects are in suchness (*tathatā*), they are equal and unimpeded. I once polished two mirrors and placed a single lamp between them, with a single image of the Buddha set before them;

Beholding how the mind and its objects mutually reflect one another, and how fundamental wisdom enters both simultaneously, one realizes within the mind an inexhaustible realm, and perceives within that realm an inconceivable mind.
The mind and its objects are layered and manifold, yet the illumination of wisdom is ever-present therein. Furthermore, by means of the mind, one realizes the Buddha within objects;

by means of objects, one perceives the Tathāgata who is nothing but mind. Thus, while the mind and the Buddha are layered and manifold, their fundamental enlightened nature is one; in all cases, they cannot be grasped.

Thus, both mind and objects vanish; illumination is inexhaustible. When principle and wisdom penetrate one another, and since mind and objects are thus, objects are mutually reflected and minds are reciprocally refined.

Chapter One: The Sublime Array of the Lords of the World.
In the Sanskrit language, it is called *Sarvalokendravyūhadharmanayavikrīḍitābhijña-parivarta*.
This is translated as "The Chapter on the Dharma-Door of the Majestic Power of the Adornment of All the Lords of the World."

The current text is preserved in an abbreviated form. "World" (*loka*) refers to time; it is synonymous with the mundane world (*saṃsāra*). "Lord" (*pati*) refers to a sovereign; it refers to various kings as well as the Buddha.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of worlds: first, the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), which is the place of transformation; second, the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), which are the recipients of transformation;
and third, the world of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*jñāna-saṃbuddha-loka*), which is the transforming lord. This lord is further divided into two types.
All kings and Buddhas preside over the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) and its sentient beings; thus, while the Buddha is not of the mundane world, he receives his title from that which he governs.
"Sublime" (*pranīta*) refers to the Dharma-gate, whose essence and function are profound, vast, and inconceivable—this is precisely what the presiding lord has attained.

"Adorned" (*vyūha*) signifies embellishment and possesses many meanings: first, the adornment of the receptacle world, such as the solidity of its ground and so forth; second, the [adornment of] the assembly...
The adornment of birth in the world refers to the fact that each of the ocean-like assemblies possesses the majestic power of their respective Dharma-gates.

Third, the adornment of the Perfectly Awakened One’s wisdom in the world refers to the fact that regarding all phenomena, he has attained supreme perfect enlightenment, his three karmas are universally pervasive, and his Dharma-gates are inexhaustible.
Therefore, while the prose sections describe the adornments of the various kings, the verses praise these virtues to manifest the adornment of the Buddha for sentient beings.
Without adornment, there would be no inspiration for the Buddha’s appearance; if the Perfectly Awakened One were not adorned, he could not serve as the sovereign.

If the vessel-world (the physical environment) were not adorned, it would not be the true abode of the Buddha. Furthermore, through the adornment by the Buddha, those who encounter him are revealed to possess virtue;

through the adornment of sentient beings acting as assistants, the Buddha’s transcendence is revealed. Such mutual adornment constitutes "wondrous adornment. Among all the sutras, there is no such extensive adornment as this; it is merely called the "Preface" at the beginning.

the term "two weeks" is used in accordance with the specific capacities of other audiences. Therefore, various sūtras and śāstras present many differences regarding the time of the initial teaching.
This refers to the *Samantaprabhāsa* and the *Guhyakādhipati* sūtras. In the second seven-day period, the Three Vehicles were taught.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is stated that the Small Vehicle was taught after the three seven-day periods had passed. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is the sixth and seventh periods;

in the *Xingxianxing jing*, the seventh and seventh periods; in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the eighth and seventh periods; and in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fifty seven-day periods. Some say this corresponds to one year according to the *Dvādaśavyūha-sūtra*.

Great Sameness (*Mahāsamatā*). Since time is not fixed, the teachings are likewise not uniform; these are all according to what is appropriate for the capacities of beings, resulting in differences in what is seen and heard.

From the perspective of the Buddha responding to the needs of sentient beings, there is no time when he does not teach. Yet, looking from the standpoint of the lack of resonance in the faculties of beings, there has never been a teaching given.

Those who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*) constantly perceive the Sūtra of a single flavor. Speaking from the perspective of the Buddha himself, there is neither teaching nor non-teaching. If one subsumes the skillful means (*upāya*), they are all one.
The seals of the vehicles differ only in their manifestations; one should not adhere rigidly to these boundless explanations.

Therefore, they should be subsumed collectively as ten stages, as has already been analyzed above. The preceding section clarified the temporal divisions. Next, the meaning of attaining perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) will be explained.

According to the different teachings, in the Hīnayāna, one severs the fetters through thirty-four moments of mind, at which point the fivefold Dharma-body is first perfected; this is termed "attainment."
Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is real and not a transformation. Within the Mahāyāna, it is shown as being accomplished through the eight phases of a transformation body;
yet, in terms of the retribution body, it is when the practices of the ten stages are fulfilled and the four wisdoms are first perfected that it is called "initially attaining perfect enlightenment.

According to reality, however, past and present sentiments have vanished and the mind has no initial characteristic; thus it is termed "initial. To illuminate without thought is designated as "perfect" (*samyak*); to perceive the mind is [enlightenment].
It is eternally abiding; this is termed "Awakening. From the beginning, there is no duality between the source and the manifestation; this is designated as "accomplishment.

With respect to the *dharmakāya*, the noble wisdom of self-awakening is neither accomplished nor unaccomplished. If one relies on this sutra, it is by means of the cloud-like bodies of the ten Buddha-dharmadhātus.

Throughout the infinite time and space of the pervasive Indra’s net, at every single thought-moment and from the very beginning, it manifests for the sake of sentient beings, complete with primary and attendant elements, encompassing the three worlds. This "beginning" encompasses the beginning of immeasurable eons and the beginning of the boundless;
in one, all are accomplished—there is neither accomplishment nor non-accomplishment; in one awakening, all are awakened—there is neither awakening nor...
It is non-awakening; words are exhausted and thought is stilled. Because it does not destroy conventional designations, it is said that "one has newly attained perfect awakening.
This is extensively revealed in the "Chapter on Manifestation" and the "Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharma. Subsuming all previous explanations, they are all manifestations of the One Vehicle.
Fourth, the specific revelation of the adornments of the locus: now, the principal figures and the assembly in this lower locus constitute the adornment of the three worlds.
Of the three [aspects], the first two are the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya* (body) and *rūpakāya* (receptacle), while the assembly is the pure land.

Their support is not in vain. First, regarding the adornment of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*): this expands upon the previous array of the field and manifests the excellence of the previously realized awakening.
It differs from the sections in other sutras; therein, each of the four matters has ten kinds of adornment, clarifying that within defilement, purity is revealed. This constitutes—
There are four distinct [ornaments]: first, the ornament of the ground; second, the ornament of the trees; third, the ornament of the palaces; and fourth, the ornament of the lion throne.
Each of these ornaments possesses three interpretations: first, they may be understood according to their literal meaning; second, they symbolize the Dharma.
That is to say, the ground symbolizes the mind-ground and the *dharmakāya*; the trees symbolize *bodhi*; the palaces symbolize non-abiding *nirvāṇa*; and the throne symbolizes...
Regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) and so forth, there are three aspects concerning causal practice:

first, to exhaustively realize the cause of the *dharmakāya* within the mind-ground, thereby attaining the superior stage of the resultant *vajra-bhūmi*; second, to take *prajñā* as the cause; third, to take the mutual guidance of compassion and wisdom as the cause;
and fourth, likewise to take the emptiness of phenomena as the cause. However, either a single causal practice may accomplish all adornments, or—
All practices may constitute a single adornment; or one practice may constitute a single adornment; or all practices may constitute all adornments.
By interpenetrating the general and the particular, the pure and the mixed are unimpeded. Here, however, we clarify only one practice as one adornment in order to manifest that which is symbolized.
Nevertheless, each encompasses inexhaustible virtues; thus, each of the four matters contains ten phrases, with the first being general and the last being specific.

Now, for the time being, we shall divide each according to the text into four parts. Regarding the ten phrases of the first stage of the mind (*cittabhūmi*), they are divided into four: the first generally reveals the essence of the stage (*bhūmi*).
Its ground is composed of solid adamant;
it is designated as "solid" and explained as "adamant. While various teachings may speak of wooden trees or grass seats, they mostly state that the seat is adamant.
Now, since the entire ground is adamant, the provisional and the real are both revealed, for it penetrates the Flower Treasury World (*Gandavyūha*). This is detailed as follows:
That Chapter. △ Second, the characteristics and endowed virtues of the fourth stage:
"The supreme and wondrous jewel wheels and various jewel flowers... (up to) the infinite manifestation of oceans of all forms and appearances."
Regarding the explanation by way of cause: first, the "single jewel-wheel" signifies that one encompasses all, because it brings about perfect conduct.
Second, the "various jewel-flowers" signify awakening others and gladdening them. Third, the "pure maṇi-jewel" signifies perfect purity and transparent clarity.
Because these three practices are used to adorn the ground of the mind, they are summarized as "serving as ornaments. The above [three] are all forms and colors; the fourth is—
Visible color refers to the distinctions of blue, yellow, and so forth; these are called the various characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).

In their manifold layers, they are as deep and vast as the ocean, mutually reflecting one another like its waves. Whether these various colors arise together or mutually encompass one another, they are empty, luminous, and transparent, manifesting in many forms of potentiality;
this is called "boundless manifestation. This arises from mastery over concealment and revelation through meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The unimpeded scattering [of offerings] is brought about by acting for the benefit of others according to their capacities. △ On the third, fourth, and fifth stages, the adornments are complete:
mani-jewels serve as banners constantly emitting light (extending to) exquisite fragrant flower garlands draped all around.
The first, the Jewel Banner (ratnadhvaja), consists of five phrases: first, its substance is the mani-jewel; second, its function is the radiance of the two lights;

third, fourth, and fifth, its adornments are distinguished by the nets and tassels. Regarding the practitioner who follows the causal stage: it is called a "banner" because it subdues Māra and overcomes externalists, and because the light of wisdom shines eternally.

The sound of their compassion gladdens those outside; their vows and practices interlace like a net; the fragrance of their precepts is aromatic; and the four means of integration hang down all around.
Therefore, as sovereign mani-jewel kings, they manifest with mastery, raining down inexhaustible treasures.
The second [sign] is rain from mani-jewels, representing the power of supernormal faculties that manifest according to the needs of beings; it signifies the raining down of the jewels of the Dharma.
Furthermore, various exquisite flowers are distributed across the ground.
Third, the ground is strewn with exquisite flowers, which is also largely due to the pervasive adornment of the mind through the practice of conduct.

Fourth, rows of jewel trees stand in formation, their branches and leaves lush and radiant, because of the establishment of virtuous deeds. △ Fourth, a single statement of the cause summarizes the function.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power (*ṛddhibala*), all the adornments of this site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) are made to appear as reflections therein.
"The Buddha’s power" indicates the cause from which they arise. Since the various types of ornaments are manifold and difficult to describe individually, it is said in general that "all appear.
They may appear within the trees, or upon the aforementioned ornaments, or within the ground; this clarifies [the extent of their manifestation].
Since every single practice constitutes a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), [the following is explained]. △ Second, regarding the adornment of the tree of awakening (*bodhivṛkṣavyūha*):
this arises from the influence of the cause of great wisdom and consists of eleven phrases, divided into four sections. The first phrase generally manifests its supreme excellence.
That Bodhi tree is lofty, eminent, and extraordinary;
it rises high and stands out in solitary majesty. In terms of its causes: its wisdom transcends the realm of numbers, which constitutes its loftiness;

its fundamental nature is never obscured, which constitutes its clarity; its fulfillment of virtues for the sake of all beings constitutes its excellence; and its state of non-dual truth constitutes its extraordinariness. In terms of its fruits:
The tree is itself bodhi. △ Second, the six bodies encompass all virtues.
With the vajra as the body—since a single body is the vajra, being the cause of the fundamental wisdom of the vajra-samādhi—it is established through correct practice and thus constitutes the tree.
The body has lapis lazuli for its trunk and lapis lazuli for its two hubs;
this is because fundamental wisdom gives rise to understanding, whereby both the internal and external are transparently clear.
The branches and twigs are composed of various exquisite jewels;
these three types of jewel branches and twigs are distinguished according to their respective objects.
The jewel leaves are lush and spreading, casting a shade like clouds.
Four branches of artificial leaves serve as adornment; wisdom, supported by meditative concentration, illuminates profoundly. Although the precious leaves differ, they together form a single canopy;
the hundreds of thousands of gates of samādhi likewise converge in a single stillness. Having shaded oneself, one shades others.
Precious flowers of various colors branch out and spread their shadows.

The five precious flowers are of different hues; when they receive light upon the branching limbs of the tree, their colors become uniform, yet as they cast shadows upon the ground, they manifest the dharmas of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), which differ according to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) while all equally receive the light of wisdom (*jñāna*), appearing as reflections within the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*).
Furthermore, they have *maṇi* jewels as their fruit, which contain radiance and emit flames, interspersed among the flowers.
Although the six flowers differ from one another, all the fruits are "as one wishes" (*yathā-manas*).

Just as the boundless ocean of practices leads toward the same enlightenment (*bodhi*), so too, when the fruit of self-benefit is accomplished, it contains radiance within; when body and mind are profoundly tranquil, it emits flames without; and when encountering objects...

This clarifies that if the fruit of benefiting others is established, when [the cause] is not yet mature, it contains its radiance; when the understanding of the Buddha-nature arises, it is like the appearance of a Buddha.
Once matured, it emits flames, flowing back as the light of the teaching. Its essence is such that the fruit accomplished through practice is no different from the fruit of the cause.
They are interspersed with flowers. Thus, the subsequent scripture says: "The Bodhisattva’s tree of wondrous Dharma grows from the ground of the upright mind," and so forth.
△ Third, the threefold mastery of wondrous function.
The trees, perfectly circular, all emit radiance (extending to) their multitudes appearing simultaneously like clouds;

they mutually benefit one another. First, relying on the wisdom of enlightenment (*bodhi-jñāna*), they emit the light of the wisdom of teaching (*śāsana-jñāna*). Next, relying on that light of wisdom, they rain down the precious jewels of the perfectly luminous Dharma.
Finally, the teaching brings forth compassion and wisdom, whereby the Bodhisattvas manifest before us; thus, practice is accomplished without deliberate thought. Therefore...
Like clouds emerging. △ Fourth, citing the cause to conclude the function:
Furthermore, because of his divine majesty and spiritual power (up to) he preaches various dharmas without end or limit.
This means that with the power of the Buddha as the cause, flowing sounds proclaim the Dharma. By the power of suchness (*tathatā*), wisdom proclaims the sound of the Dharma;
since the sound returns to the nature of suchness, it is inexhaustible. It is inexhaustible because it is vast and manifold; it is infinite because it extends vertically;
and it is called "constant" because it is uninterrupted. △ Third, explaining the adornment of the Buddha’s palace, which consists of ten phrases divided into four sections. The first is general.
Clarifying the dimensions:
The palaces and towers where the Tathāgata dwells are vast, magnificent, and pervasive throughout the ten directions.

That the palace can provide shelter and nourishment is precisely his compassion; that the hall can serve as the place of veneration and return is what is called parinirvāṇa. Thus, compassion and wisdom are mutually [interdependent].
Guide. As for the mutual support of the pavilions: they are vast and boundless because the Dharma has no exterior; they are expansive and not constricted because the Dharma is empty within;
they are magnificent and adorned because they possess all characteristics; they are beautiful and exquisite because the meaning of the Dharma is complete.
That which fills the ten directions does so because it accords with the *dharmatā*. Second, its essence and characteristics are perfectly complete:
it is an accumulation of various colored *maṇi* jewels, adorned with diverse precious flowers.
First, the single essence is the *maṇi* jewel, for it is formed by the melting together of accumulated virtues.

Second, its manifestations are manifold and adorned with various qualities, such as the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and other dharmas, through the functions of compassion and tranquility. Third, the six marvelous functions are sovereign.
The various ornaments emit streams of light like clouds;
a single stride emits radiance, showering the Dharma like clouds. The further meanings of "clouds" will be analyzed below.
From within the palace, gathered shadows form a banner;

the second is the Banner of Light, which stands out alone. "Gathered" (*cuì*) means to assemble. It is formed by the assembly of shadows received from light—meaning that at the intersection of compassion and tranquility, one receives wisdom to give rise to responsive manifestation, thereby subduing Māra and transcending.
The assemblies at the bodhimanda of boundless bodhisattvas gathered there in their entirety.

This encompasses three oceans of multitudes: the boundless bodhisattvas, those outside the bodhimanda who are also therein, and the fact that within the cause there is the correct [result], and within the result there is the cause.
This clarifies the secret confluence of the assembly of sages in nirvana.
It has a net made of the sovereign mani-jewel of inconceivable sounds that manifest the radiance of all Buddhas.
This fourth is the net of jewel-radiance of the four tones. The net serves to ward off the defilement of birds and to enhance the splendor of the hall, just as the Great Teaching serves as a net.
Externally, it wards off evil views; internally, it increases compassion and tranquility. Its teachings are all perfect and subtle, accomplished through jewels.
Thus, it can produce the Buddha’s light of wisdom and its perfect voice—the wondrous speech of inconceivable sound.
Briefly, there are four meanings: first, the sound is vast and manifold; second, that which is taught is immeasurable; third, sound is itself no-sound; fourth, one contains all.
All realms of the Tathāgata’s sovereign power of spiritual penetrations emerge from within this. This is the fifth:

the function of producing fruits, which is the great function of the primary retribution (*vipāka*). It resides within this basis; the basis and the primary retribution are fused together, intermingled yet not confused.
It is clarified that by relying on the Great Nirvāṇa, one can establish the great purpose; therefore, it is called "producing."
The dwellings and houses of all sentient beings all manifest their reflections within this.

The six [realms] appear as defiled while remaining undefiled; sentient beings are the primary reality, and their dwellings are the support. Defilement contradicts the nature of purity, yet it does not arise from it.
Delusion has no self-substance of its own; it merely manifests back upon the True. △ Fourth: Citing a single cause to reveal the vastness.
Furthermore, through the empowerment of the Buddhas' spiritual power, within a single thought-moment, one completely encompasses the entire Dharma-realm.

Because its virtues are so vast they are difficult to describe, it is now summarized: by the power of the Buddha, in a single thought-moment, one suddenly encompasses all phenomena of the Dharma-realm—both principle and phenomenon, defilement and purity.
How much more so in multiple thought-moments? Thus, while the above describes pervading the ten directions, this refers to both the universal and the particular.

Unimpeded. Gathering the assembly of bodhisattvas is the manifestation of the Buddha’s spiritual powers; this is immediately subsumed within the unimpeded. Manifesting birth in a household is the unimpeded nature of defilement and purity;
it completely encompasses the dharma-realm. Vastness and narrowness are unimpeded. A single thought-moment is able to [manifest all]—extension and contraction are unimpeded.
Furthermore, gathering the bodhisattvas is the unimpeded nature of cause and effect. Manifesting the Buddha’s spiritual powers is the unimpeded nature of the primary body and its environment. Ten...
The various palaces should now be described. △ Fourth, the ten phrases on the adornment of the lion throne, divided into four parts;
the first generally reveals its superior form.
That lion throne was high, vast, and exquisitely beautiful.

As for the "lion throne," it is where the Lion among Men resides; furthermore, because he preaches the Dharma of fearlessness, what is there to fear for one who has realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*)?
Emptiness is indeed high and unsurpassed, deep and unfathomable, and vast and boundless.
Externally, its boundaries are inexhaustible; its subtlety lies in the fact that phenomena are themselves the truth. "Excellent" means being endowed with all virtues without deficiency.
△ Second, the six essential qualities are perfectly complete:
the mani-jewel forms the pedestal.

A single mani-jewel serves as the seat, situated precisely at the center; it is that which can truly be relied upon. While the mani-jewel appears differently according to its reflections, the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā) manifests various forms according to conditions.
The wondrous principle of the Middle Way is precisely that which can be relied upon.
The lotus flowers form a net.
The flower-nets of the two concentric tiers of seats signify that their external forms are unstained;
they reflect one another in primordial emptiness, with pure and wondrous jewels forming their rims.
The three purities constitute the wheel (*cakra*). "Wheel" refers to the central platform, surrounded by a circular perimeter (*cakravāḍa*),
which is endowed with pervasive excellence and adorned with garlands of various colored flowers.
Four flower tassels hang down all around. All the various awakenings and supernormal powers extend their transformative influence to gather and sustain beings everywhere.
Halls, pavilions, towers, and multi-storied buildings, with their steps, ledges, doors, and windows—all such objects and forms are fully endowed with majestic adornment.

Adorned with the five treasures as its ornaments, the description of the halls and so forth is merely illustrative; in fact, all things are encompassed, and there is nowhere that is not adorned. Thus it is said to be "complete in essence.
This reveals the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā), fully incorporating all myriad images, for there is no thing that is not the Principle (li).
The branches and fruits of the jewel-trees are arranged in rows all around, adorned with the six precious substances;
