these represent the objects and forms interspersed above. These are the wondrous Dharma-trees of the Bodhisattvas, which branch out according to their transformations and bear fruit according to the conditions that evoke them, all while relying upon the signless (*animitta*).
This is termed "all-around" (*parikṣipta*); the mutual support between the ordinary and the holy is what is meant by this name.
Arranged in intervals. △ Third, the vastness of the two sublime functions:
clouds of mani-jewel light mutually illuminate one another.
Light emerges from each pure jewel and interpenetrates like clouds; the emptiness of phenomena is likewise. Within each and every wisdom, one knows the one.
All phenomena—each and every essence of these phenomena—manifest all-encompassing wisdom to illuminate one another.
The pearl-kings manifested by the Buddhas of the ten directions (extending to... all emit radiance and come to shine with brilliant clarity.

Second is the function of the primary and attendant jewels, which mutually illuminate one another. This means that the *maṇi* jewel manifested by the Buddha is capable of performing the work of a Buddha.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The jewel of a wheel-turning king merely rains down precious objects according to human wishes; the celestial jewel is capable of carrying out the commands of the devas;
the Buddha-jewel can perform the work of a Buddha throughout the ten directions; and the bodhisattva jewel is likewise capable of being divided and distributed."
Just as the Vaiḍūrya jewel within Mañjuśrī’s crown manifests all the Buddhas of the ten directions, the crest-jewel of the present Bodhisattva is of that same kind.
As for the phrase "the crest-jewels of the assembled Bodhisattvas" mentioned below, it is likewise so.
Regarding the use of these to adorn the seat: whenever one first attains Buddhahood, all the Buddhas manifest their forms and bestow empowerment upon them.
All Bodhisattvas personally bestow it and reverently offer it; thus, both cause and effect are like precious jewels that come together to illuminate with brilliance.
Because the Tathāgata gives rise to function from the fruit, it is called a "manifestation. When principle is perfected and understanding is full, it is termed the "King of Jewels.

Because the wisdom-illumination at the heart-peak of the Bodhisattva is perfectly pure, it is called the "Wondrous Jewel within the Topknot. Tranquil illumination and illuminating tranquility are both brilliantly pure and luminous.
Candle. △ Fourth, the expansion of the teaching through the empowerment of all Buddhas:
"Furthermore, sustained by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas... [until] the wondrous sound resonates afar, reaching everywhere."
The Buddha-realm is like space; therefore, it is called "vast. When there is a response, it arrives; because it is non-obstructive, nothing is beyond its reach.
All manifest teachings flow from the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*); thus, that which flows returns to pervade the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

It would not be manifest without wisdom; therefore, it is called "the power of the Buddha. △ Fifth, clarifying the inconceivability of the Teacher. Previously, he was merely referred to as "Buddha," but it had not yet been clarified what kind of body this is.

The Buddha. Furthermore, previously it was only stated that he "first attained perfect enlightenment," but it was not known what the characteristics of this attainment were; therefore, they are now revealed.

This means that he possesses ten kinds of profound and vast merit, which are precisely the ten kinds of inexhaustible clouds of bodies of the Dharmadhātu of Vairocana, pervading the entire Dharmadhātu—this is the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
It is not the provisional response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The text has two parts; first, a general exposition.
At that time, the World-Honored One, while seated upon this throne, attained supreme perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena.
This is the Body of Enlightenment (bodhi-kāya), endowed with inexhaustible virtues and honored by the world. When the characteristics of the seat appear, the body is immediately at rest therein;
for wisdom abides in all phenomena without before or after. Regarding all phenomena, he manifests the realm of what has been realized—namely, the two [truths].

The Three Truths are the inexhaustible Dharma. To achieve supreme perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) is to manifest the wisdom of awakening; to open the way to understanding is called "awakening" (*buddha*).

To be free from inversion is "right" (*samyak*); to reach the ultimate is "supreme" (*anuttara*); and to have attained this is called "achieved" (*saṃbodhi*). This is the explanation according to their essential characteristics.

If one were to distinguish them further: ordinary beings are deluded by inversion; the Buddha awakens from the profound darkness. Although those of the Two Vehicles possess awakening, it is not called "right," for they only know...

They hold that phenomena exist, yet they do not know the emptiness of phenomena; they merely realize the emptiness of the self, yet they do not know that the self exists. They feel aversion toward birth and death, yet speak of nirvana as empty.
Since their inversions have not been eliminated, how can they be called "correct"? Even if one were to grant them the title of "correct," it would still not be called "supreme."

Although Bodhisattvas are correct, they possess that which is superior [to them] and that which remains to be cultivated; thus, they cannot be called "supreme. Even if their status is ultimate and they are called supreme, they have not yet attained the name of "accomplishment.
Only my Buddha is able to do so; therefore, it is said he has "accomplished supreme perfect enlightenment" (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

This means that, according to the measure of reality and according to principle, he has clearly and ultimately realized [the truth], having already emerged from even the most subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). II. Detailed Explanation: This is explained by way of ten virtues.

The ten bodies are manifested separately; the text is divided into ten sections. First, the universal pervasiveness of the three karmas (of body, speech, and mind) specifically manifests the characteristics of the Bodhi-body (*bodhi-kāya*).
This is because at the time of attaining enlightenment, one acquires the immeasurable purity of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*). The text has two parts; first, the Dharma [section].
Wisdom enters the three periods of time as entirely equal.

This refers to the mental karma (*manas-karman*). It explains the aforementioned statement regarding the attainment of perfect enlightenment: whereas previously it was said "in all phenomena" (*sarva-dharma*), here it is said "in the three periods of time."

This is merely a summary of the horizontal and vertical aspects. When wisdom enters into equality, this is the accomplishment of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). Regarding wisdom, there are two, three, four, and the unobstructed wisdoms.
As for the two wisdoms, they are the wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and the wisdom that accords with phenomena (*yāvadbhāva-jñāna*).

These, in turn, have two aspects: first, through the wisdom that accords with phenomena, one penetrates the conventional; this is called "entering the three periods of time. Through the wisdom that accords with reality, one realizes the ultimate truth; this is called...
All are equal. Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "One awakens to the three truths by means of the two wisdoms. This is precisely it.

Regarding the distinction between the two types of realization, their nature is without differentiation; therefore, the three periods of time are equal. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "In accordance with ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)."

Because one awakens to all phenomena, it is called "Equal and Perfect Enlightenment" (Samyaksaṃbodhi). As for the mention of the "three wisdoms," these are conventional wisdom, ultimate wisdom, and middle-way wisdom.
This also has two meanings: first, when the ultimate and the conventional mutually dissolve and both are negated to discern the Middle, then the three periods of time are equal.
Second, only when both characteristics are extinguished does one truly enter into wisdom. Although the ultimate and the conventional are identical, their characteristics are not destroyed; that is—

In the illumination of both [subject and object], these two awakenings take the three truths as their object. Since the objects are simultaneously extinguished and simultaneously manifested, wisdom is likewise both quiescent and illuminating, flowing as a dual current.
To be unobstructed wisdom awakening to unobstructed objects is what constitutes perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

As for the "four wisdoms," they refer to the four wisdoms beginning with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Because they universally take the objects of the three periods of time as their domain, they are all—
They enter the three periods of time. Regarding "equality": the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is equality by virtue of being free from conceptual discrimination;

the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) is equality because it realizes the nature of equality; the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) is equality through its observation; and the wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*)...

Universally benefiting all with impartiality, the four wisdoms are perfectly integrated and subsumed within a single phrase. The activities of body and speech are all manifestations of these four wisdoms;
because the four wisdoms are perfectly integrated and non-dual in nature, that which is cultivated arises as that which is originally present, being neither identical nor different.
Thus, the core tenet of the sutra is not lost. Furthermore, when the subject that awakens attains this, it constitutes supreme bodhi; as for the object awakened to—
This is precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Wisdom and principle are non-dual;
thus it is the true Dharma-body. Its body pervades all worlds.
Its bodily activity (*kāyakarman*) penetrates the three worlds; therefore, it is called "all. This body of perfect enlightenment consists of these ten bodies.
In summary, this body thus pervades all three bodies without exception. The Dharma-body is omnipresent, for it is the common basis of the world.
The Wisdom-body realizes reality, for it pervades according to that reality. The Form-body is unimpeded, likewise pervading in accordance with reality.
These are all universally pervasive, yet not partially pervasive. This means that in every single atom and minute particle throughout all worlds, the Buddha is perfectly complete;
he appears when viewed as a whole, and he appears when viewed individually.

Furthermore, the lands and so forth are my very body, because outside the essence of the lands and such, there is no separate self. I am the lands and so forth, because outside the essence of the self, there are no lands.
Because they are equal, each individual body mutually merges and encompasses the others, like many lamps whose lights each pervade one another;
their voices universally accord with the lands of the ten directions.
Regarding vocal karma, there are three meanings of "conformity" (*ānukūlya*): First, conformity with diverse types of speech and sound. As the Sūtra says:
"The linguistic expressions of all sentient beings are fully expounded by a single word, leaving nothing remaining. Second, conformity with the appropriate teaching of the Dharma.
This refers to how the Tathāgata, within a single utterance, expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras. Third, conformity with universality. This refers to how the Buddha, with a single [utterance]...
"Sublime Sound. Because it is heard throughout the lands of the ten directions. △ Second, the analogy:
"For example, as empty space contains all images... [it] enters equally into all lands."
This serves as a general analogy for the three types of action (trikarma). However, the Buddha’s three actions cannot be fully illustrated by any analogy;

only space (*ākāśa*) and suchness (*tathatā*) can provide a partial indication. To employ any other analogy would constitute a slander against the Buddha. Nevertheless, regarding the analogy of space, there are points of similarity and points of difference.
Therefore, the sutra below states: "The body of the Tathāgata is not like space, for it is perfected by all sublime dharmas."
This reveals their differences; now we take up the sense of partial similarity. There are many types of similar meanings, as seen in the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences" (*Daśakṣānti*) below.
Herein are two metaphors which, when expanded, constitute four meanings: first, the metaphor of inclusion, which includes the meaning of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*);

second, the metaphor of universality, which includes the meaning of universal penetration. Using these four metaphors to illustrate the mental karma, the sutra below states: "The Buddha-wisdom is vast..."

Because it is equal to great empty space; this is the general metaphor. The wisdom of measure (pramāṇa-jñāna) encompasses and is universally pervasive; the wisdom of principle (dharmatā-jñāna) is non-conceptual and enters into realization.

Furthermore, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is the pure, perfect virtue that serves as the support for both manifest and latent seeds, capable of manifesting and generating the reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdom—this is the sense of "containing and encompassing. The subsequent scripture states: "Bodhi-wisdom manifests universally as one..."

Regarding the mental inclinations, faculties, and desires of all sentient beings, there is nothing that is manifested. The phrase "nothing is manifested" means that there is no conceptual discrimination.
The Wisdom of Equality contemplates all phenomena such that oneself and other sentient beings are entirely equal, and likewise remains free from discrimination.
The term "non-discrimination" reveals the absence of differentiation; therefore, the sutra below states: "In regard to all meanings, there is no..."
Regarding what is observed and so forth: one sees that the Great Void contains all phenomena, yet all phenomena cannot contain the Great Void;
the Great Void does not differentiate among phenomena, yet phenomena differentiate the Great Void.

This serves as a metaphor for how my dharmas cannot accommodate the Buddha’s wisdom, whereas the Buddha’s wisdom can accommodate my dharmas. Those who possess my dharmas are those who differentiate the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata does not discriminate between self and dharmas. Second, regarding the two universal metaphors: the *suvicita-jñāna* (wonderfully discerning wisdom) possesses no lack of universal knowledge, which is the meaning of "universality.
The *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom) accomplishes all things without omission, which is the meaning of "entering accordingly.
Furthermore, the subsequent scripture states: "The Buddha’s wisdom is as vast and equal as space; it universally pervades the minds of all sentient beings. This refers to wisdom.
The essence is pervasive: it fully comprehends all the deluded thoughts of the world; this refers to the pervasiveness of the function of wisdom (*jñāna*). Furthermore, it says:

"One attains a mind equal in measure to the entire dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*); this refers to the pervasiveness of realization. Because the nature of wisdom is entirely identical to the nature of form (*rūpa*), this refers to the pervasiveness of principle (*tattva*).
How is there universal entry? It is because, without destroying the subject-object distinction, there is realized knowledge. Therefore, the subsequent scripture says: "The world..."
One hears that all lands are entered by [the Buddha] in accordance with them all. The body of wisdom has no form and cannot be seen by them.
Because it accords with suchness (*tathatā*), it enters that which is nowhere to be entered; therefore, it is called "equality.
Thus, while empty space universally enters all lands, the lands do not universally enter empty space. Wherever there is a land, there must be empty space; wherever there is empty space...
In the realm of emptiness, there may be no lands. Emptiness enters into lands with impartiality, yet lands possess their own sense of "this" and "that" relative to emptiness.
Emptiness may be likened to the Buddha’s wisdom; lands may be likened to the three periods of time.
The three periods of time have their locus, and the Buddha’s wisdom is necessarily contained within it. The Buddha knows that which is the locus;

yet the three periods may lack inherent substance. The Buddha’s wisdom enters the three periods with equal impartiality, while the three periods, in relation to the Buddha’s wisdom, possess their own beginning and end.
This is merely an explanation of the non-dual as dual. If it were dual yet non-dual, the lands would be void.

Emptiness. Because the wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is of one and the same nature, they all mutually penetrate one another; by taking up one, the whole is encompassed, and this is likewise universal.
When the three worlds are thus perfectly interfused, they transcend the path of words and thought;
therefore, the Buddha-wisdom is called "inconceivable. Next, to illustrate the activity of the body with a single metaphor: even a single hair can contain the entirety of the Dharma-realm. It must...
It contains all images and manifests the bodily karma (*kāyakarman*). The second analogy states:
"For example, just as space is vast and non-material, yet it can manifest all material forms, and that space is without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
so too is the body of the Tathāgata. All the roots of goodness and karmic deeds of all sentient beings..."
"Attainment" implies inclusion. That the body of the Tathāgata is without discrimination is the second meaning.
"The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm" is the meaning of universality. Furthermore, it says:
"For example, just as space pervades all places—whether material or immaterial—neither reaching them nor not reaching them, so too is the body of the Tathāgata; it pervades..."
"All dharmas and all lands" signifies the sense of universal pervasion. "Neither reaching nor not reaching" signifies the sense of equal entry.
Subsequently, four meanings are used as metaphors for vocal action (*vākkarman*): because the Tathāgata possesses all languages within a single utterance;
and because the celestial drum of Śakradevendra produces sound without intention. Such is the voice of the Tathāgata.
Because there is nowhere it does not reach, one should know that the voice of the Tathāgata is uninterrupted, for it universally penetrates the Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, it is said that the voice of the Tathāgata is without crookedness; this is the meaning of equality, for it causes beings to rejoice according to their faith and understanding—this is the meaning of "following and entering.
Since the single metaphor of emptiness is used to universally illustrate the three karmas, it is said that the Perfectly Awakened One attains non-attainment.
The purity of the three spheres of measurement is clearly and brilliantly illuminated; this is not a product of forced interpretation. △ Second, the majesty and supremacy of the body:
the body constantly and universally occupies all sites of enlightenment (up to) like the rising sun illuminating the world.
This means that according to the inclinations of sentient beings, he manifests various images of enjoyment bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*) and lands;

because there is nothing to which these do not pervade, it is called "all places of practice" (*sarvamandala*). Briefly, there are ten types: first, the wisdom body (*jñānakāya*), which universally sits at the place of practice of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-maṇḍala*);
second, the dharma body (*dharmakāya*), which sits without sitting at the place of practice; third, the dharma-gate body (*dharmamukhakāya*), which sits peacefully amidst the myriad...

The site of practice (*caryā-maṇḍala*). The four types of emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) sit peacefully within the water-moon site of practice. These four meanings are presented for the sake of convenience.
If one were to properly categorize the sites of practice according to the bodies of majestic power (*vibhūti-kāya*), there are briefly six types:
first, the site of practice of all similar worlds, as explained in the "Chapter on Names" (*Nāma-saṃgīti*) and other texts; second, all dissimilar worlds, namely those in the form of trees.
1. As described in the "Chapter on the Formation of the World" (*Lokadhātu-saṃbhava-parivarta*). 2. Within all the seeds of worlds (*sarva-loka-jāti*). 3.
Within all the oceans of worlds (*sarva-loka-samudra*), as explained in the "Flower Treasury" (*Kusuma-kośa*) chapter. 4. Within all atoms (*sarva-paramāṇu*); the text states:
"Just as one sees the Buddha seated here in this assembly, so it is within all atoms," and so forth. 5. The infinite Indra-nets of world-dusts (*kṣetra-rajas-indrajāla*).
The *bodhimaṇḍa*, together with the ten preceding types, is therefore called "all. Regarding the phrase "the Bodhisattva," this correctly manifests the preeminence of his majestic power;

because he surpasses even those who are superior, he is specifically called a "Bodhisattva," yet this does not mean he does not transcend others. As for the phrase "like the sun," this illustrates it through a metaphor:

like the sun reflected in mountains, appearing and disappearing without concealment or manifestation, it is fully present everywhere because there is no difference in its essence. This is the metaphor.
Seated pervasively throughout the site of enlightenment, his great brilliance flows through the void, eclipsing the radiance of all else like the sun; its limits are difficult to fathom.

This is a metaphor for his majestic light, which surpasses and outshines the bodhisattvas, whom those bodhisattvas themselves cannot measure. Since it is said that he "illuminates the world," [it is clear].
Thus, they ultimately bring life to those who are blind. First illuminating the sublime heights, he speaks alone of the Bodhisattva. △ Third, the body of merit is profound and vast:
the great ocean of all merits practiced throughout the three periods of time has become entirely pure.

The virtues of the Buddhas of the three periods of time were all extensively studied in the past; now that the three temporal limits have been severed and defiled habitual tendencies have perished, all merits are completely pure.
△ Fourth, the body that takes birth according to one's will.
Yet he constantly manifests birth in all Buddha-lands.
First, following the intentions of others, he undergoes birth in every place; second, following his own intention, there is nowhere he cannot be born.
This means that compassion and *prajñā* are always in mutual accord, responding and penetrating such that they extend to the furthest reaches of the future. △ Five: Adorned with the Marks and Signs.
Adorning the body, its boundless forms and marks are perfected with radiance that pervades the entire dharma-realm without distinction;
because these forms are inexhaustible, they are called "boundless form. The ten sets of marks, numbering as many as the atoms within a lotus-treasury world-system, are called "boundless marks."

Although they are boundless, all are called "true"; thus, each and every one is boundless. All the primary marks and secondary signs, the emitted light and the constant radiance, all accord with the *dharmadhātu*;
therefore, it is said to be "perfectly complete. Because they are perfectly manifested in both vast and narrow places, they are called "without distinction."
△ Sixth, the manifestation of the Dharma through the six classes of beings:
To manifest all dharmas is like spreading a great cloud;
that is, to rain down the great rain of Dharma and sever all doubts. Therefore, the sutra below says: "The Buddha Vairocana makes this vow..."

His power pervades the entire Dharma-realm; throughout all lands, he constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel. These two lines of the sutra consist of a superior dharma and an inferior metaphor, containing many layers of meaning.
First, the cloud is a metaphor for the body, and the rain represents the preaching of the Dharma; here, the dharma and the metaphor are presented in abbreviated parallelism.
Furthermore, first the compassionate clouds arise, and subsequently the Dharma-rain falls. Although it is but a single cloud and a single rain, that which they moisten is not the same. Moreover—
According to the capacities and conditions of beings, the clouds and rain each differ; they obscure the dust and veil the sun, universally covering all with a mindless equanimity.

△ Seventh, mastery of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*): this refers to being able to manifest boundless varieties of activity within great assemblies, for all such manifestations are sovereign.
Each and every hair-tip is able to contain all worlds without obstruction; it is vast in its capacity and unimpeded.
This means that within each single hair-pore of the Tathāgata’s body, all lands (*kṣetra*) are contained without obstruction.
There are two meanings to this lack of obstruction: first, by means of a single small hair, one manifests many great lands; thus, the one and the many [are interpenetrated].
The large and the small are without obstruction. Second, these many lands within a single hair and those many lands within that [other] hair interpenetrate without being confused;
thus, concealment and manifestation are without obstruction, each manifesting immeasurable powers of spiritual transformation to teach and subdue all sentient beings.
It is universally pervasive and unimpeded, because its vast capacity is not obstructed by its universal pervasiveness.

Returning to the lands within the aforementioned hairs, he manifests through his spiritual power the generation [of beings] and, if he were to pervade the ten directions extensively, he would manifest various transformations of the three karmas to accomplish all tasks;
this is clearly and easily understood. △ Eighth, the Dharmakāya Encompasses All.
The body pervades the ten directions yet is without coming or going.
Taking the Dharma as the body, it is originally profound and pervasive; therefore, there is no coming or going. Manifesting form in reliance upon the Dharma, it returns to being like the Dharma-body:
being here is precisely being there, and furthermore, it does not depend on coming and going. 9. The Wisdom-Body Exhausts Nature and Characteristics.
The source of this is that wisdom enters into all phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) and realizes that dharmas are empty and quiescent.

"All" refers to the differentiation of phenomena; their nature is entirely empty and quiescent. Because their nature is still, they are quiescent; because phenomena lack inherent existence, they are empty. △ The Ten Powers (*daśabala*).
Sustaining the body: it is able to sustain the bodies and environments of both oneself and others.
Within its radiance, one beholds all the miraculous transformations of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; there is nothing that is not clearly seen. Sustaining the body of correct retribution:

"spirit" (*shen*) refers to wondrous wisdom, and "transformation" (*bian*) refers to manifesting the body. Both "transformation" (*bianzhuan*) and "manifestation" (*bianxian*) are termed [the body of transformation].
They are able to maintain all these transformations; they can maintain them for others, how much more so for their own affairs. The latter section is also like this:
they cause all the adornments of all Buddha-lands throughout inconceivable eons to appear manifest.

He maintains the land of dependent recompense (*niṣyanda-bhoga-kṣetra*), extending horizontally to the ends of all lands and vertically through the exhaustion of all kalpas. All its adornments are constantly maintained and made manifest.

Regarding this from the perspective of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*): if one considers it from the perspective of the three bodies (*trikāya*), then the first three sections are all termed the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), while the constant manifestation below is the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
As for the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) pervading the ten directions, within the *saṃbhogakāya*, the former is the self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*).
It is used as a retribution. The latter two are the retributions of the *parasaṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body for others); thus it says, "dwelling among the assembly of bodhisattvas.

Since various teachings speak of three bodies or four bodies, establishing distinct explanations such as the "perfected" (*niṣpanna*) and so forth, they are now all perfectly integrated. Within this single initial accomplishment, nothing is not instantaneously complete.

The ten bodies are primary, while the [other] three or four meanings are included therein. Furthermore, within a single hair-pore he harmonizes and nurtures sentient beings, and within his light he sustains buddha-lands.
Just as space is all-pervasive and so forth, these are also the ten bodies, such as the land-body (*kṣetra-kāya*) and others.

Since the three worlds are perfectly interfused, how could there be any distinction between the *vipāka* (retribution) and *nirmāṇa* (emanation) bodies? Thus, it should be understood that the Teacher is praised briefly by means of these ten virtues; yet within each individual virtue, there is nothing that is not perfectly interfused.
One should therefore set aside conceptual attachments and contemplate this. △ Sixth, the manifestation of the gathering of the ocean-like assembly. Although the assembly...

Profound and vast, it is difficult to fathom; herein, ten general gateways are briefly set forth: first, the intent of the compilation; second, the causes for the compilation; third, the discernment of categories; fourth, the determination of numbers;

fifth, the provisional and the real; sixth, the stages of the path; seventh, the sequence of before and after; eighth, existence and non-existence; ninth, hearing and not hearing; tenth, the explanation of the text.
Now, first: why have they come to the presence of the Buddha? It is for ten reasons. First, to act as a shadow and echo, serving as the principal and its attendants.
Second, to provide assistance so that [the Buddha’s qualities] may be brought to perfection, such as the assembly of those who constantly follow him, like Samantabhadra and others.
Third, to protect the Tathāgata, like Vajrapāṇi and others, who constantly and diligently guard the dwelling places of all Buddhas.
Therefore, fourth is for the purpose of adornment, such as the deities of the bodhimaṇḍa, who constantly adorn and purify the Buddha’s palace.
Fifth is for the purpose of making offerings; this includes both the offering of correct practice, such as through verses of praise, and material offerings, such as flowers and banners.
Sixth, it serves as an inspiration, for the various interlocutors who pose difficult questions in this sutra are precisely those instances.

Seventh, it serves so that those who hear the Dharma may obtain benefit and attain realization according to their capacities, as they belong to such a class. Eighth, it serves to symbolize the Dharma;

for the various peaks and groves symbolize faith, practice, and so forth, as they all share the same names, and the bodhisattvas emerging from the seats manifest extraordinary wonders—this also serves as a general symbolic representation.

First, it is for the sake of the myriad practices, because all together lead to the attainment of Buddhahood. Ninth, it is for the sake of conforming to realization, because Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others have realized and taught that [the Dharma] is not false.
Tenth, it is for the sake of overturning and revealing; that is, by showing what the Śrāvakas do not hear, it reveals that the Dharma is not shared [with them].
Because of these many purposes, the great assembly has gathered like an ocean of clouds; it is not merely for the sake of attesting to faith alone.
The second is the cause of assembly. There are also ten causes: first, because they previously accumulated roots of goodness together with Vairocana Tathāgata;
second, because they were once received by the Buddha’s four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*); third, because they heard the perfect Dharma while in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);
fourth, because they previously gave rise to the great mind (*mahācitta*) to protect all beings; fifth, because they previously made great vows to serve the Buddhas.

Therefore, for these many reasons, they are able to participate in this [assembly]: (1) because they follow the Tathāgata; (2) because they are never satiated; (3) because they delight in hearing the True Dharma with a tireless mind;
(4) because they are well able to dispel and extinguish the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*); (5) because their bodies are pervaded by the purity of merit and wisdom;
and (6) because they are born from the great ocean of roots of goodness that share the same *dharmatā*. For these many such meanings, they have attained admission here.

Assembly. Among these, there are collective causes that also accord with the general intent of the assembly; furthermore, for each group of followers, there are distinct individual causes, which may be inferred through reflection.

Third, the classification of types: based on the aforementioned general intent of the assembly, ten categories are established. First, the retinue of reflections and echoes. Second, the constantly following retinue.

1. The Assembly of the Multitude; 2. The Assembly of the Retinue; 3. The Assembly of the Three Protectors; 4. The Assembly of the Adorned Gathering; 5. The Assembly of Offerings; 6. The Assembly of Initiators; 7. The Assembly of Those for Whom the Teaching is Intended;
8. The Assembly Representing the Dharma; 9. The Assembly Witnessing the Dharma; 10. The Assembly Manifesting the Dharma. These may be understood according to what preceded.
Regarding the fourth, the enumeration of the assemblies: how could one possibly count or know the multitude of the Dharma-realm?
To speak according to the text, the total number of assemblies across the nine assemblies is one hundred and seventy-five; within the general introduction, there are forty-one assemblies.
That is to say, there is one being born simultaneously [with the Buddha], thirty-nine ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), and one on the lion throne;
if one includes those previously mentioned who flowed forth from beneath the Bodhi tree, as well as the boundless bodhisattvas within the palace, there are forty-three assemblies in total.
These forty-three [assemblies] are distributed throughout the nine assemblies. Within the first assembly, there are two groups:
the newly gathered assembly from the ten directions and the assembly from the Buddha’s brow-crevice; these added together make forty-five. In the second assembly, there are both new and old groups.
The third and fourth assemblies each have four groups, namely: the new and the old, as well as the group that has realized the Dharma, and the celestial hosts.

The fifth assembly consists of one hundred and eleven groups, namely: the new and the old groups, the groups making offerings within the "Chapter on Ascending to Heaven," numbering one hundred and seven, together with the celestial hosts, and the group that has realized the Dharma.
The sixth assembly consists of four groups, namely: the celestial hosts, those born together [with the Buddha], [the group that has realized the Dharma], and [the new and old groups].

The assembly of ordinary beings; the assembly of those who have realized the Dharma; and the two assemblies of the seventh and eighth [periods], each consisting of only one group—namely, the original assembly of Samantabhadra and others.
The ninth assembly consists of three groups: namely, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and the original assembly of celestial kings and others.

Although these original assemblies appear repeatedly, they are all included because they differ according to their respective periods. However, these various assemblies may be taken collectively as one, for there is but the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Because there are assemblies, they may be divided into two: the assembly of real beings and the assembly of emanations. Or they may be three: humans, devas, and asuras.
Or they may be divided into four: Buddhas, bodhisattvas, humans, and non-humans. Or five, by dividing non-humans into devas and asuras. Or six, by adding animals.
Or seven, by dividing devas into those of the desire realm and the form realm. Or eight, by adding bodhisattvas.
There may be nine [realms] because there are both this realm and other realms; or ten, because other directions have their respective principal and attendant [realms];

or one hundred and seventy-five, as previously explained; or immeasurable and boundless, because the categories of meaning are manifold and each is measured by a number equal to the atoms within a buddha-field (*kṣetraparamāṇu*), and so forth, as further detailed in the *New Collection on Bodhisattvas*.

The assembly of Māraprabha emerges from the multitude; all other assemblies are likewise so. Therefore, each individual assembly is without boundaries. This is still explained in terms of distinct characteristics.

If they are fused and integrated, then within each single assembly, all one hundred and seventy-five assemblies are fully present, because these assemblies of the dharmadhātu-dependent origination exist mutually within one another.
Thus far, this has been discussed with reference to a single world-system; if one were to extend it to the ten directions...
And as numerous as the atoms in lands of different types, like an infinite and inexhaustible net of Indra—this is called the number of the assembly in the oceanic gathering of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Fifth, regarding the provisional and the real: indeed, whatever can respond to and proclaim the holy teachings, and manifest their traces through its influence, is without exception provisional.

Among those who encounter the teaching, the majority are indeed real beings. Regarding the various classes of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas within the impure lands as elucidated in the various teachings, both the provisional and the real are present:
those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are real, while those on the stages are provisional; for the Dharma-body is unborn.
Because they are born into the five realms of existence. The bodhisattvas of the Pure Land are exclusively real, for they are born through the retribution of reality (*bhūtaniṣyanda*).

The various classes of śrāvakas are provisional; as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "In order to ensure that the Pure Land is not empty, [the Buddha] manifests a diverse multitude through transformation.

According to this sutra, both those born together with the Buddha and those born differently from him encompass both the provisional and the real, as they are subsumed within the reality-virtue manifested by the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*), in accordance with conditions.
Because they manifest according to their respective stages. As stated at the beginning of the second assembly: "There are none who are not in their final birth before Buddhahood.
Regarding the distinction between the provisional and the real among the ten aforementioned classes, within the assembly of "echoes and reflections" there are two types:

first, the assembly of those with realized merit (*phala-guṇa*), namely the Buddhas who bestow empowerment and realize the Dharma; they act as mutual leaders and companions, being neither provisional nor real. If [one considers] their stage...
The influence of the ultimate Bodhisattva is exclusively provisional; thus, a sutra says: "In the past he was the teacher of Śākyamuni, and now he is a disciple of the Buddha.

Since the two Honored Ones do not manifest their teachings simultaneously, [the Buddha] says, "I am a bodhisattva," and so forth. For those who are ready to receive the teaching, this is solely the ultimate truth.
The remaining eight [Buddhas] encompass both the provisional and the ultimate.
Regarding the sixth stage, some say that all are positions of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), because they are manifested through the ocean-seal (*sāgara-mudrā*) of Samantabhadra.
Others say that all are oceans of cause and effect, which cannot be seen or heard; even the World-Honored One is likewise a cause.
This is because they are manifestations of consciousness. Alternatively, all may be both cause and effect, for the effect does not abandon the cause, as it manifests according to its kind;
and because the power of vows from the causal stage assists the Buddha’s transformation of beings; and because those of the appropriate capacity are the primary focus of cultivation and progression.

Or, both may be neither, for the dependent origination of cause and effect is identical to the true nature shared by the great assembly. When this is contrasted with the preceding provisional and real [teachings], then at the stage of fruition, it is one.

Regarding "toward expedient means" (*quán*): the stage of the causal position (*yīn wèi*) encompasses both the expedient and the real. If contrasted with the ten preceding categories, the "echoes and reflections" (*yǐngxiǎng*) and the "realized dharma" (*zhèngfǎ*) encompass both cause and fruit;
the remaining eight are solely cause. The relative heights and depths within the causal stage are difficult to determine with certainty.
Regarding the seventh point, "the sequence of before and after": listing the Bodhisattvas first and the other assemblies later signifies arising from the root to manifest the branches.

Conversely, praising [the assemblies] below and subsequently clarifying the Bodhisattvas signifies returning from the branches to the root. This is truly because the root and the branches are non-dual; thus, both texts are cited interchangeably.

Furthermore, when flowing from the root to the branches, one must necessarily proceed from the small to the great; therefore, from... [self-... (Note: The final phrase "therefore, from self... appears to be an incomplete fragment of the source text.)
In the celestial realm, these are the branches; to subsume the branches and return to the root, one must proceed from the profound to the shallow. Therefore, freedom (*vaśitā*) is explained first.
This is because all of them manifest the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), being sovereign in both its regressive and progressive aspects.

Furthermore, they represent the forty stages (*bhūmi*), each of which penetrates the gate of causes and encompasses the ocean of fruits. By alternatingly citing the preceding and succeeding stages, it is intended that sentient beings do not conceive of them as superior or inferior.

Regarding the eighth [category], existence or non-existence, there are likewise ten types. First, in terms of the realms (*dhātu*), there is no existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Second, in terms of the destinies (*gati*), there is no existence in the hell realm (*niraya*);
these two are not suitable vessels [for such existence]. However, if one considers rebirth (*upapatti*), there are hell-beings who are sons of gods (*devaputra*). If one considers the object...

Furthermore, it also extends to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as it benefits all three realms. Third, regarding the continents: only Jambudvīpa is listed, because the other three are omitted for brevity or because they would present difficulties.
Fourth, regarding the vehicles (*yāna*): there are no two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), as this is a teaching unique to the Mahāyāna;
even those of the lower vehicle do not see or hear it. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If at the beginning of a Hīnayāna sūtra, only the Śrāvakas..."

I have heard that if a Mahāyāna sūtra begins by listing both bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, or if a One Vehicle (Ekayāna) sūtra begins by listing only bodhisattvas, it is therefore designated as a "unique teaching" (asādhāraṇa-deśanā).
Alternatively, if a Mahāyāna sūtra lists only those of the Lesser Vehicle, it is for the purpose of attracting and gathering them, such as the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Or, if it lists only those of the Great Vehicle, it likewise belongs to the Mahāyāna; however, because the primary and the attendant are not fully present, it is categorized differently.

Regarding the presence of both the primary and its attendants: it must be the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). Fifth, regarding the schools: there are no fourfold assemblies, because the Hinayana teachings have not yet been expounded.

Sixth, regarding the leaders: there is no human king, because the king has not yet realized [the truth]. Seventh, regarding the three groups: there are none of the "wrongly fixed" (mithyātva-niyata), because they are obstructed and separated;
for those who are like the congenitally blind, there is only benefit in the darkness. Eighth, regarding the internal and external: there are no outsiders (tīrthika), as this is not their [domain].
9. Regarding the various heavens, there are no beings in the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*), because they have entered a state of false concentration (*mithyāsamādhi*). 10.

Regarding good and evil, there are no evil Māras, because they do not cause obstruction or harm and are subsumed within the category of the heavens. These ten points are explained merely according to their superficial characteristics; in their perfect fusion (*yuanrong*), they should all be present.
Thus, there is nothing that is not fully possessed.

Regarding the ninth [category], "hearing what was not heard": from the perspective of the provisional (expedient means), those before and after all mutually hear [the teaching]. From the perspective of the real (ultimate truth), one hears it at the very assembly where one appears.
Even if one does not arise in a previous assembly but proceeds to a subsequent one, they likewise do not know one another. If, however, one considers those of sudden capacity, this is permitted.

All at once, they are fully grasped. These nine preceding sections have been briefly explained here for the sake of clarity. Whether in the middle-length or extensive versions, some points may be hidden while others are manifest;
one must not cling rigidly to the literal text.
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Vaipulya, Scroll Five;
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Vaipulya, Scroll Six (Entering the Fourth Sheet of the First Volume).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui. Commentary on the Sūtra. △ Tenth: Explanation of the Text.
In the first assembly, there are initially forty groups of followers, which are broadly divided into two categories:

the first consists of those born together with [the Buddha] (sahaja), while the remainder are those born separately (pṛthagjana). Therefore, the *Dilun* states: "Jiechuemo (Vimukticandra) belongs to the group of those born together."

Furthermore, it is said: "The assembly of those born together requests [instruction]; thus we know that those prior to the stages (bhūmi) are also included. It is clear that this does not refer to specific stages.
Other explanations, however, do not accord with the intent of the treatise. How can they be called "those born together"? There are, in fact, two meanings.

First, "various types" refers to manifesting in the diverse forms of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Bodhisattvas, having attained the *dharmatā-kāya*, appear as a single class by assuming the form of a bodhisattva like that of humans.

Second, regarding bodhisattvas being "the same," this applies across all stages; however, they are "different" in their spiritual powers and so forth, due to the distinctions within the qualities of the *dharmadhātu*.

Regarding these forty assemblies, each passage contains three parts: first, the heading; [second, the body of the text]; and third, the conclusion. [The heading is as follows: [The text continues with the specific headings for each assembly.]

First, the enumeration and classification of the assembly; second, the listing of names and the count of their bonds; third, the summary of their perfected virtues. Now, regarding the first [the enumeration and classification], there are three parts to the assembly born together with the Buddha.
First, the indication of the number and the classification of types:
they are as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-worlds.

This indicates the number. Below, the worlds are distinguished; briefly, there are three categories: first, worlds (*loka-dhātu*); second, world-systems (*cūḍika-loka-dhātu*); and third, oceans [of worlds].

What is here termed "world" is neither a world-system nor an ocean, for both the provisional and the ultimate teachings agree that a single trichiliocosm constitutes the field of transformation for a single Buddha.

It may also be called a "Buddha-field" (*buddha-kṣetra*) or a "Buddha-land" (*buddha-bhūmi*), all of which follow this same principle. As for "minute dust" (*paramāṇu*), it refers to the measure of seven *paramāṇus*.

Furthermore, it is said that if one were to grind the three thousandfold world system into fine dust, with each particle representing a single bodhisattva, their number would already be difficult to measure;
how much more so when ten such numbers are cited to signify the inexhaustible?
Surrounded by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—this distinguishes them from other assemblies. The full term is *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*; it is abbreviated here.
There are three explanations for this: first, *bodhi* refers to the fruit of Buddhahood sought, and *sattva* refers to the... [the being].
First, "transforming sentient beings" refers to the object of compassion and wisdom; the name is established based on this object, hence it is called a Bodhisattva.
Second, "bodhi" (enlightenment) is the fruit sought, and "sattva" is the person who seeks it; the name Bodhisattva is formed by combining the subject and the object.
Third, "sattva" here means "valiant," signifying that one valiantly seeks great enlightenment.

*Mahā* means "great. There are four meanings of "great": first, greatness of aspiration, because one seeks great *bodhi*; second, greatness of practice, because the two benefits [of self and others] are accomplished;
third, greatness of time, because it spans three incalculable *kalpas*; and fourth, greatness of virtue, because all the merits of the One Vehicle are fully possessed.
The former two apply generally to those before the stages (*bhūmi*), while the latter two pertain either exclusively to those on the stages or beyond. Furthermore, there is...
The various Mahāsattvas likewise do not transcend this; they are all the inner retinue of Śākyamuni Buddha, constantly following him in his movements and stillness.
Therefore, it is said that he is "surrounded by them. Second, regarding the listing of names and the enumeration: as for the sages, they have no names.

Names are established for beings; although these names may be distinguished by a thousand differences, they mostly depend upon their conduct and virtues. While all such conduct and virtues are fully possessed, they are individually designated according to what is appropriate.
This section has two parts. First, the listing of ten names that share the same title.
Their names are the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Samantabhadra and so forth.
The first ten share the same name "Samanta" (Universal) to manifest their possession of the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the Dharma-realm. The latter ten have different names.

This is to manifest the virtue of the distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, the general and the particular are fused, being one and the same Dharma-realm.

Herein, first, the "Universal" (*samanta*) among the ten names is the generality within the particular; the ten differences below "Universal" manifest that the Universal itself is capable of differentiation.

Only through this can the meaning of "Universal" be fully established. This is the common practice of all Buddhas of the past and present—the conduct of Samantabhadra—which manifests its distinctions according to each respective stage.

They are not the same. Even after attaining perfect enlightenment, one continues to practice universal inclusion; therefore, this is clarified first. Regarding the term "Samantabhadra" (Puxian): its essence and nature are all-pervasive, hence it is called "Universal" (Pu);

it manifests virtue in accordance with conditions, hence it is called "Worthy" (Xian). This refers to the universal nature itself. Furthermore, providing relief to all without exception is called "Universal";
being close to the ultimate and ranking just below the Sage is called "Worthy. This refers to the various stages of Samantabhadra. Moreover, his virtues pervade the Dharma...
The realm is called "Universal" (Pǔ). Reaching perfect harmony and goodness is called "Worthy" (Xián). This refers to Samantabhadra as he stands within his own station.

Furthermore, that there is no fruit not fully realized is called "Universal"; that one does not abandon the gateway of the cause is called "Worthy. This refers to Samantabhadra subsequent to Buddhahood. These are the Samantabhadras of their respective stations.
Compassion and wisdom are practiced in union. Following the Buddha is Samantabhadra; his ocean of wisdom is already full, yet he employs compassion that is identical to wisdom.
This is quiescent yet constantly active, extending to the furthest reaches of the future. Furthermore, "Universal" (Samanta) means that one is all, while "Worthy" (Bhadra) means that all is one.
This is explained in terms of their mutual integration and inclusion. He is listed first because he is the leader and the presiding lord of the Dharma-gates. The Dharma...
Because it is the essence of the realms; because there is no bodhisattva who does not ride upon it; because there is not a single Tathāgata who is not accomplished through it;
and because it causes all who hear it to perceive the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha within their own bodies, thereby practicing universal conduct.

Although many meanings have been explained above through analytical interpretation (*vyutpatti*), now we shall provide a combined explanation based on its specific designation. There is nowhere that is not virtuous; thus, it is named Samantabhadra (Universally Worthy). This is its very essence.
"Universal. This one constitutes the general [category], while the remaining nine constitute the specific.
Regarding the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Virtue Supreme Lamp Light Illumination:
"universal virtue" refers to virtue that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which fills the dharma-realm and is thus supreme, illuminating it exhaustively.
It is like the light of a lamp.
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Radiance Lion Banner universally illuminates the adorned lands with the three types of wisdom and decisively rises high above them.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Jewel Flame Subtle Light:
his four practices are universal, his internal conduct is perfectly pure, and the flames of his wisdom shine outwardly; therefore, he is called "Subtle."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Sound Merit-Ocean Banner possesses the five universal sounds and is endowed with all sounds, because he expounds the profound, vast, and exalted practices of the Buddha’s pure land.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Wisdom Light-Illumination Tathāgata-Sphere,
because his six wisdoms universally illuminate the inexhaustible realm of the Buddha-Dharmadhātu;
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Jewel-Crest Flower Banner.

The seventh is Universal Mind. The jewel of wisdom adorns the crown of his mind; because he excels all things with the flowers of universal conduct and so forth, there is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Joyful Voice of Universal Awakening.

The eight perceptions are universally pervasive; their nature and characteristics are fully awakened, and their sounds all accord with the capacities of sentient beings. Thus, there are none who do not turn toward them.
This is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Pure and Exhaustless Radiance of Blessings.
The ninth is the universality of blessings: because they are universally pure, accord with reality, and are inexhaustible.
Thus, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Radiance Mark.
The tenth is the universality of marks: the mark of radiance within the mark of non-radiance, because it universally benefits sentient beings. Contemplate the perfect fusion of these six marks.
...it. △ Second, listing the ten alternative names:
Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sea-Light Moon-Great-Brightness.
Just as the ten virtues and the ten mountains all rely upon the great ocean, so too do the ten stages and the ten perfections all rely upon Buddha-wisdom. Looking into the ocean...
The moon is pure and deep; it relies upon the adornment of the land through wisdom, which is both profound and pure. Like the ocean, it is vast;
like the moon, it is luminous; hence it is so named.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Cloud-Sound Ocean-Light Immaculate Treasury preaches with a voice like the roll of thunder;
hence he is called "Cloud-Sound. His eloquence is overflowing like the radiance of the ocean.

Furthermore, just as there is light upon the sea that reaches the boundless horizon, so too does the Buddha’s wisdom manifest its function, universally pervading all in a single thought-moment, purifying afflictions without end; thus he is named [Ocean-Light Immaculate Treasury].
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalagarbha-guṇaratna-śikhara-jñānasaṃbhava has cultivated the two adornments like pure jewels;
because they are secret and loftily manifest, he is called "Śikhara" (the Crest).
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Radiance, Sovereign King of Merit, has appeared as a Dharma King;
his activities are sovereign, his two adornments are perfected, and he is the light of merit.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Suvīra-padma-śekhara was born through transformation with heroic vigor;
he was unstained by the marks of transformation and rained down the profound and wondrous Dharma, like the untying of a crest-jewel.
The Samādhi of the Universal Wisdom Cloud-Sun Banner:
the clouds of compassion and the suns of wisdom mutually support and reflect one another, responding universally throughout long kalpas, rising loftily like a banner.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajranābhi of Great Diligence possesses firm and sharp wisdom;
because he is endowed with diligence, he is called "Great. Wisdom is the root of practice, just as the navel is the cause of life.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Fragrant Flame Radiance Banner (Gandhārciḥketu) has set forth through the practice of the precepts and other virtues; this constitutes his "fragrant flame. Because his knowledge of all modes is lofty and upright, he is called the "Flame Banner."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Radiance of Profound and Beautiful Sound possesses wisdom that shines everywhere;
he is one of great brilliance who accords with reality and adapts to sentient beings, hence he is named "Profound and Beautiful Sound."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Radiance of Merit and Wisdom.
His great wisdom emits light that universally illumines the realm of the Buddha, causing the characteristics of merit and non-merit to be revealed; for this reason, he is called "Great.
△ Second, the conclusion of the brief summary to reveal the extensive.
With these as their leaders, there were as many [bodhisattvas] as there are atoms in ten Buddha-worlds.

△ Third, the perfection of the gathering of virtues, in two parts. First, praising their superior virtues individually, in two sections. The first two phrases praise them with respect to their conditions.
All these bodhisattvas in the past were together [with him] (up to: ...), collectively gathering roots of goodness and practicing the bodhisattva path.
The preceding phrase concerns their past causes and shared practice, demonstrating that there is a basis for the relationship between the principal figure and his companions.

*Vairocana* means "pervasive light. Adapting it to local linguistic conventions, it should be called "Pervasive Illumination" (*Guangming Bianzhao*). However, it carries two meanings: first, the body...

The light shines universally throughout the entire dharma-realm of empty space, even unto the paths of atoms. The light of the two wisdoms shines universally through the layered dharma-realms of the ultimate and the conventional.
Body and wisdom, subject and object, merge into a single body, perfectly luminous and uniquely radiant, endowed with boundless virtues.
Therefore, this title was established. Furthermore, *vairocana* has the meaning of "various" (*vi-*), "obscuration" (*loca*), and "exhaustion" or "entry" (*na*).
This signifies that various obscurations are exhausted and various virtues are perfected. Thus, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states:
"Śākyamuni is named Vairocana because he pervades all places; his body also pervades, not merely his light. Furthermore...
It says: "The dwelling place of that Buddha is named Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-prabhāsvara*). Thus, the land itself is also light. It further says:

"It is the place established by the perfection of constancy (*nitya-pāramitā*) and the place secured by the perfection of self (*ātma-pāramitā*); this signifies the meaning of the perfection of virtue. It also says:
The perfection of purity (*śubha-pāramitā*) is the state where the characteristics of existence are extinguished; this is the meaning of the exhaustion of hindrances.

Furthermore, it is said that the perfection of bliss (*sukha-pāramitā*) is the non-attainment of the characteristics of body and mind, and the non-perception of the characteristics of all phenomena as being either existent or non-existent; this is the meaning of realization and entry. Moreover, it is said:
From tranquil liberation up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, these are the eternally abiding dharmas of form (*rūpa*).
Therefore, it is clarified that all these are immediately the True [Dharma] and constitute the Fundamental Teacher. This scriptural evidence will be analyzed in the relevant chapter.

As for the statement "collecting roots of goodness together," this means preparing the provisions for the Path (*mārga-sambhāra*). "Cultivating the bodhisattva practices" means performing what ought to be performed. How so?
They assemble because they act as both principal and associates to one another. There are three types of principal and associates: first, those of dedication; second, those of common practice;
and third, those of suchness. All are termed "assembling together."
All arise from the ocean of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness.
The latter phrase, "arising from the ocean of virtues," clarifies that they serve as his assistants. This means that the Buddha’s virtues are boundless;

having accumulated wondrous jewels, and being filled with wisdom and concentration, they are thus called an "ocean. There are four ways in which these arise: first, from the Buddha’s own roots of goodness.

First, they are born from the ocean [of the Buddha-body], because they have already perfected the ten bodies (*daśakāya*). Second, they are born from the ocean of their original teacher, for the Buddha serves as the supreme condition;
having previously taken them under his care and bestowed the Dharma upon them, he causes their practice to reach fulfillment.

Third, they are born from the ocean of other Buddhas alongside Vairocana, because it was stated above that they gather together. Fourth, they are born from the ocean of the Buddha of the *dharmatā*, because of the aforementioned ocean of virtues.
All Buddhas share a common, equal, and single flavor; they simply cultivate in accordance with their nature, which is itself the source of birth.
They do not discriminate between self and other; thus, the Sanskrit original says: "Born from the same ocean of roots of goodness as the Buddha. Second, praising by way of the virtues of practice:
Now, a Great Being must surely honor virtue and expand their deeds. With an empty mind and a body cast aside, because they honor virtue, their progress becomes equal [to that of the Buddhas].
The fruit of Buddhahood: because its vast activities extend throughout the Dharma-realm, and because its empty mind encompasses all phenomena, it does not treat the body as external;
thus its merit flows to the limits of the future, yet because it is not a self, its virtue is difficult to name. Briefly divided, there are three parts.
First, regarding the causes, practices, and virtues of self-benefit, there are three parts. First, the perfection of the practice for one's own benefit:
all the *pāramitās* have been fully completed;

the practices of the various perfections are fulfilled, meaning that they were accumulated over eighty-four thousand *kalpas* through the six, ten, and [infinite] perfections, reaching their ultimate consummation.
Because both phenomena and principle are thus perfected, it is called "complete.
The wisdom-eye is clear and penetrating, observing the three periods of time with equal vision.

The ten eyes are clear and penetrating; their discernment is termed "wisdom," and their illuminating gaze is termed "eyes. When all obstructions and veils are exhausted, there is no object of knowledge that is not known.

It is focused; therefore, it is called "luminous penetration" (*mingche*). Among the five eyes, the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) contemplates principle (*li*); since principle has no diverse flavors, it is called "equal contemplation" (*dengguan*).
Among the ten eyes, the wisdom eye contemplates phenomena (*shi*); since there is nothing that is not seen, it is named "equal contemplation.
Thus, to see phenomena in detail is "luminosity," and to profoundly penetrate their nature is "penetration. One wishes to unify all [eyes] within a single eye.
He possesses mastery over both principle and phenomena; however, here only his wisdom is mentioned.

He is fully endowed with purity regarding all samādhis, and his profound meditative concentration (*samāpatti*) is already perfected. "Samādhi" is translated here as "equipoise" (*samādhāna*); it is the mind held in equilibrium, far removed from dullness and agitation.

Because it focuses on a single object, yet it is called "various" (*nānā*); this is because all other conditions likewise focus on that same single object. True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the essential substance of this samādhi;
as it accords with objects, its specific manifestations are as manifold as the number of sensory realms. Therefore, it is called "various. Transversally, it is indeterminate and inexhaustible;
vertically, it penetrates deeply to the boundless. Therefore, it is said to be "complete. Because the hindrances to concentration are forever extinguished...
It is called "pure. △ Second, the fulfillment of altruistic practice has three phrases, which constitute the benefit of transformation through the three wheels.
His eloquence is like the ocean, vast and inexhaustible;

his speech encompasses the four types of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), which is the wheel of the correct teaching. "Eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) refers to skillfully manifesting the profound principle, while "talent" (*pratibhā*) refers to skillfully responding to the capacities of sentient beings.
It is appropriate. When all phenomena are expounded, they are vast and boundless; when the thousand difficulties are met with specific responses, they are inexhaustible.
Thus, it is like the ocean. Furthermore, when the ocean encounters the condition of wind, great waves surge like clouds; when wisdom meets an occasion for inquiry, the waves of eloquence rise.
Since the inquirer permits boundless eloquence, that eloquence is likewise vast and inexhaustible.
Possessing the Buddha’s merits, he is dignified and worthy of reverence.

His physical actions constitute the wheel of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-cakra*), meaning his three modes of activity (*trikarma*) are without fault. His wisdom is profound and unassailable; thus, he is one who possesses the Buddha’s merits.
Therefore, his external demeanor was solemn and majestic, inspiring reverence.
He knew the faculties of sentient beings and subdued them according to what was appropriate.

His mental karma involved the wheel of reading minds, and the meaning of the faculties was fully elucidated therein. The text contains both their dispositions and inclinations; as for the phrase "according to what is appropriate," it refers to the fact that the faculties...
Regarding "ripening the raw": transformations do not miss their proper time; though vessels vary in size, the bestowal of the Dharma is never erroneous.

"Transformation" (hua) refers to teaching and transforming; that is, one should accept those who are to be accepted and accepts them. "Subduing" (fu) refers to taming and subduing; that is, one should subdue those who are to be subdued and subdues them.
Because these practices are fully carried out, one enters the True Dharma. △ Third, the stage of realizing the principle and reaching its limit also consists of three phrases.

Entering the treasury of the Dharma-realm with non-differentiated wisdom is the realization of the principle of the Dharma. This means that through great wisdom, one realizes and enters the treasury of the true Dharma-realm of equality.

According to the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, there are five treasuries: first, the Tathāgatagarbha, so called because it contains the resultant dharmas while still enmeshed in afflictions; second, the svabhāva-... [text continues]

1. The Treasury of Purity (*viśuddhigarbha*): This refers to being unstained while still within the bonds of affliction (*saṃkleśa*). 2. The Treasury of the Dharmakāya (*dharmakāyagarbha*): This refers to the state of fruition (*phalāvasthā*), serving as the locus for all enlightened qualities (*guṇa*).
3. The Treasury of the Supreme Transcendent World (*lokottarāgragarbha*): This refers to having transcended the bonds and surpassed both the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.

4. The Treasury of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātugarbha*): This refers to encompassing both cause and fruit; because it externally sustains all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*)—both defiled and pure—it is called the "Dharma-realm. Internally...

Because it contains all the inherent virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is further called a "treasury" (*garbha*). This meaning is broad and pervasive; therefore, one now enters into realization.
Regarding the statement that "wisdom is without differentiation": the treasury that is realized must be equal and free from conceptual discrimination;

only when one accords with this does wisdom itself become non-differentiated. Thus, by virtue of the aforementioned principle, the subject and object are not distinct. Furthermore, this realizing wisdom and—
The treasury of what is realized is a dark unity of a single flavor, wherein there is no distinction between object and wisdom; therefore, it is said to be "without difference.

This, moreover, has two aspects: first, because they are identical in being signless, as the sutra below states: "There is not the slightest dharma that is entered by wisdom, nor is there the slightest wisdom that enters into dharmas.
Second, because they are identical with the *dharmadhātu*, then subject and object mutually encompass one another entirely.
Therefore, it is said below: "There is no suchness outside of wisdom that could be entered by wisdom, because suchness is entirely encompassed by wisdom.

Nor is there wisdom outside of suchness that could realize suchness, because suchness is completely encompassed. If they are both of one single flavor, how could it be that wisdom is made identical to its object such that wisdom would cease to exist?
An ancient master explained: "Because the characteristics of wisdom are exhausted, [wisdom] does not exist; yet it is capable of making wisdom..."
Because the characteristics are exhausted, they are not non-existent. Were it otherwise, how could all characteristics be entirely exhausted while wisdom alone remains?
Therefore, with respect to the object, it does not obstruct the ultimate yet is constantly conventional; with respect to wisdom, it does not obstruct quiescence yet is constantly illuminating.
Thus, object and wisdom are not identical: the object does not obstruct the conventional yet is constantly ultimate; wisdom does not abandon illumination yet is constantly [quiescent].
"Quiescence" means that the object and wisdom are not distinct. Since the object is empty, the two wisdoms of existence and non-existence are simultaneously fused in quiescence and illumination;
therefore, it is said they are "without distinction. The explanation provided above accords with the truth of ultimate reality being tranquil and the state of *śamatha* (calm abiding) being still.
The movement of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the illumination [of wisdom] are mutually conforming. In works such as the *Awakening of Faith*, this is explained provisionally;

however, it does not exhaust the source, for it does not allow one to name the illumination of the Real (*tattva*). When illuminating the conventional, it is not identical to quiescence. Now, to provide the correct explanation:
in terms of verbal function, they are both the same and yet different. This is because the object cannot illuminate the wisdom, whereas wisdom possesses illumination.
To speak of "quiescence" (śānti), it is different yet identical. This is because there is no distinction between the object and the wisdom (*jñāna*).

Because they are identical, there is no [discursive] mind, for the mind is forgotten in the mutual resonance with that which is other. Because they are different, the function of illumination is not lost, for wisdom differs from wood or stone.

Therefore, when true wisdom illuminates the principle (*tattva*), the object is simply quiescent; wisdom is quiescent while constantly illuminating. If one speaks in terms of illuminating the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), then...

The subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) illuminates the realm of differentiated phenomena. If one considers the integration of the ultimate and the conventional, then as for the object, the ultimate and conventional are non-dual;

as for the wisdom, the provisional and the real function simultaneously, constituting a single flavor (*ekarasa*). Yet, it does not lose its state of quiescence (*śamatha*), for although it functions dualistically, [it remains unified].
Because it is immediately quiescent. The three contemplations and the integration of object and wisdom will be analyzed in detail below.

To realize the Buddha’s liberation that is profound and vast means to realize the dharma of liberation as fruition, which refers to mastery over activity, as described in the "Inconceivable Dharma" chapter. Regarding this—
Within a single thought-moment, there are ten kinds of activities, such as establishing all the Buddha-works of the three periods of time, as described in detail in that [text].
Because these functions are identical with reality, they are profound; because these functions are boundless, they are vast, reaching to the very limits of existence.
Therefore, it is called "realization.
Being able to follow skillful means, one enters a single stage (and so on) until, together with wisdom, one reaches the end of the future.
This is the attainment of the ultimate station; that is to say, the body of Samantabhadra pervades the six stages, yet abides in any one stage through the power of the ocean of vows.
It maintains all [stages]. Thus, the older translations state: "Abiding in one stage, it universally encompasses the merits of all stages.
The present text follows the tradition of the Western Regions (India). If it were to follow this region (China), it should say: "By means of skillful means, it enters each stage accordingly;
by the power of the ocean of vows, it sustains all stages. However, there are citations from the Sanskrit original that explain this extensively.

Regarding the variations in the expansion and contraction of the number of phrases herein, it is not necessarily required that they be so. Why is this? Translating from Sanskrit into Chinese is indeed no easy task.
If the phrasing is slightly adjusted here and there, the priority is that the essential meaning does not deviate.

However, if the internal logic cannot be made coherent, one must correct it according to the Sanskrit original. If the translator’s intent seems close to the source, one should harmonize it with previous translations. This applies when the terminology differs.
The meaning is the same; why need one cite extensively? Regarding the statement that "it is always accompanied by wisdom": this refers to the clear wisdom that exhausts the limits of the future.

This text contains two meanings. First, looking back at the preceding: although one is in a single stage (*bhūmi*) within the causal state, one upholds the merits of all stages through the power of vows, such that they are all accompanied by wisdom until the end of the future, never departing from that one stage. As it is with one stage, so it is with the remaining stages.
It is likewise so. Therefore, although the causal gate extends to the end of the future, each and every stage of the Bodhisattva does not see the time of becoming a Buddha.
Second, regarding the subsequent [stage], one enters the ocean of the Tathāgata’s fruition through the great wisdom that exhausts the future;
though there are two meanings here, the former meaning is superior. △ Second, the virtues of the fruit of supreme progress, in two parts. First:
The dharma of attaining the fruit consists in thoroughly penetrating the rare, vast, and secret realm of all Buddhas and entering the secret realm of the Buddha.
This has two meanings: first, the Buddha is himself the secret realm, because his three karmas and their constituent activities are... [incomplete source text].

Because it is measured by what remains beyond [ordinary cognition]: that is to say, it is not a physical form manifesting as form; a mani jewel cannot serve as a metaphor for its multiplicity. It is not a measure of quantity manifesting as direct perception;
even one who holds it in hand cannot fathom its summit. It is all-pervasive without being divided; unity and multiplicity do not suffice to differentiate its essence.
It is entirely the Dharmakāya; even a single hair cannot exhaust its limits. This is the mystery of this body. It is the voice of the Buddha.
