This section of text is "specific" in relation to what precedes it, because it specifically concerns entering the fruition within the general possession of qualities. In relation to what follows, it is "general," as it pertains to the fortyfold assembly.
Because it marks liberation, it is now provisionally categorized with the preceding section. This passage has two parts: first, entering the fruit by means of the cause;
through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one enters the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s qualities.

This is known through subsequent cognition (*anvaya-jñāna*). It is like seeing a phoenix soar and knowing that the great void can be traversed; or beholding a dragon leap and knowing that the vast ocean can be navigated.
By the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one confirms the Buddha’s words and knows the profundity of his merit and wisdom;
by the power of faith and understanding, one gazes upon the Buddha’s transformations and knows the vastness of his compassion. This is entry into the Tathāgata’s qualities.
The great ocean is also the fruit and virtue resulting from resolute conviction and mental retention. △ Second, the function of attaining the fruit:
one attains the gates of liberation of all Buddhas and sports with supernatural powers.
Regarding the term "gate of liberation" (*vimokṣamukha*): because the obstacles to the fruit of Buddhahood are stilled and its great activity is unimpeded, it is called "liberation.

True liberation is none other than the Tathāgata; because wisdom penetrates and enters [it], it is termed a "gate. Because the multitude each realizes and accords with it, it is called "attainment. This liberation is itself the gate:
the Buddha attains its totality, while the ocean-like assembly attains its particulars. Furthermore, regarding the Buddha's liberation...
It is liberation (*vimukti*). However, the dharmas attained by the assembly are called "gates" (*mukha*), because they serve as the means for entering that fruit.
Furthermore, these gates of liberation—the dharmas attained by the assembly—which are free from obstructions and characterized by mastery, are called "liberation.
The locus entered by wisdom is also called a "gate," because one enters the fruit through liberation; thus, liberation is also so designated.

It serves as a gate; this liberation is itself the gate. However, when the general and the specific are perfectly interfused, and cause and effect penetrate one another in a state of profound non-obstruction, only then does it constitute a true gate of liberation.

Therefore, what follows may praise the virtues of the Buddha-fruit, or praise the practices of the cause, or refer to what is attained by devas and others, for the purpose of casting light upon and revealing [the truth].
Next, "wandering" refers to the playful exercise of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), which correctly clarifies the aspect of entering [the state]. Wandering...

"Playful" means entering and exiting with sovereign ease. "Supernormal power" (abhijñā) means being unfathomable and unobstructed. In terms of contemplating the mind, the non-obstruction between mind and objects is called liberation.
Because one enters this principle, it is termed a "gate. If one treats the gate as a mere gate, it cannot serve as a passage.
The gate is itself suchness; what, then, would there be to pass through? True entry is the simultaneous vanishing of both [subject and object]; this is the reality.
The gate is entered. One who enters in this manner finds that fundamental awakening (benjue) is profoundly still, reaching the ocean of the ultimate fruit.
Since the true is not external to the delusory, cause and effect are perfectly interfused; since mind and object are boundless, liberation is limitless.

△ Third, specifically clarifying the attainment of the Dharma and the praise of the Buddha. Within the assembly of forty groups, each first attains the Dharma through prose (chángxíng), which is the introduction provided by the scribe of the sutra.

The subsequent verses of praise were those recited at that time; however, because the assembly’s verses of praise were all composed simultaneously, they have been arranged in their present order for the sake of the literary structure.
Furthermore, each individual obtains one [verse] to manifest that the Buddha’s virtues are inexhaustible.
Ascending from the specific to the general, because no one among the multitude can reach its limit, Haihui says:
"The realm of the Tathāgata is boundless; each perceives it according to their own liberation. Yet, because the Buddha is inexhaustible, Samantabhadra attains ten manifestations and so forth.

Within the text, there are first three distinct categories for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). First, there are three for the devas. First, within the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are five; first, [the deva] Vaśavartin.
The Celestial King Dīrghāyus attained the Dharma.

First, he attained the liberation of the Dharmakāya, namely, the liberation door of the power of the skillful means of tranquility, [extending] from the Great Maheśvara Heavenly King of the Sublime Flame Ocean... up to [the aforementioned].

The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the space-realm (*ākāśadhātu*) are that which is pervaded. "Space" refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). The term "Dharma-realm" encompasses both the phenomenal and the noumenal:

it means that it not only pervades empty space, but also pervades all phenomena within it—such as form and mind—as well as the principle of reality that accords with the truth of both emptiness and existence.
Furthermore, while speaking merely of "space" implies a single layer of pervasion, speaking of the "Dharma-realm" implies a manifold, infinitely layered pervasion.
All are pervasive. Why is this? It is because the space-element accommodates the location of each and every atom, as well as those material things;
since everything within each atom accords with the Truth, there are therein infinitely many oceans of lands, all of which are completely filled by the great functions of the Buddha-body.
Therefore, the following verse says it is "without end. As for the term "quiescence" (*śānti*), it refers to the essence. It has two meanings:
first, it clarifies that the aforementioned great function is devoid of the characteristics of functioning, such that it does not obstruct constant quiescence;

second, because this wisdom-function is identical to quiescence and thus coextensive with the Truth, each individual function pervades all places. As for the term "expedient means" (*upāya*), it refers to the function.
There are also two meanings. First, it clarifies that the aforementioned quiescence possesses no characteristic of quiescence, and thus does not obstruct great function.

Second, internally it is identical to true nature without obstruction, while externally it responds to the various capacities of sentient beings; hence it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*). Since quiescence and function are unimpeded, it is termed "power" (*bala*).
△ Second, the liberation of the body of wisdom.
The Celestial King Light of Sovereign Renown attained the liberation door of universally observing all phenomena with complete mastery.
This has three meanings: first, by means of the universal eye, there is nothing among all phenomena that cannot be observed; second, observing one [phenomenon]...
All phenomena do not destroy facts while preserving principle. Third, within a single phenomenon, one perceives all things without obstruction;
these are both termed "mastery. △ Third, liberation through self-characteristics.
The Heavenly King Pure Merit-Eye (up to) the Liberation Gate of Effortless Practice Without Coming or Going also has two meanings.
First, knowing non-arising and so forth, one internally realizes the True Principle. Second, through effortless practice, one externally responds to the various capacities of sentient beings.
Now, regarding non-arising and so forth—the essence of the Buddha-dharma—there are many ways of explaining it; I shall briefly set forth one or two.
First, the individual explanation: non-arising and non-ceasing are applied to the object (*viṣaya*), while non-coming and non-going are applied to the activity (*caryā*).

Regarding the initial point of non-arising and non-ceasing, there are briefly five meanings: 1. With respect to the *parikalpita* (imagined nature): because this is a false attachment, there is no dharma that can arise or cease.

Furthermore, what exists as appearance (*yathābhāsa*) is precisely non-existent in principle (*tathātva*); therefore, it does not arise. What is non-existent in principle is precisely existent as appearance; therefore, it does not cease.
Neither extinguished nor arising—this is one dharma. Furthermore, because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) cannot be found when sought, it does not arise;
because it can manifest the nature of signlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇatā*), it is not extinguished. That which is not extinguished is precisely that which does not arise; this too is one dharma.

Second, with respect to the dependent origination nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*): it means that dharmas lack intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*) and arise by depending on conditions. Arising is non-arising; since they are fundamentally...
Because they have arisen, there is nothing that can be extinguished. Furthermore, because dependent origination lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it does not arise;
because it is an un-natured dependent origination, it does not cease. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Because the principle of emptiness exists, all phenomena are established.

Therefore, non-arising is itself non-ceasing, and non-ceasing is itself non-arising; they are one and the same thing. Moreover, by analyzing conditions, since there is no arising, [there is no cessation].
Arising can manifest the nature of non-arising; therefore, it does not cease. Third, with respect to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*):

because it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it lacks the characteristics of arising and ceasing. Furthermore, because it is not an object of the deluded mind, it does not arise. It is that which is realized by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

Therefore, it is not extinguished. Furthermore, because its essence does not undergo transition or change, it is not produced. Because it causes phenomena to arise in accordance with conditions, it is not extinguished. Non-extinction is itself non-production; they are one and the same thing.

Fourthly, regarding the three natures (trisvabhāva) as being interpenetrated and fused within a single phenomenon: from the perspective of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it is not produced;

from the perspective of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it is not extinguished; and from the perspective of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is likewise neither produced nor extinguished.
It is neither born nor extinguished, because it conforms to the three natures of non-substantiality (*tri-niḥsvabhāva*). It is neither non-born nor non-extinguished;
thus these four propositions are unified into a single whole, perfectly interfused and unimpeded, which can be perceived through sudden contemplation. Second, as for "neither coming nor going":

In terms of practice, this refers to right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). It turns its back on deluded attachments and thus does not "go"; it moves toward the realization of ultimate truth and thus does not "come.

Furthermore, it does not "go" because it arises from the essence to manifest its function; it does not "come" because it appears before sentient beings in accordance with their capacities. Moreover, it does not "go" as it proceeds to respond to the various needs of all beings;
it does not "come" as it constantly returns to quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*). This "not coming" is precisely "not going"; they are non-dual.
It is of a single flavor. By means of this great wisdom, one responds to conditions without thought, like a *maṇi* jewel or a celestial drum that accomplishes tasks without volition;
therefore, it is called "effortless practice" (*anābhoga-caryā*). II. General Explanation: "Neither arising nor ceasing" may also be understood in terms of practice;
"neither coming nor going" may also be understood in terms of the objective realm. That is to say, when deluded thoughts are stilled, it is like empty space.

Emptiness: what arises and what ceases? Furthermore, although great function arises, one perceives that the mind has no arising; when the function subsides, it returns to stillness, realizing fundamentally that there is no cessation.
Moreover, constantly extolling the true principle, with tranquil illumination dwelling within the breast—within this mind, what arising or ceasing could there be?
To explain "no coming or going" in terms of objects: it is like flowers in the sky, which have nothing that can come or go. Furthermore, conditions meet...
It comes, yet there is nowhere from which it comes; therefore, there is no coming. Conditions expire and it departs, yet there is nowhere to which it goes;
therefore, there is no going. Furthermore, all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*); how could suchness come or go? △ Third, the successive explanation: Moreover, why is there no arising or ceasing?
Because there is no coming or going. Why is there no coming or going? Because there is no arising or ceasing. Furthermore, since...
Without coming or going, there is neither identity nor difference; without arising or ceasing, there is neither annihilation nor permanence.
When wisdom accords with this principle, it is effortless (*anābhoga*); because it is not obstructed by arising and so forth, it is called "activity. This, then, is the arising of non-arising.
The non-arising of arising is because it is without effort (*anābhoga*); it is eternally quiescent. Because it functions, it is eternally active.

Quiescence and function are non-dual; this is liberation from effort. This constitutes the essential meaning of the True Dharma; its flavor is inexhaustible, and one should not weary of its detailed exposition.
△ Fourth, the liberation through the contemplation of meaning.
The liberation door of the ocean of wisdom regarding the true reality of all phenomena, belonging to the Great Wisdom Heavenly King Priyadarśana (up to).
The term "manifestly seeing" (*pratyakṣa*) is used to distinguish it from inferential knowledge (*anumāna*). Regarding the term "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), there are briefly three meanings:
first, observing phenomena with wisdom; because phenomena are not false, the sutra below states: "Observing conditioned phenomena as they truly are. Second...
Observing the reality of principle through wisdom—that which is called "signlessness" (animitta)—is such that signlessness is itself non-sign; this is termed the "true mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Third, by means of unimpeded knowledge, one knows the reality of non-duality. Because it exhausts reality, it is profound; because it reaches the ultimate limit, it is vast.
It is called the ocean of wisdom and is not bound by signs; this is the gate of liberation. Fifth, compassion removes the obstacles to liberation.
From the Sovereign Heavenly King Immovable Light (*Acalaprabha*) up to the Gate of Liberation through the Samādhi of Great Skillful Means:
to be free from all perils and fears is called "peace" (*kṣema*); for body and mind to be at ease and joyful is called "bliss" (*sukha*).

Because one obtains the two benefits upon seeing the Buddha, it is "peace and bliss. Because afflictions do not arise, one attains "samādhi. Because the virtues of the Buddha are inconceivable, there is "bliss and samādhi."
This is a great skillful means. △ Sixth, liberation from the hindrance of compassion:
The Celestial King Sublime Adornment Eye attained the liberation door of causing the observation of quiescent dharmas to extinguish all darkness of delusion and fear.
Sentient beings, due to ignorance, create karma; because they create karma, they undergo suffering. Because of darkness, they do not see the future;

failing to see the future, they fall headlong into calamity—there is nothing more terrifying than this ultimate folly. If one contemplates original quiescence, then the characteristic of ignorance is fundamentally empty.
If one does not even perform good deeds, how could one ever commit evil? △ Seventh: Liberation from Karmic Obstructions.
From the "Dharma-door of the Liberation through the Non-arising of the Karma of Thought regarding All Existences" of the Heavenly King Radiance of Skillful Contemplation, to:
The Buddha manifests throughout the ten directions; this is a boundless realm. Realizing its nature of non-reliance is called "skillful entry.
Since one does not even rely upon the Buddha, how could one produce the thought of karma? △ Eighth: The Liberation of Signlessness.
The liberation door of the Heavenly King Great Wisdom Delight (up to) Immovability and Non-reliance:

although his body responds to the ten directions, he is tranquil and unmoving; his wisdom proclaims all dharmas as quiescent and without reliance, not grasping at marks, for he is immovable like suchness. Ninth is the liberation of names and marks.
The Celestial King Banner of Universal Sound Adornment attains the liberation door of manifesting light by entering the Buddha’s realm of tranquility.

The Buddha’s wisdom accords with suchness; this is called "entering the realm of stillness. Because it is tranquil yet capable of responding, its body and wisdom radiate light throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, it causes sentient beings to enter the signless (*animitta*); thus it is "still" (*śānta*). Because it is nameless, it is "tranquil" (*śānti*). 10. Capable of Benefiting Oneself.
He is liberated. The liberation door for the celestial king *Yaśaḥprabhasupratividdha* (Up to: *Vipulaviṣaya*) takes that [realm] as its object.
The name of this celestial king is slightly reversed from the preceding list; the former name was *Supratividdhayaśaḥprabha*. Above.

In the following passages, there are many such instances. Sometimes the meaning remains the same while the terminology differs; sometimes there are discrepancies between detailed and abbreviated versions. These are all due to the translators' failure to properly comprehend the texts. Regarding the name of the *dharmaparyāya*, "Abiding":
as for "one's own [nature] and so forth," this refers to being free from the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper, which is a gateway to liberation that benefits both oneself and others.

"The state of self-awakening" refers precisely to being free from the distinction between the subject of cognition and the object of cognition; it is the constant, noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

It is manifested before one. As for the phrase "by means of the boundless," etc., it means that by taking the boundless *dharmadhātu* as an object of focus, one delivers boundless sentient beings and attains vast *bodhi*.
△ Second, the verse praise of the Buddha has two parts. First, manifesting the manner of the discourse.
At that time, the Celestial King Jvālāmbudhi, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic authority, spoke these verses.
[Jvālāmbudhi] was the foremost among the assembly; relying upon the Buddha’s power, he expressed his thoughts for the sake of the multitude. As the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Receiving the power of the Buddha" manifests the absence of self-conceit (*asmimāna*). "Universally observing the ten directions" demonstrates the absence of partiality.

Now, observing one's own assembly, there is only a slight difference in terms of being comprehensive or limited. Furthermore, there are four types of verses (*gāthā*) in total: the first is called the *anustubh* verse;
this does not depend on whether it is in prose or verse, but rather, any sequence of syllables that completes thirty-two syllables constitutes a single verse.
The second is called *gāthā*, which here is translated as "recited verse" (*fèngsòng*). It is also termed "non-prose verse" (*bùsòng sòng*), because it is not in prose;
or it is termed "direct verse" (*zhísòng*), meaning that the Dharma is taught by means of stanzas. The third is called *geya*, which here is translated as "corresponding verse" (*yìngsòng*).
The fourth is called *udāna*, which here is translated as "collected gift verse" (*jíshī sòng*); this means that many meanings are condensed into few words and given to others for recitation.

Because it is maintained. What follows here is precisely in the form of *gāthā* verses; all subsequent sections should be understood accordingly. For what purpose does the Sūtra frequently establish verses?
Briefly, there are eight reasons: first, because few words can encompass many meanings; second, because those who offer praise mostly do so in verse;
third, for the sake of restating [the teaching] for those of dull faculties; fourth, for the sake of future generations; fifth...

This is because it accords with their inclinations and preferences; secondly, because it is easy to uphold and practice; thirdly, because it further clarifies what was previously explained; fourthly, because it contains matters not yet discussed in the prose (*gadya*).
Now, this [verse section] primarily consists of the first two meanings, while also incorporating the fifth and sixth. Regarding the second part, the actual exposition:

the ten verses follow a specific sequence, each concluding with a distinct Dharma-gate (*dharma-paryāya*). The compilers extracted these as the prose (*gadya*), rather than using them to precede the verses.

However, within this context, there are many differences between the prose (*gadya*) and the verse (*śloka*). Specifically, while the number of characters in the verse is fixed, those in the prose vary;
furthermore, the prose concerns the Dharma attained by Deva, whereas the verse is an eulogy of the Buddha—this is certain.
If one compares the two texts against each other, they may differ in terms of cause and effect, or distinguish between essence and function, or [be mutually...]

The characteristics and shadows [of the two texts] are mutually abbreviated; sometimes the difficult and the easy are presented alternately, sometimes the dharma and the analogy differ, and sometimes the subject and the object are raised in turn.
Therefore, the transmitter skillfully reconciles them so that the two texts reflect one another, making the meaning easy to understand. This concludes the two sections on the formal exposition.
"The Buddha-body pervades all great assemblies" (up to) "appearing for the sake of saving the world.

These first two lines clarify that the aforementioned pervasion of the dharma-realm and empty space is simultaneously the pervasion of the Buddha-body; thus, all ten bodies are omnipresent and inexhaustible.
This inexhaustibility is twofold: first, the manifestation is inexhaustible, like clouds emerging from a high mountain; second, [the capacity to manifest is inexhaustible].

It is not a phenomenon subject to cessation; it is eternally abiding like space. The second phrase refers to its quiescence, because, being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it cannot be grasped as being identical, different, both, or neither, and so forth.
The final phrase concerns the skillful means (*upāya*) of combining these two to form a single power.
Since this verse describes the speaker’s own dharma, the name of the deity is not appended; the same principle applies to all subsequent cases.
"The Tathāgata, the Dharma-King, appears in the world" (up to) "this mastery is what is realized.
This first phrase refers to supreme mastery, for the Buddha is the Dharma-King because he possesses mastery over the Dharma. The second phrase refers to contemplation.
The third phrase is "universal" (pu). The final phrase concludes the teaching (jiefa), as it pertains to speaking it for others.
However, since the meaning of its concluding name is identical to that of the dharma-gate (dharmaparyāya), I fear it would be too prolix to correlate them; others should all follow this pattern.
"The Buddha’s inconceivable freedom from conceptual discrimination" (up to) "thus the pure eye is able to perceive.
The first phrase refers to effortlessness (*anābhoga*). "Inconceivable" is the thesis; "freedom from conceptual discrimination" is the explanation.

The second phrase means that the characteristics of non-arising and so forth are identical to arising and so forth. "Non-" has the sense of "not. The third phrase refers to practice. [This concludes] the long prose section.
In brief, one must first know that phenomena are unborn (*anutpāda*) before one can achieve effortlessness (*anābhoga*);

likewise, according to the verse, one must be free from conceptual discrimination (*nirvikalpa*) before one can perceive the non-arising of phenomena. Since internal realization and external application are simultaneous, the two texts appear in different sequences.
"The Tathāgata’s wisdom is boundless" (up to) "Great Wisdom enters this depth and dwells therein.
The first phrase clarifies its vastness; the second phrase clarifies its depth—this is the aforementioned ocean of wisdom.
Because the third phrase refers to personally seeing the reality of phenomena, it enables sentient beings not to become confused regarding phenomena and their underlying principles.
"The inconceivable merit of the Tathāgata" (up to) "is seen by the Akṣobhya Īśvara-deva.
The first phrase refers to the meditative concentration of skillful means (*upāya-samādhi*). The following two phrases refer to the bestowing of peace and happiness.
Sentient beings are constantly deluded and obscured by the darkness of ignorance...

(up to) "The One with the Wondrous Eye can know this expedient means. The first phrase refers to the aforementioned darkness of ignorance; that is to say, they are long lost in illusory objects, which perpetually shroud the true mind.

The second phrase causes them to contemplate stillness. The third phrase indicates that by extinguishing ignorance through its cause, one attains the blazing *sambodhi*. This "clarity" (*ming*) is the aforementioned [wisdom].
The meaning of cessation.
From "The Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous form-body" up to "observed by the gods of Good Contemplation":
the first two phrases refer to skillfully entering the boundless realm. This "boundless realm" is precisely the locus where one should abide. There is nothing [else].

This refers to goodness. Regarding the second phrase, "having no nature," it means responding as soon as there is an invocation. Regarding "having no basis," it means that thought and recollection are quiescent.
By means of this, one can cause sentient beings not to create karma.
"The Tathāgata’s voice is without limit or obstruction" [up to] "this liberation of the Deva of Joyful Wisdom.
The first two phrases refer to universally proceeding throughout the ten directions to preach the Dharma; the subsequent phrase refers to being unmoving and without dependence.
"O Lord of Gods and Humans, who has attained tranquil liberation, you behold this banner of adornment of the unimpeded Dharma.
The first phrase refers to entering the realm of tranquility; the following two phrases refer to the universal manifestation of light.
The Buddha, throughout an ocean of boundless great kalpas, awakened to this Dharma in the Heaven of Radiant Fame (*Nāma-ābhā-deva*).
The first eleven characters constitute the "boundless realm," which serves as the object of focus for seeking bodhi; it is precisely the locus of his own awakening.

The second phrase: Having taken that object as a condition, one necessarily gives rise to universal transformation; this was merely mentioned briefly in the preceding text. △ Second, the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala) has two parts.
First, the prose section on attaining the dharma.
Furthermore, from the Heavenly King Light Banner of Delightful Dharmas (up to) the liberation gate of preaching the Dharma to sever doubt:

"Universally observing [the faculties]" and so forth means that this is the bestowing of Dharma according to the faculties. It clarifies that preaching the Dharma without knowing the faculties results in no fruit; herein one attains liberation from such obstructions.

By severing doubt, faith is produced, for this is the fruit of preaching the Dharma. That is to say, one observes the capacity [of the recipient] and recognizes their affliction, acting in accordance with it.
The Root Preaches the Dharma; because there is no error regarding the medicine and the disease, doubt is removed and illness is healed.
The Celestial King Ocean of Pure Adornments attained the liberation door of causing all to see the Buddha according to their recollection.
Regarding the phrase "according to recollection," there are briefly two meanings: first, according to which Buddha one recollects, it corresponds to that name;
second, according to the depth of the recollection, one perceives the Buddha as either coarse or sublime, whereby one attains liberation in this very body.
From the Heavenly King Supreme Radiance of Wisdom (up to) the Liberation Gate of the Adorned Body Free from Dependence.
That which is the equality of the *dharmatā* is of a single flavor. To be "without dependence" is to be free from subject and object.
To have an "adorned body" is to be adorned by the realization of truth; because it is non-adornment, although it manifests in the world, it remains identical to the *dharmatā*.
Not relying on any forms of existence, one attains liberation from dependence upon existence.
This is the liberation door of the Heavenly King Sovereign Wisdom Banner, who establishes an inconceivable ocean of adornments.
To know the worldly dharmas means to know that within the world of sentient beings, mental factors differ from one another;

having known this, one manifests supernatural powers and preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and thus it is called "establishment. To establish [beings] swiftly in a single thought-moment is beyond the capacity for conceptualization by non-humans, devas, or outsiders;
by means of this, one adorns the ocean-like teaching of the Tathāgata. Through this, one attains [mastery over] the obstacle of dullness regarding the establishment of the teachings.
This is liberation.
From the Joyful Tranquility Heavenly King up to the "Unobstructed Liberation Gate of the Inconceivable Buddha-field.

Regarding the phrase "a single hair," etc., this refers to the power of the inconceivable liberation as described in the verse. There are two meanings of "unobstructed": first, [the unobstructed nature of the object]; second, [the unobstructed nature of the subject].
Considering only what is manifested, there are many lands within a single hair, yet they do not obstruct one another. Regarding both the subject and the object:
the single hair does not become large, while the many lands do not become small; thus, the one and the many, as well as their dimensions, are all without obstruction.
Furthermore, because they lack the characteristics of being large or small, this [wisdom] attains liberation from the obstacle of grasping.
The Celestial King Universal Wisdom-Eye attained the liberation door of entering the universal gate to observe the dharma-realm.
Because one gate encompasses all gates, it is called the "universal gate" (*samantamukha*); for within each individual gate, the entire dharma-realm is fully contained.
Within that state, he observes the dharma-realm with profound wisdom and attains realization; thus, it is called "entering. This, in accordance with...
Among these signs, one attains liberation through the gate of liberation known as "The Constant Manifestation Throughout Boundless Kalpas of the Heavenly King Who Delights in Bestowing Wisdom.
Sentient beings are boundless and their faculties vary; thus, he manifests various forms and preaches the Dharma in diverse ways. Once their faculties have matured...
Because it is unceasing, it manifests perpetually throughout kalpas. This constitutes liberation from the obstacle of not being born through transformation amidst diverse sufferings.
The Celestial King Radiance of the Seeds of Goodness and Wisdom enters the liberation door of inconceivable dharmas.

This means that by contemplating phenomena, one enters into principle; since this principle transcends the realm of the emotions, it is called "inconceivable. Through this, one attains liberation from all karmic retributions.
The Celestial King Stainless Tranquil Radiance attained the liberation door of demonstrating the Dharma of the essential exit for all sentient beings.
The Dharma gates are boundless. Because those who emerge from them possess ten thousand varieties of faculties, the means of emergence are inconceivable.

This is the liberation gate of the Celestial King Vast Pure Light (Mahāviśuddhaprabha), who, by manifesting through transformation, leads sentient beings to enter the Buddha-dharma and attain liberation from attachment to signs.
Through various skillful means, according to what is appropriate for each, one ultimately achieves the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñā-jñāna), which is called "entering the Buddha-dharma.
Because it manifests through great compassion and rains [benefits] equally upon all, this allows those who do not desire to benefit living beings to attain liberation.

While the previous section spoke of the "essential departure" to leave behind delusory suffering, the present section speaks of "entering the Dharma" to attain true bliss. △ Second, the verses in praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the Deva King Lovely Light Banner of the Dharma (Priyadharmābhāsaketu-rāja),
[addressing] the three classes of devas within his own assembly— since the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) are not included among those addressed— spoke these verses in ten successive stanzas,
each corresponding to the prose section.
"The realm of all Buddhas is inconceivable" (up to) "the vast intention is inexhaustible.
The first two phrases refer to the realm that is the object of doubt. The term "realm" (*viṣaya*) generally refers to the scope or the object of observation.

"Universally causing [beings] to do so" means teaching according to their faculties. "Giving rise to faith and understanding" means severing doubt; it is to believe in the Buddha’s great function within its proper scope.
Because it is difficult to fathom, one severs doubts regarding the Buddha and gives rise to correct understanding.
By believing in the realm perceived by the Buddha, one severs doubts regarding the Dharma and likewise gives rise to correct understanding.

This means that if there is doubt as to whether cause and effect exist and are not true emptiness, or whether because they are empty there is no cause and effect—now it is clarified that it is precisely through true emptiness that cause and effect can be established.
Because cause and effect are established, this is indeed the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The fourth phrase explains the term "all.
Because the Buddha takes the welfare of sentient beings as his intention, he encompasses all; therefore, he is vast and inexhaustible.
If there are sentient beings capable of receiving the Dharma, [the text] up to "the Heavenly King Sea of Adornment" views them in this way:
the first phrase causes them to recollect, while the subsequent two phrases cause them to see the Buddha.
The nature of all phenomena has no basis; this meaning is what superior wisdom can observe.
The first phrase refers to the equality of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), which is without dependence. The following two phrases refer to the adornment of the body;
that is, because one takes the nature of phenomena as an adornment, there is no place of dependence.
"According to the desires of the minds of all sentient beings" (up to) "this ocean of liberation of the King of Wisdom Banners.
The first phrase refers to the thorough understanding of all worlds; the following two phrases refer to the inconceivable ocean of adornments established in a single thought-moment.
"All the lands of the past... [up to] ...who can eloquently proclaim the delight in tranquility.
These first two lines refer to the manifestation of lands within a single pore. As stated above regarding "inconceivable Buddha-lands," these are characterized solely by their vast horizontal extent.
Now, to speak of the "past" means to exhaustively traverse the prior limit; that all these are manifested is like images appearing in a mirror.

The next phrase refers to being unobstructed, allowing those who are ready to be saved to see them—this is the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). When observed by relying on the Buddha’s mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), it is seen that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternally thus.
The inexhaustible ocean of all dharma-gates—up to the point where "the eye of wisdom can clarify these skillful means.
The first two phrases refer to the Universal Gate; the next phrase refers to the Dharma-realm; the final phrase carries the meaning of both "entering" and "attaining."
"From all the lands throughout the ten directions... to the realm of the Wisdom-Swirl of Delight.
The first two phrases refer to the various manifestations for the sake of all sentient beings. The subsequent phrase refers to its constant presence throughout boundless eons;
that is to say, although it appears or remains hidden according to the capacities of those to be trained, the Buddha neither comes nor goes, and thus it is eternally present.
"The Buddha contemplates the phenomena of the world as like light and shadow" (up to) "those with virtuous seeds and contemplative thought can perceive this.
The first line refers to contemplating all worlds; the following two lines refer to entering the inconceivable Dharma.

If discussed from the perspective of principle (*li*), "profound" (*shen*) refers to that which is profoundly non-existent; yet here, without destroying phenomena, one immediately realizes principle, and thus it is called "profoundly deep" (*shen-shen*).
To fully encompass principle to form phenomena is termed the "mysterious and abstruse" (*you-ao*). When these two aforementioned dharmas are combined, they are eternally quiescent.
This explains the meaning above. Because all phenomena are inherently quiescent, they cannot be conceived through either principle or phenomena.
The Buddha thoroughly understands all realms [of experience], up to this Heaven of Quiescence (*śāntadeva*), which is capable of awakening into and entering [this state].
The first two lines indicate all sentient beings; the next line reveals the essential Dharma.
The World-Honored One constantly [teaches] with great compassion (up to) the Pure Radiance Heaven being able to expound it.
The first two phrases refer to observing the responsive and transformational sentient beings; the next phrase causes them to enter the Buddha-dharma.
△ Third, the three dhyāna heavens, part two: first, the prose section on attaining the Dharma.

Furthermore, from the Celestial King Pure Wisdom and Renown (*Vimalakīrti*) up to the Gate of Liberation through the Expedient Means of the Path of Liberation (*vimokṣamārgopāya-vimokṣamukha*), that which is quiescent yet universally manifest is called "expedient means" (*upāya*); that which is taught is the "path" (*mārga*). This is because by means of teaching, one enters the ocean of the Buddha’s liberation.
This constitutes liberation from the obstructions regarding essence and function. Furthermore, the term "expedient means" also generally applies to entering into liberation.
This is the skillful means for liberation.
Regarding the "Liberation Gate of the Universal Manifestation Like Light and Shadow" of the Most Victorious Vision Heavenly King:
the phrase "in accordance with all" refers to those who are unable to manifest universally and thus do not attain liberation. The term "light and shadow" is used as an abbreviation.
There are two interpretations. The first holds that light produces a shadow; while the shadow resembles the substance [the object], it does not resemble the light.

When forms manifest based on wisdom, those forms conform to the inclinations of sentient beings rather than to one's own wisdom. Since they conform to these inclinations, they should be called "Universal Manifestation.

The second is like the moon in water, which is also termed a "light-shadow" (chāyā-pratibimba). This means that the Buddha-moon does not come [to the water], yet its reflection appears in the water of the mind; such reflections are manifold.
It resembles the moon; it resembles water only slightly. This is because when water moves, its light flows and surges; when water is turbid, it resembles the dark orb of the moon facing a pond.
If the water is still and clear, it is like a bright, perfect jade disk. This [comparison] also follows the inclinations of oneself and others.

This was spoken in accordance with what the celestial hosts of the Heaven of the Great Lord (Mahābrahmā) delight in; yet, as for the verses concerning the Buddha, there is nothing to which he does not respond.
The Celestial King Śāntaguṇa attained the liberation door of the great skillful means that universally adorns and purifies all Buddha-realms.
There are two aspects to the Buddha-realm: first, suchness and the dharma-nature, which is the realm realized by the Buddhas; second, the lands of the ten directions.

This is the Buddha’s realm of transformation. There are also two aspects to its adornment and purification: when one is free from signs and ceases delusion, the adornment is like the [ultimate] realm;

when one dedicates the myriad practices, the adornment is the realm of transformation. These two are unimpeded; this is the great skillful means. This constitutes the "skillful adornment within the non-existent."
They attain liberation.
The Heavenly King Sumerusvara attained the liberation door of following all sentient beings as they eternally circulate through the ocean of birth and death.
This is because his great compassion is profound and deep; thus he enters into birth and death according to them. Since sentient beings are boundless, he eternally circulates [with them].
This is to provide guidance. Herein, one attains liberation from the obstacle of abandoning sentient beings due to a lack of great compassion.
The Celestial King Pure Mindfulness-Eye attained the liberation door of recollecting the Tathāgata’s practice of taming sentient beings.

The Buddha disciplines sentient beings—sometimes through subduing, sometimes through gathering, and sometimes by employing both methods. Although his compassionate vows manifest through many doors, they all cause beings to advance toward the unsurpassed path.
If one recollects this, one will naturally undergo transformation and not be hindered by provisional means.
This constitutes a hindrance of forgetfulness regarding the supreme object of focus; from this, one attains liberation.
The Celestial King Universal Radiance Delightful to Behold attained the liberation door of the ocean of the *samantamukha-dhāraṇī* that flows forth therefrom.
Because the Buddha, by means of the *dhāraṇī* that accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), encompasses all *dhāraṇīs*, it is called "Universal Door" (*samantamukha*).
Furthermore, because it can flow forth inexhaustibly, it is termed an "ocean. This [liberation] brings about the understanding of the obstacle of delusive loss regarding hearing and reflection.
Liberation. The World-Honored Lord of Sovereignty attained the liberation door of "enabling sentient beings to encounter the Buddha and give rise to the treasury of faith.
This means that since a Buddha’s appearance is difficult to encounter, he leads them so they may meet him; since the arising of faith is difficult, he exhorts them so it may arise. Faith contains...
It is called a "treasury" (kośa) because it contains manifold virtues. As the subsequent sutra states: "Faith is the foremost wealth among all treasures.
This refers to attaining liberation from the obstacles of envy and false views.
The Celestial King Sovereign of Radiant Flames (up to) the Gate of Liberation through Hearing the Dharma with Faith and Joy.
The former causes one to have faith in the Buddha; this causes one to have faith in the Dharma. Looking up in reliance, one has faith;

understanding and comprehending, one rejoices. With faith, one can enter; with joy, one practices. Thereby one attains liberation, which is called "departure. This is for the sake of sentient beings obscured by delusion.
Obstructing the path to renunciation, yet attaining liberation,
the Deva King of the Transformation of Delighting in Contemplating Dharmas (up to) the liberation gate of being as boundless and inexhaustible as space.
That is to say: the realm of sentient beings, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the realm of discipline (*vinayadhātu*), and the realm of space are all boundless and inexhaustible.
Through the realm of skillful means, the bodhisattva’s compassion and wisdom reveal the realm of phenomena, practice within the realm of discipline, and equalize them with the realm of space;
thus, they attain liberation from all finite limitations and obstructions.
The Celestial King Banner of Transformation attained the liberation door of the wisdom of universal compassion that observes the immeasurable afflictions of sentient beings.
Through compassion, he feels pity; through wisdom, he observes. Having observed their afflictions and known their diseases and behaviors, he transforms them to deliver them.
This is liberation from the obstacles of lacking compassion and lacking skillful means. △ Second, the verse summary:
Praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the Celestial King *Viśuddhamati-yaśas* (up to) spoke in verse. There are eleven verses;
the first ten follow the sequence as in the preceding prose. Among the names listed according to the Sanskrit manuscript, this prose...

The eleventh day of the practice session: there is the celestial king named Star-Constellation-Sound-Miraculous-Adornment. Regarding the term "Miraculous Sound" mentioned below, it is abbreviated here as he has not yet returned [to his seat].
He who thoroughly understands the unimpeded nature of phenomena (until: causing all beings to together return to the ocean of liberation).

The first two phrases indicate that this is the skillful means of thorough realization, manifested in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). The latter two phrases state that this is itself the Path;
they speak of inconceivable liberation, causing all beings to return to it together.
"The Tathāgata dwells in the world without dependence" (up to) "this is the gateway entered by King Victorious Vision.
The first two lines clarify that light and shadows appear everywhere; because there is no dependence, they are like reflections. The third line establishes the meaning of the preceding two:
because there is no arising, they are like reflections that have no basis. [The text] briefly does not explain how they accord with the inclinations of the devas.
"Practicing skillful means for an ocean of immeasurable eons" [up to] "is what the deity Śāntaguṇa has realized.

The first phrase indicates the practice of skillful means over immeasurable eons, while simultaneously revealing its great significance. The following two phrases correctly clarify how these skillful means adorn the Buddha’s realm.
"Sentient beings are shrouded and obstructed by ignorance" (up to) "this liberation of Sumeru-sound.

The first two phrases refer to sentient beings perpetually wandering in saṃsāra; that is, blinded by ignorance, they obscure their inherently pure mind, create karma, and receive bodies, thereby dwelling eternally within birth and death.
The subsequent phrase refers to manifesting [the path] in accordance with them.
The unsurpassed path practiced by all Buddhas—up to—can be fully understood through the clear observation of the pure eye.
This general verse praises the Buddha’s conduct in taming sentient beings: the first line is lofty, the second is profound, and the last is vast.
The Tathāgata constantly employs the gateway of *dhāraṇī* (up to the point where it says) "Universal Radiance Heavenly King"—this is what can enter.
The first two phrases refer to the *Samantamukha-dhāraṇī*. The subsequent phrase refers to that which flows forth from it. Regarding "demonstrating and instructing":

it demonstrates what is wholesome and unwholesome, and instructs one to practice accordingly. Because it accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) without partiality, though it appears partial [to specific teachings], it is inexhaustible.
The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely difficult to encounter; this is what has been attained by this Sovereign Deva. The first two phrases refer to encountering the Buddha;
the subsequent phrase refers to giving rise to the treasury of faith. Without faith, the Buddha is difficult to encounter; it is only through the Buddha that true faith can be produced.
Having encountered the Buddha and given rise to faith, these two mutually reinforce one another. How could one not rejoice in this present singular encounter?
Faith. [The Buddha taught that] "the nature of all dharmas is ultimately without nature" (up to) "...the Heavenly King Light-Flame can thoroughly understand.
The first two phrases refer to the Dharma as it was heard; taking "absence of nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) as the true nature of dharmas. The subsequent phrase refers to...
To cause sentient beings to have faith, joy, renunciation, and purity, one then emerges from the turbidity of lack of faith;

because this constitutes the realization of the untainted (*anāsrava*), the merits of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time are fulfilled. Thus, those who delight in the Dharma are able to expound it.

The first phrase refers to those capable of subduing others; it is the cause for what preceded and the fruit of what follows. To transform the realm of sentient beings is itself the practice of subduing.
That this is boundless and inexhaustible constitutes the inconceivable. To contemplate this and bring joy to living beings is called "entry."
"Sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of afflictions" (up to) "this is the object perceived by the King of Transformation Banners.
These first two phrases refer to the immeasurable afflictions of sentient beings, namely the two types of latent tendencies—sharp and dull—as well as the rākṣasas of craving and views.
All of these are utterly terrifying. The next line [states]: "One should regard them with compassion and, through wisdom, cause them to be free from [suffering].
The Tathāgata constantly dwells within the great radiance (up to) this gateway of entry for the gods of Sublime Sound (Ghoṣavatī).
Since the prose commentary (*gadya*) is missing, I shall briefly clarify the titles based on their names. The first two phrases signify "adorned by the constellations" (*tārakā-vyūha*);

this means that the Buddha’s light flows throughout the *dharmadhātu*, as brilliant and pervasive as a net of stars. The next phrase signifies "adorned by wondrous sounds" (*svara-vyūha*), which refers to the work of transforming sentient beings;

it does not go beyond the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*). The previous mention of "wondrous sounds" merely establishes the title by citing one aspect. If one were to establish the title according to the prose commentary:
It should be said: "The liberation door of attaining the Buddha-wheel through the manifestation of light and its gathering and transforming power. △ Fourth, the two heavens of the Second Dhyāna.
First, the prose section on attaining the dharma:
Furthermore, the Heavenly King *Ramyaka-prabhāsa* (至) [attains] the liberation door of extinguishing the sufferings of the world.
There are two meanings. First, the internally realized true bliss. The sūtras and śāstras together state that there are five kinds of bliss: namely, first, causal bliss; second, resultant bliss;

third, the bliss of the removal of suffering; fourth, the bliss of the cessation of sensation; and fifth, the bliss of being free from affliction and harm. Regarding the bliss of being free from affliction and harm, there are further four kinds:
namely, the bliss of renunciation and seclusion; the bliss of the joy of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); the bliss of awakening to the Dharma; and the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.

The bliss of tranquility is now the fourth. If one takes the term "feeling" (*vedanā*) in its general sense, including both meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and awakening (*bodhi*), it encompasses both cause and effect.
As for the statement "constantly feeling," it means that because there is nothing to be felt, one feels all feelings. If one were dependent upon external objects, it would not be constant.

Furthermore, while abiding in the second [dhyāna], one is able to descend; externally, one establishes great benefit by descending in spirit and manifesting signs to eliminate the causes of suffering.

Fruit. This is the liberation door of attaining the pure, wondrous light of the Heavenly King [Nirvāṇa], which removes obstacles to the essence and function of nirvāṇa, [extending] to the liberation door of the treasury of joy and bliss for all sentient beings.

This refers to objectless great compassion, which accords with the ocean of nature; because it uproots the sorrows and afflictions of the world, it gives rise to inexhaustible joy and bliss, a treasury of names.
This attains liberation from the mind of malice and harm.
From the Celestial King Sovereign Sound up to the Liberation Gate of the Power of the Merit of All Sentient Beings:

cultivating the causes of merit brings about the fruits of the environment and its inhabitants; this is the power of merit. Though these may be brought forth by many people over many eons, it is still the power of merit.
The fusion of mindfulness and eons manifests instantaneously; this is liberation regarding time and eons.
[From] the Gate of Supreme Mindfulness and Wisdom Heavenly King [up to] the Gate of Universal Purity Like Space.
This means that by virtue of the Buddha’s power, he remains unmoved; throughout the three phases of formation, abiding, and destruction, all are like the kalpa of emptiness, eternally pure.
This constitutes liberation from transmigration and change.
The Heavenly King Delightful Pure Sublime Sound (up to) the Dharma-gate of Liberation of All Sages:
that is to say, by having faith in and delighting in the Dharma of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and by reverently practicing it, one attains liberation from the two obstacles.
The Celestial King Sound of Excellent Contemplation [up to] the Gate of Liberation through the Meaning and Expedient Means of All Grounds.
"Ground" refers to the wisdom of the grounds. "Meaning" refers to purity; that is, the ground of mind that transcends conceptualization.

"Expedient means" refers to the methods of instruction and the causes for entering the grounds, such as entering, abiding, and emerging. By means of inexhaustible eloquence, he expounds the inexhaustible Dharma.
Therefore, he is able to pass through kalpas.
From the "Dhāraṇī of the Celestial King Adorned Sound" up to the "Liberation Gate of the Skillful Means of Great Offerings," there are generally two meanings:
first, manifesting many bodies and making many offerings to many Buddhas, all of which accord with reality.

It is called "Great Skillful Means" (mahopāya), which is the meaning of the prose section. Second, because a single thought-moment manifests the eight phases [of a Buddha] throughout the entire Dharma-realm, it is called "Great Skillful Means," which is the meaning of the verse. Mastery over these is termed "Liberation" (vimukti).
The Celestial King Profound Radiance attained the liberation door of observing the inexhaustible ocean of supernatural powers and wisdom;
he attained liberation from the obstacles to meditative concentration and wisdom.
The liberation door of the celestial king Vighuṣṭaśabda (Extensive Renown), up to the skillful means of appearing in the world:
fulfilling the fruit in accordance with the capacities of beings, one attains liberation through the lack of adaptability for birth by transformation within the present body.
The Celestial King Supreme Pure Light (up to) attained the liberation door of generating a treasury of profound faith and joyful aspiration.
Seeing the clouds of the Buddha’s great vows, he joyfully aspired to follow and learn them; through this, he was liberated from the obstacle of self-deprecation.
△ Second, the praise of the Buddha in verse.
At that time, the Celestial King Lovely Light (Priya-darśana-ratna-prabha) spoke these verses:
"I recollect the deeds performed by the Tathāgata in the past; through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, may they all be seen."

The first three phrases clarify the bliss of tranquility; by collectively citing the bliss of the cause, they manifest the bliss of the fruit. The final phrase descends to the function of manifestation:
"The Buddha-body is signless and free from all defilements" (up to) "this is the liberation of Sublime Light."
The first phrase refers to the ocean of that which is conjoined. The second phrase refers to the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that is capable of responding;

because it bears the burden of great compassion, it is called "ground" (*bhūmi*). The third phrase refers to the treasury of generated joy: because sorrow is removed, there is joy; because affliction is removed, there is bliss.
The Buddha-dharma is vast and boundless (up to: the power of liberation of the Deva of Sovereign Sound.
The first phrase manifests [the capacity], while the following two manifest what is manifested.
The Buddha’s supernormal powers are without equal (up to: the skillful means of supreme mindfulness and liberation.

The first two lines refer to the universal establishment, maintenance, and so forth [of the pure land]. The next line, "pure as empty space," means that although the three calamities pervade all, the pure land is not destroyed.
However, the second and third verses appear to be somewhat disordered; I have merely explained them here following the sequence of the text.
"As numerous as the atoms in oceans of lands" (up to) "this application of the Dharma-gate of the Deva Subhavyūha.

The first two phrases refer to those who all reverently offer this with joyful devotion; the remainder refers to the noble ones (*ārya*). The next phrase refers to the aforementioned Dharma and its faithful acceptance.
The Buddha, throughout oceans of immeasurable great kalpas, [attained this] up to the Heaven of Well-Considered Sound (*Sudṛśa*). This is the meaning known therein.
The first phrase refers to abiding through kalpas. The subsequent two phrases refer to the skillful means (*upāya*) of the stages (*bhūmi*), which are boundless; these constitute the entirety.

From "The Tathāgata’s Gate of Immeasurable Supernatural Transformations" up to "This Liberation of Adorned Sound," the eight phases [of a Buddha's life] are universally encompassed throughout the verses; for brevity, the offerings have been omitted.
Empowered by majestic power, one is able to expound [the teachings] up to this liberation door of the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

The first phrase refers to prior wisdom; the second phrase refers to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); the third phrase refers to inexhaustibility and the ocean, because it purifies according to the faculties [of beings] and is thus profound and vast.
"The Tathāgata’s wisdom is boundless" (up to) "the one of vast renown, Deva, has realized this path.
The first two phrases refer to the fulfillment of the ocean of virtues; the subsequent phrase refers to his appearance in the world.
The Buddha formerly cultivated the practices for awakening (up to) the Most Victorious Light; hearing this, he was greatly delighted.

These three phrases collectively clarify the power of his former vows. In the fourth section, the conclusion, the treasury of profound faith and joyful attachment is revealed, as the text states "greatly delighted.
△ Fifth, the Heaven of the First Dhyāna has two parts. First, the prose section on attaining the Dharma.
Furthermore, from the Brahma King Śikhin [up to] the liberation gate of pure conduct free from defilement and attachment:
because his great function responds to the capacities of beings, he universally expounds the Dharma; because his function is eternally quiescent, his conduct is pure and undefiled.
Because he attains a mind free from activity, his conduct is pure; because he realizes that objects are signless, he is undefiled.
The Brahma King Prajñāprabha is able to cause all sentient beings to enter meditative concentration and abide in the gates of liberation.
The Buddha serves as the object of concentration; for when one abides in concentration, that which is perceived is profound.
The Brahma King Radiance of Skillful Wisdom attained the liberation door of universally entering all inconceivable dharmas.
The ocean of dharmas is immeasurable and is named "Inconceivable"; that which exhausts it through a single word is named "Universal Entry."
The Brahma King Universal Cloud Sound attained the liberation door of entering the ocean of all the voices of the Buddhas.
This "ocean of voices," in which the perfect sound accords with the various types of beings, requires the absence of discrimination in order to enter the voice of the Buddha.
The Brahma King Sovereign over the Speech and Sounds of the World (up to) the Gate of Skillful Means and Liberation for Teaching and Transforming All Sentient Beings.
He is born through transformation because he proceeds toward the practice of Bodhi; thus, he records [all things] by means of the clear knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).

From the liberation gate of the distinct characteristics of karmic retribution of the Brahma King Silent Radiant Eye, up to [the liberation gate of] the differences in the retributions of sentient beings:
as there are differences according to their karma, the Buddha manifests the experience of these [retributions] to cause them to give rise to right faith.
The Universal Radiance Brahma King [attains] the gate of liberation through manifesting the various distinctions of categories to discipline beings;
only by attaining mastery over all phenomena can one accordingly discipline sentient beings according to their types.
The liberation gate of the realm of the practice of tranquil extinction, from the transformation-sound Brahmā King up to the pure marks [of the Buddha].
The Buddha-body is characterized by signlessness; it is the purity of the *dharmatā*. It manifests and transforms beings, thereby constituting the practice of tranquil extinction.
The liberation door of the Radiant Eye Brahmā King (up to) "the constant and diligent manifestation of non-reliance":
because he is unattached to all realms of existence, he is able to manifest constantly; his three karmas are boundless, and there is nothing further upon which to rely.
The Brahma King Pleasing Ocean-Sound attained the liberation door of "Constantly Contemplating and Observing the Inexhaustible Dharma.
He observed that the nature of phenomena is signless, like empty space; how could it ever be exhausted? He examined their functioning as being according to conditions, like ripples on water:
as they are struck, they arise; how could they ever be exhausted? II. Verses in Praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King Śikhin, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, spoke these verses.
Regarding the "foremost assembly" (*parṣad*) and the opening of the four heavens: when combined, they constitute the Brahmakāyika [heaven], which is itself the assembly. Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The Brahmakāyikas, the Brahmapurohitas, and the Brahmakāyikaparṣadas. Here, "body" (*kāya*) refers to the assembly, and "attendants" (*purohita*) refers to the retinue.
"The Buddha-body is pure and eternally quiescent" (up to) "is seen thus, like clouds in the sky.
The first phrase [indicates] that the Dharma-body is omnipresent throughout the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The second phrase [indicates] knowing that light preaches the Dharma.

The third phrase [indicates] that conduct is pure and free from the marks of objective realms; when the cognition of objects has ceased, then even the images of great function are quiescent. The final phrase provides a general analogy.
It is revealed that clouds do not depart from space, and space does not obstruct the clouds; this serves as an analogy for quiescence and function.
The Buddha-body is thus within the realm of meditative concentration—this is what the King of Wisdom-Light has realized.

The first two phrases concern the realm of entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is precisely the nature of the mind; if one can contemplate it, this constitutes the supreme concentration (*uttama-samādhi*).
The subsequent phrase shows that although the skillful means for entry are manifold, they all lead to the same single tranquility.
From the ocean of Dharma-gates as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, up to the liberation of the Light of Well-Considered Wisdom.
The first phrase refers to the inconceivable Dharma. The following two phrases clarify the meaning of universal entry, for it is exhausted by a single word;
yet the eloquence that exhausts [the teaching] with a single word cannot be fathomed even in an ocean of kalpas, manifesting the inexhaustibility of the Dharma. This is explained in terms of...
If it can encompass [all things], then a single word expresses them all; if it can endure for a long time, then even oceans of kalpas cannot exhaust it.

Yet, a single word speaks only of a mote of dust within a world-system, which is not yet infinite. If one were to wish to express everything in a single word, then two or three phrases would contradict one another.

If a single word were to express everything, what more could be expounded throughout oceans of kalpas? How then could there be inexhaustibility? If there is further that can be expounded, then the single word has not expressed everything.

If one were to speak of them individually, they would never be exhausted; furthermore, it is impossible to repeat them. If one wishes to comprehend them as a whole, they can be fully described from a general perspective.

Yet, when they manifest in their layered and interpenetrating complexity, they cannot be exhausted. It is like ripples on water: whether struck lightly, struck heavily, or struck everywhere, each wave arises according to the impact.
Even if one were to strike until the end of the future, waves would continue to arise until the end of the future—this is the inconceivable Dharma.
"The perfect voice of all Buddhas is equal to the world" (up to) "the universal voice is realized as such by Brahmā.

Regarding the meaning of "perfect voice," the text briefly presents three senses: first, its vastness is boundless; second, it specifically expresses [meaning]; third, it is free from conceptual discrimination.
These correspond respectively to the three phrases [in the verse]. The remainder is explained as in the "Chapter on Manifestation."
Regarding "All Tathāgatas of the three periods of time" up to "the liberation of the deity Svayambhū-ghoṣa":
the first two phrases refer to the skillful means of practicing for the sake of transforming sentient beings.

This is because all Buddhas of the three periods of time take benefiting others as their direction toward Bodhi, thereby purifying their own karma. As for the subsequent phrase: since the previous section concerned the Brahmā King, it speaks of "recollection."
Now, based on the Tathāgata, his physical body manifests; if even a single hair can manifest, how much more so his entire body?
Through the differentiation of the karma of all sentient beings, [this is perceived] up to the Śāntaprabhā heaven, where they are able to realize and enter it.
The first phrase distinguishes the characteristics of karma; the second phrase distinguishes the characteristics of retribution; the third phrase shows that he appears in accordance with the world.
That all immeasurable dharma-gates are mastered up to this point is the realm of Universal Radiance.
The first two phrases refer to the taming of beings according to their respective types; because the methods of taming are sovereign, one is able to pervade extensively among all such types.
The subsequent phrase clarifies the preceding meaning, as it refers to the accomplishment of tasks without deliberation.
"The Buddha-body is like space and is inexhaustible" [up to] "the King of Transformation-Sound realized this Way.
The first two phrases clarify the Buddha’s essential nature (*dharmatā*); that is, the aforementioned purity and quiescence which are inexhaustible.

The subsequent lines briefly manifest four meanings as being like space. The next phrase states that the Buddha’s activity—his responsive manifestations—is his practice; therefore, all are like transformations (*nirmāṇa*), yet they do not lose their quiescence.
Extinction.
The physical marks of the Tathāgata are boundless. (Up to: The Celestial King Radiant Light enters this gate.
The first two phrases refer to that which is manifested as being boundless; the next phrase refers to diligent contemplation without dependence or attachment.
"The Dharma King dwells securely in the palace of the wondrous Dharma" (up to) "this liberation of King Ocean-Sound.

The first two phrases mean that he constantly contemplates the inexhaustible great function; that is, by dwelling securely in the palace of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he is able to manifest great deeds.

The next phrase means that he constantly contemplates the inexhaustible essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*). II. The various devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) [are divided into] seven. First, the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
The Heavenly King has two parts. First, the prose section on attaining the Dharma.
Next, from "The Sovereign Heavenly King" up to "the liberation door of the treasury of mastery over immeasurable sentient beings."

It is called a "Treasury" (garbha) because it manifests before the assembly of beings, exercising sovereign mastery over their discipline and bringing them to maturity through inexhaustible transformative teachings.
This is the gate of liberation known as the Joyful Entrance into the Noble Realm, presided over by the Celestial King Śubhanetra.
Contemplating that the characteristics of worldly pleasure are all suffering, one should renounce them. Contemplating the nature of worldly pleasure, one enters the noble bliss.
This is the liberation door of King Wondrous Jewel Banner Crown (up to) causing various inclinations toward desire to give rise to the inclination for practice and liberation.

The Celestial King Courageous Wisdom attained the liberation door of universally gathering all that is taught for the sake of all sentient beings, thereby severing doubts according to their inclinations and causing them to give rise to correct practice.
The Celestial King Wondrous Sound and Phrases (妙音句天王) [enters] the liberation door of universally encompassing all meanings with a single sound throughout time and place,
speaking for the sake of sentient beings, and increasing his own practice and realization.
Emulating the Buddha, they cultivate loving-kindness.

The Celestial King Wondrous Light Banner (up to) the liberation door of "Destroying All Banners of Arrogance" employs the ten powers of great compassion to crush that haughty pride, yet without a mind of crushing; therefore, it is said to be a "manifestation."
The Heavenly King Realm of Tranquility attained the liberation door of subduing all worldly minds of anger and malice.
With the light of wisdom, he illuminates all worlds, causing them to leave behind the darkness of the three poisons; thus, the fruits of the evil realms no longer exist.
Because the obstructions of anger and delusion are heavy, [the following] verses are presented in alternation.
From the celestial king Subhacakravibhūṣaṇadhvaja up to the gate of liberation wherein all Buddhas come to attend according to one’s recollection:

because the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha has become fully matured, whichever Buddha one recollects, one is immediately able to see them, as in the case of the liberation of Viśvakarman and others.
The Celestial King Flower-Light Wisdom attained the liberation door of universally manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment in accordance with the mental inclinations of sentient beings;
he manifests its attainment in response to their thoughts.
The Celestial King Indra-Splendid Light [attained] the liberation door of the sovereign dharma of great majestic power.
The mastery over quiescence and activity, manifesting in this world to harmonize and guide sentient beings, is collectively termed "sovereign power" (*prabhāva*). 2. Verses in Praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the Celestial King Īśvara, sustained by the Buddha’s sovereign power, spoke these verses:
The Buddha’s body is all-pervasive, equal to the Dharma-realm; [this extends] up to: "He is able to bring about awakening through mastery over the Dharma.

The first phrase refers to the pervasiveness of the essence (*svabhāva*); the second phrase refers to the pervasiveness of its function (*karman*). Therefore, he can manifest before [beings]. The third phrase refers to the ability to establish the treasury of the teachings (*śāsana-kośa*);
the fourth phrase refers to the mastery achieved therein, opening the treasury of the Dharma and awakening to the profound Dharma-gates—this is precisely what constitutes maturation.
All the various joys in the world (up to) the Heavenly King Sublime Eye behold this.
The first two phrases refer to the two types of joy; the next phrase causes entry [into the teaching].
From "The Tathāgata’s appearance pervades the ten directions" (up to) the liberation of the Heavenly King Valiant Wisdom.

The third and fourth [verses] may be understood accordingly. All the vast compassion found in the world up to that which was attained by the deity *Ghoṣavatī*—these three phrases collectively manifest the Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) of the Tathāgata.
Of these, the first two phrases illustrate the superior by means of the inferior, while the subsequent phrase employs a simile.
This clearly demonstrates that the worldly compassion of Maitreya has a specific form; even if it were as high as Mount Sumeru or as vast as the great ocean, it could ultimately be exhausted.

However, the Buddha’s compassion accords with his true nature (*dharmatā*); like the space within a mustard seed or the ground where a blade falls, it can never be exhausted. Furthermore, it is like space:
it universally covers, constantly encompasses, is vastly inclusive and unimpeded, indestructible, and inexhaustible. This is merely one brief illustration.
This is all. [The passage from] "the high mountain of pride of all sentient beings" up to "this liberation of the Wondrous Wheel Banner" can be understood according to the text.
"The Tathāgata’s sovereign power is immeasurable" [up to] "this gate of liberation enters through Flower Wisdom.

The first two phrases clarify that the Buddha-body is universally pervasive, being neither accomplished nor unaccomplished; the subsequent phrase shows the manifestation of perfect enlightenment in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
The ocean of immeasurable and boundless great kalpas [up to] that which is realized by the Lord of Light Heaven (Īśāna-deva).
Manifesting universally throughout the ten directions, they enter universally into all worlds; the rest all possess sovereign power and majesty.
△ Second, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven has two parts. First, the prose section on attaining the Dharma.
Furthermore, the Celestial King Subhakṛtsna has attained the liberation door of revealing all transformations of karma to others.

For the sake of sentient beings, he reveals that all conditioned phenomena are like illusions; although illusions are empty in essence, they possess functional activity which constitutes the power of karma.
Furthermore, although there is no inherent nature in that which arises from conditions, the retribution does not perish.
The Celestial King Silent Sound Radiant Light attained the liberation door of abandoning all objects of attachment.
To grasp at objects of mental deliberation is the root of the disease of delusion; if one finds nothing to be grasped within the mind and its objects, then one abandons such attachments.
The Celestial King Light of Transformative Power (up to) attained the liberation door of causing wisdom to be perfected and liberated.
Darkness is extinguished and wisdom arises, like the waxing and waning of the moon.
The Celestial King Lord of Adornment attained the liberation door of manifesting infinite, pleasing sounds.
The Brahma-voice is subtle and exquisite; therefore, it is called "pleasing to the mind. It should pervade the ten directions; therefore, it is called "boundless.
The Celestial King Light of Mindfulness attained the liberation door of "knowing all Buddhas' inexhaustible marks of merit."

This meaning has three aspects. First, regarding the characteristic of merit: because it is as numerous as the atoms in ten lotus-precious-realm worlds (*padma-garbha-loka-dhātu*), it is inexhaustible.
Second, it refers to the infinite gates of pure compassion and so forth;
because they are produced by causes, and because each cause and effect accords with reality (*tathatā*), each is inexhaustible and identical to empty space. Third, great compassion...
The practice of compassion is a mark of merit. It causes those who are blind or deaf to see and hear, all due to the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness and compassion.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there was one who, upon hearing the praise of the Buddha as possessing great merit, said in anger: "I was born and seven days had passed when my mother’s life came to an end;
how can this be called the mark of great merit? The one who praised him replied: "Though you were in the full vigor of youth, you were not violent or impetuous."
When struck, one does not become angry; when reviled, one does not retaliate. For this reason, I say that this is a mark of great merit.
When those who are enraged hear of it, their hearts are subdued. Thus, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is a mark of inexhaustible merit. This, moreover, accords with and complements the previous meaning.
From the Celestial King Supreme Cloud-Sound up to the Gate of Liberation through the Sequential Order of the Formation and Destruction of All Past Kalpas:

with the perfect wisdom of the three types of higher knowledge (*trividyā*), he comprehends the kalpas of the three periods of time. This refers to the Celestial King; for the moment, it speaks only of his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*).
The Celestial King Śakra attained the gate of liberation of awakening all sentient beings to wisdom.
