This gate lacks a verse; however, throughout the preceding and following contexts, there are frequent instances of "awakening," which is equivalent to the "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" (*kaishin’ōnyū*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Here, "opening" subsumes "showing," and "awakening" subsumes "entering. That is to say, "opening and showing" refer to the subject who transforms, while "awakening and entering" refer to the object being transformed.
Transformation. That treatise states: "Opening" has the meaning of being unsurpassed; that is to say, apart from the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), there is nothing else.
This refers to the simultaneous opening of both *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*: the nature of knowing and seeing is taken as *nirvāṇa*, while the marks of knowing and seeing are taken as *bodhi*.
These are primordially possessed by sentient beings, yet they do not manifest because they are obscured. The Buddha opens and removes these obscurations, whereby primordial wisdom [is revealed].

"Manifesting" (*khyāpana*) means "to show," as it shares the same meaning [with the preceding term], because the three vehicles share the same *dharmakāya*. "Awakening" (*bodhana*) means "not knowing," because [beings] do not know that there is only the single reality;
it now causes them to know so that they may achieve the *saṃbhogakāya* bodhi. "Entering" (*praveśana*) means causing them to realize the stage of non-retrogression;
this is the sense of "cause," for by realizing the first bhūmi and above, one attains bodhi and nirvāṇa.
The reasons for this are explained at length in that commentary.
The Celestial King Subhakūṭa attained the liberation door of emitting light that swiftly fills the void-realm of the ten directions.
Since this light accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), what difficulty could there be in its pervasiveness?
The Celestial King Priyamatī attained the liberation door of the power of indestructible diligence in all undertakings;
that is to say, because he practiced in accordance with the truth and remained untiring throughout long kalpas, he could not be crushed by any māras or non-Buddhists.
The Celestial King Flower-Light Topknot attained the liberation door of knowing all the karmic retributions received by sentient beings;
he fully understands their natures and characteristics, whether they be the distinctions between good and evil or the differences between suffering and joy.
The liberation door of universally seeing the various distinctions in the forms and types of sentient beings, from the Heavenly Kings of the ten directions [down to all others],
such that infinite categories appear instantaneously within a single pore without any coming or going— this is especially manifest as inconceivable. △ Second,
the verse praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the Celestial King Subhakṛtva, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, spoke in verse.
Excluding the seventh [section], there are only ten stanzas:
"The nature of worldly karma is inconceivable... [the various karmas of all sentient beings]."
The first phrase is general; the second phrase provides an exposition; the latter two phrases manifest the power of transformation. Regarding the activity of differentiation:
because the fruit does not perish, various contemplations of the Buddha are non-existent—this is what the Dharma-Silent Sound (Dharmatūṣṇīmbhūta) perceives.
Regarding the object apprehended by the first phrase, nothing is attained in the latter two. However, there are two kinds of objects of perception: the real and the false.

Even if one perceives the Real Buddha, it becomes a delusive affliction; how much more so in the case of the false? As for various modes of contemplation, because [the Buddha] cannot be found through the fivefold search:
to say "the Buddha exists" is the affliction of eternalism; to say "the Buddha does not exist" is the deep-seated view of nihilism. These constitute the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

It cannot be affected by the "hundred negations" (śata-apavāda). Therefore, it is non-existent [in the sense of being a conceptual object]. This is not the case for a single Buddha alone; it is likewise throughout the ten directions.

Because the manifestations of response and transformation are not the ultimate reality, one finds nothing upon seeking the real; thus, one perceives the True Body (dharmakāya). The True is without conditions (anālambana).
Even a Buddha should relinquish [this], let alone other objects.
A Buddha has cultivated all practices throughout oceans of kalpas until he enters this liberation; the adornments of its master are as can be known from verses three and four.
All the power of the various merits existing in the world [extends] to what is observed by the gods of the Light of Mindfulness (*smṛtyābhāsa*).

The first two phrases describe the characteristic of merit; the subsequent phrase describes the characteristic of inexhaustibility. The *Lakṣaṇānuvyañjana-sūtra* states: "Exhausting all the merit of human beings."
It does not equal even a single day, and so on, until it says "throughout the entire world. It does not equal even a single mark of the Tathāgata, and so forth, up to:
"all that exists throughout the three periods of time across immeasurable kalpas [is known] by the Most Supreme Cloud-Sound."
Regarding the wisdom of the devas, they know it universally; regarding a single hair-pore of a Buddha, it can manifest [all things].
The voids of the ten directions may be measured, yet even the Deva King Subhakūṭa has already been able to realize this.
The first two lines clarify that the pores transcend empty space. This means that when numinous wisdom realizes the principle, it is not like empty space;

because the true principle transcends phenomena, it is also not an object of inference. Infinite wisdom and principle cannot be analyzed; yet, according to each of its partial manifestations, they are fused and subsumed in ever-deepening layers.
Thus, the measure of a single pore immediately surpasses empty space. The next line specifically demonstrates the manner of this transcendence.
This means that although the pores are not large, they are boundless; for they are vast and unhindered. They exclude the realm of conceptual thought.
In the former case, light expands outward; in the present case, a single pore is vast within. These descriptions are merely alternating expressions.
Since a single pore is inherently pervasive throughout space, how could the ten directions ever be difficult to fill?
The Buddha, throughout immeasurable kalpas in past lives, [up to] the point where *pramuditā-prajñā* (Joyful Wisdom) was able to know this Dharma-gate:
the first phrase refers to cultivation over a long period; the second phrase refers to exhaustive cultivation; the third phrase refers to uninterrupted cultivation.
Because he possesses these three modes of cultivation, his power of progress is indestructible. As for the term "vast pāramitā," it will be explained in the fifth sutra.
The nature of karma and its causal conditions is inconceivable (extending to) "this is the entrance of Flower-Light.

The first phrase generally reveals the nature and characteristics of karma; that is, the non-perishing of retributive fruits born of conditions is precisely the non-existence of that which lacks intrinsic nature.
Therefore, one cannot conceive of it as either existent or non-existent. The second phrase states: "The Buddha spoke thus. Tianru.
This is known. The next line shows the nature of karma through the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
"You should contemplate a single pore of the Buddha" (up to) "this is what King Universal Vision has realized."

The first two phrases state that the small manifests as the great and the many as the one; this is difficult to conceive. The subsequent phrase states that when it manifests, it does not come, and when it does not manifest, it does not go; this, too, is difficult to conceive.
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Extensive Radiance, Scroll Seven;
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Extensive Radiance, Scroll Eight (Entering the Second Scripture, Part Two).
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui. Commentary on the Sūtra with Annotations.
△ Section Three: The Heaven of Contentment (Tuṣita). Part Two: First, the prose section on attaining the Dharma.
Furthermore, the King of the Heaven of Contentment attained the liberation door of the perfect wheel of teaching of all Buddhas appearing in the world.
They attain the Dharma-gate of universal characteristics. When the Buddhas are about to appear in the world, they are all born in that heaven.
At the time of their descent to be born here below, they universally respond to the entire Dharma-realm and suddenly expound the Avataṃsaka Sūtra as the mark of perfect fulfillment.
The Celestial King Joyful Ocean-Crest attained the liberation door of the pure radiant body that exhausts the realm of empty space.
His bodies of radiant form pervade the entirety of the realm of empty space and are ultimately ungraspable; therefore, they are called "pure."
The Celestial King Supreme Banner of Merit attained the liberation door of the ocean of pure vows that extinguishes the suffering of the world;
by the power of his pure vows, he extinguishes the suffering of delusion and karma.
The Celestial King Śāntiprabha (up to) attained the liberation door of universally purifying the realms of all sentient beings.
△ The fourth and fifth [sections] may be understood accordingly.
The Celestial King Ratnaśikhara-candra attained the liberation door of the inexhaustible treasury that is ever-present for the universal transformation of the world.
"Universal" means being without partiality; "constant" means being without interruption. To reveal true bliss is the Tathāgatagarbha.
The Celestial King Power of Valiant Strength attained the liberation door of realizing and revealing the realm of the perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas.
The realm of self-awakened cognition has already been entered by the Buddha; therefore, he manifests it so that all beings may awaken to its identity with all things.
This is the liberation door of the Celestial King Vajraprabha, which renders the bodhicitta indestructible.
That is to say, by means of pure merit, he solidifies the bodhicitta;
this is the liberation door of the Celestial King Star-Host Banner’s skillful means for subduing sentient beings,
looking upward to observe and looking downward to transform them.
The Heavenly King Sublime Adornment attained the liberation door of knowing the minds of all sentient beings in a single thought-moment and manifesting in accordance with their capacities;
this refers to the swift illumination and manifestation. △ Second, the verse praising the Buddha.
After a long time, the King of the Heaven of Complete Satisfaction (up to) surveyed all the hosts of gods in the Heaven of Complete Satisfaction and spoke these verses:
"The Tathāgata is vast, pervading the entire Dharma-realm... (up to) causing them to enter the inconceivable, pure Dharma."

The first half concerns the meaning of world-transcendence (*lokottara*). The upper phrase indicates that both essence and wisdom are universally pervasive; the lower phrase indicates that both compassion and function are all-encompassing.

The second half concerns the fulfillment of the wheel of the teaching. The former phrase indicates that the provisional is the wondrous gate by virtue of its reality; the latter phrase indicates that the integration of the provisional into the real constitutes fulfillment.
The Buddha’s body manifests universally throughout the ten directions... [up to] ...this entry of the *Tuṣitakūṭa* deva;
these two [sections] may be understood accordingly.
The Tathāgata, having cultivated all practices in the past... [up to] ...the supreme virtue that can know this skillful means.
The first two phrases concern purifying one's conduct through vows. The next phrase indicates that because defilement is fundamentally empty, it was previously directed toward cessation;
because the Buddha-dharma is fundamentally inherent, it is now directed toward fulfillment. When delusion is exhausted and reality is revealed, these two terms mutually support one another.
"The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is inconceivable" [up to] "the liberation gate of the Tranquil Light Heaven.

The first two phrases concern the universal manifestation based on the essence (*tattva*), like the moon entering a hundred rivers; the moons reflected in the images do not divide the substance of the moon.

This is the function (*vṛtti*) of the essence itself, and its function pervades the *dharmadhātu*. Because essence and function penetrate one another, it is "inconceivable. This refers to the second phrase.
He preaches the Dharma according to their faculties.
Sentient beings are entangled and shrouded by karma and afflictions... (up to) "the pure eyes illuminate and know, and the mind rejoices.

The first half [of the verse] refers to those sentient beings who are to be purified, for they possess the three types of defilement; the upper line provides the heading, while the lower line briefly indicates [the details].

Regarding the characteristics of delusion: pride (*māna*) is the root; arrogance (*mada*) and negligence (*pramāda*) are secondary delusions. Arrogance refers to being stained by one's own prosperity; pride refers to relying on oneself to look down upon others;

negligence is precisely the state of being unrestrained and dissolute. Arrogance serves as the basis for defiled phenomena, while pride can cause one to sink deeply into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Negligence is the source of all delusions; therefore, these three are singled out for mention. "Dissolute" (*dàng*) means to be stirred; it refers to the object—
Driven by the wind, they flutter, drift, and scatter. The second line concerns the dharma-gate of purity, which means not grasping at signs because the essence itself is quiescent.
"All the true guides of the world... [through] wondrous light, one is able to observe herein."
The first three [points] may be understood.
From "the number of atoms in the oceans of lands of the ten directions" up to "what is seen by this Banner of Adornment," it is a general manifestation.
Since one has already drawn near [to the Buddhas], one must certainly honor and support them and hear the Dharma; using what is heard to harmonize others constitutes true offering.
In the list of names, it is called the Star-Constellation Banner (Jyotiṣka-dhvaja), which serves to adorn [the assembly]. This appears interchangeably with the prose section.
That the ocean of sentient beings' minds is inconceivable—up to the point where the gods of Sublime Adornment (Sudarśana) thoroughly understand this—is [stated here].
The first half [of the verse]. "Knowing the minds of sentient beings. The upper line indicates their depth and vastness; the lower line reveals their characteristics.
Because thoughts do not abide and are as numerous as blades of grass, they are "vast. There are three meanings of "deep": first, they constantly revolve like a flowing stream, and thus do not abide;
second, their essence is quiescent, and thus they are unmoving; third, they arise falsely from conditions and have no separate basis. The next line...
He knows them all in a single thought-moment. △ Fourth, the Heaven of the Lords of Time (Kāmadeva-rāja), in two parts. First, the prose section on attaining the Dharma:
Furthermore, from "The Lord of the Heaven of Time" (down to) "the gate of liberation that causes one to forever leave behind sorrow and affliction."
When roots of goodness are aroused, anxiety and affliction are naturally eliminated.
The Celestial King Sublime Light attained the liberation door of universally entering all realms;
by means of infinite skillful means, he universally realized the realm of the Dharma-body.
The Celestial King Infinite Wisdom Banner of Merit attained the liberation door of the Great Compassion Wheel that eliminates all afflictions.
It is called a "wheel" because it crushes delusions and suffering through compassion.
The Celestial King Subhavyūha attained the liberation door of knowing the minds of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time;
by means of the three types of transcendent knowledge, he discerns their capacities and bestows the Dharma accordingly.
The Dharma-door of the Great Radiant Heavenly King of Total Retention (*dhāraṇī*)—up to—the liberation door of recollecting and maintaining all dharmas without forgetfulness.

It is called a "door" because total retention enters into principle. It is called "radiance" because it takes wisdom as its essence. If one includes its auxiliary factors, it also comprises mindfulness and concentration.

Mindfulness is clear recollection; thus, one is able to recollect and maintain. Concentration ensures there is no forgetfulness. [The four... *(Note: The source text appears to be a commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* or a similar Mahāyāna scripture, specifically concerning the "Ten Heavenly Kings of Total Retention. The provided fragment describes the first king, the Great Radiant Heavenly King of Total Retention, and his liberation door. The final characters "四無" likely refer to the beginning of a list of the four immeasurables or four fearlessnesses.)*
All dharmas, including those that are obstructive and so forth, are all that which is supported [by these gates],
from the Celestial King of Inconceivable Wisdom up to the Gate of Liberation of Inconceivable Skillful Means.
It may be known that the Celestial King Nābhi-cakra attained the liberation door of skillful means for maturing sentient beings by turning the wheel of Dharma.
Turning the Dharma and demonstrating the path to enlightenment is precisely the skillful means for maturing sentient beings.
The Celestial King Radiant Flame attained the liberation door of the vast eye that universally observes all sentient beings and proceeds to discipline and liberate them;
with his ten eyes seeing perfectly, he proceeds to discipline them according to what is appropriate.
The Celestial King Radiant Light attained the liberation door of transcending all karmic obstructions and not following the deeds of Māra.
Transcending karmic obstructions causes one to leave behind evil causes; not following the deeds of Māra means abandoning evil conditions.
The Celestial King Universal Observer of Great Renown (up to) the liberation gate of causing others to receive and practice with a pure mind.
[He] rains down the rain of Dharma equally, inducing them to advance in goodness and causing them to receive and practice it; he instructs them to sever evil so that they attain purity of mind.
This refers specifically to the devas, though the verses apply to all. △ Second, the verses in praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the King of the Ṛtu-devas (up to: surveyed all the hosts of the Ṛtu-devas and spoke these verses:
"The Buddha, throughout immeasurable and long eons... shall forever illuminate the lamp of wisdom for sentient beings."
The first half generally reveals that he has already transcended [defilements]; the second half develops the roots of goodness capable of such transcendence.
"The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is exceedingly vast" (up to) "this is the liberation of Great Radiance."
The text may be understood in its entirety.
Regarding the phrase "the nature of karma is vast and inexhaustible" up to "thus is that which the Deva of Wisdom enters":
the first phrase refers to the nature of karma. It is called "vast" because a single thought-moment creates all things; it is "inexhaustible" because...
Because the antidote has not yet been attained, there is nothing capable of stopping [the afflictions]. Because there are many gateways, the next phrase concerns skillful entry:
through wisdom one understands entry for oneself, and by revealing it, one causes others to enter. The subsequent phrase indicates that the gateways of entry are manifold.
"Turning the inconceivable, wondrous wheel of Dharma" (up to) "this is the realm of the Fire-Flame Heaven (*Yāma-deva*).
The text may also be understood accordingly.
"If there are sentient beings who see the Buddha but once" (up to) "the light illuminates the path traversed by the Heavenly King."

The first phrase refers to seeing the Buddha as the condition. The following two phrases refer to the two benefits of seeing the Buddha: first, the arising of correct wisdom, which necessarily involves transcending internal karmic obstacles;
second, the Buddha acting as the true guide, so how could one externally pursue demonic conditions? Since one does not follow demons, how could one commit demonic deeds?
Thus, all ten types of demons are abandoned, which is why the word "all" (諸) is used.
The entire assembly is as vast as a great ocean; [this concludes] up to the entry into the renown of this liberation door.
The ten [assemblies] may also be known thus. △ Five. The assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, two [parts]. First, the prose section on eleven dharmas.
Furthermore, from the time of Śakrendra, the Heavenly King, up until [the present], all clearly perceive the liberation door of great joy.

By virtue of receiving this power, they maintain mindfulness; those who mindfully recollect past Buddhas have previously entered this heaven. There are two aspects regarding the three periods of time.
First, one also contemplates the future; second, the past [factors] also have three time periods when viewed in relation to one another.
One gives rise to great joy because the objects are sublime and because one celebrates one's own merit.
From the liberation gate of the Heavenly King Universal Renowned Full Sound up to the liberation gate of the Vastness of the World Beyond Compare:
yet the Buddha-body is neither defiled nor pure, neither large nor small, and possesses neither superiority nor inferiority; it is like empty space. When clouds gather, it becomes dark;

when the sun shines brightly, it becomes bright. When colors are obscured, it seems inferior; when objects obstruct it, one speaks of it as small. Now that the clouds of delusion have vanished, wisdom...
It is luminous, therefore it is pure; because the emptiness of intrinsic nature manifests, it is vast; because wondrous color appears, it is incomparable.
Since all these are the power of liberation, it is said that it "can cause."
The Celestial King Maitreya-Netra-Ratna-Cūḍa attained the liberation door of the "Compassionate Cloud Enveloping All.
His great compassion makes no distinction between enemy and friend; it is like a cloud that, being without intention, universally covers all.
From the Celestial King named Jewel Light Banner Fame (*Ratnaprabhāketudhvaja-nāma-devendra*) up to the liberation door of manifesting bodies of various forms and majestic virtues:
because the lords of the worlds of humans and devas often rely upon their own majesty and virtue, the Buddha manifests a body that transcends theirs, causing them to feel reverence and joy.

The liberation door of the Celestial King Joyful Bliss Topknot (up to) "arising from what karmic merit" consists in knowing the distinctions between causes and effects, thereby causing sentient beings to diligently cultivate causes and effects; both of these are termed "merit."
The Celestial King Samyaksmṛti attained the liberation door of being shown the Buddhas’ deeds of maturing sentient beings;
he demonstrated how the Buddhas discipline beings, causing bodhisattvas to emulate and practice this.
The Celestial King Exalted Sound possesses the liberation door of knowing the signs of transformation during the kalpas of formation and destruction of all worlds.
He knows everything from the initial formation and subsequent destruction, through the transformations during the period of abiding, down to the subtlest lands within a single pore.
Regarding these transformations: when people of merit appear in the world, lapis lazuli manifests; when those of meager merit appear, thorns emerge.
Therein he was born.
He attained the liberation door of the Heavenly King Mindfulness-Attainment (*Smṛti*), which consists of recollecting the future practices for taming sentient beings of bodhisattvas.
Through the causes manifested by the Buddha’s body hairs, the deva’s recollection enables him to contemplate and emulate them.
The Celestial King Pure Flower Radiance attained the liberation door of thoroughly knowing the causes of the happiness of all devas.
All forms of happiness have the Buddha as their cause; because they are endowed with supreme virtues, they excel in bliss, and thus they are called "devas."
The liberation door of knowing the roots of goodness for taking birth—from the Heavenly King Sun-Eye (up to)—so as to be free from delusion and confusion.
The roots of goodness for taking birth are precisely the power of mindfulness of the Buddha; by being shown this so as not to be confused, one abandons negligence and advances in cultivation.
From the Heavenly King Sovereign Radiance (up to) the liberation gate of eternally severing various doubts:
there are many kinds of doubt, such as doubting oneself or doubting others, doubting principle or doubting phenomena. For example, upon hearing of emptiness, one doubts;

upon hearing of existence, one doubts permanence; upon hearing that both are true, one doubts their two aspects; and upon hearing that both are neither, one doubts what basis there is. Furthermore, upon hearing...

They harbor mutual doubts, such as doubting that emptiness exists when hearing of existence, or doubting that existence exists when hearing of emptiness. Now, these are opened so that they may attain awakening. II.
Verses in Praise of the Buddha.
At that time, Śakrendra, King of the Gods, spoke in verse:
In the verse, there are likewise eleven [points].
"I recollect all Buddhas of the three periods of time" (up to) "...by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they are all seen.

As for what is meant by "equality": it is because their modes of transformation and manifestation are identical. Furthermore, it is spoken of as existing merely by way of conventional designations and numerical conventions.
The "three periods" do not mean that the Tathāgata possesses past, future, or present;
rather, the Buddha-body is vast and pervasive throughout the ten directions—this path is universally praised as being able to perceive and behold it.

The first phrase signifies vastness; the second, incomparability; and the third, purity. However, the ancient masters clarify that there are six meanings through which these are universally understood:
first, "vast," meaning the entire *dharmadhātu* is taken as the body; second, "pervasive," meaning it completely pervades from a single atom to the ten directions;
third, "wondrous form," meaning it is formless, being the form of the formless; fourth, "supreme," meaning there is nothing to compare it with; fifth... [text ends]
It benefits; for its benefit of beings is boundless. It functions as light; for its radiance destroys darkness.
Thus did the Celestial King Ratnaśikhin awaken to the Tathāgata’s ocean of great compassion and skillful means.
The first half refers to Compassionate Clouds (*Maitreya-megha*). In the preceding line, the fruit is great; in the following line, the cause is profound.

All Buddha-dharmas rely upon compassion, and compassion is established based upon skillful means (*upāya*); both are termed "profound and vast," which is why the word "ocean" is employed. The subsequent line refers to "universally covering."
"I contemplate the ocean of the Dharma King’s merits" (up to) "this liberation is entered by the Flower King.
The text is all intelligible.
"If one contemplates even a small portion of the Tathāgata’s merits" (up to) "the eye of wisdom can deeply awaken herein."
The first two phrases refer to the aforementioned roots of goodness. "Those with slight merit" uses the small to illustrate the great, thereby manifesting that the cause is superior.
The subsequent phrase refers to being born among humans and devas, and thus being free from the terrors of the three evil realms.
"Within the dharma of quiescent extinction, there is great supernormal power"—this refers to what has been attained by this King of Radiance.
The first phrase is the dharma that is able to open [the way]; it is the supernormal power of the wisdom of quiescence. The following two phrases are due to universal responsiveness.

All doubts are severed. △ Six: The Son of Heaven of the Sun (2). First, the prose section on the eleven dharmas. Since he is the Son of Heaven of the Sun, he primarily elucidates the benefits of his light.
Furthermore, from "Next, the Son of Heaven of the Sun" up to "constantly acting for the benefit and liberation throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the future," [the text continues].
The names and the dharma-gates are all general designations. This means that the light of the Buddha’s body and wisdom is like that sun, illuminating without partiality;
this is called "Pure Light" (*viśuddha-prabhā*), which refers to the essence of this light. Next, the function of the light is distinguished, which briefly has four meanings:

first, with respect to the mind, it shines equally upon the high and the low, and is therefore called "Universal Illumination" (*samantaprabhā*). Second, with respect to location, it extends throughout the realms of the ten directions. Third...
In terms of time, it extends to the end of the future. In terms of its application, it is constant and uninterrupted.
Such benefit is the achievement of Great Wisdom.
[This is] the gate of liberation called "The Radiant Eye Devaputra Entering the Ocean of Wisdom."

Sentient beings inherently possess the Buddha-wisdom, which flows like a hidden current beneath the ocean. Now, the Buddha assumes various bodies according to each respective class of being and employs diverse skillful means, with the sole aim of awakening them and enabling them to realize and enter this wisdom.
From the Devaputra Sumeruprabha-pramuditadhvaja (up to) the liberation door of causing others to diligently cultivate boundless pure merits:
Sentient beings are stained by attachment and drift about without refuge; the Buddha’s virtues are unimpeded and should serve as their lord.
Cultivating accordingly to sever defilement is called "pure merit. When a single practice accords with principle, it is termed "boundless," let alone its full cultivation.
The Devaputra Pure Jewel Moon attained the liberation door of profound joy in practicing all ascetic disciplines;
because he guides compassion with wisdom and undergoes suffering for the sake of sentient beings, he experiences deep joy.
The Celestial Son *Vīryavikrāntāvinivartana* (The Valiant and Non-retrogressive) [attains] the gate of liberation that augments his vital essence and clarity (*tejas*).
His substance is free from obstructions and delusions; his function consequently becomes pervasive. Thus, it is called "unimpeded" (*anāvaraṇa*). Whether in body or wisdom, both are termed "light.

Being all-encompassing without partiality, it is called "universal illumination" (*samantaprabha*). The brilliance and sharpness of body and mind constitute the augmentation of vital essence and clarity; this clarity is luminous.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "When a king protects the Dharma, he increases three kinds of vital essence (*ojas*).

First is the vital essence of the earth, which means the five grains ripen in abundance. Second is the vital essence of sentient beings, which means their physical forms are dignified and handsome, and they are free from all epidemics."

The vital essence of the three wholesome dharmas refers to the cultivation of generosity, ethical discipline, faith, and so forth. The present text pertains specifically to the third [wholesome dharma], which augments one’s merit and wisdom;
its meaning encompasses the preceding two as well, because the power of the Dharma provides distant support.
The Celestial Son of the Radiance of Wondrous Flower Garlands (up to) attained the liberation door of causing the birth of an ocean of joyful faith and understanding.
With the two radiances of body and wisdom, he purified his physical and mental faculties; his faith and understanding were so profound and vast—how could he not be filled with joy?
From the Son of Heaven Most Victorious Banner Light (*Jiàishèngdāngguāngmíng Tiānzǐ*) up to [the liberation door] of accomplishing various sublime merits:
because during the day he diligently cultivates wholesome deeds with a focused mind.
The Devaputra Ratnaśikhara-samantāloka enters the gate of liberation called "Various Colors and Marks of Jewels.

This refers to unconditional great compassion (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*). Because he sits beneath the Bodhi tree and produces many wondrous jewels, these are called "colors and marks of jewels" (*varṇa-lakṣaṇa-ratna*);

they should rather be called "jewel-colors and marks" (*ratna-varṇa-lakṣaṇa*), for they are perfect, luminous, and precious. They take jewels as their essence and are adorned with jewels; they are endowed with the ten [perfections].

As numerous as the atoms within a lotus treasury, they are thus called "various. Each and every form and characteristic functions throughout the entire dharma-realm; this is termed "manifesting boundless realms.
All such manifestations flow from the ocean of great compassion. Because the ocean of compassion encompasses all, it makes no distinction between the worthy and the foolish.
From the Devaputra Radiant Eye (to) the Gate of Liberation for Causing One to See the Treasury of the Dharma Realm:

Wisdom removes the cataracts of delusion; the Dharma-eye then becomes pure. With pure vision, one sees the Dharma realm; the Dharma realm is itself the treasury. The treasury is as previously described.
The Devaputra Dhṛtaguṇa attained the liberation door of generating a pure, continuous mind that prevents its loss or destruction.
Because he generates a pure mind toward all Buddhas, even a single act of making an offering can cause his merit to continue until the attainment of Bodhi;
this is as described in the *Samantabhadracaryā-nirdeśa* (Chapter on Manifestation) regarding the analogy of eating a diamond. How much more so, then, for a continuous stream?
The Bodhisattva Universal Operation Radiance King (up to) the liberation door of causing the accomplishment of all activities.
It causes sentient beings to abide in their tasks, never exceeding the light of the sun; it causes people to advance in virtue, surely surpassing mere worldly principles.
△ Second, the eulogy of the Buddha in verse also consists of eleven [sections].
At that time, the Sun Deva-putra, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata’s vast light of wisdom... [and] his manifold skillful means for taming beings.”

The first half [of the verse] means "pure light shines everywhere. The second half means "constantly acting for the benefit [of others]," such as extinguishing evil and generating good, destroying ignorance and producing wisdom, and so forth;
this constitutes many skillful means.
The Tathāgata’s physical marks are boundless... (up to) ...such a Dharma-gate is obtained with joy;
two or three [verses] may be understood accordingly.
For the benefit of the world, he practiced austerities... (up to) ...Ratnacandra is able to know this skillful means.

The first half [of the verse] refers to all ascetic practices (*duṣkaracaryā*). Regarding this, there are four difficulties: first, the difficulty of turning one's back on one’s own benefit to benefit the world;

second, the difficulty that the nature of the practice is exclusively suffering; third, the difficulty of passing through various states of existence (*bhava*); and fourth, the difficulty of immeasurable eons (*kalpa*). Because he fully practices these, it is called "all.
The next line clarifies the joy of the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*), which also has four meanings. First, for the sake of sentient beings...

1. Ascetic practice (*duṣkara-caryā*): Because it fulfills one’s original vow, its meaning lies in the first phrase. 2. The two wisdoms (*jñāna*) illuminate the nature of suffering as fundamentally empty and quiescent;
thus, there is light that illuminates emptiness. 3. Universal purity and freedom from defilement, because it is not mixed with poison;
thus, universal purity is like space. 4. The fruit for oneself and others, because it is not without benefit; this corresponds to the entirety of the third phrase.
The Buddha’s manifestation of wondrous sounds without obstruction... [up to] ...this is the entrance of the deva Flower-Garland.
Regarding the meaning of the Net of Light, it is as described in the "Bhadrapāla Chapter.
All the various radiances existing in the world... [up to] ...this is the liberation of the Light of the Supreme Banner.

This refers to the "penetrating clarity" (*abhijñā*). By citing a brief example to manifest its excellence, one distinguishes that which is difficult to conceive; thus, it is able to accomplish all sublime merits. As for the statement that "the world cannot equal it":
although the world possesses much light, its benefit is not ultimate. Although the Buddha’s light may appear slight, it necessarily penetrates the true source and is inexhaustible.
Thus, by means of this single instance, all others are illustrated.
The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus... (up to) this is the power of the skillful means of the deity Guṇadevā;
the text may be understood accordingly.
Within one dharma-gate there are immeasurable gates... (up to) this is what the deity Samantavikiraṇaprabhā has realized.
The first phrase refers to the dharma-gates of illumination, which are like the solar palace where a thousand rays shine simultaneously. Taking up any single dharma, there are immeasurable gates.
Furthermore, there are two meanings: first, regarding their common characteristics. For example, within the single gate of impermanence, there are birth, old age, sickness, and death;
gathering and dispersing, union and separation, gain and loss, formation and destruction; the three calamities and the four phases; and the external vessel-world as well as the internal body.
From a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) to a single lifetime, through birth and extinction, transformation, defilement and purity, concealment and manifestation—all are gates of impermanence.
The same applies to all other phenomena. Second, regarding the fusion of their nature, they are inexhaustible. The next two phrases concern the meaning of universal movement and illumination:

as one sun traverses the heavens, day after day it is never-ending; as one gate passes through various affairs, kalpa after kalpa it is difficult to exhaust. Thus, the gates of skillful means (*upāya*) are manifold.
Ultimately, all returns to the One Ultimate. The vast has no boundaries; the great is unborn. △ Second, the Devaputra Candra:
First, the prose section on his attainment of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the Devaputra Candra attained the liberation door of "Pure Radiance Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm to Gather and Transform Sentient Beings."

This is called the "Dharma-gate," which is also a general designation. Light has two distinctions: that of body and that of wisdom. The Dharma-realm likewise has two divisions: phenomena and principle.

Phenomena consist of the bodies and minds of sentient beings, as well as the lands upon which they rely. The light of the body illuminates the body to bring about awakening and illuminates the land to bring about purification.
The light of wisdom illuminates the mind to shatter delusion and illuminates principle to make it manifest. When these two lights—of body and wisdom—are mutually identical, then...
The four dharmas illuminated therein are likewise fused; thus they are called "universal. Together they eliminate the obstacles of delusion, and all attain the name of purity.
From the Son of Heaven *Flower-King Topknot Radiance* (up to... causing them to universally enter the liberation door of boundless dharma-understanding.
With a heart of compassion, he universally observes all beings and bestows upon them many teachings, causing them to enter the boundless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
[He leads] the Devaputra *Vicitra-vimala-prabhā* (Various Pure Radiance) [and others] through the gate of liberation that revolves through various objects of perception (*ālambana*).

The *ālayavijñāna* of sentient beings is all termed the "ocean of mind. The preceding seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are termed "evolving through objective conditions" (*ālambana-pravṛtti*).

"Evolving" (*pravṛtti*) means to evolve and arise; it is also synonymous with "transmigration" (*saṃsāra*). Because their objects of perception are not uniform, they are established under various names. Thus, a sutra says:
"The ocean of the *ālaya*-consciousness abides eternally, Stirred by the winds of objective realms; Various waves of consciousness surge and arise in turn. The analogy states:
Great waves surge through the vast ocean depths; there is no end to their succession. Knowing that capacities differ, they bestow the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
[This leads to] the liberation door of the Celestial Son Peaceful Joy of the World-Mind (up to) causing him to leap for great joy.

This refers to demonstrating the noble bliss of the objects [of meditation], causing one to attain the first stage (*bhūmi*). This bliss is primordially present; though it appears defiled, it remains undefiled, and is thus inconceivable.
The Devaputra named Tree-King Eye-Light (to... guards and protects at all times, causing one to achieve the gate of liberation.
This means taking the bodhicitta as one’s home, making the two benefits one’s labor, using body and speech as oxen, and employing sharp wisdom as a plow to till the ground of the mind.
Therein, one sows the seeds of hearing and permeation, causing the sprouts of faith and understanding to grow, and giving rise to the stalks of correct practice.
They cause the flowers of awakening to bloom and obtain the fruit of bodhi. For self-benefit, they maintain constant vigilance through non-negligence;
for the benefit of others, they protect through the power of great vows capable of transforming beings, ensuring that they are not assailed by the delusions of Māra or by beasts.
Thus, from cause to fruition, they achieve accomplishment.
The liberation door of the manifestation of pure light by the devaputra (up to) causing the direct perception of the experiences of suffering and happiness:

that is to say, protecting through loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to manifest happiness, and rescuing from suffering through compassion (*karuṇā*). Causing one to perceive cause and effect, so as to abandon evil and cultivate good, is called true protection and rescue.
The Celestial Son Universal Roaming Immovable Light attained the liberation door of being able to uphold the pure moon that universally manifests throughout the ten directions;
by means of the wind of Buddha-wisdom, he upholds the moon of great compassion, causing all to clearly perceive the Perfectly Awakened One and become free from suffering and cooled.
From the Devaputra *Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña* up to the liberation gate of signlessness and lack of intrinsic nature:
All phenomena are of two kinds. The first is that which is deluded; because dependent origination is unreal, it is like an illusion;

because it is produced by conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature. The second is that which deludes; because pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) has no objective reality, it is like space; because it is a false construction.
It is signless (*animitta*). Furthermore, the dharma of dependent origination has two meanings: first, being signless like space, it is utterly swept away until nothing remains;
this is the emptiness of signs (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). Second, being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) like an illusion, karmic causes and effects are never lost;
this is the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). These two are non-dual, constituting a single dependent origination. Therefore, these two metaphors together reveal a single dharma. Since...
When one is no longer deluded regarding the subject and object, one awakens to True Suchness and perfects the fire of true wisdom.
Thus, the Moon Deva King of Pure Awakening attained the liberation door of universally initiating great functional activity for the sake of all sentient beings.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, manifesting forms endowed with the primary and secondary marks is a great undertaking.
The Celestial Son of Great Majestic Virtue and Radiance attained the liberation door of universally severing all doubts and delusions.
The light of his hair shines everywhere; how could doubts not be severed? △ Second, the verse praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the Moon Devaputra, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power (up to), spoke these verses:
The Buddha emits light that pervades the world... (up to) ...thus one contemplates the Flower-Tuft [Bodhisattva] regarding the Buddha.
The first two [verses] are understandable.
The ocean of the minds of sentient beings differs from moment to moment... (up to) ...this liberation of wondrous light.

The first phrase: "The ocean of mind turns through objective apprehension. If one considers the eight consciousnesses in terms of arising and ceasing, then that eighth consciousness is also called "turning" because it is constantly turning.
Thus it is said that "each moment is distinct": because it is constant, it is not annihilated; because it turns, it is not eternal.
They arise anew and cease anew; moment by moment they perish. Because each moment is distinct, their substance is never identical.

That *tathāgatagarbha* is eternally endowed with all merits and its meaning is likewise inseparable from them. It is like a torrential stream: apart from water there is no flow, and apart from flow there is no water.

Furthermore, it is like the waves and billows of the ocean, because they cause drifting and drowning, and because they abound in nourishing life. One should contemplate this in accordance with the Dharma.
The next phrase clarifies thorough knowledge; that is to say, this consciousness is profound and subtle, known only by the Buddha’s wisdom.

The subsequent phrase demonstrates the nature of the ocean of mind, which is itself Buddha-wisdom. It does not allow for seeking it externally; because it accords with the capacities [of sentient beings], there is joy.
"Sentient beings lack the noble bliss" (up to) "blissful contemplation;
such is the vision. These first two phrases clarify the loss of noble bliss. "Noble bliss" refers to the nirvāṇa of noble wisdom;

because it was originally present but is now absent, they remain immersed in deluded suffering. The next phrase clarifies that its nature is revealed: there is bliss that is not external to suffering. This is called [the name].
Inconceivable! Seeing one's nature brings about bliss; this nature is itself the gateway.
Such is the rare and great compassion of the Tathāgata (up to: which the deva Cakṣuḥprabha understands.
However, this is spoken in terms of the Dharma. The Tathāgata is like the master of the field; he compassionately cultivates the field of sentient beings.

His entering into existence for the sake of benefit is his activity. Seeking benefit is equivalent to seeking the fruit; entering existence is similar to plowing. Preaching the Dharma is the sowing of seeds;
exhorting toward goodness is precisely the guarding [of the crop] until it ripens—this should be understood.
The World-Honored One has opened up and elucidated the light of the Dharma (up to) such that Pure Light, seeing this, gives rise to joy.
[The Buddha] previously rescued and protected him with compassion, speaking to his fundamental mind; this light of wisdom clarifies its application.
When compassion and wisdom guide one another, they are truly able to save.
The Buddha is the basis for all merit (up to) "immovable," being able to know this skillful means.
The first phrase: the Buddha is the basis of merit; the moon is the source of coolness. The second phrase: one should say that a great wind sustains the palace, yet now it is said thus;
this is a metaphorical shift. The great earth is like the Buddha; the palace is like merit. The third phrase: that is illumination.
It has the meaning of manifestation and the meaning of coolness.
The great brilliance of the fire of wisdom pervades the Dharma-realm. (Up to: The Celestial King of the Constellations realized this path;
this may be known from the eighth [chapter].
"The Buddha is like space, devoid of self-nature" (up to) "the Celestial King Pure Awakening sees thus.

The first phrase, "The Buddha is like space," refers to the nature of the Great Enterprise (*mahā-karman*). The second phrase refers to the substance of the Great Enterprise; for if it did not benefit sentient beings, it would not be the Great Enterprise.
The third phrase refers to the characteristics of the Great Enterprise; just as there is a shadow based on light, through which movement and stillness can be known.
"By means of a mirror, an image exists through which one may discern beauty and ugliness; yet that reflection has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Know that the marks and signs of a Tathāgata are likewise so.
Thus did the Deva Vimuktiprabha realize regarding the universal manifestation of sounds from every pore of the Buddha’s body.
(Entering the third sutra). △ Second, the eight sections on the assembly of the Four Great Kings of the Eight Divisions. The first four sections all begin with a celestial being;
their meanings are explained as previously stated. First, the Gandharva King. 2. First, the prose section on attaining the Dharma.
Furthermore, the Gandharva King Dhṛtarāṣṭra (up to) "the liberation door of gathering all sentient beings" refers to the Heavenly King of the East.
This means that through both gathering and subduing, he employs manifold skillful means—whether in accordance with or contrary to circumstances—to respond appropriately to the capacities of beings;
therefore, he is named "Sovereign."
The Gandharva King Tree-Light attained the liberation door of universally beholding all adornments of merit.
This means that he causes sentient beings to behold all the Buddha’s adornments of merit; even a single hair of the Buddha brings benefit, and each and every one is likewise so.
Therefore, it is called "universal beholding."
The Gandharva King Viśuddhanetra (up to) attained the liberation door of the "Treasury of Joy Arising from Sorrow and Suffering.
Through the skillful means of compassion, joy arises when sorrow is removed. Since sorrow and suffering are as vast and deep as the ocean, the joy and bliss are likewise inexhaustible;
hence it is called a "treasury. Thus, worldly sorrow and joy arise from gain and loss, and gain and loss exist within [the realm of] phenomena.

Sincerity and falsehood, suffering and pleasure, exist within good and bad fortune; good and bad fortune exist within love and hatred. When love and hatred are exhausted, both good and bad fortune and suffering and pleasure vanish.
When sincerity and falsehood cease, benefit and harm, sorrow and joy are forever severed.
Only in this way are sorrow and suffering eternally cut off, and joy and happiness arise.
The Gandharva King Flower-Crown attained the liberation door of eternally severing the delusions of wrong views in all sentient beings;
that is to say, upon attaining the light of the Buddha’s definitive wisdom, all such delusions are eternally severed.
The Gandharva King Joyful Gait Universal Sound (up to) the liberation gate of moistening all sentient beings:

it is like the clouds of loving-kindness providing universal shade, cooling both the well-formed and the ill-formed; the vast clouds of the moisture of wisdom cause the three types of grass and two types of trees to all flourish.
The Gandharva King Delighting in Shaking His Beautiful Eyes (up to: the liberation door that causes all to obtain peace, happiness, and liberation.
He manifests his body to benefit sentient beings; he is "vast" because he universally responds in accordance with their natures, and he is "exquisite" because his marks are pure.
From the Gandharva King Subhāṣitasimhadhvaja up to the gate of liberation of the Jewel of Universal Renown:

when a Buddha appears and preaches the Dharma, this is "Great Renown. Since the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are all termed "Jewels," the meaning of causing these to be heard from afar is expressed as "universally scattering" [the fragrance].
From the Gandharva King Universal Radiance of Jewel Light (up to) the Gate of Liberation of the Pure Body of Radiance: the light from his body shines everywhere;
dust cannot defile it, and all who see him are inevitably filled with joy. His light of wisdom delights the capacities of beings, so that the accumulation of delusions does not arise.
Furthermore, because he is joyful, it is called "Great Joy."
The Gandharva King Vajradrumapuṣpadhvaja (up to) the gate of liberation that causes all who see him to rejoice:
the water of the Dharma universally nourishes the practice of Bodhi. Once this practice is established, all who see it will necessarily rejoice;
there are no longer those of the Two Vehicles, for all are Bodhi-trees.
The Gandharva King Universal Manifestation of Adornments (up to) the gate of bestowing peace, happiness, and liberation upon sentient beings.
The non-obstruction between the one and the many is called the realm of the Buddha. Because the Heavenly King’s wisdom is penetrating, it is said that he “skillfully enters” [this realm].
△ Second, the verse praises the Buddha.
At that time, the Gandharva King Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke these verses:
"The realms of the Buddhas have immeasurable gates; this Path, Samantaghoṣa, is able to awaken to and enter them all."
The first five [points] are understandable.
"The Buddha’s body is pure and all delight in beholding it" (up to) "his beautiful eyes provide excellent instruction herein.
The first phrase refers to the manifestation of the body; the second phrase means that all in the world—where "world" refers to all beings—attain peace and happiness, which is inexhaustible.

"Bliss" (*sukha*) is a general designation. It means that when a Buddha appears in the world, his shadow covers all who stand beneath it. If they are among humans or devas, he manifests increased happiness;
if they are in the lower realms of suffering, for seven days their bodies and minds experience peace and bliss, until they ultimately attain the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, it is called "inexhaustible. The next phrase specifically indicates the bliss of the supramundane cause and effect, beginning first with the cause.
The subsequent result. Both the previous life and the subsequent life are matters of sequential progression. Furthermore, taking the general meaning of the verse:
the purity of the Buddha’s body is the cause of liberation; the arising of inexhaustible bliss is the fruit of liberation.

The inexhaustible bliss of the world is both the cause of liberation and the ability to manifest a pure body, which is the fruit of liberation. Moreover, the purity of the Buddha’s body is the cause for being joyfully beheld.
Being pleasing to behold is the fruit of a pure body. That sentient beings find one pleasing to behold is the cause of peace and happiness.

Inexhaustible peace and happiness is the fruit of being pleasing to behold. Inexhaustible peace and happiness is the cause of a pure body. Being able to manifest pure karma is the inexhaustible fruit.
Such successive causes and fruits are called "gradual accomplishment."
"Sentient beings, deluded, constantly transmigrate... up to "...King Siṃhadhvaja can expound upon this.

The first two phrases concern the jewel-treasure that saves those with the capacity [for enlightenment]. "Firm" means difficult to destroy; "dense" means without gaps or intervals—where there is no empty space, wisdom cannot arise.
The next phrase refers to the actual scattering of the jewels.

Regarding the passage from "The Tathāgata universally manifests his wondrously colored body" up to "one should contemplate the Buddha with such wondrous sounds," the concluding phrase should have read:
"universally emitting precious light, one sees him thus. That it says "wondrous sounds" instead is an error by the translator.
“Wondrous Sound. Because it belongs to the preceding Lion Banner, there are immeasurable gates of great wisdom and skillful means (extending to) this well-observed Vajra Banner.

The first two phrases signify that the water of the Dharma universally nourishes; the next phrase signifies that the tree of the Path universally flourishes. Furthermore, the gates of skillful means are manifold.
This is the opening of the provisional. Entering into the practice of bodhi is the manifestation of the real. The various skillful means are solely for the sake of the One Vehicle;
this is universal nourishment.
Within a single kṣaṇa, [one attains] hundreds of thousands of kalpas [of cultivation], up to this liberation of the adornment of bliss.

The first two phrases refer to the Buddha’s realm. The next phrase refers to peace and bliss. "The Buddha’s power can manifest" means that it is unshakeable, which serves to exclude false perceptions.
It does not mean that many kalpas are compressed into a single kṣaṇa, nor that a single kṣaṇa is expanded to endure for many kalpas;
its original characteristics remain as they were, and thus it is called "unshakeable. According to those who are to be saved, the Buddha’s power causes them to see [this]. Part Two.
Regarding the second, King Kūṭadanta: first, the prose section on attaining the Dharma;
next, the gate of liberation of the Kumbhāṇḍa king Vardhana, who attains the power to extinguish all enmity and harm.
This is the Heavenly King of the South. Both internal afflictions and external enemies are termed "hostile harms. By abiding in the power of patience, he is able to subdue them both.
The Dragon Lord and Kumbhāṇḍa King have attained the liberation door of the ocean-like gateway for cultivating boundless practices.
The practice of the two benefits is called a "gate" because it leads toward the fruit; being profound and vast beyond fathoming, it is named the "Boundless Ocean.
The Kumbhāṇḍa King Adorned Banner attained the liberation gate of knowing the inclinations and understandings of the minds of all sentient beings.
Knowing their manifest desires, he tames them through appropriate transformations and benefits them;
this is the liberation door of the Kumbhāṇḍa King Ādarśamukha, who performs great luminous deeds.
For those of dull faculties, it is manifested through spiritual powers; for those of sharp wisdom, it is shown through the Dharma.
Pervading the world throughout many kalpas, it is called "Universal Accomplishment. Being like empty space, it is termed "Pure. Capable of illuminating the world, it is "Radiance."
The three wheels of transformation are the karma that has been performed.

It is the gate of liberation to the path of peace and fearlessness from the terrifying Kumbhāṇḍa kings [down to] the world’s delusions and sufferings, which are fearsome and unstable; and to bodhi and nirvāṇa, which are peaceful, fearless, and characterized by the myriad practices.
As for the path of its cause, it is that the fear of the cessation of results is brought to fulfillment.
The Kumbhāṇḍa King Subhavyūha attained the liberation door of exhausting the ocean of craving and desire of all sentient beings.
The ocean of craving and desire is deep and vast; when the sun of wisdom shines brilliantly, the false is exhausted and true clarity appears.
The Gopaka King of Wisdom attained the liberation door of the "Cloud of Radiance Universally Manifesting in All Realms."
This refers to manifesting clouds of bodies throughout all realms of existence, like the flashing lightning of supernormal powers and radiance.
The Kumbhāṇḍa King Vīrabhuja attained the liberation door of universally emitting light to extinguish mountain-like heavy obstructions.
The radiance of the body and wisdom dispels the two obscurations;
[this is] the gate of liberation called the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Great Compassion" of the Kumbhāṇḍa King Ananta-viśuddha-padma-netra, up to [the gate of] non-retrogression.

Having cultivated compassion for many eons, one ultimately extinguishes suffering and becomes non-retrogressive. Because this compassion involves manifold skillful means, it is further named a "Treasury.
It is revealed and taught in order to bring peace to sentient beings.
The Kumbhāṇḍa King Vast Face attained the liberation door of universally manifesting bodies that circulate through all realms of existence;
his supernatural powers accord with the true nature of reality, such that he flows through saṃsāra without coming or going. △ Second, the verses in praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the Kumbhāṇḍa King Vardhana (up to) spoke these verses:
"The World Teacher has accomplished the power of patience... (up to) therefore his body is most majestic and pure."
Pervasive Clarity. The Buddha has already extinguished arrogance (*māna*). Of all forms of arrogance, none exceeds pride (*māna*). To possess it is to be base and vulgar;
to extinguish it is to be dignified and majestic.
"The Buddha of old universally cultivated the ocean of all practices" (up to) "the Fearless One is able to contemplate this Dharma-gate.
The preceding four [lines] may be understood as they stand.
"Drowning in the ocean of desire, possessing manifold sufferings" (up to) "this is what the Wondrously Adorned One has realized."
The first line concerns the ocean of desire; since desire is the root of suffering, it is said to be "endowed with manifold sufferings. The following two lines concern its exhaustion and drying up;
once desire and evil have ceased, one should then expound upon virtuous conduct.
The Buddha’s body universally responds so that there is nowhere it is not seen... (up to)... thus does the Dharma-gate enter through High Wisdom (*Ghoṣadatta*).
The first phrase refers to the universal manifestation of clouds of bodies; the second phrase clarifies the equality of lightning flashes, hence the term "various.

The third phrase further clarifies thunder and rain. Thunder has two meanings: first, its distant resonance; second, its power to bring forth, meaning the arousal of hibernating insects and the growth of grasses.
As trees send forth their sprouts, the thunder of the perfect sound can be taken as a standard for reflection.
This pure and radiant light does not arise in vain; it is that which is realized by the mind of this King Viśālamukha.
△ Third, the assembly of nāga kings. According to the verse and the Sanskrit manuscript, there are eleven [sections]; however, the prose commentary omits the fifth, containing only ten dharmas.
First, the prose commentary on the attainment of the dharma.
Furthermore, from the Dragon King Virūpākṣa (up to) the liberation gate of manifesting the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings:
the first is the Heavenly King of the West; the dharma-gate and the second shall be explained according to the verse.
From the Dragon King Cloud-Sound Banner (to the point where he) expounds the liberation door of the ocean of the Buddha’s boundless names, there are six meanings throughout the verses:
first, the various realms of existence, which are the places of transformation; second, pure sound, which is the instrument of transformation.

1. The names of the three Buddhas: these are the manifestations of the teaching (dharmaparinirmita). 2. The four supernormal powers (abhijñā): these are the basis of the manifestation (parinirmāṇamūla). 3. Sentient beings: these are the objects of the manifestation (parinirmāṇālambana). 4. According to their inclinations:
this is the intention of the manifestation (parinirmāṇābhiprāya).

The Dragon King Jvālāmukha attained the liberation door of "universally manifesting the distinctions of boundless Buddha-worlds," which means that within a single pore he universally manifests infinite environments and inhabitants.
This is because the nature of a pore is capable of vast containment, and such vast containment is itself universal.
The Buddhas who are manifested likewise abide within the lands manifested inside their own pores.

Subject and object are not intermingled; the environment and its inhabitants are clearly distinguished; the large and small are perfectly distinct—this is called the differentiation of establishment. The Fivefold Stillness Sūtra states:

According to the Sanskrit original, there is the Dragon King Jvālā, who attained the liberation door of "The Tathāgata’s Compassionate Regard Causing the Elimination of the Obscurations and Entanglements of Hatred and Delusion in All Sentient Beings.
This means that when great compassion dwells within one's heart, the three poisons are simultaneously extinguished.
However, there is a version of the text that states: "The Dragon King Yaṃkhu attained the liberation door of universally manifesting boundless Buddha-worlds and establishing their distinctions.
Following this version, "establishing distinctions" refers to transforming beings according to their individual capacities.
The Dragon King Meghadhvaja attained the liberation door of the ocean of merit and great joy revealed to all sentient beings.

Because the Buddha’s great compassion is this ocean of merit, and because it is attained only after the two provisions are fulfilled, the compassionate merit of sentient beings is like the hundred rivers.
The Buddha manifests these within a single pore to signify their identical essence (*sārabhāva*). Once one knows they share this same essence, [it occurs] naturally.
The Gate of the Dragon King Takṣaka’s Attainment of Great Joy and Bliss through Manifesting Awakening and Entry, and the Elimination of All Fears.
Because his compassionate voice is conjoined with wisdom, it is called "pure. Being pure and free from craving and attachment, what is there to fear or worry about?

This concludes the section on the Dragon King Anantapada (Boundless Steps), up to the gate of liberation consisting of the sequential understanding of the Buddha’s physical body and the succession of kalpas.
That is to say, within his body, he manifested the lands and realms;
this was the liberation door of the Dragon King Pure Color Swift Movement (Vimalavarṇa-śīghravikrama), extending to the Ocean of Great Affectionate Joy and Delight.
Because he contemplates the profound and vast conduct of the Buddha in the past, he feels love, joy, and delight. The term "ocean" (sāgara) here applies to both joy and making offerings.
This refers to the liberation door of the Dragon King Universal Conduct Great Sound, known as "Delightful Unobstructed Sound."
He manifests sounds for the sake of the multitude; therefore, it is called "manifestation. There are four meanings of "sound": first, it is manifold, meaning "all";
second, it is universal, meaning "impartial"; third, it is elegant and refined according to their faculties, hence it is called "pleasing"; fourth, it is a single sound that adapts to each type.
Therefore, it is called "unimpeded. Unimpededness is itself skillful means.
[The liberation gate of] the Dragon King Without Heat and Affliction... [up to] ...extinguishing all suffering of the world.
This refers to the Anavatapta Dragon, who dwells in the Cool Lake and produces fragrant, exquisite water that flows into the four oceans and guides the hundred rivers.
He spreads clouds of compassion and pours down sweet rain; thus, he is able to extinguish all the sufferings of the world.
△ Second, the verses in praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the Naga King Virūpākṣa (up to: spoke in verse.
There were eleven stanzas:
"Behold, the Dharma of the Tathāgata is ever thus" (up to: "...he draws out those who have fallen into the perilous path."
Nāgas have four types of burning afflictions known as the "Suffering of Intense Heat," all of which now have remedies.
First, the suffering of being devoured by the golden-winged bird (garuḍa) is remedied by the first phrase, because through contemplating the Buddha-dharma, one becomes identical to the Triple Refuge.

Second, the suffering of returning to one's original form at the time of engaging in sexual desire, and third, the suffering from minute insects within the scales and shell, are both remedied by the second phrase, because one learns the equal benefits of the Buddha and others.
The fourth is the suffering of hot sands adhering to the body. The latter two lines serve as its remedy: because they cannot endure the itching caused by insects, they are cast into the hot sands;
now, through great compassion and pity, he is able to remedy this. Some say that in these four sufferings there are no scale-covered or minute insects.

Yet there is the suffering of the wind blowing against the precious robes and exposing the body; this is also remedied by the second line. Regarding the dragon, it specifically addresses the dragon realm;
the final line universally uproots [suffering] from the perilous path for all beings, including the Buddha.
"All sentient beings, with their various differences... [up to] Vāsava—thus one contemplates the Buddha.

This is explained from the perspective of the Buddha’s manifesting power. The previous passage concerning the dragon spoke of his ability to transform; furthermore, while the former "single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*) was brief in time, the present "single hair-pore" (*ekaroma-vivara*) is small in space. These two texts are thus mutually abbreviated.
The Buddha, by means of his infinite power of supernormal faculties, [reached] the Great Dragon Anāthapiṇḍada, who was able to awaken to this.
The remaining nine may be understood accordingly; however, the fifth verse is that which was previously omitted. △ Fourth, the assembly of yakṣas, in two parts:
first, the prose section on attaining the Dharma.
Furthermore, [this is] the liberation gate of the Yakṣa King Vaiśravaṇa (up to) "protecting and rescuing evil sentient beings.
He is the Heavenly King of the North. Regarding the phrase "attaining the boundless," etc.:

it means that while the virtuous find joy of their own accord without waiting for compassion to be bestowed upon them, the hearts of those who are evil are naturally biased toward their suffering. Because he skillfully employs many methods to rescue them, it is called "boundless. Moreover, this...
"O Deva, you are able to subdue evil spirits and prevent them from harming sentient beings; this is true protection.
The Yakṣa King Svayambhūnirghoṣa attained the liberation door of skillful means for universally observing sentient beings and providing their protection and deliverance.
Observing with wisdom and rescuing with compassion, they save those in suffering and protect the virtuous; because they do not stagnate in emptiness or existence, this is called "skillful means.
This is the liberation door of the Yakṣa King Adorned with Weapons (up to) liberating all extremely weak and wicked sentient beings.
Those whose karmic obstacles from evil deeds are heavy are called "extremely weak and wicked. Furthermore, being weak means lacking the power of goodness; this refers to the icchantikas.
"Evil" here signifies depravity; those who slander the Vaipulya sutras are clearly shown the wondrous principle, which serves as their nourishment and benefit.
The Great Wisdom Yakṣa King attained the liberation door of extolling the ocean of all noble merits;
he emulated the Buddha and praised the Buddha, thereby attaining the fruit of renown.
The Flame-Eyed Lord Yakṣa King attained the liberation door of the great compassionate wisdom that universally observes all sentient beings.
The two illuminations of compassion and wisdom merge into a single mind, which coexists with the *dharmakāya*;
therefore, he constantly observes the liberation gate of the Vajranetra Yakṣa King, which brings benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.
The Wondrous Voice preaches the Dharma, benefiting beings in manifold ways; its sound reaches only those who are ready for deliverance and can thus benefit them.
The Yakṣa King Brave Arm has attained the liberation door of universally entering into the meaning of all dharmas.
The teachings are vast and the principles are profound; to be able to expound even a single phrase is itself universal entry.
This is the liberation door of the Yakṣa King Courageous Foe-of-Great-Armies (through to) causing [beings] to abide in the Path so that none pass it by in vain.

To cause beings to leave the wrong and abide in the right is to provide protection. However, those who abide in the right path do not discriminate between what is wrong and what is right; this is called "inconceivable."
The liberation door of the Yakṣa King Dhana-datta (extending to): causing [beings] to constantly experience happiness;
gathering the causes of merit and receiving the fruits of happiness; and attaining increase through the light of physical wisdom.
The Yakṣa King Power-Destroyer-of-High-Mountains (up to) the liberation door of the light of wisdom born from the Buddha’s power.
Recalling the Buddha and cultivating the cause gives rise to the fruit of the ten powers; because the heavens have not yet realized the ultimate, it is called "conforming.
△ Second, the verse praising the Buddha.
At that time, the Great Yakṣa King Bahumukha (and others) spoke these verses:
"The evil karma of sentient beings is deeply terrifying; this is fully understood by the King of the High Banner."
The ten verses have clear wording and are easily understood. △ Fifth, the assembly of mahoragas, in two parts. First, the prose section on attaining the Dharma:
"Furthermore, the Mahoraga King Good Wisdom (up to) the gate of liberation for causing sentient beings to accumulate merit."

Universally manifesting majestic light is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*). Because it demonstrates the cause of nirvāṇa through an unmoving and intrinsically pure nature, it is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*).
By relying on these causes to accumulate merit, one will necessarily attain the nirvāṇa that is without dependence.
From the Mahoraga King Pure Majestic Sound (up to) the liberation gate of attaining coolness and joyful bliss:
the elimination of delusions and the realization of tranquility is the cause of coolness; coolness and joyful bliss are the fruit of nirvāṇa.
From the Mahoraga King Adorned with the Crest of Supreme Compassion (up to) the liberation door of entering the pure Dharma:
that which is good, he validates as good; that which is not good, the Buddha reveals as good. When the Good Awakening reveals non-existence, one then enters fundamental purity.
From the Mahoraga King Subhāṣitanetra up to the liberation gate of the equal marks of mastery over merit:
the marks of merit and non-merit are such that defilement cannot be attached to them; non-merit manifests as merit, which is called the mark of mastery.
That all Buddhas are non-dual is the mark of equality.
The Dharma-door of liberation for the Mahoraga King Lamp-Standard, which causes one to leave behind the path of fear of darkness:
ignorance is the black cause, which the lamp reveals; fear is the fruit of suffering, for which the banner serves as a refuge.
From the Mahoraga King Supreme Radiance Banner (up to) the liberation door of giving rise to joy:
because he knows that the Buddha’s virtues are identical to emptiness and equal to his own single nature, he experiences joy.
From the Lion-Chested Mahoraga King to the Gate of Liberation of the Lord of Rescue and Protection:

seeing principle leads to decisive judgment; hearing the profound does not cause fear; hearing the shallow does not cause doubt; and hearing that which is neither profound nor shallow, one possesses courageous resolve.
Unshaken by the eight winds, this constitutes heroic power. Having already rectified oneself, one is necessarily able to rectify others. For this purpose...
The Mahoraga King named Savior of the Multitude with Wondrously Adorned Sound attained the liberation door of generating boundless joy and bliss because he cultivated the causes of joy in the past;
thus, all who see or think of him rejoice.
From the Mahoraga King Sumerumūrdhan (up to) the Gate of Liberation of Reaching the Further Shore and Fulfillment:
when the realization of principle and wisdom is perfected, one then conditions immovability. Wisdom is the root of practice; all the perfections (*pāramitās*) are thereby made complete.
It is like the ocean receiving the hundred rivers, after which they no longer flow as such.
The Mahoraga King Delightful Radiance [attains] the liberation gate of revealing the path of equality.

He reveals the principle of the equality of all beings, demonstrates the correspondence of all Buddhas, destroys the inequality of emotional attachments, and causes the realization of the equality of nature as the path of equanimity.
△ Second, the verses in praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the mahoraga Śubhamatitejas (up to) spoke these verses:
"Behold the nature of the Tathāgata, which is pure; this wondrous radiance is able to enter [it] well."
The ten verses follow in sequence; their meaning is clear and may be understood from the text.
*Da fangguang fo huayan jing shu*, Scroll Eight.
*Da fangguang fo huayan jing shu*, Scroll Nine.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang;
recorded and annotated on the sūtra by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.
△ Sixth: The Kinnara King (2). First: Attaining the Dharma through prose exposition.
Furthermore, from the "Light of Good Wisdom" up to the liberation door of "Universally Producing All Joyful and Blissful Karmas," it is said:
all karmas that bring joy and bliss to the world arise from the Buddha.
The Gate of Liberation of the Kinnara King Wondrous Flower Banner (up to) Causing All to Attain Peaceful Bliss:
Hearing that which is profound and suits the spirit, one experiences unsurpassed joy in the Dharma, ultimately attaining the inexhaustible peace and bliss of nirvana.
The various adornments of the Kinnara King [up to] the liberation door of the treasury of pure faith and understanding.
The virtues of the Buddha are profound and vast; faith likewise encompasses them all.
The Kinnara King Pleasing Roar [attains] the gate of liberation for causing those who hear him to be free from sorrow and fear;
because he proclaims the True Dharma with his voice so that they may hear it, their false anxieties are removed and their minds become joyful.
From the Kinnara King Ratnavṛkṣaprabha [up to] the liberation door of causing awakening to objects of perception:
realizing that objects are merely mind and fundamentally empty, one establishes sentient beings in awakening.
The Universal Joy-Seeing Kinnara King attained the liberation door of manifesting all wondrously colored bodies.
It is difficult to encounter and brings benefit to living beings; thus he manifests them. Their marks are eternally adorned, and this is what is called "wondrous color."
