Their fundamental delusion is beginningless, like one born blind; though they hear metaphors, they ultimately do not recognize milk. Only when a Buddha appears in the world can they [do so].

I have explained this. The ninth corresponds to the Sanskrit original, which says: "The City-Ruling Goddess Fragrant Banner Adorned Topknot attains the liberation door of giving rise to the fragrance of the nature of all-knowledge by destroying the stench of all afflictions.

This means that even if one is like a foul object, habitual tendencies are the stench, the nature of wisdom is the fragrant substance, and benefiting sentient beings is the fragrance. As for the fragrance...
Like clouds emerging from a high mountain, their wisdom-nature is inexhaustible; like a fragrant breeze rolling up mist, their equality with emptiness is boundless.
Thus, afflictions are simultaneously extinguished along with habitual tendencies, and wisdom benefits both oneself and others.
This is the fundamental endowment of the City-Ruling Goddess named *Gandhakeśaravyūha*, who develops the purity of sentient beings.
The "Gate of Liberation through Pure and Sublime Wisdom" is also [present here], though it has been omitted in transcription; its meaning does not differ from what precedes it.
As for the verse stating "manifesting within a dream": a dream is the wandering of the spirit (*manas*), and it is also a derivative aspect of one's sensory perceptions.
If one can achieve mastery even within a dream, how much more so when awake? This is as in the case of Kātyāyana, who manifested dream-realms for his disciples, and so forth.
The City-Ruling Spirit Jewel-Peak-Luminous-Eye (up to) the Gate of Liberation for Shattering the Mountains of Obstacles of All Sentient Beings.
The two obstacles and the five hindrances are heaped up like mountains; were it not for the light of wisdom, they could not be shattered.
△ Second, the verse eulogy praising the Buddha.
At that time, the city-ruling goddess Jewel Peak Radiance (up to: spoke these verses:
"The Guide is thus inconceivable... (up to: such is the entry of Jewel Peak."
△ Second, the Sixteen Deities of the Site of Enlightenment. First, the prose section on eleven dharmas.
Furthermore, from the Deity of the Site of Enlightenment named Banner of Pure Adornment (up to) the Gate of Liberation through the Power of Vows.
The appearance of the letter is used in two ways: namely, when a Buddha appears, one immediately manifests ornaments to make offerings.
The Buddhas of the past were thus; the deity emulates them through great vows.
From the Sumeru Jewel Light Ritual Ground Deity up to the liberation door of accomplishing vast bodhisattva practices:
one accomplishes practice by means of objects and causes others to emulate them. Since the performance of giving is the precursor to all practice, the verse cites it universally.
The Dharma-door of liberation manifested by the Site-Spirit Thunder-Sound Banner-Phase (up to): within a dream, she expounds the Dharma for them;
both the dreaming and the waking states are transformations, such that time and place are simultaneously pervasive.
The Dharma-door of Liberation of the Site-Protecting Spirit Wondrous Eye Raining Flowers (up to): "Adorned with Various Jewels.

Because she possesses external jewels and internal vision, and because she practices and preaches for the sake of sentient beings despite the repeated difficulty of relinquishing them, she is said to be "able to rain [jewels]."
The Deity of the Pure Flame-Shaped Dharma-Field (up to): "The Gate of Widely Transforming Sentient Beings to Bring Them to Maturity and Liberation.

Regarding the deity of the pure flame-form, he was not included in the previous list. This refers to the dharma-field of form-and-appearance, which is exquisitely adorned in its entirety, all for the purpose of maturing sentient beings.
The Dharma-door of the Ritual Ground Deity (Dharmapathadevatā) for generating right mindfulness by preaching the Dharma according to the faculties [of beings]:
those who doubt objective realms take "mind-only" as right mindfulness; those who doubt the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) take "non-attainment" as right mindfulness.
In reality, there is neither right nor wrong; only then can it be called "right. To have no thought and no non-thought—this is true mindfulness.
No discursive thoughts arise; only right mindfulness arises. Thus, according to their faculties, they rain down the Dharma, severing doubt and giving birth to wisdom.
This is the liberation door of the Spirit Who Adorns the Site of Enlightenment by Raining Jewels, which universally rains down the Dharma of boundless joy.
The rain of Dharma from eloquence brings joy because it accords with the faculties [of beings].
The dharma-door of attaining liberation through the incense-eyed bodhisattva of the site of enlightenment, Vigorous Praise, consists in the extensive praise of the merits of all Buddhas;
because he praises the Buddhas with such depth and breadth, his name and reality are both beautiful.
The liberation door of the Vajra-Variegated Clouds Ritual Ground Deity (extending to) Adorning the Ritual Ground;
the Tree King and his retinue are all as described at the beginning of the sutra.
The liberation door of the Lotus Radiance Ritual Ground Deity (extending to) pervading the ten directions.
That is to say, his body pervades the ten directions yet there is no coming or going; his wisdom enters into all phenomena, realizing that all dharmas are empty and quiescent.
The goddess of the site of enlightenment attained the liberation door of manifesting the various powers of the Tathāgata through the radiance of wondrous light.
Because the Buddha possesses immeasurable power, his causal practices are likewise so; all are manifested through adornments.
Since he is the deity of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he attains liberation within the affairs of the site of enlightenment. △ Second, the verses in praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the goddess of the path-maṇḍala named Pure Adornment Banner (Viśuddhavyūhadhvaja), from [the point where she was seated] up to [her rising], spoke in verse.
There were eleven verses.
"I recall the Tathāgata in times past... [up to] "...this goddess Sublime Light (Prabhāsvarā) is able to hear and receive [it]."
△ Section Seventeen: The Two Devas of the Footsteps. First, the prose section on attaining the Dharma.
Furthermore, the Deva of the Footsteps named Ratnamudrā (up to) the Gate of Liberation for Causing Those Who See to Rejoice.
The first two [goddesses] may be understood as before.
From the "Goddess of Footsteps, Supreme Flower Topknot" up to the "Gate of Liberation of the Assembly Site of All Tathāgatas":
internally, she abides in every thought-moment within the principle and phenomena; externally, she establishes sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) everywhere.
The liberation door of the deity Supratisthitacaraṇa, who gathers all virtuous visions, taming infinite sentient beings through every movement of raising and lowering the feet;
by the manifestation of the Ocean Seal, every posture and deportment is none other than the work of the Buddha.
From the liberation door of the foot-traveling spirit Wondrous Jewel Star Banner (up to) Universal Rain of All Jewels Producing Exquisite Sounds,
they shower flowers and light, raining down jewels and the Dharma.
The footstep-traversing spirit Delightful Utterance of Wondrous Sounds attained the liberation door of "giving birth to an ocean of boundless joy.
Sentient beings are infinite, and they constitute the realm of the Buddha's transformation; because they see the Buddha and hear the Dharma, they give rise to joy.
From the Sandalwood Tree Radiance Foot-Walking Spirit up to the Universal Awakening of All Assemblies at the Site of Enlightenment Liberation Gate:
With a perfect voice that awakens all beings, it is like the fragrant breeze of sandalwood; by being perfumed by it even for a moment, one’s body and mind become harmonious and compliant.
The Lotus-Light Foot-Walking Spirit [up to] the liberation door of causing all sentient beings to give rise to an ocean of roots of goodness.
△ Second, praising the Buddha in verse.
At that time, the foot-attendant spirit Ratnamudrā (up to) spoke these verses:
"In the past, the Buddha practiced for immeasurable eons... having seen this, my heart gives rise to great joy."
△ Second, the eighteen classes of body-deity spirits. First, the prose section on attaining the Dharma:
Furthermore, the Body-Deity Spirit of the Realm of Pure Joy attained the liberation door of recollecting the ocean of the Buddha’s past vows.

The initial listing of locations is titled "Adorned with Flower Topknots" (*Puṣpamaulivibhūṣita*). This may be a case where the full name was abbreviated by citing only half of it, or it may be a translation error resulting from the similarity of Sanskrit phonemes;
the original Sanskrit source for this *dharmaparyāya* has not yet been verified.
The body-deity named Illuminating the Ten Directions brings forth the liberation door of causing [beings] to rejoice, be tamed, and attain deliverance.
The first three [sections] may be understood as before.
The body-deity named Pure Flower Adorned Topknot attains the liberation door of a body like space that dwells pervasively everywhere.
Because characteristics are themselves without characteristics, they dwell pervasively like space. Space is not merely void; it also pervades form.
This dwelling is not a partial dwelling; even a single atom is all-pervasive, just as the space within a mustard seed is inexhaustible. For the body and the dharma-nature cannot be divided.
The multitude of deities of immeasurable dignified conduct attain the liberation door of manifesting to all sentient beings the realm of all Buddhas.
Their dignified conduct and activities appear instantaneously without thought; this is the realm of the Buddha, difficult to conceive through words or thought.
The Liberation Gate of the Devas of the Most Victorious Radiant Adorned Body (up to): "Satisfying the physical strength of hungry and destitute sentient beings.
The Buddha is the excellent field; his appearance in the world is difficult to encounter. By making even a slight offering once, one obtains the five constants.

To speak briefly of physical strength, there are also constant life, peace and happiness, and eloquence. These five are all constant; only when they are complete can they be called "satisfaction," as one receives this retribution.
Because it is inexhaustible, they are entirely freed from poverty.
The body-host goddess Pure Radiant Fragrant Clouds attained the liberation door of removing the defilements of affliction from all sentient beings.
The light of her teeth removes impurities, signifying the purity of that which she proclaims.
The deity who guards and sustains the body attains the liberation door of transforming the demonic activities of ignorance in all sentient beings.
To be stained by the five sensory objects and to lack compassion for those in the six realms of existence is the demonic activity of ignorance.

By realizing the nature of the five desires, emptying oneself, and causing both self and others to transcend [delusion], that karma is transformed; thus it is called "guarding" and "sustaining. "Sustaining" means to guard well.
By guarding the gates of the sense faculties, collecting the distracted mind, and maintaining virtue, one remains far from Māra. Yet the delusions of Māra do not exceed the three poisons and pride;

the afflictions of Māra that distress sentient beings do not exceed three matters: namely, the five exquisite sensual desires, various instruments of suffering, and the preaching of false teachings—through which the three poisons arise.
When the three poisons are internally attached, this constitutes the activity of Māra. Now, [one must] protect...
Awareness—how can Māra affect it? This refers to the path of liberation within the verses.
[The section] from "The Universal Manifestation of the Retinue of Transformation Bodies and Spirits" up to "The Gate of Liberation of Displaying Adorned Marks."

There are three intentions [behind this]: first, although his body pervades the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), he frequently manifests as a king because he possesses sovereign power over the governance and control [of beings];

second, while possessing the eight marks of excellence, he dwells in the royal palace to look down upon and engage with sentient beings; third, within the dharma-realm, he remains beneath the Bodhi tree.
Because it is the palace of the Dharma King, [the deities] from the Immovable Radiance Body Devas (down to... all cause the arising of the liberation door of pure roots of goodness.
Because one is deluded regarding original emptiness, there is delusive suffering; that which is untainted and originally present is the pure root of goodness. △ Second, the verses.
Praising the Buddha with verses, at that time the host of deities of the Pure Joy Realm (up to) spoke these verses:
"I recall an eon as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru ago... [as seen] by the deity Immovable Light."
△ Nineteenth: Two Vajrapāṇi Devas. First, the prose section on attaining the Dharma.
Furthermore, the Vajrapāṇi Deva of Wondrous Color Nārāyaṇa [attains] the liberation door of the body of boundless color-forms.

One perceives that the body of the Tathāgata manifests universally and is not distinct; not only is every place where it appears characterized by boundless marks, but each and every individual form and characteristic is likewise without limit.
The Vajrapāṇi deity Sūryamaṇḍalaprabhāśīghravaijayanta [attains] the liberation door of obtaining infinite voices that accord with all types of beings.
The three preceding [deities] may be understood accordingly.
The Vajrapāṇi deity Subāhu-devendra [attains] the liberation door of awakening sentient beings.
In the first fascicle, his name is given as "Exquisite Faculties" (Zhūgēn Měimiào), yet it is simply called "Exquisite Arms" (Miàobì); thus both the text and its meaning are deficient.
Furthermore, he is like the Lord of Devas, who is manifested as the Lord of the World.
The liberation door of the Vajra-holding deity Lovely Radiance (Priyakara-prabha), which exhausts all things without exception;
[this door] wherein the profound depths of the ocean of Dharma and its various classifications are skillfully explained and made manifest, leaving nothing remaining.
From the Vajra-holding spirit Mahādrumameghasvara up to the liberation gate of "Gathering All Trees," regarding the spirits,
they are adorned with jewel ornaments and skillfully gather their own retinues; regarding the Buddha, he is adorned with the marks and signs of skillful means,
such that there is nothing he does not gather.
From the Lion-King Radiance Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva down to all [the others], they are fully endowed with the gates of clear understanding and liberation.
Because their cause is profound, their great merit serves as adornment; because their fruit is supreme, their marks of virtue are all luminous and complete.
The Vajrapāṇi deity Ghanajvālāśrīnetra (up to) the liberation gate of manifesting a majestic body.
"Evil" refers to the ten non-virtues. "Perilous" refers to the causes of evil, for they can cause oneself and others to fall into perilous paths.
From the Vajra-holding deity Padma-maṇi-śikhara to the liberation gate of the Maṇi-śikhara adorned with ornaments:
if taken according to the literal text, the maṇi-crest is that which rains;

if taken according to the meaning, this deity is named Maṇi-śikhara, and the crest itself is also that which rains—the ornaments of all bodhisattvas, which are what is rained down, representing bodhi.
Because the light of his wisdom is perfectly complete. △ Second, the verses in praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi deity Viśvarūpa Nārāyaṇa (up to) spoke these verses:
"You should contemplate the Dharma-King; the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus" (up to) "revealing the sphere of the Buddha's activity.
Regarding the sixth verse, as for the term *āvarta* (whirlpool): it refers to a place where water swirls and eddies, because it is profoundly deep.
Second, because of its revolutions; third, because it is difficult to cross. The whirlpools of the ocean of Dharma are likewise: first, because only a Buddha can fathom them;
second, because truth and falsehood revolve around one another, making it difficult to discern their beginning or end;

and third, because hearing of emptiness and taking it to be empty causes one to sink into the whirlpools, while hearing of existence and taking it to be existent is similarly understood. Thus, it is said that these are all the various meanings of differentiation.
The section on ordinary beings concludes.
*Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Fascicle Ten.
*Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Fascicle Eleven (Entering the Fifth Scripture).
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang;
recorded and annotated on the sutra by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.
△ From here below is the second section: the assembly of co-nascent beings (sahaja-sattva). First, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva attains all dharma-gates.
Second. The first [part] consists of the prose section, which has two [subdivisions]. First, the general indication of what is entered:
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra enters the ocean of skillful means of the inconceivable gates of liberation.
To describe the essence of the Dharma: that which is called "inconceivable" means that its number exceeds all calculation and its principle transcends both speech and thought.

That which is called the "ocean of skillful means" means that while remaining unmoved from the truth, one accomplishes worldly affairs; because one skillfully accords with the fruit through the gateway of causes, it is termed "skillful means."
They enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s merits through their skillful discernment of the Dharma; that is to say, they enter by perfecting the causes and proceed toward the ocean of the fruit.

However, since the preceding and following sections merely clarify the entry from the particular into the universal, each attains a single gate of liberation, just as the myriad rivers each flow into the sea.
Now it is clarified that the general enters the general, like the ocean entering the ocean; thus one attains the inconceivable gate of liberation.
Furthermore, this "ability to enter" is termed the "Ocean of Expedient Means," because Samantabhadra is the foremost leader of both the identical and distinct assemblies.
II. Specifically revealing ten gates to manifest their inexhaustibility.
This refers to the gates of liberation (up to) the taming of sentient beings so that they attain ultimate deliverance.
It means adorning the lands and taming the beings; that is, because one takes up a buddha-field according to the beings to be converted. As for "all buddha-fields": [it refers to]...

Vertically, it penetrates the four lands; horizontally, it encompasses the entire dharma-realm. Since the horizontal and vertical dimensions are mutually interfused, every single atom and every single land is vast, magnificent, and pure.
Thus, it is called "all. By expounding the most wondrous Dharma, it causes those to be disciplined to ultimately achieve liberation.
There is a gate of liberation called "Universally Attaining the Realm of Perfected Merit Cultivated in the Presence of All Tathāgatas.
The Buddha pervades all paths of atoms; by attaining those places and cultivating merit therein, he fully realizes that realm.

There is a gate of liberation called "The Ocean of Great Vows that Establishes All Bodhisattva Stages," which comprehensively elucidates the establishment of six kinds of bodhisattva virtues: first, the stage; second, the vow; and the remaining four are found in the verses.

There is a gate of liberation called "Universally Manifesting Infinite Bodies as Numerous as the Microdusts of the Dharma-realm," wherein the body universally responds to sentient beings according to their capacities and expounds the Dharma realized.
There is a gate of liberation called "Expounding the Inconceivable Number of Distinct Names Pervading All Lands."
The lands differ, and what is revered varies accordingly; thus, names are established according to what is appropriate, so that the resulting benefit is not in vain.
As stated in the "Chapter on Names and Titles," there are gates of liberation (up to) the manifestation of the boundless spheres of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*) of all bodhisattvas.
Manifesting a body within the midst of dust, he expounds the sphere of the bodhisattva’s practice.
There is a gate of liberation called "Manifesting the Events of the Formation and Destruction of the Kalpas of the Three Times within a Single Thought-moment.

By conforming time to the Dharma, he causes the kalpas of the three times and the formation and destruction within those kalpas to be fused and manifested within a single thought-moment. There is no... [omission].
That which is obstructed is ignorance (*moha*). However, the objective basis (*vastu*) encompasses both the agent and the object: the agents of formation and destruction are fire, water, and wind;
the objects formed and destroyed are the heavens, the earth, and the myriad phenomena.
There is a gate of liberation called "Manifesting the Ocean of All Bodhisattvas’ Faculties, Each Entering Its Own Sphere.
Although the ocean of a bodhisattva’s faculties is vast, extensive, and of many kinds, it can only enter the sphere of what they themselves know;

how could it possibly fathom the boundless dharmas of a Buddha? This demonstrates that the previously mentioned oceans of beings had not yet measured the Buddha’s virtues, whereas Samantabhadra was able to.
Knowing this principle,
there is a gate of liberation (extending to) manifesting various bodies that pervade the boundless Dharma-realm;
it clarifies that the Tathāgata’s body is identical to space, while its function encompasses the entire Dharma-realm.

There are gates of liberation that lead to the entry into the vast skillful means of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), wherein the cause is gathered and the fruit is realized; therefore, it is said that "all bodhisattva practices enter into all-knowledge.
Because the Sublime Voice proclaims this, it is said to "reveal" it. This also provides a specific explanation for the second phrase of the heading. △ Second, the verse in praise.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, having universally surveyed the ocean-like assembly, spoke these verses:
"The vast lands adorned by the Buddha [rain down] inconceivable and most wondrous Dharma."

The first half [of the chapter] concerns the purification of the Buddha-field, while the second half concerns the subduing of sentient beings; together they reveal the meaning of "purification" as pertaining to both persons and dharmas.
There are three kinds of sons of the Buddha: the first is the "external son," referring to all ordinary worldlings who have not yet been able to succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas.
There are three types of sons: first, the accidental sons, which refers to those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), because they are not born from the Tathāgata’s Great Dharma;
second, the true sons, which refers to the great bodhisattvas, because they are truly born from the joy of the Great Dharma. These are said to be pure.
This clearly indicates the third [point]. Regarding the "most wondrous Dharma," this distinguishes it from the provisional teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Because the wondrous Dharma previously purified the minds of those to be transformed, the land thus manifested also possesses pure Buddha-sons who come to be born in that realm; there, the wondrous Dharma rains down once again.
"Just as in this assembly one sees the Buddha seated" (up to) "all lands appear clearly.

The first half clarifies that [the light] pervades both the general and the particular; the second half clarifies the non-obstruction between essence and function. This is also [an example of] pervading within the general.
This demonstrates the practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas (up to) causing all Buddha-sons to enter the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

These four phrases correspond to the preceding four meanings: first, cultivating the ten superior practices; second, giving rise to the ten skillful means; third, that which is realized as the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*);
and fourth, correctly realizing the Dharma-realm and accomplishing *sarvajñā* (omniscience). The stages (*bhūmi*) serve as the general framework, while the remaining five [aspects] serve as...
Distinct.
From "The emanation-buddhas produced are as numerous as atoms" up to "vast and boundless,
all are fully expounded," the first half universally manifests the body, while the second half expounds that which has been realized.
It is extremely difficult to fully comprehend the names of the Tathāgatas and so forth, which are equal to the world.
The first four [points] may be understood as above.
The Buddha is like space, free from discrimination; [yet] all sit at the site of enlightenment and attain perfect awakening.

The first phrase refers to the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*). The second phrase refers to knowing the dharmadhātu and so forth. The latter two phrases refer to the pervasive nature of the dharma-body through its transformative functions.
Although these are briefly cited as the aspects of perfect enlightenment, they actually encompass all things; therefore, it is said above that they are "various."
The Buddha, with his wondrous voice, extensively proclaimed and elucidated [the teaching], up to: "bestowing the Dharma of equality with the Tathāgata.
The first three phrases encompass the cause; the final phrase accomplishes the fruition. △ Twenty Universal Bodhisattvas each attained one Dharma-gate.
The first Bodhisattva is not among those listed previously. This is because previously, [the list] included Samantabhadra as one of the ten "Universals" (Pūrvāḥ).
Now, since Samantabhadra is explained separately, he is added to make ten, thereby signifying perfection and completeness.

Nevertheless, while the verse contains all ten, both the seventh Bodhisattva and his corresponding Dharma-gate are missing from the prose section; furthermore, the eighth Bodhisattva and his Dharma-gate are also omitted.
The names of the ninth group of bodhisattvas shall be understood from the text as it occurs. First, the prose section:
Furthermore, the liberation door of the Bodhisattva Pure Virtue Sublime Light (up to) Adorning the Site of Enlightenment.
Adorned places where the Dharma is preached are all called "adornments.
[This includes] the Bodhisattva Universal Virtue Supreme Lamp Radiance, up to the liberation door of understanding the inconceivable realms of sentient beings.
In every atom, perfect enlightenment is attained; thus, it is already inexhaustible. This alone constitutes one gate of perfect enlightenment.

There are such immeasurable gates of attaining perfect enlightenment as are analyzed in the "Chapter on Manifestation. According to each gate through which perfect enlightenment is attained, the maturation of sentient beings is likewise so.
Therefore, it is said that the inconceivable realm of sentient beings is brought to maturity.
From the Bodhisattva Universal Radiance Lion Banner (up to) the liberation door of producing all Buddha-lands,
they cultivate an ocean of merit and adorn an ocean of lands.
From the Bodhisattva Universal Jewel Flame Wondrous Light (up to) the liberation gate of non-delusion regarding the realm of supernormal powers:
by means of profound and wondrous wisdom, he contemplates inconceivable objects; therefore, he is not deluded in many places and does not grow weary throughout many eons.
From the Bodhisattva Universal Sound Ocean of Merit Banner (up to) the liberation door of manifesting the adornments of all buddha-fields:
just as in this assembly at Jeta Grove, all pure lands are manifested instantaneously; it is thus in every assembly, appearing with distinct variations in every thought-moment.
The Bodhisattva Universal Wisdom Light-Illuminating Tathāgata-Sphere (up to) the Liberation Gate of the Treasury of the Profound and Vast Dharma-Dhātu.
Because the Dharma-Dhātu contains and encompasses the inexhaustible, it is called a "treasury. Contemplating the body of the Buddha’s Dharma-Dhātu, even a single hair-pore is without limit.
In the seven Sanskrit versions, he is named the Bodhisattva Universal Awakening Pleasing Sound; he has attained the proximity of serving [the Buddha].
The liberation door of the treasury of serving and making offerings to all Buddhas means that when the Buddha was practicing the causal path in the past, there was no Buddha he did not serve;
now that he has attained the fruit of Buddhahood, there is no assembly [of beings] to which he does not turn. It is like the hundred rivers rushing toward the sea.
From the Bodhisattva Universal Purity of Inexhaustible Merit and Majestic Radiance (up to) the Bodhisattva’s Gate of Liberation of Boundless Practices.

According to the Sanskrit original, it should be stated: "The Bodhisattva Universal Purity of Inexhaustible Merit and Majestic Radiance attained the Gate of Liberation of Vast Empowerment that Gives Rise to All Spiritual Transformations.
This means [the manifestations] pervade all lands as numerous as motes of dust, throughout kalpas reaching to the very limits of the future.

All of this is due to the power of the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). In the nine Sanskrit manuscripts, it is the Bodhisattva Samantaratnacūḍapuṣpaketu who attains the liberation door of the "Infinite Gateways of Bodhisattva Practices Arising from Universal Entry into the Conducts of All Worlds.
This very liberation door is the Dharma-door of the Bodhisattva Tejaprabha in the present sutra. This is because [the former] emerges from the eighth and ninth liberation doors.
The name "Bodhisattva" has consequently caused the ninth dharma-gate to be placed below the eighth; this is the error of the translator.
For if one lacks great compassion and does not enter into birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one cannot emerge from the gateway of bodhisattva practice.
Just as one cannot obtain jewels without entering the sea, this is the transformation of others into oneself.
This is the liberation door of the Bodhisattva Universal Mark of Supreme Light (Yi-xiang Zui-sheng Guang), which manifests the spheres of all Buddhas.
Thus, based on the essence, the function arises. △ Second, the verse summary:
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Pure Virtue Sublime Light (up to) immediately spoke these verses:
"All lands throughout the ten directions... all sufferings and difficulties shall be extinguished.

The commentary on the preceding verses has already been provided. Because it is intended to demonstrate that the Dharma-gates of the Bodhisattvas interpenetrate one another, the teaching is not formally attributed to a specific person;
the same applies to the subsequent section. △ Thirty: The various names of Bodhisattvas each attain a single Dharma-gate (2).
First, the prose section:
Furthermore, from the Bodhisattva Sāgaraprabhāmahāvyūha up to the gate of liberation through skillful means in all buddha-fields, one attains four kinds of skillful means for achieving bodhi:
first, the stages; second, the practices; third, the maturation of beings; that is, the practice.
The "stages" (bhūmi) refer to the activities performed; the "adornments of the field" (kṣetrapariśuddhi) encompass both self-benefit and benefit for others, as well as their causes and results.

Alternatively, there may be the fulfillment of a single stage and a single perfection (pāramitā), or the fulfillment of all perfections across each successive stage. The former is the general [category], while the latter nine are specific. Nevertheless, they do not transcend the aforementioned four [categories], and they primarily manifest the taming of sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Cloud-Sound Ocean-Light Free-from-Dirt Treasury [attains] the liberation door of various distinct locations;
the Bodhisattva Wisdom-Born Jewel-Crest [attains] the liberation door of manifesting pure great merit.
Universally demonstrating the extinction of delusions,
the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Pure Light of Merit and Virtue [attained] the gate of liberation of various adornments,
universally adorning the assembly.
The Bodhisattva Lotus-Crested Skillful Valor [attains] the liberation door of manifesting all Buddha-dharmas according to the capacities of beings;
the Bodhisattva Universal Wisdom Cloud Sun Banner [attains] the liberation door of dwelling eternally for immeasurable eons.
For the eternal preservation of all beings,
[this is] the liberation door of the power of the seal of all boundless dharmas of the Bodhisattva Mahāvīra Vajranābhi;
through the seal of dharma, beings are awakened.
From the Bodhisattva Fragrant Flame Light Banner (up to) the liberation door of accomplishing the mass of wisdom;
[and] from the Bodhisattva Great Radiant Virtue Deep Beautiful Sound (up to) the liberation door of the ocean of all great vows.
Together with the Buddha,
they had previously cultivated the Bodhisattva Mahāpuṇyaprabhājñānasaṃbhava’s liberation door of penetrating the profound realm pervading the entire Dharma-realm,
thereby illuminating the inconceivable state of the Tathāgata. △ Second, the verse summary.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaraprabhāmahāvyūha (up to) spoke these verses:
"The various pāramitās and the various stages (up to) all rain down the Dharma according to their respective faculties."
The text can be understood as follows:
"The True Suchness, the equal and signless body" (up to) "...universally responding throughout the ten directions to expound the Dharma.
The first phrase refers to the Dharmakāya of intrinsic purity that is realized. Regarding the term "signless," it indicates the characteristic of True Suchness; "body" (*kāya*) refers to its essence.

Regarding its meaning: while entangled [in saṃsāra], it is unstained; when emerging from obstructions, it is not [merely] pure. It is necessarily the same for both ordinary beings and sages; therefore, it is called "equality. The second phrase refers to the dharmakāya that has emerged from entanglement.
Because true thusness (tathatā) emerges from the afflictive obstructions (kleśāvaraṇa), it is called "free from defilement" (vimala). [It also emerges from] the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa).
Therefore, it is called "radiance. Furthermore, because both defilements and habitual tendencies have been simultaneously extinguished, it is called "free from stain.

Because true wisdom is perfected, it is called "radiance. As for the "pure dharma-body," this distinguishes it from that which is still entangled in afflictions; it is the body of the non-obstruction between essence and function in its state beyond entanglement.

Because it has emerged from entanglement, its application is unimpeded in all directions. In terms of principle, essence and function are non-obstructive; in terms of function, cessation and contemplation are simultaneous.

Therefore, when the fruit is attained, quiescence and illumination constitute the body. Because it is the essence of that which is employed, it is quiescent; because it is the function of that essence, it is wisdom.
Since essence and function are non-dual, they do not reside within the Buddha-body; how could there be any measure? Thus, it can universally respond to the ten directions.
This phrase specifically reveals the transformative function (*nirmāṇa-karma*). Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Mercury mixed with pure gold can coat all colors."
The image, wisdom, and the Dharma-body manifest and appear everywhere; this is precisely that meaning.
"The powers of the Dharma King are all pure" (extending to) "all lands are clearly manifest."
△ Section Eight: The Assembly of the Inner Multitudes, Part Ten. First, clarifying the place of origin.
At that time, within the Tathāgata’s lion throne... (up to)... among all such articles of adornment.
The "seat" (āsana) constitutes the general category, while the "jewels" and so forth represent the specific details. Thus, the following conclusion summarizes the extensive by means of the concise;

it does not refer solely to the wheels and other features, which is why the term "all" is used. The reason this [seat] is able to produce [these manifestations] is that the seat encompasses the entire Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).

The environment and its inhabitants (the *niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*) are fused as one, such that not even a single minute speck of dust fails to contain vast space. The lands pervaded by the seat are universally present within the seat at all times.

Therefore, they emerge from within; they are not emanations. If one considers the cause of dharma-emptiness and the seat of dharma-emptiness, then the myriad practices serve as adornments, capable of giving birth to Bodhisattvas. △ Second, revealing the various classes [of beings].
From each [of these], there emerged bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field;
for all were indeed bodhisattvas. △ Third, the listing of their names:
Their names were Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Ocean Wisdom Sovereign (through to) Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Banner of Light of Excellent Valor.
Since their places of origin are numerous, their names are likewise manifold; I have merely cited the ten principal ones above, corresponding respectively to the ten directions.
△ Fourth, the conclusion regarding the number of the assembly.
With these as their leaders, there appeared simultaneously a multitude of clouds, as numerous as the atoms within many Buddha-fields;
the ornaments were not of one kind, hence they were as numerous as the atoms of those fields. △ Fifth, the offering of clouds: this consists of the introduction, the enumeration, and the conclusion.
Each of these bodhisattvas raised various clouds of offerings (extending to) as many as the atoms contained within Buddha-worlds.
△ Sixth, the ocean of assemblies:
each of those bodhisattvas individually raised [offerings] (extending to) all oceans of assemblies at sites of enlightenment, continuing without interruption.

When the multitude of bodhisattvas has each raised clouds of offerings as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field—already inconceivable in their layered abundance, let alone their unceasing continuity—the reason all these ritual implements are termed "clouds" carries several meanings. It signifies that while their forms and appearances are manifest, wisdom perceives them as having no inherent nature;
they arise from the emptiness of the *dharmatā* as unarisen phenomena, such that both the perceiver and the perceived are utterly devoid of dependence.
It comes through application; therefore, its coming has no point of origin. It departs through the cessation of application; therefore, its going has no destination.
Yet, it can contain compassionate moisture and pour down the rain of Dharma to benefit all things, layer upon layer without obstruction—thus it bears the likeness of clouds.
This meaning of "cloud" applies to all the preceding and following texts alike. △ Seventh, reverently circumambulating the Buddha.
Having manifested these clouds, they circumambulated the World-Honored One to the right for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of times.
Facing him with profound reverence, they gazed upon him insatiably, even unto hundreds of thousands of times. △ 8. They sat in their original positions.

In each direction, not far from the Buddha, they each sat upon their respective seats in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), distinct and unmixed, like lion cubs; thus the seats of the Bodhisattvas are also called "lion" seats.
As for "sitting oneself" and "others sitting themselves," it is because the wisdom-mind manifests itself and one abides in oneself. This applies to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the sitting posture: the *paryaṅka* (full lotus) is adopted because it serves as the standard for all beings. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* quotes a verse:

"If one sits in the *paryaṅka*, the body is at ease and enters into *samādhi*, etc. △ Ninth, praising his virtuous capabilities consists of twelve phrases, divided into two parts; first, the general [praise].
The conduct of these bodhisattvas is pure and as vast as the ocean.
△ Second, the individual manifestations: each one is a distinct kind of purity and vastness, which are briefly condensed into three categories.
First, the three types of wisdom purify the three karmas extensively;
one attains the illumination of wisdom that shines upon the Dharma of the Universal Gate, reaching until one is able to enter the ocean of all eloquent dharmas.

First, realizing the universal Dharma through a single wisdom; second, the body following the conduct of the Buddha; third, speech entering the ocean of eloquence. These three meanings are sought, and they also pervade the three karmas.
Second, the attainment of the purity and vastness of the Dharma through the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*).
Having attained the dharma-gate of inconceivable liberation (up to) being able to fully contain the ocean of all dharmas:

first, attaining one's own portion of liberation; second, abiding in the stage of superior progress; third, universally possessing all the *dhāraṇīs* of the Universal Gateway stage (*samantamukha-bhūmi*).

This refers to what was stated at the beginning of the sutra: "one has already trodden upon the Tathāgata’s Stage of Universal Radiance" (*tathāgata-samantaprabhā-bhūmi*). △ Section Five: Explaining Merit.
Regarding the two aspects of the vast and great purity of wisdom, the first two [verses] clarify this directly.
Having well abided in the ground of the wisdom that is equal across the three times, one attains profound faith and vast joy.
First, because wisdom is securely established in both principle and phenomena, it is called "well-abiding. Second, because there is no merit that is not cultivated, faith and joy arise. However...

The equality of the three periods of time was already clarified at the beginning of the sutra; now it shall be briefly demonstrated further. This refers to abiding in equality based on both sentient beings and Buddhas. First, speaking in terms of the Buddhas:
all Buddhas are equal, for their Dharma-body and Wisdom-body neither increase nor decrease. If we speak in terms of sentient beings:
every birth is equal, for their afflictions, karma, suffering, and the links of dependent origination are all equal. If one considers the mutual relationship between sentient beings and Buddhas...

Regarding "mutual comparison": ordinary beings in the present compare themselves to the Buddhas of the past; by advancing in practice and attaining the fruit, they compare themselves to the Buddhas of the present;
and upon achieving Buddhahood, they ultimately compare themselves to the eternally abiding Buddhas. This is based on mutual comparison across the three periods of time.

As for afflictions (*kleśa*), for a Buddha they are originally present but now absent; for sentient beings, they are originally absent but now present. As for Bodhi, for sentient beings it is originally present but now absent. All...
The Buddha is originally non-existent and now existent; these terms "original" and "now" are spoken in reference to the distinction between delusion and awakening.

The nature of *nirvāṇa* is not subsumed within the three periods of time; therefore, one should know that it is impossible for there to be any dharma existing within the three periods. This is explained from the perspective of the purity of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).
Thus, the Buddha and sentient beings are currently equal, yet this does not preclude the distinction between delusion and awakening.
For this reason, the Three Vehicles are both differentiated and undifferentiated. The quiescent extinction (*śānti*) of sentient beings is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
the Dharma-body following conditions is itself sentient beings. Therefore, sentient beings who are not non-existent in their quiescent extinction are eternally no different from the Truth.
It is established that the *dharmakāya*, which is not a phenomenon existing [independently] but follows conditions, manifests as eternally non-different from phenomena.

Therefore, there is nothing among all phenomena of the three times—whether defiled or pure—that is not equal. How much more so when they mutually encompass one another in accordance with their true nature (*dharmatā*)!

One who understands thus is said to be "well-established on the stage of omniscience" (*sarvajñabhūmi*). Just as the earth can give birth to all things and ultimately returns to the earth, so it is with the myriad phenomena.
Relying upon the ultimate Buddha-wisdom, one returns to all-knowledge. △ Second, the threefold manifestation:
"The boundless mass of merit is utterly pure... (up to) all Buddhas who appear, whom one diligently serves with offerings."
First, by purifying prior karmic obstacles to merit, all merits are rendered boundlessly pure. Second, by contemplating the dharma-realm as empty space, one accomplishes the aforementioned wisdom.
Third, by drawing near to superior conditions, the former two are accomplished. △ Tenth, the recitation of verses in praise of the Buddha.
The ten bodhisattvas each spoke a verse, forming ten sections. Regarding the first [section], there are two parts praising the Buddha’s body and seat;
the first five verses praise the Buddha’s body for its possession of virtues.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati-vaśavarti-abhijñārāja (Sea-Wisdom Sovereign Supernatural Power King) then spoke these verses:
"Whatever the Buddhas have realized, they have all already known" (up to) "they dwell in tranquility, gazing upon one another.
First, praise of wisdom; second, praise of merit; third, spiritual powers; fourth, the profundity of the cause; fifth, the excellence of the fruit.
△ Second, five praises of the magnificence of their seats.
The Maṇi-jewel treasury emits radiance... (up to) "the Buddha is seated upon such a throne.
Since this assembly has manifested from their seats, the text praises the throne extensively. △ Second, praising the throne and the ground; the text is divided into three parts.
First, four lines directly praise the throne.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Thunder-Sound (up to) beholding the ocean-like assembly at the site of enlightenment, spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One formerly accumulated the practices for bodhi... (up to) praising the Tathāgata as he sat upon his seat."
△ Next, three verses praise the site of the assembly, which further reveals the magnificence of the seats.
The measure of the Buddha’s merit is like space; [it extends] until all sentient beings are unable to comprehend it.
This section collectively demonstrates that because the causes are profound and the virtues are vast, the offerings and services are inconceivable.
With vajra as its ground, indestructible [by anything], it completely adorns and illuminates the Tathāgata’s seat with radiant brilliance.

The first seven phrases provide specific explanations, while the final phrase concludes by describing the polishing of the precious throne. △ The subsequent three [phrases] praise the adornments of the ground;
the earth deities rejoice and leap for joy (up to the point where it says) that they are able to do so through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
The first two earth goddesses manifest offerings and adornments; the latter one manifests successive adornments through the power of the Buddha.
△ Third, the unique praise of the extraordinary virtues of the site has two parts: first, the five preceding virtues have their functions fully perfected.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jewel-Light-Tuft (Ratnārci-keśa) [from] ... spoke these verses:
"When the World-Honored One was practicing in the past... with various jewel branches spread about as a magnificent adornment."
△ Regarding the fifth section, the dissemination through the transformation of the Dharma:
You all should universally observe this ground (up to) what should be expounded upon the Buddha’s seat.
The texts of the nine assemblies and five cycles, the teachings given according to the needs of beings throughout a single transformation, have already been fully expounded upon this site.
Within each and every dharma-gate, all [teachings] are fully expounded; therefore, these grounds are all adorned and pure.
△ Fourth, praising the palace where the Buddha dwells, in two parts: first, a general explanation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāprajñāsūryavīramatī (up to) spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One sits serenely in the Dharma Hall... his body appears universally throughout the lands of the ten directions."
The subsequent section praises the location to manifest the person; thus, this verse identifies the person to reveal the location. "Ning" (凝) refers to an appearance of solemn dignity;
"sui" (睟) refers to gazing, meaning to gaze with a reverent and composed air. △ The latter nine lines specifically clarify two aspects.
The first four clarify that the substance of the palace embodies all virtues, thereby expanding upon the first half [of the preceding verse].
The Tathāgata’s palace is inconceivable; when the Buddha sits within it, he appears exceptionally radiant.
Although the palace is brilliant, the Buddha’s presence increases its luster, so that it shines forth extensively and brilliantly, illuminating the interior of the palace.
With mani-jewels as pillars of various colors, [the hall]—down to—the ocean of wisdom sits serenely within it.
To briefly distinguish the seven adornments: they are bound together by the ocean of wisdom; above, it is vast and solemn, situated in the Hall of Dharma.

This means that within, precious pillars are held; from the eaves, golden bells hang down; outside, gates and steps are aligned; above, flower canopies are spread; and precious trees reflect one another. Precious...
The necklaces hang down all around; this constitutes the seventh adornment. *Tuo* refers to a small gate; it signifies thorough penetration.

"Like clouds spreading" means that they are layered and immeasurable, succeeding one another in sequence. As for the previous description of being "serene and composed," this means the eyes do not blink;
it is specifically because there are no waves of consciousness within that the "ocean of wisdom is tranquil."
“A net of mani-jewels, banners of exquisite fragrance” (up to) “the world-transcending one of right knowledge sits here.
It is draped with jeweled nets, lined with fragrant banners, spread with flaming brilliance, and covered with ornaments.
The phrase “world-transcending” refers to the aforementioned Dharma Hall where the World-Honored One resides. “Light spreading like clouds” is like a multicolored cloud approaching.

"Day" (*rì*) signifies that the upper and lower [realms] are equally luminous. △ The latter five [perfections] represent the sovereign mastery of wondrous function; this expands upon the latter half [of the verse]:
"Universally manifesting clouds of transformations throughout the ten directions" (up to) "...all thus appear from the Buddha-palace."
He manifests clouds of *rākṣasa* bodies to harmonize and transform living beings. This precisely clarifies the previous passage concerning the manifestation of lands in the ten directions.
With *maṇi* jewels serving as trees that produce wondrous flowers, there is nothing within them that does not manifest its reflection.
The jeweled trees manifest the splendor of the three periods of time;
everywhere there are clusters of maṇi jewels... (up to) the architectural structures are adorned with extreme beauty.
These many adornments are mentioned only briefly.
The Tathāgata’s palaces are inconceivable; (extending) until each and every one contains a Tathāgata seated within.
Thus, the various adornments mentioned above are condensed into manifold adornments, with Tathāgatas seated in successive layers.
"The Tathāgata’s palace is boundless" (extending to) "there are none who do not come together toward the Buddha.
This concludes the praise of the inexhaustible assembly of the principal and the retinue. △ Fifth, the general praise of the virtues of the sovereign power of the field and the trees has two parts;
the first generally manifests them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Inconceivable Jewel-Seal of Meritorious Wisdom (up to) spoke these verses:
"In the past, the Buddha cultivated an ocean of manifold merits (up to) the site of enlightenment, adorned and pure, free from all defilements."

This refers to the power of past causes and vows, which is profound, vast, and inconceivable; through the manifestation of supernormal powers in present conditions, the resulting fruit is born pure and adorned.
△ The latter nine [verses] specifically reveal three aspects. First, the five [verses] praise the tree for its possession of virtues that adorn the site.
The King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels forms the roots of the tree (extending) throughout the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), universally adorning it.
The first two [jewels] form the trunk, towering and majestic; the next two form the branches and leaves, providing dense shade; the final one forms the flowers and fruit, radiant with fragrance.
△ Second, praising the lotus net of the site.
Observe how, from the site of the Sugata’s enlightenment (up to) the sound of bells and chimes resonating from amidst the clouds:
when lotuses are spread upon the ground, light-wheels descend; when jeweled nets fill the sky, sounds resound from amidst the clouds.
△ Third, praising the sovereign power of the tree.
From "In all lands throughout the ten directions" (up to) "the assemblies hear the sound and all behold it.
The first [of the three] is inclusion; the latter two are manifestation. △ Sixth, praising the sovereign power of the field and the tree as being fully endowed with virtues.
The transformation and the proclamation flow forth as two. The preceding nine verses each manifest a single gateway.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Hundred-Eyed Lotus-Uṣṇīṣa (until) then spoke in verse:
All the mani-jewels emit wondrous sounds, such that there are none who are not subdued and brought to purity.
△ Following this is a verse that concludes the description of the pervasive adornments:
"The Tathāgata, in the past, universally cultivated and refined [them], so that each and every adornment is of infinite kinds."
△ Section Seven: Praising the Buddha’s Ten Powers (*daśabala*). One verse for each power. The subsequent scriptural passages repeatedly clarify these ten powers;
they are the unique qualities (*āveṇika-guṇa*) of a Buddha, possessed equally by every Buddha. Bodhisattvas take these as their object when generating the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
As stated in the *Brahmacaryā-varga*: "Furthermore, within each of the powers, there are immeasurable meanings; you should ask questions at your pleasure. Therefore—

This must be known. However, it is extensively analyzed in the fifty-third [chapter] of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the fourth [chapter] of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, and the fourteenth [chapter] of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*.
Here, I shall briefly distinguish it by means of seven sections: first, the establishment of its intent; second, the explanation of its name; third, its intrinsic nature.

There are four [sections]: first, the activity; second, the sequence; third, the distinctions; and fourth, the commentary on the text. However, by understanding the names, one will know the activities;
by examining the text through comparative analysis, the distinctions will be easily seen. Therefore, the activity, the distinctions, and the explanation of the specific names are presented together.
This is also clearly demonstrated within the commentary on the text. First, regarding the establishment of the intent:

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that this reveals that the Buddha, as a Great Being, possesses true power, which causes the minds of non-Buddhists to submit, inspires the Two Vehicles to aspire toward it, and enables Bodhisattvas to emulate him so as to accomplish great deeds and ultimately attain their fruit;
therefore, it is necessary to discern this. The Tathāgata is solely the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
The power of wisdom (*jñānabala*). This power has ten functions; therefore, it is said to be tenfold.

That is to say, because one thoroughly and correctly knows the ten objects through the distinctions of time, category, continuity, and the immeasurable causes and conditions for delivering sentient beings.
Therefore, it is sufficient to speak of only ten [powers], as they fully accomplish the task. That is to say: by the first power, one knows those who can be saved and those who cannot;

by the second, the power of karma, one knows those with obstacles and those without; by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one knows those who are attached to the taste of pleasure and those who are not;

by the power of the faculties (*indriya*), one knows the degree of their wisdom; by the power of aspiration (*chanda*), one knows what they delight in; and by the power of disposition (*gotra*), one knows the direction of their deep-seated inclinations. By...

The power of knowing the destinations [of beings] is the gate of liberation for weighing the capacities of sentient beings. By the power of recollecting past lives, he distinguishes where they have previously come from;

by the power of knowing birth and death, he distinguishes the excellence or inferiority of their places of rebirth; and by the power of the exhaustion of outflows, he knows that sentient beings attain nirvana.
Because the Buddha uses these ten powers to deliver sentient beings with thorough discernment, he teaches only ten.
Second, the explanation of the name. This consists of a general overview followed by specific details. First, regarding the general name:
"Power" (*bala*) signifies the capacity to crush enemies and adversaries, and the sense of being invincible. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Because it is endowed with the functional capacity to benefit all sentient beings in every respect, it ultimately and completely overcomes all Māras and adversaries. It possesses great majesty.

Because they possess power, they are called "powers" (*bala*). The Abhidharma states: "They effectively eliminate all Māras and skillfully provide answers to questions and treatises; therefore, these ten are called powers.
Here, "ten" refers to a number, and this is an analysis based on the inclusion of a numeral (*saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa*). Their individual names shall be explained in the relevant passages.

Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (57) states: "The Buddha possesses the faculty of full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*), which has the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) as its essence.

The *Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra* states: "It has as its nature either meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), along with their associated mental states and mental factors (*caitta-caitasika*).

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* generally takes the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) as its nature. Synthesizing these textual meanings, there should be six types [of nature]: first, the most excellent essence (*parama-śarīra*).

Therefore, in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, these are of the nature of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). Second, regarding their generative essence, the *Abhidharma* includes meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as well. Third, regarding their essential nature:
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that they are of the nature of the five faculties; because wisdom is predominant, it is said that their self-nature is simply the wisdom of the ten directions.
This is why only the "power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible" (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*) is mentioned, and not the powers of faith, diligence, and so forth.

Fourth, the essence of association (*saṃprayoga*): according to the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma*), it takes the associated mental factors (*citta-dharma*) as its nature, consisting of the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*).

Fifth, the essence of the retinue (*parivāra*): it takes the five aggregates as its nature, because the untainted (*anāsrava*) matter (*rūpa*) associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*), and so forth, serve as auxiliary constituents.

Although there is no explicit textual authority for this, it must necessarily be so by logical necessity; for it serves to obstruct the defilement of transgressing precepts and assists in crushing adversaries. Sixth, based on this sūtra, [the two views] are harmonized.
All phenomena take this as their nature; for it is logically necessary that the unimpeded dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) be thus.
As for the four activities, these constitute the differentiation of characteristics, which shall be made explicit in the text.

Regarding the fivefold sequence: in various texts, there are occasional discrepancies in the order, each having its own justification. The sequence listed in this text is identical to that of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.

In the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," however, the [section on] elements (*dhātu*) precedes that on understanding (*adhimukti*). In the "Chapter on Brahma-conduct," meditative concentration and liberation occupy the third position.
The [section on] recollection of past lives follows that on the divine eye. The remainder follows this same order. This is the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
In the *Śatashāstra* (Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom) and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the fourth [power] and the twenty-seventh [chapter] likewise place dhyāna third;

the others follow this same order. To clarify the sequence according to the treatises, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The first power is the general [category], while the remaining nine are the specific [categories].
Within the first power, there are nine distinct divisions; therefore, the first power comprehensively understands all phenomena, while the subsequent nine progressively unfold [its details]."
This means that first one is made to understand the causes and conditions and their karmic retributions; thus, the power of karma arises. Next, because of afflictions (*kleśa*), one is bound;

through pure meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and liberation (*vimokṣa*), one is released. Thus, one is led from bondage toward liberation. Next, there are differences in the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya*).

Those with dull faculties create karma, while those with sharp faculties do not. Therefore, the accumulation of karma results from the two desires of good and evil, which bring about the higher and lower realms.

Roots. These two kinds of desire arise from two kinds of natures; because there are various causes and conditions for these natures, one traverses two kinds of paths, namely the wholesome path and the unwholesome path.
Next, one knows the past and examines the future. Then, through skillful means, one destroys their causal conditions and the continuity of their retribution;
therefore, it is called the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Furthermore, the *yoga* has many gateways. Next...

First, it is explained at length as in the fiftieth [chapter]. Above, according to the sequence of the treatise (*śāstra*), dhyāna was placed third because the two treatises define "brahmacarya" in contrast to one's own karma, distinguishing between those who have abandoned desire and those who have not.

In this sutra, however, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are defined in contrast to the "universal course of conduct" (*sarvatragāminī pratipad*), distinguishing between the pure and the impure; therefore, it is placed here.

7. If one’s habituation to desire has become a fixed disposition, then the realm (dhātu) is situated after desire; if desire arises from one’s innate disposition, then the realm is situated before desire.
If one clings to permanence, the recollection of past lives (pūrvanivāsa) is explained first; if one clings to annihilationism, the divine eye (divyacakṣus) is distinguished first.
For the others, there is no distinct principle; therefore, both the Sūtras and the Śāstras are definitive on this point.
Sixth, regarding the distinctions: it means that these ten powers, when compared with one another, possess both distinctions and non-distinctions;
this shall be clarified in the relevant passages.

Seventh, regarding the explanation of the text: since the primary intent of this sutra is such that all differing meanings are harmoniously integrated, each individual power fully encompasses [all others].
The ten powers extend even to encompassing the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, regarding past lives, it is said that wisdom encompasses the three periods of time;
as for the divine eye, it perceives the entirety of the Dharma-realm. It is not merely that it perceives the entirety; the Buddha-eye is like space, which is itself the Dharma-realm.

It is not merely that wisdom encompasses [all], but it can also instantaneously manifest within a single pore through its karmic power, thereby contemplating the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). How could it be anything other than this?
Regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because there are distinctions according to the gates [of analysis], the tenets of other schools are not undermined. △ The text has ten sections.
First is the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*). At that time, the Bodhisattva Suvarṇajvālāparipūrṇaprabha (up to) spoke these verses:
The Buddha formerly cultivated the practices for awakening (up to: this is the Tathāgata’s first power of knowledge (*jñānabala*). That is to say:
it is possible that a wholesome cause results in a pleasant fruit; it is impossible that a wholesome cause results in a painful fruit.

Examples such as an unwholesome cause resulting in a painful fruit can be understood by analogy with the above. "Possible" (*sthāna*) means the sense of establishing, the sense of relying upon, and the sense of arising; it is that which is able to establish.
The fruit serves as the basis for the fruit and is that which can give rise to the dharma of the fruit; therefore, it is designated by the name "basis" (*āyatana*).
To have correct knowledge regarding this is called the power of wisdom (*jñānabala*). As for its function:

it consists of knowing cause and fruit as they truly are, and being able to subdue various disputes concerning the absence of cause or evil causes. Having attained such universal knowledge, those who can be delivered are delivered, while those who cannot be delivered—
This serves as the causal basis for the following. In this passage, the first half concerns past causes, while the second half reveals the power of wisdom (*jñānabala*).

To have correct and clear understanding regarding all objects of experience is precisely what defines this power; it refers to the thorough knowledge of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). △ Second, the power of knowing the karmic retribution of the past, future, and present.
As previously stated, by equally contemplating the nature of all phenomena (up to) their pervasion throughout the ten directions, one is able to expound them fully;

this is called the *yoga* of the power of knowing one's own karma (*svakarmajñānabala*). What is here termed "all karma" refers to the three types of karma—wholesome and so forth—within the three periods of time, as well as those that accord with the present life and so on; these are all called "one's own karma.

Regarding the karma of experiencing the fruits of what one has personally performed: *Note: The text provided consists of a commentary on a specific Buddhist technical term, the power of knowing one's own karma, within the context of the ten powers of a Buddha.*

Because it is known as it truly is, how does this differ from the first [knowledge]? If one correctly understands that the wholesome and other karmas performed bring about results such as the desirable, this is due to the power of the first [knowledge].
If one understands that the ability to perform wholesome and unwholesome karmas brings about results such as the desirable, this is the power of one's own karma (*svakarmika*).
In the text, the first half refers to the past cause, and the second half to the present result. △ Third, the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñāna*).
Power. Because he cultivated great skillful means over past eons, the Buddha was able to accomplish the power of knowing the faculties (*indriya-jñāna-bala*).

This refers to the five faculties, beginning with faith (*śraddhā*). Their states of being weak, middling, or superior are termed "inferior" (*hīna*) or "excellent" (*praṇīta*). He possesses correct knowledge regarding these, as well as the capacity [to discern them].
To them, he teaches the True Dharma as is appropriate and suitable; this is his activity. In the verse, three lines concern the causes of the past, and one line concerns the fruit of the present.
△ Fourth, the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations of beings.
Just as sentient beings have differing understandings (up to: "the Buddha, by the power of his wisdom, is able to act thus"), this is also called *adhimukti* (resolute belief).
That is to say, it is when one first gives rise to faith based on another, or takes the observation of phenomena (*dharma*) as the basis.

Its antecedent consists of the inferior, middling, and superior [levels]. That which is characterized by delighting in various things is called "diverse resolve" (*nānādhimukti*), and it is also called "desire" (*chanda*).

Desire refers to faith, preference, and inclination; for example, some may crave wealth and profit, while others prefer fame, or prefer meditative concentration, or prefer wisdom—these vary in many ways.
The Tathāgata, with perfect knowledge, causes them to abandon what is impure and to increase what is pure. How does this differ from the previously mentioned faculties (*indriya*)?

They differ. The faculties (*indriya*) are established based on past lives, while wisdom (*jñāna*) varies in its extent. The liberations (*vimokṣa*) are established based on present manifestation, as their inclinations differ. The *Śāstra* states:

"If one illuminates the various faculties as primary, such that there are diverse musical performances within each respective phenomenon, this is the power of knowledge regarding the faculties (*indriya-jñānabala*).
If one correctly discriminates the differences in mental inclinations, this is the power of knowledge regarding the liberation (*vimokṣa-jñānabala*). This is evident from the text. △ Fivefold.
The power of knowledge regarding the realms (*dhātu-jñāna-bala*). Throughout the entirety of the oceans of lands in the ten directions, [all things] can be manifested within a single pore.
"Realm" (*dhātu*) refers here to "nature" (*prakṛti*); that is to say, the natures of the one, two, three, four, or five vehicles, or the natures of greed, hatred, and delusion, and so forth.

From the various types of conduct up to the eighty-four thousand types of conduct, these are called the "various natures" (*nānā-dhātu*). Nature (*dhātu*) is the seed; understanding (*vijñapti*) is the manifest activity (*samudācāra*).

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Nature is named the characteristic of accumulation. Furthermore, it says in [the same work] at section 90: "Nature is internal and desire is external;
nature performs the action, and one must necessarily undergo the karmic retribution, whereas desire may not be so. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If one illuminates the superior..."

The characteristics that arise from understanding are [determined] by seeds; this occurs through the power of understanding. If they are illuminated, they are simply the differentiation of those very seeds, occurring through the power of knowledge regarding the elements (*dhātu-jñāna-bala*).
If desire is practiced until it becomes one's nature, how can there be any distinction? For desire is merely counted as one among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
The nature (*prakṛti*) permeates all categories; this refers to the difference between the broad and the narrow. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Habitual desire becomes nature;

'nature' refers to deep-seated mental tendencies, while 'desire' refers to that which arises according to conditions. If nature is identical to seeds, how does it differ from the faculties (*indriya*)?

The faculties consist solely of the relative strength or weakness of faith and so forth, whereas nature encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome. This is because, when compared to the fruits [of practice], faith and so forth are broader and more enduring, as they are capable of producing them.
The noble paths of the three vehicles for humans and devas constitute the roots of the path. The three wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) are merely their opposites;
since they do not aspire toward the fruit [of Buddhahood], they are not even called "roots. How much less could those whose nature permeates evil be the same?
As the verse says, "All can be manifested within a single pore," this means that it is not only the Buddha’s wisdom that, like space, encompasses the nature of sentient beings.
The interior of each pore is empty; it is merely the manifestation of the realms of sentient beings. △ Sixth, the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to all destinations:
The Buddha fully knows the traversing of all places, and is able to reveal and manifest them all so that they are clearly understood.

The name of this treatise is the "Power of Knowledge of the Path Leading Everywhere" (*sarvatragāminīpratipajjñānabala*). "Everywhere" (*sarvatra*) means all. "Leading" (*gāminī*) means reaching. "Path" (*pratipad*) means the way.
This refers to the various paths traversed by sentient beings—whether paths of transcendence or paths not of transcendence—each of which is capable of reaching its respective fruit.
For example, by traversing impure paths, one reaches the five destinies; by traversing pure paths, one reaches the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. This is what it is called.
Regarding the "paths leading everywhere" (*sarvatragāminī pratipad*): if one knows the entry into such types of tracks, this is by means of the knowledge of elements (*dhātujñāna*).

If one knows all the various categories of those very tracks—namely, that such a track leads to affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and such a track leads to purification (*vyavadāna*)—this is by means of the power of the knowledge of paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipaj-jñānabala*).
In the first power, the sphere of the possible (*sthāna*) is contrasted with the impossible (*asthāna*). Within this [context]:
This merely clarifies the destination. Furthermore, the first power points to the cause as the place where the fruit is attained;
this refers to the fruit as the place that repays the cause, and thus they are not the same. In the sutra, the first phrase provides a general heading;
the next twelve characters, "In a single thought-moment one can know swiftness," indicate the time and place of what is known; the final phrase provides a detailed and thorough exposition. △
The power of knowledge regarding the dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis.
Through the power of the dhyānas and liberations, [the Buddha] boundlessly (up to) causes all afflictions and darkness to be thoroughly cleansed away.

In the Chapter on Pure Conduct (*Śīla-viśuddhi-parivarta*), he adds the defiled and the pure; thus, he thoroughly knows both the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, he knows...
The various fruits obtained based on this are called the power of knowledge (*jñānabala*). How does this differ from the power of knowing one's own karma (*svakarmajñānabala*)?

If one understands all states of existence (*bhava*) and is able to cultivate the various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), such that one can enter them and no others, this is called the power of one's own karma.

If one realizes that one relies upon such meditative concentrations as these to manifest the three types of miraculous transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) and to provide unerring instruction to those beings to be converted, this is due to the power of the knowledge of meditative concentration.
The first half of the verse refers to what is to be known, while the second half refers to its skillful application.

Regarding the statement that "the Buddha manifests [these powers]": he demonstrates his various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and manifests the three types of miraculous transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) to gladden sentient beings, to cleanse their afflictions (*kleśa*), and to cause them to depart from defilement and attain purity. △ 8. The Power of Knowledge of Recollecting Past Abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*).
The Buddha’s wisdom is unimpeded and encompasses the three periods of time (up to: all that is manifested arises through the power of recollection (*anusmṛti*).
That is to say, regarding past objects—namely, former births and past events—because they belong to a previous existence, they are called "past abodes" (*pūrvanivāsa*).

The knowledge that accompanies the recollection arising with respect to these past abodes is termed the "power of the knowledge of past abodes" (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*). The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "If one knows..."
The power of universal progression (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-bala*) consists in recollecting all the causes for rebirth in previous lives.

If one knows specific details of those past lives, such as name, clan, suffering, pleasure, and other fruits, it is called the power of recollecting former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-bala*). How is this reconciled with the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*? The treatise states:

"To know merely the events experienced in past lives, without knowing the continuity of the causal conditions of karma, is merely termed a supernormal power (*abhijñā*); even ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) possess this."
It is attained. If one additionally knows the continuity of the causes and conditions of karma, it is called "clarity" (*vidyā*); this can be attained by those of the Two Vehicles.

If one knows that the aforementioned two [types of causes] are immeasurable and boundless, it is called "power" (*bala*). Thus, power also involves knowing the cause; therefore, it should be explained comprehensively:

if one knows only the cause, it is the power of universal progression (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-bala*); if one knows both, it is the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-bala*). Yu.

Because the *gati* (going) serves as the cause for the "universal access" (*sarvatragāmin*), only the result is mentioned. In the text, the first phrase indicates the capacity for recollection. Regarding "wisdom encompassing the three times":
