since the entirety of the three times is contained within the Buddha’s wisdom, how much more so for recollective mindfulness? It is not that he does not know the three times;

rather, because it is distinguished by way of its specific aspect, it is called only "recollection of past lives" (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*). That all moments appear [in the mind] means that they are encompassed at the very moment of their manifestation.
Extremely brief. It manifests within a single pore; the place where it manifests is thus exceedingly subtle. The third phrase refers to the objects manifested and recollected.
The fourth phrase concludes by attributing this to the power of wisdom (*jñānabala*): it is not merely able to recollect, but is also able to manifest.
△ Ninth, the Power of the Wisdom of the Divine Eye (*divyacakṣus-jñānabala*).
The Buddha-eye is as vast as space... (up to) that eye is immeasurable, and the Buddhas can expound it.

This name is established solely based on its support (*āśraya*). If it were established from the perspective of its object (*viṣaya*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* calls it the "power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth" (*cyuty-upapatti-jñāna-bala*).
This means that one can correctly know death here and birth there, falling into good or evil destinies, and all matters of great or small stature, beauty or ugliness. One knows.
The cycle of birth and death in the past limit is called "past abodes. One must know that this name is obtained only after [the obstacles] are removed.
The present text states, however, "the Buddha-eye. This is because, regarding the five eyes, the other eyes exist within the Buddha as the Buddha-eye.
While such sūtras [refer to these], we now rely on the ten eyes; for the Buddha-eye can perceive the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Tathāgata. Therefore, this single power is...

This encompasses the ten powers. Taking one as an example, the same applies to the remaining nine. In the text, the first phrase refers to the greatness of the essence; the second phrase refers to the extensiveness of its function;
the third phrase refers to the superiority of its function because it is peerless; and the final phrase concludes its profundity, which is why only a Buddha can expound it.
Since it is said that he "universally perceives the dharma-realm," this is not restricted to the future alone, as this is according to the specific school’s distinction; regarding the future...
Gate: Universally perceiving the Dharma-realm. △ Tenth, the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*):
All sentient beings are possessed of various fetters (*saṃyojana*)... [omitted] ...and by all means, he causes them to be extinguished.
Regarding one’s own liberation, there is no delusion and no doubt; one also knows the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava*) and *nirvāṇa* of sentient beings.
This correct knowledge is called the power of wisdom (*jñānabala*). In the text, the first two lines refer to that which is abandoned:

the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) are the manifest states, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the seeds, and the habitual traces (*vāsanā*) are the residual impressions. The followers of the Two Vehicles cannot exhaust these traces, nor can they exhaust those of others.
Because they are subject to outflows (*āsrava*), they are not called "powers" (*bala*). The latter half [of the verse] reveals that the Buddha is able to extinguish them.

Thus, regarding these ten powers, wisdom (*jñāna*) is the essence (*svabhāva*) and power is the function (*vṛtti*). However, wisdom is itself power; there is no separate nature between them. Among these, the power of knowledge consisting in the analytical knowledge associated with the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānabala*) is explained by *appositional analysis* (*karmadhāraya*).
All the others, derived from their objects, are explained by *genitive analysis* (*tatpuruṣa*). This applies even to the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

The term "basis" (*āśraya*) is also explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. If past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) are the object, then the power of knowledge consisting of recollection (*anusmṛti-samprayukta-jñānabala*) is also explained by the *tatpuruṣa* compound.

However, these ten powers, when considered in relation to their respective functions, each possesses greatness within its own specific function, like water’s ability to purify or fire’s ability to burn;
each has its own inherent power. If considered in terms of comprehensive inclusion, the first power is the greatest. If [considered]...

The attainment of nirvāṇa consists in the great exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*). If one takes unimpeded liberation (*asaṅga-vimukti*) as the fundamental basis, then all things are perfectly equal.
*Da fangguang fo huayan jing shu*, Scroll Eleven.

composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang,
with annotations to the scripture recorded by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.
△ 8. Praising the Buddha’s fulfillment of the ten perfections through his past cultivation and his attainment of the perfection of the fruit. The eleven verses are divided into two parts;
the first verse provides a general explanation:
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Sound of the Dharma Realm (until) spoke these verses.
The Buddha’s majestic spiritual power pervades the ten directions, causing all that was previously fulfilled to be seen.
The Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is, in brief, of three types. The first is innate power (*sahaja-bala*), which refers to such things as wind not moving one's robes.
Second is the power of the noble ones (*ārya-prabhāva*), which refers to various merits such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the clear knowledges (*vidyā*).

Third is the power of the Dharma (*dharma-prabhāva*), which refers to the power of the perfected dharmas of the *pāramitās*. It causes the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) to be free from all impurities and bestows immeasurable strength upon the four limbs and hundred joints;
therefore, it is called the firm and indestructible body, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and the eternal body (*nityakāya*), which is boundless—
Regarding the "body": that which is said to pervade the ten directions is the boundless body (*ananta-kāya*). Its vast manifestation refers to the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).
That which is "without discrimination" is the body of equalizing wisdom (*samatājñāna-kāya*). That which is "the practice of great enlightenment" is the body of the *pāramitās*.
That which was "fulfilled in the past" means that all practices were first accomplished; that it "causes all who see it to appear" means that the great fruit now emerges. II. Ten Verses.

They are explained separately, with one verse for each perfection (*pāramitā*). In every case, the first half-verse concerns the cultivation of the cause in the past, while the second half-verse concerns the attainment of the fruit in the present.

The meaning of the ten perfections, as well as the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), are extensively analyzed throughout the beginning and end of this sutra; one must have a rough understanding of their characteristics.

I shall briefly set forth ten gates: first, explaining the name; second, identifying the essence; third, distinguishing the characteristics; fourth, establishing the categories; fifth, the sequence; sixth, mutual inclusion;
seventh, cultivation and realization; eighth, according to the teachings; ninth, contemplation of the mind; tenth, commentary on the text. Regarding the first, there are two further parts.

First the general name, then the specific designation. Regarding the general name *pāramitā*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that it can only be established as a *pāramitā* when it is embraced by seven kinds of supremacy (*paramatva*).
First, supremacy of abiding (*pratisthā-paramatva*), which means one must abide in the bodhisattva lineage (*gotra*).
Second, supremacy of reliance (*āśraya-paramatva*), which means one must rely upon great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
1. Supremacy of mind; 2. Supremacy of intention, meaning that one must have compassion for all sentient beings;
3. Supremacy of activity, meaning that one must fully engage in all activities; 4. Supremacy of skillful means, meaning that one must be embraced by signless wisdom; 5.
Supremacy of dedication, meaning that one must dedicate [merit] toward unsurpassed enlightenment; 6. Supremacy of purity.

"Supreme" means that one must not be interspersed with the two obstacles; thus, there is no regret throughout the three times. If any of the seven [factors] are lacking, it is not a "perfection" (pāramitā).
Therefore, each of these ten perfections is analyzed according to four propositions. Their specific names and their essential natures are as follows.
Third, the differentiation of characteristics will be explained in the relevant passages. Fourth, regarding the establishment [of the stages]:

there are exactly ten because they serve as the remedies for the ten obstacles within the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and lead to the realization of the ten *tathatā*s (suchnesses). There are exactly six because they serve to counteract the six obscurations, gradually cultivating the Buddha-dharma and gradually maturing sentient beings;
furthermore, among these six, the first three constitute the path of superior birth, which brings about great wealth, a physical body, and retinues.

Because they belong to the category of the ultimate goal, the latter three constitute the path of definitive excellence (*niyāma*), as they are able to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*) and bring sentient beings and the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*) to maturity.

Furthermore, the former three benefit sentient beings: through giving material wealth, through not causing affliction, and through enduring their affliction. The latter three counteract the afflictions:

through diligence in the application of practice (*prayoga*), they permanently subdue and permanently extinguish them. Moreover, by means of the former three, one does not abide [in cyclic existence].
Nirvāṇa. By means of the latter three, one does not abide in saṃsāra and is able to serve as the provisions for non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Regarding why there are only four of the latter [perfections], they assist the six [perfections] to bring them to fulfillment: skillful means assists the first three; aspiration assists diligence;

power assists meditative concentration; and wisdom assists insight (*prajñā*). As stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the sequence of the five is such that each preceding one induces the subsequent one.
Each subsequent [perfection] purifies each preceding one through its successive maintenance. Furthermore, the preceding ones are coarse while the subsequent ones are subtle;

thus, their sequence is such that they are progressively easier and more difficult to cultivate. Regarding the inclusion of the six aspects, each of these eleven [perfections] encompasses all the *pāramitās*, because they are mutually concordant.
As the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The meaning of *dāna* (generosity) encompasses the six: [providing] material goods (*āmiṣa*), protection from fear (*abhaya*)," and so forth.
Regarding the Dharma and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are perfections that have not yet been adorned (*apariniṣpanna*) which are not included;

there are perfections that have already been adorned (*pariniṣpanna*) which are mutually inclusive. Now, the text of this sutra must necessarily include all ten. If it were to speak of only six, [it would be incomplete].

The six [perfections] subsume the latter four; if expanded into ten, the sixth subsumes only non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), while the latter four are all subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Regarding the seventh point, cultivation and realization: these five stages involve general cultivation, reaching their ultimate consummation only at the stage of Buddhahood. The tenth point concerns the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).
In total, there are three names. During the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), the power of giving and the other perfections is still slight;
being overcome by afflictions (*kleśa*), they are merely called *pāramitās*. In the second eon, their power gradually increases and they are able to subdue the afflictions;
thus they are called "near-perfections" (*upapāramitā*). In the third *saṃkhyeya*, their power increases further, enabling them to ultimately subdue all [afflictions].
Afflictions (*kleśa*) are called the Great *Pāramitā*. Therefore, throughout the preceding and following passages, it is repeatedly referred to as the "Vast *Pāramitā*. Ninth, regarding the teaching:
while other teachings may be considered accordingly, this teaching must further integrate each and every element; it penetrates the fruit and encompasses the cause.

Tenth, regarding the contemplation of the mind: this can be understood through the intention. Tenth, the explanation of the text is divided into ten parts; first, the Perfection of Giving (*Dāna-pāramitā*).
In the past, he gave rise to great compassion for sentient beings (up to: being able to cause those who see him to feel joy.
To withhold from oneself and bestow upon others is called *dāna* (giving). Its nature consists of non-attachment and the three types of action (*karman*) it engenders.

This has three kinds: namely, giving material wealth, the Dharma, and fearlessness. The first half [of the verse] refers to the practice of giving through great compassion within the context of the causes.
These three are already included herein. This compassion is also the first three of the seven supreme qualities (*saptavidha-paramatā*).

Regarding the latter half [of the verse], which concerns the fruit: material wealth (*āmiṣa*) sustains the physical body; fearlessness (*abhaya*) benefits the mind; and the Dharma (*dharma*) sustains the Dharma-body. Thus, one attains a resultant body that is most sublime among all bodies.
Since all three gladden sentient beings, those who see them will necessarily rejoice. Furthermore, it is because they possess these seven supreme qualities that the body [is so].
It is most excellent. △ Second, the Perfection of Precepts (Śīlapāramitā).
From "In the past, within the ocean of boundless great kalpas" [to] "universally extinguishing all the heavy sufferings of the world.
Guarding against what is improper and ceasing evil is called precept (*śīla*). This has the three karmas as its nature at the time of receiving and training in the Bodhisattva precepts.

There are three kinds of precepts: the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), which gathers wholesome qualities and yields the fruit of a pure body; the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), which can eliminate the suffering of beings;

and the precept that pervades the ten directions, because the unmanifest body of precepts (*avijñapti-śīla-kāya*) is equal to all sentient beings. △ Third, the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
In the past, through the cultivation of the purity of patience (*kṣānti*), [the practitioner] universally emits light that illuminates the ten directions.

To be capable of receiving all dharmas while yet being unable to let go of them is called "patience"; this refers to patience toward living beings (*sattva-kṣānti*). Furthermore, patience is "acceptance" (*kṣamaṇa*);
patience is itself wisdom (*prajñā*). It is the simultaneous endurance of both phenomena and principle, consisting of non-anger, diligence, and discerning wisdom.

The nature of that which arises consists of the three types of karma. Patience (*kṣānti*) likewise has three aspects: patience in enduring injury from enemies, patience in accepting suffering, and patience in the discernment of the Dharma (*dharmapravicaya-kṣānti*).
As the verse says, "faithful understanding of reality" refers precisely to the discernment of the Dharma.
The perfection of physical form is the fruit of the first two types of patience; the emission of pure light is the fruit of the third type of patience. △ Fourth, diligence (*vīrya*).
In the past, through diligent cultivation over an ocean of many eons, [the Bodhisattva] manifested [all qualities] beneath the King of Bodhi Trees.
To refine the mind within the Dharma is called "diligence" (*vīrya*). To apply this refined mind toward reaching the goal is designated as "exertion" (*pragraha*).

Taking diligence and the three types of action (*karman*) it engenders as its nature, it is also of three kinds: first, donning the armor; second, gathering virtue; and third, benefiting and bringing happiness.
The first phrase encompasses the preceding two [perfections], as it refers to the armor-like diligence (*saṃnāha-vīrya*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Even if one were to dwell in hell for a single day and night consisting of a thousand great kalpas, for the sake of liberating a single sentient being. The second phrase corresponds to the third [perfection]. The latter half [of the verse] pertains to all three fruits;
since the cause is already free from the characteristics of body and mind, the fruit is able to manifest the body throughout the ten directions. △
The five *dhyānas*.
The Buddha practiced these for immeasurable eons until the stains of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) were entirely eliminated.

In Sanskrit, they are called *dhyāna*; here [in Chinese], they are translated as "calm contemplation" (*jinglü*). They take meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as their essential nature. Furthermore, there are three types, namely:
Abiding, manifesting, and accomplishing tasks: having already manifested the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and accomplished the welfare of sentient beings, those who see him rejoice deeply.

Abiding in the happiness of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), his various afflictions (*kleśa*) do not arise; furthermore, as he relies on wisdom to sever the afflictions, the afflictions of those who see him are extinguished.
△ Sixth, Prajñā (Wisdom).
The Tathāgata, having cultivated an ocean of various practices in the past... until he was able to utterly eliminate all darkness of ignorance.
*Prajñā* is the Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "wisdom" (*hui*). To investigate and seek the principles of truth is what is called wisdom. This and the following...

Fourth, all [of these] take the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) as their essence, and they are likewise of three types: first, non-conceptualization regarding the emptiness of persons; second, non-conceptualization regarding the emptiness of phenomena;

and third, non-conceptualization regarding the emptiness of both. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains them as three by way of the preparatory, fundamental, and subsequent [wisdoms], correlating them with the six perfections.
The *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā-alaṃkāra* (Yingluo jing) explains them as three by way of illuminating existence, illuminating non-existence, and illuminating the Middle Way.
This refers exclusively to the meaning of the three contemplations based on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which will be clarified below.
Since wisdom guides the myriad practices, it is said that one "cultivates the ocean of all practices. As for "endowed with," this means being endowed with the aforementioned three.
Because the cause is like having eyes, the fruit attains the two radiances of body and wisdom, which are able to extinguish all darkness. △ Seven: Expedient Means.
"Transforming sentient beings through various skillful means (upāya), without ceasing for limitless eons.
"Skillful means" (*upāya*) refers to *kauśalya* (expertise). "Means" (*fang*) signifies method; "expediency" (*bian*) signifies suitability. The four preceding [categories] each consist of two types.

Here, the first refers to the skillful means of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-upāya*) and the skillful means of deliverance (*uddharaṇa-upāya*). As the text says: "Transforming sentient beings in various ways," which refers to...
Skillful in delivering [beings], the accomplishments cultivated therein are further dedicated toward Bodhi. Those to be transformed are infinite;

as for the fruit, it extends horizontally throughout the ten directions to serve sentient beings, and in its vertical dimension, it exhausts the limits of the future without ceasing. △ Eighth: The Vow of Deliverance.
The Buddha formerly practiced for an ocean of great eons until the end of the future limit to save sentient beings.

"Vow" (*praṇidhāna*) refers to a yearning aspiration and solemn pledge. According to one interpretation, its essential nature consists of desire, resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), and faith (*śraddhā*).
It is also of two kinds: the vow for enlightenment and the vow to bring benefit and happiness to others. By virtue of the former vow, he appears in the world.
Due to his subsequent vows, even if he were to be born, it would never cease. △ Ninth, the Power of Resolve:
The Buddha extensively cultivated and refined this over immeasurable kalpas, until he universally manifested throughout all lands in the ten directions.

"Power" (*bala*) refers to that which cannot be bent or subdued; thus, whatever one contemplates and whatever one cultivates is spontaneously accomplished. This also has two types: namely, analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
What is here termed "the power of the Dharma" (*dharmabala*) refers to the cultivation performed by analytically reflecting upon all phenomena.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "By means of these two powers, the preceding six perfections are made to manifest without interruption. The Sūtra says: "It becomes spontaneous (*svarasavāhin*)."
Power. It is accomplished without a teacher and is unfailing without practice. How could it ever be destroyed? △ Ten: The Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha formerly cultivated the wisdom of the Universal Door (*pratyutpanna-mukha-jñāna*)... [up to] ...emitting light that universally illumines the lands of the ten directions.

Decisive discernment is called wisdom (*jñāna*). It refers to awakening to reality as it is. This too is of two kinds: the wisdom that experiences the joy of the Dharma and the wisdom that matures sentient beings.
The *Treatise on Non-nature* states: "By means of the six [perfections] beginning with generosity, this wisdom is established;

furthermore, by means of this wisdom, the six [perfections] are established. This is termed "experiencing the joy of the Dharma. By means of this sublime wisdom, one is able to correctly comprehend this.
Generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth benefit sentient beings. The Sūtra speaks of "universal-gate wisdom" (*samantamukha-jñāna*), which subsumes both types of wisdom in general;
when specifically assigned, the first phrase corresponds to the maturation of sentient beings, while the second phrase corresponds to the enjoyment of the bliss of the Dharma.

Since these two are non-dual, they constitute the power of non-obstruction, radiating light that shines everywhere. △ Ninth: Within the description of the *maṇi* fruit of the Bodhi tree, a praise of the Buddha.
This concerns the fruits of the practices of the ten stages cultivated in the past. The eleven verses are divided into two parts;
the first verse provides a general summary: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Cloud-Sound Pure Moon (until) spoke these verses."
The realm of supernormal powers is equal to space; [this] is fully explained within the *Maṇi* fruit, namely, the great function of the Buddha-fruit.
This is due to the practices of the previous stages (*bhūmi*) and the location where the summary is spoken. The remaining ten stages are each described in succession, one for each stage.
The meaning of these stages will be explained extensively in their respective chapters; here, they are merely summarized briefly.
"Purely and diligently practicing for immeasurable eons" (up to) "universally seeing the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: the objects perceived by the consciousness of sentient beings are themselves the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). By analogy, they evolve based on names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) through discrimination;

All possess the nature of awakening (*bodhi-dhātu*), and thus they are called Tathāgatas. This clarifies that Bodhisattvas realize and enter the ocean of the nature of sentient beings. △ Four.

Within each and every dust mote, there are as many vast lands as there are dust motes in ten Buddha-worlds.
△ Fifth, lands where Tathāgatas reside.
Within each and every land, there are the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the three periods of time.
It is in accordance with worldly convention that they are said to exist within the three periods; yet, because they fully accord with the true nature (dharmatā), they all abide within a single atom.
△ Sixth, the Bodhisattvas go to make offerings.

These bodhisattvas are all able to go everywhere to approach, attend upon, and make offerings to [the Buddhas], providing both material wealth and the Dharma. △ Seventh, assisting the Buddha to propagate the transformation:
in every thought-moment, through mastery over dreams, they cause all sentient beings to awaken according to their respective minds.
△ 8. The benefit of transformation through manifestation.
Within every thought-moment, in each and every land, [the bodhisattvas] are born into the family of the Tathāgata from the vast ocean of great vows.
Among them, Bhadrapāla awakens before the former [Mañjuśrī], who explains it by means of three meanings. First, the individual assignment and explanation: namely, by...
The first ten dharma-gates correspond to the ten benefits accomplished subsequently; one gate yields one benefit. Two gates precede [the benefits], while the remainder follow their respective order.
First, by means of the gate of mastery over dreams, one awakens sentient beings who commit evil within their dreams.

First, by means of the gate of severing evil, one causes beings to escape suffering and obtain benefit. Second, by means of the gate of Bodhisattva practices, one causes them to enter right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).

Third, by manifesting the gate of the death and rebirth of devas, one causes them to be born in heaven and experience bliss; for through negligence they perish, yet through diligent mindfulness they are reborn.
These three constitute the vehicle of humans and devas. Fourth, by shaking the world-systems, one manifests impermanence to induce weariness with cyclic existence, and by means of praise...
The Buddha’s supernormal transformations cause [beings] to rejoice, thereby accomplishing the benefit of those of the two vehicles; those below are all of the Mahāyāna.

Fifth, through great vows to adorn the buddha-fields, he causes them to cultivate merit and seek [enlightenment]. Sixth, through the speech that gathers in sentient beings, he causes them to resolve upon the Great Mind by means of the Buddha’s voice.

This is because it is the great compassion of the same essence. Seventh, by raining down the Dharma with Buddha-clouds, they cause [beings] to enter the stage of non-retrogression of the bodhisattvas;
these three aforementioned stages belong to the three levels of worthies prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*).

Eighth, by means of illumination that pervades the entire dharma-realm and through spiritual transformations, they cause them to obtain the eye of wisdom from the first ground upward, whereby they see the equal Dharma. Ninth, by means of the Buddha’s universal manifestation...

The power of liberation pervading the entire dharma-realm causes one to attain the benefit of the inexhaustible wisdom, great power, and great vows of the stages from the eighth ground upward, as well as the purification of the buddha-land.
Tenth, by means of Samantabhadra’s establishment of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one is caused to dwell in the ocean of great vows of the fruit of Buddhahood.

As for the statement "born into the family of the Tathāgata," it refers to being born because one has entered the stage of the fruit of Buddhahood; it does not mean being born into the Buddha [family] at the first ground or above.
This is the "Family. Second, regarding the "Universal Penetration": these ten dharmas above universally penetrate these ten benefits;
that is to say, either one dharma accomplishes all ten benefits, or ten dharmas accomplish a single benefit. In this way, they mutually pervade one another without any obstruction.

Third, regarding the "Individual Distinctions": it means that each of the aforementioned ten dharma-gates individually brings about awakening within as many worlds as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds.
Regarding the number of sentient beings, this is because the Dharma is of no benefit to them; later, ten [types] are beneficial.
It speaks only of the number of atoms in Mount Sumeru and does not mention the lands of atoms within the *kṣetras*. Thus, it is one's own person who is considered the beneficiary.

Since these are explained individually, the "Gate of Mastery over Dreams" also reveals that all things are like dreams; because there is unimpeded mastery over the extension and contraction [of time], it is called "mastery."

The rest may be understood as before. From the initial emission of light to the final attainment of benefit, these stages of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-transformation number eight when counted forward and twelve when traced backward;

they overlap infinitely. When the benefit of sentient beings numbering as many as the dust motes of ten Mount Sumerus is achieved in a single land, it is the same in all other lands. Therefore, it is said that in each and every land...
1. Each [benefit] is equal. 2. This benefit of all these lands occurs within a single moment of thought; it is likewise so for all other moments of thought.
Therefore, it is said to be "in every moment of thought. 3. Such benefits in every moment of thought constitute what is awakened to by a single dharma-gate;
each and every dharma-gate is thus. 4. Those many dharma-gates, in turn, constitute a single [great dharma-gate].
5. The Dharma-door of Mindfulness of What is Used: Just as with the mindfulness of what is used, so it is for the remaining instances of mindfulness regarding the Dharma-doors that are used.

6. The Dharma-door of Many Such Minds: First, one discusses a single vast world-system (*kṣetra*); as with one vast world-system, so it is for all vast world-systems numbering as many as the atoms within ten such systems.
7. The Dharma-door of Many Vast World-systems: First, one discusses a single atom; as with one atom, so it is for all the atoms within every established world-system.

It is likewise. Seven: all the aforementioned dust-motes constitute a single "Ocean of Established Arrays. As it is with one Ocean of Established Arrays, so it is with all the Oceans of Established Arrays throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
Eight: the karmic activities within all the Oceans of Established Arrays throughout the Dharma-realm constitute the transformation of a single emanated Bodhisattva.
As it is with one emanated Bodhisattva, so it is with the emanated Bodhisattvas of ten oceans of worlds.
Each and every one is thus. Ninth, all these emanated bodhisattvas are manifested by a single ray of light; as it is with one ray, so it is with each and every ray.
Tenth, those rays of light, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, are manifested from a single pore;
as it is with one pore, so it is with every single pore throughout the entire body. Eleventh, those pores throughout the entire body...

This is one bodhisattva. Just as there is this one bodhisattva, there are likewise ten billion Buddha-lands, as numerous as the atoms within those lands, each containing worlds as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds, and every single pore is exactly like this.

Thus, having previously explained these eleven layers of functional activity, we now discuss their arrival at this single assembly. Regarding such a single assembly, compared to other Buddhas’ [assemblies]...
The assembly is likewise thus. The following section of verses sets this forth in full.
Furthermore, each of the twelve preceding layers is divided into two, thereby forming twenty-four layers. For instance, consider a single thought-moment in relation to all thought-moments.
These constitute two meanings that are analogous in category; they are combined into one. The remaining eleven layers should be understood by analogy with this.

Thus, these layers overlap infinitely, each pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*. They can only be perceived instantaneously by wisdom (*jñāna*), for they are not within the domain of the mind or consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*).

In the ocean-like assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, such great functions are always thus. Regarding "The Three Lights and the Sound Spontaneously Narrate": since previously it was the light and sound that issued the summons, now likewise it is the light and sound that spontaneously narrate.

When the Bodhisattvas have reached the ultimate stage and their functions are exhausted in depth and breadth, if they did not narrate it themselves, the assembly of that time would find it difficult to know.
The ten verses are divided into two parts. The first verse generally clarifies [the subject] while simultaneously stating the location where the teaching is given.
At that time, from within the radiance of all the bodhisattvas, voices simultaneously issued forth, speaking these verses:
"From within the various radiances emerge wondrous sounds... [up to] ...able to enter the sublime path to bodhi."
△ Second, specifically revealing the excellence of qualities and functions, in three parts. First, a general revelation of the mastery of essence and function:
"Cultivating through oceans of kalpas without weariness... O Son of the Buddha, you skillfully enter this expedient means."

Compassion and wisdom guide one another; they deliver sentient beings without weariness, and throughout the ocean of all kalpas, they cultivate skillful means while constantly proclaiming that the nature of all things is quiescent extinction.
Contemplating both emptiness and existence, one enters the Dharma-gate and remains eternally tranquil.
Taking all the vows of the Buddhas of the three periods of time as one's own practice of pure karma.

Since there is no obstruction between self and others, one transforms others while purifying oneself. △ Second, a detailed account of the aforementioned mastery of manifestation, which is abbreviated compared to the previous [section]:
"In the assemblies of all Buddhas... (omitted)... entering the Tathāgata’s dharma of quiescent extinction."
His body pervades the ten directions, and his wisdom contemplates quiescence; this demonstrates that he has not merely come to this assembly.
Each and every ray of light is boundless, [extending] until one beholds the spheres of activity of all the bodhisattvas.
The light of his body enters everywhere; with the eye of wisdom, he observes all.
That a Bodhisattva can abide upon a single hair-tip is the stage of pure skillful means.
Abiding on a single hair-tip, he causes all lands to tremble; how much more so when he dwells above, upon a precious lotus flower!
Regarding the passage from "In each and every atom, immeasurable bodies" to "attaining the adornment of unimpeded intention":
within every atom there are many bodies; in every gateway, transformations differ. By taking up one instance of the gateway of death and rebirth, one may apply this analogy to all others.
Regarding all kalpas throughout the three periods of time (up to) "the one who realizes the unimpeded nature of dharmatā":

this refers to being unimpeded in the recollection of kalpas. This is brought about by the realization of profundity; since the recollection of kalpas has already been integrated, one is able to manifest dharmatā in every thought-moment.
As for "the unimpeded," both the divisible and the indivisible are unimpeded. This means that realizing the principle is not merely a matter of the indivisible.
Therefore, while it exists in all places, it is entirely contained within this one dharma; all dharmas are likewise so.

Each possesses its own fourfold body and so forth, not merely as divisions. One should contemplate that it is always present here, yet has no location. △ The final verse concludes by showing that the extensive [explanation] returns to the essential.
"Samantabhadra’s supreme practices can all be entered" (up to) "amidst all the radiances, there is a great roar.
Samantabhadra’s supreme practices enter them all; it is not merely what has been presented thus far. Therefore, it is able to manifest this mastery within the radiances.

△ Fourth, the manifestation of auspicious signs to indicate the teaching: The signs manifested above were merely to summon those with the karmic affinity; having gathered them, he is about to expound [the teaching].

Therefore, this auspicious sign has appeared once more. There are three aspects to this auspicious manifestation: first, light reveals the Master of the Dharma; second, the appearance of flowers symbolizes the meaning;
third, the appearance of the assembly symbolizes the teaching. Since the Dharma relies on people to propagate it, the principle of the Master is clarified first as the foundation of the teaching;
thus, he appears before the teaching itself. The first section is divided into six parts; the first is the intention.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause all bodhisattvas to [attain] the supernatural powers of boundless realms,
emitted light from between his eyebrows. (2) The Body.
The space between the eyebrows signifies the departure from the two extremes. Regarding its essence, one does not calculate the two extremes of existence and non-existence;

regarding its meaning, one does not cling to the extremes of the characteristics of phenomena such as permanence and impermanence; regarding practice, one does not cultivate the two extremes of suffering and pleasure;

regarding the path, one does not abide in the two extremes of the heterodox and the orthodox; regarding persons, one does not grasp at the two extremes of cause and effect; and regarding the teaching, one does not speak of the mundane...

Regarding the two extremes concerning transcendence: not perceiving the two extremes of the true and the conventional within the Truths; and regarding transformation, not being fixed upon the two extremes of the provisional and the real.
For this reason, he emits light from between his eyebrows for the sake of the assembly. Third, the names.
This light is named "The Universal Radiance of the Wisdom-Light of All Bodhisattvas, the Treasury Illumining the Ten Directions.
The first phrase causes one to attain the wisdom capable of knowing; the second phrase causes one to illuminate the objects of knowledge.

There are three meanings of "treasury" (*kośa*): first, because the light of wisdom contains inexhaustible virtues; second, because within each atom of the ocean of lands throughout the ten directions...
It is threefold because it encompasses all lands (*kṣetra*). It also extends throughout the five treasuries (*pañca-kośa*).
Because it speaks of the light of wisdom (*jñāna-prabhā*), it illuminates the first two treasuries, causing Bodhisattvas to realize them;

it illuminates the next two treasuries, causing Bodhisattvas to perfect their realization—thus attaining nirvāṇa through perfection and attaining bodhi through completion—and it illuminates the fifth treasury, causing transformation and purification. Among these three, the latter two are as follows: [text fragment].
Within the lower activities: △ Fourth, the characteristics.
Their appearance is like clouds of jewel-colored lamps.
This means their color is like lamp-clouds, shining through clearly like the sun and moon, pervading everywhere with moisture, because they rain down the rain of Dharma. As it says:
The Chapter on the Ocean of Marks. △ Five: The Manifestation of the Functional Activity of Light. First, the scope of illumination:
it universally illuminates all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.
△ Second, the manifestation of light upon the environment and its inhabitants.
Within them, the lands and their sentient beings are all made clearly manifest.
△ Third, shaking the net of those realms:
furthermore, he causes the entire web of worlds to tremble universally.
Because all worlds are reflected in overlapping layers, they correspond to one another like the openings of a net.
Fourth, the manifestation of the Tathāgata within a single atom: within each and every atom, countless Buddhas appear.
△ Fifth, raining down the Dharma according to individual capacities.

Following the diverse dispositions and desires of all sentient beings (up to) the assembly at the site of enlightenment of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, three dharmas are briefly presented, all of which are revealed below. First, the wheel-cloud demonstrates what is to be practiced; second, renunciation.
The clouds manifest that which they deliver. The three great vows manifest the master who preaches the Dharma;
this means that as he is about to preach the Universal Dharma (Pufa), he causes [beings] to know that the master’s great vows universally pervade within every atom of the lands. △ Six: Conclusion.
Having performed these acts, [the light] circumambulated the Buddha to the right and entered beneath his feet, demonstrating that there is an ultimate destination.
Realization flows from the Buddha; thus, as it was produced by causes that accord with the fruit, it must circumambulate to the right.
Because it ascends from below, it enters through the feet, for one enters into realization according to the path traversed by the Buddha. △
Second, the manifestation of flowers to signify meaning, which has two parts. First, the general indication of the manifestation of flowers:
At that time, a great lotus flower suddenly appeared before the Buddha to serve as a seat for the assembly manifested in the central space;
it generally signifies the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*, the Flower Ornament of the Buddha that is the ultimate referent (*vācya*), and specifically signifies the flowers.
Because it was purified by the Buddha of the *Tathāgatagarbha*, this lotus flower emerged before the Buddha.

While it generally symbolizes the *Avataṃsaka*, it also fully encompasses the ten gates such as "simultaneous fulfillment" (*yugapat-paripūrṇa*), as well as the teachings and their meanings; however, its primary intention is precisely to symbolize the meaning itself.
As for its sudden appearance, it signifies that phenomena arise based on principle (*tattva*), and thus it is difficult to fathom. 2. Manifesting the Adornment of Endowed Virtues.
Two. First, the ten kinds are designated.
These flowers possess ten kinds of adornments that no other lotus can equal.
By first designating these ten kinds, their inexhaustible virtues are revealed. △ Second, the ten phrases are listed individually. First, the essence is replete with all virtues.
That which is called the stalk is composed of various jewels interspersed (extending to: a wondrous net covering the top, its radiance and color pure and clear.
Because the place where the lotus seeds reside carries the meaning of "containing," it is named a "Treasury" (*garbha*).
The name "Flower Treasury" (*Gandavyūha*), which signifies that a single dharma-gate contains all [dharmas], is established on this basis. △ Second, mastery in wondrous function.
Within a single thought-moment, he manifests the infinite Buddhas [and] all the practices and vows cultivated by all Bodhisattvas.

How much more so when there are many *maṇi-rāja* jewels? These are the aforementioned essence of the treasury; the manifestation of the Buddha-bodies is the non-obstruction between the environment (*āśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Since many sounds are emitted, every sound expounds the Dharma. △ Third, manifesting the multitude to represent the teaching, in three parts. First, the manifestation.
At that time, once these flowers had arisen, in the space of a single thought-moment—
wherein "a single thought-moment" refers to the uninterrupted arising of the flowers, signifying the correspondence between the teaching and its meaning. △ Second, appearing in various places.
Within the white curl between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows,
it is represented that the teaching proceeds from what has been realized— the pure Dharma-realm— from which all teachings flow as their source, just as white is the fundamental basis of all colors.
△ Third, the correct explanation of the manifestation of the assembly in three parts.
First, the simultaneous manifestation of the principal and the retinue: There was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Sarvadharmaviśeṣaghoṣa (up to) who emerged all at once.
Because it universally explains all phenomena, it is said that "all that is explained is complete. This is called "Supreme Sound" (*jaya-svara*).
Since a teaching of the perfect Dharma necessarily includes its retinue, the text below states that there are as many *sūtras* as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds serving as its retinue.
Because the provisional and the real are without obstruction, it is called "simultaneous. 2. Prostrating and taking one's seat.
They circumambulated the Tathāgata for immeasurable circuits (until they reached their respective positions), whereupon they each took their places in successive order.

Although their roles as leaders and attendants differ, they all cultivate the causes with the expectation of attaining the fruit; thus, they circumambulate the Tathāgata. Since the text and its meaning follow one another, they rely upon lotus seats.

Because the primary and auxiliary practices are not equal, there are differences between the pedestals and the filaments. This is because the higher meaning is clarified by relying on principle. Suddenly...
And [the teaching] appears. Now, because the teaching is established by means of persons, the multitude flows from the Buddha, just as milk flows from a cow in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
△ Third, to manifest his virtuous deeds.
As for the Bodhisattva Sarvadharma-viśeṣa-ghoṣa, he is specifically questioned because he presides over this school. The text contains ten phrases, which can be briefly explained in two ways.
First, they may be vertically correlated with the ten stages (*bhūmi*) to clarify that each single phrase encompasses the merits of all ten stages.
Having realized the profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), one gives rise to great joy;

this is the Joyous Stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Having attained the realization of suchness through wisdom, one enters the wisdom that traverses the domain of the Buddhas, free from doubt or obstruction.
In the second stage, there is the morality of intrinsic nature;
this is the practice of the Buddhas, whereby one enters the unfathomable ocean of the Buddha’s Dharma-body.
In the third stage, there is extensive learning, whereby one enters the ocean of the Dharma-body.
They go to the abodes of all Tathāgatas in all lands;
they cultivate the four paths and the factors of enlightenment; they rely upon spiritual friends;
and from every pore of their bodies, they manifest supernatural powers.

On the fifth stage, one practices both [samatha and vipaśyanā] simultaneously; manifesting supernatural powers to benefit sentient beings, one universally contemplates the entire dharma-realm in every thought-moment.
On the sixth stage, one contemplates the dharma-realm, and prajñā manifests before one.
The Buddhas of the ten directions collectively bestow their power upon him.
Once these seven functions have been interconnected, the Buddhas grant them power,
enabling him to dwell securely in all samādhis.
Eighth, being without dwelling or movement, they abide in the mind of samādhi,
constantly beholding the Buddhas throughout all future kalpas as the body of the ocean of merit of the boundless dharma-realm.
Ninth, acting as Dharma-preachers, they perceive the boundless Dharma.
This extends even to all samādhis, liberations, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and transformations.

The ten [perfections] are fully perfected within the Great Consummation Samādhi (*mahāparyanta-samādhi*). Since even the first stage (*bhūmi*) encompasses the merits of all stages, how much more so for the subsequent ones;
the preceding ones are never lacking in the following. Second, explaining by way of the ultimate position: first, the principle-wisdom (*jñāna*) realizes the truth; second, the means (*upāya*).
1. Wisdom enters into practice; 2. Threefold realization exhausts the Dharma-body; 3. Constantly contemplating the enjoyment body; 4. Manifesting spiritual transformations from every pore;

5. Mindfulness and contemplation of the Dharma-gates; 6. Externally receiving the Buddha’s empowerment; 7. Internally abiding in profound meditative concentration; 8. Vertically perceiving the limit of the future.

The ten types of untimely death are not without their full resolution. Therefore, these ten phrases are subsumed into five pairs. Whether horizontal or vertical, the expressive terms must be complete;
thus, there are two explanations. Fifth, the extolling of the Buddha’s virtues: since he has manifested and arrived, one extols them according to one's capacity.
This expresses one’s own feelings of boundless devotion and manifests the Buddha’s shoreless virtues. The text is divided into two parts:

the first is the praise by the Bodhisattva between the eyebrows, and the latter ten are the praises by the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions. As soon as the assembly had gathered, the Buddha manifested an auspicious sign.
The text does not repeat itself; therefore, it has been compiled and arranged in sequence. Those with similar qualities have been grouped together and placed in one location.
Following the order of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light), the verses of *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* are presented first, followed by the ten bodhisattvas, who correspond respectively to the ten directions.
Ancient scholars did not understand this text and consequently treated the latter ten as the retinue of *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*; this is not only...

The errors in the commentaries and treatises likewise stem from transgressions in the translation. Why is this so? For instance, when the multitude emerges from between the eyebrows, both the principal and the retinue should offer praise;
yet the assembly coming from the ten directions remains silent, not uttering a single word. How utterly perfunctory are the ritual protocols between the principal and the retinue!
Moreover, according to the precedent of the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," those who arrive are all accompanied by verses of praise.

If one examines the names of these bodhisattvas closely, they correspond sequentially to those in the previous section on the ten directions; it is merely due to the translator’s lack of careful scrutiny that their names have become slightly discrepant.

In the following section, each point will be examined in detail. △ Now, first, regarding the "Exquisite Sound" (Śabdavara), the text is divided into two parts. First, the formal presentation of the verses:
therein, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, he surveys the ten directions within the assembly and speaks in verse, saying:

△ Second, the actual exposition in verse. However, within these verses, the Buddha is praised in terms of his general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which also implicitly contain all the questions; this can be understood through reflection.

The ten stanzas are divided into three parts. First, there is the direct praise of the Buddha, all of which praises the Tathāgata’s non-obstruction between essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*vṛtti*).
Within this, the first [stanza] shows that he pervades everywhere without moving from his original state.
The Buddha’s body fills the Dharma-realm (up to) and constantly dwells upon this seat of enlightenment.
The ten bodies are perfectly interfused, pervading the four dharma-realms. △ Second, not destroying the minor marks while possessing vast capacity.
Within each and every pore of the Tathāgata (up to) thus pervading the entire dharma-realm:

the former is because the phenomenon accords with the principle; this [latter] is because the phenomenon contains the principle. The preceding one and a half verses show that a single hair-pore encompasses the three worlds;
the latter half applies by analogy to the rest, meaning that throughout the entirety of the dharma-realm there are Buddha-bodies, and not a single spot where there is none.
A single hair-pore contains oceans of lands. Furthermore, a single hair-pore manifests gates of liberation, for it is where the wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwells.
As for the manifestation of many oceans of lands: through every gate, one beholds the causes of the Pure Lands. Second, praising the Buddha by way of his retinue:
because the holy sages act as attendants, they manifest the excellence of the Lord. The six verses below generally clarify the Lord and his retinue; both pervade [the following]. First:
2. The universal pervasiveness of the collective body:
"Seated within each and every land... until they completely fill the entire dharma-realm.
△ Second, there are four verses concerning the collective body's pervasion of particulars.
From the lands as numerous as the atoms of the dharma-realm (up to) flowing throughout the dharma-realm without exception;
because they are subtle and inconceivable, only universal wisdom can know them, and only universal practice can establish them. △3.
One verse concludes both the principal and the attendant.
In every atom of all lands, [the Buddhas] each rain down the Dharma rain according to their [beings'] inclinations. △ The twentieth section:
The Praise of Virtues by Bodhisattvas from the Ten Directions (ten parts). First, the East (two parts). First, the ritual for reciting verses.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva among the assembly (up to: who surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse.

Regarding the phrase "among the assembly," it refers to the ocean-like great assembly. The preceding list of names is designated as "Observation. The banner of the Lotus of the Supreme Dharma stands high;
its sovereign emergence is transcendent and supreme. This is a metaphor for similarity. Radiant Wisdom (*Prabhāmatī*) is that which is being illustrated.

The Body of the Banner. △ Second, the actual exposition of verses praising the Buddha’s two bodies—the True and the Responsive—providing a cryptic answer regarding the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and so forth, as these encompass the Buddha-ground.
The ten verses are divided into two parts: the first three praise the True Body, and the latter seven praise the Responsive Body.

In praising the True Body, both its essence and function must be seen as excellent; in praising the Responsive Body, one speaks solely in terms of its function to reveal the differences between the gates [of teaching], though in reality they are not different in essence.

[The section on] the "External" [aspects]. Now, the first part is divided into three sections: the first praises the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*); the second praises the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); and the third concludes both by synthesizing the four wisdoms, which together constitute the five dharmas of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). First, the praise of the wisdom-body: [Verse: The wisdom that is free from conceptualization, The wisdom that is unimpeded, The wisdom that is equal toward all, And the wisdom that accomplishes all tasks— These are the four wisdoms of the Tathāgata.

They are the nature of the Great Sage; They are the nature of the Buddhas. They are the nature of the Buddhas. [Commentary: This verse praises the four wisdoms of the Tathāgata. These four wisdoms are the very nature of the Great Sage and the Buddhas. They are the nature of the Buddhas. They are the nature of the Buddhas. Thus, the four wisdoms and the dharma-realm are fully present as the five dharmas. First, the praise of the wisdom-body.
The Tathāgata’s profound wisdom universally enters the dharma-realm, able to revolve through the three periods of time and serve as a guiding light for the world.

The first half-verse represents the realization of reality (tattva) as the fundamental essence; the second half-verse represents the subsequent engagement with conventional truth (saṃvṛti). Furthermore, each phrase corresponds to one of the wisdoms:

the first phrase is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is profound and subtle; the second phrase is the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*), because it is equal regarding self and others.

Because it is the very dharma-realm. The second phrase refers to the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), because it functions without obstruction regarding both specific and general characteristics.

The final phrase refers to the accomplishment of the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), because it achieves the task of guiding the world for the benefit of others. △ Second, praising the dharma-body.

All Buddhas share the same Dharma-body, which is without dependence and without differentiation; yet, in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings, they cause them to perceive the physical forms and appearances of the Buddha.
Regarding the first half [of the verse], their bodily characteristics are entirely identical. There are two meanings to this "sameness": first, the Dharma-body of the fundamental nature is identical;
as for "without dependence," it means there is no abiding basis; as for "without differentiation," it means the essence is non-dual. Second, they have already realized the Dharma-body.
The same applies to the powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth, as they are all without distinction. This is the body of unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇaprajñā-kāya*);
it does not rely on anything, is free from all conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and is thus without differentiation. The latter half [of the verse] concerns the identity of function:

because the manifestations and productions of the bodies, lands, and images of wisdom are all non-dual, this is the formless Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) that manifests forms in response to sentient beings. △ Third, the double conclusion.
Endowed with all-knowledge, one universally knows all phenomena; within all lands, there is nothing that does not manifest. The first half [of the verse] concludes the wisdom (*jñāna*):
the upper line is the fundamental [wisdom], and the lower line is the subsequently attained [wisdom]. The second half concludes the phenomena (*dharma*);
it merely cites their function, while their essence pervades both [halves], because wisdom accords with suchness (*tathatā*). As the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says: "Suchness and the one who is such."
Because wisdom is the Dharma-body. △ Second, the praise of the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) has three parts. First, manifesting the response according to the inclinations [of beings]:
The Buddha’s body, its radiance, and its physical characteristics are inconceivable; those sentient beings who have faith and joy shall all see them according to their respective capacities.

"Inconceivable" means that it is boundless according to conditions. *Guangmingjue* says: "Even if one were to contemplate the marks, features, and majestic virtue for a hundred million nayuta kalpas, they would only become more boundless," and so forth. △ Second, the body-light expounds the Dharma.
From within the body of a single Buddha, he manifests as immeasurable Buddhas (up to: "shallow wisdom cannot fathom [this]. The first transformation-body preaches the Dharma;
in relation to the preceding response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), this is a further transformation.

The next two [emanations] of light from the hair-pores preach the Dharma, and the final one concludes by praising the unfathomable Wheel of the Dharma. The meaning is explained elsewhere. △ Third: Attaining Enlightenment and Arising of Supernormal Powers.
Manifesting the body to attain perfect enlightenment in all worlds... (up to) universally manifesting supernatural powers.
All of the above are perfectly interfused. There are also ten bodies [of the Buddha], yet this is merely from one perspective. △ Second, the South: two parts.
First, the ritual for reciting the verses.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva among the assembly (who), observing the ten directions, spoke in verse:

"In the previous assembly of clouds, he was named Puzhao Fahai (Universally Illuminating Ocean of Dharma); his wisdom, assembly, and meaning were likewise identical. 'Radiance' refers to the illumination of the Dharma.
II. The actual exposition of ten verses praising the Buddha’s quiescent function and responsive virtues, answering the preceding inquiry regarding the Dharma of the objective realm.
The manifestation of the body is the delimited object; its non-arising and lack of intrinsic nature is the object of contemplation. Sentient beings and their lands are all manifested transformations.
The text has three parts: first, the four verses on how the response arises from the truth; second, one verse manifesting the truth.

The Buddha-body is eternally manifest, completely filling the entire *dharmadhātu*, constantly emitting a vast and magnificent sound that universally vibrates throughout the lands of the ten directions.

Regarding "the Buddha-body is eternal": it is eternal in the sense of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), for it transcends the three periods of time; its wisdom accords with reality, remaining serenely and eternally illuminating.
"Manifest" means being free from the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*); "appearing" means always being present before one. It is not like the self-substance of sentient beings.
It is eternal. Regarding "pervading the entire dharma-realm": because it is adorned by merit and wisdom, each of the sense organs and the marks of excellence is boundless and limitless.
The next two lines concern the constant employment of sound, for it eternally and universally experiences the vast dharma-joy of self-enjoyment.
△ The two following verses describe the arising of activity.
"The Tathāgata universally manifests his body, pervading and entering the world" (up to) "is able to enter and is able to observe.
The first [verse] concerns universally following the inclinations of sentient beings; the second, the mutual resonance of cause and response; and the third, the boundless light of the Dharma.
△ Second, the non-obstruction of essence and function.
The Buddha-body has no birth, yet it can manifest birth; (up to: all that is manifested is like a shadow.
The first two lines concern its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): no birth, yet manifesting birth. The next two lines concern its nature (*dharmatā*): non-abiding, yet abiding.
The following verse concerns its function (*vṛtti*): no coming or staying, yet universally pervasive. The final verse simultaneously negates both essence and function, meaning there is no essence.
"Swiping away non-arising" means that non-arising is the essence of the Buddha-dharma; thus, the present essence is itself no-essence.
"Having no place of abiding" swipes away the two phrases concerning nature, as even non-arising cannot be apprehended. "Swiping away the phrase of arising" indicates the manifestation of birth.
The second half of the verse swipes away the previous second stanza concerning function, for function is like a shadow. △ Third, the inexhaustibility of the Real and the Responsive.
The Buddha, in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, raises great clouds of Dharma (up to:
the interlacing of color-forms is inexhaustible. First, the inexhaustibility of the clouds of Dharma; second, the inexhaustibility of the assemblies; third, the inexhaustibility of the bodily marks.

The term "inexhaustible" refers to both [the transformation body] and the true body (*dharmakāya*). That they ultimately do not exhaust is because they are entirely identical in essence. △ Third, the two [aspects] of the Western [Pure Land]. First, the explanation.
Verse Form: At that time, there was another bodhisattva within the assembly who, having observed the ten directions, spoke these verses:
"The former name was Universal Adornment of Moonlight and Fragrant Flames; herein, 'light' refers to the light of the moon, and 'wisdom' is..."
The Adornment of Wisdom. △ Second, the ten verses of the formal exposition praise the Buddha’s body as containing all oceans;

this is the answer to the question regarding the source of empowerment, for it is through empowerment that one is able to enter. Within this, the first nine verses describe the various oceans, through which the Buddha’s virtues may be known.
This is divided into two parts. The first is general;
it describes how the bodhisattvas in this assembly enter the inconceivable stages of the Buddha, each being able to perceive the spiritual powers of all Buddhas.
△ The second part consists of eight specific sections. The first concerns the function of manifesting within atoms while pervading all things equally.
The wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) is able to universally enter all lands as numerous as atoms, up to entering the realm of the Buddha.
First, one wisdom-body enters the lands as numerous as atoms; next, one form-body (*rūpakāya*) universally manifests its functions; the latter two explain the meaning of the former:
first, the perfection of Samantabhadra’s practices; second, the equality of body and mind. II. Subtly entering into a single pore.
The function of the *kṣetra* (buddha-field):
Having realized the Tathāgata’s wisdom, it illuminates the entire *dharmadhātu*, such that in a single thought-moment, all can be manifested.
△ Second, one verse concludes the merits by attributing them to the Buddha.
In each and every Buddha-field, all Bodhisattvas universally enter the body of the Buddha, which is boundless and inexhaustible;
it is not merely a single assembly. Only when all Bodhisattvas have entered the Buddha’s body can one truly praise the Buddha.
△ Fourth, clarifying the northern direction, in two parts: first, the ritual of reciting verses.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva among the assembly who, having surveyed the ten directions, spoke in verse.
This is the same as the original title, with the addition of the character "wisdom" (慧). II. The actual exposition of the ten verses:

Praising the Buddha for manifesting function based upon his essence and turning the Great Dharma Wheel, this answers the previous inquiry regarding the Buddha’s practice. Because the Buddha turns the Dharma to transform sentient beings, this constitutes his practice.
The prose section has three parts. The first two lines provide a general summary:
Vairocana Buddha is able to turn the wheel of the true Dharma.
△ Second, there are eight and a half verses that specifically praise the ten transformations of the Buddha.
Throughout all lands in the dharma-realm, they are entirely pervasive like clouds;
they manifest birth and transformation, taking birth in every place because their cloud-like bodies are all-encompassing.
Within all the great world-oceans throughout the ten directions, they turn the wheel of Dharma everywhere through the power of the Buddhas' spiritual penetrations and vows.
This praises the transformation through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Although it is said that he turns the Dharma wheel, the intent lies in its universal application;
in all buddha-fields and amidst vast assemblies, his names and titles differ from one another.

This praises the transformation through the fruits of karma. Regarding the fact that the names and titles of all lands differ: it is to demonstrate that they belong to the same category of beings, as their karmic retributions and names are identical.
These are the three aforementioned support-bodies (*āśraya*).
He expounds the sublime Dharma according to what is appropriate and skillfully manifests transformations as required; thus he is able to sever their doubts.
Through the great majestic power of the Tathāgata and the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s vows, there is no wondrous sound that does not reach throughout all lands.
Exhortation, praise, encouragement, and transformation:

because they are praised and encouraged by sublime sounds, the bodies of the Buddhas manifest throughout lands as numerous as atoms, universally raining down the rain of Dharma upon all worlds—unborn and without distinction.
To comfort and transform beings, he rains down the Dharma rain, causing them to advance in the cultivation of the dharma of non-arising. These are the three superior vocal actions:
throughout countless billions of eons and within all dust-mote lands, he fully expounds with sublime voice all the deeds performed in the past.
They receive mental transformations; they receive and take up inquiries in order to expound upon past deeds.
Throughout the networks of light that pervade all the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, there are Buddhas who universally transform all sentient beings within those lights.

It is the transformation through the discernment of intention. Because one must first discern the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings and distinguish the differing natures and characteristics of all phenomena before being able to transform them universally, the Buddha-body is undifferentiated and fills the entire dharma-realm;
it enables those who behold the form-body to be skillfully tamed according to their individual capacities.
They initiate mental transformations and give rise to all manner of virtues and the great practices of the Three Vehicles.

For the sake of skillful training, they cause all sentient beings to see the various names and titles of all the Teachers throughout every realm in the three periods of time, explaining them in diverse ways.
It constructs mental transformations and establishes the Buddha-dharma, causing all various matters and meanings to be seen;
arising functionally based on reality, it is the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). Thus, it is called the *nirmāṇakāya*. There are no separate mind or form [apart from this].

The ten aforementioned emanations do not contradict the sequence of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*; they merely ensure that these aspects are harmonized without violating the intent of the sūtra. △ Third, the conclusion and dedication.
Assembly.
All the sublime wheels of Dharma turned by all Tathāgatas of the past and present are heard within this assembly.
△ Fifth, the Northeastern Quarter, in two parts: first, the ritual for reciting verses.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva among the assembly (up to: who surveyed the ten directions and spoke these verses:
"In the previous assembly, there was one named *Anantaguṇakośadharmasāgaravairocanapradīpa*. 'Vairocana' corresponds in meaning to 'most excellent light.
The name 'Guṇakośa' (Treasury of Merit) is no different from before. 'Ananta' (Inexhaustible) [is the same as] the second."

[This is] a title. [It is] present at the beginning but absent at the end. △ Second, the actual exposition of the verses of praise. The Buddha gathers his eminent retinue and answers the question regarding the power of the Buddha.
He praises the Bodhisattvas by way of relying upon the Buddha’s power; therefore, he concludes by saying, "abiding in the stage of power. The text has two parts.
The first stage, the fulfillment of wisdom and the attainment of the Dharma, constitutes the general characteristic.
In this assembly, the sons of the Buddha who have skillfully cultivated all forms of wisdom are persons capable of entering such a gateway of expedient means.

The final phrase has two meanings: first, it refers back to what precedes, meaning that because he possesses the transformations of the three preceding wheels, he is able to pervade every single land.
Second, it refers to the nine specific [sections] below as such skillful means. △ Second, the specific characteristics and common praise of the seven matters.
Within each and every land, he universally proclaims a vast sound, expounding the spheres of the Buddha’s conduct so that it is heard throughout the lands of the ten directions.
This first praise concerns the universal proclamation of the great sound, which possesses three kinds of greatness: first, greatness of place, because it occurs in each and every land;
second, greatness of meaning, because it expounds the Buddha’s conduct; and third, greatness of substance, because it is heard throughout the ten directions.
In each and every thought-moment, one universally contemplates all phenomena, abides in the stage of *tathatā*, and thoroughly penetrates the ocean of all dharmas.
Second, there is no passing of time in vain during the period of praise; for in every thought-moment one contemplates the Dharma and realizes the ultimate reality.
Within each and every Buddha-body, one practices the pāramitās and purifies the buddha-fields for inconceivable billions of kalpas.
Third is the ability to enter superior states, because one cultivates pure lands within the bodies of all Buddhas.
Within each and every atom, one is able to realize all dharmas; thus, being unimpeded, one travels throughout the lands of the ten directions.
Fourth, because within the atoms of defilement, which are themselves unimpeded, one realizes the Dharma and travels everywhere.
He proceeds to each and every buddha-field without exception, seeing the Buddha’s supernormal powers and entering the sphere of the Buddha’s activity.
Fifth, he is able to enter the Buddha’s realm because he sees the Buddha’s supernormal power and enters his sphere of activity. There are two such spheres of activity:
first, the sphere of wisdom, which refers to the domain of the ten powers; second, the sphere of the Buddha’s transformations, which refers to the receptacle world and sentient beings.
The vast voices of all Buddhas reach throughout the Dharma-realm so that there is nowhere they are not heard... (up to) all are able to understand them.
These are the six skillful entries into sound: the first entry is into the great voice; the next is into the wondrous voice; and the last is into all voices.
"From the ground one attains the ground; abiding within the stage of power (*balabhūmi*), the Dharma obtained through diligent cultivation for billions of eons is as follows.
Regarding "the seven excellences in knowing the grounds": "from the ground" refers to the emergence of the mind. "Attaining the ground" refers to the entry into and abiding therein.
"Within the stage of power" refers to the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*). "The Dharma obtained" summarizes the aforementioned skillful means (*upāya*).
△ Section Six: The Southeastern Direction (Part Two). First, the ritual for reciting verses.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva among the assembly who... [observing the ten directions] spoke in verse, saying:

The title is identical to the preceding. △ Second, the formal exposition of the verses of praise. The various Bodhisattvas, having awakened to and entered the profound and vast [reality], perceive the Buddha’s samādhi through the power of their own samādhi;
this is the response to the inquiry regarding samādhi. The text has four parts. First, praising the perception of the Buddha’s true essence.
All Tathāgatas are far removed from all marks (lakṣaṇa), up to the nature of mastery (vaśitā-svabhāva). There are two ways of seeing the Buddha:
first, seeing the Buddha as free from marks; second, seeing the Buddha as mastery. Regarding "being free from all marks," the *Prajñāpāramitā* states:
"One who is free from all marks is called a Buddha. The *Maitreya-śāstra* states: "Merely being free from four marks is itself freedom from one [mark]."

"Everything" refers to the self-nature and the distinctions of names and meanings. Regarding "mastery," it means that because the Bodhisattva unifies meditative concentration and wisdom, they see the Buddha with mastery. △ Second, the specific elucidation of awakening to phenomena.
Seeing the true body of the Buddha, one awakens to the profoundly deep Dharma (extending to) the ocean of all dharmas:
1. Realizing the dharma of profound principle, which manifests through the power of vows; 2. Awakening to the dharma of manifold practices, wherein merit and wisdom take form;
3. Penetrating the essence of the fruit-dharma, which is omnipresent; 4. Comprehending the teaching-dharma, which is profound, vast, and difficult to know. △ Third, praising the body.
Karma universally responds;
the single, firm, and dense body is seen within all atoms. (Up to: "It swiftly causes them to turn toward the Buddha-way.

First, it is profound; second, it is vast. As for what is meant by "firm and dense": it is equal to the Buddha’s essence and function. "Firm" refers to the Vajra-body; "dense" [refers to its impenetrability].
This refers to one of the three mysteries. Being one yet manifold, it pervades all things; being great yet minute, it manifests within the sensory dust as a response that requires no effort.
Thus, it appears while remaining without marks. In terms of the Dharma-gate, this body is the *tathāgatagarbha* (Buddha-nature).
It is "firm" because it cannot be destroyed; it is "mysterious" because it is profound and difficult to perceive; it is the "dust" of sentient beings.

The mind is such that there is nothing it does not fully possess; it has existed inherently from the beginning, and is therefore called "unborn. Its essence transcends all hundred negations, and is therefore called "formless.
The six sense-faculties of sentient beings are what are referred to as the various lands. △ Fourth, praising the attainment of the Buddha’s empowerment.
By the spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha, various bodhisattvas appear, pervading the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This consists of two parts: first, the power of this Buddha; second, the power of other Buddhas. △ Seventh, the southwest direction, part two: first, the ritual for reciting verses.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva among the assembly (omitted) who surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse.

In the preceding list of names and locations, he is called "Puhua Yanji" (Universal Flower Adorned Topknot); while there is some similarity, there are many differences. II. The actual exposition of the verses.

Praising the Buddha’s sovereign virtue in gathering and transforming living beings, answering the previous question regarding sovereignty. This is divided into three parts: first, gathering and transforming living beings without exception; second... [text continues].
First is the capacity for gathering.
Throughout all lands, one universally proclaims the subtle and wondrous sound (extending until) causing others to enter this Dharma.
