This refers to the profundity and vastness of body and speech: the preceding verse concerns speech, while the subsequent verse concerns the body. Within the description of the body, the first half [of the verse] concerns the essence; it is not subject to adventitious defilements.
Because it is defiled; this refers to the function of the latter half [of the verse]. Because it appears differently according to the objects, this also serves to resolve doubts.
It manifests forms for the sake of sentient beings without contradicting suchness, which is like space. △ Second, that which is subsumed.
If there is deep faith, joy, and being sustained by the Buddha (up to) entering the profound ocean of Dharma:
regarding the first verse, who is able to understand "internal faith and external sustenance"? Regarding the second verse, with what eye does one see? Only the superior, not the inferior.
Regarding the third verse, what phenomena are understood and seen? Namely, the three minds for each stage (*bhūmi*) throughout all stages of phenomena. Regarding the final verse, what...
The stage reaches its ultimate consummation at the final ground of the Bodhisattva, culminating in entry into the ocean of the Buddhas. △ Second, the non-obstruction of quiescence and function:
dwelling peacefully in the Buddha-lands while manifesting in all places... (until) thus beholding the Teacher.
The first verse employs universal manifestation; its essence has no coming or going. The subsequent verses employ eternal stillness; differences arise according to one's interpretation.
△ Third, the great function is boundless.
Within every single pore, various spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) are manifested, such that no one can fathom them.
First, within each individual hair-pore, all manner of spiritual powers are universally manifested; subsequently, from each individual body, the Dharma is everywhere expounded.
△ Eighth, Northwest Direction, Part Two: First, the ritual for reciting verses.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva among the assembly (omitted) who surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The former name was King Mañjuśrīprabha; here it is translated as Wēidéhuì (Vīryaprajñā). This is actually King Maṇi; only the dharma and the metaphor differ. II.
The actual exposition of the verses, praising the Buddha’s appearance in the world and his preaching of the Dharma, which are all universally pervasive virtues. [End of] Answering the Questions.
Regarding "fearlessness": because he is fearless in preaching the Dharma, this is divided into three parts. First, a general manifestation of the bodily light responding universally:
from "in each and every Buddha-field, sitting everywhere at the site of enlightenment" up to "the physical marks are not of one kind."
△ Second, distinguishing what is accomplished, in two parts. First, the light illuminates everything without exception:
within each and every atom, the radiance completely fills [them], extending to all various forms and appearances.
△ Second, there are four verses. They describe how the teaching is manifested universally:
"The Dharma realm and all lands are traversed everywhere without obstruction" (up to) "...manifesting inexhaustible dharmas in between."
First, pervading all dharmadhātu lands within and without the atoms of dust; second, pervading all lands within the bodies of the Buddhas;
third, clarifying the nature and characteristics of that which is transformed; fourth, the very power of the transformative perfect sound. △ Third, concluding the function by returning to the source:
because it is ungraspable.
In all lands, one sees the Buddha seated at the site of enlightenment; the Buddha’s body appears like a reflection, and its arising and ceasing cannot be apprehended.
This concludes the first section on the ritual of verses from the second chapter of the *Ninth Direction*.
At that time, there was another bodhisattva among the assembly (omitted)... who surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The former name was Dharmadhātu-jvālā-prabhā-mati; here it is translated as Puming (Universal Radiance), which refers to the aforementioned Jvālā. II.

The actual exposition of the verses, praising the supreme function of the Buddha’s realm into which the bodhisattva can enter, answering the question regarding supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). The text says: "Each and every one manifests..."
Therefore, it is divided into two parts. First, the supreme functions of the Buddha’s realm:
“The subtle body and physical marks of the Tathāgata are inconceivable... [until] each manifests supernatural powers.”
The first half-verse indicates its essence, namely the wondrous physical form and marks; the subsequent two and a half verses distinguish its function.
△ Second, the Bodhisattva’s ability to enter, meaning entering the realm of the Buddha, is divided into three parts. The first two [verses] concern the possession of virtuous knowledge and vision.
The Bodhisattvas of Great Wisdom enter deeply into the ocean of Dharma... [up to] the spiritual power of all Buddhas.
△ Second, there are three verses on the benefits accomplished through wisdom and vision:
"If a person possesses faith and understanding, as well as great vows... [up to] universally encompassing the entire Dharma-realm."
△ Third, there are two verses concluding the swiftness of its function:
"In as many buddha-fields as there are atoms of dust, such lands as these... the power of the bodhisattva is thus."
△ Second, the ten directions. First, the ritual for reciting verses.
At that time, there was again among the assembly a bodhisattva-mahāsattva (up to) who, surveying the ten directions, spoke in verse:

This is merely a reversal of the previous title. △ Second, the actual explanation in verse. This praises the Buddha’s perfect voice, his manifestation of the body, and his mastery of spiritual transformations, answering the question regarding the inability to encompass [the teachings].
That is to say, because this power of the vow is universally pervasive, there is nothing it cannot cause to be taken up.
This is divided into three parts; first, extolling the Buddha’s perfect voice and its virtue of raining down the Dharma.
The Buddha emits a single wondrous sound that is heard throughout the lands of the ten directions... having heard it, they proceed toward Bodhi. This [sound] possesses ten meanings:
first, it is a single wondrous sound because it is the Brahma-voice; second, it is heard everywhere because it accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*);
third, this one is many because phenomena and principle are fused; fourth, from each of those individual sounds, much [rain falls].
1. The rain of Dharma: each of those dharmas possesses all literary expressions. 2. Each is identical to the voices of all sentient beings.
3. These voices each pervade all places. 4. What is taught in each clearly reveals the principle of the purity of nature.
Ninth, each causes all beings to universally see and hear. Tenth, each and every one attains ultimate benefit.
These ten meanings unfold from a single wondrous sound, developing successively until they possess ten inexhaustible aspects; only then is it called the "perfect sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*).
The textual location can be seen [in the source]. △ Second, praising the Buddha’s merit of unimpeded manifestation of his body:
"Within every single atom of all lands throughout the dharma-realm... equal as empty space."

The first verse [is explained] by virtue of the power of liberation; it manifests as pervasive yet subtle. The next verse [is explained] by virtue of the power of the Dharma-body; it manifests such that the signs are themselves empty.
The final two verses employ the virtue of *prajñā* to elucidate the preceding verses. The first [of these two] explains the second half [of the previous verse].

Regarding the term "reflected image" (*pratibimba*), it reveals the absence of a fixed location; for when light is to the east, the shadow is to the west, and when light is to the west, the shadow is to the east. As for the substance...
The image arises from the object; it comes from nowhere. When the substance perishes, the image vanishes; it goes nowhere. Therefore, this reflection is empty and lacks substantiality.
The subsequent verse explains the first half [of the preceding verse]. It says "like space" because it cannot be grasped and so forth.
Thus, although it manifests form, it is like the moon in water—equal to space. △ Third, praising the Buddha’s sovereign mastery of spiritual transformations.
Virtue. All Buddhas throughout the ten directions enter entirely into a single pore, yet one cannot find its limit. This is because:
first, the single pore is vast enough to contain them; second, his vows are able to be universally pervasive; and third, it uses the few to illustrate the many. Furthermore—
The above is a brief correlation with ten phrases; within them, the meaning of forty phrases is contained. I cannot point them out in detail for fear of prolixity.
△ Sixth, the conclusion that [the teaching] is universally pervasive and inexhaustible, in two parts. First, the introduction thereof.
Thus, within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) of these four continents, the assembly of bodhisattvas has gathered.
Regarding the phrase "four continents," the intention refers specifically to Jambudvīpa; this is a case where the general term is used with a specific intent.

Having thus established the connection, the gathering of the bodhisattvas like clouds further highlights the excellence of the praise for those [beings] from the ten directions. Part Two: Analogizing Them.
It should be understood that it is likewise in every single place of enlightenment within each of the four continents throughout all the oceans of worlds.
This concludes the section on the distant expedient means. *The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Thirteen.
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Fascicle Fourteen (Entering the Seventh Scripture),
composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang;
recorded with annotations to the scripture by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.
Chapter Three: The Samādhi of Samantabhadra.

△ Regarding the explanation of this chapter, the four gates are the same as before. First, concerning the intent of its arrival: since the assembly has already gathered and the light has manifested the Dharma Lord, he is now about to preach the Dharma.
Therefore, the Dharma Lord enters meditative absorption to receive empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as a proximate expedient means. Thus [the chapter follows].
Next is the explanation of the title.
First, Samantabhadra represents the master who expounds the Dharma, because he teaches the universal Dharma (*samanta-dharma*).

Second, samādhi refers to the functional activity, because that which has not been realized cannot be proclaimed. Thus, this expresses both the person and the Dharma together: the samādhi of Samantabhadra. Furthermore...
This samādhi belongs to Samantabhadra. Furthermore, the realm of this samādhi is named "Samantabhadra," because the *dharmakāya* (body of the treasury) of all Tathāgatas is Samantabhadra.
Thus, Samantabhadra is identical to the samādhi; this distinguishes it from other meditative concentrations.
If one follows the Sanskrit original, this is titled "The Chapter on the Majestic Power and Miraculous Transformations of Samantabhadra’s Samādhi.

Since majestic power and miraculous transformations are all functions of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and since these functions are subsumed under their essence, it is simply called "Samādhi. Even when the Buddha bestows light and offers praise, it is entirely due to meditative concentration;
in other assemblies, entering concentration to receive empowerment and arising from concentration to preach are treated as a single chapter. Now, this [chapter] is divided.

This passage contains many words and broad meanings, intended to encourage practice and study. Regarding the "broad meaning," it refers to the establishment of the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
Therefore, compared to other [assemblies], four similarities and six differences are set forth here. As for the "four similarities," they are: entering, abiding, increasing, and emerging.

As for the "six differences," the first is a difference in number; in other assemblies, the entry and emergence occur only once, whereas in this assembly, the entry and emergence... [occur multiple times].

1. They differ in their multitude; [the latter] is of two distinct categories because it includes other dharmas. 2. They differ in their benefit; [the former] brings benefit to many upon its arising from meditative concentration.

3. They differ in their glorification; [the former] is praised by the light radiating from the pores of the Tathāgata. 4. They differ in their communal invitation; having arisen from concentration, [the Buddha] awaits the invitation of the assembly.
5. They differ in their marks of certification; in other assemblies, the mark of certification occurs only at the conclusion of the sutra, whereas here—

Having completed the chapter on benefits (*puṇya*), this chapter is established separately because it possesses all six characteristics—such as the shaking of the earth and the raining of clouds—which were not fully present in the two types of chapters (the fourth and fifth) of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.

Furthermore, while this chapter explains the fruit (*phala*), the others all explain the cause (*hetu*). Moreover, it serves as the fundamental basis for all the assemblies; whereas the seventh, eighth, and ninth assemblies, though they are fixed as fruits, are explained in a general manner.
Regarding cause and effect: furthermore, it is not a general [cause].
As for the three points of the thesis (*siddhānta*): entering the dharma-realm, the dharma-realm itself, and the Buddha’s empowerment constitute the thesis;

causing the assembly of the dharma-realm to accomplish the virtues of the dharma-realm constitutes the goal (*prayojana*). In view of the subsequent chapter, the ocean of worlds is also said to be the goal.
Fourth, the explanation of the text. The text consists of six sections. The first three constitute the section on samādhi, which is divided into two parts.
First, entering samādhi through the power [of the Buddha]: At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra (up to) "receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, he entered into samādhi."
At one time, when the verses had been spoken, the two lords manifested the Buddha’s universal virtues as belonging solely to Samantabhadra.
Third, regarding their reliance on the Tathāgata: because they were constantly in the presence of the Buddha. Fourth, regarding the seats upon which they rely:

the *Mahāsannipāta* states that because the Bodhisattvas have attained the Lotus Dhāraṇī, there are lotuses at every place where the Dharma is preached; this symbolizes that the intrinsic nature of the samādhi they enter is non-conceptual.
5. The cause of the basis, because it contains the dharmas that are the fruit of defilement; this refers to the profound and vast [state] one enters, which must rely upon power. 6.
The cause of the mental object for entering samādhi correctly, because the mind and its object are in profound accord. △ Second, revealing the name of the concentration.
This samādhi is named "The Tathāgata-vairocana-garbha-body of All Buddhas.

*Vairocana* has already been explained at length previously. Furthermore, there is another explanation: it is called the "Tathāgata-garbha-body" because it possesses these three meanings: vastness (*vi*), birth (*ra*), and cessation (*cana*).
"Body" (*kāya*) refers to essence (*svabhāva*) and basis (*āśraya*). This [body] is of two kinds: first, that which is cultivated...

It is accomplished in two ways: first, by nature; second, through cultivation. As for "by nature," both ordinary beings and sages accomplish it. As for "accomplished through cultivation," this belongs only to the Buddhas.
Because the Buddhas possess boundless compassion, it is called "vast" (*guǎng*). Because their wisdom is unsurpassed, it is termed "great" (*dà*).

Because the characteristics of birth have been exhausted, it is said that "birth has ceased. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: because it is eternally abiding apart from existence, it is called "Suchness" (*rú*).

It comes; it contains and encompasses ten thousand virtues, which is called the "hidden body" (*garbha-kāya*). This is precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) that has emerged from its entanglements.
As for what is called "original nature," it refers to the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which contains all seeds and establishes the realms of rebirth; therefore, it is called "vast.

Because original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) is immediate perception (*pratyakṣa*) and is equal to that of the Buddhas, it is called "great. Because it arises anew at every moment, it is called "birth."

It is called "quiescence" because it cannot be moved by defilement or purity, nor by suffering or pleasure; that is, the aforementioned *dharmakāya* while still enveloped in bondage is termed the "Treasury," meaning both empty and non-empty.
Emptiness acts as the container, and because it contains that which is non-empty, if one illuminates it with universal radiance, [it is revealed].
To explain Vairocana: Vairocana is the great wisdom that is capable of contemplation; the Tathāgatagarbha-body is the profound principle that is the object of contemplation.

Although this principle exists even in ordinary beings, it is only through Buddha-wisdom that it is illuminated. Furthermore, Vairocana also extends to what is primordially present (*mūla-vidyamāna*).
"Primordially present" has the meaning of true cognitive awareness that universally illumines the Dharma-realm; therefore, this is original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*).
Deluded and unaware, they fail to attain its function. Only the Buddha awakens to this and is thus able to accomplish all that can be done.

Therefore, it is said that "all Buddhas" excludes those who are ordinary; nor does it refer to causes. This reveals the environment and its inhabitants as being inseparable from the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Because there is no separate self-substance, one enters into this. Xianshou’s commentary states:

"The Buddhas pervade all" means that it is revealed that the Buddhas are nowhere not pervasive throughout the ocean of lands within the Dharma-realm, as well as all the lands contained within their atoms.
Within the atoms of all lands, there are further lands; thus they are layered upon one another, inexhaustible.

What is called the "Tathāgata’s treasury-body" clarifies that this very body, which pervades all lands, encompasses the ocean of lands throughout the entire Dharma-realm, such that there is nothing that does not exist within the Tathāgata’s body. Therefore, it is named the "treasury-body.
Consequently, there are four propositions regarding its interpenetration: 1. One land contains all lands. 2. All lands contain one land. 3. One land contains one land. 4. All lands contain all lands.
First, a single body pervades the ocean of lands; second, all lands are within the body; third, the body pervades the lands within the body;

fourth, the lands enter and pervade the bodies of the lands, such that the internal and external are identical, and the environment and its inhabitants are blended in harmony, free from obstruction or hindrance.

These are the names given because they are produced by this samādhi. Furthermore, he enters this concentration in order to expound this Dharma. Third, [the text] clarifies its essence, characteristics, and function.
The characteristics, functions, and applications of this samādhi are immeasurable and boundless; they are all explained based upon the Tathāgatagarbha.

To briefly set forth its essentials, there are thirteen phrases and ten gates. Since the final two gates subsume five phrases, they are condensed into six pairs, as each of the latter two gates constitutes one pair.
The text consists of four sections, while the meaning comprises only three points. Up to...
The following shall clarify this. △ Second, the detailed explanation.
"Universally entering the equality-nature of all Buddhas and being able to manifest various images within the dharma-realm" refers to the correspondence between essence and function;
that is, non-conceptual wisdom takes the realization of the nature of equality as its essential substance, while manifesting images within the dharma-realm.
The realm (*dhātu*) serves as the supreme function. That is to say, by means of the cause and the nature of the cause, one realizes that causal nature and establishes that resultant nature;
thus, the nature of the fruit of the fruit is revealed. In this way, the Buddha-nature possesses seven meanings: first, truth; second, reality; third, goodness; fourth, permanence.
Five are pleasures; six are the self; and the seventh is purity—the nature from which Buddhas arise. Since the beginning and the end are not distinct, how much more so is the Buddha-fruit?
Is the fruit, then, not equal? The equality of the Buddha is the Tathāgatagarbha.
Therefore, to enter solely into the body of the Tathāgatagarbha is to have already entered the equality of the Buddha. This is the first gate of harmonizing with the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the term "superior function," this indicates the gateway of manifesting all images; that is to say, it is capable of manifesting and generating the images of bodies, lands, and wisdom.
Vast and unimpeded like space, it enters into every eddy of the ocean of the *dharmadhātu* without exception.

The pair of "profound" (*gambhīra*) and "vast" (*udāra*). "Vast" means boundless, because it exists neither internally nor externally. "Great" (*mahat*) means unsurpassed, because it is the ultimate reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).

"Unobstructed" (*anāvaraṇa*) means being without hindrance, thus being identical to empty space; these establish the three aforementioned meanings and collectively constitute the gateway of the vast and unobstructed.
The final phrase refers to the gateway of entering the whirlpool of phenomena (*dharmāvarta*); "whirlpool" signifies depth.
It gives birth to all dharmas of samādhi and is universally able to encompass the dharma-realm of the ten directions.

This is the section on the initial production of the gates of samādhi, meaning that whether by way of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), all samādhis arise from this, for this is the foundation of all concentrations. It concludes with the section on the subsequent inclusion of the dharma-realm.
For this reason, because it is the essential nature of the dharma-realm,
[the Buddha] is able to manifest the ocean of the wisdom-light of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, up to the oceans of all established teachings.
The opposition between object and wisdom: the first phrase establishes the gateway to the Buddha’s wisdom, meaning that without realizing this principle, one does not possess Buddha-wisdom.

The subsequent phrase demonstrates the gateway of all objects; however, regarding the term "establishment" (*vyavasthāna*), there are generally three types: first, the establishment of the world as the environmental support (*upādāya-vipāka*);
second, the establishment of the sublime meanings within the sacred teachings; and third, the establishment of the truths through contemplative wisdom.
These marks are all the treasury of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-garbha), manifesting before one;
they contain and preserve all the powers and liberations of the Buddhas, universally capable of accommodating the boundless dharma-realm.

The "mutual containment of the internal and external" refers to the gate of the mutual containment of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu* and *adhiṣṭhāna*). This means that internally, it contains the power of wisdom regarding cause and effect;

externally, it causes all phenomena (*dharmas*) to be contained within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Because all phenomena entirely rely upon it, they manifest as the treasury of the Dharma-realm; for they are identical to true nature (*tathatā*).
From "accomplishing the ocean of all Buddha-virtues" up to "circulating and protecting so that they are never severed," this constitutes the section on the person who upholds the Dharma.

This is precisely the "gate of accomplishing and maintaining. It means that first one accomplishes the great vows of the virtues of a person who has attained fruition, and subsequently maintains the Wheel of Dharma so that it is not severed.
Because of this profound principle, the Eye of the Dharma remains eternally intact. Thus ends the [section].
Regarding the "four sections": the first four lines clarify that there is no hidden realm into which he does not enter, explaining the meaning of Vairocana’s "universal illumination.
The next four lines state that there is no virtue that does not arise, explaining the meaning of "all Buddhas.

The following two lines concern internal and external containment, explaining the meaning of "treasury" (*garbha*). The final three lines concern the perfection of virtues and the upholding of the Dharma, explaining the [remaining] meaning above.
Regarding the meaning of "body" (*kāya*): it is said that there are only three meanings. Entering into the nature of equality is the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Being as vast and equal as space is the characteristic of meditative concentration. All others are the functions of meditative concentration. These three are perfectly interfused and collectively constitute the unimpeded Samantabhadra-samādhi.
II. Classifying [the samādhi] as pervading the ten directions and all realms of dust [i.e., atoms]. This section has two parts. First, citing this world-system.
In this manner, within this world-system, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva entered this samādhi before the World-Honored One.
△ Second, the analogy with that [other] direction has two parts. First, the eleven phrases on the uniform pervasion of the Dharma-realm.
In this manner, [the light] reaches all lands manifested by the Buddha-body throughout the entirety of the Dharma-realm and the space-realm.

The first [verse] provides a general clarification, meaning it exhausts the limits of the Dharma-realm; the subsequent ten [verses] provide specific indications to demonstrate the complete pervasion of each individual realm and the entire space-realm.
Second, within space, it pervades all locations throughout the ten directions; third, within the ten directions, it pervades the three periods of time.
1) At that time; 2) within the three periods of time; 3) in the locations of subtle objects, such as the tip of a hair;
4) in all small gaps and unobstructed spaces; 5) in vast places measuring hundreds or thousands of *yojanas*; 6) in places illuminated by the light of humans, devas, the sun, and the moon;
7) in all places visible to the Buddha-eye; 8) in all places reached through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*); 9) the Buddha-body.
Regarding the phrase "the place where [they] can manifest" (the tenth sentence), it has two meanings: first, it concludes the discourse on the lands, applying to all eleven sections;
second, it establishes what follows by showing that because these lands within the body are subtle, they are infinite.
△ Second, the infinite layering.
Regarding the subtle atoms contained within this land (up to the Vairocana Tathāgata’s Treasury-body Samādhi), there are briefly four levels.
First, the atoms throughout the entire Dharma-realm. To say "this land" refers to the lands of the ten previously mentioned locations.
Second, many lands within each atom. Third, many Buddhas within each land. Fourth, before each and every Buddha, there is...
Because Samantabhadra enters this samādhi in all the aforementioned locations, his body is undivided, pervading the coarse and the subtle, the deep and the vast, level, full, and layered.
Just as this universal penetration of entering samādhi applies to these places, it is likewise so for the universal penetration of entering samādhi throughout the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Therefore, with respect to the presiding samādhi, there is only one Samantabhadra before the Buddha, because all is one.

If one considers them according to their general categories, there are as many [Buddhas] before each [bodhisattva] as there are motes of dust, because they are all-encompassing. △ Second, the bestowing of empowerment has three parts.
First, the empowerment by speech has four parts. First, the manifestation of the bodies of the Buddhas.
At that time, each and every Samantabhadra Bodhisattva [appears] before all Buddhas.

This is because there is no subsequent summary statement (kṣepaka) regarding the empowerment through speech. This is a general enumeration of the successive layers of time and place, specifically before each Samantabhadra.
△ Second, praising his attainment of meditative concentration.
Those Tathāgatas praised him with one voice, saying: "...the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Tathāgatagarbha-body.
Although this is a samādhi of fruition, it is called a "Bodhisattva Samādhi" because the bodhisattva enters it. △ Third, the basis for attaining the samādhi.
"O Son of the Buddha, this is due to the power of the vows and practices of all Buddhas of the ten directions...
There are three reasons for this: first, the concurrent empowerment of the attendant Buddhas, because the Way of every Buddha is the same; second, the original vow of the presiding Buddha."

These two serve as conditions. Third is the vow of one's own practice; this is the cause for entering meditative absorption. Furthermore, regarding the three preceding meanings, each prior one depends upon each subsequent one.
Is it not the case that others also possess such practice? Because they are the masters of the Dharma-gates and because they manifest and proclaim the Universal Dharma.
△ Fourth, the identification of the purpose for which the empowerment is bestowed. There are eleven phrases, divided into two parts. First, the general [statement]:
namely, "because it is able to turn all the wheels of the Buddha-dharma.

This passage has two functions: first, to identify the purpose for which the empowerment is bestowed; second, to reveal the characteristics of the supreme practice-vow (*adhyāśaya-praṇidhāna*). Thus, it is called the "purpose."
Furthermore, as for what is meant by this: it is for the purpose of turning the wheel of the Dharma. △ Second, the specific [explanation]:
it is for the purpose of revealing and clarifying the ocean of wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
The first [part] above summarizes the ten wisdoms; the nine [parts] below are precisely the ten oceans.
Because it universally illuminates all oceans of established realms in the ten directions without exception;
that is, it causes all sentient beings to purify their defilements within those oceans of established realms and attain complete purity.
It is the ocean of sentient beings and karma,
because it universally encompasses all great lands without attachment;
it is the ocean of worlds.
Because they penetrate all the realms of all Buddhas without obstruction,
they are the ocean of Buddhas;
because they universally manifest the merits of all Buddhas.
That is to say, because the names, the lifespans, the ocean of liberation, and the great functions of transformations are all due to merit;
and because they are able to enter into the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and increase wisdom.
It is the ocean of *pāramitās*, for it reaches the shore of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and observes all dharma-gates.
It is the ocean of turning the wheel of Dharma.
Because they thoroughly know the faculties of all sentient beings,
they are oceans of faculties;
because they can uphold the ocean of the scriptural teachings of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, they are oceans of teachings.
This is the "Ocean of Exposition," which, together with the ten knowledges [discussed] below, enables one to understand these ten. △ Second, the mental application (*manasikāra*) has two parts.
First, the application itself has two parts. First, this land has two parts. The first is general.
At that time, all Buddhas of the ten directions [bestow] the power of wisdom capable of entering the nature of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
This refers to the wisdom of the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*). As for the term "bestow," it means that the power of the Buddhas is infused to cause [this wisdom] to increase.
The nature of omniscience is precisely the ocean of fruition; the nature of wisdom is precisely power, because it is unshakable and possesses the ten powers (*daśabala*).
The final character, "wisdom" (jñāna), refers to the ability to enter. △ Second, the nine distinctions:
this is the wisdom of entering the boundless measure of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
It is precisely the ten wisdoms found within the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World. Because one possesses this wisdom, one is subsequently able to expound that [Dharma-realm].

The wisdom that contemplates those ten oceans is presented here with some omissions and in an incorrect order. This phrase refers to the third [wisdom], the Wisdom of the Ocean of the Establishment of the Dharma Realm (*dharmadhātu-vyavasthāna-sāgara-jñāna*), because it establishes that which is boundless in measure.
It is endowed with the wisdom that realizes the realm of all Buddhas—this is the fourth ocean of Buddhas. This ocean of Buddhas is a realm accessible only to the Buddhas themselves.
It is also endowed with the wisdom that knows the formation and destruction of all oceans of worlds.
The first is the wisdom that knows the vastness of all realms of sentient beings.
The second is the ocean of the karma of sentient beings; because the causes of karma are subtle, it is described as "vast."
[The phrase] "possessing the wisdom of the samādhis that are no different from the profound liberation of all Buddhas" contains two points.

First, it refers to the eighth [topic], the ocean of the Buddha’s supernormal transformations (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*). Liberation itself is the function, which is precisely what constitutes a supernormal transformation.

The term "samādhi" is added to "supernatural transformations" (*ṛddhi*) because they rely upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The second [term] encompasses the knowledge of the three periods of time. As the subsequent text states:

"In a single thought-moment, one knows the three periods of time, by virtue of the power of the Buddha’s inconceivable liberation. Because of this addition of the general phrase, these two are combined.
It bestows the wisdom of entering the ocean of all bodhisattvas' faculties;
this is the fifth.
It bestows the wisdom of eloquence for turning the wheel of Dharma through knowledge of the ocean of the languages of all sentient beings.
This is the ninth:
the body-knowledge that universally enters all oceans of worlds within the dharma-realm.
This is the seventh ocean of vows; by the power of these vows, one enters all worlds within the dharma-realm.
One attains the wisdom of the voices of all Buddhas;
this is the tenth established exposition. Furthermore, there are many other meanings regarding the faculties of a bodhisattva, such as the cultivation of the ten paths of wholesome action.
There are three roots of goodness. Cultivating the stages and perfections has diligence as its root. Gathering in the True Dharma has faith and wisdom as its root.
Nurturing sentient beings has compassion and kindness as its root. Achieving the path to Buddhahood has compassion and wisdom as its root.
This is because one thoroughly understands all such various distinctions. II. General Application.
In this world-system, all those who are before the Tathāgata, including Samantabhadra, are likewise so.
△ Second, the explanation of the cause has two parts. First, the inquiry.

Why is this? The underlying intent of the inquiry is as follows: Since all Buddhas possess the power to bestow [benefits] and the compassion to do so universally, why is it that the ten wisdoms are bestowed specifically upon Samantabhadra alone? II. The Explanation.
Because the dharma of realizing that samādhi is thus. The commentary states:
"When Samantabhadra attains this samādhi, it is the natural law (dharmatā) that [the Buddhas] should bestow [it upon him]. △ Third, the empowerment of the three bodies.
First, this land; second, the Buddha’s hand touching the crown of his head.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each extended their right hands and stroked the crown of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s head, clearly bestowing their empowerment and protection.
Furthermore, according to the Sanskrit original, it is clear that the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions do not actually come here;
yet they extend their arms—which need not be long—and simultaneously stroke his crown, each making full contact with the top of his head without obstructing one another. All of this is...
The sovereign karmic activities of the Tathāgata. △ Second, within the section explaining the functions of the hand-marks, there are ten phrases that manifest their inexhaustibility.
Part two: first, the five virtues are perfectly complete.
Their hands are all adorned with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa* and *anuvyañjana*), from which exquisite webs of light radiate, fragrances flow, and flames burst forth.

Because they possess qualities such as being long, round, slender, and straight, they are said to be "adorned with the primary and secondary marks. △ Second, the fivefold mastery of wondrous function.
Furthermore, it emits the various wondrous voices of all Buddhas (up to: "all images appear therein").
This clarifies that this hand extends throughout the ten directions and encompasses the three periods of time; it gathers cause and effect and includes both persons and dharmas.
Its profound and vast essence and function are boundless and sovereign, beyond what words can describe. △ Second, the conclusion and general application.

In this world-system, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (up to) was touched on the crown of his head by the Buddhas of the ten directions. △ Third, the section on emerging from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*).

Since the tasks to be performed were completed, there are two parts within this: first, [the emergence] in this world-system; second, [the emergence] in the two [other worlds]. First, the emergence from absorption;
second, first, the emergence of the primary meditative absorption.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva arose from this samādhi.
△ Second, the concentration of the retinue has two parts; the first is a general explanation.
From the time he arose from this samādhi (until) "the gates of oceans of samādhis as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds" arose.
This means that when one arises, all arise; for by means of this sublime concentration (*samādhi*), it is itself the ocean of all samādhis.
Other concentrations serve as its gates, as they all enter into this one. Since they are entirely identical to this, they too receive the name "ocean. △ Second, the ninefold specific analysis.
This refers to arising from the samādhi-door of all atoms, beginning with "knowing that the three periods of time are without distinction in every thought-moment" (up to).
Since the number of atoms is vast, I shall briefly list eleven of them. First is the samādhi of the wisdom that knows [all things], which means there is not even a single thought-moment of deviation;
hence it is said that "every thought-moment is without difference. Yet, this does not abandon universal knowledge, and thus constitutes skillful wisdom. Second is...
Regarding the objects of knowledge as the objective field:
the first pair of subject and object arises from the samādhi-door of all Buddha-fields of the three periods of time (up to) the samādhi-door of dwellings.
Third, the manifestation of vast lands; fourth, the manifestation of dwellings. These constitute a pair of general and specific aspects within the world.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata-garbha consciousness suddenly manifests all bodies, environments, and various enjoyments. Here, "environment" refers to the vast lands.
Enjoyment is precisely the dwelling;
it arises from the samādhi-door of knowing the ocean of the minds of all sentient beings, up to the samādhi-door of their various individual names.
Fifth, knowing the distinctions among mental activities; sixth, knowing the characteristics and names of the body—this refers to the pair of sentient beings' form and mind.
From this, one arises from the samādhi-gate of the vast clouds of Buddha-bodies that pervade all locations within the ten directions of the Dharma-realm.

Seventh is knowing the vast abodes; eighth is knowing the vast bodies. This refers to the correspondence between the primary [body] and its environment. Although it is spoken of as being like a minute particle, the intent is to manifest the vastness of the Buddha.
While space has no fixed direction, it manifests wherever there is matter. Only the Tathāgatagarbha is truly existent; all things are established in dependence upon it.
Their locations are distinct, corresponding to the practices of Bodhisattvas; thus lands may be pure or defiled according to sentient beings.
Regarding karma, because the categories of destinies differ, there is another meaning concerning the Buddha within a minute particle (*paramāṇu*):
it is the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is the true body of the Buddha. Its essence is vast and expansive, such that no one can fully know it; it eternally resides within six or seven minute particles.
Since every sentient being possesses an *ālayavijñāna*, it is said that each has an infinite great body.
He arises from the samādhi-door of the ocean of principles for expounding all dharmas.

The preceding eight [sections] were manifested through distinct gates according to specific phenomena; this [section], however, encompasses all dharmas by way of their underlying principles, and thus it says "all.
In the "Section on Principles" (*Tattvārtha-parivarta*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it is taught that all dharmas are empty, unarisen, unceasing, and without self-nature.
Nature is free from all marks and cannot be sought through aspiration. Yet, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is serene and eternally abiding;
one should know that this is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha*. As the *Saṃghabhedavastu-sūtra* (Siyi jing) says: "In every place one avoids emptiness, yet nowhere is one not separated from emptiness."

The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states that there are six modes of reasoning (*naya*). First is the mode of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha-naya*), which refers to the true reality as it is the object of the wisdom purified of the two obscurations.
Second is the mode of realization (*adhigama-naya*), which refers to attaining knowledge of ultimate reality exactly as it is.

Third is the mode of instruction (*deśanā-naya*), which refers to revealing [the truth] to sentient beings after having realized it oneself. These three constitute the basis; the latter three are their explanations. Fourth...
The principle of avoiding the two extremes: if someone asks, "What is called the principle of true meaning?
one should answer them: "It is neither existent nor non-existent; it is neither eternal nor annihilated. The five principles of the inconceivable: if someone asks, "How is it realized?
one should answer them: "It is the inconceivable. If, regarding all phenomena, one remains detached from...
Conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). At that time, one realizes the nature of true ultimate reality (*paramārtha-tattva*); therefore, one knows that all verbal expressions are not the true meaning.
Sixth, the principle of conforming to the inclinations of sentient beings: if someone asks, "How should one provide instruction? one should answer them by saying:
"Because the mental dispositions of various sentient beings differ, one should employ skillful means to reveal the true meaning in accordance with their respective desires."
This is precisely this "storehouse body" (*garbha-kāya*); that which is inconceivable is precisely this samādhi.
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga explained four intentions (*abhiprāya*), which constitute the underlying principles (*naya*) for interpreting all sūtras, as analyzed in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

Of the nine phrases mentioned above, only the third and fourth are named according to their manifestation; the remaining seven are all designated based on the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). Such are the categories of this kind.
There are as many [samādhis] as there are atoms in all oceans of worlds; when combined, they constitute a single samādhi, which is to say that this samādhi is the totality of all samādhis.
△ Second, the benefits gained by the great assembly, in two parts. First, the timing of the benefit.
When Samantabhadra Bodhisattva arises from such samādhi-gates as these, it is likewise the source by which benefits are obtained.
△ Second, the explicit explanation of the benefits obtained is stated in nine parts. First, five [parts] concern the attainment of bodhisattva dharma-gates.
Each of those bodhisattvas individually attains oceans of clouds of practice, numbering as many as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
Each phrase has a single meaning, yet all these meanings are contained within the preceding meditative concentration. Furthermore, these five phrases establish each subsequent one upon the preceding.
△ Second, the four attainments of the Buddha-fruit are the three karmas of the Tathāgata.
[From] "Clouds of the Ocean of Wisdom-Light of the Treasury of Merits, Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm as Numerous as the Dust-Motes of an Ocean of Worlds" [up to],
they attained the true wisdom of the body that illuminates the treasury.
[They attain] the ocean-like clouds of the non-differentiated skillful means of all Tathāgatas, as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds,
and the provisional wisdom of the power and function of the treasury-body.
All Tathāgatas, as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds, each manifest clouds of oceans of lands;
from the pores of their bodies they manifest lands.
Each and every Bodhisattva, as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds, [manifests] oceans of [events] such as parinirvāṇa.

The meaning of the eight phases [of the Buddha's life] should be manifested through both physical gestures and verbal expression; this is because it also involves the concealment of the body (*antarābhava*).

When Samantabhadra emerges from meditative absorption to benefit others, it is due to the mutual resonance between the path of the response and the path of the stimulus. It is like sprouts emerging in spring:

when the yang energy has long been full, a single breeze from the east causes all the buds to bloom simultaneously. So too, the multitude of Bodhisattvas have long accumulated deep roots of goodness and have practiced their vows together for a long time.
As soon as one contemplates the sublime realm, the myriad virtues are suddenly perfected; since both the hidden and the manifest are mutually sustained, why should this not be possible?
△ Second, the universal application of these categories: from "In this world, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... (up to) "...in every single atom, it is likewise."
△ Section Four: Manifesting Signs as Verification. However, because the mind that has attained benefit is joyful, and joy causes the earth to tremble, various auspicious omens appear.

This is because the members of the assembly have already attained benefit upon hearing [the teaching] to its conclusion; thus, the manifestation of signs is placed at the end. Although this particular assembly has not yet heard it, they have already previously attained benefit;
therefore, the omens are manifested first. This is because this assembly distinguishes the fruit and manifests its excellence. The text has four parts; the first is as follows:
The worlds trembled slightly.
At that time, all the oceans of worlds in the ten directions (up to... trembled slightly due to the power of samādhi, and auspicious signs also appeared.
This was caused by the dual power of cause and effect. That they "trembled slightly" indicates that this is a preceding sign. △ Second.
Adorned with various jewels;
each and every world is adorned with various jewels.
△ Third, emitting sounds to preach the Dharma.
And they emit wondrous sounds, expounding all dharmas.
△ Fourth, the Buddhas' assemblies rain down jewels.
Furthermore, from the ocean-like assembly sites of all Tathāgatas (extending to) the clouds of maṇi-kings heard throughout the ten directions.

Briefly, ten kinds are enumerated to manifest their inexhaustibility. The first three are the Treasures of Phenomenal Marks; the latter seven are the Treasures of the Transmission and Pervasion of the Dharma-transformation.

Both arise from supramundane roots of goodness. △ Fifth, the Section on Praising Virtues through the Light of the Body Hairs, which is divided into two parts. First, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent.
A universal rain of these ten kinds of great maṇi-king clouds [fell], and within their radiance, he spoke in verse.
△ Second, the actual exposition of the verses consists of ten stanzas, divided into three parts. First, a general summary of the preceding determination.
Samantabhadra dwells universally in all lands... (up to) he is able to enter immeasurable samādhis.
△ Second, specifically revealing the characteristics of his universal presence, divided into two parts: first, directly describing the aforementioned universality.
Samantabhadra constantly manifests in various bodies... (up to) it is likewise throughout the atoms of those lands.
△ Second, citing the causes to demonstrate pervasiveness, in two parts: first, pervasiveness through the power of conditions.
The manifestation of the activities of samādhi and supernormal powers is the power of Vairocana’s vows.
△ Second, the power of the cause pervades the four [aspects]. First, because it is the function that is identical to the essence, it therefore pervades.
"The physical marks of Samantabhadra are like empty space" (extending to) "manifesting universal bodies equal to all.

The first half concerns essence; the second half concerns function. His physical marks being like space refers to the *dharmatā-kāya* (Dharma-nature body). Abiding in accordance with the truth refers to the *dharmatā-kṣetra* (Dharma-nature land).
Responding universally according to the capacities of beings refers to the *saṃbhoga-nirmāṇa* (enjoyment and transformation bodies). Question: Are the *dharmatā-kāya* and *dharmatā-kṣetra* distinct?

They are distinct. If they were distinct, they could not be called *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), for that nature is non-dual. If they were not distinct, there would be no distinction between the supported and the support.

Answer: The sūtras and śāstras provide different explanations. Generally encompassing the *dharmakāya*, there are briefly ten types. As the land manifests according to the body, there are five levels.
First, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the *dharmakāya* is taken as the pure *dharmadhātu* alone. Furthermore, it also...
The *dharmatā* constitutes its land. Although its nature is of a single flavor, it is divided into two distinctions according to the characteristics of the body and the land.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Within the category of sentient beings, it is called *buddhadhātu*; within the category of non-sentient things, it is called *dharmadhātu*.
Though conventionally designated as subject and object, in reality there is no difference. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Although the essence of this body and land is without distinction..."

They are distinct, yet both belong to the Buddha-dharma. This is because their nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) differ. That is to say, the dharma-nature belongs to the Buddha and constitutes the *dharmatā-kāya*;
the dharma-nature belongs to the Dharma and constitutes the *dharmatā-kṣetra*. Since the nature varies according to its characteristics, it is described in this way.

As for the current statement that they are "like empty space," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "This body and land are both not subsumed under form (*rūpa*); although their shape cannot be described..."
Regarding its magnitude: although it corresponds to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), its measure is boundless, like space, because it pervades all places.

As with the term "space," this serves as a general metaphor for both the body (*kāya*) and the land (*kṣetra*). Alternatively, the Great Wisdom alone constitutes the *dharmakāya*, while the True Suchness (*tathatā*) realized therein constitutes the *dharmatākṣetra*.
Therefore, it is without intrinsic nature. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "The stainless and unimpeded wisdom..."
Because it is the *dharmakāya*. If that is so, why is it said that its characteristics are like space? Because the essence of wisdom is unimpeded, being identical to space.

Thirdly, it is both wisdom and suchness (*tathatā*), yet it constitutes the *dharmakāya*. The *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* both state that only suchness and the wisdom of suchness remain, which is designated as the *dharmakāya*. Thus, this body contains suchness.
As for wisdom, the land is simply suchness (*tathatā*). When both the four objects and wisdom are simultaneously extinguished, they constitute the *dharmakāya*.

As a sutra says: "The *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is neither mind nor object; the land is likewise so. Based on this principle, all sūtras state that the body and land of the Tathāgata are non-dual.
This is the statement "relying on the True" (*zhen*), which reveals the absence of subject and object; only then can it be called "relying" (*yi*).
This truly fulfills the meaning of being like space. (5) These four preceding lines together constitute the unimpeded *dharmakāya*;
whatever is spoken is all attained, and the lands are likewise so. (6) These five preceding lines—both general and specific—are mutually fused and mutually sublated;

these five vanish, and that which is beyond speech, utterly non-reliant, is taken as the *dharmakāya*, and the lands are likewise so. This above has been discussed solely in terms of the objective realm (*viṣaya*).
Wisdom is distinguished by its discernment. The seven penetrations (abhijñā) encompass the five factors (pañcāṅga), as well as compassion, vows, and all other infinite ocean-like merits;

there is nothing that this Dharma-body does not include. Because merits produced through cultivation must necessarily realize the principle [of reality], they are fused and subsumed without obstruction.

This very essence of True Suchness (tathatā) thus realized, in its aspect of magnitude (mahātva), constitutes the Dharma-nature land (dharmatā-kṣetra). Based on this meaning, [the relationship between] the body and the land...
These are vastly different. What is now called the "physical form" (rūpakāya) refers to all merits; what is called "being like empty space" refers to the nature of that body.
As the subsequent sutra also states: "To understand the Tathāgata’s body as not being like empty space is because it possesses all merits and immeasurable, wondrous dharmas."

Because it is fully perfected, the eighth [category] generally encompasses the merit of both the retributive and transformational physical forms, for there is nothing that is not subsumed within this Dharma-body.
In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the thirty-two marks and so forth are all included within the Dharma-body; however, there are three meanings [to this].

First, because the single characteristic is suchness itself, it returns to the Dharma-body of Principle (*dharmakāya*). Second, because it is manifested by the two wisdoms, it belongs to the Dharma-body of Wisdom (*jñānakāya*).
Third, as for their respective characteristics, since they are all dharmas of merit, they are called the Dharma-body.

As for its supporting land, it encompasses both nature and characteristics, being unimpeded in purity and impurity. My land is pure, yet you do not see it; sentient beings see this pure land as being consumed by fire.

Not destroying form means that it is the suchness-characteristic (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*) and yet the non-characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*). Regarding the body and the land, phenomena and principle, they mutually support one another; generally, there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
namely, the form-body (*rūpakāya*) relies on the land of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇabhūmi*); the form-body relies on the land of the dharma-nature (*dharmatābhūmi*);

the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) relies on the land of the dharma-nature; and [the dharma-body] relies on the land of phenomenal characteristics. Furthermore, by considering these single and paired factors in relation to one another, five propositions are also established, namely:

The body of form-phenomena (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa-kāya*) is based upon the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). This applies analogously to the land of form-phenomena and so forth; reflect upon this accordingly. The above still generally pertains to all Mahāyāna teachings.
The ninth [category] universally subsumes the three kinds of worlds, for they are all one great *dharmakāya*, as it possesses the ten Buddhas.

As for the three bodies (*trikāya*) and so forth, they are all the wisdom within this [state], because they are subsumed under perfect enlightenment (*samyag-abhisambodhi*). The lands are likewise so. That is to say:

The empty body manifests as the universal body; what is there that it does not possess? This belongs exclusively to the *Avataṃsaka*. Regarding the ten ascending divisions of provisional and real, only the ninth pertains to this sutra.

However, if one relies on the principle of harmonious integration and the inclusion of the "same teaching" (*samāna-śāsana*), then the preceding nine meanings are collectively subsumed under a single general category.
This is called the Tathāgata’s unimpeded body and land; Universal Worthy (*Samantabhadra*) is likewise so according to the meaning.

Regarding manifestation and concealment (*saṃdarśana-tirobhāva*), it is impossible to settle them through accumulation. Those who have attained realization do not seek [meaning] merely in the words; those with limited views are restricted by the notion of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

As for the statement above that there are five levels of lands (*kṣetra*): first, the Dharma-nature alone, which belongs to the first three bodies (*kāya*); second, the simultaneous sublation of both [nature and characteristics], which belongs to the fourth;

third, the possession of both nature and characteristics, which is the basis for the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth; fourth, the fusion of the three worlds, which belongs to the ninth; and fifth, the totality.
The aforementioned meanings constitute the tenth basis. △ Second, regarding the universality due to great vows:
Samantabhadra abides in all great vows... (up to) his emanations dwelling therein are likewise immeasurable.

This also reveals that [the manifestation] pervades the basis within the center. It is pervasive in every successive layer. That it is not seen now is because the faculties [of the audience] do not correspond;
it is because it is the body of empty space, and thus it pervades even those places where it is not seen. △ Third, the superiority of what is manifested.
The manifested lands are all adorned and pure (up to) enabling all who behold them to see them clearly.
△ Fourth, the gate of not abandoning the causal stage despite having perfected the fruits of merit:
By the power of the wisdom and merit of all Buddhas (up to) they reveal their own past practices for enlightenment.
△ Third, the source of the three bonds. Thus, mastery is inconceivable. (Reaching) the Buddha’s cloud of light, he praises his meritorious virtues. Mastery is difficult to fathom;
its manifestation is nowhere not universal. He marks his entry into one concentration, yet in reality, he wanders everywhere. This is not merely the Buddha’s light.
How could I, Yun, be able to praise and describe it? △ Section Two: The Great Assembly’s Praise and Request, divided into two parts. First, the ritual of the verses:
At that time, the entire assembly of Bodhisattvas (through) receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, praised him with one voice, saying:
The assembly previously questioned the Buddha; the Buddha revealed the Master of Dharma. As the assembly beheld him emerge from meditative concentration, they praised and entreated Samantabhadra.

The previous [assembly] consisted only of the original members, whereas this one includes both the new and the old; therefore, it says "all. Since the questions asked are the same as before, they are merely mentioned briefly here.

△ The ten verses are divided into three parts. First, eight verses praise the Master and request [his teaching] to manifest his capacity to speak. Second, the first part praises the causal [practices] of Samantabhadra.
The fruit is the virtue of profundity and vastness.
It clarifies that there is a teaching on the cause, [stating] "born from all Buddha-dharmas" (up to) "you have already adorned and purified this Dharma-body.
The three phrases clarify the cause, and one phrase clarifies the fruit. The cause has three meanings; the first is the cause.

The cultivation of the Dharma gives rise to it. This meaning applies to both the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) and the enabling cause (*upaniṣad-hetu*). Second, its arising through great vows constitutes the contributing cause.

Third, by relying on the *tathāgatagarbha* to realize true equality, this serves as the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*). True Suchness (*tathatā*) is precisely the non-empty; empty space is precisely the empty treasury (*śūnyagarbha*).
Equality and the treasury encompass the two aforementioned meanings.
Within the assemblies of all Buddha-fields (up to) "equally illuminating the ten directions so that none do not see," this praises the Buddha-field of Universal Abiding (*Samantavyūha*).
The third phrase refers to the universal cause; the remainder are all universal characteristics.
Because the cause is endowed with the adornment of wisdom, it is able to equally illuminate; because it is endowed with the adornment of merit, there is nothing that is not beheld.
Samantabhadra’s Vast Ocean of Merit... [up to] ...is able to manifest clearly by reaching all those places.
Praising his proximity to the Buddhas:
"O Son of the Buddha, we have constantly seen you [up to] ...throughout eons as numerous as the atoms in all lands."
This praises those who are constantly in meditative concentration within the realm of reality, for they do not follow after conceptualization. "Cao" (曹) refers to a class or group.
These sons of the Buddha are able to employ their universal bodies [to enter] every atom of the Dharma-realm without exception.

The praise for the perfection of saving sentient beings is complete. Regarding "microscopic particles": because there are many sentient beings within these subtle locations. The preceding five [verses] each praise a single meaning.
△ Second, praising the virtue of being able to pervade all lands as numerous as atoms and raining down the Dharma; this clarifies the presence of the fruit of teaching.
Entering into all atoms of the Dharma-realm, they expound the vast Dharma of the Tathāgata and praise the constant proclamation of the Great Dharma.
The phrase "like space" serves as a metaphor for its vastness; the preceding metaphor illustrates its inexhaustibility and non-differentiation.
Regarding "The Radiance of All Merits" (up to): "He proclaims the peerless Dharma practiced by the Buddha;
he praises the peerless Dharma. There are two kinds of peerlessness: first, the excellence of the power of the speaker, because he is endowed with the two adornments;
second, the peerlessness of that which is spoken, because he speaks of the conduct practiced by the Buddha.
"To deliver sentient beings throughout oceans of kalpas" (up to) "its sound is so vast that there is nowhere it is not heard.

This cites the cause to illustrate the result, showing that the manifestation of virtue has its origin. Because the causes have been perfected over vast kalpas, he is able to rain down the teaching through his preaching.
△ Second, citing the Dharma to formally request [instruction] and state what is doubted.
How is the buddha-field established? (Up to: Please explain according to its meaning as it truly is.
Although the questions posed in the preceding chapter involve many approaches, when their essential points are summarized, they do not exceed the three types of worlds;

therefore, each of these three phrases now manifests one of them. Furthermore, while the previous questions encompassed all assemblies in general, this [section] requires that the answer be given for the present assembly.
Therefore: △ Third, praising the assembly’s request to clarify that there are those with the capacity to hear [the teaching].
From "this great ocean-like assembly of immeasurable numbers" (至) to "all Buddhas rejoice."
This is also called "self-narration," which carries two meanings: first, with a respectful and single-minded heart, one is internally capable of receiving the Dharma;

second, the Buddhas rejoice in it, providing external and superior conditions. Therefore, it should be taught. If taught, it will above accord with the Buddha's mind and below accord with the inclinations of sentient beings.
Chapter Four: The Accomplishment of the World.

△ Regarding the initial intent [for this chapter]: Since the conditions have been fully set forth in the preceding section, what follows presents the actual subject matter, providing a general exposition of the characteristics of the fruit (phala) in response to the questions concerning the Ocean of the Establishment of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Therefore, this chapter is introduced.

Second, regarding the explanation of the names: "world" (*loka*) refers to the three times, as it falls within the past, future, and present. "Sphere" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial divisions, as there is a distinction between this and that.

Furthermore, "world" implies concealment or obscuration, while "sphere" also implies a boundary; thus, it refers to the world of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), which is subject to destruction.
It is the concealment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), indestructible dharmas that arise from true nature and are identical to unconditioned phenomena;
it is the concealment of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), destructible world. These two do not intermingle, and this constitutes their respective boundaries.

Therefore, for those who perceive the Sahā world, they see the Sahā world in contrast to the Flower Treasury World (*Huāzàng*). For those who perceive the Flower Treasury World, they see the Flower Treasury World in contrast to the Sahā world.

Regarding the term "accomplishment" (*siddhi*), it refers to the conditions that bring about accomplishment, namely the ten conditions and so forth; this is a designation that combines the agent and the object.
If one considers it as the accomplishment of the world, it follows the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. According to the Sanskrit original, it is called the "Accomplishment of the Ocean of Worlds.

The subsequent section distinguishes the "ocean," which was abbreviated by the translator. The intended meaning is that the primary and secondary marks of the Buddha-fruit arise only through hearing and cultivation, for sentient beings.
Karmic retribution has existed inherently from the beginning; therefore, it merely indicates the world-system.

Regarding the three essential themes (*piṭaka*): the theme consists of enumerating boundless supreme virtues and providing an extensive explanation of the ocean-like world-systems of all that is known.
However, its underlying intent is manifold. First, it serves as the means for causing all bodhisattvas to give rise to great faith and understanding and thereby enter [the path].
This means causing them to know that the ocean of the great compassionate practices of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas extensively covers the limitless, reaching the end of the realm of sentient beings;
thus, they may emulate these practices. Furthermore, it is because worlds are limitless and are all to be purified, and sentient beings are limitless and are all... [to be liberated].
Because they transform and deliver [beings], lands differ according to the mind; one should purify both one's own mind and the minds of others.

Worlds are layered upon worlds, inexhaustible and inexhaustible, because they are entirely filled by great practices and vows. The Buddha-realm and the realm of birth are neither identical nor different;
because one can correctly understand this, one achieves great wisdom. For those who have not yet understood, it perfumes and forms seeds; all are mental.
This is the destination. Furthermore, this chapter is presented to manifest this profound meaning. Thus, the verse below says: "Those whose minds are pure, free from all flattery and deception;
who always delight in compassion and are joyful by nature; those with vast aspirations and deep faith—when they hear this Dharma, they give rise to joy.
If they do not hear of this boundless, inexhaustible, non-dual realm, they will remain stuck..."

For those of provisional and inferior capacities, by what means could the practices and vows of Samantabhadra be accomplished? Therefore, the passage beginning with "In order to cause sentient beings...
and so forth, which was spoken by Samantabhadra himself, constitutes the essential purport of this chapter.
Fourth, the explanation of the text. The three chapters correctly present the ocean of Dharma. This is divided into two parts:
the first two chapters clarify the fruit (*phala*), and the final chapter distinguishes the cause (*hetu*). However, there are two perspectives. First, regarding the comprehensive clarification:

the first two chapters collectively answer the questions concerning the thirty phrases of the fruit, while the final chapter answers the questions concerning the ten preceding phrases of the cause. The cause is taught because it is intended to establish [the fruit].

Regarding the fruit: speaking from the perspective of the majority, the title of this section is given by citing the fruit. The second part takes up the first two chapters and provides a comprehensive answer—both general and specific—to the three questions at the end of the preceding chapter concerning the environment (*āśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhita*).
If one looks toward what follows, the extensive text primarily clarifies the environment while incidentally manifesting the inhabitants;

it sets aside the personal retribution (*sambhogakāya*) to explain it extensively in the latter section. Within that, the first chapter universally distinguishes between all Buddhas and all sentient beings.

Regarding all the oceans of lands: while the subsequent chapter specifically clarifies the adornments and purifications of our own Teacher’s land, this present chapter clarifies the conditions for the formation of these lands, and the subsequent chapter specifically distinguishes their resultant characteristics. Therefore, this chapter answers the question concerning their establishment.

Although it also clarifies aspects such as form within its discussion, these too are conditions. Now, the first section is divided into two parts; first, the general presentation of the essential outline is as follows:
The Main Body. This has two parts. First, the universal observation through the power [of the Buddhas].
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra... [up to] ...the ocean of the miraculous transformations of all Tathāgatas.
The Superior enters samādhi, inwardly attuning to its source; now, it is said that he observes universally, externally examining its manifestations.

The meaning of the ten oceans has already been explained in response to the inquiry, differing only slightly in their sequence. Once one has observed these ten, they inherently contain the remaining thirty.
Within the ocean of the Buddhas, they are equal in their physical bodies; within their great vows, they are equal in their causal foundations.

△ Second, the fourfold citation of the question and the granting of the teaching. First, the citation of the question and a brief praise. First, concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent.
Having observed in this manner, he addressed the ocean-like assembly of bodhisattvas at the site of enlightenment, saying:
"Second is the formal citation and praise. This refers to citing the thirty questions on the fruits from the latter part back to the former.
Of these, the first ten questions cite the ten inquiries concerning the oceans of worlds and so forth. "Observation" refers to observing the oceans, while "praise" refers to praising the wise ones.
Wisdom and the ocean are mutually constitutive in a reciprocal manner. This means that when one observes the ocean through one's own wisdom, it is subtle and difficult to know;
only the Buddha-wisdom can fully exhaust its depths. Because the ocean is inconceivable, the Buddha-wisdom is inconceivable; because the Buddha-wisdom is inconceivable, [the ocean is likewise so].

The ocean is profound and vast. If that is so, why not speak of "knowledge" (jñāna), but instead speak only of the "ocean"? Knowledge is distinct from the object of the ocean; how could its characteristics be known?
Furthermore, it is expressed solely as that which is realized and known; therefore, only the "ocean" is mentioned.

Regarding the ten knowledges in relation to the ocean, there are slight differences in the opening and closing of the questions, or minor discrepancies in terminology. △ Second, the detailed explanation.

O Sons of the Buddha, the inconceivable pure wisdom of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, which [extends] to all things, was previously addressed in the inquiry and contemplation as merely the "ocean of worlds.
Now, the formation and destruction [of these worlds] are added. This differs from the previous [sections] and from the section on wisdom only in being more detailed;
for within that [section on] wisdom, there is also mention of formation and destruction. As for the term "pure wisdom," it is free from...

This refers to the knowledge of obstacles. Because it involves decisive and clear discernment, the first phrase extends throughout the following sections. The term "pure" (viśuddha) is placed [at the beginning], while the rest are abbreviated.
Nevertheless, because these [obstacles] are numerous, extensive, profound, subtle, and layered to the point of being difficult to know—transcending both words and thought—they are thus described.
All say it is inconceivable.
The wisdom that knows the ocean of karma of all sentient beings is inconceivable.
"Sentient beings" refers to the distinctions among various types of retribution; "karma" refers to the differences between good, evil, and so forth. From the perspective of these distinct meanings:
These are opened into two phrases; yet although cause and effect differ, they are both equally the sentient beings to be transformed.
Therefore, this [section] and the question, together with [the section on] wisdom, are combined into one.

The inconceivable wisdom that knows the ocean of the establishment of all dharma-realms is what is universally designated as "worlds," or the methods for transforming sentient beings— namely, the established designations, skillful means, rules of conduct,
and so forth.
It is taught that the wisdom of the ocean of all infinite Buddhas is inconceivable;
they are able to manifest Buddhas in numbers that are boundless.
The wisdom that enters the ocean of all inclinations, understandings, and faculties is inconceivable.

The specific differences between the faculties and inclinations of those to be converted are difficult to discern; however, in the context of the questions, these are combined within the final five oceans, as it is necessary to know the faculties and inclinations of all five oceans.

The inconceivable wisdom that universally knows all three periods of time in a single thought-moment is such that it accords with the appropriate occasion and approaches what is to be observed; while it is generally referred to as "the three periods of time," here, because we are approaching the Buddha's wisdom, it is said that he can know them in a single thought-moment.
As for the question and the wisdom, both are called the "Ocean of the Buddha’s Liberation" because of this single thought-moment.
They universally know the three periods of time; this is because the Buddha’s inconceivable liberation manifests the inconceivable wisdom of the immeasurable ocean of vows of all Tathāgatas.
The great vows that accord with the nature of reality serve as the cause for manifesting bodies and preaching the Dharma to universally transform beings.

Therefore, among the previously mentioned ocean of names, ocean of lifespans, and oceans of wisdom, the "wisdom of universally entering all oceans of worlds within the dharma-realm" is entirely due to the power of these vows.
The inconceivable wisdom of manifesting the ocean of all Buddhas' spiritual transformations,
acting in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings through boundless miraculous displays;
and the inconceivable wisdom of turning the wheel of Dharma.
It is called the ocean of the Great Dharma-wheel that accords with its true nature (*dharmatā*). According to the inquiry, the ocean of turning the wheel is subsumed within the ocean of exposition;
yet from the perspective of contemplation, the ocean of exposition is subsumed within the ocean of the wheel. Now, these two expositions are opened up separately.
The establishment and exposition of the ocean [of teachings] is inconceivable;
this refers to the differentiation of speech and sound according to various regions, as well as the turning of the wheel of Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

This is also opened within the category of wisdom, and is termed the "wisdom of the Buddha’s vocal sound. △ Second, nine phrases: these restate the ten questions concerning the six faculties, the three karmas, and the preceding [sections].
The pure Buddha-body is inconceivable.
Up to the tenth [section], it was explained as inconceivable by way of wisdom; from here on, it is established as inconceivable directly with respect to the essence of the Dharma.

Furthermore, in view of the preceding questions, this section combines the aspects of opening and closing and abridges them to reveal their inexhaustibility; thus, while the general encompasses the particular, it specifically elaborates upon the radiance of the body.
