The first phrase above refers to the body that responds to the capacities of beings; its length or brevity is difficult to fathom.
An ocean of boundless forms and appearances universally illuminates in an inconceivable manner, manifesting gold, silver, and other such infinite varieties of color and kind.
The primary marks and secondary characteristics are all pure and inconceivable.
The marks and characteristics, numbering as many as the atoms within ten lotus-treasury world-systems, exceed even this;
they are endowed with oceans of wheels of light from infinite forms and colors, perfectly pure and inconceivable.
The size of the circular halo is inexhaustible according to the capacities of beings.
The inconceivable ocean-like clouds of light and various forms emit radiance in accordance with conditions, their colors and types being manifold.
The inconceivable ocean of sublime jewel-flames has a constant radiance like that of fire, possessing the colors of all jewels;
the inconceivable ocean of accomplished speech and sound is likewise marvelous.
The perfect voice is inexhaustible; its depth and breadth are difficult to fathom.
It manifests an inconceivable ocean of threefold mastery to discipline and bring all sentient beings to maturity.
The conversion through the three wheels refers to the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) and so forth.
It is inconceivable how they courageously tame the ocean of sentient beings such that none pass by in vain;
they are disciplined so that benefit is achieved and the fruit is not obtained in vain. Furthermore, this taming is briefly of three kinds. First, the initial...
First, one always uses gentle speech, because one should gather in those who are to be gathered. Second, one always uses harsh speech, because one should subdue those who are to be subdued.
Third, at times using gentle speech and at times using harsh speech, one brings to maturity those who are to be matured.
Because these three are possessed, there is no passing [of time] in vain. △ Thirty phrases: a summary of the above.
The first section concerns the ten questions on the perfection of qualities and functions.

From "abiding in the inconceivable Buddha-ground" up to "the inconceivable that cannot be destroyed," the preceding questions omit the two phrases regarding "transformation" and "sovereignty," as these are subsumed within "the inconceivable that cannot be grasped."
The meaning within these phrases is as previously understood, as it also exists in the ten oceans mentioned in the preceding text. Spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi*) pertain to the body;
mastery (*vaśitā*) pertains to wisdom. The rest may be understood accordingly. △ Second, the section on the scope of the exposition.
All such dharmas as these have been fully proclaimed through the power of majestic spiritual authority (*anubhāva*).
Regarding the phrase "relying on the Buddha’s power," this refers to being in the presence of the Buddha.

If one asks why the subsequent text speaks only of the establishment [of the world-system] and the ocean of worlds, it is because the sūtra has not yet reached its conclusion. Furthermore, although it has been taught...

Second, regarding the ocean of worlds (*lokadhātu-samudra*), it is likewise fully endowed with thirty questions. That is to say: because a realm must necessarily have sentient beings who rely upon and dwell within it;

because Buddhas manifest therein; because its establishment is distinct; because it is the result of the maturation of karma and conduct; and because other things are sought according to one's inclinations.
△ Third, the benefits accomplished are explained. These ten phrases are subsumed into five pairs.
In order to cause sentient beings to enter the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom (up to) and abide securely within the ocean of merit;
and to realize wisdom and accomplish blessings in response,
in order to cause the ocean of all world-systems (up to) the lineage of the Tathāgatas to never be interrupted.
The adornment of the buddha-fields constitutes a correspondence of lineage, as well as a correspondence of time and place;
it is for the purpose of causing [beings] to expound [the Dharma] throughout all oceans of worlds, reaching unto the ocean of infinite liberations.

The pair of manifesting meaning and expounding the teaching is for the purpose of causing [beings] to follow the ocean of the faculties of all sentient beings... up to... destroying all mountains of obstacles.
The pair of generating the wholesome and extinguishing the unwholesome is likewise.

In order to cause [beings] to follow the ocean of mental activities of all sentient beings (up to) dwelling within the ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows, the "Purification of Karma" and the "Universal Vow" are paired.
This also serves as the general cause for the arising of the teachings of this entire sutra. These ten [vows] also correspond to the preceding ten oceans and ten wisdoms;
fearing that it would become too verbose, they are not further correlated here. △ Fourth, praising the excellence [of the teaching] and exhorting the listeners, in two parts. Long [verse].
The section on the discernment of practice consists of eleven sentences divided into two parts. First is the general introduction:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, wishing again to inspire joy within the ocean-like assemblies at the countless sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), [spoke as follows].
This means that it causes joy to necessarily arise upon hearing the Dharma. △ Second, the specific explanation of the meaning of "joy" (prīti) is also presented in five pairs:
because it causes one to increase love and delight for all dharmas; and because it causes the vast and true ocean of faith and understanding (adhimukti) to arise.

The correspondence of generating faith through delighting in the Dharma serves to purify the body that is the treasury of the universal dharma-realm and to establish the ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows;
this is the correspondence of establishing vows based on the realization of the nature.
To cause the purification of the eye of wisdom that enters into the equality of the three periods of time, up to the great ocean of wisdom that is the treasury of all worlds;
to understand the truth and enter into the conventional,
and to give rise to the power of *dhāraṇī* to uphold all wheels of Dharma, up to the full revelation of the entire realm of the Buddhas.

The "Confrontation of Upholding the Dharma and Manifesting to the Buddha" is for the purpose of causing all dharma-gates of the Tathāgatas to be opened and expounded, up to the realization of the vast and profound nature of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
This is the "Confrontation of Opening the Dharma and Increasing Wisdom."
He then spoke in verse: II.
The Section of the Ten Verses Properly Revealing [the Meaning], divided into two parts. A. The first eight verses praise [the Buddha].
1. The Purpose for the Buddha’s Appearance: “O Ocean of Merit with Profound Wisdom... appearing in all lands.”
△ Second, distinguishing those who are vessels for the Dharma, in three parts. First, excluding those who are not vessels:
"The realm of the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to conceive... [they] cannot penetrate what the Buddha has realized."
△ Second, distinguishing the vessel of the Dharma:
Only those with pure faith, whose virtuous minds are firm... [down to] ...practitioners of Samantabhadra can attain realization.
△ Third, there is one verse concluding by returning to the power of the Buddha.
Sentient beings are vast and boundless... [up to] ...the power of the realm of Vairocana.
△ Second, the final two verses of exhortation:
All lands enter my body... [up to] ...this is non-action; you should listen attentively.

However, throughout these ten verses, there is likewise an invocation of the question by way of praise. While the preceding prose section generally reveals the inconceivable nature [of the Buddha], the following portion briefly demonstrates the characteristics of that inconceivability;
yet, although the thirty phrases are arranged without sequential order, they fully encompass all essential meanings.
I wish to provide a detailed commentary and explanation, yet I fear wearying you with excessive verbiage. △ Second, the extensive presentation of the fundamental meaning, which consists of two parts:
first, the introduction by the compilers.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed the great assembly, saying:

△ Second, the Universal Worthy’s Detailed Explanation. Within the thirty questions concerning the fruit, he extensively explains the question regarding the ocean-like establishment of worlds, while the remainder are all subsumed therein.
The text has two parts. First, the presentation of the topical outline (in three sections). First, establishing the number to demonstrate their commonality.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten matters concerning the oceans of worlds that have been, are being, and will be explained.
First, the address "Sons of the Buddha" is intended to draw the attention of those present toward their ears and eyes. Because the worlds are vast and profound, they are termed "oceans.

This means that the accumulation of lands (*kṣetra*) forms a "type" (*gotra*), and the accumulation of types forms an "ocean. The ocean has no separate substance; it is simply the collective name for all worlds.

However, as the categories of phenomena are vast and numerous, I shall briefly cite ten examples to represent their inexhaustibility. These are taught identically throughout the three periods of time to manifest their essential excellence;
furthermore, they are explicitly taught as definitive and subject to no alteration. △ Second, the enumeration of the number and listing of the differences.
What are these ten? They are: the causes and conditions for the arising of the world-ocean;
its establishment by grasping those conditions;
and the basis upon which the world-ocean rests.
Once formed, they abide according to the shapes,
external forms, and divisions of the world-oceans.
The essential nature of the world-ocean;
the internal distinctions of its essence;
and the adornments of the world-ocean.
Adorned with jewels and the like,
the oceans of worlds are purified,
and no defilements arise.
The appearance of Buddhas in the oceans of worlds;
the distinct differences among the Buddhas;
and the duration of kalpas in the oceans of worlds.
The duration of kalpas— whether long or short—
and the various transformations of the oceans of worlds change according to karma.
The gate of the non-differentiation of the oceans of worlds encompasses all with equal impartiality.
These ten also subsume the eighteen perfections, which will be reconciled in the subsequent chapter. △ Third, the conclusion of the summary and the revelation of the extensive.

O Sons of the Buddha, this brief exposition of the oceans of worlds—what has been said, what is being said, and what will be said—is such that even the wisdom of those who speak of "dust motes within an ocean of worlds" is difficult to fathom; how could it be fully recounted? Unless one has realized the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), how could one properly receive this teaching?
Furthermore, regarding the ten matters mentioned above, their quantities within each individual *kṣetra* (field) are not fixed; they are determined by a single set of conditions.
It may be one, two, three, or many; it may form four propositions, namely: one becomes one, one becomes all, and so forth.
Regarding the single type of purity, it may be one or many, or it may likewise be indeterminate, because there are buddha-fields that are purely defiled.
As for the subsequent seven matters, each is unique: that which dwells supported by space does not dwell supported by light and so forth.
The remainder may be inferred accordingly. As for their lack of distinction, all [worlds] possess it equally;

because they are equal in their essential nature and are harmoniously integrated by the power of the Buddha, they are said to be without distinction. This is why both the defiled and the pure are fully present.

Some say that all worlds are mutually identical when compared to one another, and thus name this "lack of distinction. However, this contradicts the concluding text below, which states: "Each and every world..."
The oceans of realms consist of as many worlds as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, for they are without distinction.
If one considers them in relation to one another, they are mutually identical and thus no distinct entities exist.

If these ten are compared to the world-systems (kṣetradhātu), they possess a single characteristic, yet their number is indefinite and cannot be said to be "one," because within each system there are contained many types of worlds. Pure.
First, one must not definitively state that they exist or do not exist, because within those seed-worlds (*kṣetraprakṛti*), both purity and defilement are necessarily contained.

Regarding their lack of distinction, their quantity is also uniform. As for the appearance of Buddhas and the duration of the eons, they undergo transformation according to karma; thus, one cannot say there is only one.
Yet, based on the adornment of their physical forms, one cannot say there are many, because each distinct world-system (*kṣetra*) has its own separate essence and so forth. If, by this...
Tenth: Regarding the four aspects of the ocean of lands (*kṣetrasamudra*)—its shape, its physical basis, its dwelling, and its adornments—it is accepted that these may exist as a single unit.
This is because all others necessarily involve many; as the Sūtra states, "Each ocean of worlds has various shapes.
When it is said here that there are "as many oceans of worlds as atoms," this refers to the teaching on their infinite fusion and inclusion. Some say it refers to each individual land.
To claim that all the lands within the ocean of worlds are each equal due to a single cause, and that there are as many such lands as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, is an extreme rashness.
Why? For instance, although the lands within an ocean of worlds are numerous, how could they possibly equal the number of atoms produced by grinding the entire ocean of worlds to dust?
If one wishes to establish a correspondence, then only when there is one atom for each causal condition can they be similar. How could it be otherwise?

If a single land and a single condition can fill the number of atoms within a single land, how much more so when ten such conditions, including their accumulations, are combined—conditions that equal the number of atoms in an ocean of lands?
Within each of these accumulated conditions, there already exist as many oceans of lands as there are atoms.

Thus, they collectively contain a multitude of oceans of lands, each numbering as many as the atoms in an ocean of lands. Within each land and each condition, there is a single basis and a single essence.

How could it possibly be sufficient? Nor can it be said that this refers to preaching throughout all world-oceans, because the subsequent section on "Abodes" states that within each individual world-ocean there are abodes as numerous as the atoms of a world-ocean.

Second, regarding the detailed explanation according to the chapters: since there are ten distinct matters, they are divided into ten sections, each of which begins with the causal conditions for its initial arising.
2. First, the prose section has three parts. First, the heading:
"O Sons of the Buddha, briefly stated, by means of ten kinds of causes and conditions... [they] have already been accomplished, are currently being accomplished, and will be accomplished."
Briefly stated, there are ten types that collectively constitute all Buddha-fields of the three periods of time.

△ Second, the explanation: Although the meaning of "Buddha-land" (buddhakṣetra) has many varieties, they do not exceed three. First, the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*); second, the Land of Enjoyment (*saṃbhoga-kṣetra*);

and third, the Land of Transformation (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*). If the Land of Enjoyment is divided into the self-enjoyment and the other-enjoyment, then there are four lands. In total, however, there are only two kinds, namely:
The pure and the defiled, or essence and appearance, are fused into one; this differs from other schools. Furthermore, regarding this Pure Land:

it cannot be established as a single substance, for purity and defilement would otherwise be subject to deficiency and excess. It cannot be established as having diverse substances, for the single principle is uniform and level.

It cannot be established as having no substance, for when its source is sought, it is profound and dark. Nor can it be established as having no substance, for through dependent origination, it manifests in myriad forms. Thus, form subsumes perfect fusion; there is no...

There are obstructions; since the lands are unequal, their causes and conditions are also distinct. In the current text, the ten [aspects] are divided into three sections. The first three are general clarifications.
What are these ten? They are as follows: by virtue of the Tathāgata’s supernormal power.

This means that all lands, whether pure or defiled, are accomplished through the power of the Tathāgata’s supernormal wisdom (*abhijñā*) and are assumed for the sake of sentient beings, intended to respond universally to them.

Since the Buddha presides over them all, they are all termed "Buddha-lands. Although the Lotus Treasury Ocean (*padmagarbhasāgara*) is purified by the Buddha, it contains both the pure and the defiled within it;
yet from the perspective of the Buddha, there is no land that is not pure. Thus, even that which is defiled—*
It is pure; therefore, it is inconceivable.
Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

In Sanskrit, it is called *dharmatā*, which here is translated as "the natural state of phenomena" (*fa-er*) or "the nature of phenomena" (*faxing*). If this refers to the nature of phenomena, then by means of it—
The fundamental consciousness, the body of the Tathāgatagarbha, serves as the support and basis. It constantly undergoes transformation to give rise to the external world-receptacles.
If one says this occurs "by the nature of things" (*dharmatā*), it means that if someone asks, "Why do Buddhas and sentient beings arise within these lands?
the answer is, "The Dharma is such; it cannot be further questioned. If one synthesizes these two points, it means that by the nature of things, the *garbha*—
Consciousness arises through transformation due to the karmic actions of all sentient beings.

Since karma is either wholesome or unwholesome, lands are either pure or defiled; therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* takes myriad practices as its cause. Furthermore, it says: "The multitude..."
The categories of sentient beings are the Buddha-land of a Bodhisattva. This means that although the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is one, it manifests as diverse according to karma.

Buddhas, in accordance with these diverse types, take on lands to gather and sustain sentient beings. Whether it be the subtle goodness of *nirvāṇa*, the three minds of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, or other such states, their types are not limited to one.
The first three [sections] concern the initial cause, the second the condition, and the third the cause. △ Second, the four [factors] are explained individually:
there is the cause and there is the condition, because all Bodhisattvas attain all-knowledge (sarvajñā) through them.
The cause of the land of self-enjoyment is that it is accomplished by the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*),
and because all sentient beings and bodhisattvas collectively accumulate roots of goodness.

The cause of the land of transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) refers to sentient beings and bodhisattvas who together construct a single object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), each being born according to their respective karma and conduct.
In that land, ordinary beings and sages dwell together. It is the cause for the two lower types of *paranirmita-vaśavartin* lands.
This is due to the power of the vows of all bodhisattvas to adorn and purify their buddha-fields;
specifically, it refers to those from the first bhūmi upward who cultivate the vow for a pure land, as described among the Ten Great Vows.
Because all Bodhisattvas accomplish non-retrogressive conduct and vows—
specifically those accomplished through the non-retrogressive conduct of effort from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward— the eighth stage contains the section on Pure Lands.
△ Third, the final three [sections] concern integration, subsumption, and transformation, which apply generally to causes and conditions.
Because all bodhisattvas possess mastery over pure resolute conviction (*adhimukti*),
from the eighth stage upward, they can churn the great ocean into cream and butter, transform the great earth into gold,

and exercise sovereign control over the birth of sentient beings by transforming the defiled into the pure and the pure into the defiled. Among the ten masteries (*vaśitā*), there is the mastery over the buddha-field (*kṣetra-vaśitā*).
As for the investigation of its cause: it is because pure resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and the upholding of that resolute conviction transform according to the mind;
because they flow from the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of all Tathāgatas; and because of the power of mastery attained at the time of reaching the Way.
This means that at the time of attaining perfect enlightenment, his body fills the dust-mote lands of the worlds throughout the ten directions;

thoughts and eons are perfectly interfused, established simultaneously. This arises from two kinds of causes: first, it flows from roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). [The following] concerns the cause of speech.

Second is the power of attaining enlightenment, which clarifies the function of the fruit. This represents the mutual integration of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
It is as stated at the beginning of the sutra: "In the land of Magadha, the earth was firm," and so forth.

By virtue of the sovereign power of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s vows, whether [the goal] is accomplished or not, he is always able to harmoniously integrate all things. Furthermore, while the former refers to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), this refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*deng-jue*).
Their *dharmatā*-land serves as the fundamental substance for all lands; when one exhaustively examines its cause, it is found to be assisted by what is called the "natural law" (*dharmatā*).
It serves as the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*). This is because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and all causes taken collectively serve as the contributing conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*).
Furthermore, the latter three [causes] also integrate with the preceding lands; they do not possess a separate essence. Moreover, these ten matters arise sequentially from one another.
That is to say, all Buddha-lands arise generally through the power of the Buddhas. Why is this so? Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). What is this "nature of phenomena"?
Is there a difference? It is because their karma is not the same. Sentient beings arise through karma; by what, then, is a Buddha formed?

Because they are transformations produced by the Omniscient One, there is a distinction between ordinary beings and Buddhas. Why do ordinary beings and sages dwell together? Because they collectively construct the same objective conditions (*ālambana*).
Why, then, are there lands consisting solely of Bodhisattvas? This is due to the power of the vows and practices of the Bodhisattvas. Since this arises from the power of karma and practice...
How can they be transformed? Because of the mastery of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). How, furthermore, are they integrated in successive layers?
Because of the sovereign power of the Buddha and Samantabhadra. △ Third, the conclusion.
"O sons of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of causes and conditions briefly explained [extending to] as many as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
This summary of the concise to reveal the extensive has already been explained previously. II. Verse Summary. These verses mostly manifest the cause through the result.
There are nine verses, which are grouped into eight sections; the first verse praises the spiritual power of the Buddha.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The boundless oceans of lands thus described... "...such is the power of wisdom and spiritual penetrations."
Based on this, since the ocean of boundless lands is all adorned and purified by Vairocana, the subsequent adornment of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*) is likewise clearly evident.

Speaking in terms of ultimate principle, one’s vows should pervade the entire Dharma-realm. 2. A single verse transcending [the previous] to praise how sentient beings and bodhisattvas together accumulate roots of goodness.
The Bodhisattva practices the ocean of all vows... (up to) the Bodhisattva’s lands pervading the ten directions.
△ Third: Verses on the fourth [topic], the accomplishment of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), which is the cause for the land of self-enjoyment.
The Bodhisattva proceeds toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and all vast buddha-fields are fully accomplished.
The first half [of the verse] refers to the cause; the second half refers to the fruit. The *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states:

"The pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*)—due to the maturation of the causes and conditions for the self-benefiting, untainted, and purely immaculate buddha-fields cultivated in the past—proceeds from the initial attainment of Buddhahood."
Extending to the end of the future, they continue to transform into purely adorned Buddha-lands, circular and boundless, embellished with various jewels;
this may be seen by comparing it to the sutra. △ Fourth, verses on the sixth vow for the power of purification and adornment, as well as the seventh vow for non-retrogressive practice.
"Practicing the ocean of all practices without limit (up to: in each and every land for immeasurable eons.
Regarding "practicing the ocean of all practices without limit," the *Śāstra* states: "This refers to the power of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)."

Due to the ripening of the causes and conditions for a pure Buddha-field cultivated through past altruistic and untainted practices, it is transformed into a pure land according to what is appropriate for Bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages;
these lands may be vast or inferior, or superior, changing from one state to another over time.

Although the preceding sūtra speaks of the power of vows (*praṇidhāna-bala*), it is not that there is no practice (*caryā*). To distinguish between the presence or absence of functional effort, the prose section establishes two phrases, both of which pertain to the *paranirmita-upabhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body for others).
Therefore, the verse treats them as one. The first phrase versifies the sixth [verse], and the second phrase versifies the seventh.
This is because from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one enters the stream of Dharma moment by moment, and mind after mind proceeds toward the realm of the Buddha. Hereafter—
The half-verse [of the preceding section] encompasses both textual passages. △5. One verse summarizes the third point, the karmic activities of sentient beings:
"Sentient beings are disturbed and turbid by afflictions... all oceans of lands are thus established."

Furthermore, due to the causes of karma created while being disturbed by afflictions (*kleśa*), one creates impure lands; since the desires for pleasure are not uniform, the lands experienced differ accordingly.

Because [the Buddha] previously practiced together with Bodhisattvas, there must have been much wholesome karma. This clarifies the point regarding afflictions. △ Sixth, the verse on the Bodhisattva’s superior resolve (*adhimukti*).
The Buddha-son’s treasury of the adornments of the ocean of lands (up to: all that dwells in the ten directions is likewise thus.
△ Seven verses; one verse transcends to praise the power of Samantabhadra’s vows.
A Bodhisattva is able to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra until they are pure, vast, and equal to space.
There are three aspects to Samantabhadra: first, the "preliminary" Samantabhadra, which refers merely to the arousal of the Samantabhadra-mind;

this is not what is employed here. Second, the "intermediate" Samantabhadra, which refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi); this occupies the position immediately preceding Buddhahood. Third is the "subsequent" [Samantabhadra].

Samantabhadra: This means that having attained the fruit, one does not abandon the causal practice; therefore, the long prose section is placed later. △ Section Eight consists of two verses, which instead praise the sovereign mastery of the Tathāgata.
Manifesting spiritual powers equal to the realm of empty space... this is that which is adorned and purified by Vairocana.

The preceding verse praises the function of the fruit; the subsequent verse praises the flow of goodness. The natural law (*dharmatā*) is omitted from praise because it is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmadharmatā*);
thus, it is abbreviated. Furthermore, the seventh verse [indicates] that there is a basis, while the eighth verse is in the center.
There is a basis. The ninth verse [states that] because [the lands] are fused throughout the three periods of time, the three [times] are mutually fused and subsumed without obstruction.
However, this non-obstruction comprises ten types. In various teachings regarding the lands, some claim they are merely impermanent, while others say they are transformations of the mind;

thus, principle and phenomena are separated by a vast gulf, and many fail to achieve fusion. Therefore, the essential doctrine of this present sutra must distinguish non-obstruction. First, the principle...
1. Non-obstruction of phenomena (*vastu-asaṅga*): This means that while they are entirely identical to true nature (*dharmatā*), the characteristics of the lands (*kṣetra-lakṣaṇa*) remain distinct.

As a sutra says: "The Flower Treasury World-Ocean; the dharma-realm is without differentiation, for its adornments are entirely pure. 2. Non-obstruction of formation and destruction (*saṃvarta-vivarta-asaṅga*): This means that formation is itself destruction, and destruction is itself formation, and so forth.
3. Non-obstruction of vastness and narrowness (*vistīrṇa-saṃkucita-asaṅga*): This means that while not destroying their specific characteristics, they universally pervade all. As a sutra says...
The essence and characteristics of clouds are fundamentally without distinction, pervading all immeasurable lands equally;
thus, the four characteristics enter one another without obstruction. As the subsequent text states: "By means of a single world-system, one enters all; all enter into one without exception."

Furthermore, this text states: "The body encompasses all," and so forth; such passages occur more than once. This also refers to the non-obstruction between the one and the many, wherein the five characteristics are themselves non-obstructive.
As the text says: "Because immeasurable worlds are identical to a single world. Sixth is the non-obstruction of the subtle; as the sutra says:
"Like a king of pure jewels spread out like clouds, the reflections of all Buddhas appear with brilliant clarity," and so forth. Seventh...

The non-obstruction of concealment and manifestation: this refers to the differences in concealment and manifestation among distinct categories such as the defiled and the pure, because their appearances are not identical.
The non-obstruction of the eightfold mutual manifestation: this refers to seeing all lands within a single particle, and likewise seeing particles within all lands.
They are infinitely layered, like a celestial net (*jāla-netra*). Ninth, there is the non-obstruction of principal and satellites:

in every single world-system, there must necessarily be all others as its retinue. As the subsequent scripture states: "The various oceans of lands where Vairocana formerly practiced have all been purified";
these various lands are precisely the satellites. Tenth, there is the non-obstruction of time and place; that is to say, whether at...
Within a single land, one manifests the kalpas of the three periods of time; or within a single thought-moment, one manifests immeasurable lands, as in the ninth verse cited above.
Furthermore, the subsequent text states: "All the adornments existing throughout the three periods of time are all clearly manifested within a single mani-jewel fruit."

These ten non-obstructions are simultaneously and fully present; their sovereign nature is difficult to comprehend. They are scattered throughout various texts and may be integrated through the six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*).

composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang,

△ Second, the basis of abiding encompasses both the defiled and the pure. The prose section has three parts; first, the heading:
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... there were bases of abiding as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds.
△ Second, the explanation:
It is said that they may abide in all manner of adornments;
however, the difference in their abiding arises from the distinctions in the inclinations of their minds, for the former [category] delights in such embellishments.
Some dwell supported by empty space,
because they delight in non-obstruction;
others dwell supported by the radiance of all jewels.
Because bliss is the very substance of light;
or because it abides by means of the light of all Buddhas,
out of fear of all sufferings.

Alternatively, they abide by means of all jewel-colored lights, because they delight in light that is free from substantiality; thus the light manifests as jewel-colors rather than jewels emitting light.
Alternatively, they abide by means of all Buddha-voices.
Out of reverence for the holy teachings,
or by relying on karma produced like an illusion, he dwells with a golden hand in the form of a powerful asura,
seeking divine protection.
Some abide in the bodies of all the lords of the world,
seeking divine protection;
others abide in the bodies of all bodhisattvas.
Because they are sustained by the power of the bodhisattvas' vows,
or because they abide in the ocean of all diverse adornments produced by the vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva for the sake of universally pacifying sentient beings—
how could vast worlds abide based upon small categories such as sentient beings?
This has two meanings. First, because the external is induced by the internal, it is said to "depend on the body. This, in turn, has two aspects:

first, the power of past causes, as the verse says, "sustained by the power of karma"; second, the power of present transformation, which refers to the sustaining power of the Bodhisattvas who are World-Lords, who take [the environment] under their own care.
Second, it is due to the substance and phenomena of the untainted (*anāsrava*). There is no distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles regarding this.
Obstructed, they are able to abide in mutual dependence. △ Third, the conclusion:
O Sons of the Buddha, within these oceans of worlds, there are such abodes as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
△ Section Two consists of twenty-two verses, which are divided into two parts. The first part provides a general overview:
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (throughout) observed the ten directions and spoke these verses.
Pervading the entirety of the space-realm of the ten directions, [it] appears before one everywhere and is visible to all.
All worlds abide by the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). Thus, the Sanskrit original says: "All appear through the Buddha’s supernormal power.
As for why they are not listed in the prose (*gadya*): if they were listed, the remaining nine would not be the Buddha’s supernormal power; therefore, the verse [treats them as such].
This passage subsumes the preceding ten sections; all are the Buddha’s spiritual power. △ Second, a separate verse summary of the preceding text, divided into nine parts.
First, regarding the abode of adornment:
"There are various kinds of lands... (up to) a blazing, universally manifesting ocean of light."
The subject reveals the object: because all the articles of adornment are made of precious jewels. △ Second, abiding in space:
there are some pure, luminous lands that abide supported by the realm of empty space.
△ Third, abiding by reliance on jewels:
there are those who abide within the ocean of maṇi-jewels, further dwelling in the treasury of radiant light.
△ Fourth, one verse concerning abiding by reliance on the Buddha’s light.
The Tathāgata abides within this ocean-like assembly (until: sentient beings who behold him rejoice in their hearts.
Because they receive the light of the Buddha’s teaching, they bring the world to completion. △ Five: Abiding in the Radiance of Jewel-Colored Light.
There are [ornaments] made of *maṇi* gems as adornments (up to) being covered by a net of exquisite jewel radiance.
By means of these adornments and coverings, reflections appear and abide therein. △ Sixth, there are two verses concerning the abiding of the Buddha’s voice.
There may be buddha-fields that are boundless (up to) constantly seeing immeasurably vast jewels;
this refers to the sounds of wondrous, wholesome, and unconfused [teachings], which possess majestic spiritual power. △ Seven: One verse praises the seventh and eighth abodes.
Some abide at Vajrapāṇi (up to) "constantly turning the wheel of Dharma in this place," which also reveals the teaching of the Dharma.
△ Eight verses follow, praising the abiding in the body of a bodhisattva.
Some rest evenly upon jewel trees (up to the point where it is said) this is due to the transformation by the power of karma.
Whether tree or water, all are the bodies of Bodhisattvas; because the Bodhisattvas manifest them, the prose simply mentions "Bodhisattvas.
Herein, they also rely upon the body of the Buddha. Although there is the power of vows here, it is sustained by superior past roots of goodness and is not universal.
The Vow of the Worthy One. △ Ninth, the remaining eight verses all praise the arising, abiding, and threefold aspects of Samantabhadra’s vows. First, regarding the vast lands:
because they pervade the entire Dharma-realm, it says:
"There are lands that pervade the Dharma-realm... through the power of the Buddha, they are all made visible."
The preceding verse clarifies that what is produced by pure consciousness has no substance external to the mind, and is therefore like a reflection.

The subsequent verse addresses the arising of inconceivable karma, which arises without departing from emptiness. △ Second, the explanation of mastery in governing sentient beings within subtle lands.
Within every single atom of every land (up to: Vairocana is able to manifest [all things].
However, while it is the Buddha’s power that manifests this, it is also gathered by the vows of Samantabhadra; therefore, both sections of the text equally involve the Buddha’s power.
△ Third, revealing the essential nature of the lands and concluding that they have a specific locus.
"All vast lands... sustained by the power of vast karma. The first verse clarifies that the lands exist based on their fundamental nature;
existence is non-existence. The subsequent half-verse explains the recurrence of formation and destruction like a circling wheel.
The final half-verse concludes by returning to universal vows while simultaneously manifesting vast karma. △ Third, the forms and characteristics also encompass the defiled.
Purification. Regarding the initial prose section, there are three parts. First, the heading:
"At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... [up to] ...the world-oceans have various distinct forms and characteristics."
△ Second, the explanation:
namely, they are either circular, square, or neither circular nor square (up to) having the shape of sentient beings or the shape of a Buddha.
As for "neither circular nor square," this refers to those with three dimensions or eight corners; since none are circular or square, it is said that there are "infinite varieties. Mountain.
Regarding the flame-shaped [seal]: it is like a mountain resembling a flame; one takes the upper point because it corresponds to the square and other shapes above.
The rest may be understood accordingly. △ Third, the conclusion.
There are as many such [worlds] as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds.
△ Second, the ten verses of praise are divided into two parts. First, a general praise exhorting contemplation:
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
The various distinct oceans of lands (extending to) "you all should collectively observe them.

△ Second, the remaining seven verses correctly versify the preceding meanings, while also citing the causes to manifest the results. Of these two [sections], the first two verses correspond to the ten preceding segments.
Their forms are either circular or square... [this is] due to the vastness of their karma and the non-confusion of their intentions.
As for the "mani-wheel," it is of the same category as a whirlpool. Adorned with pure flames, the verse above describes the mountain-flame gateways opening in competition;
this meaning also encompasses palaces. △ Second, seven verses on the previously mentioned infinite distinctions. First, the lands: by means of...
The diversity of causes.
The infinite and differentiated treasuries of the ocean of lands (extending to) all phenomena of cyclic existence are always thus.
△ Second, there are four verses on how sovereignty arises from the Buddha.
"Inconceivable lands within a single pore" (up to) "the Dharma of Vairocana is thus.
Regarding "inconceivable lands within a single pore," there is another principle:

it means that while practitioners dwell in their respective lands of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*), which are each different, the lands manifested by the Buddha to gather sentient beings resemble those lands of retribution; thus, they appear in infinite layers.
And they appear. Without departing from a single hair-pore. △ Fourth, the essence of the lands (*kṣetra*) refers exclusively to pure lands. This section has two parts. First, the prose:
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... (up to) ...or takes the voice of the Buddha as its essence.

Briefly, twenty kinds of essence are distinguished. However, regarding the essence of the Buddha-land (*kṣetra*), various teachings differ: some take the eight subtle particles as its essence; some take "mind-only" as its essence;
some take the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) as its essence; and some take all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) as its essence. Now, it possesses all of these.
That is to say, the various jewels and so forth are the eight subtle particles; when the Buddha’s voice is added, they constitute the nine subtle particles.

Manifesting in a single thought-moment is the sudden transformation of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). As for the Buddha’s transformations, they may be either *nairmāṇika-rūpa* (fruition-color) or all phenomena, because they cause the three worlds to act as one another.
Furthermore, by integrating the aforementioned various explanations, they constitute the essence of the unimpeded realm (*asaṅga-kṣetra*).
Regarding the "wheel of the sun-jewel," this refers to the solar disc. Fragrance permeates both substance and vapor; the Buddha stated that these constitute its essence.
Because it is the essence of unimpeded activity, and because it arises based on the powers of the Tathāgata as taught. △ Second, there are ten verses in verse form.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke these verses:
There are some oceans of lands composed of exquisite jewels, which are firm, indestructible, and rest upon jewel lotuses.
The first two lines and the sixth line of the verse refer to this indestructible vajra.
"Or the pure light arises from the unknowable" (up to) "it dwells supported by space.
This single verse praises the third and fourth [stages].
Alternatively, having pure light as its essence, it further dwells supported by light, adorned with clouds of light, serving as the common playground for Bodhisattvas.
Verse Five: All-Adorned Radiance.
There are some oceans of lands that arise from the power of vows and abide like reflections; they cannot be grasped through verbal description.
The verse describes two kinds of bodies. Regarding those born through the power of vows, it praises the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha, appearing like a reflected image;
it praises the marks of the wondrous jewels. If both matters are combined, it praises the Buddha’s transformations (*nirmāṇa*).
Alternatively, the ground is adorned with jewel wheels composed of *maṇi* gems that universally radiate the light of the Sun-Treasury (*sūryagarbha*), which are entirely filled with Bodhisattvas.
This verse describes two types of entities: the first half of the verse describes the solar wheel, and the second half describes the subtle jewels.
There are lands formed of jewel-flames that produce clouds of flames covering them above; the exquisite splendor of all these jewel-lights is obtained through the power of karma.
The verse’s mention of "jewel-flames" and the term "exquisite" also includes fragrances.
Alternatively, from the "Exquisite Marks" (Sūkṣmalakṣaṇa), various marks and ornaments arise to adorn the ground, like a crown being worn together; this arises through the Buddha’s transformation.
Regarding the verse on the jeweled crown: the jeweled crown is also a transformation of the Buddha, yet it is not a verse that directly praises the Buddha’s transformation.
Or, arising from the ocean of the mind according to what the mind understands, they abide as illusions without any fixed location—all of which are conceptual constructions.
A verse describes how the entire realm is universally manifested in a single thought-moment.
Alternatively, they take the light of the Buddhas and the light of mani-jewels as their substance, within which all Buddhas appear, each exerting their own supernormal powers.
The verse on the manifestation of the adornment of all jewels, as well as the verses on the latter three bodies, describe the mani-light;

this refers to the jewel-adorned forms of the bodhisattvas and the calyxes of the jeweled flowers. The Buddha-light refers to the Buddha’s voice, because the light of that voice constitutes the buddha-field.
Alternatively, all the adornments of the oceans of lands manifested by the power of the vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva are entirely sublime and wondrous;
they are ultimately resolved back into Samantabhadra. △ Fifth, the Adornments of the Lands. This concerns only the Pure and Radiant Lands. The text has two parts. First, the prose exposition.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva [proceeded] in this manner through as many oceans of worlds as there are atoms;

within them, some were adorned with jewels, some by persons, some by dharmas, and some by the teaching of the Dharma and the practice of cultivation, manifesting their mutual integration and inclusion.
All serve to adorn the buddha-fields (*kṣetra*). Since persons and dharmas are taken as jewels, persons—by means of causes such as preaching the Dharma—attain the fruit of adornment.
Thus, the cause is designated by the name of the fruit, and is thereby called "adornment. △ Second, the verse summary consists of ten verses divided into two parts;
the first one generally reveals the adornment of the fields.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to reiterate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The vast oceans of lands are without limit... [they] pervade all the ten directions."
△ Section Two consists of nine verses, which specifically versify the preceding prose.
From "The cloud of jewel-flames with boundless forms" (up to) "all are expounded by the Buddhas.
The first verse versifies the initial "Exquisite Cloud"; the next verse versifies the second [section], the merits of the Bodhisattvas, and the third...
The fourth is the ocean of the bodhisattvas' vows. Next, one verse summarizes and explains the karmic retributions of sentient beings:
"All Tathāgatas of the three periods of time... manifest everywhere."
The six preceding verses correspond in sequence to the latter six matters. △ Sixth, the Purification of Buddha-lands, in two parts. First, the prose explanation, in three sections.
First, the heading:
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... there were oceans of pure skillful means as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.

Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): this refers exclusively to purity. If it were defined according to the Buddha's skillful gathering of beings as appropriate to their needs, then the Buddha should preside over them all, and both pure and impure realms would be called Buddha-lands.
However, if defined according to the actual realization of practice, only the pure is so designated, not the impure. Furthermore, there are two kinds of purity:

first, mundane purity, which is so called because it is free from the impurities of desire; by taking the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) as expedient means, the upper two realms constitute the pure land.

Second is supramundane purity. This is further divided into two types. The first is the supramundane, which refers to the provisional teachings of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) that take the [Four] Truths as their skillful means;
according to these, there is no separate pure land. Speaking from the perspective of ultimate reality, however, there is a distinct pure land outside the triple world where the Two Vehicles reside;
there is textual evidence for this in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The second is the supreme-supramundane.

Purity. This means that the Bodhisattva takes the ten thousand practices as the skillful means (*upāya*) and the immeasurable adornments of the seven treasures of the true recompense as the upper layer.
Here, the text primarily clarifies the Bodhisattva while also manifesting the Two Vehicles.
Furthermore, within this supreme supramundane purity, there are two kinds: first, the ultimate reality, which is the self-enjoyment of the Buddha, free from the accumulation of marks.

Furthermore, as for the "concurrent perishing" which serves as a skillful means (*upāya*), these two states have not yet reached the ultimate; thus, from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and below, it is said in the *Renyō-kyō* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra):
"The three grades of worthies and the ten stages of sages abide in retributive fruit; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land. Within this state of non-ultimacy, there are again two kinds:
first, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one is exclusively pure, having forever severed the burdens of form (*rūpa*) and illuminating the essence in solitude.
It is established that because the spirit has no fixed location, the color and characteristics of its pure land are difficult to name.

From the second through the seventh stages [of the bodhisattva path], one has not yet transcended the triple world; because the untainted wisdom of contemplation is intermittent, it is not exclusively pure. This is according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

One enters the first stage (*bhūmi*) before it can be called a Pure Land; the abodes of the three levels of the Sages (*śaikṣa*) are all impure and not pure, because this section distinguishes between the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
According to the tenet of this sutra, however, Bodhisattvas of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) already possess a Pure Land.

Therefore, in this present passage, from "associating with spiritual friends" at the beginning to "the power of Buddhahood" at the end, all are pure expedient means (*upāya*); thus, they encompass all myriad practices (*sahasra-pratipatti*). Nevertheless...
Pure skillful means (*upāya*) is itself the cause of purity. The prose section may also function as a concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). As it is said:
"By virtue of having long-term or recent virtuous friends, one is born in a land where such virtuous friends reside. Therefore, all ten matters are pure characteristics.

Nevertheless, while they share a commonality with respect to adornment, they are distinct when categorized by their specific gates. One should know that the same applies with respect to the complete causes and conditions. Furthermore, [regarding] arising...

The "endowment with causes and conditions" applies to both the defiled and the pure; this [term], however, refers only to the pure. "Adornment" (*vyūha*) generally pertains to its fruit, while "purity" (*viśuddhi*) generally pertains to its cause.
Furthermore, the former primarily involves the cultivation of good, whereas this primarily involves the remediation of evil;
thus, in the world, the former is like applying pigments and the latter is like washing and cleansing. △ Second, the explanation.
This refers to the fact that all bodhisattvas draw near to all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) because their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are identical.
Drawing near to friends with identical roots of goodness is explained at length in the section concerning the Night Goddess *Sudhana* (or *Dharanimdhara*).
Because the vast clouds of merit increase and expand, pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
because one knows how to guide with clouds of compassion that extensively fill the Dharma-realm,
having purely cultivated vast and supreme resolute understandings.
The resolute understanding of the Dharma-gates has been thoroughly purified in all respects. The [preceding] three [stages] refer to the levels;
they pertain to the stage prior to the bhūmis, because one dwells in the observation of all bodhisattva realms.

Because one realizes the universally pervasive suchness at the very first stage, it is said that "one observes all objective spheres. Because one is born into the family of the Tathāgata, it is said that "one dwells securely.
Because one cultivates and purifies all the pāramitās until they are entirely perfected, [it is so called].

Because this is the stage of cultivation following the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), all [factors] are cultivated even if they are not yet complete; however, from the perspective of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), they may also be said to be complete.
Because one observes all the bodhisattva stages and enters into them;

for in the first stage, one advances by universally training in the practices of all ten stages, as each subsequent stage consists solely of such practice of the Dharma. Thus, the [latter] three are all contained within the first stage.
Because it gives birth to an ocean of all pure vows:
one initiates vows upon the first stage (*bhūmi*) and practices in accordance with them until reaching the eighth stage, where they are all fully accomplished;
thus it is called "giving birth to an ocean of all vows. As for the term "pure," it refers to being exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because one cultivates all practices leading to liberation:

the practices leading to liberation for the two vehicles of the nine stages consist solely of śamatha and vipaśyanā, whereas the practice leading to liberation for Bodhisattvas consists solely of unimpeded eloquence.
Because it causes the multitudes to emerge;
because it enters into the ocean of all adornments;
and because both the ten stages and the two types of adornment are fully perfected.

Because they have accomplished the power of pure skillful means, these are precisely the merits of Samantabhadra Buddha. Among the ten [purities], the first three are the causes for the purity of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), and the latter seven are the causes for the purity of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*).

Since the above intends to subsume all lands in their entirety, they are assigned sequentially according to a vertical arrangement. If, however, one considers them according to horizontal cultivation, first—
The mind may thus be fully perfected. △ Third, the conclusion:
There are such [worlds] as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
△ One verse in summary. Of the nine verses, there are two parts; the first one generally clarifies the purifier and the purified.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The various adornments of all oceans of lands Arise from the power of immeasurable pure karma."

The first half [of the verse] concerns the skillful means; the second half concerns purity. In both cases, the upper line represents the fruit and the lower line represents the cause. △ Second, eight lines separately summarize the preceding text:
"Having long approached spiritual friends... the lands are boundless and entirely pure."

The first four [verses] correspond respectively to the four purities mentioned above. Because compassion is primary in the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is said that "one practices for the sake of sentient beings.

Because it pervades true suchness (*tathatā*), it is called "vast. The fifth verse praises the purity of cultivation and practice; furthermore, it skips over the seventh verse on the purity of aspiration.
This is because the purity of aspiration extends from the first stage through the eighth stage, and since this [verse] refers specifically to the first stage, it is thus skipped.

The sixth verse praises the eighth [chapter], "Departure" (*niryāṇa*). The seventh verse praises the ninth [chapter], as well as the "Bodhisattva Grounds" (*bodhisattvabhūmi*), because the meaning of "grounds" (*bhūmi*) extends throughout both preceding and subsequent sections. The eighth verse praises the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

Thus far, these have been assigned to the prose commentary (*gadya*), though they also incorporate other meanings therein. △ Seven: The Distinctions of the Buddha’s Emergence. Part One: Prose Commentary.
Three. First, the heading:
"At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... (up to) "...there are as many distinct appearances of Buddhas as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds.
△ Second, the explanation.
That is to say, manifesting either a small body or a large body, up to manifesting the taming of boundless sentient beings—these ten matters comprise five pairs.
Regarding the ocean and the seeds, there are these distinctions: among the five, the first two correspond to the respective types [of beings];

the next one corresponds to the breadth or narrowness of the object; the next one corresponds to the suitability of the capacity; and the fifth corresponds to whether [the beings] are mature or immature. △
The three fetters (*saṃyojana*). There are such [fetters] as these, numbering as many as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
△ Second, the verses in praise consist of ten stanzas divided into three parts; first, the general introduction.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The various skillful means of all Buddhas... this is the Tathāgata’s power of skillful means."
△ Second, there are five verses. They are explained individually in sequence. These first five couplets [state]:
"The *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is inconceivable... [omitted] ...awakening the deluded masses beyond measure."
△ 34. Summary. Or, clouds of emanations issue from a single pore (up to) pervading all lands.
Since they pervade everywhere according to the mind, even a number equal to the atoms within an ocean of lands is not considered much. △ 8. Abiding for eons.

The same. This refers to the duration of the kalpa-abiding as described in the *Candrasūryagatiparivarta-sūtra*. Because it varies according to the causal factors that induce it, there are differences in length.
The text has two parts. The first, the prose section, has three sub-sections. The first is the heading.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... [remains] for as many eons as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds.
△ Second, the explanation:
That is to say, some remain for incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons... up to some remaining for unspeakable (*anabhilāpya*) eons.
Briefly stated, there are ten great numbers; furthermore, there are many other variations as indicated in the headings, the summaries, and the verses.
These apply universally across all lands and are not restricted to pure [realms] alone. For example, in the great hells, the lifespan is even longer, whereas in the human realm it is quite short;
thus, those who experience the most extreme evil or the most extreme goodness endure for a long time. Moreover, if one considers this from another perspective, it cannot be fixed definitively.
Among the ten, there are only nine, as one *asaṃkhyeya* of *anabhilāpya-anabhilāpyas* is omitted; this is all as described in the "Chapter on *Asaṃkhyeya*" (A-seng-chi-pin). △ Third, the conclusion:
There are thus worlds numbering as many as the atoms in an ocean of worlds.
△ Second, the verses in praise. Since an eon (*kalpa*) is merely a division of time and possesses no distinct ontological principle, these verses express it through a shift in poetic meter.
This section is divided into three parts; the first two provide a general summary.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The various eons within the oceans of worlds... [I] now expound them through the Buddha’s voice."
This permits the explanation of the verses above, which serve as the heading. △ Second, a general summary of what was listed above:
"I see the oceans of lands in the ten directions... [up to] ...their vows are various and each different."
This also reveals the causes for [the realms'] varying lengths; it is due to the power of vows. △ Third, there are seven verses as a summary:
"Some are purely pure, some are purely defiled" (up to) "by a single skillful means, all are purified."

Each verse has a distinct meaning: 1. Clarifying the long and short [lifespans], which apply to both the defiled and the pure; they are bound together by mental conceptions. 2. The purity of the kalpa’s duration is explained by the profundity of its causes. 3.

Listing the names of various kalpas, wherein the defiled and the pure mutually encompass one another. 4. Because the vows of the Buddhas arising in the world differ, their entry into the kalpas is not the same.
5. Unity and multiplicity are mutually fused, equally encompassing and manifesting both simultaneously. 6. The characteristics of time and phenomena.

[This] encompasses and universally enters the boundless. The seven fetters arise from thought and mind; they are demonstrated through skillful means. As for the first skillful means, it is the realization that [all is] Mind-only.
A single thought-moment and an eon both depend upon the conceptualizing mind. When the conceptualizing mind does not arise, where can long or short exist?
Being neither long nor short, this is called "purity," which does not destroy appearances. Thus, the oceans of eons are boundless. △
The second part concerns the distinctions regarding the transformations of the nine abiding kalpas. The first [section] consists of three parts; the first is the heading:
"At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... there were as many distinctions of kalpa-transformations as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds."
This is of two kinds: first, regarding only the process of karmic fruition, the kalpas of formation, abiding, and destruction are all termed "transformation";

second, regarding only the good and evil of the inhabitants during the kalpa of abiding, which causes them to transform into either defilement or purity. Second, the explanation of possessing both [aspects].
The first point refers to the preceding meaning:
that because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus, the oceans of worlds undergo transformation through immeasurable eons of formation and destruction.

As for the term "nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*), it means that phenomena proceed according to their own inherent momentum (*dharmatā*). If this is so, how does this differ from arising through the conjunction of causes and conditions? [It differs] by way of the cause...

The meaning of "condition" (pratyaya) lies in the cause; the meaning of "transformation" (pariṇāma) is manifested in the fruit. Furthermore, the causal condition is universally present, establishing only that which is indestructible;
this is like the cause for one's own enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*). △ Second, the ninth [section] explains the latter meaning.
Because sentient beings dwell in a state of defilement, the ocean of worlds undergoes transformation into defiled kalpas.
Due to encountering adverse conditions, the pure becomes defiled. As the subsequent text states: "The springs and ponds all dry up," and so forth.
Because sentient beings who cultivate vast merit abide therein, the oceans of worlds undergo transformation through kalpas of defilement and purity.
Because those who cultivate the great merit of humans and devas cause the worlds to be mostly defiled and only slightly pure, it is first described as "defiled," as the subsequent text states:
"Non-glutinous rice grows spontaneously," and so forth.
Because Bodhisattvas who abide in the stage of resolute belief (adhimukti) dwell therein, the oceans of worlds undergo transformation through kalpas of defilement and purity.

Specifically, because those prior to the [first] bhūmi have not yet severed their hindrances, these realms are not purely pure; however, because purity predominates, they were previously described as "pure."
Many sutras speak of both defilement and purity; how does this differ from what was stated previously? It may be an error on the part of the translator, or a scribal mistake.
Because immeasurable sentient beings resolve their minds upon Bodhicitta, the oceans of worlds undergo transformation during the eon of absolute purity.
Because those who have realized and generated the bodhicitta dwell in the land of enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya-kṣetra*), it is described as being "pure" alone.
Since the various bodhisattvas each travel through all worlds, the oceans of worlds undergo transformation throughout boundless *kalpas* of adornment.
Those who travel individually are the bodhisattvas from the second through the tenth stages, who sport with supernatural powers.
They may adorn a single buddha-field with many ornaments, or they may adorn many buddha-fields with a single ornament; in whichever defiled fields they arrive, they are able to adorn them.
The Bodhisattvas of all the oceans of worlds in the ten directions [transform] through immeasurable great adornment kalpas.

"Great adornment" refers to the stage of Samantabhadra; it is the adorning of lands within a single mote of dust, such as the aforementioned summoning of the assembly by means of light from the mouth.
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have entered parinirvāṇa, the adornments of the world-oceans perish and the kalpas undergo transformation.

Regarding the "perishing of adornments": this clarifies that one loses favorable conditions while evil manifests; that is to say, when the Tathāgata demonstrates his passing, his efficacious activities likewise perish.

A hundred years after the Buddha’s extinction, milk was not worth a drop of water, let alone in the present age, and even more so in the extreme period of decline, when weeds [of false doctrine] prevail.
The finest flavors; iron as the supreme ornament;
because the Buddhas appear in the world, all oceans of worlds undergo vast, pure, and majestic transformations throughout the kalpas, just as when Maitreya arrives.
Because of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers and transformations, the oceans of worlds are universally purified and the kalpas undergo transformation.

By means of the Buddha’s supernormal powers, what could possibly be impure? The case of Vimalakīrti pressing the earth with his toe, or the threefold purification of the land in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, are precisely examples of this.
Regarding the ten matters mentioned above, the first is general while the others are specific; they do not go beyond [the manifestation of] karma. Furthermore, the first...

The first two belong to ordinary beings; the next four to bodhisattvas; and the final three to Buddhas. Furthermore, from the perspective of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, that which is defiled is made pure;
from the perspective of ordinary beings, that which is pure becomes defiled. △ Third, the conclusion.
There are as many such [worlds] as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds.
△ Second, the verses in praise:
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
All lands arise in accordance with the power of karma... (up to) all are universally pure.
The ten verses follow their respective order as explained previously. △ Ten Non-differentiations. Part one: The prose section has three parts. First, the heading.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed [the assembly]... [up to] "...there are world-oceans as numerous as atoms, which are without distinction.

This means that while the preceding nine sections distinguished various worlds based on their differing characteristics and their defilement or purity according to karma—due to the existence of distinctions among sentient beings—the present section speaks of "no distinction" because their nature is non-dual. Thus, the verse says: "Arising from the nature of karma."
Furthermore, from the perspective of provisional establishment, there are various distinctions; however, when speaking from the perspective of ultimate reality, all things are without distinction.
For example, within the teachings, the mention of the three vehicles constitutes a distinction, whereas when the *Avataṃsaka* is taught, all are without distinction.
Furthermore, because all are employed by the Buddhas, each is harmoniously integrated and equal without distinction.

Thus, the distinctions of the preceding nine are the differentiation within this non-differentiation; and this present non-differentiation is precisely the non-differentiation of the preceding nine differentiations.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "While sentient beings see it burning, the Pure Land is not destroyed. Both are mutually identical.
Based on this meaning, it is said that within the Pure Land there are eighteen perfections; each accords with reality because they are all universally pervasive.
△ Second, the explanation:
namely, within each and every world-ocean, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in a world-ocean, which are without distinction.
The number of worlds contained within the ocean is equal to the total number of atoms in the ocean; thus, each atom constitutes a world-realm. This already embodies the meaning of inclusion.
Within each and every world-ocean, the majestic power manifested by all appearing Buddhas is without distinction.
The Buddha manifests his majestic power equally;
in every single ocean of worlds, all places of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) pervade the dharma-realm of the ten directions without distinction.
These places of enlightenment are identical because they are identical with true nature (dharmatā).
In every ocean of world-systems, there is no difference among the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Tathāgatas,
because these assemblies are identical as they are constantly accompanied by their retinues.
In every ocean of world-systems, there is no difference in the light of all Buddhas (extending to) the skillful means of the Wheel of Dharma.
The names and sounds of the next four radiances, as well as their dharmacakra and skillful means, can all be understood from the text.
The seven preceding [radiances] are all based on the single principle of immovability, yet they are universally pervasive and without distinction.
Within each and every ocean of world-systems, all oceans of world-systems universally enter into a single atom without distinction;
atoms contain oceans of lands.
Within each and every ocean of world-systems, every single atom likewise manifests [all things] therein without distinction.
The mundane dust-like forms and the Buddha-lands: these two, in terms of their indestructible characteristics, extensively contain all things without distinction. △ Third, the conclusion:
"O Sons of the Buddha, the oceans of worlds are without distinction... [up to] ...without distinction in number equal to the atoms of dust."
△ Second, the verses in praise.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning (up to) observing the ten directions, spoke these verses:
"Within a single mote of dust are many oceans of lands... by the power of his vows, he pervades the world."

The ten verses follow their respective order to verse the ten meanings mentioned above; however, the sixth verse concerns the body (*kāya*), differing from the preceding ones only in name and substance.

While the preceding [verses] dealt with a general, undifferentiated state, the present one clarifies the meaning of the non-differentiation of layered and integrated inclusion within the sensory objects (*viṣaya*).

If it were said that this refers to a commonality of activity, why would it not also mention the commonality of affliction (*kleśa*) and the commonality of suffering (*duḥkha*)? How could this possibly be the world-system (*lokadhātu*)?
"Is there nothing at all like this within the ocean? Below this, the eighth fascicle of the sutra begins.
○ *The Chapter on the Flower Treasury World*, Fifth.
△ Regarding the initial intent for its inclusion: the preceding chapter generally elucidated the oceans of Buddha-lands; now, this chapter specifically elucidates the land of our own Teacher.
Regarding the "fruit of the adorned basis": it follows next because it answers the inquiry concerning the world-ocean.

Second, as for the explanation of the title: according to the Sanskrit original, it is fully titled "The Chapter on the Light of the Universally Pure Ocean of Merits of the Flower-Treasury Adorned World-Ocean.
The translator, finding this too verbose, made it overly concise; therefore, this [title] strikes a middle ground.
It should be titled "The Chapter on the Lotus Treasury Adorned World-Ocean. This means that the "treasury" (*kośa*) refers to the place where the lotus nurtures its seeds;
since this world-system (*kṣetra-vyuha*) and its worlds are now contained within a great lotus, it is called the "Lotus Treasury.
Furthermore, because every single realm therein possesses pure merits as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds, it is so named.
The world-system is adorned; because it is profound and vast, it is called an "ocean" (*sāgara*).

As for the claim that the world-system is supported by an ocean and thus given the name "ocean," this likely does not reflect the intended meaning of the text, since it is later referred to as the "Flower Treasury Adorned World-System Ocean" (*kusumatalagarbhavyūhālaṃkāralokadhātusāgara*), indicating that it resides within a flower.
Its Sanskrit term *vyūha* refers to that which adorns, namely the adornment itself. Its light from the ocean of pervasive, pure merit...

"Manifest" (*ming*) refers to the characteristics and functions of the adornments. Since function depends upon substance, the word "manifest" is employed. In the present text, the substance is cited as encompassing the function, thus simply saying "Flower Treasury" (*Huazang*).

While this may be acceptable from the perspective of conventional phenomena (*shi*), for what reason is it called the "Ocean of Lands" (*Chashai*)? Its characteristics and forms are as previously described. Briefly stated, there are two reasons:
first, with respect to sentient beings, the Tathāgata’s storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is itself the fragrant ocean, which is also the ocean of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Based on the foundation of non-abiding, this is called the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). It is also the wind of false conceptualization (*parikalpa*).

Within this ocean, there are causal and resultant characteristics—the nature-virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—which are the flowers of the true cause (*tathatā-hetu*). These are the future resultant dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
Because it encompasses and contains all things, it is called a "storehouse" (garbha). If one regards the dharma-nature as the ocean, the mind is the flower;

the manner of its containment is likewise. However, within the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of this storehouse consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna), half constitutes the external vessel-world, as it is not grasped or appropriated (anupātta).
Half constitutes the internal body; it is grasped as self-nature because it gives rise to perceptions and sensations. For what reason is the Tathāgata-garbha consciousness thus?
Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because it is drawn forth by karma and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Second, regarding all Buddhas:

it means that by the wind of great vows, they sustain the ocean of great compassion, producing the flowers of boundless practices and containing within them the fruits of the two benefits—both defiled and pure—which are layered without end.

Because there are obstructions, the characteristics of the lands they bring forth resemble them. For this reason, in the "Appearance" chapter (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*), worlds are frequently used as metaphors for the Buddha’s virtues.
Upon closely examining the meaning of the text, it is found that the worlds are like the Buddha’s virtues because of those virtues.

Regarding the three aspects of the fundamental intent (*abhiprāya*): specifically revealing that the Master’s primary and secondary environments encompass the three worlds, integrating them inexhaustibly, constitutes the fundamental intent (*mūla*).
Causing all bodhisattvas to give rise to faith and understanding, thereby accomplishing their practices and vows, constitutes the goal (*prayojana*). The remainder is as in the preceding chapter.

It is merely a matter of general and specific distinctions. The manner in which these are integrated and subsumed is also seen in the preceding text. When Xianshou established the Flower Treasury Contemplation (*Huazang guan*), there were again ten virtues;
they are largely the same with minor differences, as explained in that text.
