Fourth, the explanation of the text. This chapter is divided into three sections, which follow the sequence below: first, explaining the name "Flower Treasury Adorned World. Now, for the first [section], "The Flower Treasury:
Cause, Effect, and Essential Nature," there are two parts. First, the prose section has two parts; first, citing the fruit and attributing it to the person.
This reveals the profundity and vastness of the causal conditions.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying: "[From here until] 'this is Vairocana Tathāgata.
This refers to this ocean of lands as being my original teacher, purified through the cultivation of causes. Furthermore, these causes are profound and vast; there are three [aspects to them].
Regarding the "superior characteristics":

in the past, while practicing the bodhisattva path for as many eons as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, he practiced for a single long duration spanning eons as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of lands; thus, it was not merely three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
In each eon, he draws near to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds.
Furthermore, throughout many eons, he encounters many superior conditions, not only meeting victorious ones such as Śākyamuni Buddha.
At each and every Buddha-field, one purifies and adorns world-ocean-microdust-count great vows.

Third, regarding the many superior conditions: at each [Buddha-field], one purifies many great vows, such as the vow to purify lands and so forth, rather than merely purifying a single [state] such as the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because of these three layers, it is said to be "profound and vast. However, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Aśvabhāva-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, and other texts...
The teaching of the Three Vehicles is intended for the specific needs of a single direction and a particular class of worlds; it definitively speaks of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Now, according to the One Vehicle, this applies universally to the ten directions as well as to realms shaped like trees and so forth; therefore, it is said to be "as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of lands. Thus, the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states:
"For the sake of sentient beings of shallow understanding, I speak of practicing for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; however, in reality, there is no such [limit]."

The measure is incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. One cultivates all supreme practices; furthermore, time has no separate substance and is established based upon phenomena (*dharma*). Since phenomena are inexhaustible, time is likewise infinite.

How much more so when mindfulness and kalpas are perfectly interfused—how could one possibly cling to literal interpretations of the texts? Second, regarding the manifestation of the essence and characteristics of the fruit:

since the planting of the causes was profound, the fruit must necessarily be vast and profound. However, as for the measure of the lands (*kṣetra*) upon which they rely, the various teachings do not...
The same applies here. In the Hīnayāna, there is only this single Sahā world. In the Triyāna, there are teachings of both the Great and Small [vehicles]:

some take Akaniṣṭha as the ultimate reality, while others maintain that there are distinct pure lands elsewhere. Now, in the realm of the Ten Buddhas of the Ekayāna, the Great and Small are mutually unimpeded.

The pure and the impure are mutually integrated. For the time being, based on a single aspect, one speaks of having boundaries and surfaces; yet in reality, even a single layer extends horizontally without limit.
How much more so when each successive layer contains within its dust motes the entire Dharma-realm! However, according to the detailed exposition below, there should be ten matters:
first, the foundational wind-circle; second, the fragrant ocean sustained by the wind; third, the lotus flower emerging from the ocean; fourth, the ocean of lands sustained by the flower.
1. Mountains surrounding the terraces; 2. The precious ground on the faces of the terraces; 3. Fragrant oceans upon the ground; 4. Fragrant rivers between the oceans; 5.
Trees and so forth between the rivers; 6. A summary of the manifold adornments. In the present text, only one river is missing.
The text is divided into four sections: first, the supporting wind-circle; second, the supported fragrant ocean;

third, the lotus flowers emerging from the ocean; and fourth, the ocean of lands supported by the flowers. Regarding these lands, there are both general and specific causes, as seen in the preceding text.
To clarify the specific meaning, we shall first explain how a single cause produces a single result. Now, the first section: the wind-circle.
The causes for this are the great vows and so forth, as explained previously. Within this section, there are three parts. First, the general enumeration of the numbers:
"O Sons of the Buddha, this Flower Bank Arrayed World-System... is supported by wind-circles as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru."
△ Second, a brief listing of names.
The lowest wind-circle is named "Abiding in Equality" (up to) "Clouds of Platforms of All Jewel Colors and Fragrances. It is called "Abiding in Equality" because:
first, it universally sustains all positions; second, it accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). The remaining names may be understood accordingly.
The winds are all beneath; the jewels are upon the surface of the terraces. They are held from afar by power. △ Third, specifically citing the supreme [wind]:
"O Sons of the Buddha, those wind-circles as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru... [up to] ...are named 'Treasury of Supreme Majestic Radiance'."
Regarding the mention of the supreme one: its superior power is able to sustain the ocean of fragrance; therefore, it is given that name. △ Second, the supported ocean of fragrance:
it is able to sustain the fragrant water ocean adorned with universal light mani-jewels.
It is named thus because mani-jewels emit light that universally illumines all things, adorning the seabed and its shores as well as the fragrant waters of various jewel-hues.
Furthermore, the *ālayavijñāna* is called the "ocean" because its qualities are profound and vast; its continuous flow is called "water" because it is of the nature of momentary change (*kṣaṇika*).
Moreover, the Buddha-nature is called "water," and its distant permeation is called "fragrance" because it is heard but not yet realized. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also says:
Some people smell the fragrance. △ Third, the lotus flowers that emerge:
In this ocean of fragrant water, there is a great lotus named *Vividly Radiant Filament-Fragrance Banner*.
Its filaments emit extraordinary light and also produce a supreme fragrance; because it rises high and subdues [all others], it is given this name. Furthermore, as for what it emits...
The myriad practices are each the awakened nature; therefore, they are called "radiance" (*prabhā*). That they are all able to universally permeate is the meaning of "fragrance.
△ Fourth, the ocean of lands that are sustained.
The Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean resides therein (up to): the lands, oceans, multitudes of trees each have their distinct classifications;
the four directions are even and level, collectively manifesting the overall form; it is pure and firm, revealing its essential nature;

the Diamond Enclosure and so forth specifically clarify what is contained therein, which will be detailed below. This serves as the foundation: first, the mountains; second, the lands; third, the oceans.

The four trees are each separately distinguished, which collectively manifests their manifold adornments; however, one river is omitted here because it will be specifically manifested below, and thus it is briefly indicated here.
Below, there is also a brief verse. △ Second, the verse summary. Now, between the prose (long-form) and the verse summary, there are ten patterns forming five pairs:
namely, presence and absence, expansion and brevity, separation and combination, priority and posteriority—these constitute eight; the ninth is occasional transposition.

In some cases, after a verse has been recited, it is recited again; therefore, the commentary on the verses cannot be treated as a single uniform pattern. One should apply this principle to both preceding and succeeding sections. Briefly, there are four types of examples in this text:
first, the causes from past lives and present conditions, where the prose [of the sūtra] is separated and the verses are combined; second, the characteristics of the fruits achieved.

The Sūtra is extensive while the Verse is concise; the three present conditions of the wind-circle are concise in the Sūtra and extensive in the Verse. Fourth, regarding the mountains, lands, oceans, and trees, they exist in the Sūtra but are absent from the Verse.
The ten verses are divided into two parts: the first two verses concern the characteristics of the superior cause.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One, in the past, throughout all realms of existence... [omitted] ...now in this world there are no defilements."
This explains how causes give rise to effects. △ Second, the remaining verses praise the characteristics of the fruit, in four parts. First, the verse on the wind-circle:
"Emitting great radiance, it dwells pervading space... by the power of former vows, it abides in mid-air."
All of these are sustained by the preceding phrases, while the subsequent phrases are capable of sustaining them. The first half-verse sustains the fruit through the fruit;

the latter verse clarifies both the fruit and the causes that bring it about. The first half constitutes the vow to be free from obstacles, so as to bring about purity; the second half constitutes the vow of unimpededness.
Because it abides in emptiness. △ Second, the verse on the ocean of fragrances:
"Various firm and solid adornment oceans... universally reaching the ten directions with blazing radiance.
Seeking this, one understands the name. △ Third, there are three and a half verses praising the lotus.
"Flames form circles, adorned with exquisite flowers" (up to) "universally responding to the minds of all beings without exception.
The first one and a half verses explain the various radiant filaments, thereby revealing that this flower has jewels as its substance. The next verse explains the meaning of fragrance;
it clarifies this through the Dharma. From within the jewels, Buddhas emerge; the Buddha is the sovereign of the world, just as [fragrance issues forth from the source].

The first explains the meaning of "substance" (*dravya*) as the sense of its fragrance wafting afar; the latter explains the meaning of the "banner" (*dhvaja*). "Manifesting the Buddha" has the meaning of being loftily elevated;

"taming beings" has the meaning of subduing and overcoming. △ Fourth, there are two verses clarifying mastery over the *kṣetra* (buddha-fields), summarizing the aforementioned ocean of supported fields.
All the atoms within the Flower Treasury World (up to) all its adornments emerge from this.

The first verse is sovereign because each [atom] accords with the nature (*dharmatā*); this is the "Gate of Simultaneous Endowment and Correspondence. One should contemplate the mind and the atoms accordingly.

As for the manifestation of Buddhas through the light of jewels, it is because the primary body (*svābhāvikakāya*) and the environment (*bhājanaloka*) are mutually interfused. The subsequent verse concludes by returning to the universal cause.
Therefore, it is able to contain and encompass all. △ Second, the detailed exposition of the arrangement and adornment. This section has six parts. First, the mountain of wheels (*cakravāḍa*).
This is that which is formed by the Master’s own pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), which internally contains and externally guards [virtue]. Within the prose commentary, there are three sections.
First, a general presentation of the basis.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying... [up to] "...dwelling upon the lotus-flower of the Sun-Special-King (*sūryaviśeṣarāja*).
As for the ground upon which the mountain rests—that is, the area surrounding the base of the earth—it is the ground where the Sun-Jewel King (*sūryamaṇirāja*) resides.
Therefore, the old sūtra says: 'He dwells upon the ground of the Lotus-Sun-Jewel-King. There are also those who say: 'Upon the great flower, there is yet another [ground].'"
It seems inconsistent in meaning for this lotus to be that upon which the mountain rests. As for why the ground receives this name:

the previous description of the flower as having "various radiant filaments" (vicitra-prabhā-kesara), and the statement in the verse that "flames form a wheel," as well as the mention of "emitting pure light from among all jewels," clearly show that this flower has jewels as its substance. Thus, it is like a pearl within the solar disc.
The King took it to be a lotus flower; this is a general designation for flowers. △ Second, the specific manifestation of its essence and characteristics:
sandalwood and mani-jewels constitute its body.

Previously, it was taken as "hard and sharp" and merely called *vajra*; now, to clarify its possession of virtues, there are briefly ten characteristics. The first phrase describes the body as a whole form:
the *maṇi* jewel is perfectly luminous, and the *candana* sandalwood is richly fragrant; these are all virtues of the precepts.
The king of majestic jewels forms its peaks;
these mountain peaks are said to rise in solitary loftiness, subduing all evils with their majesty,
while exquisite fragrant maṇi-jewels form its terraces.
Regarding the "mountain-rim" (*parikhā*): there are two ancient interpretations. First, it refers to the curved portion of the mountain;

second, it refers to the mountain’s belly protruding outward like a lion throne, with the crescent moon serving as the rim. According to the subsequent verse, the rim resides at the base of the mountain and serves as its support.
It is established by both the *Jvālā-garbha* and the *Vajra*.

Regarding the conditions for the formation of the mountain, three matters were previously cited, each having its own distinct substance. Now, it is revealed that the *vajra* internally contains flames and light, which pervade and constitute its very substance.
Just as in the world, earth and stone combine to form a mountain, because the *vajra* is all-pervasive, it is called "Gold" (*Kāñcana*).
Regarding the names of the wheels: the upper four represent the perfection of the essential body, while the lower six represent the adornment of external features.
All fragrant waters flow through their midst, [extending] to a net of mani-jewels that hangs down and covers them all around.
They are all situated amidst the mountains; their patterns and manifestations are clear and may be known. △ Third, the conclusion on the inexhaustibility of its virtues:
There are such arrays of exquisite adornments, as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
△ Third, the Verses on the Encircling Mountains consist of ten verses, divided into two parts. The first six concern the physical characteristics and adornments of the mountains;
five of these specifically elaborate upon the preceding [description], while the first verse provides a general summary of the encircling mountains.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The great oceans of worlds are without limit... these arise through the spiritual power of the Tathāgata."
The first phrase is that which is surrounded; the next two phrases are that which surrounds; the final phrase states the reason. Regarding the term "boundless" (*ananta*), there are two meanings:
first, it indicates multiplicity through its general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), and thus it is called "boundless," though in reality it signifies having a limit.

Second, that which lies outside the surrounding mountains is the "limit of the boundless"; because it does not obstruct principle (*li*) while being identical with phenomena (*shi*), it is now described as "boundless."
Regarding "the limit": it is the limit that is limitless, for its unchanging characteristic is itself the principle (*li*).
△ Second, there is one verse summarizing the preceding mountain-rings, the mani-jewel rings, the exquisite fragrance rings, and so forth, up to the pure wheel-enclosures where they abide.
△ Third, one verse on the three realms of existence. This verse describes the substance of the mountain:
"With solid maṇi-jewels as its treasury... (omitted)... both inside and out it is transparent and entirely pure.
△ Fourth, the conditions for the formation of the mountain.
"Accumulated from vajra-maṇis... emitting pure light that universally adorns with beauty.
△ Five [verses], consisting of two stanzas, praise the aforementioned adornments such as water and so forth, as well as the addition of garments and other items.
The streams of fragrant water flow in immeasurable colors (up to): clouds of light shine constantly and perfectly in all directions.

△ Second, four verses distinguish the sovereign and wondrous functions of the mountains, also revealing the non-obstruction between the environment and its inhabitants, which corresponds to the concluding passage of the preceding section.
The immeasurable and boundless great bodhisattvas (up to) the Buddha’s sovereign power may cause it to pervade everywhere.
△ Second, the jeweled ground on the terrace surface. This is that which is accomplished through the meditative concentration of the essence of the mind-nature. The prose section has three parts.
First, indicating its location.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly... [up to] all the great earth within the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains.
△ Second, the specific manifestation of the adornment of the essence and characteristics.
All are composed of vajra, adorned with firmness, and indestructible.

The substance of the first ground is designated as "vajra" and explained as "firm and indestructible. Since the entire ground of the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha) is pervaded by vajra, the site of the supreme bodhi ground penetrates throughout the Flower Treasury.
It is pure and level, without elevations or depressions;
the second stage is equally pure and flat, while the eight lower stages are all adorned with wheels made of mani jewels.
Adorned with precious wheels,
with various jewels as its treasury,
it stores within it a storehouse of jewels.
It is interspersed with various maṇi jewels in the diverse forms of all sentient beings,
alternating with other rare gems;
it is strewn with powdered jewels and carpeted with lotus flowers.
Scattered are powdered jewels; spread are lotus flowers—these two phrases are explicit.
Fragrant-treasury maṇi-jewels are distributed among them;
the precious fragrant-treasury maṇis are distributed therein.
All manner of ornaments pervade like clouds (up to) adorning with every kind of embellishment.
Filled with such ornaments, they are simply called "all ornaments. As for the quantity of these ornaments: they are the adornments of the Buddha-fields of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
As for that which constitutes the adornment, it manifests inexhaustible ornaments.
With exquisite maṇi jewels forming its net (extending to) being arrayed therein like the net of Indra.
It is covered with a jeweled net, adorned with shimmering reflections. What is the purpose of this net? It universally manifests the images of Buddhas. What is the appearance of this net?

It is arranged like the net of Indra (the celestial net). Furthermore, this net of Indra manifests infinitely within itself, thereby perfecting the aforementioned universal manifestation of the Tathāgata’s realm;
thus, each and every individual realm is also inexhaustible. △ Third, the summary.
[The] Conclusion:
"O Sons of the Buddha, this world-ocean of lands possesses such adornments as these, numbering as many as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.

II. Verses in Praise (consisting of ten verses, divided into two parts). The first seven verses further distinguish the preceding [sections] into three; the first four verses correspond to the preceding [section].
Eight lines.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"That ground is level and exceedingly pure... (omitted)... universally covering the earth as an adornment."

The phrase "small and out of order" indicates that there is no superiority or inferiority among those preceding it. The phrases "repeated" or "expanded" indicate that the meanings are not restricted to a single method.
Fearing prolixity, I have not provided a word-for-word correspondence; this may be understood through the general sense. △ Second, the verse on the ornaments like clouds.
Dense clouds arise and spread, filling the ten directions... (up to) ...within this jewel, there is nothing that is not seen.
△ Thirty-one verses. These eulogize the Indra’s Net.
All the mani-jewels possessed by that ground... (up to) ...all lands likewise enter within it.
This means that since one jewel already encompasses all things, the atoms within those lands likewise encompass all things;
this is the principle of "layer upon layer" (*zhongchong*). △ Third, the summary:
"The Flower Treasury World-realm adorned with wondrous jewels... [omitted] ...all such divine transformations."

The summary of their respective affiliations: the first verse summarizes the affiliation with the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); the next summarizes the affiliation with the power of the Buddha;
and the final one summarizes the person capable of knowing [this]. *Da fangguang fo huayan jing shu*, Scroll Fifteen.
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Fascicle Sixteen (Entering the Second Half of the Eighth Scripture),
composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang,
with annotations on the scripture recorded by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.

△ Third, regarding the fragrant oceans upon the ground: since the aforementioned great ocean is the *ālayavijñāna*, this now clarifies that within the "flower of the mind" (*cittakusuma*), all seeds are subsumed.
Since each and every seed is not separate from the ocean of the *ālaya*, there are thus many fragrant oceans.
Nevertheless, each one is endowed with the qualities of its nature, and thus all possess adornments. The prose section is divided into two parts. First, the general enumeration of the number:
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying... [up to] "fragrant water oceans as numerous as the atoms of Buddha-fields."

According to the subsequent descriptions of the world-systems (*kṣetra-vyuha*) and the Sanskrit manuscript, both contain "ten unspeakable numbers" (*daśānabhilāpyāni*). Here, ten characters are missing;
this is likely either an omission by the translator or an error in transcription. The same applies to the section where the systems are subsequently enumerated.
2. Specifically Revealing the Adornments: According to the subsequent summary, it should state that each fragrant ocean possesses a certain number of adornments.

[The section on] "Adornment" is omitted in the current text. If one were to extract the meaning according to the text, the term "all" refers to all oceans, collectively having wonderful jewels as their floor and so forth.
There are twenty phrases in total; the first ten clarify the essential nature and characteristics of the ocean.
1. The bottom; 2. The banks; 3. The net; 4. The water; 5. The flowers; 6. The sandbars; 7. The sound; 8. The light; 9. The manifestation of supernatural powers by the people who guard it;
10. The extensive conclusion that is inexhaustible.
The entire bottom is adorned with all manner of exquisite jewels, such that all adornments appear therein.
The adornments of the stairways consist of various jewels; all these are the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
The first verse describes the steps and railings; the next verse, the groves of trees; the third, the blooming flowers;

the fourth, the banners and insignia; the fifth, the excellence of the city; and the sixth, the walls and pavilions. "Liao" (繚) means to encircle or wind around. The seventh verse concerns the adornments dedicated to the Buddha:
first, the causes from the past; second, the manifest power. The fragrant rivers between the four seas correspond to each individual thought-moment.
This is the correspondence of time; it is the flow of merit. The prose section also has three parts. First, the enumeration of the number:
"At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying... [until] the river of fragrant water circulates by turning to the right."
△ Second, the identification of the ornaments.
All have diamond for their banks;
since there is no distinction among the banks of any of the rivers, it is said that "all have [diamond for their banks]."
It is adorned with pure light maṇi-jewels;
its shores are embellished with pearls,
and it constantly manifests clouds of precious-colored light from all the Buddhas.
It manifests the radiance and colors of the Buddhas,
as well as the vocal sounds of all sentient beings,
producing diverse and varied tones.
All the places where that river has eddies and whirlpools, as well as their various forms, all emerge from within it.
The eddies cast reflections;
nets of *maṇi* jewels and clusters of precious bells adorn it.
A network of bells hangs down and covers it;
all the adornments of every ocean of worlds appear within it,
collectively manifesting manifold splendors.
Maṇi-jewel clouds cover its summit (extending to) all the miraculous activities of the Buddhas.
Jewel clouds cover the top, manifesting the holy reliance and the primary realm.
Furthermore, they emit wondrous sounds extolling the names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
They also emit wondrous sounds,
and from within that fragrant water, clouds of light-flames of all kinds of jewels constantly emerge in an uninterrupted succession.
The water surges forth as clouds of light, inexhaustible throughout long kalpas. △ Third, the conclusion regarding the extensive number:
If explained in detail, each and every river possesses adornments equal in number to the atoms within an ocean of worlds.

Having already circled the small seas and small rivers, there still remain adornments as numerous as the atoms within a sea of lands (*kṣetrasamudra*), which further manifest the significance of the boundary-marking;
these are not merely matters of physical phenomena, but all represent the non-obstruction between the one and the many. △ Second, the verse summary.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Pure fragrant streams fill the great rivers, ...until... The reflections of all Buddhas appear with brilliant clarity."
The first half-verse praises the diamond nature of the banks; the next one and a half verses praise the jewel-adorned banks;

the third [set of] three verses praises the clouds of light and vocal sounds; the subsequent three [sets] all praise the whirlpools and the reflection of images; and seven verses praise the hanging canopies of net-patterned tassels.

Furthermore, all the adornments appear in their entirety. The preceding section manifested the adornment of the physical environment; this section explains the practice of the path. Eight verses manifest the Buddha’s reliance (the environment) and the supported (the Buddha).
Nine verses describe the emanation of wondrous sounds. Ten verses describe the clouds of light emerging from the waters. △ Fifth, the Flower Forests between the Rivers.
The prose commentary has three parts; first, the general introduction.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly, saying: [omitted] "all were adorned with various kinds of exquisite jewels.
△ Second, the specific manifestation:
each [lotus] has as many petals as there are atoms in four continents, [omitted] "with rows of various jewel trees following one another in succession."
Two distinct matters are specifically revealed: namely, the lotus and the tree; one each for water and land. In reality, there are many such matters.

However, this particular section differs slightly in its literary structure; rather than listing ten matters to manifest their inexhaustibility, it mentions only two, thereby illustrating their multiplicity through successive progression—from the first white lotus to the final jewel tree.
From each and every tree, there constantly emerge all manner of *maṇi* jewel-kings that fill the ground.

As for these jewel-trees, they produce five kinds of functions: first, the emergence of clouds of adornment; second, the radiance of the jewel-kings; third, the pervasive filling with the fragrance of flowers;
fourth, the production of sounds that expound the Dharma; and fifth, the raining of jewels upon the ground. Within these five, there are both general and specific [functions].
Distinct. The former is general while the latter is specific. There are eight distinct items that pervade the three worlds, namely:
from the Lotus-Mouth Cakra-Maṇi-Ratna-Rāja (up to) the Universal-Downward-Spreading-Light-Network-Cloud Maṇi-Ratna-Rāja.
The sixth stage above manifests the vessel.
It manifests the mani-jewel king of the spiritual transformations of all Buddhas;
this is the single manifestation of perfect enlightenment.
The King of Maṇi Jewels manifests the ocean of karmic retributions of all sentient beings.

This single manifestation of the world of sentient beings displays the retribution of evil karma through such things as the forest of sword-leaves, while the celestial wish-fulfilling trees display the retribution of virtuous karma.
Within the groves of men and women, those born in the morning that fall by evening—all these are the ocean of karmic retribution.
There are as many such [trees] as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds.

To conclude the section on the trees raining jewels: since there are already as many [trees] as there are atoms in an ocean of lands, the same applies to the four preceding categories—clouds and so forth—each being likewise.
Within a single tree, there are already the various adornments of many oceans of lands. Next, following the example of the *pundarīka* [lotus]:
The flowers are likewise identical to the trees. Each flower and each tree contains as many atoms as there are in the four continents; every single one is thus.
Just as with these flowers and trees, there should further be objects numbering as many as the atoms in an ocean of lands;
therefore, they constitute an inexhaustible adornment. △ Third, the summary.
The ground between those two rivers of fragrant water is each and every one fully endowed with such adornments.
△ Second, the verses in non-sequential order. This section is divided into three parts. First, the jewel trees.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The ground is level and utterly pure... [omitted] ...all of which he expounds extensively through his ten powers."
△ Second, the white lotus:
the *maṇi* jewel, the wondrous *puṇḍarīka*, (until) all manifest inexhaustible radiance.
△ Third, there are three verses praising the cause of the adornment.
All the adornments existing throughout the three periods of time (up to) are entirely pure according to their respective inclinations.
This is due to the power of the Buddha; his essence and function are unimpeded, appearing while remaining eternally as they are. However, these three verses have many underlying intentions:
the first verse concerns the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), the second concerns the Perfectly Awakened One’s wisdom, and the third concerns sentient beings. To clarify this one [point]...

Within a single phenomenon, the adornments of all three worlds are manifested; the text merely abbreviates these descriptions. Furthermore, first it clarifies that a single fruit can manifest [these adornments];
next, it applies this by analogy to all adornments; finally, it clarifies that every atom is likewise so. This proceeds from the concise to the extensive, and from the coarse to the subtle.

Moreover, first it clarifies the power of the Buddha; next, it reveals the power of his vows; and lastly, the power of his responsiveness to the inclinations of beings. Furthermore, first is the fruit...
Regarding the subsequent causes: may they encompass both cause and effect. Furthermore, regarding the initial [self] and the subsequent [other]: may they encompass both self and other.
Moreover, the first clarifies that essence is non-essence, for its substance is fundamentally unborn; the next clarifies that marks are non-marks, for their manifestation has no coming or going;

and the final clarifies that while not destroying marks, each is seen differently, thereby manifesting the adornments of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*). All these are beyond words and transcend thought.

This cannot be sought through ordinary sentiment. △ Sixth, the concluding summary of the adornments. Although the preceding sections have spoken of adornments, they have not yet exhausted the subject.
Now, the individual realms are collectively revealed; whether explicitly stated or not, each is fully endowed with adornments of merit as numerous as the atoms within oceans of lands.
Therefore, the text says: "All realms. The prose section consists of two parts.
First, the heading indicates that the adornments are difficult to fathom:
"At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... [up to] the inconceivable adornment of the world-ocean.
Second, the inquiry and explanation of the reasons for this.
Why is this? O Sons of the Buddha, [it is] adorned by pure merits.
The phrase "pure merits" contains two meanings: first, it refers to the adornment by numerous fruits, which are themselves the pure merits;
second, it refers to each individual fruit being adorned, having arisen from many causes of pure merit. This is viewed from the perspective of the cause in relation to the fruit.
This should be understood through four permutations: namely, many causes producing a single effect, one cause producing many effects, and so forth.

Therefore, with respect to each individual phenomenon, it is called "inconceivable. Thus, a verse says: "It arises solely from the Tathāgata’s past conduct, through his supernormal powers and the force of his vows"—this refers to the cause.
As for the adornment of the result, there are briefly five aspects. The first is to cause [the multitude] to be pervasive.
First, it is given to all. Second, it is made constant, so that there is never any lack or exhaustion. Third, it is made sublime, pleasing the minds of all beings.

Fourth, it accords with the nature [of reality], being without birth and without marks. Fifth, it is sovereign, melting into seamless integration. These five meanings are fully contained within the verses;
because they encompass these five aspects, it is called "inconceivable. Moreover, cause and effect are mutually identical. II. The verses contain:
Tenth. This is divided into two major sections. First, the excellence of the adornment and function of the fruit. Within this, first is the specific explanation of the adornment and function.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to reiterate this meaning, observed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
In every place within this ocean of lands, [it reaches] throughout all oceans of lands, pervading them entirely.
△ Second, the conclusion on the conditions for manifestation:
All manifested Buddhas are like illusions, [appearing] thus in all lands.
△ Third, regarding the many types of fetters:
all matters concerning the Tathāgata’s sovereign supernormal powers (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna), up to [the attainment of] everything, are seen within the jewels.
△ Second, regarding the correspondence between cause and effect.
All the various transformations throughout the ten directions arise from the power of spiritual penetrations and vows.
Because they take the practice of vows and spiritual penetrations as their cause, one obtains the fruit of transformations that are like reflections in a mirror.
If there are those who can cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra— up to universally manifesting their bodies to purify all buddha-fields—
they take the supreme wisdom of Samantabhadra as the cause, and thereby attain the fruit of purifying all buddha-fields within a single atom.
From inconceivable billions of great eons down to a single kṣaṇa, [the Buddha] can manifest everything within that instant.
Because taking long-term proximity to spiritual friends as the cause, he attains the fruit of sudden manifestation in a single kṣaṇa.
The lands of all Buddhas are like empty space... (up to) ...they abide therein by the power of their original vows.
This reveals the intent of the pure cause, so that others may emulate and practice it. The first half concerns the realm of wisdom:
"adornment is non-adornment" refers to the land of self-enjoyment, which is all-pervasive and peerless; it is the land of *dharmatā*, whose essential nature is unborn. Both of these are non-existent.

The marks [of the Buddha’s body] are such that his compassion is perfectly responsive; his adornment is an adornment without adornment, yet his adornment pervades the entire Dharma-realm; his dwelling is a dwelling without dwelling, yet he eternally abides within the lands.

△ Third, the network of lands sustained [by the Buddha], which explains the terms "world" and "realm" in the title of this chapter. Furthermore, whereas the preceding section clarified the fundamental land (*mūla-kṣetra*), the present section distinguishes the derivative worlds (*anta-kṣetra*);
thus, it encompasses both the defiled and the pure. The text has three parts: first, the announcement to the assembly and the granting of permission to speak.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed [the assembly] (up to): "What kinds of worlds exist? I shall now describe them.
△ Second, the dual presentation of the two chapters:
"O Children of the Buddha, these unspeakable (up to) worlds as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields."

The two chapters designated here refer to the world-systems (*kṣetra*) and the world-system arrays (*kṣetraprakāra*). Now, since the world-system arrays depend upon the ocean of world-systems, and all world-systems depend upon the world-system arrays, their relative breadth and narrowness can be understood.
From what is the name [of these chapters] derived? It is intended to clarify that worlds are boundless, employing skillful means to manifest their multiplicity.
Therefore, this name is established. It is called a "seed" (*gotra*) because many worlds are accumulated together in one place, encompassing all various categories.
Such types are further numerous, profound, vast, and boundless; therefore, they are called an "ocean" (*sāgara*).
It is like a multitude of fish being gathered to form a single kind, while fish, dragons, turtles, and tortoises, along with mountains, springs, and islands, constitute many different kinds.
All of these are entirely contained within one great ocean. As for the statement that worlds are infinite:

beyond the oceans there are further oceans, and these oceans are without end. If such types have no distinct substance and are formed by aggregating the realms (*dhātu*), why does the subsequent text state that they possess physical form?
Although the name "type" is established based on their category, what prevents this type from having its own distinct existence?
As for its substance (*tattva*): it is like many bee-holes that together form a single hive; how could this hive not have its own distinct substance?
The previous mention of fish and dragons was merely a partial metaphor. Following the latter sense, it may also be termed "lineage" (*gotra*).

Depending upon this lineage, one is able to produce the world, just as depending upon a single stalk of grain, there are many grains. The old scriptures refer to this as "nature" (*prakṛti*), which generally emphasizes the former sense.
Regarding this meaning, fearing that it might be confused with the essential nature (*svabhāva*), it has been changed to "seed" (*bīja*).

As for the statement that there are "unspeakable [numbers]," according to the subsequent text, both the fragrant oceans and the seeds each have ten unspeakable [numbers]. This is also present in the Sanskrit original; the word "ten" (*daśa*) has simply been omitted here.

This is mostly due to errors in transcription. △ Third, the extensive explanation of the two chapters, in two parts. First, a general clarification of the differences among the world-systems (*kṣetra-vyuha*).
Regarding the explanation of the chapter on world-systems, in two parts. First, the prose section, in two parts. First, the listing of the ten gates.

O Sons of the Buddha, those world-systems within the ocean of worlds—though these ten gateways differ in their specific world-system types—all of them remain inseparable from the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha) upon which they depend; therefore, it is said "within the ocean of worlds.
The ten matters enumerated here are entirely different when compared with those in the Chapter on Accomplishment (*Siddhi-parivarta*), as the latter applies universally to all [worlds].

The Ocean. This clarifies all the world-system arrays (*kṣetrajāla*) within a single ocean. When viewed individually, they may exist or not exist in relation to one another; they possess the causes and conditions for their arising;
they are purified, Buddhas appear therein, and they endure through kalpas and undergo transformations. That which exists here may be absent there;

their spatial boundaries, their rows and entries, and the five factors such as their sustaining power—these may exist there while being absent here. Their bases of support, their physical forms, and their adornments...
The formal arrangement is no different; the names for "this" and "that" are identical, appearing interchangeably before and after, totaling fifteen instances.

All of these manifest the ten [perfections], collectively expressing their inexhaustibility. Where there are differences, they reveal the manifold aspects of the meaning; where there are similarities, they prevent confusion with those that are entirely distinct. Why is this so?
Because while the former possesses [the elements] and the latter lacks them, the preceding section provides a general clarification, establishing the cause and effect, whereas in this section...

This is the formal analysis. As for which world it is, this is because it is that upon which [the world] depends and abides; other points may be inferred accordingly. However, as it is the same as what preceded, it has already been explained as before.
Since it does not concern my present task, I shall now explain it.
Each abides according to its own [place], each has its own shape, and each has its own essential nature.
The first three are the same as before;
each has its own location.

If its spatial extent were complete, it would pervade the entire Dharma-realm such that there is nowhere it does not exist; yet it is neither identical to the triple world nor separate from the triple world.
If considered according to its appropriate locations, throughout the ten directions, it is designated by different names based on whether one faces toward it or turns away from it.
Each enters individually;
they enter by way of the gate. Regarding the dharma-gates, this refers to the three liberations. Furthermore, they manifest mutual entry without coming or going.
Each is individually adorned,
as previously described;
each has its own distinct boundaries.
In terms of phenomena (*dharma*), they vary according to circumstances, as their breadth and narrowness differ. In terms of the Buddha’s domain, it is boundless throughout the ten directions;
each individual array constitutes a path, which can be understood through phenomena. In terms of the Dharma, it refers to great mindfulness, wisdom, and practice as the pathways for wandering.
Each is without distinction, as before;
each is sustained by the power of empowerment.
That is to say, food can cause one to abide; this is in terms of the Dharma. It is sustained by the vast flavor of the Dharma and the joy of bliss.
Furthermore, these [qualities] emerge reciprocally, as they manifest the inclusion of the eighteen perfections within the fifteen perfections of a Buddha’s pure land.
Regarding the "eighteen," these are: color, shape, dimension, location, cause, fruit, principal [ruler], retinue, assistants, attendants, sustenance, activities, and the gathering of benefits.
Fearlessness, dwelling place, pathways for roaming, vehicles, gates, and supports—how are these subsumed? These constitute the causal conditions;
that is, the perfection of causes. Dwelling refers to the support. Shape corresponds to color-form (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*). As for substance, it subsumes two kinds.
First, it encompasses manifest color (*varṇa*), because its essential nature consists of the radiance of the seven treasures. Second, it encompasses the fulfillment of results;

the various results corresponding to different types of beings can be understood as being transformations produced by the pure consciousness associated with the Buddha’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).

Therefore, the preceding verse says: "Alternatively, a single moment of mind universally manifests as its essence. Third, regarding adornment, it encompasses three aspects, namely: first, it encompasses abiding.
First, the dwelling: the Tathāgata’s adornments serve as the place of residence. Second, the gathering of assistants: because of the adornment of bodhisattvas.

Third, the gathering of retinues: because there are other assemblies. Regarding the three types of pure gathering: first, the gathering of activities, which refers to performing what is beneficial for sentient beings;
second, the gathering of benefit, which refers to manifesting liberation and extinguishing their afflictions and calamities.
Third is the fearlessness of gathering [beings], which means being free from calamities within and free from external terrors. Herein, based on abiding, two perfections are gathered:

first, the perfection of the leader; second, the perfection of the vehicle, as it is said that there is but one vehicle (*ekayāna*), and so forth. This constitutes the delimitation of its spatial extent.
The two names are identical. "Array" (*paṅkti*) refers to the path; "entry" (*praveśa*) refers to the gate. "Sustaining power" (*baladhāraṇa*) means maintenance (*upastambha*).

Among the eighteen [attributes], there is no mention of abiding for an eon (*kalpasthiti*) or transformation (*pariṇāma*); however, since these are semantically equivalent to the "fruition" (*phala*) and are subsumed under "activity" (*karma*), they may also be established as twenty perfections (*sampad*), which does not contradict reason.
This is because abiding for an eon means reaching the end of the future, and transformation refers to the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata.
The mastery of transformations is the universal purification and transformation of the oceans of worlds; this is the meaning of "perfection" (*pariniṣpanna*).

Although the term "without distinction" (*nirviśeṣa*) does not appear in that text, it is precisely because of this [mastery] that perfection is revealed. All other [descriptions] are according to the circumstances, which is why it says "each and every.
If there is no difference, how can it be said that they are "each and every"? This is because the matters that are without distinction are of many kinds. If one were to...
These ten [aspects] may also be subsumed within the ten [aspects] of the "Chapter on Accomplishment" (*Siddhi-paṭala*); however, fearing excessive prolixity, they are not detailed here.
Furthermore, within each of the preceding sections, many perfections are fully present; as each is integrated and subsumed [within the others], this system differs from other schools.

II. Extensive Explanation According to the Gates: Only three are explained—namely, the basis, the abode, the shape, and the essential nature. Although the remaining seven are treated briefly, their meanings...
The above has been explained. Now, the first section is divided into two parts. First, the enumeration:
"O Sons of the Buddha, this world [system]... (up to) ... rests upon the ocean of mani-jewel kings of the voices of all Buddhas."
△ Second, the summary:
If these were explained in detail, they would be as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds.
△ Second, the shapes: Part one lists twenty kinds.
O Sons of the Buddha, those various world-systems (up to and including) some that take the form of various ornaments,

or those that take the form of revolving shapes— which refers to forms that fold, crumple, move back and forth— and those that take the form of altars— which refers to altars constructed by piling up earth.
The ground was cleared to form a leveled altar (*śmaśāna*). *Khaḷaka* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "bamboo basket.
△ Regarding the subsequent summary of the different counts of atoms: if explained in detail, they are as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
△ III. The Threefold Nature. Part 2. First, the enumeration.
"O Sons of the Buddha, those [world-systems] have as their essence all world-seeds (up to) pure sounds;
they are also of twenty kinds. The first ten are material forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*); the latter ten are sounds (*śabda*). The interpretation of this assembly is as before. △ Second, the conclusion.
If these were explained in detail, they would number as many as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
△ Second, the Verses of Response consist of ten verses, divided into six sections; the first verse describes one stage.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The world-systems are firm and wonderfully adorned... (omitted) ...some abide upon seas of fragrance."
△ Second, there is one verse concerning their shapes, arrays, and abodes.
[It describes] the forms of Mount Sumeru, the cities, trees, and mandalas (up to) how they are each individually arrayed and established.
△ Three verses on the essential nature:
"Some have a nature that is pure radiance" (up to) "the sound of the Buddha's merits is likewise.
△ Four verses on the three matters.

The various distinct gateways of each world-system (kṣetra-vyuha), extending to the peerless and immeasurable and pervading everywhere—this refers to the entry point indicated by the first two lines of the verse. The subsequent line concerns the location, and so forth, as adorned by the four lines.
In the remaining two stanzas, there is the fundamental characteristic of the vast world-systems, namely their boundaries, whether broad or narrow, and how they mutually interpenetrate one another.
The verse introduces the theme. In the first stanza, the many enter into the one; in the latter stanza, the one and the many mutually enter one another.

All enter, yet there is no entering. To enter would destroy dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); not to enter would destroy its inherent function. Furthermore, it is precisely by way of non-entry that one is able to enter.
Moreover, because the essence is fundamentally empty, there is neither coming nor entering; because the appearances are not destroyed, they remain as they originally were.
No difference. Because the nature (svabhāva) fuses with the phenomena (lakṣaṇa), they are able to enter into one another. △ Fifth, the verse on non-difference:
"Within the atoms of all lands... all sentient beings are fully tamed."
This means that because the sensory objects and the Buddha-ocean are equal and without distinction. △ Sixth, the verse on the empowerment of power:
"The Buddha-body pervades all lands... universally transforming all sentient beings."
Both the principal and the attendant [elements] are sustained by spiritual power. The words "universally transforming" include the flavor of the Dharma as well. **2.

Specifically Explaining the Fragrant Oceans of Buddha-lands.** To explain these two chapters together: it means that the fragrant oceans depend upon the ocean of lands, the land-divisions depend upon the fragrant oceans, and all lands depend upon the land-divisions.
The prose section is divided into three parts; first, a general enumeration of what the various oceans depend upon.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva again addressed the great assembly... [omitted] ...arranged like the net of Indra.

Although the preceding sections have merely indicated the world-systems (*kṣetra*) and the two chapters on the worlds themselves, within the descriptions of their locations it is consistently stated that they "rest upon the oceans.
Therefore, the number of these oceans is enumerated. This Ocean of Many Fragrances is situated upon the ground of the Ocean of Worlds; thus, it is called the "basis" (*āśraya*).

Regarding the phrase "like the net of Indra" (*indrājāla*): its general distribution resembles a chariot wheel. As for its specific characteristics, it refers to the net of Indra’s palace, formed by threading celestial pearls.
A single large pearl is placed at the center; next, pearls of successively smaller size are threaded through and encircle it.
In this manner, they continue to alternate and surround one another, winding around for hundreds of thousands of turns. Whether above, below, or in the four directions—
[The faces] face each other. Viewed from all four corners, the rows and ranks are perfectly aligned.

Although this Fragrant Sea is now situated upon the surface of the earth, its distribution is similar [to the celestial array], and it further carries the meaning of "interpenetrating layers. Therefore, it is said to be "like" [that].

△ Second, the specific enumeration of the various seas and lands. The text is divided into three parts: first, the examination of the central sea; second, the examination of the right [sea]; [and third, the examination of the left sea].
[This section] revolves around the ten oceans (*daśa-samudra*). It subsequently clarifies the oceans governed by these ten oceans.

However, each of the ten oceans governs oceans as numerous as the atoms within unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra-rajas*). Taken collectively, there are unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields multiplied by ten;
yet when explained in sequential order, there are only one hundred and eleven oceans, the remainder being indicated by abbreviation. Now, first, the central [ocean]:

The first ocean is divided into two. From the Ocean of Radiant Fragrance, flowers emerge. This constitutes the third [element] for upholding the world-system (*kṣetradhātu*). First, regarding the name of the fragrant ocean:
"O Sons of the Buddha, this most central fragrant-water ocean (extending to) has a base of mani-king banners."
Because it emits light through many flowers, and because the practice of the Bodhisattva serves as its cause. △ Second, the names of the flowers are given:
there emerges a great lotus named "Adorned with the King of All Fragrant Maṇis."
This is because it is adorned with fragrant *maṇi* jewels; furthermore, it arises from the base of the *maṇi*.
In terms of the Dharma, it is accomplished through the perfect clarity of the myriad practices (*sādhana*). Since the ocean can possess flowers, it receives the name "Flower";
since the flowers depend upon the ocean, it takes the name "Ocean Base. △ Third, the name of the world-system (*kṣetra-vyuha*).
There is a world-system that abides upon it (up to: having all ornaments as its substance.
In terms of the phenomenal aspect (*vastu*), this is because the light of jewels shines afar; in terms of the dharma-aspect (*dharma*), this world-system is precisely the seed contained therein.
Each and every one of them possesses the meaning of the great light of wisdom universally illuminating the dharma-realm; this is because their inherent virtues mutually adorn one another.
△ Second, the worlds supported [by these lands] has three parts. First, a general enumeration of the great number.
There are worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields arrayed therein.
△ Second, the specific description of the central [array]: there are twenty tiers of vast primary fields.

According to the headings and the concluding summary, these all number as many as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields; however, the current text lists only the number of atoms in nineteen Buddha-fields. This is because...
There are twenty tiers. Those capable of encircling the stūpa number as many as the atoms within two hundred and ten Buddha-fields.
The twenty tiers shall be explained in detail below, divided into twenty sections. In the first tier, there are seven matters.
At its very bottom is a world-system (extending) to the limit of the adamantine ornamented radiant wheel (*vajra-alaṃkāra-prabhāsa-cakra*).
"Limit" (*pratiṣṭhā*) refers to the boundary upon which the world-system rests, such as the adamantine base (*vajratala*).
It rests upon various jewel-maṇi flowers.
As for its resting place, according to this name, it is largely the same as the lotus upon which the world-systems (kṣetra) rest;
however, the ancient commentary states that above the flowers produced from the aforementioned boundless sea of fragrance, there is yet another flower that supports this single world-realm.

As illustrated by the various tiers above, each has its own distinct support; therefore, this explanation is given. Consider how it would not be contradictory for the very lowest tier to rest upon the collective lotus.
Its shape is like that of a maṇi jewel.
As for its shape: it is said that the mani-jewel has eight facets; it is neither square nor round. Thus it differs from the eight corners [of the lower tiers].
Clouds of all manner of jewel-flower adornments completely cover its summit.
Above, it was covered by a retinue of worlds as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, which were surrounded on all sides, ablaze, variously established, and variously adorned.
The Buddha’s name is Pure Eye, Lamp Free from Defilement.
In his original realm, the Buddha is named Free from the Defilement of the Two Obstructions; his eye of wisdom is pure, illuminating the world like a lamp.

Yet the virtues of a Buddha are boundless; each [name] follows a single specific meaning. From the second tier upward, there may be eight matters, namely: adding the fact that he is distant from this place.

Because they are proximate, there may be nine matters; this is due to the addition of the term "pure" (*viśuddha*). By analogy, if this term were absent, it would encompass both the defiled and the pure.
Above this, the number of lands gradually increases for the retinues; the various matters in the intermediate layers can be understood by inference.

Clouds of Brahma-sound mani-kings cover its summit... (down to) the Buddha named Fragrance-Light Joy-Power Ocean.

Regarding the statement that "its form is like empty space," Jingfayun states: "The sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna alike teach that the essence of empty space is devoid of form or substance and possesses no visible characteristics.
That it is now said to have form is an error resulting from a scribal corruption of the text. In the Sanskrit original, it says 'three' (tri)."
*Maṇḍala* (circular), *divyabhavana* (celestial palace), *gagana* (space), *alaṃkāra* (ornamented canopy/covering), *saṃsthāna* (shape).
In the reversed script, *saṃsthāna* (shape) should be placed before *maṇḍala* (circular), and *gagana* (space) placed above *divyabhavana* (celestial palace).
Then, they are joined together as follows: "Its shape is circular, resembling the celestial palaces of the gods dwelling in space."
These are ornaments used to cover its top. Jingfa’s [interpretation] is correct and possesses profound logical consistency.
Now, I shall explain it according to the sutras; there is likewise reason for this. That is to say, although space has no form, it is spoken of in accordance with worldly convention.

According to secular texts, space is designated as "heaven" (tian), and heaven is described as a circular vault whose shape is like a griddle. Therefore, when the books speak of heaven, they describe its circumference and expanse.
The plains. This is also as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "The Brahmā King is the father of sentient beings," which is likewise a conventional expression.
From [the worlds numbering] as many as the atoms in thirteen buddha-fields (up to) the World-Honored One, Vairocana Tathāgata.

Above this, passing through worlds as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field (until one reaches) the Buddha named Supreme Sound Pervading the Dharma Realm.

Above this, passing through worlds as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field, [one reaches a world] whose shape is like that of the svastika (卍).
Regarding its shape being like a svastika, Jingfa says: *Śrīvatsa* is not originally a letter; it is rather the mark of one who possesses virtue.
A direct translation is "Auspicious Ocean-Cloud. Its manifold virtues are as deep and vast as the ocean, and its benefit to sentient beings is like a cloud.
Since antiquity, the Tripiṭaka has erroneously translated *lakṣaṇa* as "evil *kṣara*," thereby using "xiāng" (相) as the character for it; thus, it has been a mistake.
However, these marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are regarded as the accumulation of all auspicious and myriad virtues. Consequently, they are designated as "myriad" (*wan*);
this is intended as a linguistic abbreviation that implies the full meaning, and should properly be called "myriad marks" (*wanxiāng*).
The Clouds of Fragrant Water-Seas of Maṇi Trees... [up to] the Buddha named Invincible Power Universal Radiance Banner. △ Sixteenth Layer.

Summary of the Remainder. Herein, it is not merely a summary of the number; it also collectively reveals the basis for the preceding text.
Regarding the section on "Abiding" and so forth, the text is divided into four parts. First is the summary of the total number:
"O Sons of the Buddha, these [worlds] throughout the ten directions... [up to] as many vast worlds as there are atoms in a buddha-field."

This refers back to the original world-system (*kṣetra-vyuha*). As for how many [worlds] are included therein, the world-system thus delimited must certainly be the central world-system (*maulakṣetra*), because the subsequent text specifies this as the "unspeakable Buddha-field" (*anabhilāpya-buddhakṣetra*) and it is further encircled by two additional layers.

Within the vertical interval above, there are nineteen Buddha-fields, yet they are described as being "unspeakable" because they are discussed from a lateral perspective; otherwise, would that not be the case?

At the very bottom of a single world-system (*kṣetra-vyuha*) is a single sovereign world-system (*adhipati-kṣetra*). Thus, one should know that as previously described, when discussing sovereign world-systems both horizontally and vertically, they are unspeakably many.
Therefore, the text concludes by stating their location: "and they are situated within the seas of fragrant water."
Reflect upon this. △ Second, the summary of the categories of forms has three parts. First, a general listing of the ten gates:
each with its respective basis of abiding, each with its respective shape (up to) each with its respective power-maintenance surrounding them on all sides.
Since it is stated that they "surround" on all sides, it is clearly understood that they extend outward. II. The detailed explanation of the ten gates:
namely, worlds in the shape of revolving forms numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, up to worlds in the shape of gateways numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.

Regarding the shapes of the worlds, there are eighteen phrases. Compared with the shapes of the previous world-systems (*kṣetra-vyuha*), those shaped like Mount Sumeru and those shaped like ornaments are omitted;
all others are entirely the same. The only difference here is that these are categorized according to the worlds themselves. △ Third, the conclusion summarizing the total number.
There are thus as many such [worlds] as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
△ Third, the conclusion regarding the retinue:
Each of these individual worlds is surrounded by ten Buddha-fields (up to) vast worlds encircling them on all sides.
However, there are two layers of primary and secondary [realms]. Each of these refers to the aforementioned number of atoms of unspeakable realms.

If one looks back at the preceding text, the primary lands extend directly upward with their surrounding numbers gradually increasing; here, they are described in terms of their general characteristics, hence it is said that each has "ten times the atoms of a land.
Furthermore, this is intended to manifest the meaning of inexhaustibility.
In each of these worlds, there are further as many worlds as there are atoms [in a world] serving as their retinue.
The aforementioned statement contains two meanings: first, it refers collectively to the number of the surrounding and the surrounded as previously described.
It encircles one world-system. To avoid excessive elaboration, it says "as above. Second, "as above" likewise uses ten buddha-fields as that which performs the encircling.
According to this [interpretation], it seems the translator’s phrasing is prolix while the principle remains obscure;
why not simply say that each [field] further contains a number of buddha-fields equal to the dust motes? If one follows the former meaning, then the translator’s skill is evident.
△ Fourth, indicating the location.
Regarding all the worlds thus described (up to) those surrounding this sea, within these rivers of fragrant water:
"in" refers to the Fragrant Ocean itself; the phrase "and being in the fragrant river" clearly indicates that they extend laterally.
(Entering the Ninth Sūtra). △ Second, explaining the ten oceans of right-turning spirals. These are the ten oceans surrounding the Ocean of Subtle Flower Radiance (*Sūkṣmapuṣpābhāsamudra*).

next, there is a fragrant water ocean named "Stainless Flame Treasury" (extending to) having the "roaring sound of the bodhisattva practices" as its essence.

His body is all-pervasive, equal to the true *dharmadhātu*.

The true realm can cause material forms to interpenetrate with it; within the dust-motes and hairs of the dharma-realm, each layer completely pervades all others, such that all buddha-fields are manifested as arising therein.
Second, the characteristic of compassion: not abandoning causal practice, there is nothing that is not produced;
one proceeds to all sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and reaches their respective locations.

He approaches [the Buddha], who is endowed with boundless, wondrous, and pure colors.
These four color-attributes are serene and eternally abiding; thus they are called "wondrous colors. Since every color is boundless, it is said that he is "endowed" with them.
There is no substantial fruit; this is called purity.
Nothing in all the worlds can eclipse it. It possesses five superior characteristics:
its physical form overwhelms the great assembly; its majestic virtue strikes terror into the hosts of Māras; and its powers and fearlessness are perfected.
How could it be outshone?
It is endowed with all the marks of jewels, each distinct and luminous.
With the six noble marks and infinite jewel-marks, it is perfectly bright and precious, surpassing even the noble emperors; therefore, it is called "distinctly clear."
All palaces manifest their images therein.
This is the seventh mark of correspondence: without moving, it appears everywhere like an image in a mirror, such that all sentient beings are able to see it with their own eyes.
Eighth is the mark of non-obstruction: when there is a response, this vision arises; mountains and rivers do not obstruct it.
Boundless transformation-buddhas emerge from his body.
Ninth is the mark of transformation: transformation flows from the Real; its source is without difference.
Various colored lights fill the Dharma-realm;
the ten auspicious marks and the radiance of the body’s wisdom-light universally resound throughout the world. These supreme virtues above are largely the same as at the beginning of the sutra.

Just as [the Buddhas] appear and sit within this Pure Radiant Fragrant Water Sea (up to the point mentioned), they likewise manifest their bodies and sit therein.

that light is named "The Sound that Initiates All Roots of Goodness."
Because they activate past seeds and give rise to new wholesome states, there are three types of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

First, those that produce meritorious and immovable karma, taking the three qualities of generosity, patience, and wisdom as their roots. Second, those who, weary of suffering, seek its cessation, taking faith and the other [faculties] as their roots.

it fills all lands throughout the ten directions;

If there are sentient beings who should be disciplined, the light touches them and they immediately attain self-awakening.

and the fever of all delusions is stilled.

It crushes the mountains of all obstructions.

for those who have not yet believed in the Great [Vehicle], it inspires them to enter and abide [in the path].
They give rise to supreme roots of goodness.

causing them to be forever free from all calamities and terrors.

The Buddha’s virtues are perfected; he is called the "Wheel that Subdues Obstructions. Because he possesses knowledge within meditative concentration, he is called the "One who Accepts his Vow.
He has realized the universal gateway dhāraṇī of all Buddha-dharmas.

It accords with the vastness of essence and function;
it realizes the great adornment of great compassion that tames all sentient beings.

He realizes the great compassion of the Universal Cloud Sound,
which is like the thundering sound of the Dharma-clouds and is able to uproot the source of suffering;

Knowing that which is apart from names is the Dharma; this Dharma, too, should be relinquished, relinquished in accordance with reality.
One realizes the great supernormal power (abhijñā) of the vast treasury of skillful means and equality.

One realizes and increases the power of resolute belief and attains great vows;
throughout the entire realm of sentient beings, one bears the burden without weariness. To cause others to attain resolute belief is the nature of the great vow.
One realizes the gate of eloquence that universally enters the light of all-knowledge.

first, three dharmas of meritorious qualities; next, four dharmas of cultivation through perfuming; and finally, three dharmas for initiating transformation. They are called "great" because they are manifold.
[The term] "one who" refers to one whose objective realm is boundless, who is vast and expansive in accordance with the nature [of reality], and whose wisdom penetrates and thoroughly understands;
such individuals are collectively given the name of "Realizers. *Da fangguang fo huayan jing shu*, Scroll 18.

Extensively Revealing the Dharma Gates, Part Five. First: The Buddha Turning the Wheel of Dharma.

At that time, that Tathāgata, wishing to subdue [sentient beings] and, according to their mental dispositions, cause them all to obtain benefit, taught through the application of the Buddha’s liberation.
