This has two parts; first, the general [overview].
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the Bodhisattva Mahāteja (Great Radiance) [attained] the light of the ocean of Dharma accumulated over his past lives.

This refers to the aforementioned Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, which is precisely what the Buddha had previously accumulated. Having seen the Buddha and obtained benefit, he was subsequently conferred the name "Bodhisattva. Part Two: Specific Explanations.
This refers to the light of wisdom of the samādhi of attaining the equality of the collection of all dharmas (*sarvadharma-puñja-samatā-samādhi-jñānāloka*).

Wisdom is the essence; "light" refers to its function. Because the objects illuminated differ, it is divided into eleven [categories]. The first is the light of wisdom of profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the "collection of all dharmas," there are briefly three meanings: first, the three collections such as right determination (*samyak-niyata*) and so forth; second, the wholesome...
The three clusters, beginning with the unwholesome, collectively encompass all things; they do not transcend the two categories of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.

These two states mutually include one another, and their single flavor manifests as their true nature; thus, they are called "equality. To realize this within meditative concentration is termed that samādhi.
All phenomena enter entirely into the wisdom-light that abides within the initial mind of bodhi.
This is the second great mental illumination: namely, that all subsequent causes and effects enter the initial mind. Briefly, there are three meanings:
first, because the subsequent cause is attained through the initial [moment], it is said that "all enter. If one practices the path until reaching it, the learner stands at the very first step.
The reward is contained therein. Second is the bodhi of the direct mind, which is right mindfulness of *tathatā*. Within the gate of *tathatā*, all dharmas are subsumed.

Third is the manifestation of the three virtues, in which the beginning and the end are perfectly interfused; for at the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one immediately achieves perfect awakening.
The light of the wisdom of the pure eye of the Universal Radiance Treasury throughout the ten directions and the dharma-realm;
the illumination of the great wisdom of the three greatnesses. As for "dharma-realm," it refers to the greatness of the essence that is illuminated.

"Universal radiance" refers to the greatness of its characteristics, because the light of wisdom universally illuminates the meaning of the dharma-realm and contains the nature-virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

It is called the "Treasury. Since delusive confusion is fundamentally empty, it is termed "pure. To see clearly is called the "eye"; this seeing-nature, though within the physical eye, is identical to the Buddha-eye.
It observes the light of wisdom from the ocean of great vows of all Buddha-dharmas.
The fourth is the light of wisdom of the four great vows, because one knows that all Buddha-dharmas have vows as their foundation.
The fifth is the light of wisdom of the five great practices, because one enters this through the boundless ocean of meritorious qualities and pure conduct.
It is the light of wisdom of the treasury of great power and swiftness that proceeds toward non-retrogression.
Sixth is the light of swift wisdom, which refers to entering into the unborn, wherein effort does not regress and there is great power without effort;
it is called such because a single practice encompasses many.
Within the *dharmadhātu*, there is the light of wisdom that emerges from the wheel of liberation through immeasurable powers of transformation;
the light of wisdom of the seven supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*); and the three wheels of activity. Without these, liberation is impossible.
They enter the light of wisdom of the ocean of the perfection of immeasurable merit;
they are the light of the eight great blessings and wisdoms, which illumines the adornment of merit.
They realize the light of wisdom of the ocean of the accomplishment of the adornment of the definitive understanding of all Buddhas.
The ninth is the light of wisdom of the ninefold analytical knowledge. It is the Buddha’s power of supreme resolve, which forms an ocean of adornments.
It is the light of wisdom of the ocean of supernormal powers that realizes the infinite manifestation of Buddhas throughout the dharma-realm before all sentient beings.
The ten great illuminations of wisdom universally pervade the dharma-realm;
they are the light of the wisdom that understands all the powers and fearlessnesses of the Buddhas.

The eleventh is the illumination of the Buddha’s wisdom-virtues, which subdues Māras and restrains outsiders. Since the final three pertain to the realm of the Buddhas, one merely understands and knows the remainder.
It can be known through realization. [The terms] "attainment" and "entry" are used. △ Third, praising and describing in verse, in two parts. First, the cause:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Great Majestic Radiance (up to) spoke these verses by virtue of the Buddha’s awesome power.
△ Section Two: Ten Verses, divided into three parts. The first verse indicates the benefit, essence, and function:
"Having heard the Buddha’s wondrous Dharma, I have attained the light of wisdom; by means of this, I see the deeds performed by the World-Honored One in the past."
△ Second, the manifestation of what is seen through its function. The first seven verses show the causes:
the differences in names, titles, and bodies in all places of birth, up to seeing the path traversed by the Buddha.
Finally, there is the fruit of seeing [the Buddha].
I contemplate the ocean of Buddha-fields as pure, great radiance, and the quiescent realization of the Dharma-realm of awakening, which is all-pervasive.
△ Third, there is one verse expressing a vow to emulate [the Buddha].
"I shall, like the World-Honored One, extensively purify the oceans of lands and cultivate the practices for enlightenment through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.

This refers to the cultivation of the great vows at the beginning of the preceding chapter. △ Fourth, the propagation and transformation of sentient beings has three parts. First, the clarification of self-awakening.
O Sons of the Buddha, at that time, the Bodhisattva Great Majestic Radiance (up to) attained realization in his mind before the Tathāgata.
△ Second, turning [others] to awakening:
for the sake of all worlds, he manifested the practices and vows of the Tathāgata (up to) those of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
This displays ten dharmas. There are both similarities and differences between these and the eleven wisdoms of clear illumination previously attained by oneself.
△ Third, the benefit of others:
causing sentient beings as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru (up to) to achieve the pure lands of the Tathāgata.
△ V. Encouragement by the Five Tathāgatas. There are eleven verses. The first three praise the attainment of the great fruit of the Dharma through the arousal of the bodhicitta.

At that time, [the Buddha] spoke these verses for the sake of the Bodhisattva Mahātejaḥprabha: [Verse 1] All mountains of merit... (up to)... for the Bodhisattva Mahātejaḥprabha, he spoke in verse: [Verse 2] ... [Verse 3] ... (Note: The original text provides the structural outline and the opening of the first verse; the full translation of the verses would follow this pattern.)
"Excellent! O you of great majestic light, treasury of merit, and wide renown... (until) one shall attain such wisdom.
△ Second, there are four verses which, by contrasting the inferior with the superior, reveal the excellence of progress. This is the perfection of advancement.
Those of inferior practice cannot know this expedient means (upāya), [and so forth] until: "they shall attain the unsurpassed path.
△ Third, there are two verses: External application combined with internal wisdom leads to decisive realization without doubt.
"All Buddhas of the three periods of time shall together fulfill your vow" (up to) "you will be able to know this skillful means.
△ Fourth, there are two verses. By citing one example, other practitioners will immediately attain it.
Because he made offerings to me with great light, he obtained great majestic power (extending) throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
△ Second, meeting the Buddha Adorned with the Good Eyes of the Pāramitās. Part One: Concluding the preceding and introducing what follows.
"O Sons of the Buddha, you should know... (up to) "...the lifespan is fifty billion years.

This refers to the period when the subsequent Buddha is about to appear; therefore, the kalpa and lifespan are discussed collectively. To clarify the number of intermediate kalpas is intended to manifest the appearance of many Buddhas.
Regarding the statement of human and Buddha lifespans, it is because the Buddha's lifespan is brief while the human lifespan is long, thereby [attaining] majestic power.

Kāśyapa served three Buddhas throughout his life. △ Second, the actual manifestation of the appearance of the Buddha, in five parts. First, the appearance of a Buddha after the previous one has passed into extinction:
After that Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, another Buddha appeared in the world... [until] he attained perfect enlightenment beneath the great forest of the *cakra-vartin* tree.
This means that wisdom guides all practices so that they all reach the other shore; because one perceives the nature clearly and distinctly, it is called the "Good Eye.
Since the fruit is adorned by the cause, this is termed "Adornment. △ Second, observing the signs and obtaining benefit, in two parts: first, observing the signs.
At that time, the youth Mahātejas saw that Tathāgata attain equal and perfect enlightenment and manifest supernatural powers;
this was the cause by which he immediately obtained benefit. △ Second, the obtaining of benefit, in two parts. First, listing the ten kinds.
One immediately attains the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) known as the "Gate of the Boundless Ocean-Treasury.
As for this *nien-fo san-mei*, it is the father of the Bodhisattva; therefore, it is explained first. Even up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), one does not depart from the mindfulness of the Buddha.

Regarding the "Gate of the Boundless Ocean-Treasury": that which is accumulated is called a "treasury" (*kośa*), and that which is deep and vast is termed an "ocean" (*sāgara*). However, briefly stated:
There are three meanings. First, because one sees many Buddhas within this meditative concentration (*samādhi*). As the subsequent text states:

"Taking the Buddha as the object of focus, one contemplates him with single-minded devotion without abandoning it; such a person attains the vision of the Buddha, whose magnitude is equal to the mind. It is through mindfulness that one is able to see."
This is why it is called a "gate. Each and every Buddha-virtue is an infinite ocean-treasury; because one can know them through mindfulness, it is called a gate. What is this "infinite ocean"?
There is an ocean of practice and vows cultivated throughout oceans of kalpas, which accomplishes the form-body (*rūpakāya*);

there is an ocean of marks and signs, which accomplishes the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*); there is an ocean of eloquence, which establishes the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); and there is the name...

There is the ocean of names; there is the ocean of cultivating the various factors conducive to enlightenment; there is the ocean of merit; there is the ocean of dwelling in peace for sentient beings; and there is the ocean of pure lands.
Each of these oceans is boundless, and each gives rise to a treasury of accumulated qualities. These three kinds of boundless, supreme virtues arise from the recollection of the Buddha;
therefore, this single gateway is profound, vast, and an accumulation of treasures. What is the recollection of the Dharma-nature body?

This accords with the principle of suchness. By recollecting the body of merit, one accomplishes boundless virtues; by recollecting the body of marks and signs, one realizes boundless characteristics.

There are no obstructions that are not extinguished, and there are no virtues that do not arise. All are condensed within a single word, which is collectively termed "recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti*).
From this, universal awakening is attained; therefore, it is called a "gate. Yet even this single gate cannot be fully described.
He immediately attained the dhāraṇī named "The Ocean of Dharma of Great Intellectual Power," which upholds great wisdom and enables one to penetrate profound teachings.
He also immediately attained great compassion, named "Universally Following Sentient Beings to Subdue and Liberate Them."
Responding universally without conditions,
one immediately attains the name "Great Compassion Pervading All Realms like a Cloud," which equally removes all feverish afflictions.
He immediately attains great joy, named "The Power-Treasury of the Ocean of Merits of All Buddhas.
This is the ocean of the Buddhas' profound virtues, an accumulation of power and function; the bodhisattva, taking this as an object of focus, experiences joy pervading both body and mind.
One immediately attains great equanimity (*upekṣā*), which is called the equality and purity of the *dharmatā* like space.

Compassion (*karuṇā*) causes the mind to be sorrowful; joy (*muditā*) causes it to be agitated. When one deeply accords with the *dharmatā*, it becomes as vast as space, and both compassion and joy vanish, resulting in equality and purity.
One immediately attains what is called the *prajñāpāramitā*, the body of the pure *dharmadhātu* which is by nature free from defilement.

This is the awakening to the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is free from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). If there were something to be abandoned, it would not be true abandonment.
Knowing that the self-nature is already free, one no longer abandons anything. This abandonment of abandonment is the true *dharmadhātu*. As for the true *dharmadhātu*, it is primordial...
Purity. The purity of the *dharmadhātu* is the purity of *prajñā*. When *prajñā* is pure, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally pure.
Since all phenomena are pure, there is neither purity nor impurity; this is true purity. Real-mark *prajñā* (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā*) is the substance of all phenomena.
Contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*) merges with this, and it is upon this that all virtues depend; therefore, it is called the "body."
He immediately attained the supernormal power named Unobstructed Light Manifesting Universally;
because it functions in conjunction with universal wisdom, it manifests universally without obstruction.
He immediately attained the eloquence named Skillfully Entering the Stainless Abyss.
Entering deeply into the Dharma and departing from the defilement of verbal expression, one immediately attains the light of wisdom called the "Pure Treasury of All Buddha-Dharmas.
This wisdom illuminates the Buddha-dharmas, purifies the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and contains all virtues. △ Second, the conclusion.
In this manner, he attained thorough penetration into ten thousand such Dharma-gates.
As his practice progressed through successive stages, they are referred to as "ten thousand. The term "thorough penetration" explains what was previously stated as "attained immediately.
△ Third, praising his virtues and exhorting others to visit him, in two parts. First, the delivery of verses, in three sections. First, extolling the rare and auspicious encounter.
At that time, the youth Mahātejas, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, spoke these verses for his retinue:
“Throughout inconceivable billions of eons... (until) now he has come to see the second Buddha.”
△ Second, praising the Buddha’s supreme virtues in three parts. First, the three types of bodily karma:
"The Buddha’s body universally radiates great light... this is manifested by the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of this Buddha."
△ 2. Three types of verbal action (*vākkarman*):
Each and every pore manifests clouds of light (extending to) the taming of all sentient beings.
△ 3. One type of mental action (*manaskarman*).
The Buddha’s supernormal powers are boundless... (up to) ...for the benefit of sentient beings, he has attained perfect enlightenment.
△ Third, there are two verses exhorting the assembly to follow together:
"You all should give rise to a heart of joy... (up to) ...you shall attain mastery like the Dharma King."
△ Second, the benefit of hearing the verse:
From "O sons of the Buddha, the youth Mahāteja" (up to) "immeasurable sentient beings resolve their minds on Bodhi.
△ Fourth, the retinue’s collective return.
At that time, Prince Mahātejas, together with his parents, went to the presence of the Tathāgata Suvilocanavyūharāja.
△ Fifth, awakening through hearing the sutra, in three parts: first, the Buddha preaches the sutra for them.
That Buddha, for their sake, preached the *Dharmadhātusvabhāva-samatā-sūtra* as its retinue.
The principal sūtra refers to the *Dharmadhātusvabhāva*, which is the *Mahāvaipulya*. "Pure Buddha" refers to the *Śubhabuddha*. "Adornment" refers to the *Avataṃsaka*.
The fact that it has many retinues demonstrates the perfection of this teaching. △ Second, the benefits obtained by those suited to the teaching.
When that great assembly has heard this sutra, there are likewise ten benefits.
Since it refers to a "great assembly," some individuals may obtain one, some two, three, or four, while others may possess all ten.
Because their majestic radiance was first realized [by the Buddha], they are not mentioned here in detail; however, the term "great assembly" already implies them. Therefore:

The Buddha then praised him. Regarding these ten matters, there are briefly two interpretations: first, they are correlated respectively with the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), either taking the meaning of the stages or taking the meaning of the perfections.
Attaining pure wisdom is called "entering all purifying skillful means.
To realize that all phenomena are originally pure is called "pure wisdom. Not grasping at the marks of purity is called "skillful means";
this is the wisdom of realization upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*).
On the first stage, one attains the light of detachment from defilement.

On the second stage, one is detached from the defilement of immoral conduct; this is the obstacle removed, and it illuminates all categories of wholesome qualities, which is the light of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Attaining the name of the wheel of the pāramitās is called the manifestation of the adornment beloved by all worlds;
this is precisely the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Patience is the supreme adornment, the source of all that is beloved.
One attains the expansion of the wheel of practice, named "Universal Entry into All Buddha-fields with Boundless Radiance and Pure Vision.
There is no field that is not entered, no phenomenon that is not illuminated, and no vision that is not pure. This constitutes diligence in expanding all practices.

Explaining this according to the meaning of the stages (*bhūmi*), one uses the various factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) to incinerate inexhaustible delusions and achieve boundless light.
He attains the wheel of practice for proceeding toward [enlightenment], named "Stainless Cloud of Merit and Radiant Banner.
He proceeds toward all practices and is able to enter the mundane world. Because his perfection of dhyāna has increased, his nature is free from defilement;
he engages with the mundane to transform sentient beings, forming clouds of merit, and because he does not lose sight of the true principle, he serves as a radiant banner.
Attaining the realization that enters accordingly is called the "Vast Radiance of the Ocean of All Dharmas.
When prajñā manifests before one, it is called "entering accordingly and realizing. Its illumination of profound dependent origination is called the "Light of the Dharma-Ocean."
Attaining a progressively deeper engagement in practice is called the adornment of great wisdom.

When effort has already receded and one is about to enter the state of effortless spontaneity, this constitutes profound engagement; the unimpeded integration of the provisional and the ultimate constitutes the great adornment.
Attaining the ocean of wisdom through empowerment is called "effortless cultivation" (*anābhoga-bhāvanā*) and the "supremely subtle vision.
To see the true nature of phenomena while cultivating effortlessly is what constitutes the supremely subtle vision.

Because one further attains empowerment through this wisdom, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states that the final three stages are identical in their dispelling of ignorance and identical in their state of effortlessness. Therefore...
The stage that is not [merely] consecrated is the wisdom of consecration.
It attains the manifestation of great radiance, known as the "Tathāgata’s Ocean of Merits," whose marks and light-shadows shine everywhere.
It clearly discerns the medicine and the disease; this is the mark of the ocean of merits. Its eloquence responds universally, like the flowing light of the moon's reflection.
Attaining the pure wisdom of the power of birth from vows is called the "Treasury of Resolute Belief in Immeasurable Vow-Power.
Because wisdom is perfected and free from obstructions, one then gives rise to resolute belief in the vows of the Buddha; hence it is said "birth.
Second, regarding these ten gates above, their names are established according to each individual matter; they do not necessarily correspond entirely to the stages (*bhūmi*). Or...
This applies to all positions. Or, they may not follow the sequence, as there are infinite individuals who attain realization differently;

thus, Samantabhadra’s skillful exposition contains manifold meanings within its text. △ Third, the Tathāgata’s praise and narration has two parts. First, six [verses] praise his possession of supreme virtues and his future attainment of the ultimate fruit.
Then that Buddha spoke these verses for the Bodhisattva Great Majestic Light:
"Excellent! O ocean of merit and wisdom... [omitted] ...adorned with stainless arrays throughout the oceans of all lands."
All [of these] have already been attained in the first half; the latter half shall be realized. Only the three lines of the fourth verse constitute the cause.
△ Second, there are four verses clarifying that the practice is equal to the Buddha’s cause, and that one shall realize it as the Buddha did.
"You have already entered my bodhisattva practice" (up to) "you shall attain the great merit of Buddhahood.
In all these cases, three phrases cite the Buddha’s practice, while the final phrase aligns with the Buddha’s virtue.

However, the descriptions and praises herein largely coincide with what was previously mentioned regarding the benefit gained from encountering the light and what was attained before the great assembly; the meaning must surely follow from what has been stated above. This may be understood.
Examine this by means of your own mind. △ Third, the encounter with the Buddha Supreme Merit Ocean (Guǐ Zuìshèng Gōngdé Hǎi Fó), in six parts.
First, the time of the Tathāgata’s appearance:
"O Sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Paramita-Sun Eye... [until] the youth Great Majestic Light received the position of a Wheel-Turning King."
This refers to the period following the parinirvāṇa of the previous Buddha. △ Second, the explicit explanation of the present age:
In that Great Forest of Maṇi-flower Branch-wheels (up to) it is named the Ocean of Supreme Merit.
One who establishes this title fulfills the ocean of merit; there is nothing further to surpass it.
△ Third, the Great King of Wheel-Turning, Mahātejas, went to make offerings. [From the passage] he offered a great jeweled pavilion adorned with mani-gems to the Buddha.
△ The Four Buddhas preach the sūtra for him.
At that time, those Tathāgatas, within that grove, [preach] as many sūtras as there are motes of dust, serving as his retinue.
Because he perceives the Universal Dharma (Samantadharma), it is called the "Universal Eye" (Samantanetra). Because its nature is wisdom, it is called "Radiance. How much more so, then, a single eye?
This refers to the ten eyes. When they are fused without obstruction, there is no dharma external to the eye; this is the truly universal eye.

Because seeing is triggered by various conditions, each condition serves as a faculty. Since the cause is submerged within the fruit, all conditions are termed "eyes. Thus, form itself is entirely the eye.
One constantly perceives forms without conditions; the entire eye becomes form. One always speaks of "seeing," yet it is not the self.
△ Fifth, the Benefit of Majestic Radiance.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Great Majestic Radiance, having heard this Dharma... [up to] ...is named Great Merit Universal Radiance.

The five perfections are all merit, but meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the greatest. Being quiescent yet illuminating nothing that is not, it is called "Universal Radiance" (*Samantaprabhā*). The following passage demonstrates the function of this concentration:
because one attains this *samādhi*, one is able to fully comprehend the oceans of merit and non-merit throughout the past, present, and future.
Regarding the terms "merit" (*puṇya*) and "non-merit" (*apuṇya*), there are briefly two meanings. First, merit is that which is wholesome, while non-merit is transgression.
Second, merit refers to the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), while non-merit refers to the nature (*svabhāva*). Because both nature and characteristic are fully understood, the Sūtra says:
"Merit is itself the nature of non-merit. This is "profound" (*gambhīra*); "fully understanding" is "vast" (*vipula*). Therefore, there is the expression "ocean," as when one first encounters it.

The Buddha. Those who have attained only ten [qualities] do so because their own power has not yet surpassed [that of others]. Those next to the Buddha who have ten thousand [qualities] do so because the Way has become even deeper.
Now, there is only one [remaining], because the Way is already perfected. Six. The Tathāgata’s Prophecy consists of eleven verses and is divided into four parts.
The first four [verses] reveal his bodhicitta.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses for the Bodhisattva Mahātejaḥprabha:
“Excellent, O Mahātejaḥprabha of great merit! ... This is your great light capable of entering.”
The first verse contains aspiration; the second verse contains compassion; the fourth contains the light of wisdom; and the third combines diligence.

Because these collectively guide the three mental states, the bodhicitta becomes perfected, and one shall attain sublime wisdom. △ Second, the four verses above [describe] entering the realm of the Buddha.
"You are able to fulfill these vast vows... (until) once you have mastered them all, you shall attain Buddhahood.
△ Third, there is one verse showing the characteristics of the fruit, which is to attain equality with all Buddhas.
As you have seen within the ten directions... that which those with boundless vows shall attain.
△ Fourth, there are two verses praising his present ability to benefit others by abiding in the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Now, from "this assembly in the ocean-like gathering at this site of enlightenment" (to) "the universal practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
△ Fourth, meeting the Buddha named Universal Renown Lotus-Eye Banner. Part four: first, the appearance of the Buddha among humans.
O Sons of the Buddha, regarding that Great Forest of the Mani Flower Branch-Wheels (up to) the Lotus-Eye Banner of Universal Renown:

in terms of its characteristics and categories, it is a blue lotus; in terms of its virtue, its mind is unstained. Its characteristics and virtues are lofty and manifest, and its renown is proclaimed abroad.
It crushes the heterodox and draws all beings to take refuge; therefore, it is called a "banner" (*dhvaja*). △ Second, the Heavenly Kings present offerings, in two parts. First, the Bodhisattvas.
He proceeded to the celestial palace of the Heaven of Reporting [One's Deeds].
At that time, Mahātejas passed away there (and was reborn) under the name Vimalapuṇyaketu.
This city is one of those listed at the beginning of this chapter. △ Second, knowing that the Buddha is worthy of refuge, he held flowers and waited.
They made offerings.
Together with the assembly of devas, they proceeded to the Buddha’s abode, raining down clouds of precious flowers as an offering.
△ Third, the Tathāgata preaches the sutra.
At that time, that Tathāgata expounded for them a vast number of sūtras—as numerous as motes of dust—as his retinue.
There are briefly three kinds of skillful means (*upāya*): first, provisional bestowal without reality, which is the crooked and clever skillful means;

second, the principle is fundamentally beyond words, yet one speaks by means of words, which is the great skillful means; third, where the provisional and the real are without obstruction, this too is the great [skillful means].
Skillful means: when both phenomena and principle are illuminated, it is called the Universal Gate. △ Fourth, the benefit received and the return:
At that time, having heard this sutra, the assembly of heavenly kings... [up to] ...departed from the site of enlightenment and returned to their original abodes.

Having heard the aforementioned Universal Gate, one enters into and dwells securely in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), wherein the joy of the Dharma is inexhaustible; thus it is called a "Treasury" (*kośa*).

By means of this, one realizes and penetrates the ocean of all true marks (*dharmatā*). Within this eon, there were Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms of ten Mount Sumerus, yet here only four are mentioned.

Furthermore, there is no connection between the past and the present, nor accounts of those who attained realization or benefits in the present; this is because the transmission of the sutra has not yet been completed.
As for those who would reconcile [the accounts], they should say: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Majestic Light was none other than Vairocana Buddha.
From here below, one enters the twelfth fascicle of the sutra.
Chapter Seven: The Names and Titles of the Tathāgata.
△ This chapter will be explained through a fivefold analysis.

First, regarding the intent of its inclusion: first, we clarify the sequence of the sections. Having previously presented the fruit [of Buddhahood] to inspire faith and joy, this section now clarifies the capacity [to attain it].

It follows next because it gives rise to faith and understanding regarding cause and effect. Regarding its arrival at the second assembly: among the various forms of understanding that arise, faith is the foremost;
furthermore, while the preceding section presented the objects of faith, this section clarifies the practice of being able to have faith, and thus it follows next.

Regarding its arrival at the third chapter: the preceding chapter presented the objects of faith through the accomplishment of causes, conditions, and effects, whereas this chapter presents the fruit.
This section distinguishes the causes and clarifies the practice of faith. Among the three types of karma within the fruit, the body is taken as the general category and thus appears first.
Furthermore, it serves as a remote response to the previous inquiry regarding the "ocean of names and titles."
Second, the explanation of the names is also threefold. First is the title *The Section on Cultivating the Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Giving Rise to Understanding*.

This means that by cultivating the perfect causes of the five stages, one accomplishes the full fruit of the ten bodies, causing all bodhisattvas to understand these characteristics; thus, they give rise to the understanding of "cultivating the causes to accord with the fruit.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-saṃbandha* (dependent compound). Second is the title of the assembly, which refers to the location as the "Universal Radiance" (*Samantābhāsa*).
Regarding the term "Hall" (dian), there are three interpretations. First, the hall is made of jewels, and its light shines everywhere. Second, the Buddha emits universal radiance from within it.
Third, the Buddha expounds the Dharma-gate of Universal Dharma within the hall, and the light of his wisdom illuminates the world.

Therefore, its name is established. According to the first meaning, it follows the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound; according to the latter two, it is a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compound. Regarding the dharmas, it is called the "Assembly of Faith, Understanding, and Practice.
The names of the three chapters have already been explained in the "Chapter on the Tathāgata Manifesting Signs. That which summons the essence is called a "name" (*nāman*);
that which expresses virtue is a "title" (*abhidhāna*). While "names" are specific, "titles" are general; all Buddhas universally possess the ten titles. This concludes the explanation of the names.
Because [the suffixes] such as *ka* and so forth differ, the Tathāgata is explained as one category within the ten [categories].
Depending on the capacity of sentient beings and their specific virtues, distinct names are established. Since these express virtues, they are both "names" (*nāman*) and "titles" (*abhidhāna*).
The name and title of the Tathāgata is analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.

The three thematic principles (*abhiprāya*) are also threefold. First is the *principle of classification*: taking cultivation as the cause and cultivation as the fruit as the theme, it aims to lead all bodhisattvas to practice and enter [the path].

Second is the *principle of convergence*: if one considers the stages collectively, taking the subsumption of positions through faith, understanding, practice, and virtue as the theme, it aims for the universal attainment of the Buddha-fruit; for faith enables one to certainly reach the stage of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, viewed from a proximate perspective, taking faith alone as the primary principle (*śāstra*) and the attainment of the state [of Buddhahood] as the goal (*prayojana*).

If one follows the extensive classification, these three lower grades constitute one part of the tenfold primary principle; namely, that the fruit-function accords with the capacity [of beings] and pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*, which is taken as the primary principle, and the arising of faith based upon this is taken as the goal.
Thus, this is also called the cause and fruit of the "correct retribution" (*samyag-vipāka*), and it is also the object...
Faith. In what dharma-gate does one have faith? One has faith that the name of the Buddha’s body is equal to that of sentient beings; thus, one knows that my own name is like the name of the Buddha.

One has faith in the Buddha’s dharma-gate, which is established according to what is appropriate; thus, one knows that my deluded thoughts regarding the causes and effects of suffering and its accumulation are likewise entirely the dharma-gate.
One has faith in the Buddha’s mental karma, whose radiance shines everywhere; thus, one knows that one's own mind is not without awareness.
The virtuous masters of antiquity also took the aforementioned three categories and subsumed them under the classification of results. Regarding the three categories as the primary tenets (*zong*):

the first reveals the Buddha’s name and title, taking universal pervasiveness as its tenet; the second takes the transformation and edification of beings according to their capacities, bringing benefit, as its purpose (*qu*). Alternatively, both of the former two may be taken as the tenets.
Generating faith is the vehicle.

There are four questions and answers. Question: Regarding the five cycles of the distinctions and equality of cause and effect, since the two meanings are not the same, why are they divided into separate names and then combined into one?
Answer: It is because they universally generate the understanding of both distinction and equality; thus, apart from their cultivation and arising, they are so described.

Question: What is the purpose of this exposition? In the previous assembly, the fruit was presented primarily to engender faith. Why, then, are the three aspects—the Name and so forth—repeatedly presented here? Answer:
Generally, there are two principles by which faith is engendered in relation to an object: first, to designate the objective phenomenon so as to clarify its locus;
second, to subsume it within the mind so as to bring about the practice of faith. The previous assembly relied on the first principle; this assembly relies on the latter.

Regarding the meaning: furthermore, in the previous assembly, the fruit was extensive while the cause was brief; thus it was called "presenting the fruit. In this assembly, the cause is extensive while the fruit is brief;

therefore, they are collectively subsumed as the cause. This is merely a matter of shifting the sequence between the preceding and the main text for the sake of brevity. thus, it is not the same as what is explained in the seventh assembly regarding the fruits produced. Herein, the object of faith is distinguished in its own right.
Because it is based upon [the state of concentration]. Question: Why does he not enter meditative absorption? Answer: Because he has not yet entered that stage, as his nature is not yet fixed.
If that is so, are the ten concentrations not mundane wholesome states (*vyagrakuśala*)? However, regarding the formal protocols for preaching the Dharma, there are generally four permutations:

first, preaching after entering concentration, as in various assemblies; second, entering concentration after preaching, as in the *Anantārthasūtra* and others; third, preaching within concentration, as in the ninth assembly.
Because there is no utterance of words, there is the fourth "non-entry into discourse. Thus, the texts in this *Śraddhābalādhāna* chapter and those in the seventh assembly are not few;
the ninth [assembly] serves as a manifest proof that only the one who can speak has attained eternal permanence, because he is unimpeded in the arising of his activity.

The seventh [assembly] serves to manifest that he is always in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Furthermore, "entry" is for the purpose of receiving empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), but since he does not require empowerment, it is not necessary.

"Entering. Regarding the statement that one enters later: this is because it refers to being in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and because one is about to arise from it. Thus, we know that movement and stillness are nothing but phenomena (*dharmas*).

Since the sages have no fixed rule, the subsequent text distinguishes the function of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*): in one direction one enters into correct concentration, while in the other directions one remains the same;
arising and emerging are described as faith, wherein concentration and distraction are sovereign and unimpeded. In the other assemblies, [the Buddha] strokes their heads, and this is explained later.

[The Buddha] assembled [the assembly]. After he had preached, he patted their heads. Thus one knows that the structure of this sutra is both vertical and horizontal, and cannot be fixed by a single standard.

Fifth, the explanation of the text: if categorized according to meaning by chapter, within the ten divisions, these following three chapters constitute the "Division of the Universal Response to Capabilities through the Function of the Result.
If categorized according to the Dharma, within the ten divisions of the assembly... this one [chapter].
This shall be the second assembly, the Assembly for Accomplishing Virtue through Faith. Now, the section on the fourfold question-and-answer concludes here.
This is the seventh assembly, which corresponds to the second division, the Section on the Application of Understanding through Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit.

If one were to follow the general sequence of the assemblies, the question-and-answer portions should have been divided directly; however, following the current textual arrangement, this single assembly is divided into three parts: first, the introductory section (nidāna); second, the request...

Section Three: The Section on the Exposition. Now, first is the introductory section (*nidāna*), which is fully as presented at the beginning of the sutra; it differs only slightly by adding "Universal Radiance" (*Samantaprabha*).
Briefly divided, there are three parts: first, the indication of the principal figure, the time, and the location.
At that time, the World-Honored One was at the Bodhimanda of the Dharma of Araṇya in the kingdom of Magadha.
△ Second, the specific exposition of the three matters has three parts. First, the specific exposition of the time of the teaching.
He first attained perfect enlightenment.
△ Second, specifically indicating the place of teaching:
He sat upon the Lotus Treasury Lion Throne in the Hall of Universal Radiance.
It is located approximately three *li* to the southeast of the Bodhimaṇḍa, at a bend in the River Sītā. The nāga of that river constructed this for the Buddha.

Here, the general is cited to encompass the particular; the name of the country was previously indicated to include its branches, and the designation of the site was mentioned above to include its specific features.
Thus, from the "Immovable" [Bodhi] tree, it extends throughout the ten directions. 2. Specifically manifesting the virtues of the presiding deity.
Sublime realization is entirely fulfilled;

this is precisely the manifestation of the attainment of perfect enlightenment. According to the beginning of the eighth assembly and the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and other texts, it is taught that the Buddha possesses twenty-one kinds of merit. The text contains the first ten phrases, which are also a brief explanation. Regarding the term "sublime awakening" (*miaowu*) mentioned in the preceding phrase:

in the Jin dynasty translation of the *Sūtra*, it is called "Excellent Awakening" (*shanjue*), while in the *Śāstra* translation, it is called "Perfect Awakening" (*zhengjue*). This is because the Sanskrit term *samyak* encompasses both "sublime and excellent" (*miaoshan*) and "perfect" (*zhengdeng*).

The translators accordingly rendered it as "awakening," which is synonymous with "enlightenment. Because it simultaneously illuminates both the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is termed "sublime awakening. [The following section is incomplete.]
These various phrases differ from those pertaining to the causal stage; therefore, they are further described as "fulfilled.
The two courses are eternally severed.
Both afflictive obstructions and cognitive obstructions, as well as saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, are termed the "two courses. That neither of these manifests before one is called "eternal severance."
To penetrate the dharma of signlessness and pure suchness is what is called "the dharma of signlessness. "Penetrating" means to fully comprehend.
This is to abide in the abode of the Buddhas.
The Tathāgata abides eternally in great compassion, spontaneously benefiting and gladdening all beings. Furthermore, he constantly dwells in the sublime, celestial, and Brahma-abodes.
Having attained the equality of a Buddha, both that which is realized and the means of realization, as well as his transformative activities, are all equal to those of all Buddhas.
It leads to the state of non-obstruction,
because it can counteract the obstacles to liberation through the path;
it is a dharma that cannot be reversed.
Because the Dharma he teaches cannot be overturned by non-Buddhists,
his conduct is unimpeded;
as he traverses all worlds, neither the adversities nor the favors of Māra can obstruct him.
Establishing the inconceivable and stabilizing the teachings, for they transcend words and thought;
thus one universally perceives the three periods of time.
Regarding the objects of the three periods of time, because one understands and discerns them—whether as phenomena or principles—without error, these nine distinctions are complete.

The formation, subsistence, differentiation, and dissolution of the first general phrase may be understood by applying this principle through reflection. △ Third, the perfection of the auxiliary wings has two parts.

Together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields (up to) they all came together from other directions.

It is bound to a single stage. This text primarily concerns the manifested characteristics (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
Thus it is said. △ Second, praising his supreme virtues:
"Universally and skillfully observing.
Although his virtues are immeasurable, he is praised briefly for one wisdom. "Skillfully observing" means being able to perceive and know. "Universally" has two [meanings].
Regarding the meaning: first, the entire assembly universally possesses these virtues. Second, there are three meanings to the universal contemplation of the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*):

first, skillfully knowing marks (*lakṣaṇa*); second, skillfully knowing the markless (*alakṣaṇa*); and third, skillfully knowing that these two are unimpeded. From here below, the objects of contemplation are clarified;
all of them fully possess the three aforementioned meanings.
The realm of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, the world-realm, and the nirvana-realm—extending to the conditioned and unconditioned, the past, present, and future—constitute ten phrases.
The first is the general subject, namely those to be converted. Next, as for where these beings come from: they arise from the world-realm due to delusion regarding the dharma-realm.
[I] shall cause them to abide in the fruit of nirvana and purify their various karmic fruits; therefore, one must recognize the activities of the mind.

Illness. The medicine of words and meaning causes one to weary of the mundane world and to rejoice in the supramundane. One does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), nor does one dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Above, the ten dharmas were examined through horizontal observation; now, one penetrates the three periods of time through vertical observation: observing that *nirvāṇa* has been known and will be realized in the present and future;

that various karmas have been performed and will be performed in the present and future; that retributions have been received and will be received in the present and future; and that mental activities have already occurred in the present.

The preceding section provided a general summary to collectively manifest the cause of the interpenetration and sequential arrangement (*saṃbhinnakrama*) of practices; this section, by contrast, focuses on the specific divisions to manifest the characteristics of the distinct causes.

Although the subsequent twenty phrases are entirely identical [to those previously mentioned], the former was general while this is specific. Furthermore, the former concerned that which is believed, whereas the present passage distinguishes that which is accomplished.
Because the essence of that which is believed and that which is accomplished is shown to be non-different, the phrasing is identical throughout.

If one were to categorize them solely by their meaning, they could also be divided into three parts: the first ten phrases inquire about the Buddha’s virtues, which are the causeless response to sentient beings;

the subsequent ten phrases inquire about the stages of the Bodhisattva’s practice, which constitute the greatness of the fruition resulting from those causes; and the final ten phrases [inquire about] the [resultant] state.

The supreme virtues of the Buddha-fruit manifest the results produced by the causes; thus, taking the Buddha as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), one gives rise to the perfuming of the cause, and through this cause, the fruit is accomplished. "Much learning and repeated practice—there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharmakāya, and there is nothing that does not return to realize this Dharmakāya. This is precisely its meaning.

the latter forty phrases consist of inquiries by means of citing examples. The meaning does not differ from what preceded. However, regarding the basis and that which is accomplished, the text should have them reciprocally;
it is merely a case of abbreviation, as there was no desire for prolixity. Therefore, the direct raising of questions in the first assembly is precisely this.

Just as all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in all worlds of the ten directions, for the sake of bringing all bodhisattvas to fulfillment:

It is so that the lineage of the Tathāgatas may not be severed;
first, it continues the Buddha-lineage above, and second,
it provides protection and refuge for all sentient beings.
Second, how does it follow by means of saving sentient beings?
It is by causing all sentient beings to forever leave behind all afflictions.
Third, how does it save them so that they may be free from delusion?
Because they fully understand all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
because they know how to rescue others by understanding their faculties and conduct;
and because they expound all dharmas.
Fifth, by what means does it provide relief? Because it administers the medicine of the Dharma and because it purifies all defilements.
Sixth, what benefit does it accomplish? It eliminates the defilement of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Because it permanently severs all webs of doubt;
second, because it resolves doubts regarding the Truth of the Path by uprooting all expectations.
Third, the hope of uprooting suffering, because it destroys all bases of attachment.

Fourth, the realization of the cessation of the bases of attachment; furthermore, this constitutes the practice of a bodhisattva, being endowed with both compassion and wisdom. Possessing this compassion and wisdom—

For what purpose is this? It is so that the lineage of the Buddhas may not be severed. What are the characteristics of the non-interruption of the Buddha-lineage? It is said that one accomplishes the three virtues:

by rescuing and protecting sentient beings, one accomplishes the virtue of benevolence (*upakāra-guṇa*); by eternally severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), one accomplishes the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*);

and by fully understanding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one accomplishes the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). There are three types of conditioned phenomena: first, mental formations; second, objective formations; and third, [the formations of the body].
The objects of comprehension are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which are impermanent and signless; this is what is comprehended. How does one protect and expound upon all dharmas?

How does one eternally sever and purify all defilements (*saṃkleśa*)? To eternally sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) means that both their seeds and their manifestations are simultaneously extinguished, thereby eliminating all defilements—referring here specifically to the manifest delusions. How do these become wisdom? It is by eternally severing the net of doubt; this is wisdom.
What benefit is there in achieving anything? It is to sever all hopes. What benefit is there in eliminating delusions? It is to extinguish all attachments.

As for all who are attached—whether to existence or emptiness, to practice or to its fruit—they must not cling to any phenomena. When right wisdom manifests before them, they compassionately rescue sentient beings so that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed;
this is the essential core of a bodhisattva’s practice, and it is also the fundamental intention of all Buddhas.
Each of the questions posed herein possesses this very benefit. Furthermore, it explains that all bodhisattvas achieve what is to be accomplished.

How do they accomplish the non-interruption of the Buddha-lineage? It is by accomplishing it for themselves and protecting sentient beings, thereby accomplishing it for others. How do they protect them?
It means being free from the two obstacles, permanently severing afflictions, and being without the obstacle of afflictions. One clearly understands...

As for this afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*), what are its characteristics? They are craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*). To eliminate all defilements:
