Each has its own chapter; as for the single "Ten Summits" (*Daśa-śīrṣa*), the text of the answer does not clarify it. There have been many ancient interpretations. One says:

according to the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, there is a dharma-gate concerning the "Mind-Ground" (*citta-bhūmi*) following the ten patiences (*daśa-kṣānti*); this refers to these Ten Summits. This principle is also logically consistent.
However, where that sūtra speaks of them, there are ten [chapters], yet at the beginning there is no mention of the Bodhimanda assembly; it merely says, "sitting in the four directions."

In the *Thousand-Ray King’s Seat* and the *Sublime Light Hall*, the ten world-oceans are expounded. The second, third, and fourth [assemblies] are identical in location and dharma to the third, fourth, and fifth assemblies here.
The sequence of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) in the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations is also the same.

However, in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, the ten meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are expounded; in the first dhyāna, the ten adamantine minds (*vajracitta*) are expounded; and in the second dhyāna, the ten vows (*praṇidhāna*) are expounded. In the third dhyāna...

It speaks of the ten patiences (*daśakṣānti*). It states that in the palace of Mahesvara within the fourth dhyāna, the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground was taught by Vairocana Buddha of the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbhalokadhātu*), which serves as my own source;

it does not mention a subsequent assembly at the Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*) or the successive events at the Gabled Hall in Jetavana. Furthermore, these points are difficult to reconcile. Moreover, there is further fruition following this intermediate stage.
Question: That "Buddha-ground" (*buddha-citta-bhūmi*) is equivalent to the subsequent "Tathāgata-ground" (*tathāgata-bhūmi*) and so forth; it is not the "Ten Summits" (*daśa-mūrdhan*).

Some say that the answer in the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* (or *Mahāsāṃghika-vaibhāṣika*), when compared with the *Ratnakaranda-sūtra* (*Ābharaṇa-sūtra*), indicates that there is a distinct "Summit-position" (*mūrdhan-pada*) for the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), as it represents the ultimate limit of the causal stage.
Now, within the *Saṃghāṭa*, ten great numbers are taught, and since this is the pinnacle among those numbers, it is called the "Ten Summits. Although that question mentions ten...

Answer: There are many [interpretations]. It is not tenable because it would also contradict the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* (or *Śrīmaladevī-sūtra*), which states that these are not of the same category as the higher meditative attainments (*dhyāna*). Some say:
In the "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Āyuṣka-prakaraṇa*), the ten successive Buddha-lands are described, each being the crown of the one below, culminating in the Buddha-field of Bhadraśrī;
these are called the "Ten Crowns. Furthermore, in the second section on the names of Buddhas, these eleven worlds are designated as the "Foremost" (*agra*).
Therefore, by citing only these eleven [kalpas] at the beginning and the end, it reveals a lifespan numbering more than a million asaṃkhyeya worlds;
this serves as the heading. Since a "heading" (śīrṣa) is the "top" (mūrdhan), yet there is no separate question regarding them, it seems there is some slight logic [in this].
However, merely citing these ten realms as the opening of a question to correspond with the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth is highly inconsistent.

Now, it is said that neither the new nor the old Sanskrit manuscripts contain the term "patience" (kṣānti). Yet, it is present within the dialogue; thus we know that the "patience" mentioned there is precisely this "summit" (mūrdhan).
As for the "ten summits," they represent the ultimate limit of the stage of causes. The ten concentrations and ten supernormal powers all belong to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
The ten patiences (*kṣānti*) are situated at the end. Furthermore, they receive the name "Summit" (*mūrdhan*). Question: Regarding the stages (*avasthā*), why is it called the "Summit"? Answer:

Because it refers to the patient acceptance (*adhivāsana*) of the Dharma-gates, which is fixed by the seal of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*), it is called "patience. It is not because it is the ultimate limit of the stage;

for if one does not possess the ten patiences, it is not the [Summit] stage, and if one does not have the ten patiences, one has not reached the ultimate limit of the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*). These two texts clarify this further; thus, at the end of the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences":
It says: "One who penetrates this gate of patience achieves unimpeded wisdom and transcends all multitudes, turning the unsurpassed wheel," and so forth.

Since it speaks of "transcending," this carries the meaning of the "Summit" (mūrdhan). This is because its doctrinal characteristics are similar to the "Patience" and "Summit" dharma-gates among the four roots of goodness (*catvāri nirvedhabhāgīyāni*).

Otherwise, if there were no separate question regarding patience, what would be the purpose of answering [about the summit] in the void? Even if one wished to establish [this point], [it would be redundant].
Tenth: One should explain that the Ten Faiths are to be transcended. Although the Ten Faiths have not yet established a formal stage, they nonetheless accord with the Dharma-realm;
their cultivation of vast and great practices and their sublime qualities and functions are distinct, and thus they are answered in a separate assembly because there must be a corresponding inquiry.

Alternatively, if the four grades from the Ten Patiences downward are used together to answer the question regarding the "Summit," there is no loss in principle, as both are the ultimate point of Equal Enlightenment (Samyagbodhi). Part Two.
The twenty questions concerning the fruits achieved are entirely identical to the second section of the text from the first assembly.

First, the internal virtues are perfected, followed by the exposition of the *tathāgata-bhūmi*, the realm of the *tathāgata* (extending through) the mastery of the *tathāgata* and the unimpededness of the *tathāgata*.
The Tathāgata’s spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*) was previously termed "the Buddha’s empowerment" (*buddhādhiṣṭhāna*), which refers precisely to the empowerment of spiritual power.

Regarding supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), they refer to external functions being unobstructed; regarding spiritual power, it refers to internal capacity and efficacy. In the "Chapter on Transcending the World," each of these has ten matters.
Their characteristics are distinct from one another. As for the term "unimpeded," it means that there is nothing capable of obstructing what the Tathāgata performs.
This is the same in meaning as the phrase "incapable of being grasped" mentioned in the preceding text. △ Second, the manifestation of essence and function.
The Tathāgata’s eye and the Tathāgata’s ear (up to) the Tathāgata’s wisdom and the Tathāgata’s supremacy:
eloquence is vocal action; wisdom is mental action; and supremacy is bodily action. This is according to the previous assembly.
It lacks only the single phrase regarding the Buddha’s radiance; the rest is as explained previously.
The text of the response is also as cited previously from the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Ocean of Inconceivable Marks. However, since that was a general summary, this passage is cited here.
The cited text is the direct answer, and it is appropriate for the speaker to cite it again now. △ Third, the final phrase.
He concludes with a formal request:
"I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will likewise speak for me.
Since it was so for that Buddha, this case is analogous; he requests that the teaching be the same as that one, which is why he uses the word "likewise" (亦). △ Third.

The Section on Exposition (*Vyākhyāna-bhāga*). Within this, the first six assemblies answer the questions posed here. Following the length of these questions and answers, the structural outline (*śāstra-vibhāga*) is also divided into three parts:

first, the initial three chapters answer the question regarding the fruit that serves as the basis; second, from the chapter "Clarifying the Questions" (*Prasnaprakāśana*) onwards, they answer the question regarding the causes to be cultivated;
third, from the chapter "Inconceivable" (*Acintya*) onwards, they answer the question regarding the fruits to be accomplished. Regarding that equality...
The cause is the cause of the result; the middle [cause] is the cause. The result is the function of this result, and thus it is subsumed under the result.
This chapter is divided into two parts: first, the Tathāgata’s manifestation of signs, which answers by virtue of his mindfulness of the request and because he has realized the ultimate limit;
second, Mañjuśrī’s verbal response, which acts as an assistant to the Lord and manifests through conventional speech. Regarding the first part, there are two subdivisions.
First, the Buddha manifests supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the various bodhisattvas, manifested supernatural powers for each according to their respective kind.
"Knowing the thoughts" refers to receiving their mental requests; "manifesting supernatural powers" refers to answering by displaying signs. For each according to their kind...
This has three meanings: first, because what is appropriate for those who harbor doubts varies;

that is to say, some may manifest forms to be seen, sounds to be heard, or provide silent assistance to bring about understanding—all of which are manifestations of supernatural power (ṛddhi), as the body of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-kāya) appears instantaneously and perfectly clear.
Second, because the categories of those who harbor doubts differ. Third, because the specific objects of doubt vary; that is to say:
If those with doubts regarding the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā) see the wheel-marks on the Tathāgata’s feet emitting light that pervades the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and so forth;

if those with doubts regarding the ten abodes (daśa-vihāra) see the toes of the Tathāgata’s feet emitting light beyond the dust-particles of a hundred lands where bodhisattvas assemble, and so forth—just as it is with this single instance of emitting light, so it is with all other marks.
Therefore, we know that the manifestations appearing in the first assembly pervade the nine [assemblies].

Assembly. This assembly manifests supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that extend to a certain portion [of the audience]. The compilers of the canon have arranged them in sequence according to their meaning.

Therefore, in the following three assemblies, there are all references to not departing from the Bodhi tree. Second, the ocean-like assembly gathers, and the Buddha answers the first ten questions by manifesting signs.
He answers the question regarding the Buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra*) by manifesting light within those fields. Those fields are golden in color.
These are the adornments of that land. Since they are composed of gold, they also constitute the substance of the land.

Because the bodhisattvas of that land are adorned with the great jewels of the bodhisattvas who adorn the land, it is also a pure land. It is a purely pure buddha-land because it consists solely of bodhisattvas.
They have purified their brahma-conduct because this land has accomplished the practices for purifying the buddha-field. Thus, it is also a pure land.
Because that which is cultivated is pure. The five phrases above have already answered this; they answer both the questions and the responses.

The five phrases concerning the primary retribution and the land each having a Buddha, as well as seeing the Tathāgata seated within the Lotus Treasury, answer the question regarding the Buddha’s dwelling. The manifestation of supernatural powers and the emission of light answer the question regarding his majestic power.

The names such as "Immovable Wisdom" answer the question regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Seeing the Buddha turning the wheel of the Dharma is... [the answer to the question regarding the turning of the wheel].
Answer: This is the teaching on the Dharma. That the Buddha attains perfect enlightenment is the answer regarding Bodhi.

Although the text appears later, its meaning is fully contained herein, for it is this very manifestation of the light of awakening that is revealed. The assembly of multitudes from the ten directions constitutes ten sections;
within each direction, there are eight items: first, the distance; second, the name of the land; third, the title of the Buddha; fourth, the chief disciple; fifth, the retinue... [and so forth].
6. Approaching the Buddha; 7. Paying homage upon arrival; 8. Transforming seats and sitting down. Regarding the distance from here being as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields:

in the previous assembly, because the causes and conditions of what is to be believed were explained as profound and vast, it was necessary to gather from afar from beyond the Flower Treasury World (Gandavyūha), from the oceans of lands in the ten directions. Now, because the causes and conditions for generating understanding are being explained, [the gathering] gradually increases.
Because they are being cultivated, only the lands adjacent to Sahā are gathered; this is because their practice through faith is the most inferior.

Furthermore, it is said that from ten onwards, the numbers gradually increase up to the "Dharmadhātu" chapter, where the oceans of lands are gathered. It does not initially say "one," but directly says "ten."
Because it manifests the inexhaustible; because "dust motes of lands" is used to compare with other superior things; and because there must be that which is manifested, stages are differentiated.

It is not the case that those at the stage of initial faith and so forth are excluded, for this applies universally; thus, both the conclusion and the proof are spoken of equally throughout the ten directions.

Furthermore, following delusion, it is called "external," while the place of awakening is called "coming"; yet in reality, the Buddha-lands have no inherent distance or proximity. All lands are named [as such].
"Form" (*rūpa*) indicates that faith is coarse and manifest; it also indicates that it is clearly evident and capable of engendering faith.
Regarding "the Buddha is named 'One of Equal Wisdom'": if one has faith but lacks wisdom, ignorance increases. The wisdom within faith is the realization of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
Regarding "the Lord is named 'Chief'": in Sanskrit, this is *Śrī*. It has four meanings: first, chief; second, supreme; third, auspiciousness; fourth, [glory].
Virtue. For this reason, the translators have used different terms at various points; now, we shall employ them consistently.
Faith is taken as primary because it encompasses all stages, because it is most excellent among the successive practices, and because it is extremely difficult to attain.
It is auspicious for one to first give rise to faith within the midst of birth and death. Furthermore, faith is able to increase all virtues, such as wisdom and merit.
Because these ten bodhisattvas equally represent the gate of faith (*śraddhā*), they are all named Śrī.

Yet, because each attains all dharmas through a specific gate, there are further distinctions, which shall be explained in the subsequent text. There is also a tradition stating that *śrī* in Sanskrit means "auspiciousness" (*maṅgala*) here;
alternatively, *śrī* means "head" (*mūrdhan*), which is likewise a valid principle. Regarding the statement that their retinues are as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, this represents...
Each and every practice encompasses inexhaustible virtues. "All approach the Buddha" means they possess a direction toward him. The rest is as in the previous assembly.
Furthermore, the names of the Bodhisattvas and so forth below are all symbolic of the Dharma. "Bodhisattva" symbolizes the practices one performs; "original land" symbolizes the principle realized;
and the "name of the Buddha" symbolizes the wisdom attained. Now, first, there are eight sections concerning the East.
Having manifested these supernatural powers, [he beheld that] in the eastern direction, beyond as many worlds as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, there was a world named Golden.
The name of the soil signifies that the nature of the mind is undefiled; it forms a vessel through its interaction with conditions, serving as the fundamental substance.
The Buddha’s title is "Immovable Wisdom" (*acala-jñāna*).

This name for the Buddha signifies that original wisdom is like space, transcending both the subject that perceives and the object perceived. It is profoundly still and immovable; movement itself is delusion.

It is not because of the nature of wisdom; furthermore, even if one were to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, it would not differ from that of an ordinary being. Thus, the wisdom of original enlightenment abides in the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind.
In that world, there is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī.
The leader was named Huida. Throughout the various realms of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, through discernment, accords with fundamental wisdom; thus he distinguishes cause and effect.
Together with a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, he came to where the Buddha was. Having arrived, he performed [prostrations].
Having paid homage, he manifested a Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne in the eastern direction and sat upon it cross-legged (the throne appearing in its original location).
To the south, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, there is a world named Wondrous Color.
Being unstained yet stained, and being stained yet unstained—both are difficult to comprehend; therefore, it is called "wondrous color.
The Buddha is named Unobstructed Wisdom.
Non-nature is not obstructed; following conditions, non-nature is not obstructed.
In that [assembly] there was a bodhisattva named Chief of Enlightenment (Bodhimukha),
who realized the nature of the mind.
Together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, he arrived at a world named Lotus Color (Padmavarṇa).
Having realized the emptiness of sentient beings, he is like a lotus, unstained by them.

The Buddha’s name is Jñānāndhakāravidhvamsana (Destroyer of the Darkness of Ignorance). There is a bodhisattva there named Vasumitra (Wealth Chief), who teaches and transforms others through the wealth of the Dharma; he is indeed Jñānāndhakāravidhvamsana.
Together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields... there is a world named Campaka Flower Color.
Its nature and characteristics are not in conflict; it is solely the purport of the One Vehicle. This is what is meant by "only smelling the campaka flower."
The Buddha’s name was Viniyatakīrti.
He was well-versed in the fruits of karma and never transgressed the rules of decorum.
Among his followers was a bodhisattva named Ratnaśrī.
The ultimate and the conventional are not in conflict, for they are both worthy of being cherished.
Together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, [he arrived at] a world named Utpalavarṇa.
If one possesses this wisdom, it is supreme, like the blue lotus. The Buddha is named Mingxiangzhi (Wisdom of the Radiance of Marks);
that is to say, he is clear regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), and his mind is pure and lucid in understanding the virtues of the Buddha.
In that [world] there was a bodhisattva named Guṇaśrī (Virtue-Head),
who had thoroughly realized the merit of the Tathāgata’s manifestation and preaching of the Dharma;
together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, he arrived at a world named Suvarṇa (Golden).

Luminous and pure, it is worthy of veneration; hence it is called "golden. The Buddha is the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); taking the Buddha as one's object of focus, he is thus identical to Mañjuśrī, relying upon the Golden Realm (*Suvarṇadhātu*).
The Buddha’s name is Ultimate Wisdom (Kūṭasthajñāna).
He is the field of merit of equanimity, and thus he is called Ultimate Wisdom.
There is a bodhisattva there named Chief of Eyes (Akṣimukha).
The Field of Merit (puṇyakṣetra) guides and illuminates like eyes leading the body.
Together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, [he arrived] at a world named Ratnavaṛṇa.
It was perfectly luminous and precious; therefore, it was called "Jewel" (ratna).
The Buddha’s name is Most Victorious Wisdom (*Jinshengzhi*).
He is called Most Victorious Wisdom because he can spur all practices.
Among his followers was a bodhisattva named Foremost in Diligence (*Jingzinshou*).
The True Teaching is profoundly deep; it must rely upon diligence.
[Together with] bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, [he went] to a world named Vajra-color.
Attaining the firmness and sharpness of Wenruo, one takes on the color of a vajra.
The Buddha’s name is Sovereign Wisdom (Svatantra-jñāna).
Only when one is able to practice within the Dharma does one attain sovereignty.
In that [world] there was a bodhisattva named Dharmottara.
Although dharma-gates are numerous, they must ultimately reside in right practice.
Together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, [he traveled] to a world named Crystal Color.
The essence of wisdom is pure, like crystal; it is transparent and unstained.
The Buddha’s name is Brahma-Wisdom (*Brahma-jñāna*);
because it can purify all practices, it is called Brahma-Wisdom.
In that [assembly] there was a bodhisattva named Jñānaśrī.
Although the Buddha’s aids to the path are immeasurable in their gateways, wisdom is the foremost among them.
Together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, [he went] to a world named Samavarṇa.
Because the fundamental nature is observed as being eternally equal, the Buddha is named Wisdom of Observation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). Among them is a bodhisattva named Bhadramukha (Worthy Face).
From the Buddhas of the past to the Buddhas of the future, there is a single path of purity; because of this inherent goodness, he is called "Worthy" (*bhadra*). He is able to know this.
Worthy one, this is the power of observation.
[The ten bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-fields,] proceed until they sit cross-legged upon lion thrones.
Furthermore, among the ten Buddhas, immovability is the essence, while all others are its functions. Among the ten bodhisattvas, the text...
The "Distinguished" (Viśiṣṭa) is the general [category], while all the others are specific. Since the general guides the specific, the nine bodhisattvas do not depart from Wondrous Virtue (Mañjuśrī).

Following this precedent established by what precedes and follows, I have briefly provided this explanation; one should simply empty oneself to seek it therein. If one does not believe in this principle, [it will remain unapprehended].
What concern is this profound Dharma-gate of mine?
*The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Nineteen;
*The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Twenty (entering the fourth page of the thirteenth scripture).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang;
recorded and annotated on the sutra by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.
△ Fourth, Mañjuśrī’s verbal response. First, praising the rarity of the assembly.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva [arrived]. These bodhisattvas were truly rare and extraordinary.
As for why the Buddha, when the assembly had previously raised their doubts, commanded Mañjuśrī to answer them: it was because Mañjuśrī manifested his residence in this land;

he possesses the ten signs of birth; he has come from another direction; his essence contains the myriad virtues; he subdues Māras and restrains outsiders; his eloquence is unfathomable; and he transforms sentient beings.

Pervading every direction of the dust-motes, its influence encompasses the three periods of time. Having realized the Way in a previous kalpa, he was already titled the Honored King of the Dragon Lineage;
now, manifesting the realization of Bodhi, he is further called Maṇiratnasañcaya. He is truly the Mother of the Buddhas of the Three Times; how could he be merely the teacher of Śākyamuni?
Following his radiance and influence, all beings behold him alike. Therefore, regarding his teaching, why wait for an invitation? His reverence is equal [to that of all].

Because it is the Buddha; why then would he not wait for an announcement? It is by receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and because the Buddha’s intention has granted permission that, once the assembly has mentally made their request, the Buddha then manifests his signs.
Were it not for a Great Being of supreme dignity, how could there be such a profound and secret resonance with principle? Thus, above, Samantabhadra was shown by means of light;
this is the subtle empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) bestowed upon Miaode (Ghoṣadatta). If this is so, why did Samantabhadra make a further request after the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) had ended?

The *Vyākhyāyukti* states that because what is believed is extremely profound and subtle, why would one not enter meditative absorption? This is because the fruit follows from the cause, as they are identical in their convergence with faith.
The rest is as explained above. Why is there no additional [explanation]? Because there is no fixed [rule]. Furthermore, it is by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

This is due to the power of the profound spiritual influence (*adhiṣṭhāna*). There are briefly five meanings for praising the rarity of the assembly: first, because the resonance between cause and response is remote and difficult to encounter;
second, because their virtuous conduct is fully realized within, and thus they are praised collectively; third, because names are used to manifest the Dharma, which is exceedingly rare;
fourth, because the initial arising of faith and practice is unprecedented; and fifth, because this single assembly is itself an assembly equal to the empty *dharmadhātu*.
△ Second, the summary of the questions and general praise:
"O sons of the Buddha, the buddha-fields are inconceivable... [up to] the three types of awakening are all inconceivable.
Regarding the manifestation of the Buddhas apart from the substance of the lands (*kṣetra*), this refers to the aforementioned majestic virtue. *A* means "non-" (*na*). *Anuttara*...
"Anuttara" (Supreme) means "above all. "Samyak" (Right) means "correct. "Sambodhi" (Perfect Enlightenment) means "pervasive. Furthermore, "three" refers to the threefold pervasiveness.

"Bodhi" means "awakening," signifying that the Way cannot be further added to; thus it is called "Supreme" (Anuttara). To know without deviation or partiality is "Right Pervasiveness" (Samyak-sambodhi).
△ Third, the inquiry, praise, and general explanation.
Why is this? This interrogates the aforementioned "inconceivable" statement. The subsequent explanation states:
"O Sons of the Buddha, all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions know that the inclinations and desires of sentient beings are diverse."
The capacities that can be moved are infinitely diverse; the Tathāgata responds universally, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
This vastness is inconceivable, as fully revealed by the concluding verses.
They teach the Dharma to subdue beings according to what is appropriate for them, and they teach the Dharma according to what is suitable; their underlying intentions are inconceivable.
In this manner, they continue until they equal the realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space.

Furthermore, regarding "equality with the Dharma-realm": by citing a single teaching, one equals all other numerous gateways; these gateways are inexhaustible, their measure equaling the Dharma-realm, and these Dharma-gates are inconceivable.
△ Fourth, extensively revealing the inconceivable, in two parts: first, a general revelation of its many aspects.

O Sons of the Buddha, regarding these four continents within this Sahā world, the Tathāgata first takes the Sahā world as the primary example to briefly manifest ten kinds of distinctions that are manifold in their variety. Following the concluding summary below, these actually pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
Within these ten phrases, nothing is excluded from the three types of action (trikarma).
Regarding various bodies:
a single body constitutes the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Because it manifests as the differences of the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), it is called "various. Various names.
The second is called "invoking reality through names. This will be extensively analyzed below.
Third, there are differences in various colors and forms, such as gold and silver, and distinctions in the thirty-two marks and so forth.
Various heights and statures:
their four physical forms range from three feet to sixteen feet, even up to being boundless.
There are various lifespans as well.
Fifth, the limit of the lifespan: it may be for immeasurable kalpas, or less than a hundred years, down to appearing in the morning and passing away in the evening;
thus there are various such locations.
The six bases refer to the bases of transformation, which differ according to their defiled or purified nature and consist of various faculties.
The seven faculties refer to the eye and so forth, which manifest differently according to individual karmic retribution.
There are various places of birth;
within the eight places of birth, there are distinctions such as the kṣatriya and others.
There are also various types of verbal karma.
Ninth, regarding the function of speech: according to various dialects and sounds, it is established in manifold ways through diverse observations.

Tenth, regarding circumambulating and looking about to respond to the capacities of all beings, one further observes their survival or demise, safety or peril, and what is permissible or forbidden, illuminating them with wisdom.
The various objects are shown in many ways so that all sentient beings may each have their own distinct knowledge and vision.
The commentary states: "Now, each sentient being, according to their own capacity, attains self-knowledge and vision, thereby achieving subduing."

△ Second, the detailed exposition according to the gates. This section is divided into three parts. First, up to the end of this chapter, there is the analysis of the distinctions among the names of the bodies, answering the question regarding the Buddha’s dwelling and extensively elaborating on the eight phrases such as "various bodies," since characteristics such as form all belong to the body.

Second, in the Chapter on the Four Truths, there is the analysis of the pervasiveness of the verbal teachings, answering the question regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha. [The third part follows] near...
Extensively elaborating upon various verbal activities: the third section, "The Chapter on the Awakening of Radiant Light," describes the luminous wheel of light that shines exhaustively.
It answers the three aforementioned questions regarding majestic virtue, the *dharmatā*, and bodhi. It extensively elaborates on various observations;

as for its five phrases concerning the secondary environment (*pratyaya*), they merely respond by manifesting their signs, as these were already extensively explained in the previous assembly. Now, first, to elaborate upon the aforementioned names: yet, for the sages, there are no names.

Names are established for things. If they are established according to their virtues, those virtues are boundless; if they are established according to circumstances, they are equal to the realm of sentient beings.
Although there are many such types, all are established as appropriate for generating goodness and extinguishing evil, and are based upon the realization of principle.
The Ocean Seal manifests instantaneously; one should not give rise to attachment. The text has four parts. First, within this Sahā world-system, there are naturally ten billion [worlds].
Regarding the first, these four continents, each passage consists of three sections.
O Sons of the Buddha, regarding why the Tathāgata designates these four continents within this world-system of four continents:

formerly it was said that the intention was to take Jambudvīpa as the primary focus; thus, while the words are general, the meaning is specific, because the Buddha does not appear in the other three continents.
Nevertheless, although he does not appear there, with the exception of Uttarakuru, it is possible for him to dwell in the others. Below, all...
Following this, the names are listed.
One name is Sarvārthasiddha, which is Siddhārtha;
for there is no matter that he does not accomplish.
He is sometimes called the Full Moon,
for his delusions are severed and his wisdom is perfected, providing the cooling shade of his grace;
he is also called the Lion’s Roar.
He is named "Definitive Explanation" (Niyata-vyākaraṇa). Alternatively, he is named Śākyamuni.
"Śākya" means "Capable One" (Śakya), because he belongs to the Śākya clan. "Muni" means "Silent One" (Maunī), because he accords with the principle of tranquility.
He is sometimes called the Seventh Sage because he is the last of the Seven Buddhas.
If one takes the perspective of the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Aeon), he is simply the fourth. "Sage" is a metaphor, as he is free from the defilement of desire.
He is also named Vairocana,
as explained extensively above;
he is also named Gautama.

This refers exclusively to the clan name (*gotra*). Here it is called "Lord of the Earth" (*Dharaṇīndra*), because from the beginning of the kalpa, they have been inherited generation after generation as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*).
However, what was mentioned above as "Śākya" refers to the ancestral lineage; this [term] refers to the clan name.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states: "The clan name of Śākyamuni is Gautama. The *Buddhanāmasūtra* is likewise.
He is also called the Great Śramaṇa;
this is translated as "the one who has stilled evil. Since there is no evil that he does not still, he is further titled "Great.
He is also called the Most Victorious.
Because he is the ultimate among the noble ones and his virtues are unsurpassed, he is called the "Teacher" (*śāstṛ*).
He guides sentient beings so they may leave behind perilous difficulties, and he reveals the various jewels within the ocean of birth and death. Thus, the name contains [these meanings].
There are many meanings. I shall briefly explain these ten; fearing that the text might become overly prolix, the remainder shall be explained only as needed.
In this manner, these ten [thousand] items cause all sentient beings to each have their own distinct knowledge and vision.
Summary. △ Second, the ten realms adjacent to each of the four continents, which constitute ten sections. First, the eastern direction:
the location is indicated, the names are listed, and the summary follows the previous example.
O Sons of the Buddha, to the east of these four continents, there is a world called Well-Protected (Sugupta).
This is the general designation for the four continents; the others are all to be understood in this manner.
There, the Tathāgata is sometimes named Vajra and sometimes named Chinnapravāda.
Because it is realized as being beyond words, and because there is no one capable of criticizing it—
through such means numbering ten thousand, he causes all sentient beings to each have individual knowledge and vision.
△ Second, the southern direction.
O Sons of the Buddha, in this southern continent of Jambudvīpa (extending as far as the Tathāgata), he is there sometimes named Śakra,
the Lord of Gods and Men, who is able to accord with the minds of sentient beings.
Some call him Ratnayaśas, some call him Vimala (up to: causing all sentient beings to each have their own distinct knowledge and vision.
△ Third, the West.
O Sons of the Buddha, to the west of these four continents (up to: the Tathāgata there is called Varuṇadeva.

It benefits all things; because its celestial light is pure, it is called "Joyful to Behold" or "Supreme King," [and so on] until: it causes all sentient beings to each have their own distinct knowledge and vision.
△ Fourth, the northern direction.
O Sons of the Buddha, to the north of these four continents (up to) there is a land called Airāvaṇa.
In full, it is called Airāvaṇa. *Airā* means "sovereign" (*īśvara*), and *vaṇa* means "sound."
This is the sovereign power of the perfect sound (*pariṣphuṭa-svara*).
It is also called the "Supreme Gift" or "Austere Practice," [extending] until it causes all sentient beings to each individually perceive and know.
△ 5. Northeastern Quarter.
O Sons of the Buddha, in this northeastern quarter of the four continents... [omitted] ...causing all sentient beings to each individually know and see.

O Sons of the Buddha, from this four-continent world in the southeast... [omitted] ...causing all sentient beings to each have distinct knowledge and vision.

O Sons of the Buddha, from this four-continent world in the southwest... [omitted] ...causing all sentient beings to each have distinct knowledge and vision.
△ 8. Northwest. O sons of the Buddha, these four continents in the northwest... (extending to) causing all sentient beings to each have distinct knowledge and vision. △ 9. Below.
Sons of the Buddha, next below these four continents, [down to] causing all sentient beings to each have distinct knowledge and vision.
△ Tenth, the Upper Direction.
Sons of the Buddha, next above these four continents, [up to] some are named "Like a Blazing Fire."
As a raging fire consumes firewood without discriminating among the trees and forests, so does the Buddha’s wisdom benefit sentient beings without selecting between the worthy and the foolish.
Whether they are called upholders of the precepts or followers of the One Path, it causes all sentient beings to each attain their own distinct knowledge and vision.
Question: Other holy teachings state that within the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains, ten billion [worlds] are spread out horizontally, with the various heavens above and the hells situated below.
How can this [text] say that there are four continents both above and below? Answer: What is taught in this scripture is such that phenomena accord with principle and are harmoniously integrated.
Wherever the teaching is expounded is considered the center; even if one reaches the very zenith vertically and extends laterally to the Cakravāḍa Mountains, it remains so.

There are the ten directions, which act as mutual leaders and companions, unified as a retinue. Their fundamental number is not many; the fusion of the worlds of the ten directions is likewise based on this.
Therefore, this is explained briefly. Regarding the integration of the Sahā world, there are five general ways in which its unchanging and changing aspects are transformed:
first, that which is fixed according to phenomena, as taught in the Hīnayāna; second, that which is seen differently according to the mind, such as by Śāriputra.

First, regarding the Brahma King: from the perspective of the Buddha, it is fundamentally neither pure nor defiled. Second, it revolves according to the Dharma, as described above in the mutual relationship between the principal and its attendants.
Third, it penetrates into every atom, as previously explained in the assembly. If discussed in general terms, there are five further meanings for all other pure lands:
namely, the meaning of the mutual entry of all lands, the meaning of their mutual identity, and the meaning of one containing all.
The meaning of the mastery over breadth and narrowness, and the meaning of the overlapping Indra’s net, are both as explained in the various preceding and following passages.
△ Third, the summary of Sahā World:
"O Children of the Buddha, this Sahā World... (up to)... causes all sentient beings to each have their own distinct knowledge and vision."
△ Second, the neighboring worlds of Sahā. These are located beyond the ten billion [worlds]. The text covers the ten directions. First, the eastern direction:
it indicates the location, lists the names, and provides a summary; each subsequent direction follows this same pattern.
"O Sons of the Buddha, from this Sahā world to the east... [and so on].

As for why only nine names are listed—namely, those ending with "Incomparable Wisdom" (Asamajñāna)—a comparison with the Jin translation reveals that one instance of "Hearing-Wisdom" (Śrutamayī-prajñā), following the section on "Opening and Clarifying the Meaning," is missing.
In this way, these hundreds of billions of various names cause all sentient beings to know and see them individually.
△ Second, the South.
O Sons of the Buddha, from this Sahā world to the south... [omitted] ...some are named Original Nature, some are named Diligent Mind.
The names listed are only two; both the new and old sūtras alike omit eight names. This must surely be due to omissions in the Sanskrit original.
Judging by preceding and succeeding examples, it is certain that this alone should not be abbreviated.
In this way, these hundreds of billions of various names cause all sentient beings to know and see them individually.
△ Third, the West.
O Sons of the Buddha, from this Sahā world to the west... [causing all sentient beings to know and see them individually].
△ Fourth, the northern direction.
O Sons of the Buddha, from this Sahā world to the north... [omitted] ...causing all sentient beings to each have distinct knowledge and vision.
△ Fifth, the northeastern direction.
O Sons of the Buddha, in the northeastern direction of this Sahā world... [omitted] ...causing all sentient beings to each have distinct knowledge and vision.
△ Sixth, the Southeastern Direction.
O Sons of the Buddha, in the southeastern direction of this Sahā world... [omitted] ...causing all sentient beings to each have distinct knowledge and vision.
△ 7. Southwest: O Sons of the Buddha, from this Sahā world toward the southwest... [omitted] ...causing all sentient beings to each have distinct knowledge and vision. △ 8. Northwest.
O sons of the Buddha, in the northwestern direction from this Sahā world—[up to] it is named *Dharmanidhyapti* (Fixation on the Dharma), or it is named *Jālapraticchanna* (Enveloped by a Net).
Regarding the eleven names: [the phrase] "only this has the remainder" does not constitute a complete textual structure; herein, *dharmanidhyapti* is appropriate.

This is precisely the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) previously released; it is also a leakage from the Sanskrit original. As for those who noted these omissions, they mistakenly placed them upon the palm leaves.
In this way, through hundreds of millions of various names and titles, all sentient beings are led to have distinct cognitions and views.
△ Ninth, the lower direction.
O Sons of the Buddha, in this Sahā world, proceeding further downward [until] it is called "Indra’s Bow.
It is the bow of the Tathāgata’s mindfulness and concentration; because with its bright and sharp arrows, it can shoot the asuras of karma and afflictions. Thus it is.
The old translation says "Dharmajīvin," intending Śakra, because he rules as the Lord of Heaven through the commands of the Dharma.

The current version says "His Bow," referring only to a single object. If one uses the term "palace" (gong-shi), taking the location to represent the person, it is largely the same as the Jin edition.
Some are named "The Abode of Impermanence" and some are named "Awakening to the Source" (extending to) causing all sentient beings to each have distinct knowledge and vision.
△ Tenth, the Upper Direction:
O Children of the Buddha, in this Sahā world, next in the upper direction (extending to) causing all sentient beings to each have distinct knowledge and vision.
△ The third category applies universally to all. That is to say, throughout the ten directions:
"O sons of the Buddha, as it is in this Sahā world, so it is likewise in the four intermediate directions and above and below."

Following the "Chapter on the Four Truths," this point is further raised; by analogy with other directions throughout the ten quarters, they are likewise like the Sahā world, mutually serving as both primary and secondary.
△ Fourth, explaining the reasons for these distinctions.
As when the World-Honored One was formerly a bodhisattva, [he taught] up to such knowledge and vision while preaching the Dharma.

This is because he accords with sentient beings; herein there are two intentions. First, since he himself has already attained accomplishment through various conventional designations and so forth, he now likewise follows the ancient example to mature others by means of these distinctions. Second, when he was formerly a bodhisattva, he [taught] according to the capacities of beings.
Regarding the harmonizing of beings: at the present time, he appears in the world and establishes names according to his original nature.

Just as in the past he taught sentient beings to empty out delusory objects, now that he has attained perfect enlightenment, he establishes names that transcend such realms. Others all follow this pattern, thereby attaining the expression "bringing to maturity," which applies to both oneself and others.
Chapter Eight: The Four Noble Truths.
△ An explanation of this chapter is provided through a fivefold analysis.

First, regarding the intent of its inclusion: this chapter elaborates upon the various types of vocal karma mentioned previously, thereby answering the prior question concerning the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.

This also serves as a distant response to the previous question regarding the ocean of teachings expounded by the Buddhas of the past assemblies. Having known that the Buddha is worthy of taking refuge in, one next knows that the Dharma is worthy of looking up to.
The former name was established according to the nature of things; now, the Dharma follows the differences in the capacities of sentient beings. Therefore, it follows [the discussion of] the Buddha.

Second, the explanation of the names. Regarding the term "Four Noble Truths" (*catur-ārya-satya*): "Noble" (*ārya*) means correct. It refers to the untainted, correct Dharma because it is attained within the mind.
"Truth" (*satya*) has two meanings: first, reality; second, thorough examination. As for "reality," this is distinguished in terms of the object.

That is to say, it does not deviate from the characteristics as they have been described, because it is real, because it is true, and because it is definitive. This refers to the world... [text continues]
The two kinds of supramundane causes and effects are necessarily devoid of falsehood and cannot be mistaken. To say they are "truths" (*satya*) refers to their clarity through wisdom;

for when noble wisdom contemplates them, it finds them to be strictly non-false. Although ordinary beings possess suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), these are not strictly real to them and thus cannot be called truths.
Because unerring noble wisdom knows the objects with strict certainty, they are called the Noble Truths (*āryasatya*). Therefore...

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 95, states: "They are called truths (*satya*) for two reasons: first, by way of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*); second, by way of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

Worldly fools possess the former but not the latter; the noble ones (*ārya*) possess both. Therefore, they are universally designated as 'Noble Truths' (*āryasatya*). The four are suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
collectively they are termed the 'Four Noble Truths,' which is an explanatory compound based on number (*saṃkhyā-vigraha*). What are their nature and characteristics? Oppression is called..."
Suffering refers to contaminated form and mind. Its increase is called origination, which refers to karma and afflictions. Cessation is called quiescence, meaning nirvana.
The path is called renunciation, meaning calm abiding, insight, and so forth. This is explained according to their characteristics and applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Hīnayāna, the three [truths] have the characteristic of existence (*sa-lakṣaṇa*), while cessation (*nirodha*) is without characteristics (*a-lakṣaṇa*).

In the Mahāyāna, all four noble truths are without characteristics. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "To understand suffering as being without suffering is called the Noble Truth of Suffering; this means to realize that it arises from the four conditions."

When one is empty, one transcends the fishing trap; when one awakens to the essential principle, one achieves greatness. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Ordinary beings have suffering but no truth (*satya*);
those of the two vehicles have both suffering and truth, yet lack reality; Bodhisattvas have neither suffering nor truth, yet possess reality.
This means that if suffering were itself the truth, how could the sufferings of the three miserable realms be the truth? Although the followers of the two vehicles examine and know [this],...

...yet they do not penetrate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and do not perceive the ultimate reality. Furthermore, although those of the Two Vehicles know the characteristics of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*), they do not know its immeasurable characteristics.
Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "Suffering has immeasurable characteristics, which are not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* says that there are one hundred and ten [characteristics] of suffering. Nevertheless, although these names differ in this sūtra, they are in fact [the same].
The expressed meanings differ, for names necessarily summon their corresponding realities; this is the meaning of the immeasurable Four Noble Truths.
Taking a single realm and a single truth as a basis, there are ten thousand *saha* worlds; thus, the Four Noble Truths possess four hundred billion times ten thousand names and meanings.

These texts and meanings are comprehensive and vast, encompassing both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). When one thoroughly investigates these four truths through the text, they are not merely emptiness alone, but constitute the ultimate reality.
Truly, now one realizes that the aggregates and sense bases are all suchness (*tathatā*). There is no suffering to be abandoned; ignorance and the afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves bodhi.
There is no origin to be severed; birth and death are themselves nirvāṇa. There is no cessation to be realized; extremes and deviations are all the Middle Way. There is no path to be cultivated.
Where there is no suffering and no origin, there is no mundane world. Where there is no cessation and no path, there is no supramundane.
In this interval, there is neither grasping nor abandoning; it is the single ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Therefore, within this one category, both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as well as the finite and the infinite, are all contained therein. According to the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), these are further examined through ten aspects, which shall be clarified below.
Regarding the three aspects of the fundamental tenets (*śāstrārtha*): based on the boundless ocean of truths, names are established differently according to faculties and meanings.

Throughout the entire world-system, these constitute the fundamental tenet; the objective is to benefit sentient beings, and the purpose is the harmonious cultivation of life. Furthermore, both of the aforementioned [aspects] constitute the fundamental tenet.
The arising of pure faith serves as the vehicle.

Fourth, the removal of obstacles: since difficult questions have been clearly set forth, the Buddha responds with his verbal activity by expounding the Dharma. Question: The Dharma taught by the Buddha has many gates;

why does he present only the Four Noble Truths? Answer: Although the names belong to the Hīnayāna, their meaning extends to both the Great and Small Vehicles, encompassing both phenomena and principle.
It is complete. This means that the two truths of suffering and its origin are the worldly cause and effect; they are to be known and abandoned, and because they are unchanging, they are established.
The two truths of cessation and the path are the supramundane cause and effect; they are to be realized and cultivated, and because these matters are definitive, they are established.

Through knowing, abandoning, realizing, and cultivating, one is able to transport sentient beings to the other shore. While the world undergoes change, this alone remains unchanging; how much more so, then?

There is no limit and no effort [required to encompass it]. What meaning would not be included? Therefore, by means of this, the distinctions are revealed. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of refuting false attachments and guiding sentient beings:

that is to say, by expounding the limited Dharma of the Four Truths for those Śrāvakas, one causes them to abandon their attachments and leads them into the boundless ocean of truths of the One Vehicle;
thus, these distinctions are established. Why do all four truths carry the term "suffering"? It is said:

Regarding the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering and so forth: because it is the origin (*samudaya*) that gives rise to suffering, it is called the "Origin of Suffering" (*duḥkha-samudaya*). The cessation (*nirodha*) that exhausts suffering is named the "Cessation of Suffering" (*duḥkha-nirodha*).
Reaching the path to the cessation of suffering is named the "Path to the Cessation of Suffering" (*duḥkha-nirodha-mārga*); one cannot speak of it simply as the "Path of Suffering."

Because the Path does not produce suffering, as it is not identical with origination; nor does it extinguish suffering, as it is not identical with cessation. Rather, it is that which can realize the extinction of suffering;
therefore, it is called the "Path to the Extinction of Suffering."
The fifth section, the "Correct Explanation of the Text," consists of two parts. First, the introductory address:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
△ Second, the formal explanation has four parts: first, the names of the *satya* (realms) of Sahā; second, the ten adjacent realms; third, the general application to all [realms];
and fourth, the infinite network of primary and attendant realms. Now, compared to the preceding chapter, this section is abbreviated regarding the separate mention of the four continents.
Within the first two [parts], for each of the directions, there are two sections: first, the specific name of each *satya*; second, the summary of the number and its analysis.
[Note: However, regarding the establishment of these names, some are designated by way of the effect based on the cause, while others take the name of the cause based on the effect.

Whether categorized according to phenomena (*dharma*) or principles (*tattva*), and whether collectively or individually, they should be understood as they appear in the text. First, within the Sahā world-system, the four internal truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*) are enumerated, which constitute four distinct sections.
First is the Noble Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-āryasatya*).
O sons of the Buddha, this Noble Truth of Suffering is called "guilt" (pāpa) in this Sahā world;
"guilt" means to crush, for it refers to the crushing and destruction of both form and mind.
It is also called "oppression."
Unpleasant mental objects oppress the body and mind; these two together manifest what is generally termed "the suffering of change" (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
It is also called "clinging to objects," "the suffering of pursuit," or "the accumulation."
The suffering of the five aggregates of clinging is also called "thorns";
this name is established by way of analogy, just as when a thorn has not yet been extracted.
It is also called "relying on the faculties," because suffering can give rise to all evils;
it is also called "deceptive."
Within lower suffering, one can give rise to the perception of pleasure;

this is also called the site of an ulcer or abscess, which serves as a metaphor for the two types of suffering. Where there is an ulcer or abscess, its very nature is suffering, just like the suffering of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). If [to that] further...
Contact by the hands and so forth, which adds suffering upon suffering, is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

It is also called the "practice of the foolish" (*bāla-carita*), which refers to the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), because it is the practice of fools. It is like not perceiving a hair placed on the palm of the hand, yet perceiving it if placed in the eye.
Internally, one suffers from unease. Yet the fool does not perceive this pervasive suffering (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), which is like hair on the palm of one's hand;
instead, they seek to abandon suffering because it is suffering. All such actions are the conduct of a fool. △ Second, the Noble Truth of the Origin (*samudaya-satya*).
O Sons of the Buddha, regarding the Noble Truths of Suffering and its Origin (up to the Truth of Cessation), they are also termed "bondage" or "destruction.
The first two [truths] reveal this universally: that those possessing karma and afflictions are bound to the three realms and destroy their roots of goodness.
Alternatively, they are called "the sense of attachment" or "deluded conceptualization.
The next two specifically reveal the afflictions;
alternatively, they are called "entry," or "determination," or "concomitance," or "the root of perversion."
The remainder mostly consists of pervasive karma and afflictions. △ Third, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering:
O Sons of the Buddha, this Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is, in this Sahā world, also called "Non-contention" (araṇa).
The afflictions (*kleśa*) are called "contention" (*raṇa*).
They are also called "separation from dust" (*viraja*), or "tranquility" (*śānti*), up to being called "cessation" (*nirodha*) or "the reality of essence" (*bhūtatathatā*).
As for "reality," it does not consist merely in the extinction of delusions; rather, it is the eternally abiding *dharmakāya*, which constitutes the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
This is the meaning. Therefore, it is next stated that they "abide in their own nature" (*svabhāva-vyavasthita*), because they are originally extinguished.
Alternatively, they are called "abiding in their own nature.
△ Fourth, the Noble Truth of the Path (*mārga-āryasatya*).
O Sons of the Buddha, the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering is also called the "Practice of the Rishis" or the "Ten Treasuries.
The Ten Treasuries refer to faith, hearing, and so forth, as explained in the "Chapter on the Ten Treasuries. △ Second, the conclusion of the enumeration and the clarification of its intent.
O Sons of the Buddha, in this Sahā world, there are as many as four hundred *koṭis* of ten thousand names [for the Truths].

Compared to the previous enumeration of names—wherein one set of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*) had ten thousand names—now, within a single set of four worlds (*cāturmahādvīpaka*), each Truth (*satya*) likewise has ten thousand kinds of names.
Since the Four Truths (*catuḥsatya*) are applied across ten billion worlds (*koṭi*), there are thus four hundred *koṭis* of ten thousand names.

"To subdue all according to the minds of sentient beings" reveals the meaning of their distinct differences. △ Second, distinguishing the neighboring directions of the ten quarters. Regarding the "Secret Instruction on the East," there are two parts.
First, listing four [truths]. First, the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
O Sons of the Buddha, in this Sahā world—[from "up to"]—some call it "Analysis," yet none have the power [to analyze it];
when pushed back to its conditions, it is found to be no substantial entity.
Some call it "The Basis of Action," some "Extreme Suffering," some "Agitation," and some "Material Form."
Because all that has form is suffering. △ Second, the Truth of Origination:
"O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Origination of Suffering" (up to) "is also named attachment or the source of illness."
The source of illness refers to the existence of objective referents (*ālambana*);
it is also termed "names and numbers.
△ Third, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (up to its other names): it is also called "subduing" or "a portion.
Because delusions arise from false conceptualization, they are divided into parts as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; yet in principle, they cannot be divided, and thus may be termed "a portion."
It is sometimes called "faultless," sometimes called "free from craving," and sometimes called "definitive.
△ Fourth, the Noble Truth of the Path:

O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the cessation of suffering (up to) is sometimes called "the fierce general" and sometimes called "the supreme practice."
That which is reached is cessation (*nirodha*).
It is also called "transcendence" (*vyutkrānta*), or "possessing skillful means" (*upāyayukta*), or "supreme eye" (*paramacakṣus*), or "contemplating the directions" (*dig-vilokana*).

"Contemplating the directions" refers to contemplating the Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*). There are further four directions, as described in the "Chapter on the Ten Concentrations" (*Daśasamādhiparivarta*). △ Second, the conclusion.
The Buddhas’ Sons secretly instruct the world (up to: causing all sentient beings to be fully tamed according to their own minds.
△ Second, the Southern Most Victorious [Land]. Part One: Listing the Four. First, Suffering.
O Sons of the Buddha, what is called the Noble Truth of Suffering in this Sahā world is termed "Abundance" (Puṇyavardhana) in that World of the Most Victorious.
"Abundance" is the direct translation, while "Most Victorious" is merely a translation based on its meaning.
It is called "terror," or "segmentation" (up to), or "erroneous discrimination," or "possessing power.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death are like four mountains closing in upon a person; though one may be a worthy hero in this world, no strength can compete with them. △ Second, the Collection.
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (up to its various names) is also termed "the adversary" or "that which is not one's own property.
One's own fundamental nature is pure; how could delusive confusion have anything to do with it?
It is also called "evil guidance," "increasing darkness," or "destroying wholesome benefit.
△ Third, the Cessation [of Suffering]:
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (extending to) is also called "beneficial" or "the meaning within meanings."
In terms of its function, it is virtuous and meaningful; in terms of its principle of cessation, it is even more excellent.
It may be called "immeasurable," or "that which should be seen," or "that with which one may dwell together," or "unconditioned."

△ Four Paths. O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (up to) is also named "the ability to incinerate," because it burns away afflictions with the fire of wisdom.
It is called the supreme grade of accomplishment, or the definitive [attainment], or the nature of liberation, or that which is capable of delivering [beings].
△ Second, the conclusion:
O Sons of the Buddha, in the most excellent world, the Four Noble Truths are taught to bring all sentient beings to subdual according to their respective minds.
△ Third, the second section on the Western Land of Freedom from Defilement. First, the enumeration of the four [realms]. First, suffering:
"O Sons of the Buddha, in this Sahā world... (up to) it is also called 'False View' or 'Innumerable.'"
"Without number" means that the three periods of time have no limit. △ Second, the Accumulation:
"O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Accumulation of Suffering... (up to) ...is also named 'the base and lowly' or 'increase.'"
Because afflictions give rise to further afflictions and karma,
they are called "heavy burdens," "producers," or "coarse and wild.
△ Third, cessation.
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (up to its full extent) is also named the Supreme Faculty, or it is named the Convergence.
It is called "convergence" because it is the convergence of phenomena with the cessation of their objects, and the convergence of phenomena with the cessation of their principles.
It is called "having no dependence," or "extinguishing delusions" (up to) "ultimate," or "breaking the seal.

The aggregates (*skandha*) of suffering in the world are like a wax seal pressed into clay: when the seal is broken, the impression is formed. As soon as these aggregates cease, those aggregates arise in succession.
What is now called "breaking the seal" means they will never arise again. △ Fourth, the Path (*mārga*).
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (up to its other names) is also termed "the limit of all existence" (*bhavānta*).
When reality is illuminated, birth and death can be exhausted. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

"Because the true Dharma, the speaker, and the listener are difficult to encounter, therefore, regarding birth and death, there is neither finitude nor infinity. This means that these three factors are difficult to encounter.
It is not that there is a limit. That which is difficult to attain may yet be attained; if it is attained, then birth and death will have an end.
Alternatively, it is called "receiving a full entrustment":
karma is entrusted to the Truth of Accumulation (samudaya), where it is temporarily received and then vanishes; karma is entrusted to the Path (mārga), from which it can never be lost.
It is also called "Ultimate Accomplishment" or "Pure Discernment.
△ Second, the conclusion:
"O Sons of the Buddha, in the world-system Free from Defilement, the Four Noble Truths are taught (up to: causing all sentient beings to be fully tamed according to their own minds."
△ Fourth, the Abundance of the Northern Quarter, in two parts. First, the enumeration of the four truths. First, suffering:
"O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of Suffering in this Sahā world is, in that world of Abundance, [the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering]."
"Abundance" (*Puṇyavat*) is a name from the southern region. In the preceding chapter, this direction was called "Abundant Joy" (*Puṇyavardhana*).

In Sanskrit, it is *Pūrvavideha* (the *deha* being pronounced with the *ti* rhyme). "Abundant Joy" captures the essential meaning, whereas the translator was not careful and merely conflated the two names.
It is called the locus of attachment and defilement, or the root of perilous harm, or a portion of the ocean of existence—
referring to one part of each of the twenty-five states of existence.
It is also called the accumulation of formations, or the root of differentiation (up to), or that which is constituted by enumeration.
The essence of number is itself accumulation (*saṃcaya*), because it is that which is formed by accumulation. △ Second, Accumulation:
"O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Accumulation of Suffering" (extending to) "is also named 'the inexhaustible' or 'the numerical division.'"
Regarding these categories: if there were not a single principle to unify them, then delusions and karma would differ in ten thousand ways.
Some are called "unlovely," while others are called "capable of seizing and biting.
"Seizing" (*jué*) means to clutch; "biting" (*shì*) means to gnaw. Their collective harm is like that of malevolent birds and beasts.
It is sometimes called coarse and vulgar things, sometimes called attachment, sometimes called vessels, and sometimes called movement.
△ Third, Cessation.
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (up to) is also called "that which is not to be cultivated."
Because cultivation has reached its ultimate limit,
it is called "having nothing to see," or "having nothing to do," or "having already eliminated and destroyed.
△ Fourth, the Path (mārga).
O sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (up to) is also named "Immeasurable Life.
This refers to the realization of cessation, which is eternally constant; it is now designated by the name of its fruit.
It is called "Thoroughly Understanding," or "The Ultimate Path," or "Invincible.
△ Second, the conclusion:
"O Sons of the Buddha, in the overflowing world, the Four Noble Truths are taught (until) all sentient beings are brought to subjection according to their minds."
△ Fifth, the two [realms] of the Northeastern Quarter. First, the listing of four. First, Suffering:
"O Sons of the Buddha, this Sahā world... (up to) ...is called various conceptual proliferations, or it is called the nature of hell."
Prior to entering the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), there is always a tendency toward falling back;
this may be termed "non-substantiality," or "the burden of desire," or "fundamental emptiness.

These are identical when explained in terms of their essential nature, which corresponds to Vimalakīrti’s thorough penetration of the emptiness of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). △ Second, the Collection.
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (up to its further names): it is called "the swift" or "that which is able to grasp.
Because of delusive confusion, the rākṣasīs of craving and views perversely seize and grasp it.
It may be called "conceptualization," or "having fruit," or "that which is ineffable," or "that which is ungraspable.

Since the essence of delusion is fundamentally empty, there is nothing that can be grasped. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Regarding this deceptive false grasping, what is there to be grasped therein?
The Buddha taught such a Dharma desiring to demonstrate the meaning of emptiness."
Or it is called "transmigration.
△ Third, Cessation:
"O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering" (up to) "or it is called 'distancing from evil,' or it is called 'renunciation.'"
△ Fourth, the Path.

Regarding what the sons of the Buddha call the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (up to): "It is subsumed within the world, or it is called 'beyond words' (*nirabhilāpya*).
As for both cessation and the path being called "beyond words": the nature of cessation is beyond words; the path causes one to leave behind words.
It is called "Non-contention," or "Instruction" (up to) "Supreme Wisdom," or "Ability to Comprehend the Meaning.
△ Second, the conclusion:
"O Sons of the Buddha, by grasping the world, they preach the Four Noble Truths (up to) causing all sentient beings to be tamed according to their minds."
△ Section Six: The Two Benefits in the Southeastern Quarter. First, the enumeration of the four [realms]. First, suffering:
"O Sons of the Buddha, in this Sahā world... (omitted)... it is also called 'Non-firm' or 'Like a Thief'."
The five aggregates of clinging are suffering because they harm and injure me;
they are called old age and death, or the product of craving, or growth and birth, or the sharp blade of suffering.

△ Second, the Truth of the Origin of Suffering (*samudaya-āryasatya*). O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (extending to) is also named "retrogression" or "lack of power.
It possesses no strength or capacity for transcending birth and death. When it is governed by wholesome dharmas, it no longer opposes them.
It is called "loss" or "separation," up to being called "grasping" or "intention.
△ Third, Cessation:
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (up to) is called the "root" or the "cause of relinquishment."
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is without cause, yet its essence is the fruit. The path to enlightenment (*bodhi-mārga*), when viewed in relation to this, is also a cause;
only solitary *nirvāṇa* can be called the "fruit of fruits. Therefore, it is said that [the latter] abandons the cause.
It is sometimes called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and sometimes called the non-continuous (*anuprabandha*).
△ Fourth, the Path:
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (extending to) is sometimes called the Seal of All (*sarvamudrā*).
Because there is nothing that is not thoroughly examined and resolved. The meaning of the "seal" (mudrā) will be explained later.
It is also called the "Treasury of Samādhi," or "Attainment of Radiance," up to being called the "Root of Non-transmigration."
△ Second, the conclusion:
"O Sons of the Buddha, for the benefit of the world, [the Tathāgata] has preached the Four Noble Truths (up to) causing all sentient beings to be fully tamed according to their own minds.
△ Seventh, the second section on the Freshness of the Southwest. First, the listing of the four; first, suffering.
O sons of the Buddha, in this Sahā world (up to) it is called the Place of Bondage, or it is called Deviant Practice;
its essence is not the Right Path, because its nature is that of such practice.
It is sometimes called "Following Feeling," sometimes called "Lack of Shame or Remorse" (up to), sometimes called "The Nature of a Torch," or sometimes called "Abounding in Sorrow and Affliction.
△ Second, the Accumulation:
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Accumulation of Suffering is, in those rare worlds, sometimes called "Extensive Ground."
Because it gives rise to the tree of great suffering,
it is called "that which leads," "far-reaching wisdom" (or "reaching"), "that which attaches to a place," or "the master of the house.
The master of the house is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Or it is called "continuous bondage.
△ Third, Cessation:
"O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering" (up to) "or it is called 'the severance of the sphere of activity.'"
Because the path of the mind is severed,
it is called "non-dual.
△ Fourth, the Path.

O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (up to) is also named the "Vast Road," for both the sages of antiquity and the saints of later times have traveled upon it without weariness.
It is called the "Cause of Equality," or the "Pure Expedient Means," or the "Supreme Vision.
△ Second, the conclusion:
O Sons of the Buddha, in few worlds the Four Noble Truths are taught (up to) so as to discipline all sentient beings according to their minds.
△ Section Eight: The Joyful [Land] in the Northwest, Part Two. First, the enumeration of the four [realms]. First, Suffering:
"O Sons of the Buddha, this Sahā world... (omitted)... is also called 'Evil Dwelling' or 'Nature of Suffering and Affliction.'"
First, regarding omissions: the *Puyi* (Universal Translation) lacks the section on "arising," while the *Tangyi* (Tang Translation) lacks the section on "cessation. Second, regarding the collection:
"O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of Suffering and its Accumulation" (extending to) "is also called non-substantial phenomena, or called bottomless."
Because their afflictions are deep, they do not practice the training of the Path; they continue to drift and sink.
They are sometimes called "those who grasp," sometimes "those who abandon the precepts" (up to), sometimes "those with narrow and inferior views," and sometimes "those who are a mass of defilements."
△ Third, Cessation.
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (up to) is also named "the destruction of the basis.
Body and afflictions serve as mutual bases for one another in an endless cycle; only by realizing the principle of cessation can one [bring this to an end] forever.
It is called "Destruction," or "Heedfulness," or "Reality" (up to), or "Mastery," or "Non-arising.
△ Fourth, the Path.
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (up to) is also named "vast nature.
The path is called vast because there is nowhere it does not reach.
It is also called "Exhaustion of Discrimination," or "Divine Power" (up to), or "Encompassing Liberation.
△ Second, the conclusion:
"O Sons of the Buddha, in the world-system of Joyful Speech, the Four Noble Truths are taught (up to) so as to fully subdue all sentient beings according to their minds."
△ Ninth: The Lower Direction’s Barrier [Gate]. Part Two. First, the enumeration of the four. First, Suffering:
"O Sons of the Buddha, in this Sahā world... (omitted)... it is also called 'like a fragile vessel' or 'composed of what belongs to me.'"
Because I perceive its existence,
it is called the body of the various realms of existence (*gati*), or the numerical flow (*saṃsāra*), or the tasteless, or coming and going.
△ Second, the collection.
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (duḥkhasamudayasatya) is also termed the "limb of sensation" (vedanāṅga) or the "mind of self" (ātmacitta).
It is, in other words, the view of self and craving (ātmadṛṣṭi-tṛṣṇā). It is also termed "mixed with poison," "empty renown," "contrariety," "feverish affliction," or "trepidation."
△ Third, Cessation.
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (up to) is also named "Vast" or "Factor of Enlightenment," because it is the locus of awakening.
It is sometimes called "freedom from defilement" and sometimes called "absence of obstruction.
△ Fourth, the Path:

O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (up to) is sometimes called "ultimate reality" and sometimes called "the meaning of entry."
Because it is able to enter the ultimate truth of the cessation of suffering (*nirodha-satya*),
it is called "the ultimate nature" (*prakṛti-paryanta*), or "the manifestation of purity" (*viśuddhi-prabhāsa*), or "salvation" (*paritrāṇa*), or "supreme practice" (*agracaryā*).
△ Second, the conclusion:
"The sons of the Buddhas, in the world-system of the Gate-Keypad, preach the Four Noble Truths (up to) causing all sentient beings to be tamed according to their minds."
