△ Second, the Ten Directions: Vibration of Sound (Vijṛmbhita-ghoṣa). Part One: Listing the Four [Sufferings]. First, Suffering:
"O Sons of the Buddha, in this Sahā world... up to... in that world Vibration of Sound, it is called 'Concealing Faults' (Guhya-doṣa)."
Because it is the locus where the disease of delusion resides, it is called the "world" (*loka*), the "basis" (*āśraya*), or "pride" (*māna*).
Pride has the function of producing suffering; here, the name of the effect is applied to the cause.

It is also called the nature of defiled attachment, because its nature causes one to become attached. It is like the suffering inherent in the change of pleasant sensations; who would call that "suffering"?
It is also called a swift current.
Because it is momentary in nature, it is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
Alternatively, it is called "unpleasant," which is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*).
It is called "concealment" (*saṃvṛti*),

because it conceals the cause of suffering (*duḥkha-hetu*), because it conceals the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) within pleasure, and because it conceals the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) within that which is neither painful nor pleasant. Alternatively,
it is called "swift extinction" (*kṣipra-nirodha*).
This is the suffering of saṃsāra.
It is also called "difficult to tame.
Who would not wish to abandon it? Yet none are able to escape it. Only by not shrinking from weariness and suffering can one finally tame it. Part Two: Accumulation.
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (up to) is also named "reaching the ultimate limit.
It brings forth fruits without interruption, and the experience of suffering is inexhaustible.
It is also named "universal conjunction," "differentiation," or "gateway."
Because it enters the realms of suffering,
it is called "floating and moving" (pāta) or "concealing and covering" (channa).
△ Third, cessation (nirodha).
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (up to) is also named "the ungraspable.
If it is grasped, it does not cease.
It is also named "reversion," "freedom from contention," or "the small."
If it is made small, there is no interior; it cannot contain a single thing.
It may be called "Great.
If it is made great, there is no exterior; it is the nature of the Dharma-realm.
It is also called "Wholesome Purity," "Inexhaustible," "Vast and Expansive," or "Peerless.
△ Fourth, the Path:
O Sons of the Buddha, that which is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (extending to) is also called "Invincible."
Where there is delusion, it must be destroyed; one is not destroyed by delusion. It is like light extinguishing darkness: where there is no darkness, there is nothing for the light to extinguish;
yet darkness cannot extinguish light—how could they possibly oppose one another?
It is called "Infinite Meaning," or "Able to Enter Wisdom," or "Exalted Meaning.
△ Second, the conclusion:
O Sons of the Buddha, in the world-system Vimalasvara, the Four Noble Truths are taught (until) all sentient beings are brought to subdual according to their respective minds.
△ Section Three: The Three Categories Pervading Both [Realms]. First, Saha World is cited as a category for the Eastern [directions].
"O Sons of the Buddha, in this Saha world... (up to) causing all sentient beings to be tamed according to their minds."
△ Second, citing the eastern direction as an example to represent the remaining nine.
As it is with the east, so it is with the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
△ Fourth, the inexhaustibility of the primary and its associates (pramukha-parivāra). Part one: citing this case as an analogy for that.
O Sons of the Buddha, just as in the Sahā world there are the aforementioned worlds of the ten directions—
with the Sahā world as the principal and the worlds such as Guhyaka and so forth as its companions— so it is throughout all worlds that reach the limits of space. △ Second,
illustrating this by means of that.
In all those worlds, there are likewise [the Buddhas] who, according to the inclinations of their minds, bring about their subduing;

thus one knows that the Secret Instructions and so forth take the entirety of the world-systems as vast as space as their domain. The gathering of their retinues is likewise inexhaustible and inexhaustible.
This is still spoken of in reference to worlds similar to this Sahā world, for among the enumerated totals, they are equal in number to a hundred.

Because of these [ten] billions, there are other worlds of different types with various tree shapes and so forth; each of these types pervades all of space and extends throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
This constitutes a layer upon layer of inexhaustible infinity, which is not what is being described here.
All of this is for the purpose of taming sentient beings.
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Vaipulya,
Scroll Seventy-one (Entering the Lower Volume of the Forty-third Scripture),
composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jin Water. Commentary on the Sūtra with Annotations.
△ Second, the entry into the functioning of all dharmas, in four parts. First, clarifying the ten phrases of realization and entry.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters this wheel of wisdom of samādhi of great majestic power (*mahā-tejas*), the first phrase clarifies the meditative concentration that realizes it.
Although "samādhi-wheel of wisdom" (*samādhi-jñāna-cakra*) follows the Sanskrit word order, it should properly be rendered as "wheel of wisdom samādhi" (*jñāna-cakra-samādhi*).
Because this concentration is preeminent, it is named "of great majestic power. Next, the dharma realized is revealed; namely, realization...
Regarding the dharmas of the fruit of Buddhahood: first, there is a general clarification, which states that one is able to realize and attain all Buddha-dharmas;

the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*) serves as the realization, while the conditioned fruit (*saṃskṛta-phala*) is termed "attainment" (*prāpti*). The remaining eight phrases are specific distinctions.
One is then able to enter into all Buddha-dharmas;
by entering into and realizing them,
one is able to achieve accomplishment.
The accomplishment of the Śākya-attainment is thus able to fulfill [the requirements];
this fulfillment applies to both [types].
Then one is able to accumulate;
when accumulation reaches completion through its causes,
one is then able to purify.
Purity means the exhaustion of hindrances;
thus one is able to abide securely, and through meditative concentration, one is able to abide securely.
Then one is able to penetrate and comprehend; wisdom is that which penetrates and comprehends,
being in accord with the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

When both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) have vanished, one is in accord with the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); this constitutes realization and entry. △ Second, clarifying the characteristic of being free from realization:
yet this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not form such thoughts (up to) various inclinations or various realms.
Because it is realized precisely through non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*), one does not even conceptualize the object of unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*);
how much less so the various phenomena that are realized? △ Third, the inquiry: Why is this so?
There are three points of inquiry: first, by what means is it proven that there is no discursive thought (*manasikāra*)? Second, why does a single concentration yield manifold fruits?
Third, how is it that through a fixed cause one obtains the dharma of the fruit? △ Fourth, the explanation has two parts; first, a brief and specific explanation.
Answering the first three inquiries:
such is the essential nature of the bodhisattva’s samādhi;
it is a single essential nature because it is free from conceptualization.
Thus it is boundless.
Although the essential nature of these two meditative absorptions is one, their functions are boundless;
such is their excellence.
Third, by way of its excellence: this refers to the principle that the fruit is obtained through the cause. △ Second, the detailed general explanation:
this means that the text is extensive and the meaning is universal, universally clarifying the aforementioned three phrases. This section is divided into two parts. First, the general heading.
These are the various objects of this samādhi;
"objects" refers to the focal points of meditative concentration.
These are its various powers.
Majestic power (*prabhāva*) is the function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Its various modes of profound penetration constitute the realization and verification of that concentration. All three are the essence of concentration; since all are described as "various," it was stated above that they are "boundless."
It possesses three aspects and is moreover manifold; therefore, it is called "extraordinary and supreme. △ Second, the specific manifestation:
there are twenty-eight phrases, and each phrase contains the aforementioned three meanings.
"Entering the gate of ineffable wisdom.
"Entering" has the same meaning as "penetrating deeply" mentioned previously. "Ineffable" has the meaning of "boundless. "Gate of wisdom" has the meaning of "objective sphere.
Since wisdom resides in speech, speech is designated as the gate of wisdom. In other versions of the text, some phrases may lack the sense of being boundless; this is likely due to textual omission.
This is abbreviated.
They enter the adornments free from conceptual discrimination;
they enter the adornment of the non-duality of merit and wisdom.
One should know that they enter the boundless, supreme pāramitās, up to the immeasurable, ineffable, and vast wisdom of a nayuta;
they enter the vision of the boundless, sublime treasury of the Buddhas.
One enters the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha;
one enters the sphere of activity without ceasing.
Within the realm of compassion and wisdom, one contemplates and delivers beings without rest.
Entering the Dharma-factors that Assist the Path through Pure Faith and Resolve (up to) Entering the Knowledge of the Minds of All Buddhas.
△ Third, the Universal Virtue that is Inexhaustible, Part Four. First, the direct manifestation of its inexhaustibility.
O Son of the Buddha, these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas [extend] to the adornment of the Buddha-realm of the past.
That is to say, it is not only the various functions listed above; they can also enter many samādhis in every thought-moment, which likewise cannot be fully exhausted.
△ Second, the inquiry. Why is this?
The intent of the inquiry is as follows:
Since one enters [the meditative states] many times in every thought-moment, why does one not reach exhaustion? △ Third, the explanation of the text contains ten phrases.
"Because one knows that all phenomena are ultimately inexhaustible.
The commentary explains: "The objects of this samādhi are ultimately inexhaustible. This is a general statement followed by a specific explanation.
Because one knows that all Buddha-fields are boundless, up to knowing that all phenomena which are the objects of the illusory mind are immeasurable.
△ Fourth, the analogies. Within this, there are three analogies illustrating the aforementioned inexhaustibility; each has both an analogy and its application (*yoga*).
In the first two applications, further interrogation and explanation are added. The first is the analogy of the wish-fulfilling gem that accords with every request.
O Son of the Buddha, just as a wish-fulfilling jewel never exhausts its power no matter what is requested from it,
so too does the concentrated mind inexhaustibly produce dharmas according to their requirements.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this (up to) "neither exhausted nor ceasing. Why is this? The underlying intention of the inquiry is:
by what means of emergence are they inexhaustible, unexhausted, and non-ceasing?
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the conduct of Samantabhadra (up to) being like reflections, because they neither increase nor decrease.
The explanation of this meaning states: "One realizes that many illusory phenomena are all identical to reflections; they arise when conditions meet. How could there be any exhaustion?"
The essence neither increases nor decreases; how could there be any exhaustion or cessation? △ Second, the analogy of the distinct arising of minds:
"O Son of the Buddha, it is as if ordinary beings each give rise to their own minds... [continuing] until... they flow on in succession without interruption, being inconceivable."
This is a metaphor for the inexhaustibility of objects of perception.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (up to) because of the immeasurable dharmas of the universal gate of illusion.
△ Third, the parable of the dragon king’s descent has two parts. First, the metaphor.
"O Son of the Buddha, it is as if Nanda and Upananda... [this is] the realm of effortless mastery of all nāgas;
this serves as a metaphor for entering the inexhaustible Dharma. △ Third, the application [of the analogy], in three parts. First, the explicit explanation of entering the Dharma.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this.
The merging of drops is like the axle of a chariot; that is to say, by entering the vast Dharma, they abide in this samādhi and enter the gates of all the samādhis of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
The first phrase is general; the remaining phrases are specific.
These range from the gate of wisdom, the gate of dharmas, and the gate of seeing all Buddhas, up to the gate of the unspeakably vast net of illusions (*māyājāla*).
As for this "net of illusions," everything is illusory, mutually arising through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and interpenetrating one another like reflections.
One knows the gateways of worlds, from the inconceivable distinctions up to those possessing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and lacking intrinsic nature.

Because the nature of worlds is empty, they lack intrinsic nature; because they follow conditions through defilement and purity, they possess intrinsic nature. Furthermore, because they are lands of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-kṣetra*), they possess intrinsic nature;
because they are lands of phenomena (*vastu-kṣetra*) arising from conditions, they lack intrinsic nature. Moreover, because pure lands accord with principle, they possess intrinsic nature.
Because defiled lands are falsely established, they have no inherent substance.
Know that there are unspeakably unspeakable gateways of sentient beings' perceptions (extending to) the various Buddha-lands situated inverted or upright.
"All are called 'gateways' because they are entered by both self and others. △ Second, the timing of entering the Dharma:
within a single thought-moment, one knows all things as they truly are;

this corresponds to the time of the rain falling previously. △ Third, the characteristics and functions of the time of entry: this corresponds to the previous state of being boundless, inexhaustible, and without limit.
It forms a sphere of activity. Within this, there are three parts; first, ten phrases clarify its characteristics.
Thus, when entering [this state], it has no boundaries and no exhaustion.

It is like merging with boundless clouds and raining without end. Next, it merges with the sphere of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*); "non-action" means the absence of effortful application (*anābhoga*).
Without weariness or aversion;
the body does not tire and the mind does not grow weary;
without interruption and without ceasing.
It does not seek cessation; it does not temporarily rest;
it neither regresses nor loses [its state].

This means that because one has not yet entered [the state], one enters [it] constantly, and thus there is no regression; because one has already entered [it], it is eternally constant, and thus there is no loss.
Among all phenomena, one does not abide in what is not the proper place.
Since there is no phenomenon that enters nor any gateway [through which it enters], one does not abide in what is not the proper place,
but constantly engages in right reflection.
Because there is no mind that does not accord [with reality], there is neither sinking nor uplifting;
this is precisely the characteristic of entry. △ Second, clarifying its functional activity.
Seeking all-knowledge, one is forever without retreat or abandonment (up to: the physical body of marks and signs is never severed.
Entering each and every gate, there is always this activity; yet gate after gate is inexhaustible. △ Third, the interrogation and explanation of the reasons, in two parts. First, the interrogation.

Why is this? There are two points of inquiry. First: how could it be that a Bodhisattva does not attain Buddhahood through the fulfillment of their practice, yet the scope of their karmic activity remains without limit?
Second: even if one were to arbitrarily demonstrate its inexhaustibility, that might be acceptable; however, why is it that within each and every gateway, there is such activity?

This is inexhaustible. △ Second, the explanation also has two parts. First: It is said that because the Bodhisattva fundamentally acts for the sake of sentient beings, and since these beings are inexhaustible, their application is also inexhaustible.
Second, the explanation of the latter meaning states: Since both sentient beings and the world are like empty space, the application is inexhaustible through any single gate.
This is like the space within a mustard seed; by this, it is established not only through one gate.
Many. Even a single thought-moment can accomplish many tasks. The text has three parts. First, the analogy:
For example, when fire is kindled, it continues to burn without ceasing for as long as the necessary conditions persist.
Fire follows the conditions of its fuel; where the fuel is abundant, the fire remains. This is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s sphere of birth, whose vast application of means is without limit.
△ Second, the application [of the analogy]:
"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this" (up to) "causing all sentient beings to be entirely without remainder."
△ Third, the inquiry and explanation. Why is this?
The intent of the inquiry is:
for what reason does the Bodhisattva initiate such manifold karmic activities?
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva desires to deliver [beings] (up to) fulfilling all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
The commentary explains: "In order to universally deliver sentient beings and fulfill universal vows. △ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation to practice, which has two parts.

First, the conclusion and exhortation to diligent cultivation: This means that because this Bodhisattva’s mind reaches the limits of the realm of sentient beings, its application is certainly boundless; therefore, one should cultivate [it].
The Practice. Part Two. First, the presentation of the dharmas to be practiced:
"For this reason, all bodhisattvas.
These five characters encompass the following two sections. The dharmas to be practiced consist of eleven phrases; of these, the first ten phrases are as follows.
This section separately clarifies the functional activity (*karmavṛtti*) of the wheel of non-obstruction (*asaṅgacakra*).

Within it, the preceding passages are cited in reverse order because such types of functional activities are manifold. As in the analogy of damming a dragon, "types" refers to the multiplicity of entries into the Dharma.
Such an objective sphere is precisely the focal object of meditative concentration, just as in the previous analogy of the deluded thought taking an object;
such is its majestic power.
This immediately and comprehensively reveals the function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It is like the previous analogy of the jewel that can produce [all things];
such is its vastness. These three aforementioned types are all entirely vast, each being limitless, as previously described in the section on the "Invisible Samādhi" (*adṛśya-samādhi*).
Because it reaches the limit,
it is thus immeasurable and its number cannot be exhausted; as in the previously mentioned entry into the gates of ineffable wisdom and so forth, it is simply boundless.
Thus it is inconceivable, transcending both mind and speech; for, as before, one does not form such thoughts as "there are so many bodhisattvas.
Thus it universally illuminates.
All are accompanied by wisdom. As previously stated, although one knows that all phenomena are without activity, one is nevertheless able to manifest all manner of activities;
this is because of the clear illumination of the provisional and the real.
In this way, all Buddhas abide manifest before one.

When their essence and function are equal to the Buddha-realm, then all Buddhas are manifest before one. This is as previously described regarding the stage of the Ten Powers (daśabala-bhūmi), which leads to the attainment of omniscience (sarvajñā).
In this way, they are protected and remembered by all Tathāgatas;
being protected and remembered by the Tathāgatas, and having already been taken into the care of the Buddhas of the past, they are now included within the number of the Buddhas of the future.
Thus, one accomplishes past roots of goodness;

it is not merely that present mastery is exercised, but past goodness is also perfected. This is because, as in the previous case of the perfection of merit, the understanding and desires are entirely purified.
The final phrase cites the name and essence of the meditative concentration.
Thus, within this samādhi of the unimpeded and immovable mind.
△ Second, showing the signs for encouraging cultivation, in two parts. First, a brief indication of abandoning faults and advancing in virtue.
Diligently cultivate [the path] to be free from all feverish afflictions, until one accords with the realm of samādhi and enters the stage of inconceivable wisdom.
△ Second, the specific demonstration of transcending faults and advancing in virtue has two parts. First, transcending faults.
Not relying on words and letters, not clinging to the world (up to) being unstained by worldly affairs and not discriminating among objects.
△ Second, advancing in virtue:
Regarding the wisdom of all dharmas, one should simply abide therein (up to) knowing the proper time to preach the Dharma without ceasing.
△ Second, the summary and manifestation.
O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice in this way... [up to] ...they thus embrace all sentient beings.
If taken distantly, this connects back to all preceding sections; if taken closely, it connects back to the passage on the advancement of virtue mentioned above.

I wish to correlate each point individually, yet I fear that doing so would result in overly prolix text. △ Third, the fulfillment of the meditative concentration and the resulting benefits. The text belongs to this concentration, while its meaning encompasses the previous nine.
Within this, there are four parts. First, the external response of the Buddhas' empowerment and benefit (five sections). First, distinguishing the basis for the empowerment.
"O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [attains] such great wisdom-samādhi—this refers to the time when he is in meditative concentration.
△ Second, revealing the Buddhas who bestow empowerment."
Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers throughout each of the ten directions, appeared before him.
△ Third, the actual manifestation of the signs of empowerment.
The Tathāgata bestows the power of mindfulness so that there is no loss of recollection (up to: all are fully accomplished without being in vain.
△ Fourth, the application of their function:
O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thus fulfills (up to: he turns the subtle and wondrous wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas.
△ Second, the inquiry into and explanation of the reason for this has two parts.
First, the inquiry: "For what reason?

The intent of the inquiry is as follows: Since the universal practice is already fulfilled, why is it necessary to continue practicing the conduct of harmonizing sentient beings until the end of the future? △
The second explanation: "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... manifests great mastery in the samādhi of vast practice.

The intent of this explanation is as follows: because the nature of unobstructed vows is thus; because he has already perfected his great vows; and because he is truly capable of taming [sentient beings].
△ Second, the fourfold benefit of the perfection of internal virtues. First, restating the perfection of the causes for abiding in meditative concentration:
"O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... abides in the lion’s-leap wisdom (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-jñāna*), with unimpeded mental activity."
This concludes the preceding summary. △ Second, the specific exposition of that which is fulfilled:
"His mind constantly dwells in the ten great dharma-treasuries... (up to) such that no worldly wisdom can describe it."
The ten [manifestations] are inexhaustible. △ Third, the summary of the ultimate consummation:
"O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already reached (attained) the manifestation that subdues all sentient beings."
△ Second, the inquiry into and explanation of the reasons for this, in two parts.
First, the inquiry: "For what reason?
The intent of the inquiry is: by what means can a bodhisattva fulfill such a multitude of virtues? △ Second, the explanation.
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi-dharma in such a manner.
△ Third, the benefit of subsuming the fruit of Buddhahood, which has three parts. First, the explicit explanation:
"O Son of the Buddha, by means of this samādhi, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... causes [beings] to enter the supreme wisdom."
△ Second, the inquiry: "For what reason?
The intent of this inquiry is: "The aforementioned are the virtues of the Buddha; how can they be encompassed? △ Second, the explanation: "Abiding in these three..."
[This is] obscure. It is because [the Buddha] is able to cause all that he undertakes to be without remainder, being identical to the Tathāgata. Within this, there are three parts.
First, the actual manifestation of karma without remainder; therefore, in each case, it says "all."
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice in this manner, they abide in the equality of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
△ Second, the clarification of the characteristics of their activity:
within this Dharma, they perform such actions and do not perform other actions.

The first phrase provides a general indication: acting based on what was previously undertaken, one does not perform any other insufficient karma. The subsequent portion clarifies the meaning of that action:
abiding in a mind that has not yet reached fulfillment, abiding in a non-distracted mind, up to abiding in a resolute mind and abiding in an unchanging mind.
The following is a summary of what preceded:
"Thus one contemplates, thus one performs the action, and thus one brings it to completion.

△ Third, the repeated explanation in response to objections: that is, to elaborate on the preceding statement that one performs such actions and does not perform other actions. This section has three parts.
First, a brief summary:
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has no discrepancy between speech and action; his speech is as his action, and his action is as his speech.
This "action as it is" encompasses both body and mind. △ Second, the inquiry.
Why is this? The intent of the inquiry is: "Why does one not perform other [deeds]? △ Third, the extensive explanation. The intent of the explanation is:
"If one performs something different from the former, one is not a bodhisattva. The text contains ten similes, which constitute ten sections, each with its own application (*yōjaku*). First, gold...
The analogy of the indestructible diamond (*vajra*):
for example, just as a diamond receives its name because it cannot be destroyed and there is never a time when it is separated from that indestructibility,
so too is the essence of practice firm and stable.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: [he continues] until finally there is never a time when he is separated from the dharmas of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
△ Second, the analogy of the slight color of pure gold:
For example, just as pure gold receives its name because it possesses a wondrous color, and there is never a time when it is separated from that wondrous color.
This is like external adornments resulting from wholesome karma.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (up to the point where it says): "He never at any time departs from all wholesome karmas.
△ The Analogy of the Radiance of the Sun-Disk.
For example, just as the Sun Deva Prince receives his name from the orb of light and never at any time is separated from that orb of light—
this being a metaphor for the perfect clarity of wisdom—
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (until: he never at any time is separated from the light of wisdom.
△ Fourth, the parable of the four peaks of Mount Sumeru:
For example, just as the King of Mountains, Sumeru, with its four jewel peaks, never at any time abandons those four peaks.
This is a metaphor for the transcendence of the roots of goodness.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (up to): there is never a time when they abandon the roots of goodness.
They do not join with the four peaks; if they were to join, it would be by joining them through the four practices of a Bodhisattva. △ V. Five Greats.
The analogy of the earth’s capacity to support:
just as the great earth receives its name from supporting all things and never at any time abandons that capacity to support,
so too is the analogy for the bearing of great compassion.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: (up to) there is never a time when he abandons great compassion.
△ Sixth, the analogy of the great ocean containing water:
For example, the great ocean derives its name from containing all waters, and there is never a time when it abandons its water.
This is like a great vow that nurtures universally.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this, never for a moment abandoning the vow to deliver sentient beings.
△ Seventh, the analogy of the military general clarifying the metaphor of battle.
For example, just as a military commander who has mastered his skills never at any time abandons that proficiency—
this being an analogy for practicing meditative concentration to ward off enemies—
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who likewise never at any time abandons this practice.
△ 8. The Parable of the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) Protecting the World:

Just as a Cakravartin King governs the four continents [until] he ensures that none suffer untimely death and they constantly experience happiness; this serves as a metaphor for how objects [of merit], when purified by meditative concentration, produce their corresponding results.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this, [proceeding] until he causes them to reach ultimate purity.
△ Ninth, the analogy of planting seeds and their growth:
For example, when a seed is planted in the earth, it is able to cause the stems and leaves to grow.
The analogy of the increase of things through cultivation:
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this, [up to] being able to cause the wholesome dharmas of all sentient beings to increase.
△ Second, the analogy of seasonal rain producing seeds; first, the analogy.
For example, just as a great cloud bestows heavy rain during the summer months, even increasing all seeds, so too does the rain of Dharma universally bring about fulfillment.
△ Second, the synthesis of the two [analogies]. First, the formal synthesis.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this (up to) practicing the bodhisattva path and raining down the great Dharma rain, and so forth.
As for the phrase "and so forth" (乃至), it omits the initial stage of birth and directly joins with the final accomplishment; this is because [the rain] falls in accordance with the proper time.
By attaining these fourteen kinds of benefits,
one can bring all sentient beings to ultimate purity,
for they obtain the fruit of wisdom and purify the two obstacles.
It is ultimate nirvana;
because one attains the fruit of cessation and realizes the signless dharma,
it is ultimately secure and peaceful.
Because one abides in great compassion as the fruit of having attained grace, one reaches the ultimate further shore;

because one attains the purity of the basis, one reaches the fruit of the ultimate further shore. The preceding four [perfections] are for one's own benefit; the remaining ones are all for the benefit of others.
He attains ultimate joy;
he thoroughly understands the conduct of sentient beings; he causes others to rejoice; and by being free from the ten fears himself, he rejoices within himself, having ultimately severed all doubt.
Having attained the severance of doubt,
one becomes the ultimate field of merit for all sentient beings and achieves the state of being worthy of offerings; the following seven phrases are accomplished on this basis.
It causes their acts of giving to become entirely pure (up to) establishing all sentient beings in the state of omniscience;
the text may be understood accordingly. △ Second, the interrogation and explanation, which has two parts. First, the interrogation.
Why is this? The purport of the inquiry is:
by what power of practice does the Bodhisattva preach the Dharma and thereby accomplish such great benefit? △ Second, the explanation. The purport of the explanation is:
because they have attained great wisdom and realized the *dharmadhātu*, they are even able to adorn and purify immeasurable sublime practices; how much more so [the aforementioned benefit]?
Does this establish [the nature of] sentient beings? The text has two parts. First, the heading:
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish these dharmas... up to... inconceivable and immeasurable practices."
△ Second, the explanation of the text has three parts. First, the listing of the merits to be purified:
namely, being able to purify all wisdoms because of seeking omniscience (up to) constantly seeing all Buddhas appearing in the world.
△ Second, the summary of its vastness and multiplicity:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi... up to "...unspeakably pure merits.
This is because it would be difficult to exhaustively describe them individually. △ Third, the revelation of the causes capable of purifying [them].
By the power of the pure and refined roots of goodness that are of the same category as the spheres of these samādhis—
wherein "roots of goodness of the same category" refers to each individual root of goodness being dedicated to the dharma-realm so as to become a sovereign with its retinue.
By the power of the aspiration for vast vows and joyful resolve (up to) the power of inexhaustible merit that is without counterpart, one transcends all worlds.
Because the merit cultivated through correspondence with the *dharmatā* is equal [to it], one transcends the world.

Since the *dharmatā* does not coexist with the false, it has no counterpart. △ Fourth, the benefit of being truly identical to the fruit of Buddhahood, in two parts: first, the actual manifestation of this identity.
The Buddha said:

"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi... [This section] first sets forth the thesis and subsequently raises the inquiry, [stating that he] is equal to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
What are these ten? They are listed below:
namely, attaining the various marks and signs and manifold adornments, up to [attaining] the realm of all Buddhas and becoming equal to all Buddhas.

The name "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambuddha) is established on this basis. △ Second, the interrogation and selection through question and answer. First, there are two questions. The first restates the previous point of being equal to the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra... [up to] ...having attained such a Dharma as to be equal to all Tathāgatas.
△ Second, the statement of his own doubts:
Why is he not called "Buddha"? Why is he not called "One of Ten Powers" (up to) why is he not called "One Who Abides in the Reality-limit"?
The first nine phrases express doubt and are not termed "fruits. The final two phrases ask why one would not relinquish the cause:
why is it that when practicing the vows and conduct of Samantabhadra (up to the point of being unable to reach the ultimate limit of the *dharmadhātu*), one might abandon the Bodhisattva path?
△ Second, the response has two parts. First, praising the question and restating the doubt:
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed Puyan Bodhisattva (extending to) "...cannot abandon the bodhisattva path."
△ Second, the direct answer to the question has three parts. First, the explanation by way of Dharma:
"O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... this is what is called the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra."

The text consists of eleven sections, which answer the preceding eleven questions in sequence; these are easy to understand from the wording, yet the underlying meaning remains difficult to perceive. Specifically, one might ask:
how is it that having already entered the ten powers (*daśabala*), one can still practice universally and without ceasing? This is now illustrated collectively through a metaphor:
it is like a person practicing recitation who, although they have already attained mastery, continues to review it repeatedly rather than resting content with long-term proficiency. Below...

The Parable of the Fragrant Elephant: This illustrates that although their characteristics appear similar, their essence is different. Thus, the *Sūtra of the Necklace* states: "Equal Enlightenment is illumination within stillness;
Wondrous Enlightenment is stillness within illumination. This is also like comparing the stage where effort is perfected to the stage of effortless spontaneity.

Furthermore, it demonstrates that the attainment of the fruit does not abandon the cause, for throughout the limits of the future, one remains in the universal stage of Samantabhadra following the [ten] stages. [Section on the Divisions within the Parable]
Third: First, the excellence of the primary and secondary adornments of the Elephant King is presented.
"O Son of the Buddha, it is as if the Elephant King Airāvaṇa were dwelling within a cave of the seven treasures on Mount Suvarṇakukṣi."
Ilāpatra, here translated as "Fragrant Leaf," constantly dwells on the side of the first golden mountain.
The perimeter of his cave is entirely composed of the seven treasures... [up to] ...well-tamed, virtuous, and compliant, with no contrary thoughts in his mind.
△ Second, the simile of the sovereign miraculous transformation of the elephant king:
If Śakra, Lord of the Devas, intends to travel about, he manifests seven tusks upon each and every head.
According to the "Chapter on Worthy Excellence" (Xianshou pin), there are only six tusks; perhaps the translator, following the later pattern of three times seven, stated there were seven ears.
If this is intended as a symbolic representation, why would it not be acceptable?
From each tusk, seven ponds are manifested (continuing until) the elephant and the gods appear so similar to one another that no one can distinguish which is the elephant and which is the god.
This is precisely what is intended here, used as a metaphor for the meaning of a Bodhisattva being equal to a Buddha.
△ Third, being able to manifest while not destroying the fundamental essence.
O Son of the Buddha, that elephant king Airāvaṇa (up to) receives celestial pleasures no different from those of the devas.
△ Third, the correspondence with the Dharma, in four parts. First, being adorned with all practices.
The Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, are likewise thus. Integrating the aforementioned [teachings on] the environment and its inhabitants,
they cultivate the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva until they reach the further shore of all Bodhisattva practices and vows.
△ Second, clarifying that cause and effect are unimpeded, in two parts. First, clarifying the purpose for practicing unimpeded conduct:

it is because one desires to establish oneself upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimanda*), to accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), and to attain supreme perfect awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Combined with the aforementioned sovereign spiritual transformations, the former constitutes the fruit and the latter the cause.
This increases the vast practices and vows of Samantabhadra, leading to the liberation of all sentient beings from suffering and affliction.
△ Second, the correct manifestation of the unimpeded mode of practice has two parts. First, the general explanation:

Not abandoning the path of Samantabhadra while manifesting the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment, because the cause and effect of the *dharmadhātu* are without obstruction. △ Second, the specific explanation has three parts. First, the manifestation of the result through the gate of the cause.
Practice. The text contains four fruits.
It manifests unspeakably unspeakable gateways to the attainment of perfect enlightenment;
this is the fruit of wisdom.
They manifest the gates of turning the wheel of Dharma in unspeakably unspeakable ways,
teaching the fruits of the Dharma;
they manifest the gates of abiding in the profound mind in unspeakably unspeakable ways.
The fruit corresponding to *prajñā* manifests the gates of the transformation of *nirvāṇa* within unspeakably unspeakable, vast lands; this is the fruit of severance.
△ Second, revealing that the fruit arises from causal practice.
In unspeakably unspeakable varieties of worlds, [the Bodhisattvas] cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra and attain perfect enlightenment.

This clarifies that the fruit arises from causal practice; furthermore, regarding the time of attainment, it is explained that [the manifestation] differs according to the capacities of sentient beings. △ Second, the section on the causal practices for manifesting the fruit.
Furthermore, throughout all Buddha-fields, [he manifests] the various methods of teaching and subduing sentient beings.
△ Third, concluding by establishing the indestructible cause and manifesting its fruit.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
from this point downward, it is shown that while the fundamental essence remains indestructible, one is able to manifest;
yet the original body itself is not extinguished.
Thus, the cause is not destroyed; it remains intact within the cave without change.
Through the power of practice and vows, it manifests such transformations in all places, thereby being able to manifest the fruit.
This corresponds to the "Supernatural Transformation of Heavenly Deities. △ Fourth, the interrogation and explanation, which consists of two parts. First, the interrogation.
Why is this? The intent of the inquiry is as follows: Since cause and effect are distinct, how can the effect manifest within the gate of the cause, and how can the effect further become the cause?

Second, the intent of the explanation is as follows: Because the method for harmonizing sentient beings ought to be thus. This section has two parts; first, the explanation of the intent of the effect acting as the cause.
This is because [the Buddha] desires to manifest the sovereign spiritual power of Samantabhadra, up to the point of being able to realize all-knowledge through sovereignty.
△ Second, the explanation of the intention behind manifesting the fruit based on the cause, in four parts. First, the explanation according to the Dharma (the teaching).
"O Son of the Buddha, you should observe this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (up to) the sovereign enjoyment of all-knowledge dharmas;
that is to say, the manifestation of the fruit without abandoning the cause. △ Second, the preceding metaphor is cited to illustrate [this].
Just as the elephant king Airāvaṇa does not abandon his elephant body [yet] becomes identical to the various devas without distinction.
△ Third, the application by means of the Dharma.
The Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, are also like this: [from "up to"] they have no conceptual discrimination within the Buddha-dharma.
The preceding clarifies how the cause is not abandoned while manifesting the fruit; the following clarifies how the fruit is not destroyed while manifesting the cause.
Although they know that all phenomena are universally equal, they continue to cultivate the characteristics of bodhisattva practice without interruption.
△ Fourth, the praise of excellence:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells thus... [the passage continues] ...the mind of such a person shall attain purity."
△ Third, the summary of the three fetters.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the Bodhisattva’s (up to) the vast wisdom of the sublime mind of the Great Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel.
△ Third, the general summary of the ten numbers.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten great samādhi-wheels of the conduct of Samantabhadra in which the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas abide.

Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Ten Pervasions.

△ First, the intent of the introduction: This is to answer the ten questions concerning supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) posed in the second assembly. Two chapters are used to clarify the vastness of their karmic function;

this supernormal power follows the preceding meditative concentration (*samādhi*) because of the sequential order of their meanings. Furthermore, it is because supernormal powers are brought forth based upon meditative concentration.

Second, regarding the explanation of the names: "Abhijñā" (shentong) is the general term. That which is called "divine" (shen) refers to wondrous functions that are difficult to fathom; that which is called "penetration" (tong) refers to sovereign mastery without obstruction.

These wondrous functions are infinite, and the number ten is employed to manifest their perfection. As for why the Jin-period *Sūtra of the Original Vows* (Benye jing) refers to them as the "Ten Clarities" (Shiming), it is as follows: [text continues].

Because it illuminates exhaustively without omission. However, regarding "penetration" (*abhijñā*) and "clarity" (*vidyā*), the sūtras and śāstras differ. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle three, states:
"To know directly the matters of past lives is penetration; to know the causes, conditions, and karmic actions of the past is clarity," and so forth.
Now, according to this sūtra, penetration is exhaustive illumination, which may also be termed clarity, as explained at length in the text.

To manifest this perfect principle, it is opened up and formed into ten types of supernormal powers (abhijñā). II. Second, the inquiry into their number and the detailed explanation, in two parts:
first, the general inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Second, the detailed explanation of the ten. First, the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna-abhijñā). Part one: the heading.
"O Son of the Buddha, by means of the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva..."
Regarding the initial designation here as "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracitta-jñāna*): it is so called because this wisdom takes the minds of others as its object (*ālambana*).

If one were to name it directly according to its object, it should be called "supernormal power of discerning the distinctions of mind" (*cetaḥparyāya-abhijñā*), for it is able to know all various types of minds, whether they be those of ordinary beings or those of kings.
This is named according to its predominant object. Regarding the cognition that takes another's mind as its object, various explanations differ. Master Sthiramati says:

"The Buddha’s wisdom takes another’s mind as its object by apprehending its actual substance (*bhāva*); all others [of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas] merely perceive a transformation of an image (*pratibimba*). Master Dharmapāla, however, maintains that even the Buddha perceives an image.

He argues that if it were to take the actual substance as its object, one would be apprehending a phenomenon external to the mind, which would undermine the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). It is simply that the image is extremely similar to the actual substance.

Regarding the substance [of this teaching], there are differing reasons for its basis. According to the school of Yogācāra, Dharmapāla’s interpretation is correct. When viewed from the perspective of the present sutra in relation to the preceding one, it is likewise not erroneous.

This is because, while encompassing the objects that serve as conditions, the mind does not destroy those objects; thus, both subject and object are simultaneously absent, yet their existence is not obstructed.
In the ultimate sense, "mind-only" is neither identical nor different [from its objects], for when correctly taking another as the condition, that very other is itself. Because...

It is the Buddha-mind that is the sentient-being mind; it is not the case that the sentient-being mind is the Buddha-mind. This serves as the object of cognition (*ālambana*). It is the Buddha-mind that is the sentient-being mind;
it is not the case that the sentient-being mind is the Buddha-mind. This serves as the subject of cognition (*ālambaka*).

Because they are thus fused and integrated, they are neither identical nor different. If one were to posit sentient beings as existing separately apart from the Buddha, one would have to undergo further transformation.
[This] shadow, however, deviates from the true meaning of *vijñapti-mātra*. △ Second, the explanation of the characteristics has two parts. First, knowing a single moment [of time] has three parts.
First, the general: knowing the distinctions among the minds of sentient beings within a single trichiliocosm.
△ Second, there are thirty distinct types of mind, excluding the third, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). These are fully present in the Jin translation. Within this section, there are two parts;
first, eight [types] are presented as a general exposition based on their characteristics.
What are called the wholesome mind and the unwholesome mind—
these two, in terms of their intrinsic nature, encompass all minds in general.
[There are also] broad minds and narrow minds.
These two are distinguished by their practice, as they encompass both altruistic salvation and solitary self-cultivation;
these two are distinguished by their retribution, as they involve either a great mind or a small mind, and a vast body or a small body. The former four are exclusively wholesome.
The "mind that follows birth-and-death" and the "mind that turns away from birth-and-death":

these two are distinguished by way of orientation. While "following" pertains to all three natures—with the wholesome being exclusively impure (*sāsrava*)—"turning away" is exclusively wholesome and pertains to both the impure and the pure (*anāsrava*).
△ Second, the twenty-one minds are specifically explained according to persons.
The mind of a śrāvaka, the mind of a pratyekabuddha (up to) the mind of pratyekabuddha practice, and the bodhisattva practice—these six are categorized according to the vehicles (*yāna*).
The first three are results; the latter three are causes. These correspond respectively to the aforementioned generation of the mind and the expansive and narrow minds.
The minds of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, [up to] the kinnaras, and mahoragas—
these eight classes are categorized by type as the aforementioned "conforming to birth and death" and the "great and small."
The human mind is not merely the human mind; it is the mind of hell (up to) the mind of hungry ghosts—the minds of sentient beings in various states of suffering.

The five [realms] beginning with hell are explained in terms of the destinies (*gati*) and also follow the cycle of birth and death; these are unwholesome minds. The remaining two may be understood accordingly. △ Third, the conclusion.
In this way, he fully discerns and knows the various minds of immeasurable and diverse sentient beings.

The preceding section distinguishes the clarity of the perceiving faculty; the following section distinguishes the thoroughness of the perceived objects.

"Mindfulness" refers specifically to the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), which is the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) of recollecting past lives. △ Second, the explanation of its characteristics has two parts.
First, knowing all matters has two parts. First, the general [explanation].
He is able to know the events of his own past lives throughout unspeakably unspeakable numbers of eons, down to the count of atoms.
△ Second, the specific details:
namely, he fully understands all such matters as being born in a certain place with such a name, such a clan, and so forth.
△ Second, knowing the matters of the noble ones, in two parts. First, manifesting multiplicity by way of the realms:
Furthermore, he recollects as many buddha-fields in the past (up to) all such things he is able to recollect.

Furthermore, he can fully know [the deeds] from the unspeakably unspeakable [eons] back, up to the planting of roots of goodness.
Furthermore, one knows their causes because the Bodhisattva has attained the eye of the nine periods of time, seeing them as if they were present.
If it were otherwise, if past phenomena had not fallen away, they could not be called "past"; if they had already fallen away, there would be no phenomenon that could be known.
If you claim that one remembers and knows simply because a seed existed within the mind in the past and its reflection appears before one, [this is not so].
This would mean seeing only one's own mind and not seeing those external phenomena. Furthermore, having never experienced those events, one should not be able to recollect or know them.
Moreover, one would see only the present and not the past; how, then, could this be called "recollection of former abodes"? △ Third, the conclusion.
This is called the third supernormal knowledge of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom of recollecting past lives throughout kalpas of the past limit.
△ Fourth, the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom of the future limit of kalpas, in three parts. First, the heading.

△ Second, the explanation of its characteristics has two parts. First, knowing the ordinary [kalpas] has two parts. First, clarifying the kalpas upon which it relies.
One knows all the kalpas within as many world-systems as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
This is merely by means of designating many fields to manifest many kalpas; it is not that they have a limit or boundary.

Furthermore, the subsequent sections all extend to the end of the future, because the objects of knowledge in this stage are identical to those of a Buddha. △ Second, the manifestation of the phenomena that depend [upon these fields].
One can thoroughly know all sentient beings within each and every kalpa, as extensively explained in the section on the Ten Grounds (*Daśabhūmika*).
However, according to the Mahāyāna school, phenomena in future lives lack both substance and function; how, then, can they be known?
Based on the provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*), one perceives the causal seeds in the present and thereby knows the characteristics of the future fruits.

It is not that one perceives the substance (*svabhāva*) of future phenomena. According to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) school, within the nine periods of time, both the substance and function of the present exist;
we now know this as it truly is. However, because it is not the "present of the present," it is called the "future.

If this existence were an intrinsic existence (*svabhāvataḥ sattā*), it would be identical to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). If it is an existence by conditions (*pratyaya-sattā*), since those conditions have not yet met, how can it be said [to exist]?

There is. If one examines it from the perspective of the present time, both the conditions and the nature are non-existent, because the present and the future are definitely not existent [at that time].
If one examines it by following the future time, since this is the "present" of the future, it is still as if it exists now.

△ Eighth: the supernormal knowledge of the adornment of the form-body (rūpakāya). Part three: first, the heading.

They receive their names based on what is manifested; this is a designation established by way of possession (*sadhana*).

△ Second, the explanation has three parts: first, knowing the formless, because form is itself emptiness; second, clarifying the ability to manifest form, because emptiness is itself form; third, explaining both the formless together.

This concerns the manifestation of forms. It is because there is no obstruction to compassion. First: Because one realizes that the dharma-realm has no fixed, substantial form, its entire substance is emptiness;
yet it is not a void of annihilation. Within this emptiness there is no form, yet it does not obstruct form.

Since both existence and non-existence, as well as concealment and manifestation, are entirely sovereign, one is then able to manifest various forms according to the inclinations [of beings]. Therefore, this is explained first. Second, the formal explanation.
The passage consists of six sentences.
One knows that all phenomena are far removed from the characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).

The first sentence provides a general understanding that the nature of form is devoid of characteristics and that there is no phenomenon whatsoever that exists as empty. The remaining five sentences provide specific [explanations].
It clarifies what kinds of characteristics are absent:
it is devoid of differentiated characteristics,
such as coarse and subtle, long and short, and so forth, because they share the same essence of non-arising.
There are no manifold characteristics,
because various distinct characteristics are empty.
There are no infinite characteristics.
Because it is free from manifold characteristics; furthermore, because it is neither large nor small and transcends all dimensions, it lacks the characteristic of conceptual discrimination.
It is merely a false discrimination, for even when sought, it cannot be found. Both the views of form and emptiness are grasped through emotional attachment; they are thus [identical to] non-...
This is because the two views have been severed. Above, it pervades both form and manifestation;

there are no characteristics of yellow, red, or white, for these manifest colors depend upon form to exist. △ Second, it clarifies that which manifests color, because emptiness is identical to form. Text.
2. First, the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent one is introduced.
In this way, the Bodhisattva enters the Dharma-realm and is able to manifest their body in various forms.
Because form that is itself emptiness constitutes the wondrous form, and because emptiness and form are non-dual, the aforementioned true emptiness is established. Not...
Two yet two; manifesting these wondrous forms, form and emptiness are fused and identical as the true *dharmadhātu*. Conditioned origination is inexhaustible;
from the one, the many appear. △ Second, specifically revealing their differences.
What are called "boundless forms" and "immeasurable forms," up to "forms that fully embody all the practices of Samantabhadra," number one hundred and three.
Some are named according to their formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while others receive their designations based on their qualities and functions (*guṇa-vṛtti*);

these may be sought through the power of the mind. Nevertheless, they are all forms that accord with the *dharmadhātu*, and are not like [ordinary] matter characterized by transformation and obstruction (*rūpaṇā*). They exist merely as manifestations in accordance with conditions.

Establishing the names of the forms. △ Third, a dual explanation of the purpose for which formless beings manifest forms. Because they do not obstruct compassion, there are two parts. First, the conclusion of the preceding section:
"O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter deeply into such [states]... they are able to manifest these various kinds of physical bodies."
△ Second, revealing that which is for the sake of others:
causing those to be converted to see [the Buddha] and causing those to be converted to remember [him], up to performing various beneficial activities for the sake of those to be converted.
All ten phrases may be known. △ Third, the conclusion:
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s (up to) eighth incalculable [aeon] wisdom of the form-body supernormal powers.
△ 9. The Supernormal Knowledge of Knowing All Dharmas (Sarvadharmajñānābhijñā). Three parts. First, the heading:

"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of the supernormal knowledge of knowing all dharmas, receives this designation from the known dharmas of the ultimate and conventional truths, etc. △ Second, the explanation of its characteristics, in two parts. First, the clear understanding of the dharmas. That is to say:
The first part clarifies the realization of phenomena and principle within; the second clarifies the manifestation of the Dharma, which benefits sentient beings externally.

This is also because the former clarifies that phenomena are eternally the principle, while the latter clarifies that the principle is constantly manifested as phenomena; thus, function and quiescence are mutually unimpeded. Regarding the first [of these two], there are again two sections.
First, the reality is revealed by way of transcending words.
One knows that all phenomena have no names.
The first three phrases exclusively reveal reality; because the preceding phrase [states] that names lack the power to apprehend objects, there is no seed-nature (*gotra*).
Conditioned arising is devoid of intrinsic nature;

it neither comes nor goes, for its essence is utterly free from coming and going. Below are three phrases that reveal reality through mutual contrast. However, there are three ways of explaining these three pairs.
The meaning is that they are neither different nor non-different.

"One" refers exclusively to the manifestation of reality; since they are empty through mutual dependence, they are said to be "non-different" because their distinct characteristics are mutually absent.
To preclude divergent claims, it is said that they are "not different. Yet, since no characteristic of being non-different can be apprehended, it is said that they are "not not-different.

Second, regarding the simultaneous manifestation: in essence they are non-different, but in their characteristics they are not non-different. Third, regarding the simultaneous negation of characteristics.

Because it is the very nature, it is not different from nature; because it is the very characteristic, it is not non-different. Furthermore, because the characteristic is non-characteristic, it is not different;
because the nature is non-nature, it is not non-different. Thus, it is free from the two extremes and does not abide in the middle way. The following two pairs should be understood by analogy.
It is neither manifold nor non-manifold; neither dual nor non-dual.
△ Second, revealing reality by means of the two kinds of emptiness:
it is without self and without peer.
Furthermore, the first three pairs exclusively reveal the ultimate reality. Because the latter pair— being without "mine" and "I"— serves as a point of comparison,
[the dharmas] are unborn, undying, immovable, and indestructible.

The other two [meanings] may be understood accordingly. The subsequent pairs of contrasts below also admit of these three interpretations; they should be known by analogy with what precedes. For now, let us explain them according to the manifestation of reality:
there is neither reality nor unreality.
Because both the empty and the real are manifested through conditions, they are of one mark and yet markless.
Since the dharma-nature does not coexist with the true [duality], it is of one mark; yet even this "one" is not truly one, which is why it is called "markless."
It is neither non-existent nor existent;
both existence and non-existence are dharmas. Because they exist in mutual dependence and opposition, they are non-existent.
It is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma.
Dharma and non-Dharma are merely provisional designations; when sought according to ultimate reality, both the remedy and that which is remedied are entirely quiescent.
All other cases should be understood accordingly.
Not following the mundane, yet not not following the mundane... (up to) neither according to principle nor not according to principle.

△ Second, explaining the proclamation of the Dharma; this consists of three parts concerning the external benefit of sentient beings. First, restating the preceding attainment of wisdom as the basis for initiating activity.
This Bodhisattva does not grasp at conventional truth (up to: does not establish words, for they accord with the nature of quiescence.
△ Second, the actual explanation of the manifestation of the Dharma:
Without abandoning any vows or views, knowing the meaning and the Dharma, they spread the clouds of Dharma and pour down the rain of Dharma.
△ Third, the unimpededness of quiescence and activity. First, quiescence does not impede activity:
although one knows that the true mark (*dharmatā*) is ineffable, [one] teaches that all phenomena arise entirely from conditions.
△ 2. Activity does not obstruct quiescence:
Although there is verbal expression, there is no attachment... (up to) although one gathers in sentient beings, one does not abandon the ultimate reality.
△ 3. Quiescence and activity are non-dual.
He does not regress from the non-dual Dharma (up to) universally raining down the rain of Dharma without missing its proper time.
△ Third, the conclusion:
This is called the ninth supernormal power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the wisdom of all dharmas.
△ Ten: The Supernatural Power of Knowledge regarding the Cessation Samādhi of All Dharmas, which encompasses three [categories]. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, by means of the supernatural power of knowledge of the cessation samādhi of all dharmas, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva..."
"Regarding the extinction of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-nirodha*): it means that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are all inherently quiescent in their very essence.

This is the extinction of principle (*li-mie*), which differs from other schools that explain only the extinction of phenomena (*shi-mie*). [In those schools,] only the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are extinguished while the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are not;

the eighth consciousness is merely extinguished as a phenomenon. Therefore, they cannot establish certainty through the extinction of principle to serve as proof. Thus, there is both concentration and distraction."

There is no obstruction. Because principle is identical with phenomena, there is no obstruction to cessation; because phenomena are identical with principle, there is no obstruction to function. Therefore, the text says:

"Although one enters [cessation] in every thought-moment, one does not abandon the Bodhisattva path," and so forth. This is neither a state of mental concentration nor is it merely the arising of function from the body.
It is not that both concentration and distraction are utterly severed; rather, it is simply the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle.

Therefore, the *Saptabhūmika-śāstra* states: "Although one practices the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one does not realize it; one can enter it moment by moment and emerge from it moment by moment. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"Without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one manifests all modes of deportment. These are all expressions of this same principle.

Since phenomena and principle are not identical, the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) that is the extinction of all dharmas is not something other than extinction; thus, extinction itself is supernormal power.
This encompasses both interpretations. △. Second, the two interpretations. First, clarifying that the essence and function of samādhi are sovereign. First, the heading on entering samādhi:
"In every thought-moment, one enters the samādhi of the cessation of all phenomena."
△ Second, clarifying the unimpeded function:
it neither retreats from the Bodhisattva path nor abandons Bodhisattva activities.

The first two phrases generally indicate non-retrogression regarding what has not yet been done, and non-abandonment regarding what is currently being performed. This specifically distinguishes the cessation of phenomena to reveal the Truth.
Cessation. The remaining phrases clarify this individually.
[The Buddha] does not abandon the mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion (up to) teaching various dharmas through skillful means.
△ Second, mastery over the duration of entering meditative concentration has three parts. First, length and brevity according to the mind.
When this Bodhisattva dwells in samādhi, he remains according to his mental inclination for as long as unspeakably unspeakable kalpas.
△ Second, his deportment is never errant.
The Bodhisattva enters this samādhi of the extinction of all dharmas (up to) being neither weary nor lax, and being inexhaustible.
△ Third, the samādhi of unimpeded arising of function, wherein concentration and distraction proceed together.
Although there is no activity whatsoever regarding either existence or non-existence (up to the point where) supernatural powers and transformations never cease.
The first six phrases are the Dharma; the final two phrases are the analogy.
For example, just as light and shadow appear everywhere yet remain tranquil and unmoving within samādhi—appearing universally while being silent and mindless—so it is with the Bodhisattva.
According to the capacity of beings, they appear to diminish or fill, yet their essence neither comes nor goes.
△ Third, the conclusion.
This is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s supernormal knowledge of the wisdom that enters the samādhi of the cessation of all phenomena.
△ Third, a general praise of their superior capacity, in two parts. First, manifesting superiority by contrasting it with inferior forms.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in such a state of wisdom, it is inconceivable, for those of inferior capacity cannot fathom it.
△ Second, manifesting excellence through excellence.
Except for the Buddhas and those who have attained this supernormal power (ṛddhi), no one can fully measure, extol, or praise the merit of this person;
it is only the Buddhas and their like who can fathom it. △ Fourth, the conclusion of the number and the discernment of the fruit.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s [attainment] up to the supernormal power of unimpeded knowledge regarding all three periods of time.
Chapter Twenty-nine: The Ten Endurances (Daśakṣānti).

Regarding the initial intent for its inclusion: it is for the purpose of answering the ten questions posed by Samantaprabha on the Ten Summits. The meaning has been explained as previously stated. The preceding two...
Having already clarified that meditative concentration (samādhi) is universally extensive, this section now distinguishes the profound depth of wisdom (*prajñā*); therefore, it follows next.

Second, regarding the explanation of the names: "patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to patient acceptance, understanding, and confirmation; it is the illumination and penetration of observation through wisdom, which, by relying on the Perfect [Teaching], manifests the ten stages.
Regarding the three essential principles (*zongqu*): taking profound wisdom and practice as the principle, and attaining the fruit of Buddhahood—unimpeded and inexhaustible—as the goal.
Now, this practice of patience (*kṣānti*), in terms of its stages, resides in the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) for the purpose of severing subtle ignorance and afflictions.

However, from the perspective of perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*), it actually pervades all five stages; this is stated according to its ultimate manifestation. Its essence is none other than wisdom (*jñāna*). It is not...

This is the same as other schools, wherein patience (*kṣānti*) is the cause and wisdom (*jñāna*) is the fruit. Although they constitute a single wisdom, they are explained differently according to their respective meanings as two, three, four, five, and so forth;
thus the various teachings differ. Now, in this Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), ten patiences are therefore taught.

Fourth, the correct explanation of the text. The text consists of prose and verse. Within the prose section, there are four parts. First, citing the number and praising its excellence. Second, citing the number:
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "...there are ten kinds of patience."
△ Second, praising its excellence:
If one attains this patience, one reaches the stage of the unimpeded patience of all bodhisattvas;
that is, the causes pertaining to one's own level are perfected.
All Buddha-dharmas are unimpeded and inexhaustible;
this is the fulfillment of the fruit of supreme progress. △ Second, listing the names to reveal their essentials.
First, the inquiry into the number: What are these ten?
△ Second, the listing of names.
That is to say:
the first three refer to the Dharma, while the latter seven refer to metaphors.
The patience of sound (*śabda-kṣānti*).
Regarding the teaching: this refers to being patient with the sounds of the teaching; it is named after its object, the patience toward sound. It is the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*).
In terms of practice, it is because it accords with all dharmas; thus, "accordance" (*ānulomika*) is itself "patience" (*kṣānti*).

Regarding the principle of the non-arising of dharmas, it is the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). If one considers it in terms of the wisdom of non-arising and the afflictions...
When affliction does not arise, there is no arising; this is "patience" (*kṣānti*). This applies to both interpretations.

Furthermore, if these three types of patience are explained according to their general characteristics, the first two are both preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), tending toward it, while only the last one accords with it.

If one considers them according to their respective stages, the three types of patience (*kṣānti*) are distinct. This is because it is only upon reaching this stage that there arises the "patience conforming to non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

"Conforming" here refers only to conforming to the principle; it is not yet the "patience of conformity" (*anulomikī kṣānti*). If that is so, how does this differ from the "conforming patience of non-arising"?

The former conforms generally to both phenomena and principle, whereas the two dharmas [of the latter] are different. As the verse on non-arising says: "One also conforms in knowing that dharmas exist," and so forth. Furthermore, based on the five...

The stage of patience (*kṣānti*) shall be quiescent. Herein, the meaning is clarified by means of the three types of patience; therefore, it corresponds to the non-arising [of dharmas], as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* (Dishichi).
The subsequent seven are explained by way of analogy and are all *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds, meaning "patience that is like an illusion," and so forth.
The patience like an illusion, the patience like a flame, the patience like a dream (up to) the patience like a transformation, and the patience like space.
Guangtong says: "The first four metaphors refer to sound; lightning and transformation metaphorically represent the patience of conformity (*anulomikī-kṣānti*);

space represents non-arising. Lightning is what we now call the metaphor of the shadow. Furthermore, it is said that 'illusion' refers to the characteristic of arising while there is no arising; 'flame' refers to the characteristic of an object while there is no object; 'dream'..."
That which is "knowing" has the characteristic of non-knowing; an echo has the characteristic of non-hearing; lightning has the characteristic of non-abiding.

Now, since it is called a "reflection," one should say it has the characteristic of non-manifestation. A transformation has the characteristic of non-existence; emptiness has the characteristic of non-action.

These are the metaphors, yet they are restricted to a single characteristic, whereas the meaning of that which is illustrated applies to many phenomena. Although this is not explicitly stated in the text:

There is no logical error here. Furthermore, the Venerable Master Xianshou said: "Contemplate consciousness as an illusion, perception as a mirage, sensation as a dream, mental formations as an echo, volitional formations as lightning, and form as a magical creation.
Contemplate all aggregates, elements, and sense bases collectively as being ultimately empty, like space.
This interpretation accords with the meaning of the subsequent verse; therefore, the present metaphor of the shadow also serves as a simile for this.
Regarding the practice: according to the fifth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, all eight metaphors illustrate the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Nevertheless, they differ from one another because the doubts to be dispelled are distinct.

First, when outsiders hear that the characteristic of the dependent nature exists only as false conceptualization and lacks ultimate reality, they immediately give rise to doubt, wondering: "If it does not exist..."
Regarding the true meaning: what objective sphere of activity could there be? Therefore, it is said to be like an illusion;

that is, what is conjured by a magician—how could the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as objects of perception have any reality? The second doubt is: "If there is no reality, how can the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arise?
Therefore, it is said to be like a shimmering mirage (*marīci*), which is not water but appears as water; thus, the mind arises falsely. The third doubt is: "If there is no reality..."
How could there be the enjoyment of the pleasant and the unpleasant? Therefore, it is said to be like a dream. Within a dream, there are in reality no signs of men, women, and so forth;
from what, then, could there arise the experience of enjoying the pleasant, the unpleasant, and so on? It is the same during the waking state. Fourth, the doubt: [as follows].
