△ Second, the actual manifestation of what was being contemplated:
"How inconceivable are the buddha-fields of all Buddhas... (up to)... how inconceivable is the liberation of all Buddhas?"

Regarding why these ten dharmas are all called "inconceivable": it is because the aforementioned functions of the fruit transcend the realm of ordinary cognition and are free from the characteristics of verbal expression.

Therefore, the meanings of these ten phrases are manifold; they pertain equally to both the True (Dharmakāya) and the Responsive (Nirmāṇakāya), and must not be understood exclusively from the perspective of the Responsive alone.
However, these ten questions subsume the preceding Universal Radiance [Chapter] and the results achieved by the subsequent twenty phrases.
Regarding the questions: "body" subsumes the six sense faculties; "wisdom" subsumes the Buddha’s realm, the Buddha-ground, and the three questions concerning the most supreme;

and "mastery" subsumes five: first, spiritual power (which refers to supernormal powers); second, the ten powers; third, the four fearlessnesses; and fourth, the samādhis. These are all expanded upon previously and synthesized here.
Within the preceding "objective realm" (*viṣaya*), there is the differentiation of the land, that which is transformed, and the objective basis;
within the preceding "practice" (*caryā*), there is the differentiation of the manifestation of the lineage of original vows. This lineage is precisely the practice of compassion and wisdom.

This is because the original vow is distinguished as practice solely from the perspective of the cause, whereas manifestation is the practice of the Buddha Samantabhadra. Thus, manifestation and practice are mutually related.

Regarding "broad and narrow": the *Prakaraṇa-pāda* (Chapter on Manifestation) appears below; "practice" is one of its aspects. Thus, while the former [refers to] non-obstruction, this [refers to] opening up liberation.
Because unimpeded activity is called "liberation," the reason for opening and closing is to manifest that the meaning has no fixed direction.

As for the term "mostly the same," it is to manifest that they are not different. Sound itself is eloquence (*pratibhāna*); although there is no distinction between opening and closing, in name there is breadth.

The essential meaning is largely the same as the previous section. These ten characteristics of the meanings have already been explained in the second assembly and will be further elucidated below in the text on the "Section on the Exposition.
△ Second, the Section on the Bestowal of Power has three parts. First, the causes for the bestowal of power.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas and perceiving their mental dispositions through his spiritual power, then bestowed empowerment upon them by means of his supernatural might.
This constitutes the second section: Manifesting the Signs of Empowerment.
Because the three karmas are augmented: the preceding phrase serves as the general [statement], while the following three phrases are specific.
Wisdom encompasses, light illuminates, and majestic power fills [all].
Regarding "the mind, speech, and body are illuminated by light," this refers to the light of the teaching (*deśanā-prabhā*). △ Third, the purpose for which the augmentations are performed.
In order that the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha may fully explain these virtues, there are eight phrases;
he abides in the fearlessness of the Buddha.
Externally, one restrains fearlessness;
internally, one realizes profound stillness by entering the Buddha’s Dharma-realm. This is the excellence of mental action (manas-karman).
They attained the majestic power of the Buddha;
their majestic power was fully internalized,
and their supernormal powers were sovereign.
The divine power penetrates outwardly; this is the excellence of bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
Attaining the Buddha’s unimpededness and possessing the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is the excellence of vocal action (*vākkarman*).
Vast observation: observing the capacities and teachings universally is "vast";
it is the knowledge of the sequential order of the lineage of all Buddhas.
Knowing that there is no difference in their nature is the sequential order.

Abiding in the skillful means of the ineffable Buddha-dharma and bestowing predictions with dexterity is the skillful means; these all describe his virtues. This is why he is added as the Blue Lotus Treasury.

This is because the fruition-merit (*phala-guṇa*) is beyond words and is manifested by means of causes; because cause and fruition are simultaneous; because the nature-merit (*svabhāva-guṇa*) is untainted and most preeminent;
and because a single merit contains all merits. △ Third, the ten phrases of the section on realization (*pratyakṣa-bhāga*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Blue Lotus Treasury (up to the point stated) will then be able to know and see all Buddha-dharmas.
The first four [points] above concern self-benefit; the last three below concern the benefit of others.
Observing sentient beings with a mind of great compassion (up to) practicing all the dharmas of the bodhisattvas.
The preceding [stages] are self-benefit; the latter three are superior progress.
In a single thought-moment, one gives birth to the Buddha-wisdom (up to) being fully endowed with *dhāraṇī* and eloquence.
△ Fourth, the section on the teaching has two parts. First, the general announcement by receiving power.
Relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, he addressed the Bodhisattva Padmagarbha.
[The reason for] addressing Padmagarbha is that without a mind identical to the Buddha’s, one would have no means to receive the Buddha’s virtues. Furthermore, it is named "Lotus" (Padma);
the specific color "blue" is not mentioned because it is unimpeded in its capacity to speak and is most transcendentally supreme. △ Second, the actual manifestation of the Buddha.
Regarding "Virtue" (*guṇa*), there are briefly two meanings. First, this chapter collectively answers ten questions for the five preceding chapters;

this specific chapter answers [the question concerning] the Buddha-nature (*buddhagotra*), because the Buddha takes merit as his nature. Next, there are two chapters that answer [the questions concerning] the Buddha-body.
The next chapter answers the fundamental vows; the final chapter answers the manifestation of that land. It is asked:

since the first assembly has already been explained extensively, the remainder is either yet to be transmitted in the sūtra or is subsumed within the preceding and following sections. Second, this chapter fully answers the ten questions;
that is to say, the Buddha’s virtues are immeasurable, yet they are briefly manifested through thirty-two gates, each of which possesses ten aspects, thus totaling three hundred and twenty.
The one hundred and twenty kinds of virtues manifest inexhaustibility. Previously, by means of the first ten [verses], the essential principles were indicated and the questions briefly answered.
In providing a complete answer to the ten questions, all that remained was to skip over the individual responses and proceed to answer the preceding ten questions in sequence.
Now, it is said that the thirty-two gates answer the ten preceding questions in their respective order; thus, within each gate, all ten answers are contained. This is because...
This demonstrates that the Buddha’s virtues are complete and all-encompassing, and it also shows that the questions posed are extensive and inclusive;

thus, the titles of the sections are numerous, differing from those previously mentioned, in order to reveal that the Buddha’s virtues are boundless. The text is divided into ten parts: the first two sections answer the question regarding the land;
the next two sections answer the question regarding original vows; and the third pair of sections answers the question regarding spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Question: [The following sections] answer the question of manifestation with four and two gates; the question of the Buddha-body with five and five gates;
the question of voice with two gates; the question of wisdom with three gates; the question of mastery with eight gates; the question of unimpededness with three gates;
and the question of liberation with three gates. This includes both the body and mastery.

In the preceding *Samantaprabhā*, because there were many questions, the gates [of explanation] were also numerous; however, the text generally consists of three parts: the thesis (*uddeśa*), the explanation (*nirdeśa*), and the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*).
The characteristics of these meanings will be made manifest in the text as it proceeds. Now, regarding the first two gates which answer the question concerning the buddha-field:
the field is that which is relied upon and in which one dwells, and thus it is divided into two. The first gate clarifies the dharma-gate of its eternal abiding.
The latter section clarifies that his abiding pervades the dharma-realm; it is not merely a land, nor does it exist within spatial locations, for it is the true land.
Now, the first part of the text has two sections. First, the heading.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have immeasurable abodes.
△ Second, the explanation of their characteristics:
namely, as follows.

The text contains nine phrases that reveal how the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; these implicitly answer ten questions, thereby showing that all ten questions constitute bases of abiding.
The following sections should be understood in this same manner.
Perpetually abiding in great compassion,
he gives rise to a responsive mind to answer questions concerning spiritual lineage; because compassion constitutes his spiritual lineage,
he dwells in various bodies to perform the deeds of a Buddha.
The body that expounds the Dharma answers the question regarding the Buddha-body;
abiding in an impartial mind, it turns the pure wheel of Dharma.
The intention to turn the Dharma answers the question regarding the original vow, for the original vow is impartial and benefits all beings.
Having given rise to the four types of eloquence, they expound immeasurable teachings.
Because they possess the eloquence that can turn [the wheel of Dharma], the eloquence that responds to sounds, and the eloquence that issues forth in answer to questions,
they abide in all the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas.
Regarding the Dharma that is turned forth: it answers the questions of those who possess mastery, for mastery is inconceivable.
It abides in a pure sound that pervades immeasurable lands;
its resonant voice turns and reaches throughout all lands, for these lands are where the sound arrives.
Abiding in the ineffable and profoundly deep *dharmadhātu*, one answers with wisdom the principles manifested therein; for wisdom is able to abide within the *dharmadhātu*.
Thus, one abides in the manifestation of all supreme supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The supernormal power of transformation answers the question regarding supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*).
Abiding in the ability to reveal the ultimate Dharma without obstruction, it explains the benefits of expounding the Dharma;
this answers the question regarding non-obstruction. The text consists of only nine phrases, omitting [the phrase] "manifesting. Alternatively, it may apply to all [categories].
[This is] a phrase. It appears because [the Buddha] is able to perform all that was previously mentioned in the nine [preceding] cases.
Answer: Since the ten questions in this chapter are thus, the two initial assemblies may be understood by analogy. △ Second, "Pervading the Dharma-realm," which clarifies his universal abiding;
that is, the six sense organs and three karmas pervade the lands of the Dharma-realm. The text is divided into three parts. First, the heading.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of dharmas that universally pervade the immeasurable and boundless Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

"Immeasurable" refers to phenomena (*dharma*), while "the boundlessness of the Dharma-realm" refers to principle (*tattva*). These two—phenomena and principle—are non-obstructive, as is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena;
these together constitute that which is pervaded. II. Listing and Explanation.
What are the ten? They are as follows: all Buddhas universally enter all realms of existence (*gati*) without being stained or attached.

This answers the three questions. First, it directly answers that their bodies are omnipresent throughout all realms of existence; this signifies both their compassionate nature and their manifestation.
All Buddhas possess boundless [qualities], up to abiding in the unimpeded and equal Dharma-body.
The following six phrases describe the specific characteristics of this body; they also simultaneously answer the six questions concerning the Universal Radiance Eye and so forth.
By producing sublime sounds, he answers the question regarding sound.
All Buddhas possess boundless, unimpeded liberation and the manifestation of inexhaustible great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

They answer three types of questions: namely, the ninth is the "unimpeded answer" (*asaṅga-vyākaraṇa*), the tenth is the "liberation answer" (*vimokṣa-vyākaraṇa*), and the supernormal powers answer with "mastery" (*vaśitā*).
All Buddhas possess boundless [realms] (extending to...), yet they do not give rise to defiled attachment therein.
This is the separate answer regarding the lands.
All Buddhas possess boundless [realms] (extending to...), and they are able to thoroughly penetrate all Buddha-dharmas.
This answers the questions regarding the original vows and wisdom. △ Third, the conclusion:
"O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha... [up to] ...the dharma-realm which is boundless."
△ Section Two: Two Gates. Answering the Questions on the Original Vow (2). First, it clarifies how, by virtue of his vow, he manifests the eight phases of appearance.
"O Sons of the Buddha, all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of wisdom that arise in every thought-moment."

However, it is intended that the essence [of this] consists of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). From that wisdom of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), the eight signs and so forth arise; it is not that wisdom itself arises.
The subsequent sections follow this pattern: first a heading, then an inquiry, followed by an enumeration and a conclusion.
What are the ten? They are as follows: all Buddhas descend from the heavens to immeasurable worlds;
they descend by virtue of their vows.
Within a single thought-moment, all Buddhas are able to manifest the taking of birth by Bodhisattvas in immeasurable worlds.
Regarding the lineage of birth:
all Buddhas are able, within a single thought-moment, to manifest in immeasurable worlds the going forth into homelessness and the training in the Way,
as well as the training in the Path of Liberation.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, manifest their appearance from beneath the Bodhi tree until they attain equal and perfect enlightenment.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma throughout immeasurable worlds.
Regarding sounds:
in a single thought-moment, all Buddhas [transform] to teach and transform sentient beings, make offerings to all Buddhas,
and manifest births to adorn their lands.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, manifest various Buddha-bodies beyond verbal expression. All Buddhas,
within a single thought-moment, [manifest] the sovereign treasury of all-knowledge of the Tathāgata.
Because the Tathāgatagarbha is adorned with sovereign characteristics and adorned with merit,
all Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, [reach] immeasurable and innumerable pure sentient beings.
Because it is unimpeded,
all Buddhas attain equal and perfect enlightenment within a single thought-moment (up to) throughout the three periods of time;
this is because it is wisdom that is perfectly and universally knowing.
These are the ten.
△ Second, clarifying that vows do not miss their time:
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have ten kinds of non-missing of time.

Their movements and abidings depend upon conditions. When the faculties ripen, they manifest; when their fundamental [karmic] maturation is exhausted, they abandon it. It is not that their vows are incomplete.
However, if the opportunity for maturation is lost at the critical moment, they would then violate their original vow.
What are these ten? They are: first, all Buddhas manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment without missing the proper time;
second, all Buddhas bring those with whom they have a karmic connection to maturity without missing the proper time.
May these vows be fulfilled through our shared affinity.
All Buddhas bestow predictions of enlightenment upon Bodhisattvas without missing the proper time;
they know their spiritual lineage and grant them their predictions.
All Buddhas manifest spiritual powers in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, never missing the proper time;
they act with mastery.
All Buddhas manifest the Buddha-body in accordance with the understanding of sentient beings, never missing the proper time.
Manifesting the body.
All Buddhas abide in great equanimity without missing the proper time;
their wisdom abides in equanimity.
All Buddhas enter all villages without missing the proper time;
their six sense faculties are unimpeded.
All Buddhas gather those of pure faith without missing the proper time.
The Pure Land gathers those with faith.
All Buddhas discipline wicked sentient beings without missing the proper time;
they use powerful sounds to subdue the wicked.
All Buddhas manifest inconceivable buddha-supernormal powers without missing the proper time;
this is inconceivable liberation.
These are the ten.

△ Section Three: Two Gates. Answering the Question on Lineage (gotra), there are two parts. The first gate clarifies both the *vipāka* (retribution) and *nirmāṇa* (emanation) lineages, as both are authentic and true.
"O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of incomparable and inconceivable realms."
Their essence and characteristics transcend words and thought; therefore, they are called "inconceivable. They are beyond the reach of those in lower stages;
therefore, they are called "peerless. What are these ten? That is to say, all Buddhas [pervade] throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions.
Manifesting his body,
he is able to reveal all Buddha-dharmas through the single meaningful phrase spoken by all Buddhas. His voice—
All Buddhas emit a single ray of light that is able to universally illuminate all worlds.
They emit this light by virtue of their vows; it is the light obtained through their original vows.
All Buddhas are able to manifest all bodies within a single body;
all Buddhas are able to manifest all worlds within a single location.
Buddha-lands:
All Buddhas, within a single wisdom, are able to decisively comprehend all phenomena without any obstruction—
this is wisdom.
All Buddhas are able, within a single thought-moment, to travel everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions with sovereign ease.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, manifest the immeasurable majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the lineage of majestic power:
all Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, universally take as their object the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the minds of sentient beings, without confusion or disorder,
and without the obstruction of confusion.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are identical in essence and non-dual with all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
their bodies of liberation are likewise identical.
This is the tenth.
The preceding five sections have all provided a brief indication and response to the ten questions; what follows might be considered too prolix, so let the expositor explain as appropriate.
△ Second, explaining that the Dharma-body alone constitutes the spiritual lineage (gotra).
Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to produce ten kinds of wisdom.
From within the state of non-substantiality (niḥsvabhāva), they bring forth their wisdom, for it is not a wisdom that arises from a response to a question.
What are these ten? They are: [the wisdom of all Buddhas] up to the wisdom that fully understands arising and ceasing; these constitute the ten.
There are ten phrases. Each phrase is divided into two parts: the first part recognizes that the nature is precisely the nature of no-nature, serving as the capacity for production;
the second part is the manifestation of the functional wisdom that arises therefrom. △ Fourth, there are two sections answering the question regarding manifestation. 2.
The first gate clarifies universal manifestation and constant manifestation.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of dharmas of universal entry;
it is only when they are without appearance or disappearance that they constitute true manifestation.
What are the ten? They are as follows: all Buddhas [possess] three kinds of mastery for the universal transformation of sentient beings.
These three kinds of mastery refer to the transformations of the three types of action (trikarma).
All Buddhas are fully endowed with [the power] to universally manifest all Buddhas of the three periods of time in a single thought-moment.

If this is so for all Buddhas, how much more so for one's own body? Furthermore, the manifestation of one is the manifestation of all, because the Buddhas of the three periods of time possess no dual essence, as explained in the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā*.
All Buddhas are fully endowed with [these qualities], up to and including universally establishing the number of kalpas throughout the three periods of time; this constitutes the tenth.
II. Clarifying the Characteristics of Manifestation:
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of vast dharmas that are difficult to believe and accept.
This means that its great function is boundless; therefore, it is called "vast and great. Because ordinary and inferior beings cannot fathom it, it is difficult to believe and accept.
What are these ten? They are: [all Buddhas] (up to) abiding within the ten powers—these constitute the ten.
△ Section Five: Five Gates. This answers questions regarding the Buddha-body, which is divided into five parts. First, it generally demonstrates the absence of faults:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of great merits that are pure and free from faults."
Because the three karmas of the Tathāgata proceed in accordance with wisdom, these three karmic activities do not depart from his body.
What are the ten? They are: [all Buddhas] ... up to ... being pure and free from faults; these constitute the ten.
In this section, there are many points that correspond to the ten characteristics of the body as presented in the "Chapter on Manifestation. II. Explaining the Non-arising of Faults:
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of ultimate purity.
To distinguish it from purity through causes, it is called "ultimate. Because the afflictions, hindrances, and all defilements never arise again, what are these ten?
They are: the ultimate purity of all Buddhas (throughout) and all their retinues.
The first five phrases refer to the purity of the body of merit;
they signify that all the lineages of the Buddhas are ultimately perfected, and that the marks and signs of their form bodies are ultimately pure.
These two form-bodies are the Dharma-body of all Buddhas, which is unstained and ultimately pure.
This is the Dharma-body.
The wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) of all Buddhas, characterized by the unimpeded and ultimate purity of the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The liberation and mastery of all Buddhas, having accomplished what was to be done and reached the further shore, which is ultimately pure.
Finally, there is the purity of the body through the single-minded arising [of the thought of enlightenment] and so forth.
These constitute the ten.
△ Third, the karmic functions of the three bodies.
O Son of the Buddha, that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to universally observe all worlds (up to this point) constitutes the tenth.
This is also largely identical to the description of the bodily marks in the "Chapter on Simultaneous Manifestation. △ Fourth, the correspondence with wisdom.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of inexhaustible oceans of wisdom-dharma (up to) these ten.
This is because the six sense organs and the three karmas of the Tathāgata are all in accord with profound and vast wisdom;
it is also because they are distinct, expansive embodiments of wisdom. △ Fifth: Uninterrupted Activity and Function.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of eternal dharmas (extending to) "because they are boundless"; these are the ten.
They assist the mental karma within the body of the Buddha, for it is constantly employed without interruption. Section Six has two gates.
First, answering the question regarding sound; second, explaining how to discern and teach by means of sound, which simultaneously answers the question of Puguang regarding eloquence.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have ten kinds of discourse on the immeasurable... these are the ten.
△ Second, clarifying the various ways of preaching the Dharma:
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have ten kinds of performing Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings.
That is to say, the six sense objects and the four great elements, as well as all movements and activities, are able to manifest the Dharma and accomplish its benefit;
there is nothing that is not a Buddha-activity. It is not limited to vocal sounds alone, as stated in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra.

What are the ten? They are as follows: first, all Buddhas [perform] the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings; second, [all Buddhas] have what they receive [which serves] as the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings; third, [all Buddhas] perform the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings through their bodies; fourth, [all Buddhas] perform the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings through their voices; fifth, [all Buddhas] perform the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings through their mental activities; sixth, [all Buddhas] perform the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings through their physical manifestations; seventh, [all Buddhas] perform the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings through their vocal manifestations; eighth, [all Buddhas] perform the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings through their mental manifestations; ninth, [all Buddhas] perform the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings through their physical transformations; tenth, [all Buddhas] perform the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings through their vocal transformations. Thus do all Buddhas perform the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings.

Both of these involve wisdom; they do not constitute [true] acceptance because they are undertaken for the sake of accomplishing *dāna*. They cause others to emulate the Buddha’s practice of having few desires.
Furthermore, it is by means of non-acceptance that one accepts all sensations.
All Buddhas perform the Buddha-work for sentient beings by means of earth, water, fire, and wind (up to) this being the tenth.
△ Seventh, there are three sections answering questions on wisdom. First, it clarifies that wisdom is supreme.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of most excellent dharmas.

This single section comprehensively elucidates the wisdom of the provisional and the real regarding cause and effect, while simultaneously answering the question of Samantaprabha concerning the most excellent [wisdom].
Because this wisdom is most excellent, it concludes by stating that one "dwells in the stage of the Ten Powers," which also answers the question regarding the Buddha-stage.
What are the ten? They are: the firmness of the great vows of all Buddhas... [and so on] ...these are the ten.

Four of these correspond to the practice of the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); the remainder may be considered accordingly. △ Second, explaining wisdom as being free from obstructions.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have ten kinds of unobstructed abodes.
Because their wisdom is unimpeded, they are entirely without obstruction.
What are these ten? That is to say, all Buddhas are able to go to [all places]—this constitutes the ten.
△ Third, the benefit of accomplishing wisdom. Because one possesses internal adornments of wisdom, one externally possesses all manner of adornments. This section has three parts. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of most excellent and unsurpassed adornments."
Because it transcends all lower stages, and because there is nothing superior above it that can surpass it, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
△ Second, regarding the ten distinct meanings, the title itself clearly indicates the conclusion. First, the body of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana-kāya*).
What are the ten? [They are] the first supreme, unsurpassed adornment of the body of all Buddhas.
△ Second, the perfection of voice:
all Buddhas are fully endowed with... the second supreme, unsurpassed adornment of speech.
△ 3. Adorning the mind with merit:
All Buddhas possess the ten powers (up to) the third supreme and unsurpassed adornment of the mind.
△ 4. Emitting light.
All Buddhas are able to emit [light], up to the fourth supreme and unsurpassed adornment of radiant light.
△ Fifth, the Smile:
When all Buddhas manifest a smile, it is the supreme and unsurpassed adornment of manifesting a smile.
The bestowal of the prophecy of enlightenment has many such causes and conditions, which are further elucidated in the "Chapter on Transcending the World.
Sixth, regarding the Dharma-body: all Buddhas possess a Dharma-body that is pure and unimpeded.
Because True Suchness has emerged from its entanglements, it is said to be pure and unimpeded; this is the Dharma-nature Dharmakāya.
Because fundamental wisdom reflects back upon itself, one attains ultimate penetration into all phenomena and abides in the Dharma-realm without limit or boundary.
This is precisely the wisdom-dharmakāya. Wisdom accords with the dharma-realm; both are without limit or boundary.
Although it exists within the world, it is not defiled by the world.
This is the nirmāṇa-dharmakāya.
Having realized the true nature of the world, one practices supramundane dharmas.

Because the dharma-body of merit is adorned by wisdom and principle, one realizes the true nature of the world, thereby accomplishing the aforementioned non-intermixture and giving rise to the aforementioned supramundane state.
By practicing supramundane dharmas, one’s merits become complete.
The path of language is cut off;

this is the Dharma-body of empty space, which is also the Dharma-body of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). Its essence transcends the hundred negations, and words cease within the four propositions, for it can only be realized through direct correspondence with awakening.

Transcending the aggregates, elements, and sense bases reveals this as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). By overturning the outflow-tainted aggregates, one forms the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*).
If one overturns the elements and sense bases, then the six external objects likewise become the land-body; thus, the ten bodies are perfectly interfused, and the true Dharma-body is realized.
This is the sixth most supreme and unsurpassed adornment of the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.
△ Seventh, the Constant Light:
All Buddhas possess infinite (up to) the most supreme and unsurpassed adornment of the eternally wondrous light.
△ Eight: The wondrous colors such as gold.
All Buddhas possess boundless wondrous colors.
The preceding phrase serves as the general [heading], while the remaining five are the specific [details].
Adorned with lovely, wondrous colors and pure, wondrous colors (up to) the eighth, the most supreme and unsurpassed wondrous color-adornment.
△ Ninth, possessing the true and the responsive lineages:
all Buddhas are born from within the Buddha-lineage of the three periods of time.
The seed of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is precisely suchness, because it is without intrinsic nature; thus the seeds should be understood.
By accumulating the jewels of manifold virtues, one attains ultimate purity, reaching the ninth [stage]: the adornment of the most supreme and unsurpassed lineage.
△ Ten: Great Compassion.
All Buddhas, by the power of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), [attain] the permanent cessation of bodily activity (*kāyakarman*) through the absence of all craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
This arises necessarily in conjunction with wisdom (*jñāna*); therefore, there is no craving. Because movement accords with the Path (*mārga*), bodily activity is permanently stilled.
The mind is well-liberated;
having attained the supreme state of non-craving,
those who behold it never grow weary.
This constitutes the cultivation of superior practice and tranquility; these are all meritorious qualities, free from attachment and views.
It constitutes the cultivation of inferior great compassion—the great compassion that protects and delivers all worlds, the foremost field of merit, and the unsurpassed recipient.
Since they constitute the foremost field of merit, there is none superior to them among those who receive offerings;
they compassionately benefit all sentient beings, adorned with the virtues of great loving-kindness and great compassion.
△ Third, the three fetters.
These constitute the ten.
*The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 75.
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Fascicle Seventy-Six (Entering the Second Half of the Forty-Sixth Scripture),
composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang,
with annotations to the scripture recorded by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.

△ Section Eight has eight sections. The answer to the question regarding mastery (*vaśitā*) is divided into eight parts. The first section provides a general explanation of mastery, which also encompasses empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
This section consists of two parts; the first is the general overview.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of sovereign dharmas.

△ Second, the detailed classification: these are entirely identical to the ten kinds of sovereignty found within the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), though here they are more profound and vast; the text merely differs in its arrangement.
First is mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*).
What are the ten? They are as follows: [the attainment of] all Buddhas... this is the first sovereign dharma of all Buddhas.
The *Śāstra* on the Sūtra states: "Because of the manifestation of the Dharma-gate that is without middle or limit. △ Second, mastery over the mind.
The teaching and transformation of sentient beings by all Buddhas—up to this point—is the second sovereign power (*vaśitā*) of the Buddhas.

Because they possess the wisdom of entering samādhi throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and because they observe the capacities of beings while remaining in samādhi, their transformations do not miss the proper time.
△ Third is the sovereign power of resolute belief (*adhimukti-vaśitā*).
All Buddhas are able to cause [the transformation] throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space; this is the third sovereign dharma of the Buddhas.
Because they can transform [realms] into large or small, pure or impure according to their understanding. △ Fourth, mastery over wealth.
All Buddhas, by means of their supernormal powers (up to this point), possess this fourth sovereign dharma of the Buddhas:
because they adorn, sustain, and maintain all worlds with immeasurable ornaments. △ Fifth, mastery over life.

All Buddhas behold a single sentient being... (up to) this is the fifth sovereign dharma of all Buddhas, because they maintain their life-span throughout unspeakable eons. △ Sixth, mastery over the wish-fulfilling [mind].
All Buddhas are able to go everywhere; this is the sixth sovereign dharma of the Buddhas.
Because they manifest transformations at will throughout all lands. △ Seventh, mastery over wisdom.
All Buddhas, desiring to discipline [sentient beings] and so forth until they achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
manifest the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of a Tathāgata, as well as the marks and signs of physical adornment and the three types of awakening (*tri-bodhi*).
Yet, regarding all Buddha-dharmas, he has not yet attained manifest awakening (up to: nor does he abide in the stage of one still in training).
Because the realm of sentient beings is boundless and their capacities have ripened accordingly, he must respond in every thought-moment;

yet, since his true accomplishment occurred in the past, the Buddha is not newly awakened in the three periods of time, nor is he unawakened. Furthermore, it is revealed that although he abides in the stage of training...
Moment-to-moment awakening, because it is free from the characteristics of awakening; not awakening within the three periods of time, because it is also free from non-awakening;
not abiding in the stage of training, yet fully knowing, seeing, penetrating, and attaining unimpeded, immeasurable wisdom and immeasurable mastery.
That is, the ten powers (*daśabala*) and so forth.
To teach and transform all sentient beings and bring them to discipline is the seventh sovereign dharma of the Buddhas.
△ Eighth, mastery over karma (*karmavaśitā*).
All Buddhas are able to perform the Buddha-work of the ear-faculty through the eye-faculty (and so on), up to the eighth mastery of dharmas.
This is because the vast Buddha-work of the mutual functioning of the six faculties is the activity of a Buddha;
yet it does not involve transformation, for each faculty remains unchanged, being inherently complete from the beginning. △ Ninth, mastery over birth.
From "the pores of the bodies of all Buddhas" (up to) "this is the ninth sovereign dharma of all Buddhas," because they manifest birth in all worlds. △ Tenth: Sovereignty over Vows.
Because all Buddhas manifest the attainment of *sambodhi* at will, according to their own minds, regarding the Buddha-lands and the times, there are four sections in the text.
From "In a single moment of thought, they manifest all worlds" up to "they manifest the sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas."
In each and every thought-moment, many Buddhas appear;
they attain Buddhahood within a single category of realm, such as those vast and magnificent worlds adorned with various wondrous lotuses, extending through various kalpas of pure worlds.
The second category reveals the remaining realms;
as it is in a single moment, so it is in all moments throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons.
The third category reveals the remaining moments.
"In a single thought, all appear.
This fourth section summarizes the profound and vast. Regarding "all appear": it means that in a single thought, all forms and all spiritual powers of the dharma-realm manifest.
To abide immeasurably in a single thought-moment because nothing ever manifests,
yet without having employed even the slightest power of skillful means— this is the tenth sovereign dharma of all Buddhas.
Because the Tathāgata Acala employs even a slight skillful means, he is said to be "sovereign.

Of the ten preceding sections, only the third and the eighth have been explained by taking their essential meaning; the remaining eight all discuss the literal text of the sūtra. △ Second, Sovereignty of Perfection.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of immeasurable, inconceivable, and perfect Buddha-dharmas;
these are what were previously termed the "ten masteries. Because these may exist [in part] at the eighth stage, they are here revealed as the ten kinds of perfection of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, it is only when not a single dharma lacks mastery that one can speak of "perfection."
What are these ten? They are as follows: all Buddhas, up to and including, fully accomplish all Buddha-dharmas.
These all Buddha-dharmas are precisely the realization and accomplishment of bodhi, the ten powers (*daśabala*), and so forth.
All Buddhas have fully accomplished all roots of goodness.
These roots of goodness encompass both merit and wisdom.
All Buddhas have fully accomplished all meritorious virtues.
Its merit consists solely of blessings.
It can be known that all Buddhas are able to teach and transform [beings], such that those who see them obtain benefit and their merit is never in vain.
All Buddhas possess the equal and true Dharma of all Buddhas;
that is, they possess the teachings of the Wheel of Dharma.
All Buddhas, having performed their Buddha-works, invariably manifest entry into nirvana—this is the tenth.
△ Third, the three skillful means. First, the general overview:
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of skillful means.
This is because they have attained mastery over all dharmas, as their provisional and ultimate teachings are equal and unimpeded. △ Second, the specific ten. First, verbal expression:
Mastery. What are the ten? [From] "All Buddhas" [to] "this is the first skillful means.

Knowing that reality is ineffable and transcends the conceptual proliferation of movement and agitation, yet giving rise to provisional teachings to reveal roots of goodness—therefore, it is [the first].
Mastery. △ Second, mastery of knowledge and vision:
All Buddhas know all dharmas... this is the second skillful means.
Verifying that there is neither subject nor object of perception, yet not obstructing the true knowledge and vision of phenomena;
being neither bound nor liberated, one attains great sovereign mastery. △ Third, the manifestation of sovereign mastery.
All Buddhas are eternally free from all marks (up to) this being the third skillful means:

the markless knowing of marks, and the natureless entering into nature. They are also able to manifest the reliance on and the correctness of [the environment and its inhabitants] to harmonize and guide sentient beings.
△ Fourth, mastery over the three periods of time.
All Buddhas abide in the *dharmadhātu* (up to) this being the fourth skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

They realize the principle of the three periods of time [past, present, and future] in their mystery, yet they manifest throughout the three periods to benefit sentient beings. △ Fifth, mastery over nature and characteristics.
The physical, verbal, and mental activities of all Buddhas—[extending] to this—is the fifth skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
These three activities are profoundly still, yet they encompass and manifest [all things]. △ Sixth, mastery in taming sentient beings.
All Buddhas know all dharmas (up to) this being the sixth skillful means:
knowing that they are neither identical nor different, yet perceiving all dharmas. △ Seventh, mastery over time.
All Buddhas, within a single moment of time (up to...)—this is the seventh skillful means.
Knowing the proper time to enter [absorption], they neither abide nor abandon it, yet without destroying the duration of years and kalpas, they expound the Dharma without ceasing.
△ Eighth, mastery of eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
All Buddhas eternally abide in the dharma-realm, accomplishing the immeasurable fearlessnesses of all Buddhas.

To eternally abide in the dharma-realm is to be quiescent and without abiding; yet they accomplish the ten analytical knowledges (*daśapratibhāna*) and expound the Dharma with immeasurable fearlessness.
And there is incalculable eloquence because the numbers are so vast;
there is immeasurable eloquence.
Because it cannot be fathomed by the mind,
its inexhaustible eloquence is such that even if one were to speak of a single matter for an entire kalpa, it would never be exhausted.
Uninterrupted eloquence,
because there is no interval in its unrestrained and free-flowing eloquence;
boundless eloquence.
Because it establishes arguments by touching upon various categories,
it is an uncommon argument;
for it is something that does not exist among those of inferior status.
Inexhaustible eloquence,
because it cannot be challenged or defeated;
true eloquence.
Because all [teachings] accord with both phenomena and principle,
they employ skillful means to reveal all phrases and arguments;
there is not a single phrase or meaning that cannot be made manifest.
He possesses eloquence regarding all phenomena,
for there is not a single dharma that he cannot expound.
According to their faculties, natures, inclinations, and understandings— [extending] to that which is good in the beginning, middle, and end— he brings them all to ultimate completion.
The virtue of being clearly explained consists in possessing the seven excellences; alternatively, it may be expanded into ten. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (85) states:
first, it is excellent in the beginning because one experiences joy at the time of hearing; second, it is excellent in the middle because there is no difficulty or suffering at the time of practice.

It is "good in the middle" because it relies on the practice of the Middle Way, remaining far removed from the two extremes. It is "good in the end," meaning that it ultimately abandons all defilements and so forth;

as the present text states, "all are completely perfected. There are many further explanations regarding these points in various sūtras and śāstras, but fearing prolixity, I shall not elaborate further.
The remaining seven sūtras are omitted here.
This constitutes the eighth skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
△ Ninth, mastery over the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-vaśitā*).
All Buddhas abide in the pure Dharma-realm (up to) being far removed from all false conceptualizations and attachments;
they speak while remaining free from speech, and thus they are without conceptual attachment.
Thus, to ultimately reach the other shore is the ninth skillful means. △ Tenth, the function of quiescent realization.
Within this, there are two parts: first, knowing the primordial quiescence; second, the actual manifestation. First, the direct manifestation:
All Buddhas know all dharmas; because they are non-apprehendable, they are not elements (*dhātu*).
△ Second, the explanation for establishing this:
yet they do not destroy any dharmas [up to] being neither with causes and conditions nor without causes and conditions.

This means that the nature of form and so forth is non-existent; it is not made non-existent by being negated. Therefore, one does not destroy the various dharmas. Thus, emptiness is itself devoid of karma and so forth.
△ Second, the non-abandonment of the arising of function.
And being able to discern right determination and wrong determination—this is the tenth skillful means.
△ Third, the conclusion:
"O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of skillful means accomplished by all Buddhas."
From here below begins the forty-seventh fascicle of the sutra.
△ Fourth, the vast buddha-activities clarify the mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). This directly answers the questions concerning the supernormal powers from the previous two assemblies.
The text has three parts; first is the general overview.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of vast buddha-activities.
This means that within the eight signs and so forth, there are all great functions, because they are subtly interpenetrating. By means of this, they gather and transform sentient beings. Therefore—
This is called "Buddha-activity. The first part provides the title; the second part reveals its excellence.
It is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable (extending to) except for the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual authority.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the two [sections].
First, the inquiry: What are the ten?
△ Second, the explanation of the ten. First, clarifying the Buddha-activities of ascending birth, in four parts. First, specifically clarifying that which can encompass.
That is to say, it refers to the sphere of activity of all Buddhas, from the exhaustion of empty space up to immeasurable wisdom.
△ Second, the vastness of what is encompassed:
it encompasses all humans, devas, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, asuras, and so forth.
△ 3. The excellence of what is subsumed:
Great compassion is unimpeded, reaches the great ultimate, and equally benefits all sentient beings.
△ 4. The benefit accomplished by that which is subsumed.
Either causing them to be born in the heavens or causing them to be born among humans (up to this point)—this constitutes the first vast Buddha-activity.
△ Second, the Buddha-activity of descending in spirit and dwelling in the womb has two parts. First, the internal perfection of wisdom and virtue.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas proceed from Tuṣita Heaven until they achieve the vast and wondrous treasury of adornment.
△ Second, the external application of supernatural powers has two parts; first, performing buddha-work in a single place at a single time.
Having received his final body, he dwells in the Great Jewel-Adorned Pavilion (until) arising from various samādhis to perform buddha-work.
△ Second, a general summary of performing buddha-work across time and place.
O Son of the Buddha, at that time the Tathāgata was within his mother’s womb... [up to] thus, through various skillful means.
In this section, there are many places; following the *Gopā* [chapter] below, there are as many as ten layers. Here, five are briefly cited, each subsequent one expanding upon the preceding.
In all directions— namely,
the Sahā world together with as many worlds as there are atoms in thirteen surrounding realms— they abide without interval throughout the ten directions; thus,
they constitute the entire net.
Above those lands, there are further surrounding subsidiary lands that encircle them, forming a network of interlacing lattices;
thus, they all revolve around the central sea, which is the tenth right-turning sea.
In every way, throughout the entirety of the Flower Treasury Ocean of Lands,
because of all the world-systems within it; in all worlds.
Because it pervades the entire dharma-realm, performing buddha-work in this manner constitutes the second vast buddha-work.
△ Third, the buddha-work of manifesting birthplaces and palaces has two parts. First, manifesting birth within non-birth; this is the aspect of the birth ceremony.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas, through all their wholesome karmas, manifest birth in a royal palace for the sake of sentient beings.

△ Second, being unstained while dwelling in what is stained. This refers to the characteristics of the royal palace; herein there are four parts. The first three concern the perfection of one's own training.
All Buddhas have already renounced all forms, desires, palaces, and musical entertainments, remaining free from any attachment or defilement.
This absence of defilement is meditative concentration.
They constantly contemplate that all phenomena are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, and that all objects of pleasure are entirely unreal.
This first is wisdom;
upholding the Buddha’s pure precepts to ultimate perfection—this is morality.
△ Second, clarifying the four minds that take pity on sentient beings.
Contemplating all the ladies of the inner palace, wives, concubines, and attendants (up to) attaining mastery over the mind and giving rise to great equanimity.
△ Third, gathering and benefiting through the possession of virtues:
possessing the Buddha’s merits, manifesting birth within the dharma-realm (up to) causing them to awaken in the interim so that their minds attain purity.
△ Fourth, the gathering and benefiting [of beings] is profound and vast.
Although he dwells within the inner palace, he is beheld by all (until: this is the third great Buddha-activity).
△ Fourth, the Buddha-activity of renunciation has two parts. First, clarifying the intent of renunciation.
O Sons of the Buddha, all Buddhas likewise abide in various [states] (throughout the passage) cultivating pure conduct to benefit sentient beings.
△ Second, the characteristics of leaving the household life:
At the time of leaving the household life, one discards worldly deportment (throughout the passage) to become for all time a lofty banner of wisdom for the world.
Because the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind] benefit both oneself and others, this constitutes the fourth vast buddha-activity.
△ Fifth, the buddha-activity of attaining enlightenment has three parts. First, true awakening is primordially perfect.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas possess all-encompassing wisdom and have already known and seen all immeasurable dharmas.
△ Second, the fulfillment of the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*):
from attaining supreme perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree until the cultivation of all merits has been entirely perfected.
△ Third, the manifestation of the Dharma to benefit sentient beings.
Its Bodhi-maṇḍala is fully adorned... (up to) this constitutes the fifth vast Buddha-activity.

This is the sudden exposition of the *Avataṃsaka*. △ Sixth, the Buddha-activity of turning the wheel of Dharma. Its meaning encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate. The text has two parts. First:
Section.
The Buddha-sons: all Buddhas turn the wheel of the non-retrogressive Dharma in order to cause all bodhisattvas not to retrogress.
Only the Bodhisattva Vehicle encompasses the four types of non-retrogression.
He turns the immeasurable wheel of Dharma so that all worlds may fully understand it;
he penetrates the five vehicles so that the world universally understands them;
and he turns the wheel of Dharma that awakens all beings, being able to let out the great, fearless lion’s roar.
By opening up the provisional and revealing the ultimate, it causes one to awaken to the knowledge and vision that exist with certainty;
by turning the Dharma-wheel of the treasury of wisdom regarding all phenomena, it opens the door to the Dharma-treasury and removes the veil of darkness.
It penetrates the Three Piṭakas, for the Three Piṭakas eliminate delusion and the three obstacles;
it turns the unimpeded wheel of Dharma, which is equal to empty space;
it is exclusively the Sudden Teaching, for both phenomena and principle are simultaneously transcended.
He turns the wheel of non-attachment by contemplating that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent;
he turns the wheel of the Middle Way because it does not cling to the two extremes;
and he turns the wheel that illuminates the world so as to purify the Dharma-eye of all sentient beings.
The dharmas of conventional truth, because they purify that which is known;
the wheel of the dharma of omniscience, because it is turned and revealed so as to pervade all dharmas of the three periods of time;
and the Buddha-dharmas alone, because their wisdom is all-pervasive knowledge.
It turns the single Dharma-wheel of all Buddhas, because all Buddha-dharmas are not mutually contradictory;
it is solely the Perfect Dharma, because there is no diversity of flavors. △ Second, the conclusion.
All Buddhas perform buddha-work through such distinctions in mental conduct as these;
this constitutes the tenth wheel, the infinite vehicles, because they are expounded according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Inconceivable! All ten are perfectly interfused; this is what is meant by "inconceivable.
This constitutes the sixth vast buddha-activity.
△ Four on the Buddha-activities of the seven modes of deportment. First, specifically citing the benefit of beings upon entering a city:
"O Son of the Buddha, when all Buddhas enter among all sentient beings, there are none who hear them and do not rejoice."
△ Second, universally manifesting the benefit of sentient beings through majestic deportment:
"The form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of all Buddhas are pure... [omitted] ...all perform the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings.
△ Third, manifesting the benefit of sentient beings through speech and discourse.
"All Buddhas of the past" (the term "past," *xi*, is absent from the Jin edition;
it refers to the benefit of the present). If one speaks of the "past," this is to cite the cause in order to manifest the fruit;
it must therefore be the character "universal" (*pu*). △ Fourth, the summary of its profundity and vastness.
All Buddhas, by means of such [practices] as these... this constitutes the seventh vast buddha-activity.
△ Eighth, the fourfold buddha-activity of initiating practice. First, the dwelling in physical and mental tranquility.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas may perform the work of a Buddha while dwelling in an araṇya;
"araṇya" refers exclusively to mountain forests.
Or they may perform the work of a Buddha while dwelling in a place of tranquility.
Tranquility extends to cities and towns,
or one may perform the Buddha-work while dwelling in secluded places;
"secluded" refers to locations devoid of things.
Or they abide in the state of a Buddha and perform Buddha-works (up to) performing Buddha-works without rest.
△ Second, the arising of the practice of seeking upward in response:
Or they assume a celestial body to seek all-knowledge (up to) performing Buddha-works by seeking all-knowledge.
△ Third, the practice of silent transformation below:
at times he preaches the Dharma, and at times he remains in silence (until: performing buddha-work even where it is not a [conventional] sphere).
△ Fourth, advancing in practice according to the divisions of time.
Or remaining for one day, or remaining for one night (up to this point)—this constitutes the eighth vast buddha-activity.
△ Ninth: The Buddha-Activity of Arising Function. Part Two: First, the basis upon which the function arises.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas are the treasury from which pure roots of goodness arise.
Because they are able to give birth to this treasury of merit,
they cause all sentient beings, within the Buddha-dharma, to attain the brilliance of wisdom and to realize awakening independently, without relying on others.
△ Second, the explicit explanation of the manifestation of activity.
From "Or manifesting nirvāṇa to perform Buddha-work" (up to) "this is the ninth vast Buddha-work. △ Tenth, the Buddha-work of nirvāṇa.
This is one among those that specifically reveal the function. Within this, there are three parts. First, the explanation of nirvāṇa.
The benefit of compassionate longing:
when all the Buddhas, sons of the Buddha, enter parinirvāṇa, they perform the work of a Buddha through lamentation and yearning.
△ Second, the benefit of the distribution of relics.
Furthermore, they transform and deliver all devas and humans (up to) forever acting as a refuge for the world.
△ Third, the summary of benefiting beings:
"O Son of the Buddha, although the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have entered parinirvāṇa... this is the tenth vast buddha-activity."
If these ten points are correlated with the answers to the ten questions: first, the answer to the original vow; second, the seed-nature and the land;
third, unimpededness; fourth, liberation; fifth, manifestation; sixth, voice; seventh, the Buddha-body;
eighth, wisdom; ninth, mastery. △ Third, the conclusion.
"O Son of the Buddha, these buddha-activities are immeasurable and vast (until: ...), except for that which is empowered by the majestic spiritual authority (*anubhāva*) of the Tathāgata.
△ Fifth, the Dharma of Non-dual Sovereignty.
Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of sovereign dharmas of non-dual conduct that clarify fearless sovereignty.
Because they respond to the question posed by Samantaprabhā regarding fearlessness, they are clear, precise, and decisive in their actions;
because they are free from doubt, they are non-dual; and because they do not fear the challenges of others, this is called sovereignty.
What are the ten? They are as follows: [the first four]—namely, that the wisdom of all Buddhas is definitively non-dual—can be understood from the preceding section. [The next six are:
that all Buddhas fully know the three periods of time... [and so forth], up to: that the speech of a single Buddha is definitively non-dual.
These three [points] encompass two meanings: first, the integration of phenomena through principle; second, the mutual entry of all things.
All Buddhas fully know that the nature of the three periods of time is without differentiation and is definitively non-dual.
These two are solely based on principle.
All Buddhas fully know all Buddhas of the three periods of time... this constitutes the tenth. There are three meanings:
first, because they are cultivated with the same nature; second, because they mutually dedicate [merit]; third, because they mutually serve as the principal and the attendant. △
Sixth, the elucidation of abiding in all dharmas.
Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have ten kinds of abidings by which they abide in all dharmas.
This elucidates mastery over samādhi and simultaneously answers the question regarding the Samādhi of Universal Radiance. Therefore, there is nothing in which the Tathāgata does not abide.
Samādhi. Therefore, he dwells pervasively in all things.
What are the ten? They are: all Buddhas dwell in awakening... (up to)... these are the ten. △ Seventh:
knowing all phenomena exhaustively without remainder.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of knowledge that comprehend all phenomena without exception, manifesting the mastery of the Ten Powers.
This also serves as a response to the question posed by Samantaprabha regarding the Ten Powers; thus, the wisdom of the Ten Powers illuminates all objects of cognition without omission.
What are the ten? They are: knowing all past phenomena exhaustively without exception... [and so forth] ...these are the ten.
△ Eighth, Great Power. This clarifies mastery over spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) and also answers the question regarding the ten powers of Samantaprabha.
The text has three parts; first, the heading.
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds [of qualities].
"The Ten Powers" (*daśabala*) is a specific designation, while "Great Nārāyaṇa" and so forth are general appellations. Therefore, in the following list, we rely solely on the general names.
Thus, each of the "Ten Powers" indicated in the heading applies universally throughout the subsequent specific sections. Among these, there are ten gates in the specific section: first...
If one sets forth the ten powers (*daśabala*) indicated in the preceding heading, they constitute one hundred gates.

Ancient masters have sequentially correlated the ten powers in the heading with the ten qualities of heroism (*daśa-vīrya*) listed below—namely, identifying the first [power] as "vast power" (*vaipulya-bala*) and so forth.

However, this approach fails to include the preceding ten [powers] within the individual gates, thereby failing to establish the one hundred gates; it also renders the remaining gates devoid of the meaning of "vastness. This concerns the first gate.
There is no supreme [element] above it. If one wishes to pair them according to their excellence, they should be paired in reverse order;
for its vast power pervades the entire dharma-realm.
The supreme power,
because it is unsurpassed;
the immeasurable power.
Because it is immeasurable;
because its great majestic power is to be revered.
The power that is difficult to obtain,
for it is attained by the Buddha alone;
the power of non-retrogression.
Because it acts without yielding,
it is the power of firmness; because its essence is solid, it is the power of steadfastness.
The power that cannot be destroyed,
because its conditions are indestructible;
the inconceivable power of all worlds.
Because he transcends invocation, thought,
and recollection, no sentient being has the power to move him; he is unshakable.
The Dharma of the Great Nārāyaṇa Banner and Valiant Prowess.
△ Second, the interrogation and explanation, in two parts.
First, the interrogation: "What are the ten?"
The second section, the "Explanation," is divided into ten parts. First is the power of the indestructibility of body and life;

this is now assigned in reverse order to the present context, namely, the power of being unshakable, because not even a single hair is moved. This passage has two parts: first, the explicit clarification of being unshakable and indestructible.
That which is called the indestructible body of all Buddhas (extending to... rains down from it without ever causing any harm.
This means that neither sentient nor insentient conditions can destroy it. △ Second, illustrating its excellence by way of analogy.
If there are sentient beings who are sustained by the Buddha (up to) the foremost dharma of the heroic vigor of the Nārāyaṇa Banner,
it is like causing Jīvaka to enter fire to retrieve a child, or entering a prison to inquire about a crime. △ Second, the power of containing and sustaining within a single pore.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas [up to] the second great Dharma of the courageous Narayana-bannered heroism is inconceivable;
yet because sentient beings do not realize it, [it remains hidden]. △ Third, the power of holding up the great mountain with a single hair.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas [possess] the third Dharma of the Great Narayana Banner of Valiant Prowess, which is indeed indestructible.
This is because even while supporting massive great mountains, their body and mind suffer no fatigue or injury.
In this text, "swiftly traversing vast strides" means that the lands traversed over many eons are the measure of a single mountain; yet these mountains are themselves boundless.

How much more so when many mountains exist within a single hair-pore, and how much more so when many hairs remain held there throughout an entire kalpa; this is truly what is called an inconceivable realm.
△ Fourth, the power of mastery over the functions of meditative concentration.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas [possess] up to the fourth Dharma of the Great Nārāyaṇa Banner of Valor and Prowess;
this is because they abide in firm and stable resolve.

△ The Universal Manifestation of the Power of the Dharma. This is the voice of non-retrogression, for it is inexhaustible, being without change or interruption.
Part Two. First, clarifying that a single body manifests the Dharma in three sections. First, revealing the multiplicity of what is taught:
"O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas are able, within a single body... [to manifest] as many words, phrases, and meanings as there are atoms in a Buddha-field."
△ Second, clarifying the permanence of what is taught:
Thus, these teachings are expounded in full, beyond even the ineffable and ineffable (until) the turning of the Wheel of Dharma is without end.
△ 3. Showing the essence of what is taught:
namely, the wheel of Dharma expounded through wisdom (up to) the wheel of Dharma adorned with various forms of eloquence and fearlessness.
△ 2. Clarifying the turning of the Dharma by multiple bodies.

Just as a single Buddha-body, by means of supernormal powers, reaches the fifth stage of the Great Nārāyaṇa Banner of Valiant Dharma—this is the teaching of the eternal and constant, which is boundless before and after. Those who are born blind cannot see it even when facing it;
according to what they perceive through their own resonance, they speak of its beginning and end. △ Sixth, the marks and virtues that subdue the power of Māra.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas [possess] up to the sixth dharma of the great Nārāyaṇa-bannered valor and strength, which is indeed difficult to attain.
Yet, all ten are difficult to attain. Because the world abounds in demonic delusions, this one is specifically designated by the name "difficult to attain.
△ Seventh, the power of the universally penetrating perfect sound.

"O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas [up to] the seventh Dharma of the Great Nārāyaṇa Banner of Valor and Prowess is itself majestic power (*tejas*), for upon hearing it, all are tamed and subdued. 8. The Power of the Unobstructed Mind.

This is the Power of Immeasurability, for it is free from both the measurable (*pramāṇa*) and the non-measurable (*apramāṇa*). The text has two parts; first, freedom from the obstructions of dust-like afflictions (*kleśa*).
"O Son of the Buddha, the minds of all Buddhas are without obstruction" (up to) "transcending all conditioned and unconditioned verbal expressions.
△ Second, the unobstructed arising of function.
Regarding the unspeakable and boundless realm... up to: the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*) and the mind being well-liberated.
As for "the mind being well-liberated," it is by way of three characteristics: first, because of the thorough and complete knowledge of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
second, because of the abandonment and realization of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) associated with them; and third, once the afflictions have been abandoned, regarding all...
Abiding in detachment from craving, he dwells in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This concludes up to the eighth great quality: the courageous and heroic Dharma of Nārāyaṇa’s Banner.
△ Ninth: the subtle and secret power of the Dharmakāya.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas [up to] the ninth, the Great Nārāyaṇa Banner of Valiant Dharma, constitute the supreme.
This collectively subsumes the preceding eight and the subsequent one, for there is nothing further to be added. The text enumerates twenty-five bodies;
these are either the reality of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), the response-body of reality, the characteristic of the nature (dharmatā), or the wisdom of the principle (tattva).
The ten bodies are perfectly interfused as a single body of the Dharma-realm; they cannot be categorized as either *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) or *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
Therefore, it is called the "Supreme and Most Subtle Mystery. △ Tenth, the Power of Wisdom that Perfectly Accomplishes Practice: this is the power of vast majesty.

Because the causal practice is like the ocean, the resultant wisdom universally pervades the five boundless realms. Its great function is limitless. The text has four parts; first, the perfect purity of the myriad practices.
O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas equally awaken to the fact that the activities of body, speech, and mind are entirely without confusion.
△ Second, the perfection of the function of wisdom:
abiding in what the Buddhas abide in, within the lineage of all Buddhas, one attains non-retrogressive wisdom and enters the number of all Buddhas.
△ 3. Sovereignty over movement and stillness:
Although one has already realized that which is ineffable (up to), one is able to know and see it all through unimpeded wisdom.
△ 4. Boundless function.

O Son of the Buddha, all the Buddhas [up to] the tenth quality, the Dharma of the courageous Narayana-bannered heroism—these ten powers above do not transcend the three karmas; this may be inferred accordingly. △ Third, the conclusion.
O Son of the Buddha, all these Buddhas are like great Nārāyaṇas... [omitted] ...except for those empowered by the supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*) of the Tathāgata.
△ Ninth: Three sections. Answering the section on unimpededness. First, it clarifies that what is accomplished is definitive and nothing can act as an obstruction.
O Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of definitive dharmas.
These are called "definitive dharmas" because they pertain to a specific category of world-systems; in world-systems of a different category, they may not necessarily be so.
Furthermore, they are called "definitive" because they refer to what the Buddhas are certainly able to perform.
What are these ten? They are as follows: all Buddhas invariably proceed from Tuṣita [to birth]; these constitute the ten.
△ Second, clarifying that they cause others to be without obstruction:
O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of swift dharmas.
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, it brings swift benefit to those who behold it, yet those of meager merit do not see it.
What are these ten? They consist of ten phrases in five pairs.
That is to say, if anyone should behold any of the Buddhas, they will swiftly attain the fulfillment of supreme merit,
leave behind the evil realms, and perfect excellent virtues.
If anyone beholds any of the Buddhas, they will swiftly attain rebirth in the pure and wondrous heavens,
establishing wholesome causes and experiencing joyful fruits.
If anyone beholds any of the Buddhas, they will [attain] the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Eliminating doubt and fulfilling the great resolve,
all Buddhas— whether they have not yet entered the stage of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), or up to those whose worldly faculties have become pure— [possess] all faculties.
Beginning with the entry into the stage and ending in complete purity, if any among all Buddhas should behold this, they will swiftly attain fearless eloquence; this is the tenth.
They purify the two obstructions and possess the four analytical knowledges. △ Third, they maintain unimpeded mindfulness.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of pure dharmas that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, should constantly recollect.
Citing that the Buddhas are free from the two kinds of obstruction, he exhorts beings to mindfully uphold [this teaching].
What are the ten? They are: all Buddhas’ past causes and conditions... (up to)... this is the tenth.
△ There are thirteen sections that answer questions on liberation. The first section elucidates liberation from the obstacles to wisdom:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of abodes of omniscience."
Because wisdom rests securely upon both phenomena and their underlying principles, it is called "abiding. Due to being free from all obscurations, one is able to know everything.
What are these ten? They refer to all Buddhas, within a single moment of thought, [attaining] up to [the realization that] this constitutes the tenth.
△ Second, liberation from the obstacles to meditative concentration.
Sons of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-samādhis.
Because they are free from obstacles, their application is vast; because they constitute an immeasurable essence, they are profoundly inconceivable. Among these ten kinds:
First, each [of these powers] is clarified as being present within meditative concentration;
subsequently, they are universally applied in a single moment of thought. What are these ten? They are: all Buddhas are constantly in right concentration... (up to) this is the tenth.
△ Liberation through the Functioning of the Three Karmas.
The Buddha-sons, the World-Honored Buddhas, possess ten kinds of unimpeded liberation.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "Bodhisattvas possess inconceivable liberation; the Buddhas possess immeasurable liberation. Regarding this:
It acts without obstruction because it is liberated from hindrances; therefore, within each single atom, it simultaneously performs subtle functions.
Now, to answer the ten questions individually:
what are these ten? They are as follows: "All Buddhas" (up to) "unspeakably many Buddhas appear in the world."
Answer: Manifestation.
All Buddhas are able, within a single atom, to turn the pure wheel of Dharma for unspeakably many Buddhas.
Answer: Sound.
All Buddhas are able, within a single atom (up to: *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings), to transform and subdue an unspeakable number of sentient beings.
This answers the original vow; for the vow was made to transform all [beings] until none remain.
All Buddhas are able to manifest within a single atom unspeakably, unspeakably many Buddha-lands.

This is because the former concludes with the description of the lands themselves.
All Buddhas are able to manifest all supernatural powers of the past, future, and present within a single atom;
this is the answer regarding mastery.
All Buddhas are able to manifest all sentient beings of the past, future, and present within a single atom.
Answer: It is unimpeded benefit. Because sentient beings are without obstruction, all Buddhas are able to manifest all Buddha-activities of the past, future, and present within a single atom.
Answer: It is liberation, for there is nothing it does not accomplish. Since each individual gate answers all ten questions, one knows that it encompasses and subsumes them inexhaustibly;
therefore, it is called "inconceivable. However, as this passage lacks a formal conclusion at its end, it appears that the scripture has not yet reached its completion.
Alternatively, because it manifests the inexhaustibility of the Buddha’s virtues, the "Ocean of Marks" and subsequent chapters still provide further answers.
Because of the previous question,
