Chapter Thirty-Four: The Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Ten Bodies and Marks. Regarding the intent of this chapter:

The preceding chapter explained the dharma of fruition in general; this chapter specifically reveals the excellence of its marks (*lakṣaṇa*). It answers, in the near term, the questions concerning the Buddha-body raised in the previous chapter;

and in the distant term, it answers [the inquiry regarding] the six sense organs, such as the Universal Radiance Eye, demonstrating that it is not only the eyes and other organs that are all-pervading.
Within the *dharmadhātu*, each [of these bodies] possesses manifold marks and functions that are difficult to conceive.

Regarding the second point, the explanation of the names: the "Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata" (*daśatathāgatakāya*) designates the person and reveals their virtues. The term "Ocean of Marks" (*lakṣaṇasāgara*) reveals the marks based on that person.
The Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata are all explained as previously stated. Their wondrous forms, which are the fruits of merit, are brilliantly renowned as "marks"; these are the marks of virtue.
Because it is profound and vast, it is called an ocean. Thus, the sutra text describes ten sets of marks, as numerous as the atoms within a lotus-receptacle world-system (*padma-garbha-loka-dhātu*).
The substance of these marks is vast; each and every function pervades everywhere, so their functions are vast; each and every one is inconceivable, mutually merging and interpenetrating.
The essence and function [of these marks] are profound. Such characteristics belong exclusively to the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao); this is why only the ten bodies (daśakāya) are indicated.
The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisāgara-sūtra* distinguishes three categories of these characteristics: first, the briefest summary, which speaks of thirty-two marks;
second, the brief explanation, which speaks of eighty-four thousand marks; and third, the detailed explanation, which speaks of immeasurable marks. As it says:
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was preached for Samantabhadra, Bhadramukha, and others; it is an alternative name for this very scripture.
Among the three [categories], the first is common to both the provisional and the small vehicle (*hīnayāna*), as it shows [the Buddha] to be like a human being, being upright and composed.

The second pertains exclusively to the Mahāyāna, because Bodhisattvas cultivate the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*. The last pertains exclusively to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), meaning that the One Vehicle cultivates the non-... (the text is incomplete).

Because it is the fulfillment of all practices. Furthermore, the first [aspect] refers to the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); the second, to the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*); and the last, to the ten bodies.

This is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound referring to the ocean-like marks of these ten bodies. Moreover, the first is seen by both ordinary beings and sages; the second, only by those on the stages (*bhūmi*); and the last, only by those with the capacity for the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

However, these penetrate all five stages. If one speaks of their substance (*tattva*), the first consists of form and color; the second consists of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*);
and the last consists of the inexhaustible Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). If one speaks of their causes, the latter two encompass both the pure and the mixed, as explained in the first assembly.

Therefore, each and every mark and fruit completely pervades the Dharma-realm. The causes of the first two marks are as described in treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The *Saṃcaya-gāthā* and other sūtras explain this extensively, as discussed in a separate chapter.

Regarding the threefold thematic intent (*abhiprāya*): the primary theme (*piṇḍārtha*) is the explicit teaching of the inexhaustible ocean of signs; the ultimate goal (*prayojana*) is to cause sentient beings to collectively cultivate inexhaustible practices until they reach manifest realization.
Next is the formal explanation of the text. The text is divided into three parts. First, the announcement to the assembly and the granting of permission to speak:
"At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... [until] expounding the ocean of marks possessed by the Tathāgata."
The reason Samantabhadra speaks is that the ocean of marks is universally pervasive; he causes [beings] to practice universal conduct so that they may attain universal marks.
Since Samantabhadra is originally the presiding host of this assembly and his previous discourse has reached its conclusion, he now speaks.

Alternatively, as the sutra text at the end of the preceding chapter has not yet ended, there should further be a separate response to questions regarding the lands and so forth. △ Second, the actual presentation of the characteristics, briefly cited:
Regarding the ninety-seven marks, within each mark there are five aspects: first, the locus; second, the enumeration of names;

third, the adornment of the essence; fourth, the functional activity; and fifth, the summary of the number. These may be abbreviated and not fully present, as should be understood from the specific text.

Alternatively, some may include additional benefits, which are subsumed under "functional activity. However, since names are established solely based on the essence and its function, they are all categorized according to essence and function.

Explanation of the Names: Some names derive solely from the essence (*svabhāva*) or the function (*karman*), while others derive from both. These should be understood according to the specific textual passages.
Where the name does not correspond in meaning to the essence or the function, it is a case of textual abbreviation; the meaning, however, is fully encompassed.

If one were to discuss each aspect in detail according to its respective location, there would be ninety-seven sections, as the sutra itself indicates their sequence. For the present purpose, they have been grouped together according to their thematic categories.
Based upon the eighteen locations, this is divided into eighteen sections, beginning from the crown of the head and ending at the feet;
this constitutes the sequential contemplation of the Tathāgata’s ocean of marks. Now, first, regarding the crown of the head, the text has three parts: first, a general indication by way of location.
O Son of the Buddha, upon the Tathāgata’s crown there are thirty-two adornments of jewels.

To manifest clearly the reality of the adornment of the essence, it is said that they are all adorned with *maṇi* gems and the like; this also reveals the perfection and purity of the adornment of the jewel of wisdom.
Within each and every mark, there are both the two adornments of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*), which may be explained according to what is appropriate.
The marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*); because they are the marks of a great man. △ Second, the individual enumeration of names and characteristics.

Regarding the thirty-two marks, each textual passage contains only four [elements], as the single category of "basis" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) has already been indicated in general. The reason why there are specifically thirty-two marks in this context is that... [the principle].

In truth, there should be many; however, to manifest their perfect interpenetration—wherein one is all—even within a single crown, the thirty-two features of the provisional teachings are fully present.
If this is so, why is it not the same for the others? It is because the crown is manifested as the most supreme. As the *Sūtra on the Birth of Goodness* states:
The merit of all the worlds does not equal the merit of a single hair-pore of the Tathāgata. The merit of all the hair-pores does not equal the merit of a single secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*).
The merit of all the secondary marks does not equal a single primary mark (*lakṣaṇa*). All the primary marks do not equal the ūrṇā-kośa (the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows).
The ūrṇā-kośa does not equal the uṣṇīṣa (the invisible crown protuberance). Thus one knows that [the latter] is superior. This is according to the primary and secondary marks. As for the marks...
To clarify this: if categorized by the beings who possess them, those who delight in excellence are superior; thus, they subdue humans, for they take pleasure in excelling over them.
In other contexts, however, it is taught that those who delight in excellence are subtle. △ Third, the actual explanation of the text.
Among these, there is a mark of a great man named "Illuminating All Directions by Universally Emitting Immeasurable Nets of Great Radiance.
Regarding the four [aspects] within this first mark: first is the enumeration of the names; the names are established according to their functions.
Adorned with all manner of exquisite jewels, their hair is everywhere soft, supple, and dense.
Their two bodies are majestic;
from each one emanates the light of mani-jewels, until the physical marks and signs of a Buddha appear in their entirety.
The functioning of the three karmas constitutes one [category].
The four enumerations of fetters (saṃyojana) follow this same pattern in the four subsequent sections.
Next is a mark of a great man called Buddha-Eye Radiant Cloud.
The meaning of "cloud" is as described in the first assembly.
It is adorned with various kinds of *maṇi* kings, [extending] up to the light emitted from the *ūrṇā-kośa* between the eyebrows.

The "adornment of the body" (*kāyālaṃkāra*) explains the meaning of "light. The emission of light from the *ūrṇā* mark is as described in the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" (*Nirmāṇalakṣaṇaparivarta*).
That light universally illuminates all worlds.

The "activity" (*karman*) explains the meaning of the "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakṣus*), for there is nothing that the Buddha-eye does not illuminate. All other adornments of the body and activities are likewise [to be understood].
Consider this accordingly.
This constitutes the second mark of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa), extending up to [the description of] being adorned with a *maṇi-rāja* jewel.
The term *maṇi* means "intention" (*manas*); therefore, it is not the same as the "wish-fulfilling" (*cintāmaṇi*) jewel.
Constantly emitting the radiant light of the Bodhisattva’s flaming lamp (up to) producing sublime sounds that fill the Dharma-realm.
Regarding the analysis of their functional efficacy: all such manifestations are brought forth from the great ocean of merit and wisdom of the Buddhas.
The cause is also subsumed under karmic activity.
This constitutes the eleventh mark of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa), [extending] up to being fully adorned and pervading the Dharma-realm.
This explains the karmic activity.
Spontaneously he expounds the four bodhisattva practices, the sound of which pervades the entire ocean of the dharma-realm.
Regarding these four bodhisattva practices, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, "Bodhisattvabhūmi," states: "In brief, all bodhisattvas have four practices."

First, the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*); second, the practice of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); third, the practice of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); and fourth, the practice of maturing sentient beings.
These constitute the fourteen successive marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), which serve as his ornaments, culminating in the wheel with its thousand spokes.
The Sanskrit text states: "Possessing a thousand-spoked wheel,
pure both internally and externally, [extending] from the past to the wondrous treasury of wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
it displays the two lights of body and wisdom, both manifesting wisdom."
These constitute the twenty-first mark of a Great Man (up to): "The Tathāgata’s pure eyes serve as his adornment.
This refers generally to the ten eyes; what follows below reveals their functional activities.
The light illuminates all worlds throughout the ten directions;
it also comprises both the light of the body and the light of wisdom, as well as the pure eyes and their radiance.
This explains the aforementioned "universal illumination," within which there universally appear all the various ornaments belonging to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
This is the meaning of the supreme wheel, for it is the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
Furthermore, it emits sublime sounds that expound the inconceivable and vast ocean of the Dharma; this is the twenty-sixth.
From the twenty-seventh to the thirty-first, the adornments are omitted, as they are already contained within their names.
Because they exist.

Next, there are the marks of a great man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa), beginning with the mark named "Cloud of the Buddha-ocean Illumined by Light" and extending to the "Cloud of Adornments of the Entire Dharma-realm.
The following section distinguishes their essential nature and adornment.
It is situated most centrally;

this abode is at the very summit, distinguished as a special location, and is thus said to be "situated in the center. From this, one should know that all other [features] encircle this mark, though they are not explicitly mentioned here for brevity.

It gradually rises upward, clearly manifesting its characteristic. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle five, states: "The Tathāgata’s crown has a bone-protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) the size of a fist.
The *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states: "It is like a clenched fist," which refers to the characteristic of being prominently raised.
Adorned with a Jambūnada-gold Indra-net, [and so forth, up to] this is the thirty-second.
△ Third, the summary of these adornments:
O Son of the Buddha, upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, there are these thirty-two kinds of marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) which serve as his magnificent adornment.
△ Second, there is only one mark between the eyebrows. From here downward, all subsequent passages have their respective bases; thus, there are five sections.
Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata possesses the mark of a great man between his eyebrows.
The locus is named "Pervasive Dharma-Realm Cloud of Radiance";
this is its manifest name.
Adorned with mani-jewel flowers (up to) like the sun and moon, penetratingly clear and pure.
Its essential majesty is illuminated: if these marks are gathered, they spiral to the right like an overturned bowl of lapis lazuli;
if extended, they possess ten facets. It is adorned with great radiance; from a single jewel-light, many colors emerge, manifesting within and without.
All are empty; this is precisely what it means to be thoroughly penetrating.
Its light shines universally upon the lands of the ten directions (up to: and further produces wondrous sounds that proclaim the ocean of Dharma, clarifying its functional activity.
From "further produces" onwards refers to the light of the Dharma (*dharmaprabhā*). Therefore, the name of this light is derived from its function.
Established.
This constitutes thirty-three in the enumeration of fetters (saṃyojana). △ Third, the eye has one characteristic.
The Tathāgata’s eyes possess the mark of a great man (up to: this is the thirty-fourth.
△ Fourth, the nose has one mark.
The Tathāgata’s nose possesses the mark of a great man (up to: this is the thirty-fifth.
△ Fifth, the tongue has four characteristics. The first is the characteristic of the broad and long tongue.
The Tathāgata’s tongue possesses a mark of a great man called the Cloud that Manifests the Reflections of Sound.
The upper part reveals its name; the lower part is adorned with majestic splendor.
It is embellished with various exquisite jewels, accomplished through the roots of goodness cultivated in past lives.

That these past virtues have been perfected here refers to the adornment of the cause. The reason for specifically explaining the cause in this way is to enable the thorough exposition of the One Vehicle.
His tongue is broad and long, covering all the oceans of worlds.
To speak of its substance: for a person of merit, the tongue reaches the nose; for a Buddha, it reaches the hairline.

In other Mahāyāna teachings, it is explained that through the manifestation of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), it reaches the Brahma-world or covers the trichiliocosm. Here, however, we speak directly of its actual substance.
It then covers everything without relying on supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi*). Next, the functional activity is distinguished:
if the Tathāgata shines forth with a serene and joyful smile (extending to) pervading all lands for immeasurable eons.
The phrase "expounding the Dharma" explains the sound above; the phrase "manifesting the Buddha" explains the image above.
This constitutes the thirty-sixth [mark].
△ Second, the marks of the tongue and the palms.
The tongue of the Tathāgata further possesses the mark of a great man (extending until) it resembles the light emitted from between the eyebrows.
"Palm" refers to that which is near the root. Next, the functional activity is explained.
That light universally illumines all Buddha-fields, which are composed solely of atoms and possess no inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
As the light shines upon these fields, those who are ready for deliverance need not rely on further contemplation to deconstruct the aggregates;
they spontaneously understand that the Buddha-fields are merely formed by the conjunction of atoms—what inherent nature could there be?
Within the light, there further appear immeasurable Buddhas... (up to) this constitutes thirty-seven.
△ Third, there are two aspects. Both reside at the tip of the tongue; they may dwell on the left and right, or above and below.
Examining their textual function, there is only the unfolding and rolling up [of the tongue], yet the two meanings differ. Now, following this section, first one rolls back the ocean of Buddhas.
The tip of the tongue.
The Tathāgata possesses the mark of a great man at the tip of his tongue (extending to...)—this is the thirty-eighth.

On the tip of the Tathāgata’s tongue there is another mark of a great man (up to... this is the thirty-ninth.

On the upper palate of the Tathāgata’s mouth there is a mark of a great man (up to... this is the fortieth.

On the lower tooth of the right molar of the Tathāgata’s mouth, there is a mark of a Great Man (up to) this being the forty-first.
This refers to the four large canine teeth located on the left and right, above and below. Therefore, when the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*, these four teeth did not shatter.
"Fǔ" (輔) refers to the cheeks; there are also sources that state it refers to the *vakra* bones.
On the upper right molar of the Tathāgata’s mouth is a mark of a great man called the Jewel-Flame Sumeru-Treasury Cloud.
It is named "Sumeru" because it manifests the Sublime Height.
Adorned with a treasury of maṇi jewels, [it extends] throughout the void of space, distributing the milk of the Dharma.
The fourth consists of the three dharmas of Dharma-milk and so forth. These share the same function of expounding the Dharma; insofar as they nourish the Dharmakāya, they are termed "Dharma-milk.
Because the "Dharma-lamp" illuminates and clarifies the myriad objects of experience, it is called "realization."

The Dharma Jewel causes [the practitioner] to become perfectly pure; therefore, it is called a "jewel. It expounds the Dharma of the Nirvana of the Three Virtues and likewise accomplishes the benefit of the Nirvana of the Three Virtues.

the Tathāgata’s teeth possess the mark of a great man (up to) this is the forty-fifth.

The Tathāgata’s lips possess the mark of a great man called "Cloud Manifesting All Jewel Radiance.
The upper part reveals its name; the lower part adorns its substance.
It emits the color of Jāmbūnada gold and the hue of a lotus flower;
its lips are beautifully red like the rising sun or the petals of a red lotus.
It possesses the vast radiance of the colors of all jewels.
Next, the functional activity is distinguished:
illuminating the dharma-realm and causing it all to be completely pure constitutes the forty-sixth [mark].
The two preceding [marks] should each be further divided into upper and lower [sections]. △ Tenth, there is one mark on the neck.
The Tathāgata’s neck possesses the mark of a great man (extending to... which is deep blue, well-formed, soft, supple, and smooth.
"Deep blue" means its shape is like that of a crabapple (*jinzū*), and it has three folds; this has already been explained above.
He emits the pure light of Vairocana... (up to) this is the forty-seventh.

On the Tathāgata’s right shoulder is the mark of a Great Man... (up to) this is the fifty-second.
Two on the right and three on the left; perhaps these are also omitted. △ Twelve: There are twelve marks upon the chest. The first is in the center:
upon the Tathāgata’s breast is the mark of a great man shaped like a svastika, named Auspicious Ocean-Cloud (Śrī-sāgara-megha).
The *svastika* should be translated correctly as "Auspicious Ocean-Cloud" (*śrī-samudra-megha*), because it is named according to its form. First, the form is indicated;

then, the character *fa* (乏) should be replaced by *cao* (艸), and placed beneath the name to signify that it belongs to the essential category. In this way, there will be no contradiction between the preceding and following parts.
Adorned with mani-jewel flowers... (up to) this is the fifty-third.

Emitting great radiance that universally illumines the ten directions... (up to) this is the seventy-second.

On the Tathāgata’s right hip there is a mark of a great man... (up to) this is the seventy-ninth.

therefore, they must be summarized. Yet, as a summary cannot exhaustively convey the full meaning, they must also be revealed in detail. First, the Flower Treasury (Gandavyūha).
The characteristics of the dust-motes are already boundless; how much more so, then, are the ten Flower Treasury worlds, which are infinitely inexhaustible.

Chapter Thirty-Five: The Merits of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiance. Regarding the initial intent of this chapter:

The preceding chapter elucidated the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*), while this chapter establishes the minor marks (*anuvyañjana*). Although the primary and minor marks differ, both serve to adorn the body.

This serves as an answer to the previous inquiry concerning the body and the six sense organs, such as the eyes, as well as the question regarding mastery (*vaśitā*). The minor marks exist in dependence upon the primary marks; [this chapter further treats] their merits (*guṇa*).

Because they are inferior to the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*), they are explained next. The function of these inferior virtues brings about immediate benefit; conversely, this reveals that the greatness of the primary marks and their virtues is inconceivable.

Second, regarding the explanation of the names: "Tathāgata" designates the person to indicate his virtues, while the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) and so forth manifest the virtues as residing in that person. The secondary marks...
The "essence" (tǐ) follows along with the major marks because its virtuous form is excellent. "Radiance" (guāngmíng) is the function;

"merit" (gōngdé) refers to virtue, meaning that light is emitted from the excellent [marks], and this light benefits sentient beings by manifesting the virtue of those excellences; thus it is so named.
Whether one says "the Tathāgata’s secondary characteristics" (*anuvyañjana*) or "the Tathāgata has secondary characteristics," both interpretations are applicable.

Regarding the three points of essential purpose (*abhiprāya*): the essential purpose is to clarify the excellence of being preeminent, and the objective is to cause sentient beings to cultivate reverence.
Next, the explanation of the text has two parts; first, the brief [explanation] has two parts. First, the excellence of the fruit is indicated.
At that time, the World-Honored One [spoke].

Regarding the fact that the Buddha himself spoke these words, there are two intentions: first, because the causal stage of the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* has reached its conclusion and the fruit of this chapter has attained its ultimate limit, both of these chapters were spoken by the Buddha himself;
second, because [the teachings] employ inferior characteristics while their application is inconceivable, he feared that sentient beings might not believe them.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke of himself, addressing the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi.
There are two meanings to this address as "Ratnapāṇi" (Jewel-in-Hand): first, it refers to the secondary mark (anuvyañjana) of the hand; second, because he is the master of this gate.
One should hold this in high esteem, for it is the hand that gives rise to faith.
"O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses the secondary marks (anuvyañjana).
The phrase "possesses the secondary marks" is a general statement; it specifically refers to the excellence of the soles of his feet, as its name is identical to those mentioned later.
He is named King Paripūrṇa.
Because his virtuous functions are all-encompassing, he is called "Complete. He is the most supreme of kings, possessing sovereign power to gather and benefit others.
From within this secondary mark (anuvyañjana), a great radiance issues forth, with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) rays of light as its retinue.
Regarding "the radiance is blazing and intense": it is like the sun possessing its attributes. By means of this, one is further able to gather a retinue of hundreds of thousands and so forth;

this manifests a great number. Furthermore, it says "seven" because of purifying the seven branches [of the path], cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), and illuminating the seven stages (*bhūmi*).
△ Second, manifesting by citing the causes: this is for the purpose of manifesting excellence. This has several layers. First, by—
The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) are profound and vast; words cannot fully encompass them, and for this reason they are set aside.

However, following the teaching of the "excellent," there are many further secondary marks. Since there are already eighty secondary marks corresponding to the thirty-two primary characteristics, those of the ten Lotus Treasury [Buddhas] possess even more.
To cite but one example: among the three [types of excellence], the superior is placed first, yet here only the inferior is mentioned; therefore, it is clarified.

Venerable Sir: Each of the four soles of the feet possesses one excellence, which in turn has manifold rays of light; yet we speak of only "one ray. Even for a single ray within the state of the five fruits (*pañca-phala*), it cannot be fully described;

thus, it is manifested by means of its cause, and the benefit is accomplished through the light of the cause. This is so even when the three stages are simultaneously perfected—how much more so for a single ray of the fruit?

Such is the case through successive progression; how much more so regarding the various marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and how much more so when speaking collectively of all the virtues of the Tathāgata’s fruition?
The ocean transcends words; this is also the meaning here. The text has two parts. First, the scope of the light’s illumination:
"O Son of the Buddha, when I was a bodhisattva... [it] illuminated worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields."
This refers to the light emitted from the "excellent" (śubha) marks previously described; therefore, no separate location for the emission of light is specified.

Yet, this is not the same as the previous light, because the excellent marks are manifold. △ Second, the benefits accomplished by the light, which has two parts. First, the benefit of being freed from suffering now and purifying past roots of goodness.
The sentient beings in the hells within that world (up to... all gave rise to joy, leaping for gladness, and offering congratulations.
△ Second, the transformation of retribution and birth in heaven, whereby they obtain the benefit of hearing the Dharma.

This demonstrates his past causes: that his mind was never indolent and that he had practiced under the Tathāgata, planting various roots of goodness (kuśalamūla).
Pervading through seeing, hearing, and so forth, by drawing near to spiritual friends, one will certainly hear the Universal Dharma and become of the Vajra lineage.
The great majestic spiritual power of Vairocana manifests its present conditions.
Having passed away from that life, they were reborn in this heaven.

Because the connection between cause and effect is abbreviated in the text, the "connection" refers here to their birth in heaven. In reality, however, the cessation of suffering as well as the attainment of the Pure Eye and so forth all result from these two types of causes and conditions.
Thus, one knows that the Buddha’s light shines impartially; it does not [shine only upon those who] have planted [the seeds].
This is a virtuous cause. There is no superior benefit like this. Why does a single ray of light suddenly accomplish such benefits?
It is because it is manifested by inexhaustible merit and because it flows from the pure Dharma-realm; it is not like the eighty secondary marks of the provisional teachings.

The text has two parts. First, an extensive explanation of the benefit of purifying past wholesome roots from the preceding section:
"O Son of the Buddha, beneath the soles of the Bodhisattva’s feet are wheels with a thousand spokes... constantly emitting forty kinds of light."
It crushes the suffering of the lower realms. The light from the thousand-spoked wheels beneath his feet consists of forty rays;
these represent the forty stages, for there is nothing they do not illuminate.
Among them, there is a light named Pure Merit;
setting aside a detailed explanation for brevity,
it is able to illuminate worlds as numerous as the atoms within billions of nayutas of buddha-fields.
The limit exceeds what was previously stated.
Following the various karmic actions of sentient beings, they all reach the end of their lives and are reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.

There, they purify their afflictions and perfect their virtues; therefore, the previous light is given names such as "Pure" (*viśuddha*). By using the heavy to illustrate the light, [the text] cites Avīci Hell.

"Having been born in the heavens, you shall hear the sound of the celestial drum... [until] ...you shall enter the Vimala-samādhi; you should pay homage."
△ 2. Doubt arises after hearing.
At that time, the sons of the gods, having heard the sound of the celestial drum, [wondered] from what cause this subtle and wondrous sound was produced.
△ 3. General indication of the cause.
At that time, the celestial drum addressed the sons of the gods, saying: [up to] "...accomplished through the power of various roots of goodness.
△ Fourth, the explicit explanation of the exhortation has four parts. First, using oneself as an analogy for the Buddha, it shows that there is no self and no coming.
"O sons of the gods, as I speak of a self, yet do not cling to a self—so it is likewise; they have not come from the ten directions.
This passage consists of two sections, each containing both a simile and its application. The first simile illustrates the absence of self; the second illustrates the absence of coming.
△ Second, using others as a simile for oneself, it reveals that "coming" is in fact no-coming.
"O sons of the gods, it is as if you were formerly in hell... [and so on] "...it is likewise not from the ten directions.
This passage contains three metaphors, all of which are clear upon examination. However, evil karma and roots of goodness are the causes and conditions for coming;
since these causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), "coming" is in fact "no-coming. It is not that some pre-existing phenomenon comes from somewhere within the ten directions.
Therefore, that which is called "causes and conditions" is itself wisdom. The nature of wisdom is fundamentally not subject to causes and conditions;
how can one think in terms of "what causes and conditions exist"? △ Third, using oneself as an analogy for the inconceivable realm of the Buddha.
O sons of the gods, it is as if from a single *anuvyañjana* (minor mark) among the billions of *nayuta* buddha-fields, a single ray of light is emitted.

Regarding the "raising of the hand" (*hasta-vyañjana*): this refers to raising [the hand] specifically to manifest superiority, to save those below and lead them upward; thus, while the light of the foot is raised, here, because he is manifesting supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), the hand is mentioned.
The manifestation of immeasurable sovereign spiritual powers (up to) cannot even be known, let alone by ordinary sentient beings.
△ Fourth, the formal exhortation to go and visit, with two sections on the admonition not to remain behind. First, the general admonition and exhortation.
"O sons of the gods, you should go to where that bodhisattva is; do not again become greedily attached to the pleasures of the five desires.
Part Two: Extensive Explanation, in two sections. First, the explanation of the preceding admonition.
Attachment to the pleasures of the five desires obstructs all roots of goodness.
This is an analogy for the higher Dharma.
O sons of the gods, it is as if the kalpa-fire were to burn Mount Sumeru until it is entirely consumed, leaving nothing behind that can be found.
The subsequent combination is as follows:
when greed and desire entangle the mind, it is likewise impossible to ever give rise to the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha.
△ Second, the explanation of the preceding exhortation has six parts. First, the direct explanation.
"O sons of the gods, you should recognize kindness and repay it.
2. The reverse explanation:
"O sons of the gods, there are sentient beings who do not know how to repay kindness; they frequently meet with untimely deaths and are reborn in the hells."
△ 3. Manifesting the aspect of his grace:
"O sons of the gods, in the past, while you were within the hells, you were illuminated by this light; your bodies were transformed, and you abandoned that place to be born here.
△ 4. Exhorting them to go and increase their merit.
"You all should now swiftly dedicate [your merit] to increase your roots of goodness.
△ Fifth, showing the Dharma so that they may practice: this refers to the teaching on the two kinds of emptiness.
"O sons of the gods, like my celestial drum, I am neither male nor female... [up to] ...various sublime palaces and gardens."
The analogy of being neither male nor female is used to reveal the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Just as my celestial drum is neither born nor extinguished, so too is it neither born nor extinguished.
The analogy of non-arising and non-ceasing is used to reveal the emptiness of phenomena. △ Sixth, the exhortation to practice and the resulting benefits:
"If you can awaken to and understand this, you should know that you will enter the Samādhi of the Seal of Non-reliance."
Once one has realized non-arising, both subject and object are simultaneously severed; being utterly without support, it is called "non-reliance.
With this seal of wisdom, one seals all phenomena, neither grasping nor retaining them; the mind abides in itself in peace, and is thus termed *samādhi*.
△ Five sections on the exhortation to approach the Buddha. First, the offering of incense does not exceed [the proper time].
At that time, having heard this sound, the sons of the gods desired to pay their respects and behold him, yet they were unable to see him.
△ Second, hearing of her location.
At that time, a certain son of heaven spoke as follows: (up to) she was dwelling within the womb of Lady Māyā, riding upon a sandalwood pavilion.
△ Third, observing that he would descend to be born below.
At that time, the sons of the gods, using their divine eyes, observed [him] (up to) being served and honored by the gods of the Brahma and Desire realms.
△ Fourth, they resolved to go forth.
The assembly of devaputras all had this thought: (up to) ten nayutas of their retinue wished to descend to Jambudvīpa.
△ Fifth, the instruction on the ritual for seeing the Buddha, in two parts: first, instructing them to recognize the manner of birth so as to cause them to abandon crooked views.

Because they previously did not encounter [the Buddha], and now behold his descent into birth, they remain attached to existence and non-existence, and harbor sentiments of "self" and "other. Therefore, he reveals the essence and its function to manifest the absence [of duality].
The arising and manifestation of birth. The text has three parts. First, the Dharma; second, [the commentary]. First, admonishing against distorted views.
At that time, a voice issued from a celestial drum, proclaiming: (up to) "it is not by means of this life that one dies and is born in that other realm."
△ Second, the demonstration of his correct view:
He merely employs supernatural powers to cause sentient beings to see according to what is appropriate for their minds.
Thus it is known that what is produced through the Buddha’s transformation is not a birth following death. △ Second, the analogy.

"O sons of the gods, just as I am now able to produce sound without being seen by the eye, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who enters the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement; he likewise cannot be seen by the eye. (Section Three: Synthesis)
The Dharma-body is unborn; it is pervasive yet invisible, yet it is able to manifest birth in every place.
Since there is nowhere it does not arise, it is present everywhere. Wherever there is a responsive capacity, it is seen therein as well; why then need it descend further?
Jambudvīpa, free from discrimination,
manifests the virtues of those destined for birth; it sweeps away all views so that one is born through non-discriminative wisdom, not by way of existence.
Regarding the place where he was chosen to be born:
having eliminated arrogance,
although he dwelt in a royal palace, he remained free from arrogance.

Free from attachment, surrounded by the devas, yet remaining free from attachment. △ Second, instructing on the arousal of the bodhicitta and admonishing against faults, so that they may attain vision.
This has three parts: first, indicating the instruction; second, inquiring as to the method; third, the formal instruction according to the Dharma. Now, one who wishes to repent their transgressions—

One must recognize twenty kinds of minds, both adverse and favorable. First, one should identify the ten kinds of minds that accord with birth and death (*saṃsāra*), which serve as the objects to be remedied:

1. The false discrimination of a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*), giving rise to the view of a body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). 2. Possessing internal afflictions while encountering external adverse conditions, causing the mind of "I" to flourish. 3.
Having both internal and external factors present, the mind ceases to engage in wholesome deeds and takes no joy in the goodness of others. 4. [The fourth item continues...]
1. They indulge their three karmas, committing every kind of evil. 2. Although these five matters are not extensive, their evil intentions are pervasive. 3.
These six evil mental states continue in succession, uninterrupted by day or night. 4. They conceal and deny their faults, unwilling to let others know. 5.

They act with arrogance and insolence, showing no fear of the evil realms. 6. They lack shame and remorse, having no dread for ordinary beings or sages. 7. They repudiate causes and deny the existence of karma.
As a result, one becomes an icchantika. Next, ten kinds of thoughts that oppose the cycle of birth and death arise; these are to be overturned and eliminated in reverse order:
first, clearly believing in cause and effect; second, feeling self-reproach and self-blame; third, fearing the evil realms; fourth, not concealing one's flaws;
fifth, severing the continuous stream of [defiled] mind; sixth, generating the bodhicitta; seventh, cultivating merit to compensate for transgressions; eighth, rejoicing in the goodness of others.
Ninth, mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions; tenth, contemplating the emptiness of the nature of offenses. All three of these sections are present here, though their order differs.
Previously, they were arranged according to the sequence of mental arousal; here, they are presented in terms of their relative superiority and inferiority.
Now, first, there is the general presentation of the instruction.
O sons of the gods,
this text consists of four sections that remedy the six aforementioned faults conducive to saṃsāra.
You should all resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Generating the bodhicitta serves as the basis for repentance. Because it is the root of all practice and encompasses all virtues, it is explained first.

It is the opposite of the fifth evil mind previously mentioned, which was pervasive, endangering oneself and others; now, one generates a heart of compassion that covers the entire dharmadhātu to extensively benefit sentient beings.
Purifying the mind and abiding in virtuous deportment, one causes the three karmas to be purified;
this constitutes the essence of confession. The first phrase refers to the practice of ceasing evil, while the meaning of the second phrase encompasses both ceasing and performing.
This reverses the sixth [hindrance], the continuity of an evil mind, and reverses the seventh, the concealment and denial of one's faults.
I repent and eliminate all karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*), afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), retributive obstructions (*vipākāvaraṇa*), and obstructions to vision (*darśanāvaraṇa*).

Now I repent for these four obstructions, which are the very non-virtues to be extinguished—namely, delusion, karma, and suffering. Regarding the two obstructions of karma and its retribution, they differ in terms of cause and effect.
Since I have already repented the obstruction of retribution, I now stand in awe of the evil realms (*durgati*), reversing my previous lack of fear. Thus, O sons of the gods...
Since this has just been introduced from that [previous section], it is not explained in detail here. Among the afflictions (*kleśa*), there are two types: sharp and dull.

Because the severance of the roots of goodness by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is the most terrifying, the hindrance of views (*dṛṣṭivaraṇa*) is explained separately. Furthermore, because the hindrance to the objects of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is also a hindrance of views, it is treated thus. The rest is as explained elsewhere.
With bodies as numerous as all sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm, [one proceeds] until all obstructive faults and evils are repented and eliminated.

One directs the mind universally so that nothing remains unexhausted. Since past transgressions have already pervaded all objects of experience, one now repents those former errors by universally mobilizing the three karmas (body, speech, and mind) to equal the realm of sentient beings. Before each and every Buddha and assembly of beings, one confesses and discloses them.
Confession: Having already confessed before all beings—humans, devas, ordinary persons, and sages—one then engages in the second stage, which is self-reproach and self-rebuke.
This reverses shamelessness and lack of remorse; as the mind operates universally, it causes the body and speech to follow suit, beginning with prostrating with the head.
The entire body is unified as a whole, with the five wheels [of the limbs] touching the ground. Regarding the statement that this is "pervasive," by what means is it pervasive?

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The three karmas are well-purified and pervasive. This constitutes the fourth stage: cultivating merit to remedy past transgressions, which reverses the previous state of unrestrained indulgence in the three karmas of body and so forth.
△ Second, the inquiry into the method.
When the sons of the gods had heard these words... [up to] "...how can one repent and eliminate all faults and evils?
The preceding scripture was still brief, and its further meaning was not yet exhausted; therefore, he next inquires about it. △ Third, the correct teaching according to the Dharma.

This correct teaching observes that the nature of offenses is empty, while simultaneously revealing the false conceptualization of a self and persons, the denial of cause and effect, and the encounter with adverse external conditions.
The text is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies the cause for the production of sound:
at that time, the celestial drum, through the power of the roots of goodness of the Bodhisattva’s samādhi, produced a voice and proclaimed:
△ Second, the actual exposition of the instruction has five parts. Now, first, the specific contemplation on the emptiness of karma:
"O sons of the gods, Bodhisattvas know that all karmas [arise]... and are collectively accumulated, abiding within the mind."

Karma is the cause of retribution, as it is the foremost of the three obstacles. It does not pre-exist with a substantial body coming from the ten directions; this precisely reveals the meaning of emptiness.
It arises solely from inversion and has no place of abiding.
He explains the reason for emptiness: because the ocean of karmic obstructions arises from false conceptualization, it lacks intrinsic nature.
Thus, the bodhisattva clearly perceives this with certainty, free from all doubt.
Now, this wisdom of emptiness is associated with the mind; when one knows it thus with certainty and without doubt, one is called a Bodhisattva.

△ Second, the general contemplation of the four obstacles. The text contains both a metaphor and its application. By means of the metaphor, conventional existence is shown; in reference to the ultimate truth, it is non-existent.
The text has two parts. First, the analogy:
"O sons of the gods, just as I, the celestial drum, speak of karma and speak of its maturation.
This raises the subject of what is to be remedied, namely, the two obstacles of karma and its maturation.
To speak of practice, to speak of precepts, to speak of joy, to speak of peace, and to speak of all samādhis constitutes the remedy.
This involves practicing what is good and ceasing what is evil; it brings joy to others and brings peace to others. (Part Two: Synthesis)
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise in this regard: to speak of "I" and "mine" is itself an obstacle of views;
to speak of "sentient beings," or of greed, hatred, and delusion, is likewise so.
This refers to the afflictive obscurations and various types of karma.
The preceding section clarifies that these exist according to conventional truth, while the following section distinguishes that they are ultimately non-existent in the absolute sense.
In reality, there is no self and nothing belonging to a self (*ātman* or *ātmīya*). (Up to: searching throughout the ten directions, it is entirely unobtainable.

The two characters "existence" and "non-existence" [represent] a condensed illustration of the three obstacles. Since there is nothing belonging to a self, this overturns and refutes the first [obstacle].

One forgets the conceptualization of self and person. III. Specifically Refuting the Delusions of View (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*). Because the delusions of view are profound and perilous, they are extensively refuted. The text contains three metaphors.
The first drum is an analogy for that which is heard as being without arising or ceasing.
O sons of the gods, it is like this: my voice neither arises nor ceases (until) wherever there is cultivation and accumulation, one receives its retribution.

This analogy shows that although karma has no arising, it still elicits retribution according to its cultivation. One contemplates the emptiness of karma in order to dispel the attachment to its existence;

yet, if one were to claim it is empty [in the sense of non-existence], the Buddhas would not manifest in transformation. Therefore, this now clarifies that it is not a nihilistic non-existence, thereby overturning and refuting the tenth [view] which denies cause and effect.
△ Second, the analogy of sound having no coming or going.
"O sons of the gods, just as the sounds produced by my celestial drum—from its coming or going—are all ungraspable;
this is a metaphor for returning to the Middle Way. This is the analogy followed by the application.
O sons of the gods, if there were coming and going, there would be the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.

If it were definitively existent, it would be eternal; if it were definitively non-existent, it would be annihilated. Both are likewise dualistic. Therefore, by simultaneously refuting the two views of coming and going, one reveals the transcendence of annihilationism and eternalism.
All Buddhas never preach the existence of dharmas characterized by annihilation or permanence, except as a skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity.

If there were something that comes, one would fall into the view of permanence; if it departs without returning, one would fall into the view of annihilation. Therefore, although it is empty, it is not annihilated;
although it exists, it is not permanent. △ Third, the analogy of the drum sound following the mind.
"O sons of gods, it is like my voice (extending to... which causes all sentient beings to see it according to their own minds;
this is a metaphor for seeing the Buddha through the mind, thereby dispelling the mind's external attachments.

The master of confession causes them to truly contemplate the Buddhas of the ten directions, overturning and breaking through external adverse conditions. IV. Contemplating Retribution in Relation to Karma. Part One: The Substance of a Mirror Image.
The analogy of emptiness:
O sons of the gods, it is as with a crystal mirror... [the various karmic fruits and retributions] have no place from which they come or to which they go.

Although the analogy exists, it is non-existent; that is to say, the reflection in the mirror appears in dependence upon the mirror, yet the image neither comes nor goes. Retribution follows [from karma in the same way].
Since karma is born [of conditions], how could there be coming or going? △ Second, the analogy of the illusionist’s deception of the eyes:
"O sons of the gods, it is like an illusionist who deceives the eyes of people; you should know that all karmas are likewise so."

This metaphor illustrates that although karma and its retribution do not exist [in an ultimate sense], they nonetheless exist. Furthermore, karma is like an illusion; moreover, an illusion is neither existent nor non-existent—it is the Middle Way.
△ Fifth, the summary of the benefits of repentance.
If one understands in this way, it is the true repentance; all evil deeds will be entirely purified.
△ Sixth, the benefits gained through seeing and hearing, in two parts. First, clarifying the benefits for the other assemblies.
When this Dharma was being taught, hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas [of beings] (up to) gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled Bodhi.
Because the sound [of the teaching] was heard everywhere through the power of samādhi. △ Second, the benefits obtained by those present; this has two parts.
First, the primary benefit, which also has two parts. Now, first, the benefit of attaining the Dharma.
At that time, because the sons of the gods heard the teaching on Samantabhadra [up to] "attaining the Samādhi Adorned with All Powers," all [versions] contain the character "hence" (故).
This meaning seems to function as a recapitulation of what preceded as a cause, implying that they saw the Buddha for their benefit.

Since there was no prior instance of attaining the tenth stage, what would there be to recapitulate? For this reason, the Jin translation lacks the character "hence" in all cases; it should simply read "heard."
Because of the teaching on the vast and universal dedication of Samantabhadra, one immediately attains the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and acquires the Samādhi Adorned with All Powers (*sarvabalālaṃkāra*).
The former phrase refers to attaining the stage; the latter phrase refers to accomplishing practice. One partially attains the ten powers (*daśabala*) for the sake of adornment.
△ Second, the benefit of seeing the Buddha, in three parts: first, clarifying the causes for seeing [the Buddha].
Because they have repented and eliminated all heavy obstructions through pure actions of body, speech, and mind equal in number to all sentient beings.
△ Second, the actual manifestation of seeing the Buddha:
that is, seeing hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields... [up to] ...the power of even a small portion of the *vimala-samādhi* (stainless samādhi).
△ 3. Raising Offerings with a Heart of Reverence.
At that time, those devaputras offered the aforementioned flowers.
"Aforementioned" means that they had previously carried these flowers and proceeded to where the Bodhisattva was; although they had presented them as offerings, they had not yet been scattered.
Therefore, from each and every pore of his body, he further emanated clouds of various exquisite flowers equal in number to all sentient beings.

As for the flowers emerging from the pores: because he had already attained the stages (*bhūmi*), and as these flowers represent the beginning [of that attainment], they are mentioned briefly here. Above...
Among the items they hold, there are incense canopies and so forth; therefore, as seen in the subsequent passages, the seeing of the incense and the seeing of the canopies both bring about benefit.
They offer these to the Tathāgata Vairocana, scattering them over the Buddha, and all of them abide upon the body of the Buddha.
△ Second, the mutual attainment of benefit, which has two parts: first, the benefit from smelling the fragrance; second, the benefit from seeing the canopies.

Both of these derive from the previous offering and do not exceed what is presented in the text. Within the former [the benefit from smelling the fragrance], there are three sections. First, the Dharma.

These clouds of incense rain down universally upon immeasurable Buddha-fields (until: those whose bodies are touched by the fragrance find their bodies peaceful and blissful, for by being freed from hindrances, they attain the joy of liberation). △ Second, the analogy.
For example, when a bhikṣu enters the fourth dhyāna, all karmic obstructions are completely extinguished.
This is analogous to how the fourth dhyāna is free from the eight calamities. △ Third, because these obstructions are extinguished, one attains pure roots of goodness;
this constitutes the aspect of benefit. The text has two parts. First, the manifestation of what is extinguished.
If there are those who hear this, those sentient beings—up to those whose afflictions are equally distributed (*sabhāga-carita*)—number twenty-one thousand.
These constitute the eighty-four thousand afflictions. Regarding this, there are two ancient interpretations. The first states: "The roots of the afflictions are ten;
however, each individual delusion possesses ten further powers, thus totaling one hundred. These should be divided into nine grades (*navavidha*). Now, however, [it is only]...
Because the superior grade is heavy, it is divided into three; because the middle and lower grades are light, each constitutes one grade, thus forming five grades in total.
With one hundred [instances] per grade, this results in five hundred. Furthermore, these arise in relation to internal and external objects of oneself and others:
that is, the five sense-objects of oneself are termed "internal," while the five sense-objects of others are termed "external. Within each of these sense-objects, there are again five [factors].

One hundred [instances] become five thousand. When each is separately deluded regarding the Four Noble Truths, they become twenty thousand; adding the original one thousand, there are twenty-one thousand in total.
When these are further correlated with the three poisons and the equal portion (of ignorance), they constitute the eighty-four thousand afflictions, as the scriptural text itself fully demonstrates.
Second, some say that the ten unwholesome paths are the root, which develop and mutually reinforce one another. One...
Each [of these] has ten, thus totaling one hundred. Furthermore, if categorized according to delusion regarding the five objects (*viṣaya*) of self and others, there are one thousand.
When directly deluded regarding the ten truths (*daśatattva*), and since those ten truths consist of the four truths, three truths, two truths, and one truth, they total ten thousand.

Alternatively, it is ten thousand because of delusion regarding the ten truths such as the "truths established by teaching," or because of delusion regarding the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*). Thus, there is delusion...

The ten truths (*daśatattva*) differ in their emptiness (*śūnyatā*), thus dividing into twenty thousand. Alternatively, regarding the delusion concerning the ten wholesome paths and the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional (*satyadvaya*), these likewise divide into twenty thousand.
Together with the original one thousand, the remainder is as explained in the sutras. Both systems possess reason; one may choose between them according to one’s own inclination.

There is another alternative interpretation, as found in texts such as the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*, which does not represent the intent of the present sutra. △ Second, clarifying its capacity to extinguish:
one thoroughly understands that all such things are entirely empty and delusive.
This means that one realizes the fundamental emptiness of delusions, such that they do not arise at all. Thus, the Jin translation states: "All these afflictions are entirely extinguished.
Having known this, one accomplishes the pure roots of goodness of the Sovereign Radiance of Fragrant Banner Clouds.
Because delusions are extinguished, there is purity; as delusions perish, wisdom manifests, resulting in sovereign radiance and the fulfillment of roots of goodness.

The "fragrant banner" refers to the tongue-faculty possessed by those in the ninth stage, which will be explained in detail below. △ Second, the passage on the benefits of seeing the coverings has two parts.
Now, first, the actual clarification of the benefits obtained.
If there are sentient beings who see his canopy (up to the point of) the roots of goodness planted by the Golden Net Wheel-Turning King, which are as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River—

according to the Jin translation, it says "the roots of goodness planted by one Ganges River's worth of Wheel-Turning Holy Kings," namely the White Pure Jewel Net Wheel-Turning Kings and others— it is evident from this that there are many wheel-turning kings, not just one.

The abundance of its virtues is thus great; the Sanskrit original is likewise so. As for the term "Pure Golden Net" (*vimala-suvarṇajāla*), according to the first volume of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing), the position of the golden wheel is within the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*).

From the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, these are all lapis lazuli wheels, distinguished by an increase in the number of jewels. Thus, we know that the "Jewel Net" (*ratnajāla*) in the old translation refers to a superior "Golden Net."

Therefore, that sutra says: "On the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one wears necklaces of a hundred jewels and possesses a wheel-marked banner (*cakra*) of seven precious gems, serving as the Four Heavenly Kings;
even ten thousand sons of merit serve as one's retinue. One beholds a hundred Dharma-bodies and travels through a hundred Buddha-fields.
Each of these numerical attributes increases until the seventh stage, where one uses thirteen precious gems for the wheel-marked banner. Regarding the eighth stage, it simply states:"
Regarding the "Great Jewel Spoked Wheel" (*mahāratnacakra*), it is stated in the *Ninth Ground* (*navamī-bhūmi*) that the spoked wheel is made of white cloud jewels (*pāṇḍaramegharatna*).

In the *Tenth Ground* (*daśamī-bhūmi*), it is stated that the spoked wheel consists of the jewel-light garlands of a million supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the fearlessness-jewels (*vaiśāradyamaṇi*).

If one follows the *Jin* (Chinese) translation, the term "white and pure" (*pāṇḍara-viśuddha*) refers to the Ninth Ground; thus, it accords with the preceding text regarding the "fragrant banner clouds" (*gandhaketur-megha*) arising spontaneously.
In the light, if that pure white jewel is merely that which is equalized, then there is no loss in [calling it] the golden net.
If one takes the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as the pure golden net, this precisely corresponds to the ten stages;

taking the fearlessness jewel (*abhaya-maṇi*) as the meaning of purity, and because its scope of gathering and transforming beings is identical to the ripening fruit gathered in the tenth stage, it is realized as the ten stages. Its...
The meaning is clear. Therefore, this king emits light below; those who encounter it also ascend to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
"One *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*" refers to those from the ninth stage and below, up to the tenth abode of the copper wheel.

This is because the scope of those transformed by these ten stages is such that the preceding positions are as numerous as the sands of a river. Thus, the Jin translation says: "The Jewel-Net Wheel-Turning King," and so forth. "And so on" (*ādi*) [indicates the inclusion of others].

This refers back to what precedes. △ Second, the increase in benefit through gathering and transforming sentient beings has two parts. First, the benefit of attaining the stage has three sections. First, the Dharma:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this position of a Wheel-Turning King... [he] teaches and transforms sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms [of those realms]."
The direct clarification of the scope of the Bodhisattva’s gathering and transforming has already been explained as before. △ Second, the analogy:
"O Son of the Buddha, it is like the world of a bright mirror... [until] never for a single thought-moment was there any interruption."
The upper part of the analogy concerns the teaching and transformation of sentient beings through the Dharma;
it states that if there are sentient beings who hear the name of that Buddha, they will certainly attain rebirth in that Buddha’s land.
The lower part of the analogy, in its application, concerns encountering this radiance and attaining the ten stages (*bhūmi*). △ Third, the synthesis.
It is likewise for a Bodhisattva who dwells securely in the sovereign position of a Universal Monarch with a Pure Golden Net.
The first phrase summarizes this:
if anyone should even momentarily encounter its light...
According to the *Jin* (Dunhuang) edition of the sutra, it is likewise as follows: [the text] omits the phrase "emanating the light of sovereign Maṇḍarava.

In the current edition, this is reflected in the subsequent section where the metaphor is applied. If it were simply stated that "one encounters this light," since there has been no prior mention of the emission of light in the preceding text, what would one encounter?
One will certainly attain the tenth stage of a bodhisattva.
Regarding the attainment of the ten stages, within this chapter there are three layers, all of which involve attaining the ten stages; these are called "successively increasing benefits.
First, the sons of the gods hear the drum preaching the Dharma and realize the ten stages. Second, from the pores of these sons of the gods...
Flowers emerge, together with the aforementioned fragrant canopies. Those who behold them realize the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
This is precisely the radiance emitted by the three types of Wheel-Turning Kings of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*). Sentient beings who encounter it likewise attain the Ten Stages.

These three realizations are all equal in rank; they are simultaneously and instantaneously accomplished. According to individuals, there are as many varieties as atoms in the dust of the world, yet they are all but a single manifestation of the Bodhisattva.
Regarding the "excellent" [marks]: by the power of a single ray of light, it is even more difficult to describe the excellence of the remaining rays and so forth.
This is because of the power of the roots of goodness cultivated through prior practice;
it thus reveals the cause for the sudden benefit previously mentioned. This is because, upon hearing the Universal Dharma, one cultivates universal goodness. △ Second, the accomplishment.
The benefit of virtue has two parts. First is the analogy:
"O Son of the Buddha, just as one who has attained the first dhyāna, though not yet at the end of life... (up to) "...those who have attained all the dhyānas are likewise.

The meaning is this: having cultivated and attained the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the form realm within the desire realm, one uses the eyes of the desire realm to see the objects of the form realm; this is the analogy.
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s sudden realization of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they perceive the realms of the ten stages without yet having transformed their ordinary body;
this is due to the power of the Dharma. Thus, that which takes three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be reached in a single thought-moment, clarifying that the one encompasses all.
That which does not exhaust itself within a single stage even over aeons as numerous as dust motes clarifies that all encompasses the one. Such slowness and speed are both entirely sovereign.
This is the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), not any other school. II. Combining the two. First, the explicit explanation of the benefits gained:
"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, dwelling in the Pure Golden Net... all attain the tenth stage of a Bodhisattva."

This is merely restating the scriptural passage from the preceding "Synthesis" (saṃgraha) section, which states that the stages (bhūmi) are established based on virtues; thus, it is restated for this reason.
Otherwise, there would be two instances of emitting light, each resulting in the attainment of the ten stages.
Having accomplished immeasurable light of wisdom (up to) accomplishing such pure physical eyes (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
That is to say, the aforementioned virtues as well as the ten eyes are all achieved based upon the physical eyes of an ordinary body; therefore, they are summarized here.
△ Second, the delineation of the scope of the object: this reveals that the range of the physical eyes is vast. If even the physical eyes are thus, [how much more so the others].
The remaining eyes are profound and subtle, beyond description. The text has three parts. First, a provisional analogy is established to demonstrate the multiplicity of objects.
Within this, there are three sections; the first concerns the vastness of a single layer of objects.
"O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were someone who, using [billions of nayutas] (up to) completely integrated them all into a single buddha-field.
△ Second, the question-and-answer reveals its vastness, causing faith to be established and benefit to be realized.
"Ratnapāṇi, what do you think? ... [they] shall attain the unsurpassed wisdom of a Tathāgata.
△ Third, by again multiplying the previous number, he further manifests its vastness.
Bao-shou, suppose there were another person who [traversed] a thousand billion Buddha-fields (and so on), proceeding successively until eighty such turns had been completed.
△ Second, the actual explanation of being able to see.
All such vast Buddha-lands (up to this point) can be clearly seen within a single thought-moment.
To see the atoms of those aforementioned vast lands with the physical eye is already a supreme excellence; how much more so in a single thought-moment!
He also saw as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten billion vast Buddha-fields;
he clearly beheld these many Buddhas,
just as the pure radiance of a vaidūrya gem illuminates worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields.
He clearly perceives the marks of the Buddha; he is without the mind of discrimination, for there is neither coming nor going.
△ Third, the conclusion on the virtues and their source: "The jeweled hands are all thus pure golden nets... [omitted] ...accomplished by roots of merit and goodness."
It returns to the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*). At the end of this chapter, the scripture has not yet reached its conclusion.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang;
