Chapter Thirty-Six: The Practices of Samantabhadra.
△ First, regarding the intent of the introduction: first general, then specific. "General" refers to the two chapters which clarify the causes and conditions for manifestation;

therefore, they follow next. They are also called the "causes and conditions of equality," meaning that the previously mentioned differentiated causes are integrated to form this perfect cause of Samantabhadra, and the previously mentioned differentiated fruits are integrated to form the fruit of the manifestation of *xingqi* (nature-arising). Furthermore...

The previous section concerned cultivation through production (*bhāvanā-utpāda*); this section concerns cultivation through manifestation (*bhāvanā-vyakti*). If that is so, why is there no further separate question?

Furthermore, why is it that at the end of the preceding chapter on the differentiated fruits there is no auspicious sign, whereas at the conclusion of the proof of the cause of equality, there is an auspicious sign?

It is precisely by this principle that it is shown to be a reconciliation with what preceded; for if there were another separate question, there would be a disjunction, and [this] is intended to reconcile with what preceded.
It is not that they are separated by auspicious signs; rather, the Universal Dharma is rare and marvelous, such that there are distinct auspicious signs for both cause and effect.

Furthermore, there ought to have been auspicious signs previously, as it would prove that the transmission of this sutra was not yet complete; their absence is therefore due to this. Specifically regarding this chapter, the sequence follows the order of principle: first the cause, then the fruit.

This also serves as a distant response to the initial inquiry regarding "what was practiced" in the second assembly, as well as to the *Acintya-parivarta* (Chapter on the Inconceivable), which addresses the request for the nature of the lineage (*gotra*).
Although these were already answered previously, they are now elucidated again because the latter two [chapters] are profoundly subtle;

they are like the ocean of marks (*lakṣaṇa-samudra*) and the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), the most exquisite among the exquisite. Ancient masters have treated this separately as a distinct section concerning cause and effect.

Second, regarding the explanation of the names: the first [name] generally elucidates the meaning of the two categories. It is called "arising of cultivation based on nature" and "arising of function based on nature.
Because their differentiated characteristics are exhausted and the essence of cause and fruit is uniform, it is termed "equal cause and fruit.

Furthermore, the cause is the cause of the fruit, its magnitude pervading the Dharma-realm; the fruit is the fruit of the fruit, its sphere being like space. Both cause and fruit are thus inexhaustible.
Regarding the future limit (*āyati*), it is called "manifestation" because it brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings. Specifically, this is the title of the chapter.
"Samantabhadra" identifies the person to manifest the Dharma, clarifying that these practiced dharmas are not sequential dharmas. "The practitioner" manifests the Dharma;

it is not within the category of persons that the Dharma being practiced is correctly explained, nor does it describe the human body. "Universal" (*samanta*) means that his virtues pervade the *dharmadhātu*. "Bhadra" means being supremely compliant, harmonious, and virtuous.
It is called "virtuous" (*bhadra*). To cultivate practice based on one's nature is called "conduct" (*caryā*).

Although the conduct of Samantabhadra appears frequently by name in various sūtras and its details are extensive within this chapter, I shall now briefly manifest it by condensing it into ten meanings to represent its inexhaustibility.
First, the universality of what is sought: this means one must seek to realize that which all Tathāgatas have equally realized. Second, the universality of those to be transformed... [one]... First.
1. Universality of sentient beings: because all the numerous sentient beings within the tips of a single hair are transformed and perfected.

2. Universality of what is to be severed: because there is not a single delusion that is not severed. 3. Universality of the practice of phenomena: because there is not a single practice that is not performed.

4. Universality of the practice of principle: because the aforementioned practices of phenomena all penetrate the source of principle, as it is inherently complete. 5. Universality of... [text incomplete]
1. Universality of Obstructed Practice: Because the two aforementioned dharmas mutually penetrate one another. 2. Universality of Unobstructed Practice:
Because each and every practice is infinitely integrated through fusion. 3. Universality of Arising Function: Because there is no function that is not possible and none that is not all-pervasive.
4. Universality of the Sphere of Practice: Because the preceding eight gates are practiced throughout the Indra-net of lands. 5. Universality of the Sphere of Practice... [text continues]
At that time, "Universal" (Samantata) refers to the time that exhausts the three periods;

because the contemplation of kalpas is perfectly interfused and has no end, the aforementioned ten practices are interpenetrating yet unmixed, entering into one another in layers of depth. Therefore, Sudhana enters into a single pore of Samantabhadra.
The dharma-gates thus attained surpass all other spiritual friends by an unspeakable multiple. Furthermore, the ten superior practices may be collectively subsumed into two.

If these are explained according to the subsequent stage of Samantabhadra, they represent attaining the fruit without abandoning the cause, continuing until the very end of time as the practice of Samantabhadra.
When the dharma is manifested through the person, it is the practice of Samantabhadra; if categorized by stage, it is the former.

Samantabhadra within the stage is one who has become a person through virtue; simply practicing universal conduct is called Samantabhadra, and Samantabhadra is also simply conduct, being named after that practice.
If one refers exclusively to Samantabhadra as the stage, then the practice of Samantabhadra would have no application for those in lower stages.
A detailed explanation of Samantabhadra is as established in the analysis of the first assembly.
Regarding the three aspects of the fundamental principle (*tātparya*): first, there is the general, followed by the specific.
Generally, two chapters clarify equality, taking cause and effect as the fundamental principle and the reconciliation of prior distinctions as the goal.
Specifically, this chapter clarifies equality, taking the perfect cause as the fundamental principle and the accomplishment of the fruit of equality—non-duality—as the goal.
The commentary on the text has two parts: this chapter distinguishes the cause, while the subsequent chapter clarifies the fruit. Within the former [section], there are two parts:

first, the prose; second, the verses. Within the prose, there are two sections: first, the actual exposition, which has two sub-sections. First, it clarifies the statement of the cause, which has two parts. The first is the designation of what was previously stated in brief.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra again addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"When Samantabhadra speaks, he uses human terms to represent the Dharma.
O Sons of the Buddha, as previously expounded [up to this point], I have briefly described a small portion of the Tathāgata’s realm."

The phrase "as mentioned above" has three meanings: first, it refers proximately to one category of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) to briefly explain a small portion of their power and function for the sake of sentient beings in the heavy-obscuration hells, as a full explanation would be inconceivable;

second, it refers generally to the aforementioned results (*phala*) as a limited object, because the ocean of results is beyond words; third, it refers distantly to the previously mentioned differentiated causes (*hetu*).

[The section on] the Result. Although the preceding text contains the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), because it follows expedient means, the five stages proceed gradually, and cause and result are distinguished separately;

as it accords with the capacities and ailments of beings, it has not yet exhausted the source of the Dharma. Therefore, it is called the "partial teaching" (*shaofen*). This serves to reveal that what follows below concerns the equality of cause and result;

explained according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), cause and result are perfectly interfused, and thus it is called the "vast teaching" (*guangdashi*). △ Second, the interrogation and explanation.
There are two parts to this. First, the inquiry: "Why?
The intent of the inquiry is:
for what reason was it called a "brief explanation" in the preceding text? Second, the explanation.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, act for the sake of all sentient beings.
The commentary on this passage has two meanings. First, it establishes the foundation of *śamatha*. As for why the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world:
it is because sentient beings possess ten kinds of faults and evils, such as ignorance (*avidyā*). Rather than explaining these extensively, they first clarify the distinctions [between them].

Regarding "other causes" and so forth: second is the arising of subsequent [retribution]. This means that once sentient beings have become exceedingly numerous and their obstructions and burdens are inexhaustible, then the treatment of one is the treatment of all, and the manifestation of one is the manifestation of all.
Since sentient beings are inexhaustible, cause and effect likewise extend to the very limits of the future. Because what preceded has not yet been exhausted, the ten faults are next explained.
Lacking wisdom,
first there is ignorance,
which leads one to commit evil.

The second is the performance of unwholesome conduct; in the Jin translation, this is termed "all fetters" (*paryavasthāna*), which are likewise afflictions. These two constitute the general category.
The subsequent six are all ignorance (*avidyā*) consisting of the conceit of "I" and "mine."
Three [aspects] can be known:
attachment to the body;
fourth, clinging to the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi). Therefore, the *Six Stages* (*Ṣaḍbhūmi*) says: "The worldly acquisition of a body arises entirely from clinging to a self."
Perversion and doubt— such as the five perversions,
the three perversions, the four perversions, and so forth— which cannot be decisively resolved;
and wrong view.
Sixth, the discrimination of deviating from correct principle;
seventh, the discrimination of pervasive conceptualization.
It is constantly associated with all fetters and bonds;
eight fetters and bonds always follow it,
as it flows along the stream of birth and death.
The nine meanings pertain to karma and suffering; that is, they are a flow of cause and effect that distances one from the path of the Tathāgata.
Because they constitute ten paths of deviant conduct, this phrase summarizes the faults of all the preceding points.
Therefore, he appears in the world.

The designations such as "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) and so forth are as explained in the usual [treatises]. △ Second, the formal presentation of the present meaning. Regarding the conduct of Samantabhadra, the text has two parts.
First, clarifying the vastness and multiplicity of that which is to be remedied: since a single delusion constitutes one million obstacles, then one obstacle is all [obstacles].

Regarding the meaning of "obstruction": this applies equally to both afflictions and secondary afflictions; here, it is explained according to their gravity. The text has three parts. First, the general heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, I do not see a single dharma that constitutes a greater fault than [to] give rise to a mind of anger toward another bodhisattva."
It identifies the poison of anger as the most grave. Apart from anger, one searches everywhere and finds no other evil more severe than anger.
Thus, the Jin translation states: "Among all evils, there is none that surpasses the arising of a single thought of anger.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra* also says: "A bodhisattva would rather give rise to a hundred thousand thoughts of greed than give rise to a single thought of anger."
Because nothing surpasses this in its ability to obstruct and harm the great compassion of a bodhisattva, the same is said regarding the bodhisattva’s virtuous precepts.

To give rise to a mind of anger toward another bodhisattva—should one harbor anger toward a bodhisattva—the transgression is even more grave, for it causes the bodhisattva to abandon their great practice. Therefore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the various devas and Māras...
Seeing that the various bodhisattvas were mutually criticizing one another, he was constantly greatly joyful. △ Second, the interrogation and explanation, in two parts. First, the interrogation:
"For what reason?
△ Second, the explanation, in two parts. First, the general manifestation.
O Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva [acts toward] another bodhisattva... this immediately results in the accomplishment of one million gates of obstacles.
△ Second, the inquiry and enumeration of their names and characteristics:
What are these one million obstacles?
Although the headings number one million, they are briefly set forth here as one hundred gates. The ancients categorized them by their respective positions into five sections, namely:
the obstacle of not seeing bodhi, the obstacle of not hearing the true Dharma, [and so on] up to the obstacle of being among evil rākṣasas.
They obstruct the ten stages of faith and practice.
They range from obstructing the delight in the Buddha-dharma to obstructing the joy in seeing and hearing the Buddha’s sovereign supernatural powers.
They obstruct the ten stages of abiding.
The obstacle of not attaining the various faculties of a bodhisattva (up to) the obstacle of not guarding and maintaining the various practices of a bodhisattva;
the obstacle that hinders the practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The obstacle of delighting in slandering the words of omniscience (up to) the obstacle of not resolutely generating the great vows of a bodhisattva.
These hinder the practices of the Ten Directions. Below this, they hinder the practices of the Ten Stages.
They hinder dwelling together with Bodhisattvas; they hinder hearing the unobstructed Dharma; and they hinder speech from being like that of a mute sheep.
The "mute sheep" refers to an obstruction of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*). Because one is born in a remote region where the Dharma is not heard, there is nothing spoken from the mouth;
this is an obstruction of the tongue-faculty (*jihvā-indriya*), which will be explained clearly below.

Because they lack the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), there is the obstruction of the impairment of the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) [extending to] the obstruction of the lineage (*gotra*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
An ancient commentator concluded: "The myriad practices of a Bodhisattva do not exceed these five. To give rise to even a single thought of anger suddenly obstructs them all.
This interpretation is not without reason; for example, if one seeks the Dharma with a thief’s mind, how could it obstruct anything less than the ten [perfections]?
Is this the practice of the stages? This ignorance obstructs all wholesome dharmas such that even faith does not arise; how much less so the subsequent stages?
Furthermore, the dharma-realm that is obstructed is like an imperial net, layer upon layer; the obstructor is identical to the obstructed, and both are likewise without obscuration.
Thus, one knows that "one million" is merely a brief explanation. △ Third, the conclusion.
If a son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva, gives rise to a mind of anger toward other bodhisattvas—from [the first] up to [the last]—[this is the fault].
△ Second, the two profound and subtle remedies. First, within the main text of the correct manifestation, there are separately six stages, each with ten practices.
The first is the initial cultivation; the latter five constitute the realization of benefits. Therefore, the latter five sections successively rely upon the first. This is...
The former subsumes the latter; that which remedies one thing remedies all. Although there is a sequence in their exposition, their attainment constitutes a single retention (*dhāraṇī*).
Now, the first section is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the title and the exhortation to practice.
Therefore, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas (up to) should diligently cultivate ten kinds of dharmas.
II. Inquiry into the number, enumeration, and conclusion: What are these ten?
Among these, ten dharmas are subsumed into five pairs to distinguish five kinds of cultivation. The first two concern the person and clarify the cultivation of humility and respect;
that is to say, not abandoning any sentient being in one's mind and conceiving of all bodhisattvas as the Tathāgata.
Because of honoring those above and loving those below, the next two [verses] clarify true and correct cultivation by way of the Dharma:
never slandering any of the Buddha's teachings and knowing that all buddha-fields are inexhaustible.
Because one understands the matters through compliance with the teaching, the next two [stages] clarify the vast cultivation in terms of mental activity:
one generates profound faith and delight in the bodhisattva practices and does not abandon the bodhicitta, which is equal to space and the dharma-realm.
One delights in the great practice because of the firmness of the great resolve. Next, the following two [verses] concern the cultivation of increasing excellence through wisdom:
one observes awakening, enters the powers of the Tathāgata, and diligently cultivates unimpeded eloquence.

The wisdom that realizes the fruits of the internal sense-bases gives rise to superior discernment externally. The latter two [perfections] clarify long-term cultivation in terms of compassion and vows:
teaching and transforming sentient beings without weariness, and dwelling in all worlds with a mind free from attachment.
Sentient beings are inexhaustible; one transforms them through compassion without weariness. Worlds are boundless; one vows to abide therein without attachment.
These constitute the ten. △ Second, the twenty kinds of purity. First, following the previous section to introduce the subsequent one.

O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (up to the point mentioned) is able to fulfill ten kinds of purity, it is because they have achieved freedom from defilement based on the correct practice performed previously. △ Second, the enumeration of the number and listing of the names.
What are the ten? They are formed sequentially from the preceding ten phrases, namely:
the thorough penetration of the purity of the profound Dharma.
First, because of not abandoning any sentient beings, one attains the purity of the profound Dharma;
for since all sentient beings possess buddha-nature, they are true within their very delusion, and thus constitute the profound Dharma.
First, purity through associating with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);
second, purity through protecting and upholding all Buddha-dharmas by virtue of honoring those who are superior.
Third, by not slandering [the Dharma], one is able to protect the Dharma and thoroughly comprehend the purity of the realm of space.
Fourth, by knowing it to be inexhaustible, one comprehends it as being like space.
They enter deeply into the purity of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Fifth, because the bodhisattva practices do not depart from the dharma-realm,
they are able to enter deeply and observe the purity of the boundless mind.
Sixth, because they know that the bodhisattva’s mind is equal to empty space, they observe it as boundless;
their roots of goodness are purified in common with all bodhisattvas.
Seventh, observing that all bodhisattvas share this same contemplation, they are able to enter the power of the Buddhas; therefore, these are called "roots."
They do not cling to the purity of various eons,
because they cultivate the eightfold path with tireless diligence; they do not cling to the calculation of eons,
as they observe the purity of the three periods of time.
Ninth, because of being insatiable in emanation; by observing all sentient beings of the three times—whether already transformed or not yet transformed—one practices the purity of all Buddha-dharmas.
Tenth, by abiding in the world, one is therefore able to cultivate all Buddha-dharmas.
These are the ten.
△ Third, the ten kinds of vast and great wisdom, in two parts. First, connecting the preceding to introduce the subsequent:
"O Son of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in these ten dharmas, they then become fully endowed with ten kinds of vast and great wisdom."
Once defilements have been brushed away, fundamental wisdom is spontaneously luminous. Because this knowledge accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), it is called "vast.
△ Second, the inquiry into the number and the enumeration of names: What are the ten? They are: the wisdom that knows the mental activities of all sentient beings (up to) this being the tenth.
These are also formed from the preceding ten and the subsequent ten; however, there are instances of expansion and contraction, which I fear would be too cumbersome to correlate here.
The expositor may explain as appropriate. △ Fourth: The Ten Kinds of Universal Entry. Part One: Building upon the preceding to initiate the subsequent.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in these ten wisdoms, they then attain entry into the ten kinds of universal penetration (*samanta-praveśa*).

Phenomena accord with principle and merge; they have been entered from the beginning. Wisdom realizes that this is the natural state (*dharmatā*), such that there is no realm through which it does not pass.
Thus, both body and mind are able to penetrate one another. Furthermore, these ten arise from the preceding three and can be understood through the power of intention. △ Second.
The enumeration of the names of the categories is as follows.
What are the ten? They are: (1) all worlds entering into a single hair-pore; [and so on, up to] (10) that which is not a faculty entering into all faculties.
Regarding "that which is not a faculty": objects, consciousness, and principle are all not faculties.
To enter all perceptions into a single perception, and so on, up to entering the present single lifetime into all three periods of time—these constitute the ten.
△ Fifth: The Ten Kinds of Supreme and Sublime Minds. Part Two: First, following upon the preceding to initiate the subsequent.
After the Buddha-son Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has observed in this manner, he abides in ten kinds of supreme and wondrous minds (*viśiṣṭa-citta*).

Because they accord with the Dharma as previously described and their fundamental nature is perfectly interfused, they render the two—phenomena and principle—unimpeded, benefiting beings in accordance with their capacities;

these are called "supreme and wondrous minds. They arise from the preceding four [minds] and may be understood according to one's inclination. II. Inquiry into the Number and Enumeration of the Names.
What are the ten? They are: dwelling in the languages of all worlds... [and so forth] up to these being the ten.
△ Sixth: The Ten Kinds of Skillfulness. Part Two. First, connecting the preceding to introduce the subsequent.

O Sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas abide in these ten kinds [of practices] up to the ten kinds of skillful knowledge regarding the Buddha-dharma, because of the aforementioned non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, they are now able to decisively resolve both the provisional and the ultimate; this is called "skillful knowledge."
△ Second, the inquiry into the number and the enumeration of names. What are the ten?
There are eleven phrases; the last two are combined into one, while the others follow their respective order. These are formed from the preceding ten.
That which is called the skillful wisdom that thoroughly comprehends the profound Buddha-dharma is such that words themselves vanish when spoken; this is termed "profound.
It is the skillful wisdom that gives rise to the vast Buddha-dharma.
Second, because it is without dependence, it gives rise to vastness and proclaims the various skillful wisdoms of the Buddha-dharma.
Third, just as form arises depending on space, it is thus able to expound all varieties.
One realizes the skillful wisdom that enters into the equality of the Buddha-dharmas;
because one abides in the four [stages] free from the two extremes, one realizes equality.
One clearly understands the skillful wisdom that distinguishes the various Buddha-dharmas.
Fifth, by means of comprehending the profound secrets of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*),
one distinguishes [the conventional] while awakening to and understanding the skillful wisdom regarding the non-differentiation of the Buddha-dharmas;
sixth, non-differentiation— the two texts are identical in full.
7. Skillful wisdom that deeply enters the adornment of the Buddha-dharma.
If there is no doubt or confusion, this constitutes the adornment of the Buddha-dharma. 1.
Skillful wisdom that enters the Buddha-dharma through expedient means.
Eighth, by means of an impartial mind, one accomplishes a single skillful means;
through immeasurable skillful means, one enters the skillful wisdom of the Buddha-dharma.
Ninth, regarding the phenomena of the three periods of time, they are categorized according to the gate of differentiation; for this reason, it is called "immeasurable skillful means."
Knowing that the boundless Buddha-dharmas are without distinction, [he attains] skillful knowledge of non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas.
Tenth, by abiding in the power of the Buddhas, he knows that his own power for the boundless Buddha-dharmas is non-retrogressive.
These are the ten.
Just as it has been explained through the successive transitions from the preceding ten, the same principle should apply to the preceding four sections.
Thus, through these successive transitions, one does not depart from the initial cultivation; therefore, within each single dharma, all are fully present. △ Second, the conclusion and exhortation.
"O Sons of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have heard this Dharma, [up to] it is entirely equal to the Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Because a single practice can encompass all practices, they swiftly attain Bodhi. The second major section, the text of the proof, has two parts.
First, the manifestation of auspicious omens as proof, which has two sub-sections. First, within this world-system.
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha and because the Dharma is thus, (it reached as far as) raining clouds of the preaching of the Dharma through unspeakable spiritual powers.
△ Second, the summary extending to the ten directions.
In this world-system of four continents (and so on), it is likewise throughout all worlds in the ten directions.
△ Second, the realization of the bodhisattvas also has two parts. First, this land.
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha and because the Dharma is thus, [it extends] to the profound Dharma of the prediction of the greatest vow.
As for the profound Dharma of prediction, one quickly attains Bodhi with little exertion of effort.
"O Sons of the Buddha, we are all named Samantabhadra.
As for those who share the name Samantabhadra, it is because we all possess this same practice.
We have each come from the world-system called Universal Excellence (Samantavijaya)."
Because this universal Dharma is the most supreme,
at the abode of the Tathāgata Universal Banner Sovereign (*Samantadhvaja-īśvara*),
this practice achieves fruition, arising loftily and without obstruction.
They have come to this land entirely through the spiritual power of the Buddha (up to) coming to this site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to bear witness for you.
△ Second, the conclusion of the pervasion:
"In this *bodhimaṇḍa*, as we [are] in ten Buddha-fields (up to) so it is in all worlds."
△ Second, the re-exposition by means of verses, which has two parts. First, the preliminary narration. Initially, the verse protocol is stated:
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra (extending until) surveyed the ten directions as far as the Dharma-realm.
△ Second, the intention of the verses.
Desiring to reveal and elucidate the bodhisattva practices (up to) causing them to attain awakening, he speaks these verses.
These contain ten intentions, all of which are fully present within the verses. △ Second, the actual verses consist of one hundred and twenty-one verses. Great.

Within a single atom, one perceives all worlds, [and so on] until: "one is able to discern and know them all."

penetrating deeply into the subtle wisdom that discriminates all worlds (up to: except for the revelation of the Buddha.

the Various Names of Worlds and Tathāgatas (up to) Attaining the Further Shore.

Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Appearance of the Tathāgata.
△ Regarding the intent of this initial section: The preceding chapter elucidated the cause that accords with the fruit; this chapter discriminates the fruit that arises from such a cause.
Although their essence is equal, the two aspects are not conflated. The sequence of first the cause and then the fruit follows the logical order of meaning.

Furthermore, it serves to answer the thought that arose in the "Inconceivable" chapter and to respond to the questions concerning the "practice" asked in the second assembly. This concludes the exegesis.
As before. Second, regarding the explanation of the names: "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One) is a person who possesses the Dharma; it is a general designation for the three bodies and ten bodies.

"Manifestation" (prādurbhāva) is the Dharma that relies upon the person; it is a collective name for the fruition-function and the transformative-function. Although the Tathāgata is seen as described above...
The text states: Because they manifest in response [to sentient beings], the ten bodies are again distinguished. Each of the ten bodies possesses the meaning of manifestation;

however, for now, we shall clarify this by relying upon the three bodies. Yet, "coming" is itself manifestation; thus, to distinguish between person and phenomenon, it is explained with clear illustration.
Therefore, I shall clarify this further. If we speak according to the *dharmakāya*, the Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
To manifest eternally in accordance with reality is called "appearing. Thus, the subsequent passage says: "He universally manifests all things, yet there is nothing manifested. It also says:

"The essence is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing," and so forth. If one relies on the *saṃbhogakāya*, having mounted the path of reality (*yathābhūtamārga*) and come to achieve perfect enlightenment, one is therefore called a *Tathāgata*.
Because the qualities of the original nature are suddenly and simultaneously manifested, it is termed "appearance.
Thus, the subsequent text says: "When the Tathāgata achieves perfect enlightenment, regarding all meanings, there is no doubt; he perceives them universally."

"All sentient beings attain perfect enlightenment," and so forth. If one relies on the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), it comes to transform sentient beings by riding upon the vehicle of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience);
therefore, it is called "Tathāgata. This refers to the simultaneous manifestation of great activity that accords with the capacities of beings. Thus, the verse says:
"By the power of original vows, he manifests the Buddha-body, causing [beings] to see the Tathāgata’s great spiritual transformations. It further says: "In accordance with..."
Regarding power: beneath the Bodhi tree, one attains perfect enlightenment through various bodies.

Now, because the newly enlightened Buddha and the anciently perfected Buddha have never been two distinct entities, and because the new perfection and the ancient Buddha appear to be distinguished as Dharma-body and Reward-body yet respond without fail to the proper time, the Responsive is identical to the Real.
Because the Responsive arises in accordance with the Nature, the Responsive is identical to the Real. Thus, the three Buddhas are perfectly interfused within the ten bodies.

It is unimpeded; thus, by distinguishing between the responsive and the manifest, one reveals the perfection of the Real. For this reason, the Jin translation names this chapter "The Nature-Arising" (*Xingqi-pin*).

Although the character "nature" (*xing*) was added for interpretive purposes, it does not deviate from the underlying principle. This is because, although the response arises from conditions, it does not contradict nature;
because there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm; and because when purity supplants defilement, nature itself arises. If it were apart from conditions...

Because the nature (*dhātu*) is ineffable, the Bodhisattva Nature-Arising (*Prakṛtyutpāda*) is added below to represent that which is expressed. Although delusion is identical to the nature, it does not accord with the nature;

therefore, since the meaning of "arising" contains many implications, we speak directly of "manifestation. This is because [the Buddha] manifests from the nature, from causes, from the truth, and from responsive resonance.
If one were to say that this only explains the manifestation of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), one would not only lose the preceding point regarding the nature...
Based on these two meanings, it is still insufficient to reveal the profundity [of the term]. How, then, could it integrate the previously mentioned differentiated fruits?

If "Tathāgata" (如來) is taken to mean "manifestation" (現), then Tathāgata is simply manifestation; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. If one distinguishes between the person, the dharmas, and the three bodies (*trikāya*), all are manifestations of the Tathāgata, as they are distinguished from and emerge out of what is other.
Third, the fundamental tenet (*siddhānta*): it takes the manifestation of equality as its tenet and the integration of differentiated fruits as its objective.

Fourth, the correct explanation of the text: the text consists of seven sections. The first is the section on the bestowal of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is divided into two parts; the first concerns the empowerment of the light from the *ūrṇā* (the hair-tuft between the eyebrows) bestowed upon the requester. Text.

Third: Within the first light there are ten meanings, which are grouped into three categories. The first concerns the source of its emergence; the second concerns its name and essence; and the remaining eight concern its functions.
First, the source of the light’s emergence:
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from between his eyebrows.

Emitting it from between the eyebrows signifies the realization of the Middle Way, for it is free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence; it signifies the Way of Non-abiding, for it is free from the two extremes of the Real and the Responsive.
Within the mark of the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*):
as for the "white tuft," it symbolizes that which is manifested, because its nature is stainless; it signifies manifestation, because it is the fundamental source of all teachings.
△ Second, distinguishing the names and essence of the light.
He emits a great light named "The Appearance of the Tathāgata," because it is as has been described.
Thereafter follow eight sections, all of which pertain to the activity of light. △ Third, the light of the retinue; this refers to the activity of the cause.
It has immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeyas of light rays as its retinue.
It encompasses all dharmas, for they are all produced from it. △ Fourth, the manifestation of activity.
That light universally illumines all worlds throughout the ten directions, the entirety of space and the dharma-realm, circling them ten times to the right.
△ Fifth, the act of reverence,
which manifests the Tathāgata’s immeasurable mastery.
6. The activity of awakening:
awakening countless multitudes of bodhisattvas and shaking all worlds throughout the ten directions.
7. The activity of cessation.
It eliminates all suffering of the various evil realms.
△ Eighth, the activity of subjugation:
it outshines and eclipses all the palaces of the māras.
△ 9. Manifestation of Activity:
Revealing all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, as well as all their assemblies at the sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
△ 10. Reabsorption of Activity.
Having performed these actions, they came and circumambulated the assembly of bodhisattvas to the right.
△ Second, the actual description of the signs of empowerment:
[the light] entered the crown of the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagarbha-samudgata-guṇa-vyūha.
The reason this Bodhisattva is singled out for special treatment is that he is manifested according to his name. "Nature" (*prakṛti*) has two meanings:

first, the sense of "lineage" (*gotra*), because it is that from which [the Buddha] arises; second, the sense of "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*), because whether in the true or the responsive body, all arise from this.
There is also an interpretation which states: "The Wondrous Virtue of Nature-Arising" refers to Mañjuśrī preaching this Dharma-gate, and thus he is given the title "Nature-Arising."

One who provides this explanation does not contradict the great principle. This is because Mañjuśrī’s great wisdom acts as the manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*), while the Dharma-realm of Samantabhadra acts as that which is manifested (*abhivyajya*);
together they bring about the appearance of Vairocana. Furthermore, it is because his practice and realization are perfected that the Buddha appears.
As for [the light] entering through the crown of the head, this is a sign of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); for only the pinnacle of sublime wisdom can manifest it.
△ Third, the addition of two [sections]. First, the entire great assembly rejoices together, knowing that the Dharma is about to be bestowed.
At that time, all the members of this assembly [realize that] he will surely expound the profound Great Dharma.
△ Second, Subhūti receives the mandate. This consists of two parts: knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has commanded him to seek out the speaker;
and first, the prose section on the physical and mental prostration. At that time, the Bodhisattva *Tathāgatagotra-subhūti* (至) turned his mind single-pointedly toward the Buddha and spoke in verse:

"Kǔ" (kneeling) means to kneel. △ Second, the verses of praise and invitation consist of ten stanzas, divided into two parts. First, five stanzas praise [the Buddha], which is further divided into two.
The first stanza is a general praise expressing reverence.
The Great Wisdom arising from the merits of Perfect Enlightenment... (up to)... for this reason, I now pay respectful homage.
△ Second, four verses specifically praising:
Having ascended to the shore of the signless realm... (up to)... sharing the same nature as all Buddhas.

The first three verses praise the fruit [of the teaching], and the last one praises the cause. △ Second, the five verses of the request: the first verse is a personal account of the benefit received, which constitutes the acceptance of the essential meaning:
"The Teacher has emitted this great radiance... and it has returned again to enter my body."
△ Second, there is one verse. It conveys the intent of the assembly to request [the teaching]:
"Having well studied the definitive Dharma... therefore I cause you to request the Dharma King.
△ Third, there is one verse. It praises the assembly as being capable of hearing [the teaching].
He causes this entire assembly to be purified... (until) such noble and excellent ones have all gathered together.
△ Fourth, there is one verse describing the Buddha’s command to request [the teaching]:
"O Honored One, Teacher of the World, who brings benefit... (until) cause me to inquire about the Unsurpassed Dharma."
△ Section Five: One verse concerning the primary seeker of the Dharma.
[The verse asks: "Who, within the profound realm of the Great Sage... [down to] ...the Honored Guide of the World, pray reveal it?

Having already grasped the Buddha's intention, he does not formally entreat the Buddha. △ Section Two: Regarding the empowerment of the speaker by means of light from the mouth, this demonstrates that which was requested.
Therefore, there are three parts within the text. First, the light also consists of ten [aspects]. First, the place of emergence:
"At that time, the Tathāgata [emitted light] from his mouth.
That it is emitted from the mouth signifies that the path of teaching is transmitted and communicated. Second, the name of the light.

He emits a great light named "Unimpeded and Fearless," which enables one to attain unimpeded eloquence, to have no fear of the great assembly, and to [fathom] profound principles. △ Third, the karma of causes.
With hundreds of thousands of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light as its retinue.
△ Fourth, the manifestation of activity:
it universally illumines all worlds throughout the ten directions, as far as the reaches of space and the entirety of the Dharma-realm, circling them ten times to the right.

Manifesting the various sovereign powers of the Tathāgata.
△ 6. The Activity of Awakening.
Awakening immeasurable multitudes of bodhisattvas, they cause all worlds throughout the ten directions to tremble.
(7) Ceasing karmic activity:
they eliminate and extinguish all suffering in the various evil realms.

eclipsing all the palaces of the māras.

Manifesting all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and their entire assemblies at the sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
[This concludes] the tenth fascicle on karma.
Having performed these deeds, they came and circumambulated the assembly of Bodhisattvas to the right.
△ Second, the explicit explanation of the signs of empowerment.
Entering the mouth of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra:
that the light enters the mouth is because it is taught through oral transmission, as spoken by the Buddha. That he is empowered by Samantabhadra is because he is universal...
Because it is the fruit of virtuous conduct, the Dharma-realm that is realized is manifested through principle. △ Third, the attainment of benefits:
Once the light had entered, [it pervaded] the body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (up to) with the exception of the Tathāgata’s lion throne.

"Except for the Tathāgata," [it is said], because this distinguishes between teacher and disciple. △ Second, the main body of the text is divided into two parts. First, the inquiry that raises the matter:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Virtue of the Arising of the Nature of the Tathāgata... [up to] "the world is unable to know what auspicious sign this is."
△ Second, citing examples to provide the answer. The answer is the main point itself.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra said (up to): "Now, manifesting this sign, he shall expound his Dharma."
△ Third, the manifestation of auspicious omens as proof of accomplishment:
When these words were spoken, the entire great earth shook everywhere, manifesting a rare wonder.
This is because signs already appeared as soon as its name was heard. As for the shaking of the great earth, it signifies that the Great Dharma is about to...
Manifesting [this], because the great delusions were about to collapse, he produced the light of immeasurable inquiries into the Dharma.

As for "producing the light of inquiries into the Dharma," it refers to secretly bestowing wisdom to assist in the arousal of the request. △ Third, the Section on the Request, which is divided into two parts. First:
The prose section has four parts. First, the general request for the teaching:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra... [requesting] that the Dharma of manifestation be explained to me.
Second, praising the assembly as being capable of hearing it.
"O Son of the Buddha, these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions [of bodhisattvas], up to those with immeasurable merit, have all assembled here.
△ Third, praising the virtues of the speaker by specifically extolling ten matters.
O Son of the Buddha, you have already served and made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas;
having made offerings to so many Buddhas, you must certainly have heard this before.
Having accomplished the most supreme and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva and perfected that wondrous conduct through prior cultivation,
they have attained mastery over all gateways of samādhi.
Mastery over meditative concentration, because it has a basis;
entering the secret realm of all Buddhas,
because of direct realization and entry.
Knowing all the Buddha-dharmas,
because one knows the path of teaching,
one cuts off all doubts and delusions.
In order to eliminate the doubts of others,
he is empowered by the supernatural might of all Tathāgatas;
because of this supreme empowerment.
Knowing the faculties of sentient beings, because he thoroughly discerns their dispositions and capacities,
he preaches the true Dharma of liberation according to their inclinations.
Because he is able to teach in accordance [with reality], he expounds the Buddha-dharma in conformity with the Buddha’s wisdom, thereby reaching the further shore.
Because he has attained the profound meaning that accords with wisdom, he reaches the shore. Thus, at the end, he summarizes the ten virtues.
There are such immeasurable merits as these.
Since there are those who speak of these virtues, it is appropriate that they should now speak. △ Fourth, the headings are set forth and a specific request is made:
"Excellent!"
The first phrase praises what is excellent. Following the three preceding sections, ten distinct matters are presented to manifest inexhaustibility.
"O Son of the Buddha, please explain the dharma of the appearance of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."

This is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). By the collective assembly of many conditions, the manifesting phenomenon (*dharmaprādurbhāva*) is established. A phenomenon (*dharma*) contains both the aspect of sustaining (*dhṛti*) and the aspect of functioning (*vṛtti*). The remaining nine are the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*):
the physical form, speech and sound, mind, and mental factors.
That is, the three secrets of body, speech, and mind;
the objective sphere,
which is the object of cognition and also the delimited domain.
The practices to be performed are cultivated in reliance upon their respective objects; they encompass both cause and fruit,
thereby accomplishing the Way.
One accomplishes the path to Bodhi and turns the Wheel of Dharma.
Having attained Bodhi, the mind turns the Wheel of Dharma.
Even unto manifesting entry into parinirvāṇa, one should attain bodhi;

yet one must certainly manifest nirvāṇa. The roots of goodness produced by seeing, hearing, and drawing near [to them]— [The Sanskrit for the above is: yāvat parinirvāṇasaṃdarśanena bodhim abhisaṃboddhavyam avaśyaṃ ca nirvāṇaṃ saṃdarśayitavyam | dṛṣṭa-śruta-vijñātôpāstija-kūśalamūlam ||
Whether they exist or have perished, seeing or hearing them all brings benefit. These nine matters comprise the beginning and end of a single transformation.
Some say that the first is the Dharma upon which others rely, while the remaining nine are the virtues that depend upon it; this too is a reasonable interpretation.
"I pray that you will explain all such matters as these.
This concludes the formal request. II. The Request in Verse: Ten stanzas, divided into three parts. The first praises his virtues and introduces the request, summarizing the preceding three sections.
Then the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagunajñānābhibhū (up to) addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, speaking in verse:
"Excellent is your unimpeded great wisdom... (up to) having heard this, the sons of the Buddha all rejoice."
△ The second section consists of four verses. It presents the dharmas and makes specific requests, summarizing the preceding fourth segment. [The text asks:
"How does a bodhisattva accord with and enter [the stages]... what benefits are there? We pray that you will proclaim them."

△ Section Three consists of five verses. These verses praise the virtues [of the Buddhas] and entreat them [to teach], encompassing the final three sections [of the treatise]. Within this section, there are four parts.
First is the general praise and entreaty:
"All these Bodhisattvas join their palms... [until] ...may you, for the sake of purifying sentient beings, explain [this]."
△ Second, there are two verses concerning the method of exhortation. [The text continues:
"I pray that you will provide causes, conditions, and parables... up to "...the Buddha’s bodhi is likewise.
Because the Dharma is profound and difficult to comprehend, he requests that causes and parables be taught. △ Third, there is one and a half verses praising the assembly's capacity.
Having heard [this],
[beings] in ten directions across thousands of myriads of Buddha-lands [develop a thirst and yearning for the subtle and profound meaning].
△ Four and a half verses conclude the request for what is to be taught.

I vow to fully expound the vast Dharma of the Tathāgata’s appearance with a pure mind, proclaiming it with clarity, without error, and with complete textual and semantic perfection. △ Fourth, the Section on Exposition.
This is divided into two major parts: first, the specific answers to the ten questions; each of the ten sections contains both prose and verse, and each is complete in its entirety.
10. Now, first, the answer regarding the method of manifestation. The prose section has two parts: first, the announcement, praise, and profundity.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... (up to)... "O Son of the Buddha, this place is inconceivable."
△ Second, the threefold detailed exposition according to the meaning. First, the extensive response to the preceding causes and conditions through the Dharma-exposition. First, the heading:
That is to say, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, appears in the world by means of immeasurable dharmas.
This is the general statement that multiple causes bring about the fruit of manifestation. △ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts. First, the inquiry followed by a general explanation:
"For what reason? It is not through a single condition nor through a single matter that the appearance of the Tathāgata is accomplished."

"Conditions" refers to the conditions that bring about accomplishment; "matters" refers to the essential substance of that which is accomplished. The preceding section provides a reverse explanation, while the following provides a direct explanation:
it is through ten immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* matters that accomplishment is attained.
The previous mention of "immeasurability" (*apramāṇa*) was a general characteristic. Now, ten types of immeasurability are clarified here to demonstrate inexhaustibility.
In reality, there are hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya numbers of immeasurabilities. These ten immeasurabilities each pervade the ten similes.
Regarding the phrase "hundreds of thousands," the ancients said: "By including the ten immeasurabilities within [each of] them, the ten similes are thereby completed."
One hundred. Following this, ten phrases within the "Conjunctions" (jie) each take the preceding one hundred categories to form one thousand;

therein further distinct meanings arise, thereby constituting the "Infinite" (wuliang). These are now listed individually below. Within these ten categories, each category states that they are established "by means of infinite causes";
thus, it need not wait for mutual interpenetration (*xiangru*). It is known from this that the terms "hundred" and "thousand" are merely numerical designations.
This is merely a general designation. △ Second, the specific enumeration is clarified through inquiry:
What are the ten? They are as follows: [from "the past" to] "because they are formed by the bodhicitta of all sentient beings."
First, one initially gives rise to the great mind, vowing to appear [in the world]. Therefore, what are the characteristics of this mind?

Thus one knows that there is no body, for it is known to be like empty space.
Because it is like space, both delusion and views are simultaneously extinguished;
thus one knows equality, for one knows that all sentient beings are without self.
Because there is equal selflessness, there is but a single flavor.
Thus one knows that knowledge is inexhaustible, because it pervades all buddha-fields without end;
and by virtue of this inexhaustibility, all vehicles are universally transformed.
Thus one knows that knowledge is non-retrogressive, because it reaches the limit of the future without interruption.
Because there is no interruption in the future limit, the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed.
Thus one knows that it is indestructible; one knows the Tathāgata’s wisdom because it is without opposition.
That which is without opposition is precisely unimpeded wisdom.
Thus one knows that non-dual knowledge observes the conditioned and the unconditioned with equanimity.
This equanimous observation of the conditioned and the unconditioned subsumes the three wheels and returns them to unimpeded wisdom.
Thus one knows that all sentient beings obtain benefit because their original vows of dedication have been spontaneously fulfilled.

Since they originally acted for the sake of sentient beings, they cause them to benefit and spontaneously fulfill [their aims]. If one merely applies each of these points to the preceding ten gates, one has not yet grasped the essential meaning.
II. The Verse Summary consists of thirty-seven verses, divided into three parts. First, praising the profundity and granting permission.
It is explained in two parts. First, praising the profound and the immeasurable; second, [the specific explanation]. Within the first part, there is one verse that praises it in general.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"The Great Heroes of the ten directions, most unsurpassed... (down to) supreme in merit, transcending the world.
This verse summarizes the preceding proclamation of inconceivable words. △ Second, there are ten verses that specifically praise [the Buddha].
"The merit of the Ten Powers is boundless" (up to) "now I behold the Great Supernatural Transformation of the Tathāgata.
This sequentially follows the preceding verses. Within the final summary, these eleven lines also constitute the ninth stanza, which summarizes the ninety-two lines.

Since the previous section was a summary of metaphors, this current section likewise serves as a general summary of those metaphors. Thus, the metaphor clarifies both the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
This, then, is primarily explained in terms of "nature" (*prakṛti*). The ancient designation "Arising from Nature" (*xingqi*) is all the more justified for the following reasons:

first, that which is "without limit or measure" corresponds to the meaning of "immeasurability"; second, that which is "unfathomable even within a single hair-pore" corresponds to the meaning of "vastness"; third, that which is "unobtainable at the very limit of space" corresponds to the meaning of "non-arising.
However, this third point seems to be a restatement of the fifth [point], the metaphor of being like space, while the sixth seems to be a restatement of the... [text ends].

Third, the analogy of non-arising and non-ceasing: because the meanings grasped differ, they are each treated according to their sequence. Fourth, "that which cannot be known" refers to being apart from mind and consciousness.
Fifth, "pervading all things and not being one" is precisely the meaning of space. Sixth, "the equality of essential nature" is the meaning of equality and selflessness.
Seventh, whereas the previous [verse] pervaded all lands, this [verse] pervades the three periods of time; thus it is stated in the text.

They merely alternate with one another. Eighth, because they are unchanging, they persist until the end of time. Ninth, because they transcend verbal expression, they are non-dual and without counterpart.

Tenth, because they manifest bodies through their original vows, they are able to accomplish benefit. △ Second, the admonition to listen and the permission to speak, in two parts. First, the admonition to listen and the exhortation to practice.
"If one wishes to know the realm of the Buddha" (up to) "causing the mind to be unimpeded in whatever it is directed toward.
The first half of this verse says, "The pure mind is like space," which reveals the meaning through a general metaphor; the second half reveals it specifically.

First, being free from grasping and rejecting is like that pure space because it is devoid of clouds and obscurations; this is true cessation (*śamatha*). Second, there is no obstruction when contacting objects.
Like that pure sky, because it is without obstruction, this is true contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). This contemplation is not something produced;
its intention is to illumine objects, whereby that which is illumined is boundless. Because the essence of this cessation (*śamatha*) is detached and free from forgetfulness, all grasping is stilled.
If this is so, then without polishing or refining, one is spontaneously pure. This purity that is not produced by purification is to silently tread upon the realm of the Buddha.
This is the essential point of the mind; those who study later should contemplate and practice it. △ Second, the section on the limits of the teaching.
"Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, you should listen well" (up to) "I shall now speak of all roots of goodness.
The first half-verse concludes the preceding section and introduces what follows; the subsequent one and a half verses correctly demonstrate the scope.

Ten categories are cited, though the category of "practice" is omitted briefly because it is subsumed within the three types of action (*trikarma*). The category of "Perfect Enlightenment" is omitted because it is subsumed within the category of the "Teacher. Alternatively, [it may be omitted]...
Omission: none. △ Second, the verses on the ten preceding metaphors, which constitute ten sections. First, the metaphor of the construction of the great trichiliocosm, which consists of four verses;
as this is the general [introduction], the text has two parts. First, the general manifestation of manifold conditions.
For example, from the initial establishment of the world up to the cause for the arising of the ten powers, none can fathom it.

The first [example] is the illustration; the latter is the application to the Dharma. All subsequent cases follow this pattern. △ Second, there are two verses that specifically reveal the characteristics of conditions.
For example, it is like the clouds pouring down rain at the beginning of a kalpa... (up to) universally guiding [beings] to bring them to the attainment of the unsurpassed fruit.
△ Second, there are eighteen verses which, in their respective order, versify the nine preceding sections of the sutra beginning with "pouring down a great rain."
It is like a great rain called "The Torrential Downpour" (extending to "...causing all delusions and afflictions to be extinguished").
Each section contains two verses; the first eight texts are explicit. The ninth says: "The skillful means rely on wisdom. This "wisdom" refers to that which appeared previously in the verse.
However, unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-prajñā*) is the Buddha’s true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). The middle two [sections] are both provisional (*upāya*). Within this, as for wisdom—

This is precisely knowing the skillful means of affairs; according with the capacities of beings and harmonizing with the ultimate, it constitutes the unimpeded correspondence between the provisional and the real.
Initially, this constitutes the simultaneous movement of compassion and wisdom. △ Third, the conclusion on the inexhaustibility of the teaching.
The Tathāgata appears within the boundless Dharma (up to) the state beyond analogy, wherein he provides analogies for that which is without analogy.
