Here, we shall briefly clarify that the preceding phrase serves as the general heading, which fully possesses the twenty-one kinds of qualities listed below.

Therefore, it is called "wondrous realization. These are all fully explained below in detail. Of these, the first four pertain to self-benefit, while the remaining ones all pertain to the benefit of others.
Within the former [four], there are four: first, the virtue of wisdom; second, the virtue of abandonment; third, the virtue of grace; and fourth, the virtue of equalizing activity.
The two modes of activity are forever severed.

The first refers to being unimpeded in every respect regarding the objects of knowledge; this is the name for the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*) as described in the *Sūtra on the Transformation of Merits*.

"Non-dual" (*advaya*) refers to their non-manifestation. Regarding the term "non-," it should be understood in the sense of "absence. This signifies "forever severed," meaning that the merit of the Buddha’s wisdom is free from [obstructions].
Regarding the knowledge of obstacles: unlike the śrāvakas, who possess ignorance regarding extremely distant times and places, [the Buddha] has both knowledge and ignorance;
thus, these constitute two modes of practice. Now, since there is no ignorance, it is said that [obstacles] are forever severed.
One realizes the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*).
Second, regarding the non-dual nature of existence and non-existence, there is the merit of being able to enter the most supreme purity of *tathatā*.

That sūtra is called "the approach" (*gati*); "the approach to the dharma of signlessness" means that "approaching" (*praveśa*) has the sense of realizing this very [dharma]. However, as for the essence of the dharma of signlessness...
It is precisely suchness (*tathatā*). Because it lacks the two characteristics of existence and non-existence, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).

Among all phenomena, it is the most pure and free from adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*), causing oneself and others to enter into excellence. Within the terminology of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), it is called the most supreme purity.
Abiding in the Buddha-abode.
Third is the merit of performing the Buddha-activities effortlessly and without cessation. Vasubandhu’s commentary states:

"This means abiding in that which the Buddhas abide in, which is a state of non-abiding. This explains the sūtra: within this abiding, one constantly performs the Buddha-activities without [interruption].
There is a cessation; this is the exegesis of the commentary.
One attains equality with the Buddha.
Fourth, within the dharmakāya, there is the merit of non-differentiation regarding the basis, the intention, and the activity. That is to say, all...
The Buddhas have three matters that are without difference: first, their wisdom as the basis is identical; second, their altruistic intentionality is identical;
and third, their activities of retribution and transformation are identical. Therefore, they are said to be equal.
One arrives at the state of non-obstruction.
Fifth is the cultivation of the merit that serves as the antidote to all obstructions. Vasubandhu’s commentary states:

"This means that at all times one constantly cultivates awakened wisdom (*buddhi-jñāna*), because it serves as the antidote to all obstructions. This clarifies that awakened wisdom is the means by which all [obstructions] are remedied.
"Obstructions" refers to the two obstructions (*dvividhāvaraṇa*); these are that which are to be remedied.

"Unalterable dharmas" refers to the sixth [perfection], the merit of subduing all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), meaning that one cannot be shaken by others through either the path of teaching (*śrutamārga*) or the path of realization (*adhigamamārga*).
The sixth is the merit of being unimpeded while living in the world, such that one is not obstructed by worldly dharmas; this means that the eight worldly concerns,
such as gain and loss, cannot bind one.
Establishing the inconceivable:
the eighth is the establishment of the merit of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), meaning that one abides in the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), for it cannot be conceived by others.
He universally perceives the three periods of time.
Ninth is the merit of bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*); that is, because he predicts the past and future as if they were all present.
His body is constantly pervasive throughout all lands.
The tenth is the merit of manifesting the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) for all the world;
that is to say, because these two bodies pervade the two types of realms.
Wisdom is constantly clear and penetrating regarding all phenomena.

Eleventh is the merit of severing doubt. This means that because one has achieved excellent certainty regarding all objects oneself, one is able to resolve the doubts of others and comprehend all modes of conduct.
The twelfth [point] concerns causing [beings] to enter into the merit of various practices. Since the two commentaries on the root text are easy to understand, they are not explained here.
The intended meaning is that one thoroughly understands the dispositions and behaviors of all sentient beings and causes them to enter [the path] according to their faculties.
It exhausts all doubts.

Thirteenth is the merit of generating sublime wisdom in the future; that is to say, when a śrāvaka says that he possesses no roots of goodness whatsoever, the Tathāgata knows that because of a subtle goodness from long ago, they will produce [roots of goodness] in the future.
No one can fathom his body.

Fourteenth is the merit of manifesting according to their respective inclinations (*adhimukti*); that is, he manifests golden color and so forth in accordance with the various inclinations of sentient beings.
Although he manifests this body, it is without conceptual discrimination, like a *maṇi* jewel; therefore, no one can fathom it.
The wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas;
fifteenth, the merit of the application for the purpose of disciplining sentient beings based on immeasurable supports.
This means that, by virtue of the immeasurable supports of bodhisattvas, they initiate applications out of a desire to discipline all sentient beings, with the Buddha as their sovereign influence.
Power. Having the hearing of the Dharma as the prerequisite, one obtains sublime wisdom.
It is received and entrusted to bodhisattvas of various classes, transmitted from one to another in continuous succession, revolving without interruption.
By this, one realizes the wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas and others. The meaning is that the Buddha-wisdom is what is sought by all bodhisattvas and others.
One reaches the Buddha’s ultimate shore of non-duality.
Sixteenth is the merit of fulfilling the perfection (*pāramitā*) of the equal *dharmakāya*.
"Equality" has the meaning of non-duality; the non-dual *dharmakāya* serves as the basis for the perfections.
He is fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s impartial liberation.
Seventeenth is the merit of manifesting differentiated Buddha-fields according to their respective inclinations (*adhimukti*). Herein, liberation is itself inclination;
according to the dispositions of sentient beings, the Tathāgata’s inclination is able to manifest the [Buddha-fields] as is appropriate for those inclinations.
The earth of silver and so forth is the same for every Buddha; therefore, it is called "equality.
It refers to the realization of the Buddha’s ground of equality, which is without middle or limit.
The eighteen [qualities] are the merits of the three types of Buddha-bodies being without spatial limitation. Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "That is to say..."
The Buddha’s Dharma-body cannot be delimited by such-and-such a spatial extent; likewise, its Enjoyment and Transformation bodies cannot be said to occupy only such-and-such worlds,
but pervade the entire dharma-realm.
Nineteenth is the merit of constantly manifesting benefit and happiness for all sentient beings until the very limit of saṃsāra, which is equal to the realm of empty space.
Twentieth is inexhaustible merit, meaning that the Buddha’s true wisdom is as inexhaustible as space; this [twentieth] is omitted in the present sutra.
Finally, reaching to the limits of the future, there are twenty-one phrases in total, both general and specific; their meaning is as previously explained.
However, while the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* treats this in terms of the *saṃbhogakāya*, this [text] treats it in terms of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*). How is this known?

Although being in the kingdom of Magadha is a *nirmāṇakṣetra* (transformation land), since the text already praises the merits of the *saṃbhogakāya*, it is clearly understood that both the *vipākakāya* (retribution body) and the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) are intended.
Because the two lands of the body are fundamentally interfused, there is no need to restrict [the vision] to those before or after the stages (*bhūmi*);

thus, one knows that the five positions (*pañca-avasthā*) can all universally attain this vision. △ Third, the perfection of the world of sentient beings. This section has two parts: first, praising their virtues;
second, listing their names and praising their virtues. In the former, many people possess these virtues; in the latter, superior individuals possess them. Within the former, there are two parts.
First, the number is cited to specify [the assembly].
[They have come] together from unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddhas... to various lands.
△ Second, manifesting their possession of supreme virtues, in three parts: first, the general heading.
They are fully endowed with the skillful means and wisdom of a bodhisattva.
This is explained in two distinct parts. The text consists of nineteen phrases; in its general meaning, it does not transcend skillful means and wisdom. This is divided into two sections.
The first ten verses praise his own virtues.
That is to say, from "being well able to observe all sentient beings" up to "skillfully entering immeasurable methods of expedient means.

The first eight [verses] all possess both wisdom and expedient means; they represent the arising of function based on the essence. The latter five all consist of being "well able to... [and so forth].
First: knowing that all sentient beings are empty and non-existent, yet not destroying the fruits of karma;
knowing emptiness, yet not destroying the realm of karma.
They skillfully know the various distinctions among the mental activities, faculties, objects, and expedient means of sentient beings.
Discerning the differences in their capacities, they clearly recognize them;
they are able to receive and uphold all the Buddhas' teachings of the three periods of time, attaining personal realization and subsequently explaining them to others.
He maintains the Dharma to transform others.
Regarding all immeasurable phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds, he thoroughly observes them and knows that they are without duality.
The latter two [verses] clarify that through skillful means and wisdom, all things return to reality. The two sets of nine phrases praise his superior and progressive virtues.
In a single thought-moment, one is able to fully attain all the wisdom possessed by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The preceding section generally clarifies the swift attainment of the fruit-wisdom; the following eight sections are all the functions of that fruit-wisdom.
In every thought-moment, they are able to manifest [all things], until their pure conduct and vows are entirely fulfilled.
△ Third, the summary:
All Tathāgatas, even if they were to speak for boundless eons, could not exhaustively describe such immeasurable merits as these.
△ Second, listing the names and extolling their virtues, in two parts. First, listing the names and concluding with the count:
Their names are Bodhisattva Universal Wisdom (up to) as many as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields.
△ Second, the explicit praise of their virtues.
They have all fully accomplished the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
The text contains ten phrases: the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific.
Their profound resolve and great vows are all fully perfected;
their aspirations accord with reality and are fulfilled because the Universal Eye is complete.
Thus, they are able to travel to every place where any Buddha appears in the world to request that he turn the wheel of Dharma.
They are leaders in gathering the teachings for the sake of universal transformation;
they are well able to receive and uphold the Dharma-eye of all Buddhas and maintain the True Dharma because they possess universal wisdom.
They do not sever the lineage of all Buddhas;
they do not interrupt the Buddha-seed because they universally perceive the existence of its nature.
They skillfully know the sequence of the appearance of all Buddhas in the world, their prophecies, their names, and their lands.
He knows the Buddha’s transformative manifestations because his light universally penetrates all.

He attains equal and perfect enlightenment and turns the wheel of Dharma; he manifests as a Buddha in worlds where no Buddha exists, demonstrating the attainment of Buddhahood while observing that such a world is ultimately non-existent.
It is able to bring all sentient beings who are defiled by afflictions to complete purification,
because it illuminates the source of their capacity for both purity and defilement;
it is also able to extinguish all obstacles of the bodhisattvas.
Because it is the banner of wisdom that crushes the obstacles of others,
one enters the unimpeded and pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*),
realizing the awakening to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) within that realm. Regarding these nine preceding phrases, if explained individually, the first phrase constitutes the vow.

The remaining eight constitute the practice (*caryā*). Generally speaking, these are all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra. His former vows are now fulfilled, as in the case of the Ten Great Vows;
they are the practices of Samantabhadra manifested through present conditions. Therefore, the summary verse says: "Accomplishing the practices and vows.

Furthermore, these ten phrases are universally possessed by ten types of persons. The text of the first phrase says, "Because they have all been accomplished," yet each phrase also individually manifests one specific person.

Regarding these virtues: because they clarify the names [of the ten stages], the general phrase is for the sake of Samantabhadra. The remaining nine follow in sequence as previously assigned and explained.
This section constitutes the "Accomplishment of the Multitude. △ Second, the Section on Samādhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra entered the vast samādhi.
He is called "Samantabhadra" because he is the presiding master of this assembly and because he expounds universal conduct.
It is named "Adorned with Buddha-Flowers.
Because the myriad practices unfold to adorn the Dharma-body, the ocean of the mind—the gateway of practice within the Dharma-realm—is taken as the essence of samādhi, for it sustains the infinite.
To expound the Dharma and perfect the practices is its function; it is by relying upon this essence that [the practices arise]. △ Three.
The Section on Arousing [the Resolve].
When entering this samādhi, all worlds throughout the ten directions undergo the six types of eighteenfold earthquakes.
This first clarifies the shaking of the earth in order to awaken the various capacities of sentient beings.
A great sound issues forth that is heard by all without exception.

This is because the sound is manifested later in order to cause them to hear the Dharma. While the former cases involved empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) but lacked initiative (*samutthāna*), this case involves initiative but lacks empowerment.
The former indicates that understanding arises from external conditions; thus, there is empowerment by another. This indicates that practice arises from...

Because it has already been established, it arises spontaneously. Furthermore, this indicates that conduct (*caryā*) arises based on understanding (*adhigama*), as there is no separate dharma [between them].

Therefore, one does not add "comprehending" to "conduct" to form "conduct-as-comprehension. One must also enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The Sage’s intentions are manifold; they cannot be standardized by a single rule. △ Fourth, the section on arising.
Thereafter, he arose from that samādhi.
The three meanings have been explained as before. △ Fifth, the request for the distribution [of the teaching] has three parts. First, the statement of the intent of the question:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, knowing that the assembly had already gathered, addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying:
The assembly has gathered and the time for preaching the Dharma has arrived; this is the intended meaning of the inquiry.

Why is it that in the sūtra texts of previous assemblies, the question was posed first and the determination followed later, whereas here the order is reversed? There are two reasons for this: first, the ritual of preaching is not fixed.

Previously, the sequence expressed the gravity of the Dharma and the response of the audience; here, it clarifies the depth of compassion and the observation of the capacities of beings before the desire to preach arises. Now that the assembly has already gathered...

Therefore, he first enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*) so that [the audience] may know the speaker. Second, regarding the signified meaning and the intention behind his coming, it clarifies the entry from the phenomenal (*lakṣaṇa*) into the ultimate (*tattva*) in order to establish correct understanding.
Herein, the intent is to clarify that one relies on the essence (*tattva*) to give rise to function (*vṛtti*), thereby establishing correct practice; thus, it is not the same [as the previous case].

As for the questioner, "Universal Wisdom" (*Samantamati*), this refers to wisdom that accords with the *dharmadhātu* and is capable of initiating practice. As for the "single person" who asks, it refers to practice...
It is already established as being unique, for it is not like [other] expositions. △ Second, the actual presentation of the inquiry. There are two hundred questions.
In the *Du shi jing* (Sūtra on Transcending the World), which circulates separately, there are six rounds of question and answer. Within each round, a question is first posed followed by an answer;
the earth trembles and auspicious omens appear, manifesting the benefits and providing verification. The virtuous masters of antiquity all relied upon that text to structure this sūtra.
This is divided into six sections. The first section consists of twenty lines, which inquire about the practices of the ten levels of faith:
"O Son of the Buddha, please explain for us what constitutes a bodhisattva... [and so on] ...up to what constitutes the exposition of the Buddhas."
△ Section Two contains twenty phrases. It asks about the ten stages of practice (*daśavihāra*).
What is the arousal of the mind of Samantabhadra... (up to) ...what is transformation?
△ Section Three contains thirty phrases. It asks about the practice of the ten practices (*daśapratipatti*).
What is the power of sustenance (*baladhāraṇa*)? ... up to ... what is the entry into unsurpassed enlightenment through ocean-like wisdom?
△ Fourth, there are twenty-nine phrases that inquire about the practice of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*).
What is the abiding like a jewel... (up to) what is the activity and what is the body?
△ These five sections comprise fifty phrases that inquire about the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
What is karma? What is the body? (Up to: What is the sphere of activity?
△ Six: there are fifty-one phrases concerning the inquiry into the practice for the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of results.
What is the observation [up to] why the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha demonstrates parinirvāṇa?

In the fourth section, although there are thirty phrases, because one phrase of the sūtra text serves as a general heading by means of its unimpeded function—marking it as an empty phrase—there are only twenty-nine phrases therein. This section contains fifty-one phrases. This is from this sūtra.

From beginning to end, the entire text passes through three cycles, explaining six stages (*ṣaḍ-avasthā*). This constitutes the second [section], which explains [the stages] in terms of practice (*caryā*), because the practices of Samantabhadra encompass all six stages.
Therefore, the *Lokottara-parivarta-sūtra* (Dùshì jīng) initially requests:

"I only pray that you will explain the practices of all bodhisattvas from beginning to end, so that there may be no doubt. Although that sūtra does not explicitly bestow the [six] positions, [they are nonetheless implied].

Since it is stated that [the practice] proceeds "from beginning to end," and the final section further clarifies the matter of attaining Buddhahood, we know that this must certainly refer to the practices of the six stages (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*).
The reason this sutra does not intersperse the text with question-and-answer sessions is that its intent is to capture the preeminent practices within the stages, rather than the stages themselves.
If it were not integrated in this way, how would it differ from a mere fixed enumeration of the stages?
Regarding the causes and effects of differentiation, this sutra (the *Avataṃsaka*) throughout its upper and lower sections, as well as the *Mūlaprakṛti-karma-sūtra* and others, delineates six stages.

All of these take the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), which have not yet attained entry into the stages, as the primary starting point—namely, the three levels of worthiness (*tri-piṭaka-bhadra*) and the ten sages (*daśa-ārya*), culminating in Equal Enlightenment (*sama-saṃbodhi*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).
Why is it that here one does not open [the discussion] with Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) but instead takes up the stage of Faith?

This has a profound meaning. Both that [previous section] and this one intend to focus on the stages (*avasthā*); they establish their discourse by taking the stages as the basis. The intent of the present passage, however, is precisely to clarify the practices (*caryā*).

The practice of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) resides at the very beginning of practice. As for the stage of Equal Enlightenment, it possesses three meanings; alternatively, it may be subsumed within the preceding ten [stages].

The stage of "Excellence in Ground" (*bhūmi-viśeṣa*) is either subsumed under the subsequent [stage], as it is then designated as "Buddha," or it is established as a distinct position, being the "Stainless Stage" (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

Now, to explain its practice, it is therefore subsumed within the perfection of the cause. Although the scriptural text contains fifty-one phrases, only the final four belong to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbuddha*);
the rest all pertain to Equal Enlightenment (*samaya-jñāna*). If this is so, then regarding the term "based upon" (*niśritya*) used herein:
If you argue that because one relies on the bodhicitta and so forth, this must be the stage of "Abiding in the Initial Resolve" (Cittotpāda-vihāra), this objection is even more untenable.

At the beginning of the second stage, one first gives rise to the Universal Good Mind (Samantabhadra-citta); would this not then be the stage of "Abiding in the Initial Resolve"? Furthermore, at the very beginning of the Ten Faiths (Daśa-śraddhā), is there not likewise the arising of the resolve?
Therefore, the Worthy Head (Bandhuprabha) said: "When a bodhisattva resolves the mind to seek bodhi, it is not without causes; nor is it without conditions and so forth.

These are precisely that upon which the arousal of the mind relies. To fail to investigate this principle and instead vainly cite supporting authorities [is futile]. △ Third, the conclusion and request for an explanation.
Excellent, Son of the Buddha! I pray that you will expound such teachings as these.
*Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 85 (Entering the Second Half of the Fifty-third Scripture), composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui. Commentary on the Sūtra with Annotations.
△ Section Six: Exposition. The text has two parts. First, the general announcement:
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the various bodhisattvas, including Puhui and others, saying:

△ Second, the direct response to the preceding two hundred questions. One question is answered with ten, thereby manifesting their inexhaustibility and completing the two thousand [verses] of Samantabhadra’s supreme practices.
Lord Ying (Ying Gong) sighed in admiration: “Two hundred questions arise like clouds; two thousand answers pour forth like water from a jar.
To explain these two thousand [verses], there are briefly five introductory gates: first, an analysis according to cause and effect; second, an analysis according to practice and stages (*bhūmi*).
Third, revealing the universal and the particular; fourth, clarifying the comprehensive inclusion; fifth, discerning the aspects of practice. The preceding questions follow this pattern.
Now, for the first [section], there are four parts: First, regarding the major positions: among the six stages, the first five are causes and the last one is the fruit;
alternatively, the latter four gates are the fruit and all the others are causes. Second, regarding detailed discernment: each individual gate of practice penetrates to the Buddha.
Because the fruit [is attained], the conclusion of each section invariably results in the attainment of Buddhahood; this constitutes the second [category], the universal cause-and-effect.

Third, some [sections] belong entirely to the cause, because they demonstrate the attainment of Buddhahood through the stages and practices of Samantabhadra. Fourth, others belong entirely to the fruit, as many subsequent passages state:
"Although one has attained Buddhahood, one does not cease the Bodhisattva practices. Regarding the second [category], the stages and practices, there are likewise four [points].
The meaning [of this] is as follows: first, the formation of stages through the accomplishment of a bundle of practices, because they constitute six divisions;

second, the general attribution to the stages, because all practices are practiced within the stages; third, the general attribution to the practices, because the essence of Samantabhadra’s practice does not depend on the stages;
fourth, a single practice pervades all six stages, because each stage is cultivated universally. Only when there is such non-obstruction is it truly the practice of Samantabhadra. However—

Wen Zhengxian explains the latter two sections as follows: because one attains the stages by grasping the practices, and because while the stages are empty, the practices are real, he presents both the questions and answers together without dividing them into six rounds;
this is his intent. Regarding the "universal and particular" (san-pu-bie): it means that a single aspect of practice must necessarily pervade all things, yet it remains eternally unmixed.
Because they are unmixed, the six meanings are distinguished; because they necessarily pervade, [the universal and particular are established].

Therefore, the meaning of "universal" (pu) encompasses all; it is like a brocade pattern where various colors form a design. It is both eternally universal and eternally particular, with every thread interpenetrating the others, as if embroidered.
The practice of the Dharma is likewise: the universal is itself the particular, and the particular constitutes the universal, all without obstruction.
If this is so, then since both the universal and the particular are fully present, why is it specifically called the "Universal Worthy Practice" (Samantabhadra-caryā)?
It does not mean that one maintains universality while being unable to discern particulars; nor does it mean that by making distinctions one loses the good.
In truth, it means being able to discern particulars without destroying universality; therefore, it is called the practice of Samantabhadra.

Furthermore, universality necessarily entails particularity, yet merely speaking of one particularity does not necessarily entail universality—just as, for example, a single thread is not brocade. This is because [the thread] is not within the brocade.
Regarding the "threading" [of the stages], there are four ways of comprehensive inclusion. First, inclusion by way of stages: each of the six stages includes all stages;
thus, a single stage possesses two thousand practice-gates, totaling twelve thousand. Therefore, the aforementioned scripture states:
"Within a single stage, the merits of all stages are fully present. Second, inclusion by way of gates.
1. Each of the two hundred gates individually encompasses all gates of practice, thereby forming twenty thousand gates (two hundred times two hundred).

This constitutes forty thousand practices. 2. Third, by subsuming practice within practice—since each single practice fully encompasses all practices—there are two thousand sets of two thousand practices, which constitute four *zhào* (ten trillion) practices. 3. Fourth, by subsuming the extensive through the concise, these two thousand [practices]...
[The practice of] action. The concluding verse below states: "Like a single mote of dust upon the great earth;

by means of this brief explanation of a single mote of dust, one does not depart from the vastness of the ten directions. Therefore, even when the vast is subsumed, there is nothing that is not exhausted.
This is the infinitely equal *dharmadhātu*, which transcends the boundless void. Thus, the subsequent verse says: "The void may be measured, but the Bodhisattva..."

"Virtue is inexhaustible"—this is precisely what is meant by this. Fifth, the analysis of the characteristics of practice follows the text for its explanation. The explanation of the distinctions among the provisional characteristics is divided into six sections.
Now, for the first two hundred phrases, the answer addresses the twenty questions concerning the stage of faith and practice (*śraddhā-caryā*).
This section is further divided into three parts: first, nine gates clarify the fulfillment of one's own practice; second, eight gates clarify the perfection of superior practice; third, three...
The section on the two practices within the gates has been fully explained. Now, the first gate is treated as a single category, which is divided into nine sections.

Generally, however, each of the two hundred gates consists of five parts: first, the general heading; second, the inquiry into the number; third, the enumeration and explanation; fourth, the conclusion regarding the number.
Fifth, the manifestation of the superior benefits of cultivation. Alternatively, the latter two may be omitted, or the fifth may be omitted; this should be understood from the text as it appears.
In the present section, all five are complete; first, there is the general heading.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of reliance (*āśraya*).

First is reliance on the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), because it is that upon which the arousal of practice depends. This means that by relying upon the bodhicitta and so forth, one accomplishes the myriad practices.
As the "Chapter on the Wise and Virtuous" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*) states: "When a Bodhisattva resolves their mind to seek bodhi, it is not without cause, nor is it without basis."
The conditions and so forth. △ Second, the inquiry into the number: What are the ten?
△ Third, the enumeration and explanation.
That is to say:
for each of the ten phrases, the name is first stated and the meaning subsequently explained;
because one takes the bodhicitta as a reliance and never forgets it.

Regarding "relying on the bodhicitta": all ten [perfections] are called "reliances. Since they are already the foremost among all practices, and since the bodhicitta is the very first among these ten, it is the root of the myriad practices;
thus, it penetrates and stands at the head of the two thousand gates of practice. The commentary states:
"Not forgetting" means that if one forgets the bodhicitta while cultivating various roots of goodness, this is the work of Māra.
Because of karma, one relies on this non-forgetfulness to be able to accomplish the myriad practices; this phrase serves as the general heading.
This is because, by relying on a spiritual friend, one attains harmony and becomes as one.
Although one may possess a superior resolve within, if one does not rely upon virtuous friends externally, one’s practice will not reach fulfillment.
Therefore, the Great Sage said to Sudhana: "Seeking virtuous friends is the primary causal condition for unsurpassed bodhi. The commentary explains:
"If one's mental conduct does not accord with [the teacher], how can they be my friend?"
Because one relies upon roots of goodness to cultivate, accumulate, and increase them;
for if one does not cultivate and increase roots of goodness, what benefit is there in meeting a spiritual friend?
Because one relies upon the perfections to practice them fully.
Whatever wholesome practices one cultivates must reach the other shore, for all dharmas serve as the basis for ultimate liberation;

both apply to oneself and others. The preceding [seven] all rely on the Dharma, while the final three rely on persons.
Because all bodhisattvas rely upon the same identical wisdom,
their superior companions share that same wisdom.

for there is no sense of "self" or "other," as they mutually serve as leaders and companions, supporting and benefiting one another, sharing the same essential nature, being the very practice of oneself, and because self and other are mutually identical.

just as in the first phrase; likewise,

The teachings of the non-Buddhists are also remnants of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma.
Regarding all linguistic phenomena, they give rise to the notion of a "path of speech.

One should conceive the thought of all Buddhas as one's compassionate fathers;

namely, abiding oneself in the bodhicitta and also causing others to abide in the bodhicitta, so that the mind attains peace and security.
The first line is the fundamental basis. The next two [lines] concern the elimination of faults:
having personally attained ultimate freedom from anger and strife, one should also cause others to be free from anger and strife, so that their minds attain peace and stability.
This is the *araṇā-samādhi* (the samādhi of non-contention), which is free from all contention.

Having personally departed from the dharmas of the ordinary and the ignorant, one also causes others to depart from the dharmas of the ordinary and the ignorant, so that the mind attains peace and stability.

This transcends the ordinary and the small. "Ordinary" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); "ignorant" refers to those of the ignorant dharmas of the Hīnayāna. The next two [stages] involve progressing toward the wholesome.
One diligently cultivates roots of goodness oneself and also causes others to diligently cultivate them, until one abides in the path of the *pāramitās* and attains peace of mind.

one is born into the family of the Buddhas oneself and should also cause others to be born into the family of the Buddhas, thereby attaining peace of mind.
Entering the stage:
one deeply penetrates the true dharma of selflessness (up to) the true dharma of selflessness, and the mind attains peace and stability.
Entering the dharma.
From not slandering any Buddha-dharma (up to) not slandering any Buddha-dharma, one’s mind attains peace and security and enters into benefit.
Regarding "slandering," there are two meanings. First is the coarse [form]: to say, for instance, "This is not the Buddha-dharma" and so forth; its fault is even greater.
The second is subtlety. This means that if one’s speech does not accord with reality, the fault is slight; yet without this subtle slander, one cannot realize the truth.
Only when the latter two causes are perfected can the fruit be fulfilled.
Having fulfilled the vow for the bodhi of omniscience (up to) attaining peace and security through the mind of the inexhaustible treasury of wisdom.

Having already abandoned faults and perfected virtues, one verifies one’s own practice and realizes that it will inevitably bring about its corresponding fruit. For this reason, one is able to know for oneself that one has received the prediction (vyākaraṇa).

Seeing the truth, one feels profound compassion; thus, the resolve generated is extraordinary, and there is no doubt that the fruit will be attained. If, however, it arises from a distaste for suffering induced by others, it is not extraordinary, and the prediction of enlightenment is not yet certain.
Never abandoning any bodhisattva practices, they know they have received their prediction; practicing without weariness, they know they have received their prediction;
dwelling through all kalpas while performing bodhisattva practices, they know they have received their prediction.
Cultivation over a long period;

This explains the practice for receiving the prediction; it does not clarify the distinct characteristics of the prediction itself, as is done in works such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

this is divided into eight segments. Now, at the beginning, the Bodhisattva is first introduced with a general outline.

Manifesting the body. △ Second, questioning the number: What are these ten?

these are the times of transformation. The following three sections all serve to fulfill the preceding point that [the Bodhisattva] knows everything in a single thought-moment without exception.
...as well. △ Second, the inquiry into the number: What are the ten?

This refers to entering past kalpas, entering future kalpas, and so on, up to entering incalculable kalpas.
The first five [phrases] involve direct entry; the latter five phrases involve entry by way of mutual identity (*samāropa*).
Entering countable eons is itself entering incalculable eons, continuing until entering all eons is itself a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).
This mutual entry of characteristics has two meanings: first, because those characteristics of the eons are themselves wisdom, one enters them;

second, because those characteristics of the eons mutually contain and enter one another. It is simply that by entering what contains, one enters what is contained therein, and so forth. The rest is as before.

these constitute ten.

The aforementioned five gates are all entries through wisdom; the fourth and fifth entries also pertain to entry through the body. △ Sixth, the exposition of the five [entries] regarding the three periods of time. First, the general heading.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten ways of explaining the three periods of time (*tryadhvan*).

Although the preceding kalpas and this world differ in length, they are all equally temporal divisions; all are established through the distinct formation of the "Ten Periods of Time" (*daśādhvan-viccheda-dharma*).
II. Inquiry into the Number.
What are these ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, [as follows].
The first nine are specific, while the last one is general. Within the specific [categories], there are three for each of the three time periods; thus, they constitute nine time periods.
Regarding the past period, it speaks of the past period (up to) the past period speaking of the present period.
Because the past consists of dharmas that have already arisen, the past of the past is not called inexhaustible.
In the future, one speaks of the past; in the future, one speaks of the present; and in the future, one speaks of the inexhaustible.
Because the future is that which continues to arise, the future is called inexhaustible.
The present is spoken of in terms of the past, the present is spoken of in terms of the future, and the present is spoken of as equality.
The present is the present; this can be seen in the very fact at hand. This is because it serves as the model for the "present" within the past and future.
Therefore, it is called "equal. Since the two "presents" of the past and future cannot be perceived, the name "present" is established merely in relation to what precedes and follows it.
In the present age, it is taught that the three periods of time are but a single thought-moment.
Now, how is it that these three periods constitute nine? An ancient commentary states: "They are explained as nine for the sake of meaning, but in reality there are only five."

The Master Yì said: "If one considers them by way of five days—taking the first three as the three periods of the past, taking the last three as the three periods of the future, and taking the middle three as the three periods of the present—then according to this interpretation, advancing [in time], there is no substance to the nine periods, and retreating [to the past], they exceed the count of the three periods. How, then, can a single thought-moment possess all nine?"
Now, my view is not so. One should take nine days and broadly divide them into the three periods of time, which mutually function as conditions and origins (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Since it does not rely on this [sequential model], but rather takes the mutual dependence of the three periods as the condition and origin, the nine periods are thereby established. That is to say: the past has the present and future as its causes;
within the past, there are again the present and future. The present and future each have their own causes, and the same applies to the other two periods. This is...

This is because each of the three periods of time possesses these three [aspects]. Thus, the *Madhyamaka* states: "If a phenomenon arises from a cause, that phenomenon is not different from its cause.
When the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* refutes attachment, it identifies it as a fault for there to be three within one; this clarifies the function of avoiding such faults.
Thus, within the one there are three as its virtues; by taking illness and making it medicine, how excellent this is!
The phrase "that is, a single thought-moment" in the summary statement was established by viewing the preceding nine periods of time in relation to one another.

Now, the intent here clarifies that all branches are subsumed back into the root, not departing from a single thought-moment. This very single thought-moment is the present; it is the past, and it is also the future.
The future is the past; it inherently possesses the three periods of time. The characteristics of the three periods are mutually dependent, and thus the nine [periods] are complete.
Therefore, by unifying the one, the nine are contained within it; though there are nine, they are eternally one. By distinguishing the nine from the one, though it is one, it is eternally nine.

The non-obstruction between the nine and the one transcends results and cuts off words; yet, by provisionally employing ten to achieve perfect fusion, it serves as an entrance gate. How much more so when formed through the accumulation of thoughts?

World. Is it not the case that there is no world outside of mindfulness? Furthermore, because there is no mindfulness and so forth; and because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is identical. These constitute four meanings.

Therefore, in the Jin translation it is called the "Three Worlds," while in the *Du shi jing* (Sūtra on Crossing the World) it is called "Entering the Three Abodes.

namely, knowing all established conventions, knowing all languages, (up to) knowing all regulations, and knowing conventional designations.

It can be exhausted.

What are the ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, the knowledge that discerns the differences among sentient beings (up to) the knowledge that discerns the differences in all paths of speech.
△ 4. Summary of the number.
These constitute ten.
△ 5. Benefits of cultivation.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and distinguished wisdom.
[Section] Two: The Five Dhāraṇīs. First, the general heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of dhāraṇīs, by which they are able to maintain the ultimate.
As the preceding text says: "They practice the various pāramitās, supreme liberations, and so forth. △ Second, the inquiry into their number.
What are the ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, the *śrutadhāraṇī* (dhāraṇī of hearing and retention), because it retains all dharmas without forgetting or losing them.
The first is the retention of the sound; the next four are the retention of the meaning.
One practices the dhāraṇī through skillful contemplation according to reality, because the mind does not become distracted while hearing the true Dharma.
Next, the four [dhāraṇīs] concern the function of hearing and retaining what is extensively taught.
The *Parmanirghoṣa-dhāraṇī* (Dhāraṇī of the Perfect Sound) is for the sake of understanding the inconceivable, because it enables one to hear all the dharmas that are preached.
The last one [the *dhāraṇī*] subsumes the aforementioned meanings, for it is the *dhāraṇī* of all Buddha-dharmas that abides by means of the Tathāgata’s powers and fearlessnesses.

Furthermore, the first four [verses] respectively uphold the teaching, practice, principle, and fruit. The subsequent two [verses] again clarify the upholding of practice, namely, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Therefore, next, one [verse] clarifies the inconceivable principle; next, two [verses] further clarify the teaching; and finally, one [verse] further clarifies the fruit.
△ Fourth, the summary of the number:
these constitute ten.
△ 5. The Benefits of Cultivation:
If bodhisattvas wish to attain this Dharma, they should diligently practice and study it.
△ 3. The Explanation of the Ten Kinds of Buddhas, Part Four: First, the general heading.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva speaks of ten kinds of Buddhas.
That which is able to support and that which is supported are both the Buddha-dharma. Now, having realized the ultimate nature of the Lord of Dharma, the preceding passage states:
Thus, one attains consecration and ascends to the rank; for upon the fulfillment of the mind of the ten stages of faith, one immediately attains Buddhahood. △ Second, the inquiry into the number:

What are these ten? Now, these ten Buddhas are identical in both name and meaning to the ten kinds of Buddhas seen [in the following section], though their names differ from those of the ten bodies mentioned previously.
There is both similarity and difference; the underlying meaning is not distinct. △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment, so called because he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment; this is precisely the aforementioned Body of Bodhi.
The Buddhas of Vows;
the Buddhas of Rebirth in Tuṣita—these are entirely the same as before.
The Buddhas of Karmic Retribution.
Because it is produced by the causes of the myriad practices, it is the body adorned with the marks and signs;
because it maintains the Buddha’s own body through the preservation of relics, it is the body of empowered sustenance.
The Nirvāṇa Buddha:
because a transformation body must manifest extinction, this refers to the aforementioned transformation body.
The Dharma-realm Buddha: [this refers to the ultimate nature].
Because it is the truly untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), it is the aforementioned Dharmakāya.

Because mind is the Buddha and because all things depend upon mind alone, it is the Vaśitākāya (Body of Sovereignty); for even though its radiance can subdue others, the mind is supreme. As it is said:
The Buddha of Samādhi, who subdues Māra and others through a mind of loving-kindness,
is eternally in meditative concentration; thus, he is the body of merit, for concentration is the supreme form of merit.

The Buddha of the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-buddha*). Because one realizes the intrinsic nature, this is precisely the aforementioned body of wisdom; for both the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) are inherently possessed.
Therefore, it is stated below that one "clearly perceives."

The Buddha who accords with desire (*yathābhiprāya-buddha*) manifests in whatever way is desired; because he does not fail to appear, he is the "mind-born body" (*manomaya-kāya*). Thus, the Jin translation calls him the "Buddha according to wish" (*yathāruci-buddha*).

However, while the Buddha is established in terms of internal awakening, the "body" (*kāya*) generally refers to external characteristics; therefore, the names established differ. Further details are as explained in other chapters.
Briefly, it is as in the Eighth Stage. △ Fourth, the summary of the number:
these constitute ten.
△ Second, there are twenty gates that answer the previous twenty questions, clarifying the ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*). This is the same as the ancient masters.
This is divided into four parts. First, six sections specifically clarify the meaning of the stage of "Generating the Resolve" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*).
Second, six sections clarify the internal virtuous practices accomplished within the remaining nine stages. Third, three sections clarify the external transformative practices within those stages.
Finally, five sections clarify the unimpeded and preeminent practices. This is not without reason; here, we follow the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.

The text consists of twenty sections, which sequentially clarify the ten stages of practice (*caryā*). However, these are mutually related to the preceding practices through a combination of elaboration and brevity, serving as mutual reflections.

This is because the practices within the stage of realization (*adhigama*) are infinitely extensive. If one relies on their perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*), every practice universally pervades all others;

yet, if one does not destroy their distinct characteristics, they do not hinder their sequential order. The first four sections clarify the first stage of practice, while the second and third stages each have two [sections].

Section on the Gates. There are four or five gates, each with one [section]; the latter five consist of two gates. Now, for the first part: the first four gates clarify the Stage of Generating the Resolve (*cittotpāda-vihāra*).
The first one provides a general clarification, while the latter three specifically manifest it. Now, for the first [of these], there are five parts; the first is the general heading.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas give rise to ten kinds of Samantabhadra-minds.

In the preceding section on the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), within the context of their own respective stages, they gave rise to the mind by taking the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Buddha as their object; this merely expanded upon the scope of the arousal of the mind.
Now, the characteristics of the arousal of the mind are explained in detail, being clarified through a concise illustration. As for the "Samantabhadra-mind," it is none other than the bodhicitta.

The bodhicitta is explained in terms of its fruition; the Samantabhadra-mind is described according to its characteristics and functions. It extends horizontally throughout the dharma-realm and vertically through all of future time.
△ Second, the inquiry into the number.
What are the ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, because of generating the mind of great compassion to rescue and protect sentient beings... [up to] ...because of relinquishing all that one possesses.
The first three [perfections] involve the mind that protects sentient beings through compassion;
the subsequent six give rise to the aspirational mind, which takes the aspiration for omniscience as its primary focus because it joyfully seeks all Buddha-dharmas.
Seeking the wisdom of the fruit: this refers to taking the ten powers of the Buddha as one's object, generating a mind adorned with merit, and training in all bodhisattva practices.
Thus, one seeks the causal practice.
One generates a mind like a vajra, because one is never forgetful throughout all places of rebirth;
thus it is vertically exhaustive.
One generates a mind like the ocean, because all pure and white dharmas flow into it; thus it is horizontally pervasive.
Extensive and pervasive. These four are all vows for upward-seeking;
they give rise to a mind like the king of great mountains (extending) to the point of bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
These two [types of] patience and giving are both vows for downward-transforming others.
Because one gives rise to the ultimate mind of *prajñāpāramitā* through skillfully contemplating that all phenomena are non-existent, there follows the single mind of wisdom;
this is precisely the Bodhi of the three minds. Furthermore, the preceding seven [minds] protect against the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*):

the first three protect against a narrow mind, the subsequent four protect against a small mind, and the remaining three protect against a mind of afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus, they differ from those of ordinary people and the Lesser Vehicle; this is Bodhi.

Focus the mind. Furthermore, the first three [vows] are: "I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings. Because there is no stinginess in delivering beings, this constitutes all-encompassing giving (*sarvadāna*).
Next is one: "I vow to realize the unsurpassed Buddha-way. Next are three: "I vow to study inexhaustible Dharma-gates.
Finally are three: "I vow to sever boundless afflictions. These are the Four Great Vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*). One arouses the mind by contemplating these principles.
△ 4. Summary of the Number.
These constitute ten.
△ 5. Manifestation of the Benefits.
If bodhisattvas abide in this mind, they will swiftly achieve the skillful wisdom of Samantabhadra.
△ Second, the Dharma of Samantabhadra’s Practices, in five parts. First, the general heading.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of Samantabhadra-practice methods.
These specifically clarify the bodhicitta; this gate is precisely the mind of great vows. △ Second, the enumeration of the number.
What are these ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, the vow to abide through all future kalpas (up to) the method of the conduct of Samantabhadra for attaining unexcelled bodhi.

This is also identical to the aforementioned "progressive practice" (*viśeṣa-gamana-caryā*), namely, diligently making offerings to the Buddhas and delighting in dwelling within *saṃsāra*, and so forth.
Since the wording and intent are the same, I fear that further elaboration would be redundant and confusing. △ Fourth, the conclusion regarding the number.
These are the ten. △ Fifth, the manifestation of benefits:
If bodhisattvas diligently cultivate this dharma, they will swiftly attain fulfillment of the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
△ Third, a detailed explanation of the mind of compassion, in five parts. First, the general heading:
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion by observing sentient beings through ten ways.
△ Second, the inquiry into the number: What are the ten?
△ Third, the enumeration and explanation.
This refers to the arising of great compassion by observing that sentient beings are without refuge and without protection.
The first phrase serves as the general summary; it means that externally there are no virtuous friends upon whom to rely, and internally there are no personal virtues upon which to depend.
The remaining nine [phrases] constitute the specific details.
Observing that the nature of sentient beings is untamed (up to: being bound by the fetters of desire), he gives rise to great compassion.
These sentient beings who seek the five superior desires merely indulge their greedy passions before their eyes.
Observing sentient beings submerged in the ocean of birth and death, he gives rise to great compassion;
for these beings who seek only existence are thus submerged in the ocean of birth and death.
Observing sentient beings who are perpetually afflicted by the suffering of illness (up to) the loss of all Buddha-dharmas, he gives rise to great compassion.
The latter three refer to sentient beings who seek a false holy life (*mithyā-brahmacarya-gaveṣin*); for they are afflicted by ignorance and wrong views, and they desire only false dharmas.
△ Fourth, the summary of the number:
these constitute ten.
△ 5. Manifesting the Benefits.
The Bodhisattva constantly observes sentient beings with this mind.
△ 4. The Causes and Conditions for Arousing the Mind. There are four parts; first, the general heading.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of causes and conditions for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas to give rise to the bodhicitta.

These are distinguished from the "mind of wisdom" (prajñā-citta) because they involve contemplating objects and inferring principles; since the ways in which the mind is generated are distinct, this section and the preceding section on the causes and conditions for generating the mind within the "stage of self-practice" (svacaryā-bhūmi) are mutually abbreviated and implied. 2. Inquiry into the Number.
What are these ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, generating the bodhicitta for the purpose of teaching, transforming, and subduing all sentient beings.
The first five take *sattva* as their object; the one above is the general [category], while the four below are the specific ones.
One generates the bodhicitta for the purpose of eliminating the mass of suffering of all sentient beings.
One causes delusory suffering to cease.
One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of endowing all sentient beings with perfect peace and happiness,
thereby attaining true cessation.
One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of severing the ignorance of all sentient beings and severing the accumulation of that ignorance.
One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of bestowing the Buddha-wisdom upon all sentient beings.

Having realized the True Path, one then infers the principle of the Four Noble Truths of Non-action and gives rise to the Bodhicitta. Subsequently, the latter five [stages] take Bodhi as their condition;
for the sake of reverently making offerings to all Buddhas (up to) causing the Buddhas to rejoice, one gives rise to the Bodhicitta.
These two are the causes of merit and wisdom;

for the sake of beholding the physical marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana*) of all Buddhas, up to their powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), one generates the bodhicitta.
These three are the desired fruits of merit and wisdom. However, the preceding two sections contain two meanings: first, they fulfill the aforementioned generation of the mind.
Abiding in the middle practice. Second, accomplishing the lower stage of the "dwelling that purifies the ground" (viśuddhabhūmi-sthāna) through middle practice;

this refers to the ten kinds of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which are the causal conditions for the single mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) among the ten minds within one's own category (*svabhāga*).

The first five are precisely the first five minds within that same category: 1. benefiting, 2. great compassion, 3. bringing happiness, 4. pitying, and 5. abiding securely. The latter... [text continues]
These five phrases lack each other in mutual correspondence. △ Fourth, the summary of the number:

these constitute ten. △ Second, there are two sections. This primarily explains the practice within the stages and dwellings of the ground. First, approaching virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), four [points]. First:
General Summary:
"O Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva generates the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment... they should give rise to ten kinds of minds.
This section concerns the cultivation of superior progress through drawing near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Within this textual heading, it also serves to clarify the underlying intent. △
Second, the inquiry regarding the number. What are these ten?
Third, the enumeration and explanation.
This refers to giving rise to a mind of service, a mind of joy, a mind free from opposition, a mind of compliance, and a mind free from seeking anything else.
To be "free from seeking anything else" means not seeking fame, gain, or even [the teacher's] faults.
With a single-minded focus,
he first attends to six matters regarding his spiritual friends, and subsequently cultivates four qualities in common with them:
a mind of shared roots of goodness, a mind of shared vows, a mind identical to the Tathāgata’s mind, and a mind of shared perfect practice.
△ Fourth, the summary of the number:
these constitute ten.
△ Second, the four fruits of associating with spiritual friends. First, the general heading.
O Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to such a mind, they will attain ten kinds of purity;
these are the fruits of superior progress and approaching a spiritual friend. Therefore, it is stated in the summary: "By giving rise to such a mind, one attains these ten."
This refers to the aforementioned thorough comprehension of meaning, practicing in accordance with the Dharma, remaining far removed from delusion, and dwelling in immovability.
In Sanskrit, this is called *pariśuddhi*, which has two meanings: first, universal purity, which refers to these ten types.
Second, "Utmost Purity," which corresponds to the sixty-fourth section below. △ Second, the inquiry into the number:
What are the ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation.

That which is called the purity of the profound mind (up to) the thorough comprehension of all languages refers to the purification of the three karmas of the first six [perfections] and the purification of the essence of the latter three.
It is the purity of eloquence in skillfully expounding the boundless (up to) being fully endowed with the sovereign powers of a bodhisattva.
These three purify function;
through the accomplishment of the purity of the retinue, one reaches the past and eliminates all karmic obstructions.
These two purify the retribution of the primary and its attendants.
The great vows are pure because they lead all bodhisattvas (up to) liberation by means of the vehicle of Samantabhadra.
The latter two vows are the purity of practice. △ Fourth, the summary of the number.
These are the ten.
△ Third, there are two sections clarifying the practices within the dwelling of cultivation. First, the five self-contained *pāramitās*.
First, the general heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pāramitās.
This gate is their own stage of practice (*sva-pratipatti*). By opening up a single wisdom, they perform tenfold observations; now, the cultivation of these ten perfections is revealed in general.
△ Second, questioning the number.
What are the ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), because of completely relinquishing all that one possesses.
The ten pāramitās are all explained by way of their general characteristics; each one contains manifold meanings. Therefore, it is said that "all are relinquished," and so forth.
This ranges from the śīla-pāramitā, which purifies the Buddha’s precepts, up to the jñāna-pāramitā, which enters into the powers of the Buddha.
Wisdom is itself skillful means; it is the provisional wisdom that advances toward the power of the Buddha.
It is established under the name of "wisdom" because the perfection of aspiration is fulfilled, thereby manifesting all sovereign functions of Samantabhadra.
Supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are the power of strength (*bala*). In the Jin translation, they are called "spiritual powers" (*shenli*).
The perfection of phenomena (*dharmapāramitā*) is so named because it universally enters into all Buddha-dharmas.
Phenomena (*dharma*) are precisely wisdom (*jñāna*); this name "phenomenon" is established based on that which is known. △ Fourth, the conclusion of the enumeration.
These are the ten. △ Fifth, the manifestation of benefits:
"If all bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas... [up to] the unsurpassed great wisdom pāramitā."
△ Second, the five [aspects] of the superior progress of wisdom through realization. First, the general heading:
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has ten kinds of wisdom through realization.

These are accomplished by means of prior practice; they consist of non-perverted penetration that accords with both phenomena and principles, because of their skillful awakening and knowledge. △ Second, the inquiry.
Number. What are the ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation.

That which is called the "wisdom of the infinite distinctions of all worlds" (up to) the "wisdom of realizing liberation" refers to the aforementioned ten dharmas of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gāmin*).

There are also abbreviated references to the observation of the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*) and so forth; however, fearing that they would become too prolix and difficult to comprehend, they have been omitted.
△ Fourth, the summary of the number.
These are the ten. △ Fifth, the manifestation of benefits:
If bodhisattvas abide securely in these dharmas (up to) they understand all Buddha-dharmas and attain equal and perfect enlightenment.
△ Section Four: Clarifying the Practice within the Stage of Noble Birth through a Single Door; Part Five. First, the general heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has ten kinds of realization-knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).

These are his own natural practice (*svabhāva-caryā*); because he has previously attained thorough understanding, he is able to realize them. By virtue of this realization, regarding the holy teaching..."
Born therein. △ Second, the inquiry into the number:
What are the ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation.
This refers to knowing that all dharmas have a single characteristic (up to) knowing that all dharmas exist within a single thought-moment.
The three preceding [sections] comprehensively know all dharmas.
[It further includes] knowing the mental activities of all sentient beings without obstruction (up to) knowing the wholesome and unwholesome actions of all sentient beings.
These five are an expansion of the previous "knowledge of sentient beings.
They consist of knowing all the vows, practices, sovereign mastery, sustaining power, and transformations of all bodhisattvas;
these are subsumed within the category of karma among the aforementioned karmic activities.

Knowing that all Tathāgatas are fully endowed with the ten powers and have attained equal and perfect enlightenment, one immediately knows that nirvāṇa stands in contrast to saṃsāra. As for their supreme practice, it consists solely in realizing the Buddha-dharma;
since there are no distinct characteristics of practice, they are not explained in detail here. △ Fourth, the conclusion regarding the number.
These are the ten. △ Fifth, the manifestation of benefits:
If bodhisattvas abide securely in these dharmas, they will attain skillful means regarding all dharmas.
△ Section Five: One Gate. This consists of the five practices within the "Abiding in the Fulfillment of Skillful Means. First, the general heading:
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of power.
If based on the Sanskrit original, this is named "Accumulation" (*saṃcaya*), which carries the meaning of being "endowed with skillful means.
The ninety-fifth section below is precisely the Ten Powers (*daśabala*). △ Second, the enumeration of the numbers.
What are these ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, the power of entering into the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (up to) the power of profound and clear understanding regarding all phenomena.
The sixth stage is the power of liberation; the remaining four are the powers of higher seeking.
These include the skillful power that, regarding all spiritual friends, causes the mind set on omniscience never to regress.
In the preceding ten stages (*bhūmi*), it was merely stated that all practices cultivated are for the sake of sentient beings, yet it was not known what those practices were.

Now, the specific practices to be cultivated are revealed; furthermore, upon entering [this stage], one immediately attains thorough penetration, including the superior progress and the understanding of sentient beings and so forth.
△ Fourth, the summary of the number.
These are the ten. △ Fifth, the manifestation of benefits:
If bodhisattvas abide securely in these dharmas, they will possess the unsurpassed powers of the Tathāgata.
△ Section Six has two gates. It clarifies the Abiding in the Right Mind. This gate consists of five parts concerning the equality of one’s own practice.
First is the general heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has ten kinds of equality."
Because one realizes equality, the mind remains steadfast and unmoved upon hearing praise or blame. Now, the term "equality" generally possesses three meanings.

First is equality of phenomena (*vastu-samatā*): this refers to the mutual comparison of the ten categories, such as saying that all sentient beings equally possess Buddha-nature, up to the fact that all Buddhas are identical in their single Dharma-body, single mind, and single wisdom. Second is equality of principle (*tattva-samatā*).
This means that these ten categories are equal because they are one with True Reality. Third, "the mind is equal": by realizing the preceding two points, one identifies them within the mind;
thus, regarding the ten objects, no sense of high or low arises. △ Second, the inquiry into their number.
What are the ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, equanimity toward all sentient beings.
This means that because there is neither enemy nor friend, all phenomena are equal;
for one does not give rise to discrimination between good and evil.
All lands are equal, for whether they appear defiled or pure, there is no distinction of high or low.
All profound intentions are equal.
Because they emerge from the same true path,
all roots of goodness are equal;
there is not a single root of goodness that does not lead to Buddhahood.
All bodhisattvas are equal,
for they regard their fellow practitioners as themselves;
all their vows are equal.
Because each and every great vow extends to the limits of the future,
all the pāramitās are equal; it is not said that prajñā is superior to dāna and the others.
All phenomena are equal,
for each and every phenomenon thoroughly penetrates both fact and principle.
All Buddhas are equal.
It is not said that this is [the Buddha], for he is the most supreme. △ Fourth, the conclusion of the number:
these constitute ten.
△ Fifth, clarifying the benefits of cultivation.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, equal dharma of all Buddhas.
△ Second, the five phrases on the true meaning of the Buddha-dharmas. First, the general heading.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of phrases concerning the true meaning of the Buddha-dharma for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
These constitute the practice of further advancement; although they differ slightly from the preceding section, their meaning is largely the same. △ Second, the enumeration of the number.
What are these ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, that all phenomena are merely names.
The first [verse] refers to the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
because it is entirely without reality, all phenomena are like illusions... up to "all phenomena are pure in karma.
The next four [verses] refer to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and those five [verses] refer to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
All phenomena are merely produced by words;
for they are spoken of through provisional names within that which is without name or characteristic.
All phenomena are the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), all phenomena are without characteristics (*animitta*), and so on, up to all phenomena being the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The remaining four each have one meaning. △ Fourth, the summary of the number:
these constitute ten.
△ Fifth, the manifestation of the benefits of cultivation.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will skillfully enter the supreme, true meaning of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
△ Section Seven has two gates, clarifying the practice within the stage of non-retrogression. The first [gate] consists of five parts concerning one's own nature; the first is a general heading.
The Buddha’s sons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, discourse on ten kinds of dharmas.
Because they are able to proclaim these profound and vast dharmas, those who hear them spoken do not regress in mind. △ Second, the inquiry into their number.
What are the ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, preaching the profound Dharma, preaching the vast Dharma, [and so on] up to preaching the Dharma that gives rise to the powers of a Tathāgata.
He speaks of the nature of karma and so forth, thereby establishing the powers of the Tathāgata.
He teaches the dharmas corresponding to the three periods of time and explains the methods for causing Bodhisattvas not to regress.

He expounds these according to what is appropriate, ensuring that Bodhisattvas do not fall back. Within the twenty-eighth [chapter] on Nirvāṇa, the matter of regressing and not regressing is explained in detail.
The signs of regression.
[This concludes] the teaching on the dharmas that praise the Buddha’s merits (up to) the dharmas corresponding to the realm of all Tathāgatas.
The remaining eight may be understood accordingly. △ Fourth, the summary of the number.
These are the ten. △ Fifth, the manifestation of the benefits of cultivation:
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed skill in preaching the Dharma.
△ Second, the fivefold superior progress. First, the general heading:
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of upholding (*dhāraṇī*), which means receiving, maintaining, and practicing them;
it is not merely reciting them with the mouth. △ Second, the inquiry into their number.
What are the ten? △ Third, the enumeration and explanation:
namely, upholding all accumulated merit (throughout) up to upholding the power of the supernatural transformations and playful mastery of all Buddhas.
△ Fourth, the summary of the number.
These constitute ten.
△ Fifth, the manifestation of the benefits of cultivation.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the sustaining power of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom.

△ Section Eight has two gates clarifying the practice within the stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūta*). This is the first gate, which consists of five parts concerning their own-level practice (*svabhūmi-pratipatti*).
First is the general heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of eloquence.
△ Second, the enumeration of the items: What are these ten?
△ Third, the detailed explanation:
This refers to the eloquence of non-discrimination regarding all phenomena (up to) the eloquence of non-attachment toward all phenomena.
Because there is no fault in the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, there is the eloquence of non-attachment.
The eloquence that thoroughly realizes the emptiness of all phenomena (up to) the eloquence that causes the minds of all sentient beings to rejoice.

Because one knows the inclinations and desires of the minds of sentient beings, one brings joy to others through this eloquence. The remaining eight [types of eloquence] may be understood accordingly. △ Fourth, the conclusion of the enumeration.
These are the ten. △ Fifth, the manifestation of the benefits of cultivation:

namely, the sustaining power of the Buddha, the sustaining power of the Dharma, and the sustaining power of sentient beings.

The first three [categories] of the Three Jewels constitute the Jewel of the Dharma as the object of support (*ālambana-dhāraṇa*). Sentient beings constitute the Jewel of the Saṃgha, because the Saṃgha of Bodhisattvas belongs to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).

because it performs the deeds of compassion;

Because they correctly initiate practice;
because they are sustained by the power of aspiration; and because their practice is maintained by aspiration.

That [stage] possesses the sustenance of offerings (*pūjā-dhāraṇa*) and the sustenance of the eon (*kalpa-dhāraṇa*), but lacks the sustenance of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-dhāraṇa*) and the sustenance of wholesome power (*kuśala-bala-dhāraṇa*). This is because it pertains to the eighth stage.
This subsumes the eons. He, by means of his practice, subsumes this wholesome power; because he gives rise to offerings based on the object [of refuge], there is no difference between them.

The other names are identical. This is fully as explained in that commentary. Since the number and names differ, one should explain them according to their names. Herein, there is no Jewel of the Saṃgha.

next, "receiving and upholding" (*śrutadhāraṇa*) was explained as receiving, internalizing, and practicing; now, "powerful upholding" (*baladhāraṇa*) refers to empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and sustaining support.
Therefore, these terms do not overlap. △ Fourth, the conclusion of the enumeration.

△ Three on Deeply Entering the Buddha-dharma: First, the heading.

While the preceding sutra passage clarifies the anticipation of future attainment, this section distinguishes their present capacity for realization and comprehension;
that is to say, it concerns the aforementioned practice of the gift of Dharma. Thus, that text states: "I shall fully study all that the Buddhas have studied, and realize all-knowledge."
Knowing all dharmas, one preaches them for the sake of sentient beings.
