△ Third, the explanation.
That is to say:

in the first six [verses], there is the character "enter" (入); in the latter four, the character "know" (知) is used as the initial term. These two expressions—“entering and realizing” (證入) and “knowing” (了知)—are mutually illuminating.
Among them, the first four [verses] concern entering the receptacle world (器世間).
Entering all worlds of the past (up to) entering the number of worlds of the present;
"number" refers to their quantity.
This is the course of worlds.
"Practice" refers to the causes of the lands,
as explained in the context of the world-systems. "Explanation" refers to the teaching of the Dharma within each respective result.

The world is pure. "Purity" refers to the essence of the *kṣetra*. This constitutes the general essence; the three preceding [sections] clarify it specifically, while the following one reveals it collectively.
It enters into all worlds in their various modes of arising.
The various natures refer to the distinctions between defilement and purity; these constitute distinct entities.
They enter into the various karmic retributions of all sentient beings and enter into the various practices of all bodhisattvas.
The first two [knowledges] pertain to the world of sentient beings; the latter four pertain to the world of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
They know the successive [lives] of all past Buddhas, including their lands and assemblies, as well as their preaching of the Dharma and their taming of beings.
The first three [knowledges] enter the Buddhas of the three periods of time; the last one enters the Dharma.
It knows the worldly dharmas, the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of Tathāgatas;
it knows the distinctions among the five vehicles.
Although one knows that all phenomena are entirely without discrimination, one teaches various dharmas;

this clarifies the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the ultimate. Because the nature does not destroy the characteristics, although there is no discrimination, one speaks of various things.

In this context, "discrimination" (vikalpa) refers to differentiation. Therefore, the Jin translation states: "Although all dharmas are neither one nor different, yet one speaks of oneness and difference;
all these enter the dharma-realm because there is nothing to enter."

This explains and establishes the preceding meaning. It means that because one completely enters the *dharmadhātu*, there is no differentiation; yet because there is nothing to enter, it is described as being manifold. Why is this?
If there were a separate place of entry, then at the moment of entry, the original characteristics would be lost, and one could not speak of the manifold.
Since each phenomenon is inherently empty, it is called "entering the *dharmadhātu*. Because there is nothing distinct to enter, the various categories are not destroyed.
It has been sown. Above, this was distinguished through knowledge; below, it is clarified through exposition.
As taught according to the Dharma, there is nothing to be grasped or attached to.

Now, one who expounds the Dharma should do so in accordance with the Dharma. Since the Dharma is the simultaneous fusion of the provisional and the ultimate, the exposition likewise is an exposition of non-existence.

namely, extinguishing all obstructive karma and giving rise to a mind of fearlessness.
Obstacles are difficult to extinguish;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one must protect and uphold the True Dharma with a fearless mind,
for the bequeathed Dharma is difficult to preserve.
To subdue all māras, one should resolve upon a fearless mind;
for evil māras are difficult to subdue,
one must resolve upon a fearless mind that does not begrudge even body or life.
It is difficult to relinquish body and life;
one shatters all the heterodox and false arguments of external paths and gives rise to a mind of fearlessness,
yet these external paths are difficult to crush.
Causing all sentient beings to rejoice and give rise to a mind of fearlessness;
for the minds of beings are difficult to satisfy.
Causing the entire assembly to be completely joyful and give rise to a mind of fearlessness.
The great assembly was difficult to gladden;
yet he tamed all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, up to mahoragas, giving rise to a mind of fearlessness.
These eight classes of beings were difficult to subdue.

Having departed from the stages of the two vehicles and entered the profound Dharma, they give rise to a mind of fearlessness. It is difficult for those of the inferior vehicle to depart [from their own stage];
thus, they practice the bodhisattva conduct for unspeakably unspeakable eons with a mind free of weariness, giving rise to a mind of fearlessness.
The higher practices are difficult to cultivate. Regarding these ten difficulties, he is entirely without fear; how could he fear sentient beings troubling or harming him?

Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of inconceivability, which consist of the virtues they encompass.

the first three concern the roots of goodness individually. Aspiration and knowledge that accord with the nature are called "inconceivable.

first, four concerning conduct (*caryā*); second, three concerning wisdom (*jñāna*). Wisdom pertains to internal clarity, while conduct pertains to external manifestations. Now, the first part.
Having resolved upon the bodhicitta and cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva, their roots of goodness are never lost; they are non-conceptual and inconceivable.

practicing the bodhisattva path, he manifests his descent into the world (and so on) to inconceivably rescue and protect sentient beings.
Through the cultivation of causes, the fruit of the eightfold marks is perfected.

Although they are able to manifest the ten powers of a Tathāgata (up to) the inconceivable teaching and transforming of sentient beings, they manifest the fruits while never abandoning their great functions;
all of these are difficult to conceive. △ Second, the latter three are categorized according to wisdom. This section has three parts.
First, regarding the mutual identity of the two truths, one knows all phenomena.
Among the eight [sections], ten phrases are condensed into five pairs: first, the object; second, the mind; third, that which pervades all; fourth, that which pertains to cultivation.

They arise. The five are precisely what are called "names" (nāman), and they are also the five dharmas: first, appearance (nimitta); second, conceptual construction (vikalpa); third, suchness (tathatā); fourth, correct wisdom (samyag-jñāna);

and fifth, name (nāman). Each of these has two meanings. First, when taken directly as the essence of the dharmas: non-appearance is the ultimate (paramārtha), while appearance is the conventional (saṃvṛti);

they are constantly mutually identical. The same applies to the following four pairs. Second, regarding the five pairs of delusion and awakening: for the most part they are the same, with only minor differences.
They are different.
That which is signless is itself a sign;
by being deluded regarding signlessness, one establishes signs.
Characteristics are non-characteristics;
awakening to the non-characteristic nature of characteristics is precisely suchness.
Non-discrimination is discrimination.
To be deluded regarding non-conceptualizing correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) is itself the formation of conceptualization and discrimination;
such discrimination is [itself] non-discrimination.
To awaken from false discrimination is precisely non-conceptualizing correct wisdom.
That which is not existent is existence.
To realize that it is non-existent is true suchness.
Existence is non-existence.
If one clings to existence as being existent, it is not truly existent;
non-action is action.
If wisdom were non-action, that would be correct wisdom.
This is non-action. If there were anything to be done, it would not be the correct wisdom of action;
it would not be the teaching that is truly taught.
It is known that "naming" is not "speaking"; it is "true speaking" that is called "naming.
To say that "speaking" is "naming" means that naming possesses speaking; it is not that speaking itself is naming.
Inconceivable. △ Second, regarding the three matters: they are fused yet not fused.
One knows that the mind is equal to bodhi; one knows that bodhi is equal to the mind; and one knows that the mind and bodhi are equal to sentient beings.

Furthermore, one does not give rise to the inversion of thought, the inversion of perception, or the inversion of view.

because all dharmas entirely enter the Dharma-realm, there is nothing that enters.

They enter entirely into the Dharma-realm; therefore, it is said that they are mutually identical. Because there is nothing to enter, one should not differentiate between the Buddha-dharma and other phenomena within the world.
This means that because each phenomenon is inherently empty of itself, they are called mutually identical; there is no dharma to be obtained within the world.

One knows that all phenomena are non-dual;
one cannot seek them within one another,
for they are unchanging.

△ Section Five has six gates, clarifying practice within the absence of delusion and confusion. Within this, there are three parts. The first two gates clarify the practice of non-delusion;
the next two gates clarify the practice of non-confusion; and the final two gates clarify how these two practices together give rise to merit.
Although delusion and confusion may have commonalities, they are explained here according to their specific distinctions. Furthermore, these three sections are as follows:
The three meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). The first is the absorption that benefits sentient beings; the second is the absorption of dwelling in the joy of the true Dharma;

the third is the absorption that draws forth and produces merit. Now, for the first [of these], there are two parts. First, the five points on the gate of not being deluded regarding skillful and esoteric terminology. First, the heading.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of skillful esoteric speech (*saṃdhā-bhāṣita*).
Having already clarified internal practice above, the present section distinguishes external verbal expression as its counterpart. The text states:

"By means of right mindfulness, they skillfully understand all worldly discourse and are able to maintain the discourse of all supramundane dharmas," and so forth—all of these are termed esoteric speech.

Generally speaking, there are five [reasons for this]: first, because it explains the profound and secret Dharma, as in the "Chapter on Manifestation" where it is called the "Tathāgata’s Secret Treasury," and so forth;

second, because a single word expresses all dharmas, as stated above regarding the Tathāgata’s "single utterance," and likewise the four realities and nine meanings of the *śruti* (hearing) of the Ṛṣi, the sound *go*, and so on; third, because one is near yet does not hear, as in the case of the body...

The Master is seated; though distant, there is no separation, like Maudgalyāyana seeking a sound. (4) Words are near while the meaning is distant, such as saying that the Three Vehicles are the ultimate.
Words are distant while the meaning is near, such as saying that obtaining fire during the cold season is called *nirvāṇa*.
This is also called "concealing the real to speak of the provisional. (5) Using different words to speak of different dharmas, such as [saying] that what is perceived is not solid.
[This refers to] "steadfastness" and so forth.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are the ten?
△ Third, the explanation.
This refers to the skillful secret language found throughout all the Buddha’s sūtras.
The first [category] possesses five aspects because it is comprehensive and constitutes the entirety of the teaching.
It ranges from the skillful secret language regarding all places of rebirth up to the skillful secret language regarding the manifestation of perfect enlightenment.
These two contain two meanings: namely, that they indicate something while being [taken as] real; this is the fourth meaning.
Both of these are profound and esoteric teachings; this is the first meaning.
From "the skillful secret language regarding the karmic retributions of all sentient beings" (up to) "the skillful secret language of identical accomplishment.

The others [of the preceding categories] are subsumed under the first two, or alternatively, they may all be combined with the five; this can be understood through reflection. △ Fourth, the conclusion.
These are the ten.
△ Fifth, the exhortation:
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed skillful and subtle secret speech.
△ Second, the wisdom of skillfulness that is not deluded. This section has five parts. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of skillful analytical wisdom."
Since his external speech was already secret and his internal wisdom was further skillful, he was free from the darkness of delusion in benefiting sentient beings.
Thus, that text says: "The Bodhisattva, in the presence of a spiritual friend, hears the True Dharma, namely the profound Dharma and so forth.
The words and meanings are for the most part identical. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? Part Three:
The Explanation. They are:
the skillful analytical wisdom that enters all lands, up to the skillful analytical wisdom that enters all Buddha-dharmas.
△ Fourth, the conclusion.
These constitute ten [sections].
△ Fifth, the exhortation.
If bodhisattvas abide therein (up to) the unsurpassed skillful wisdom that discriminates all dharmas.
△ Second, the dhyāna of dwelling in the joy of the True Dharma, which is the practice of non-distraction. Both gates are the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In the first gate, the entry into samādhi is clarified through five points concerning the differences in the manifest locations, etc. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of entry into samādhi.
As that text says: "They skillfully enter all doors of meditative concentration. Herein, ten are clarified, all of which apply universally to everything.
△ 2. Inquiry: What are the ten?
△ 3. Explanation:
That is to say:
a general exposition on the different ways of entering meditative concentration by taking these ten objects as conditions; specifically, the ten gates differ in the objects they take as conditions.
[This ranges] from entering samādhi in all worlds up to abiding for all kalpas.
The first five [phrases] concern the successive stages; the latter five concern the interpenetration and perfect fusion.
From arising from samādhi and manifesting inconceivable bodies (up to) entering samādhi without rest.
The ninety [mental states] are all one yet manifold. Thus, it is said: "In a single thought-moment, one attains countless samādhis.

This is spoken from the perspective of the majority in relation to what precedes and follows, and is judged as the essential substance of concentration; it is not that its function is absent. △ Fourth, the conclusion.
These are the ten.
△ Five: Exhortation.
If all bodhisattvas dwell securely therein (up to) the Buddhas' unsurpassed skillful samādhi-dharma.
△ Second, the explanation of universal penetration (*paryāpanna*). This means that the categories of understanding are all universally present within the five [realms]. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has ten kinds of universal penetration.
This is analogous to what is taught in the Hīnayāna regarding the ten bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), which serve to cause samādhi to gradually expand and broaden. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, the universal entry of sentient beings (up to) the universal entry of various offerings to all Tathāgatas.

The preceding section clarified all cases, such as the bodies of sentient beings—namely, the bodies of children and so forth—which, although capable of being entered by all [elements], do not necessarily occur simultaneously.
Now, this section concerns the entry into one specific category, wherein each [element] pervades everything, just as when the ocean first comes, everything is water. △ Fourth, the conclusion.
These are the ten.
△ Fifth, the exhortation:
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme great wisdom that universally enters all phenomena.
△ Section Three has two gates, clarifying the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) that possesses the merit of inducing [birth]. The first gate clarifies that its activity is unimpeded;
therefore, it is called the "five liberations. First, the heading:
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten gates of liberation, namely, the inconceivable liberation (*vimokṣa*; in Sanskrit *vimokṣa*, here translated as "superior liberation").
This refers to a preeminent function, which is also achieved by relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to accomplish the eight liberations. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, "the body pervading all worlds" (up to) "the gate of liberation of the playful exercise of supernormal powers."
△ Four conclusions.
These constitute ten.
△ Five exhortations.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed gate of liberation.
△ Second, there is no obstruction regarding objects; hence it is called the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Just as one relies on the four dhyānas to induce the six common applications of these powers.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are these ten?
△ Third, the explanation:
namely, the supernormal knowledge of the skillful means of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-abhijñā*) up to the supernormal knowledge of the skillful means of being unimpeded.
If these ten are subsumed under six categories, the first four are as previously understood; the next five constitute the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*).

According to the minds of sentient beings, there appear inconceivable (up to) unspeakable transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) through the power of skillful means and supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).
Finally, by exhausting all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), one attains enlightenment (*bodhi*).

From "following the inconceivable minds of sentient beings" up to "the supernormal power of the skillful means wisdom of *samyak-saṃbodhi*," these differ according to their respective stages and are slightly distinct from the ten [supernormal powers]. △ Four: Conclusion.
These are the ten.
△ Fifth, the exhortation:
"If all bodhisattvas abide therein" (up to) "manifesting various [forms] to cause them to practice and learn."
△ Section Six has two gates. The first gate correctly elucidates the essence of practice within the stage of the Good Manifestation (Sudṛśa). First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of clarity belonging to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."
This clearly reveals the essence of practice, which is precisely *prajñā* (wisdom). Therefore, it is called "clarity of wisdom.

Furthermore, as all these are wisdoms in which the provisional and the real are unimpeded, they are termed "skillful means" (*upāya*). This is not like the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), which are categorized into five practices solely based on their fundamental nature and merely according to their relative intensity or subtlety. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? Part three:
the explanation has two sections. The first seven concern a single wisdom alone, which is divided into three parts. The first three concern those to be transformed, namely:
"knowing the karmic retributions of all sentient beings" (up to) "the skillful wisdom-illumination that is like a vajra."
First, the phenomenon; second, the principle; third, returning to the principle from the phenomenon. △ Next, the three [sections] concerning the transformer:
the ability to employ immeasurable, subtle, and wondrous sounds (up to) the skillful wisdom and clarity of not undergoing rebirth.
The first also concerns phenomena (*dharma*). The second phrase concerns principle (*li*). The last returns phenomena to principle. △ Third, abandoning the conceptualization of a subject:
returning [all] to Prajñā.
This is the skillful wisdom and illumination that relinquishes all spheres of ideation and sensation.
Through mindfulness, contemplation, and observation, one eliminates [distractions] and does not grasp at objective realms; this is for the sake of skillful entry into principle.

△ Second, there are three subsequent phrases that distinguish the three modes of dual practice. First, it clarifies the skillful wisdom of non-explanatory explanation and non-accomplishing accomplishment.

To know that all phenomena are neither with marks nor without marks (up to: to analyze and expound upon them throughout immeasurable kalpas—this refers to the illumination of the dual negation and the stillness of cessation.
It transcends the path of words yet is able to differentiate; it illuminates phenomena and possesses discourse.

It is not "with marks" in order to dispel marks, nor is it "without marks" in order to dispel non-existence. Through the single nature it dispels multiplicity; through the absence of nature it dispels existence. Thus, both nature and marks are simultaneously quiescent.
Abiding in the *dharmadhātu*, one attains the skillful wisdom-illumination of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This is an attainment that is non-attainment; it is the essence of the *dharmadhātu*, which in reality has nothing to be attained. To illuminate this *dharmadhātu* is precisely what is called "attaining Buddhahood.
2. Explaining the Wisdom-Illumination that Arises from Non-arising. This section has three parts. First, the direct explanation of the condition that is without conditions.
This also reveals the transformation that is without transformation. Within this, there are two parts. First, it clarifies the absence of conditions:
"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows all sentient beings... because he has thoroughly realized that taking birth is unobtainable."
This refers to the true mind of sentient beings; because it accords with principle, it cannot be apprehended. If there were no conditions (*pratyaya*), there would be nothing to transform.
△ Second, clarifying that the true mind follows conditions without destroying dependent origination, and thus there is indeed that which is transformed. This section has two parts.

First, knowing those to be converted. This passage consists of three sections. The first section contains eight phrases, which specifically identify the characteristics of the conditions and thereby reveal the causes—namely, ignorance and so forth.
Knowing conditions:
"conditions" refers to karmic formations.
Knowing phenomena.
That is to say, one recognizes name-and-form and so forth,
and knows the objective sphere; that is to say, one experiences contact with and the reception of sensory objects.
Knowing and practicing.
That is, one takes up existence in the present;
thus, birth is known.
Birth itself is the link;
its cessation is known as old age and death.

Know that all verbal expressions arise in accordance with conventional conditions; they do not depart from the three periods of time. △ Second, there are twelve phrases in six pairs, which comprehensively inform one of defilement and purity, delusion and awakening.
One knows delusion and knows the departure from delusion (up to) knowing birth-and-death and knowing nirvana.
To be deluded regarding principle is to be inverted, confused, and defiled; awakening is the reverse of all this.
Knowing that which can be known and knowing that which cannot be known, one clings to the former and does not cling to the latter.
Conventionally, both are obtainable; in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), neither is obtainable. Whether there is attainment or non-attainment depends upon the principle.
Attachment and non-attachment are distinguished by means of wisdom. △ Third, knowing the activities of the mind:
knowing stillness and knowing movement.
Stillness refers to the fundamental nature; movement refers to adventitious defilements.
One knows departing and one knows returning.
To follow the adventitious defilements is to depart and fail to return; to perceive the original nature is to return to the source and revert to the root.
One knows arising and one knows non-arising.
There is returning and there is departing; both are the arousal of the mind. When one returns to abide in the state where both are absent, all is tranquil and nothing arises.
To know destruction is to know transcendence:
when the mind arises, all that is wholesome is destroyed; when it does not arise, one transcends the veils and entanglements.

Knowing maturity means knowing that contact with objects is quiescent; this is what constitutes maturity. The former [type] extends to both self and others, while the latter involves knowing the faculties and capacities [of beings], referring exclusively to oneself.
He knows the various faculties and knows how to discipline them.
"Faculties" refers to the six sense organs; not being led astray by their objects is precisely what constitutes discipline. △ Second, the summary of dual practice:
according to what is appropriate for each case, he employs various means of teaching and transformation, never failing to maintain the conduct of a bodhisattva.
This means that wisdom conforms to and transforms according to [the needs of beings], yet does not lose its state of non-action. △ Second, the interrogation and explanation:
Why is it that the Bodhisattva acts solely for the benefit of sentient beings (up to) and does not contravene anything performed in the world?
The reason for this is that he generates the aspiration for the sake of sentient beings. △ Third, the conclusion of the name:
This is the luminous wisdom of skillfulness regarding the many *pratītyasamutpāda*.
△ Third, the luminous wisdom of equalizing transformation. Part one clarifies that reality does not obstruct expedient means.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is unattached toward the Buddha [up to] because his mind is vast and equal to the Dharma-realm.
△ Second, clarifying that skillful means do not obstruct reality:
knowing the various ways of teaching the Dharma and knowing the number of sentient beings [up to] being immovable and destined to achieve perfect enlightenment.
△ Third, the title of the section:
The skillful wisdom and illumination that equally ferries all sentient beings across the ocean of birth and death.
△ Fourth, the enumeration of the sections.
These are the ten.
△ Fifth, the exhortation to practice:
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great, skillful wisdom-illumination.
△ Second, explaining liberation through the removal of the cognitive hindrance (jñeyāvaraṇa), in five parts. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of liberation.
Because they are liberated from the two hindrances. In Sanskrit, this is called *vimukti*; here it is translated as "liberation" (*jie tuo*). This differs from the previous [category]. △ Second...
Question: What are the ten?
△ Third, the explanation.
That is to say, liberation from afflictions and liberation from wrong views;
these two are the liberation from the obstacles of affliction and all forms of grasping.
The karmic obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*) has grasping as its predominant activity.

Liberation from the aggregates, bases, and elements constitutes the retributive obstruction (*vipākāvaraṇa*). Among these, the first four liberations counteract the three obstructions [of afflictions, karma, and retribution], while the latter six liberations counteract the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Surpassing the liberation of the two vehicles—
this first excludes the inferior.
From "the liberation of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" up to "the liberation that is able to fully comprehend all three periods of time."
The remainder all manifest excellence. △ Four, the conclusion:
"These constitute the ten.
△ Five, the exhortation.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas (up to) teaching and maturing all sentient beings.

△ Section Seven has two gates, clarifying the practice within the stage of non-attachment. The first gate clarifies roaming and acting according to one's inclination; the second gate clarifies dwelling and finding delight.
Both universally encompass the twofold benefit [of self and others], employing provisional and ultimate skillful means without any attachment. Now...
The first five [sections]. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of groves for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, that birth and death are the pleasure groves of the bodhisattva (extending) until they pervade all worlds throughout the entirety of space.
△ Four conclusions.
These constitute ten.
△ Five exhortations.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, sorrow-free, and great practice of bliss.
△ Second, dwelling in contentment, in five parts. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of palaces.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are these ten?
△ Third, the explanation:
namely, that the bodhicitta is the palace of the bodhisattva (up to) because it performs the sovereign activity of a king of all dharmas.
Regarding the four Brahma-abodes: they are the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), as they are also the cause of form. Therefore, the *Dulouji* (Lokottaraparivarta) says: "Cultivate the four Brahma..."
Practice loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. The remaining nine [immeasurables] may be understood accordingly. △ Fourth, the conclusion:
These constitute the ten.
△ Fifth, the exhortation.
If bodhisattvas abide therein (up to) attaining sovereign mastery of supernatural powers within a single world.

△ Section Eight has two gates, clarifying the practice within the stage that is difficult to attain. The first gate concerns the internal aspiration and delight. Aspiration is the essence of practice;
it has five parts. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of delight.
Because they dwell in palaces, their minds rejoice in supreme bliss. △ Second, the inquiry:
What are these ten?
△ 3. Explanation:
That is to say, because one delights in right mindfulness and the mind is not distracted, [it continues] until: "one utterly destroys all the teachings of heterodox paths. △ 4. Conclusion.
These are the ten.
△ Fifth, the exhortation:
If bodhisattvas abide securely in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed dharma-bliss of all buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
△ Third, the fivefold adornment of external virtues. First, the heading:
"O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of adornments, because they are fully adorned with various virtues through their vows. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, because the adornment of power is indestructible... [and so on] ...because there is no regression in seeking all-knowledge.
△ Four conclusions.
These constitute ten.
△ Five exhortations.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain all the unsurpassed dharma-adornments of the Tathāgata.
△ Ninth, there are two gates clarifying the practice within the stage of wholesome dharmas. The first gate clarifies immovability through external conditions;

the second gate clarifies not abandoning [the resolve] within the internal mind. Furthermore, this clarifies the firmness of the mind, while the latter clarifies deep penetration; both possess the meaning of "power" (*bala*).
Now, the first section is divided into five parts. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to ten kinds of immovable minds.
Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? Part Three: The Explanation.
Namely, being able to relinquish all that one possesses (up to) having a mind that is neither regressive nor wavering.

Among the ten, the second and the ninth constitute the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*); the remainder are all the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*). Within the eighth category, there are ten:
first, faith (*śraddhā*), which is the accomplishment of faith rooted in the faculties (*indriya*).
Because it gives rise to the fruit of Buddhahood,
it is "unturbid faith," as it is not mixed with the turbidity of lack of faith.
Pure faith, because it is pure and free from afflictions;
supremely pure faith.
Because it is free from subtle conceptualization,
it is stainless faith; because it is free from the stains of the knowable, it is stainless faith.
The faith of clear penetration:
because one serves the source,
it is the faith that reverently makes offerings to all Buddhas.
Because it is directed toward the state of fruition,
faith is non-retrogressive;
because its own nature is firm, it is steadfast.
It cannot be fully exhausted,
for virtue is inexhaustible;
nothing can destroy faith.
Because it is conditioned by the movement of the lower [realms],
there is great joy and leaping faith;
because one realizes *tathatā* (suchness).
The accomplishment of the immovable mind gives rise to all-knowledge (up to) the faithful acceptance and non-slander of the immovable mind.
△ Fourth, the conclusion:
these constitute the ten.
△ Five Exhortations:
If all bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, immovable mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā).
△ Second, the five points on not abandoning [the resolve] within the inner mind. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of non-abandonment of the profound and great mind.

Because it is immovable, they are able to exhaustively penetrate both principle and phenomena. Since the principle is profound and the phenomena are vast, it is called "profound and great. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? Part Three: The Explanation. They are as follows:
the profound and great resolve to never abandon the fulfillment of all Buddhas [up to] the gathering of all Buddha-dharmas.
△ Four conclusions.
These constitute ten.
△ Five exhortations.
If Bodhisattvas abide therein, they are able not to abandon any of the Buddha-dharmas.
*The Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll 86;
*The Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll 87 (Entering the latter half of the fifty-ninth sūtra).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang;
recorded and annotated on the sūtra by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.
△ Nineteen sections clarifying the practice within the stage of reality. First, the five aspects of the observing wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of wisdom-observation.
Because they do not abandon the profound and great, they are able to observe. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, skillfully and analytically expounding all dharmas, up to the unimpeded wisdom of contemplative observation.
The previous question used the term "contemplation" (觀) merely as a synonym for "wisdom" (智慧). One should reflect accordingly upon these ten phrases. △ Four: Conclusion.
These constitute the ten.
△ Five: Exhortation.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme great wisdom of observation.
△ Second, the five [aspects] of the knowledge of teaching the Dharma; first, the heading.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas preach the Dharma.
Because they are able to contemplate within, they are able to preach without.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are these ten?
△ Third, the explanation:
namely, it is said that all phenomena arise from conditions and that all phenomena are entirely like illusions.
The first two statements explain the conventional; the following eight explain the ultimate.
It is taught that all phenomena are without conflict;
there is nothing dualistic to be contested.
It is taught that all phenomena have no limits.
Its essence and virtues are both vast;
it explains that all phenomena have no basis of reliance,
and its characteristics are profound and far-reaching.
It is taught that all phenomena are like a vajra,
their essence being firm and sharp;
it is taught that all phenomena are entirely suchness (tathatā).
It is suchness, immovable;
it teaches that all phenomena are entirely quiescent,
its essence transcending the hundred negations.
It is taught that all phenomena are entirely transcendent;
though enmeshed in bondage, they are undefiled.
It is taught that all phenomena abide in a single meaning, perfected in their intrinsic nature.
The essence and characteristics are of one flavor. △ Four, the conclusion:
"These constitute the ten.
△ Five, the exhortation.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will be able to skillfully expound all dharmas.
△ Third, the wisdom that is free from hindrances, in five parts. First, the heading:
"O Sons of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of purity."
This is the wisdom that is free from hindrances; in the Jin [translation], it is called "Stainless.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are the ten?
△ Third, the explanation.
What are called "purity of the profound mind," "purity of severing doubt" (up to) "purity of all roots of goodness"?
Although they are equally pure, that which is purified differs. Among these ten, there are differences in their expansion and contraction when compared with the seven purities;
this is easy to understand from the text. The seven purities are as explained at the beginning of the fifth stage. △ Fourth, the conclusion.
These are the ten.
△ Fifth, the exhortation:
"If all bodhisattvas abide therein, they shall attain the supreme, pure Dharma of all Tathāgatas."
△ Five: The Seal of the Wisdom of Thorough Determination. First, the heading:

"O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of seals for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, because they definitively seal and authorize all phenomena through pure wisdom. Therefore, in the Jin translation, these are called "Wisdoms."
Seal. The benefit of the seal subsequently formed is also the Seal of Wisdom (jñāna-mudrā), just like the three seals of the Dharma (dharmamudrā) and so forth.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are the ten?
△ Third, the explanation: First, regarding the patience of enduring adverse conditions, one’s wisdom remains unshakable.
What is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s knowledge of the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditioned formations (up to...)—this is the first seal.
△ Second, the determination of the practice of patience toward harm from others.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees sentient beings who are foolish and deranged... this is the second seal.
△ Third, the patience of discerning phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā-kṣānti*).
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva hears it said that [the Dharma] is associated with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)... this is the third seal.
Regarding the profound Buddha-dharma, they possess faith, patience, and certainty. △ Fourth, the certainty of attaining Buddhahood and liberating sentient beings:
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects thus: "I have generated the profound mind... (up to) "...this is the fourth seal."
△ Fifth, the definitive knowledge that the Buddha’s wisdom is boundless.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that the Tathāgata’s wisdom has no limit (up to) this is the fifth seal.
△ Sixth, the seal of being irreversible from the Buddha-fruit of one’s resolve.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [regarding] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi... this is the sixth seal.
△ Seventh, the seal of never regarding body or life, because of practicing the Dharma of intimacy.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva path without regard for body or life... this is the seventh seal.
△ Eighth, those who have already attained decisive understanding and entered the Mahāyāna Dharma.
If a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees a good man or a good woman... this is the eighth seal.
△ Ninth, the Seal of Resolving on the Equality of Deliverance:
A Bodhisattva-mahāsattva causes all sentient beings to attain a mind of equality... this is the ninth seal.
△ Tenth: Resolving that the essence of the Buddha is identical, such that causes are perfected and fruits are fulfilled.
From "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva shares the same roots of goodness as all Buddhas of the three periods of time" (up to) "this is the tenth seal."
△ 4. Conclusion: O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten seals of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
△ 5. Exhortation.
By this, the Bodhisattva swiftly accomplishes the supreme wisdom-seal (jñāna-mudrā) of all the dharmas of the Tathāgata, which is fully perfected.
△ Five: The Penetrating Illumination of Wisdom. First, the heading.
O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of illumination by the light of wisdom for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
Because they are fixed by seal, they shine through all things without obstruction.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are these ten?
△ 3. Explanation:
This refers to the knowledge of the light of illumination that fulfills all *pāramitās*, knowing with certainty that one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. △ 4. Conclusion.
These are the ten.
△ Fifth, the exhortation:
If all bodhisattvas abide securely in these dharmas, they shall obtain the illumination of the supreme wisdom of all buddhas.
△ Section Six: The Fivefold Knowledge of Peerlessness. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has ten kinds [of knowledge] (up to) such that none among the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can equal them."

Because of the aforementioned thorough illumination, one does not dwell with partial attachment; rather, one dwells simultaneously in both phenomena and principle, which is called "being without equal.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are the ten?
△ Third, the explanation:

That which is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s contemplation of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)—up to "this is the tenth peerless dwelling"—all involve the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the real.
Whether it be the function of quiescence itself, or the quiescence within function, and so forth, all are clearly manifest as can be known.
△ IV. Conclusion.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of peerless abodes of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
△ V. Exhortation.
If all bodhisattvas abide therein (up to) the peerless abiding in all Buddha-dharmas.
Below this begins the fifty-fifth sūtra.
△ Seven: Non-inferior Wisdom, five parts. First, the heading.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas give rise to ten kinds of non-inferior minds.
Previously, it was stated that they are "without equal" when compared to those below; now, it is stated that they are "without inferiority" when compared to those above.
Because they resolutely undertake ten superior matters, they are called "non-inferior. This is why the Jin translation also uses the term "without timidity. II. Inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
the ten phrases consist of five pairs. First is the pair of subduing Māra and restraining outsiders.
The Buddha-son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, forms this thought... (up to)... this is the second [resolve]: the mind that is not inferior.
△ Second, the counteraction of pride through delighting in others and oneself.
Furthermore, one reflects: "I shall [strive] for all sentient beings... This is the fourth mind that is not inferior.
△ Third, the correspondence of accumulating merit to achieve wisdom.
Furthermore, one forms this thought: "I shall accumulate all merit" (up to) "this is the sixth mind that is not inferior."
△ Fourth, transforming those below to edify those above forms a pair.
Furthermore, one reflects: "I shall edify them with the unsurpassed [teaching]... (up to) "...this is the eighth mind that is not inferior."
The preceding four were explained individually. △ Fifth, the correspondence between the culmination of compassion and wisdom; this constitutes their simultaneous practice.
The former is the compassion within wisdom, yet compassion and wisdom are practiced together.
Furthermore, he forms this thought: "When I practice the bodhisattva path... this is the ninth mind that is not inferior.
Although he feels compassion, he does not seek karmic retribution. △ Second, the wisdom of that very compassion, wherein the provisional and the real are practiced together, has four parts.
First, the objects of knowledge are enumerated.
Furthermore, one reflects thus: "All Buddhas of the three periods of time... [down to] the realm of all quiescent nirvāṇa.
△ Second, the subject that knows is distinguished.
In this way, all such various dharmas—from [the realization of] suffering up to—have been fully seen, fully realized, fully cultivated, and fully abandoned.

That is to say: knowing suffering and awakening to its forgetting; seeing the principle and realizing cessation; cultivating the path and abandoning the origin. △ Third, brushing away the mark of that knowledge.
However, within this, there is no discrimination and it is free from discrimination... (up to) there are no merits and no objective spheres (*viṣaya*).
Because one is able to know non-discrimination, there are no merits; because that which is known has no variety, there are no objective spheres.
△ Fourth, the convergence upon the Middle Way. This consists of two parts: a detailed exposition of the dual practice. First, a general exposition of the Middle Way.
Neither existent nor non-existent, neither one nor two.
△ Second, the mutual clarification of object and wisdom:
by means of non-dual wisdom, one knows all dualities... (up to) ...by means of inexhaustible wisdom, one knows all that is exhausted.

All [these] know the provisional through real wisdom, manifesting the unimpeded simultaneous practice of both. Within this, the distinctions are discussed vertically in terms of transformational differences, while they are distinguished horizontally in terms of diversity.
△ Third, the manifestation of function from the essence itself, thereby clarifying the simultaneous practice of both.
By means of the wisdom of the ultimate dharma-realm regarding all worlds... this is the tenth mind that is not inferior.
△ Fourth, the conclusion:
"O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of non-inferior minds generated by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas."
△ Five Exhortations:
If bodhisattvas abide in this mind, they will attain all the most supreme and non-inferior Buddha-dharmas.
△ Eight Superiorities of Wisdom (5): First, the heading.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses ten kinds of mountain-like superior resolve (*adhyāśaya*) regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because they are free from inferiority, their myriad practices transcend all others, and their height is difficult to gaze upon;
because they resolutely act for the sake of the supreme, they proceed directly toward Bodhi and cannot be shaken. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? Part Two: Explaining the Ten. First, the diligent cultivation of the wisdom that realizes [the truth].
"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly applies his attention... (up to) "...this is the first mountain-like superior mind."
△ Second, constantly contemplating the principle realized:
one perpetually contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, and that there is nothing to be apprehended. This is the second mountain-like superior mind.
△ Third, cultivating the untainted internally.
Vowing to practice the bodhisattva conduct for immeasurable eons—this is the third mountain-like superior mind.
△ Fourth, externally associating with virtuous persons.
For the sake of seeking all Buddha-dharmas, one should serve spiritual friends with an impartial mind, without any divergent aspirations,
such as seeking fame and profit or other pursuits,
and without any intention to steal the Dharma.
Having heard the words from another and understood them, one steals the Dharma. The *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states that such a person falls into hell as swiftly as an arrow shot.
This serves as a warning for future students.
Only giving rise to a sense of reverence and an unprecedented resolve—this is the fourth mountain-like superior mind.
△ Fifth, the Lord of the Perfection of Great Patience:
If there are sentient beings who revile, insult, or slander [him] (up to the point where they cause it to increase further without ceasing).
Regarding the further increase of the great vows: it is like fire when fuel is added.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva [regarding] all phenomena... this is the fifth mountain-like superior mind.
△ Sixth, decisively transcending the realm of Māra.
Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish supreme and great merit (up to) dwelling in the realm of the Buddha, they do not become attached despite achieving these excellent virtues;
they sustain themselves solely with the joy of the Dharma. Thus, all realms of Māra become the realm of the Buddha.
The object.
This is the sixth mountain-like superior mind.
△ Seventh, diligent and courageous cultivation.
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, practice the bodhisattva path without ceasing. As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"Though the fool practices for but a short time, his mind of indolence suspects that it has been long; the Buddha, throughout immeasurable kalpas, regards diligent vigor as but a moment."
This is the seventh mountain-like superior mind.
△ Eighth, not abandoning evil persons.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows all sentient beings... [as above] ...this is the eighth mountain-like superior mind.
△ Ninth, the Buddha of Solitary Distinction, etc.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further forms this thought... (up to) this is the ninth mountain-like superior mind.
△ Tenth, the dual practice of the provisional and the real, in four parts. First, the formal exposition of the dual practice.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva performs such contemplation (up to) the vow for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
△ Second, the interrogation and explanation, in two parts. First, the interrogation.
Why is this? There are two points of inquiry. First: cultivation must accord with principle; since principle is ultimately unattainable, why not abandon one's vows?
Yet if one does not abandon one's vows, what is the use of contemplating non-existence? Thus, there is an obstacle whether one proceeds or retreats. Second, the explanation.
The Bodhisattva seeks all dharmas but finds nothing to be attained, up to and including *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This explanation also has two meanings. First, it says: if there were anything to be attained, one would not attain *bodhi*; because there is no attainment, *bodhi* is brought forth.
Although one does not abandon one's vows, one must contemplate non-attainment. Second, it says: the dharma of non-attainment does not exist [in a fixed location].
One attains the external; yet one must seek all dharmas before reaching the ultimate source of non-attainment.
Therefore, if one wishes to realize non-attainment, one must not abandon the vow for bodhi. △ Third, the conclusion establishing the dual practice.
Therefore, although there is nothing to be apprehended regarding phenomena... his mind is neither startled nor terrified by this.
△ Fourth, revealing his freedom from faults:
he does not form such thoughts as "if all phenomena... [up to] "...seeking the path of unsurpassed bodhi."
This means that because one does not fear emptiness and does not seek it [as an object], this is the tenth mountain-like superior mind.
△ Four: Conclusion.
O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of mountain-like superior resolve of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
△ Fifth, the exhortation:
If all Bodhisattvas dwell securely within these [resolves], they will attain the superior resolve of the Great King of Mountains of Unsurpassed Supreme Wisdom.
△ Ninth: The Five on Profound and Vast Wisdom. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has ten kinds of entry [into] the ocean-like wisdom that reaches up to *samyaksambodhi*."
It is not merely that he seeks to ascend to the loftiest heights; it is also that his essence of wisdom encompasses all.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are these ten?
△ Third, the explanation, which has two parts. First, the four [stages] correspond to the four immeasurable realms.
That which is called "entering all infinite realms of sentient beings" (up to) "this is the fourth ocean-like wisdom.
△ The subsequent six [wisdoms] are all derived from the opening of the infinity of the Buddha-realm. First, one enters the roots of goodness of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, regarding the past, future, and present... this is the fifth ocean-like wisdom.
△ Second, entering the realm of the Buddhas of the past.
In every thought-moment, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... this is the sixth ocean-like wisdom.
△ Third, entering the realm of future Buddhas:
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the future world... this is the seventh ocean-like wisdom.
△ Fourth, entering the realm of the Buddhas of the present.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the world of the present... this is the eighth ocean-like wisdom.
△ Fifth, making offerings to many Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [regarding] the unspeakable... this is the ninth ocean-like wisdom.
△ Sixth, seeking manifold dharmas:
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in the presence of all Buddhas... this is the tenth ocean-like wisdom.
△ 4. Conclusion: "O Sons of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of ocean-like wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas regarding the three types of *sambodhi*.
By means of this causal ocean, one enters the resultant ocean. △ 5. Exhortation.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the ocean of the supreme, great wisdom of all Buddhas.
△ The fourth major section contains twenty-nine gates, answering twenty-nine phrases regarding practice within the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Including the general phrase on non-obstruction, there are thirty gates. The ancient masters divided this into three parts; the first consists of eleven gates.
The first section clarifies the firmness of the essence of practice within the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Next, twelve gates clarify the mastery of the application of practice.
Finally, seven gates clarify the perfection of the virtues of practice. Herein, these are also sequentially correlated with the ten dedications.
Among them, the first four gates clarify the first dedication; the second and third dedications each have two gates; and the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh [dedications]...
Each has but a single gate. The eighth dedication corresponds to the ten non-obstructions; the ninth has three gates, and the tenth has four gates, as shall be understood from the text itself.
Herein, first, the four gates clarify the practices within the stage of the Dedication of Saving and Protecting Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings.
This is divided into four parts. First, the clarification of the roots of goodness of dedication, which is further divided into four: first, the heading.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of jewel-like abodes for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is because the roots of goodness in which they abide are noble and perfect. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation: First, serving many Buddhas.
"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to go to [all of them]... This is the first jewel-like dwelling.
△ Second, hearing and upholding the Dharma.
From being in the presence of inconceivable Tathāgatas... this is the second jewel-like dwelling.
△ Third, mastery over rebirth.
Passing away from this world-system and manifesting birth in another (up to) this is the third jewel-like abiding.
△ Fourth, the teaching on the primary and secondary dharmas:
knowing that all dharmas emerge from a single dharma, one is able to analyze and expound each of them individually.
First, one proceeds from the root to the branches, as in the *Anantārtha-sūtra*: "All phenomena arise from a single dharma.
This single dharma is what is called "signlessness" (*animitta*), because the various meanings of all phenomena ultimately converge into this one meaning.
Next, by subsuming the branches back into the root, the preceding meaning is explained and established.
This constitutes the fourth [stage], the Abiding Like a Treasure.
△ Fifth, Mastery over Knowledge and Severance.
One knows how to weary of and become detached from the afflictions, and one knows how to bring the afflictions to rest.
On the path of accumulation, one knows how to weary of and bring them to rest;
one knows how to guard against the afflictions.
The path of preparation (prayoga-mārga) provides protection;
knowing that it eliminates and abandons the afflictions (kleśa),
the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) cuts them off, eliminating them so they are no longer grasped.
While practicing the bodhisattva path, one does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) until finally reaching its further shore.

This entry into realization via the path of liberation differs from that of the two vehicles; for only by retaining afflictions without severing them can one ultimately achieve their total abandonment and realization.
Having skillfully trained in the methods of skillful means (upāyakauśalya), they attain complete fulfillment without their bodies ever becoming weary.

How could they fail to realize [the goal]? Because they have skillfully trained in the boundless Buddha-dharmas and fulfilled their former great vows, it is like an arrow shot into the sky that remains fixed because its notch is caught.
This is the fifth dwelling like a treasure.
△ Sixth, the simultaneous practice of compassion and wisdom:
knowing the conceptual discriminations of the minds of all sentient beings... [up to] this is the sixth dwelling like a treasure.
Seventh, the unimpeded knowledge of the nature and characteristics [of phenomena]: knowing that all dharmas are of one and the same nature... this is the seventh jewel-like dwelling.
Eighth, the attainment of non-attainment.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva seeks the Buddha but finds him unobtainable... this is the eighth jewel-like dwelling.
△ Ninth, contemplating emptiness to fulfill vows:
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows skillful preaching of the Dharma... this is the ninth jewel-like dwelling.
△ Tenth, practicing without weariness.
Regarding the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s state of being unsurpassed (up to) not being startled, not being terrified, not being deluded, and not being confused:
the former [section] clearly manifests this, while the latter provides the explanation and establishment.
Because one knows that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is inconceivable... this is the tenth jewel-like dwelling.
△ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation:
"O Son of the Buddha, these are the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ [jewel-like dwellings]... whereby they attain the unsurpassed great wisdom-treasure of all Buddhas."
△ Second, the fourfold protection through great vows. First, the heading:
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives rise to ten kinds of Mahāyāna vow-minds that are like adamant.
Although all dedications involve vows, this one is placed first because it concerns both future tasks and present practices;
it is without limit, requiring a firm mind that exhausts their very bounds. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? Second, the explanation of the ten: First, the vow to know that the Dharma-gates are inexhaustible.
"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... [up to] "...this is the first diamond-like resolve for the Great Vehicle."
△ Second, the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva forms this thought... [up to] the second adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind.
△ 3. Adorning the Buddha-field.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forms this thought... [up to] the third, the Vajra-like Mahāyāna vow-mind. △ 4. Dedication.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva forms this thought... [up to] the fourth adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind.
△ Fifth, making offerings to the Buddhas.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva forms this thought... [up to] the fifth adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind.
The first three vows concern the fruit of Buddhahood; the first five are all based on what will be accomplished, and are discussed horizontally as being boundless.
The subsequent two are based on what is currently enacted, and are both vertically profound and without limit. △ Sixth: Non-attachment to seeing or hearing.
O Son of the Buddha, from the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... this is the sixth, the adamantine-like resolve of the Great Vehicle.
△ Seventh: Patience and Non-distraction.
O Son of the Buddha, if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is subjected by sentient beings to [any of these], up to and including having his eyes gouged out or his head cut off—
where "cutting off" means decapitating him—
he is able to endure all such things, up to and including the seventh: the adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind.
The first two vows are for severing afflictions; the latter three shall likewise be accomplished. △ Eighth, universally throughout time and place, one practices the two benefits.
From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... up to "...this is the eighth adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind."
△ Ninth: Accomplishing boundless great conduct through the essential core of the mind.
O Son of the Buddha, from the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... this is the ninth adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind.
△ Third, the three aspects of quiescent arising of function. First, awakening to quiescence:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that the Buddha is unobtainable... [omitted] ...dwelling in nirvāṇa, dwelling in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)."
△ Second, the manifestation of activity.
Yet he does not abandon any of his great vows (up to) not abandoning the adornment of worlds.
△ Third, the explanation and establishment. Within this section, there are three layers of inquiry and explanation. First instance.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not abandon or distance his mind from all sentient beings.
This means that the reason [the Bodhisattva] acts through function while remaining in quiescence is that he does not abandon compassion due to the wisdom of his original vow.
△ Second section.
Why is this? Because all phenomena (*dharmas*) are non-existent [and so forth], one clearly and distinctly illuminates the nature of all phenomena.
The reason wisdom does not abandon compassion is that wisdom also exists for the sake of sentient beings. △ Third, the latter section has two parts. First, the inquiry.
Why is this? The underlying intent of the inquiry is: why must these two proceed together? △ Second, the explanation has two points. First, all Buddhas are thus.
All Buddhas abide in quiescent extinction... how could I now abandon great compassion?
△ Second, my former vows are superior.
Furthermore, I previously made vast and great vows... up to the tenth, the adamantine Mahāyāna vow-mind.
△ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation:
"O Son of the Buddha, this is the unsurpassed great supernormal wisdom of adamantine nature of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
