△ III. The Purpose of Dedication. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of great initiations for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
namely, the initiation of dedication, so that it may be brought before them. △ II. The Inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation.
First, the six [aspects] of self-perfection. Of these, the first three concern the greatness of meritorious action.
The Buddha-son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, forms this thought... (up to)... this is the third great undertaking.

△ Second and third, the greatness of the activity of transformation (*nirmāṇa-karman*). Furthermore, one forms this thought: "I shall teach, transform, and subdue [beings]... and thereby adorn all worlds.
This adornment is also for the purpose of gathering in sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgraha*).
This is the fifth great undertaking... up to... this is the sixth great undertaking.
△ Second, the four superior advancements; the first two superior advancements comprise merit.
Furthermore, he forms this thought: "Those Tathāgatas are immeasurable and boundless... (up to) "...this is the eighth great undertaking.
△ Regarding the latter two superior advancements—the arising of transformation—there are two parts. First, the realization of the essence.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects thus (up to): "This is the ninth great undertaking.
△ Second, the manifestation of activity.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects thus (up to): "This is the tenth great undertaking."
△ 4. Conclusion. "O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds of great undertakings of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
△ 5. Exhortation.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas (up to) being fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom.
△ Fifth, the fulfillment of what is to be accomplished, in four parts. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of ultimate great matters.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are these ten?
△ Third, the explanation:
namely, from "respectfully making offerings to all Tathāgatas" up to "the ultimate great matter of the True Dharma of all Buddhas.
△ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation.
These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, [they will attain] the ultimate state of great wisdom.

△ Second, there are two sections clarifying the practice within the indestructible dedication (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*). First, the direct clarification of the four types of indestructibility. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of indestructible faith.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are these ten?
△ Third, the explanation:
namely, the indestructible faith in all Buddhas (up to) the indestructible faith in the subduing of all sentient beings.
This has been explained previously within the ten points of meaning. △ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation.
These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain unshakable faith in the supreme great wisdom.
△ Second, the dedication of practice, which consists of four parts. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
△ Second, the inquiry: What are these ten?
△ Third, the explanation:
This refers to those who possess profound internal understanding and receive a prediction of enlightenment;
they comprehend the Buddha’s mind.
One who is able to give rise to the various roots of goodness of a bodhisattva in accordance with the truth receives the prediction of enlightenment;
one who possesses the roots of goodness conducive to liberation and cultivates vast practices receives the prediction of enlightenment.
The great practices have already been cultivated. Regarding the upper three [stages], they mostly concern the three types of noble persons (*śaikṣa*).
There is receiving the prediction of enlightenment in the presence [of the Buddha] and receiving the prediction of enlightenment not in his presence;
these two refer to being face-to-face versus not being face-to-face. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "For those who are not in this assembly, you should [act as their teacher]..."
It is proclaimed that by realizing bodhi through the testimony of one's own mind, one receives the prediction [of enlightenment].
On the first bhūmi, one realizes suchness (tathatā).
One attains the prediction [of enlightenment] upon achieving patience (*kṣānti*).
At the eighth stage, one achieves patience;
by teaching and disciplining sentient beings, one receives the prediction.
On the ninth stage, one possesses the methods for training and transforming others;
having reached the ultimate limit of all kalpas, one receives the prediction of enlightenment.
On the tenth stage, the three great kalpas are fulfilled.
All bodhisattvas attain the prediction of enlightenment through mastery over their practices;

having realized equal awakening, they enter the profound mystery (*chongxuan*), and thus they are said to possess "mastery. This is as recorded in the case of Maitreya and others. If one considers them according to the sequential arrangement of stages (*xingbu*):

This stage of dedication consists only of the first five; they are included here for the sake of convenience. If considered from the perspective of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), however, they all pertain to these ten.
△ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation.
These are the ten; if bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will receive the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas.
△ Third, there are two sections. Second, practicing the dedication that is equal to all Buddhas. First, being equal to the roots of goodness of the Buddhas, which has four parts. First, the heading.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of [vows] whereby all roots of goodness are entirely dedicated.

This section correctly clarifies "equality with the Buddhas. The Buddha is the true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); "equality" (*sama*) carries the meaning of being identical. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, "by means of my roots of goodness, [I shall] accord with the mind of the spiritual friend" (up to) "by means of my roots of goodness, [I shall] accord with the mind of the spiritual friend."
The mind is precisely compassion and wisdom as its essence.
One should accomplish this in such a way that there is no separate accomplishment [other than this], so that through my roots of goodness, I may be equal to my spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Being thus equal, one accords with the principle.
"Thus accomplished, not otherwise accomplished" (repeated as "thus accomplished, not otherwise accomplished").
The remaining [phrases] each have their own distinct meaning; yet they are all said to be "identical" because they share the same essence (*ekasvabhāva*) and no dual characteristics are perceived.
Therefore, the heading states: "By this, one is able to dedicate all roots of goodness. △ Fourth, the conclusion.
These are the ten; if bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme dedication of roots of goodness.
△ Second, the accomplishment of the practice of dedication has four parts. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten ways of attaining wisdom.
As that text says: "Abiding in this samādhi, they enter the realm of profound and pure wisdom," and so forth. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? Part Three: The Explanation.
That is to say, attaining wisdom through mastery over giving... [and so forth] ...attaining wisdom through variously adorned speech and sound.

△ 4. Conclusion and Exhortation. This constitutes the tenth [chapter]. If all bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas... (up to) ...the unsurpassed, manifestly realized wisdom (*abhisamaya-jñāna*) of all Buddhas.
△ 4. Within the practice of dedication to all places, there are four parts. First, the heading.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of generating immeasurable, boundless, and vast minds.
Because they are immeasurable and boundless, there is nowhere they do not reach. Since their objects are immeasurable and boundless, the mind is as vast as those objects.
△ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, generating immeasurable [vows] before all Buddhas... up to generating an immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind.
△ Four: The Conclusion and Exhortation.
This constitutes the tenth [chapter]. If all bodhisattvas abide in this mind... (up to) ...the boundless and vast ocean of wisdom. △ Five:
Within the practice of the inexhaustible treasury of merit, there are four sections. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of treasuries (*nidhi*).
Because all dharmas contain these ten meanings, they are called "treasuries. When observing them as they truly are, those who are deluded do not see them;
therefore, they are called "hidden" (*vinigūḍha*). △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, knowing that all dharmas are the treasury for initiating meritorious conduct (up to) the treasury for generating joyful pure faith.
Each of these consists of ten; these are called the inexhaustible merits. △ Fourth, the conclusion of the contemplation:
"If bodhisattvas abide in these ten dharmas... they are able to fully subdue all sentient beings."
△ Six: Following and conforming to the practice of dedicating all roots of goodness with firm resolve. Part Four. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of discipline for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas."

The previous section extensively treated giving (*dāna*) as the primary practice to clarify the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*); the present section briefly distinguishes ethical discipline (*saṃvara*) as the fundamental practice.
Since all roots of goodness accord with the principle of equality and truly pervade everything, the eighth fascicle states:
"All roots of goodness are made to reach fulfillment. This "fulfillment" carries the meaning of being in accordance with firmness. 2. The Interrogation.
What are the ten? Part Three: The Explanation.
That is to say, the discipline that brings all Buddha-dharmas (up to) all pāramitās to complete fulfillment.
These ten phrases of universal clarity encompass all that is wholesome and beneficial, leaving nothing unfulfilled; they pervade all virtues, which can be clearly understood.
△ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation:
These are the ten. If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme discipline of great wisdom.
△ Seven: The fourth section within the dedication that accords with all sentient beings in their equality. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of mastery belonging to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."
They possess the ten masteries because they are able to act in accordance with them.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are the ten?
△ Third, the explanation.

That which is called mastery over life (*jīvita-vaśitā*) refers to [attaining] perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) throughout unspeakable eons (*anabhilāpya-kalpa*) in the ten directions with fearlessness.
The meaning of the ten masteries is as explained in the Eighth Stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*). △ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation.
These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, [they attain] wisdom, spiritual power, and mastery over enlightenment.
Below this, one enters the fifty-sixth sūtra.
△ Eighth, the practice within the dedication of the aspect of true suchness (*tathatā*).
Because there is no obstruction regarding true suchness, the fruit of that stage is described as: "Abiding in this stage, one attains the equality of all lands.
Equality is both the cause of non-obstruction and the meaning of non-obstruction. Furthermore, it says: "One attains the Buddha’s immeasurable and perfect body. (1)

The passage beginning with "The body fills all worlds" precisely clarifies the meaning of non-obstruction. It consists of four sections; the first is the general heading, which comprises ten chapters.
Within this, there are three parts, the first of which is the heading itself.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of non-obstruction.
The preceding section clarified mastery (*vaśitā*), which refers to the spontaneous nature of activity; this section clarifies non-obstruction, revealing that activity is free from constraint.
△ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the enumeration:
namely, the unimpeded function of sentient beings (up to) the unimpeded function of spiritual power and the unimpeded function of power.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of unimpededness (*anāvaraṇa*): first, knowledge (*jñāna*), and second, objects (*vastu*). Among these ten [bases], some are general and some are specific.

However, regarding the unimpededness of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-anāvaraṇa*), it mostly refers only to knowledge, as in the cases of the bodies [of Buddhas] and lands. It mostly refers only to objects, as in the case of sentient beings and so forth.

There are instances where both objects and knowledge are involved. Nevertheless, unimpededness regarding objects necessarily involves knowledge; however, the objects of unimpeded knowledge do not necessarily involve objects. (2)
All are the function of the essence itself; therefore, they are collectively termed "unimpeded functions. Yet, all ten penetrate both self-benefit and benefiting others.
For now, we shall explain them according to the aspect of transformation (*nirmāṇa*). First, there is that which is transformed; second, the place of transformation;

and the remainder are all those that transform, namely the transformative teachings and the transformative bodies, which can be understood through reflection. II. General Inquiry into the Ten Chapters.
"O Son of the Buddha, what is the unimpeded activity of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva regarding the equality of all sentient beings?
△ Third, the detailed explanation according to the chapters, which consists of ten sections. Each passage contains four parts: the heading, the inquiry, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Now, first is the unimpeded function regarding the sentient beings to be converted. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of unimpeded functions regarding sentient beings for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
Second, the inquiry.
What are these ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, the unimpeded function of knowing that all sentient beings are without sentient beings.
Because one has realized the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
one knows that all sentient beings are sustained merely by conceptualization,
and that their unimpeded functioning is a manifestation of mind alone. These two constitute ultimate wisdom.
To preach the Dharma for all sentient beings without ever missing the proper time is the unimpeded function [of wisdom].

Preaching the Dharma according to the appropriate time is precisely expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). The aforementioned three are distinguished as unimpeded in terms of wisdom; the remaining seven are unimpeded in terms of phenomena (*dharma*).
The unimpeded function of universally manifesting throughout all realms of sentient beings;
the unimpeded function of being able to manifest sentient beings and place them all within a single pore without any crowding or obstruction.
Having recently gathered a single hair,
he manifests all worlds in other directions for the sake of all sentient beings, displaying his unimpeded power so that they may all see them;
thus he reveals distant lands in other realms.

For the sake of all sentient beings, he manifests the unimpeded function [of the Buddha], from the forms of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors up to the attainment of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
The remaining four [bodies] all manifest as the bodies of preeminent leaders. △ Fourth, the conclusion.
These are the ten.
△ Second, the fourfold unimpeded function regarding lands. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of unimpeded functions regarding lands."
△ 2. Inquiry: What are the ten?
△ 3. Explanation.
This refers to making all lands into a single land (extending up to) manifesting this universally to all sentient beings through unimpeded function.
To know that lands are inexhaustible is precisely the penetration of the wisdom-penetration (*jñāna-abhijñā*) and the object-penetration (*vastu-abhijñā*). Therefore, the Jin translation states:
"In all lands, one deeply enters inexhaustible skillful means. The *Dushi jing* states: "That which is entered within all Buddha-realms is inexhaustible; all are penetrated."
This is the matter. The remaining nine are only unimpeded in terms of phenomena (*vastu*). "Profound" refers to subtle lands; the rest can be understood accordingly. △ Fourth, the conclusion:
These constitute the ten.
△ Section Three: The Fourfold Unimpeded Function of the Dharma. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of unimpeded function regarding the Dharma.
That is to say, all are based on wisdom; because they are entirely sovereign, they are able to know and expound all dharmas that are unimpeded in their nature and characteristics."
△ 2. Inquiry: What are the ten?
△ 3. Explanation.
This refers to knowing that all phenomena enter into a single phenomenon (up to) the unimpeded function of not contradicting the mental understandings of sentient beings;
such that the one and the many immediately interpenetrate without destroying their original nature.
From the *prajñāpāramitā* all dharmas are born (up to: causing all to awaken through unimpeded function.
True wisdom gives rise to skillful means;
knowing that all dharmas are beyond words, it causes sentient beings to all attain awakening and entry through unimpeded function.
To reveal the non-textual through the textual;
to know that all phenomena enter into a single characteristic while being able to expound immeasurable characteristics of phenomena without obstruction;
and to manifest many characteristics through a single teaching.
The unimpeded function of knowing that all phenomena are beyond verbal expression, yet being able to teach infinite dharma-gates to others;
the unimpeded function of skillfully revolving the universal wheel of syllables (*pramukha-akṣara-cakra*) through speech that is no-speech regarding all phenomena.
A single word fully encompasses the meaning of the syllable *vṛtta*.
As explained in the section on Megha, all phenomena enter into a single dharma-gate; thus, his teaching is inexhaustible and possesses unimpeded function.
Each gate mutually encompasses the others.
By causing all phenomena to enter into the Buddha-dharma, it brings about the unimpeded function through which all sentient beings attain awakening and understanding.
Thus, the conventional is subsumed within the ultimate.
He knows that all phenomena have no limit and possess unimpeded function;
he knows them horizontally as being boundless.
He knows that all phenomena have the limit of non-obstruction, and he possesses the inexhaustible, unimpeded function of preaching for the sake of sentient beings.
Vertically exhausting its limits. △ Fourth, the conclusion:
"These constitute the ten.
△ Fourth, the unimpeded function of the body, in four parts. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of unimpeded functions of the body.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are these ten?
△ 3. Explanation:
That is to say, from "the bodies of all sentient beings" (up to) "the unimpeded function of manifesting the bodies of all sentient beings.
△ 4. Conclusion.
These are the ten. △ Five:
The Unimpeded Function of Vows, Part Four. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of unimpeded functions of vows."
△ 2. Inquiry: What are the ten?
△ 3. Explanation.
This refers to the unimpeded function [of the Bodhisattva] that, by means of all the vows of a Bodhisattva, thoroughly satisfies the realms of all sentient beings.
△ Fourth, the conclusion:
These constitute the ten.
△ Section Six: The Unimpeded Function of the Object-Sphere, Part Four. First, the heading:
"O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of unimpeded functions regarding the object-sphere.
That is to say, within these ten types of objects—superior and inferior, and mutually contradictory—they manifest the inferior within the superior, turning them about without impediment. This is...
This constitutes the scope of the Bodhisattva’s stage. △ Second, the inquiry: What are the ten?
△ Third, the explanation.
This refers to [the qualities] from "abiding in the realm of the *dharmadhātu* without abandoning sentient beings" up to "the unimpeded function of tranquil deportment.
△ Fourth, the conclusion:
These constitute the ten.
△ Section Seven: The Unimpeded Function of the Ten Knowledges (Four Parts). First, the heading:
"O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of unimpeded function of knowledge (*jñāna-asaṅga-prayoga*).
Although there have been instances of knowledge in the preceding sections, each was categorized according to its respective primary class; now, however, they are treated exclusively as such."

As for the function of that wisdom: yet wisdom is not manifold; it is distinguished by reason of the dharmas. Following the dharmas with respect to wisdom constitutes the unimpeded [knowledge] of dharmas (*dharmapratisaṃvid*);
following wisdom with respect to the dharmas—△ second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, the unimpeded function of inexhaustible eloquence; the unimpeded function of never forgetting any of the *dhāraṇīs*.
These two are the wisdoms of emanation (*nirmāṇa-jñāna*);
they possess the unimpeded function of being able to definitively know and definitively teach [the Dharma] to all sentient beings, administering medicine according to their respective needs.
These three are the wisdoms that know those to be converted (*vineya-jñāna*).
In a single thought-moment, one is able to enter the unimpeded function of the Tathāgata’s ten powers.
This constitutes the ultimate entry into Buddha-wisdom; the preceding six [powers] are all provisional wisdoms.
By means of unimpeded wisdom, one knows all kalpas of the three periods of time, reaching to the point where there is no interruption—this is the unimpeded function.
These two— the unimpeded wisdom of the non-obstruction between the provisional and the real—
possess the unimpeded function of knowing the thoughts of all sentient beings through the thought of a single sentient being, and so on, up to understanding the languages of all sentient beings.
These two constitute the wisdom of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena. △ Fourth, the conclusion: "These are the ten.
△ Eighth, the unimpeded functions of the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), in four parts. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of unimpeded functions of supernormal powers (abhijñā).
△ Second, the inquiry: What are these ten?
△ Third, the explanation:
This refers to the unimpeded function of manifesting the bodies of all worlds within a single body,
as well as the supernormal power of innumerable form-bodies.
The unimpeded function of hearing and receiving all the teachings expounded within the assemblies of all Buddhas within a single assembly of a Buddha;
the divine ear;
and the unimpeded function of awakening the minds of all sentient beings within the mental thoughts of a single sentient being.

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds: by means of a single sound, they manifest the various verbal expressions of all worlds, such that each person attains understanding; this is their unimpeded function of discerning speech and terminology.
Within a single thought-moment, one manifests all kalpas of the past limit (up to the point where) one attains the unimpeded function of complete knowledge and vision;
this is the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). Therefore, the *Dushi jing* names it "seeing previous lives."
To cause all worlds to be fully adorned through unimpeded function;
to travel to all Buddha-fields through pervasive adornment—this is its specific meaning.
To universally enter all three periods of time through unimpeded function.
The future eons are included; since the past has already been clarified, all three periods of time are mentioned together.
It emits the great light of the Dharma, manifesting the unimpeded function of the bodhi, the practices, and the vows of all Buddhas and sentient beings.
This is the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-jñāna-abhijñā*). Therefore, Dushi (Dharmarakṣa) said:
"The practices established by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas radiate the light of the Dharma to illuminate them; this is precisely the illumination of the Buddha-Dharma by the light of the Dharma."
It is the unimpeded function of the bodhisattva’s roots of goodness, which skillfully protects all devas and nāgas (up to the ten powers of the Tathāgata).

This is precisely the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). As Dūshī translates it: "Because one knows and sees all things equally. That is to say, seeing that there is something to be done, one protects and guards it.
According to the Jin edition, the tenth [verse] states: "O Son of the Buddha, briefly stated, the bodhisattva’s impartial contemplation of all phenomena..."
The supernormal power of mastery over phenomena (*dharmābhijñā*) is precisely the samādhi of the cessation of all phenomena (*sarvadharmakṣaya-samādhi*).

Because it penetrates the equality of quiescent extinction, the *Dushi jing* (Sūtra on Crossing the World) states: "The Bodhisattva is equal; he quiets all sounds and, through this equality, governs sentient beings.

This passage is omitted in the current text, which merely provides a brief illustration; thus, it does not proceed by way of exhaustion. In its general purport, it does not differ from the ten supernormal powers (*daśābhijñā*).
Section on Analysis. △ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation:
These are the ten; if bodhisattvas attain this unimpeded function, they are then able to universally enter all Buddha-dharmas.
△ Ninth, the fourfold unimpededness of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of unimpeded applications of spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*).
While supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) generally refer to external functions that are unobstructed, spiritual powers generally refer to internal capacities for mastery.
Therefore, among these, the ten powers (*daśabala*) mostly concern such things as containing and encompassing [the universe] within a single hair. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are these ten?
△ Third, the explanation:
namely, by means of unspeakable worlds [up to] causing all sentient beings to fully attain awakening and understanding through unimpeded function.

This refers to the power of the body (*kāyabala*), while the latter refers to the power of wisdom (*jñānabala*). If one were to subsume these powers under the category of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the ten kinds of spiritual powers would be nothing more than the single supernormal power of the basis of psychic transformation (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*).
Since the powers of the body and wisdom are thus distinguished as two distinct types, among the ten supernormal powers, the power of the basis of psychic transformation is mentioned only briefly.
△ Four conclusions.
These constitute ten.
△ Regarding the unimpeded function of the ten powers, there are four [sections]. First, the heading.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of unimpeded functions of power.
Because the powers of both compassion and wisdom are entirely unimpeded, they also possess unimpeded functional efficacy; this is explained here from the perspective of their predominant aspects.
△ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, the unimpeded function of the power of sentient beings (extending to) not abandoning any sentient being.
△ Fourth, the conclusion.
These constitute the ten [points].
△ Fourth, the general conclusion on the benefits.
O Son of the Buddha, this is called the Bodhisattva’s [stage] up to the gate of skillful manifestation of unimpeded activity.
Whether desiring to accomplish or not to accomplish, one has already attained non-obstruction; attaining the fruit without abandoning the cause further manifests this non-obstruction.
△ Ninth, there are three gates clarifying the practice of the dedication of liberation that is neither bound nor attached. This contains one hundred gates in detail.
This is revealed through liberation from bondage and attachment, whereby one accomplishes the sovereign wisdom and activity of Samantabhadra.
Herein, I shall briefly distinguish three aspects, divided into three sections: first, the gate of sporting according to one’s will; second, the gate clarifying that the realm is immeasurable;

and third, the gate clarifying the efficacy of wisdom and activity. All of these arise from being without bondage and without attachment. Now, for the first section, there are four parts; first, the heading.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of playful mastery (*vikrīḍita*).
They act according to their will, having achieved perfection, and they move and enjoy themselves with sovereign ease.
△ Second, the inquiry: What are these ten?
△ Third, the explanation: these are subsumed into five pairs.
That is to say, taking the body of sentient beings as the body of a buddha-field (and so forth, until) not destroying the body of a buddha-field is the bodhisattva’s playful sport (*vikrīḍita*).

Although they manifest through the characteristics of the primary and secondary, the defiled and the pure, they do not destroy their original nature; this clearly demonstrates the meaning of "playful sport" (*līlā*).
It is like worldly play that indulges the passions, for it causes neither harm nor agitation. All other cases should be understood in this same way.
Manifesting the bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas within the body of a Buddha (up to) is the bodhisattva’s playful exercise (*vikrīḍita*).
Manifesting the bodies of the Great and Small Vehicles interchangeably,
and manifesting the body of one who has attained perfect awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) within the body of a bodhisattva’s practice (up to) is the bodhisattva’s playful exercise.
Cause and effect manifest reciprocally.
Manifesting a body of birth and death within the realm of nirvāṇa, up to entering into nirvāṇa, is the playful sport (*vikrīḍita*) of a bodhisattva.
Birth and death and nirvāṇa manifest reciprocally.
Entering into samādhi while manifesting walking and standing (up to) that which is inexhaustible—this is the bodhisattva’s play (*vikrīḍita*).
It is mastery over concentration and dispersal: first, arising from within samādhi to manifest activity while remaining constantly in samādhi;
subsequently, entering samādhi while manifesting activity and remaining constantly active. △ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation.
These are the ten; if bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the play of unexcelled great wisdom.
△ Second, the immeasurability of the sphere of activity, in four parts. First, the heading.
O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of spheres of activity.
These encompass two types of spheres: first, the sphere of playful practice; for this reason, the Jin translation refers to them as "supreme practices" (*śreṣṭha-caryā*).
The second refers to the realm of distinct boundaries; that is, because only Bodhisattvas are able to manifest appearance and disappearance without obstruction.
△ Second, the inquiry: "What are the ten?
△ Third, the explanation.
That which is called "the manifestation of the gateways of the boundless dharma-realm" (up to) "fully employing skillful means to bring about awakening" is the domain of the bodhisattva.
The first three [of these] are the domains traversed by practice; the latter seven are all domains of formal limits.
From the body of the Tathāgata, the bodies of bodhisattvas emerge (up to) the attainment of perfect enlightenment; this is the domain of the bodhisattva.
△ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation:
These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, (up to) they enter the domain of unsurpassed great wisdom.
△ Third, the function of the three knowledges, which has four parts. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of powers.
△ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, the power of the profound mind, because it is not mixed with any worldly sentiments.
Because he seeks [the Dharma] with single-minded intensity, it is explained as being "unmixed.
Because his superior mental power does not abandon any of the Buddha-dharmas, he deeply seeks the Buddha-dharmas; the Buddha-dharmas themselves are the "superior" element.
Because all that is undertaken through the power of skillful means is brought to completion.
As for "bringing what is undertaken to completion," it is due to expertise; the three aforementioned [powers] are for self-benefit:
the power of wisdom realizes all mental activities, while the power of aspiration fulfills all that is sought.
These two constitute the power of benefiting others, because their practice continues without interruption until the end of the future, and because they do not abandon the Mahāyāna.
These two pertain to both types of benefit [for self and others]. The preceding seven constitute the power of one's own nature (*svabhāva*).
Because of the power of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi-bala*), [the Buddha manifests] within each and every pore [up to] the various faculties, dispositions, and desires of all sentient beings.
These are the three powers of supreme progress. △ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation.
These are the ten; if bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, [they attain] the supreme ten powers of all-knowledge.
△ There are fourteen sections clarifying the practice of the immeasurable dedication within the *dharmadhātu*. This is divided into three parts.
The first section clarifies the roots of goodness to be dedicated. (Four parts. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of fearlessness.

What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation of the ten. First is the fearlessness of hearing and retaining.

△ Second, the fearlessness of eloquence (*pratibhāna-vaiśāradya*).
From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva receives the consecration of the Tathāgata" up to [the description of] the second fearlessness of the Bodhisattva.

O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are empty; this constitutes the Bodhisattva’s third fearlessness.
Having thoroughly realized the two kinds of emptiness, he does not fear deluded thoughts, and his four modes of deportment remain flawless; it is for these reasons that he is fearless.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is protected by the power of the Buddhas... this is the fourth fearlessness of a Bodhisattva.

O Son of the Buddha, the physical, verbal, and mental actions of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... this is the fifth fearlessness of a Bodhisattva.

O Son of the Buddha, from the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi onwards, this constitutes the sixth fearlessness of the Bodhisattva:
not fearing any māras or non-Buddhists. △ Seventh, the fearlessness of right mindfulness.
O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already attained accomplishment... this is the seventh fearlessness of a Bodhisattva:
fearlessness regarding forgetfulness. △ Eighth, the fearlessness of skillful means.

not fearing birth and death, like one who has well-repaired a ship and thus does not dread the perils of the sea. △ Ninth: Fearlessness in the Mind of Omniscience.
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva never forgets or loses [this resolve]... this is the ninth fearlessness of the Bodhisattva.

not fearing an inability to transform and give birth to beings. △ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation.

What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation. First, the practice for one's own benefit:
"O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, without relying on the instruction of others... (up to) "...cultivating the six perfections and the uncommon dharmas."

The Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, are universally able to embrace [the teachings] up to the uncommon dharmas of diligently gathering in sentient beings.
△ 3. Practice of Seeking the Supreme.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas skillfully dedicate [their merit] (up to) seeking the Buddha’s wisdom and unshared qualities.

O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reaches skillfulness [in means], not clinging to his own happiness but exerting himself solely in transforming and delivering others.

"O Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas accomplish the Buddha-dharma;
by relying upon these ten, they are able to achieve it. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, not being separated from spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to accomplish the Buddha-dharma... up to... entering the realm of the Ten Powers to accomplish the Buddha-dharma.
△ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation.
This constitutes the ten [points]. If all bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas... [up to] ...the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom.
△ Third, the threefold explanation of practicing while remaining free from faults. Part one: the heading.
O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of retrogression from the Buddha-dharma that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should avoid.
[The text] enumerates ten specific faults to cause them to be avoided in general. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, [1] disparaging spiritual friends and falling away from the Buddha-dharma... up to [10] harboring resentment toward bodhisattvas and falling away from the Buddha-dharma.
△ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation:
These are the ten; if bodhisattvas distance themselves from these dharmas, they enter the bodhisattva’s path of non-arising.
△ Fourth, there are five gates that clarify the practice within the fourth bhūmi, divided into three parts. The first gate clarifies the purification of the antidotes.
There are four causes for the increase of practice. First is the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, there are ten paths of departure from birth for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
The first three stages are analogous to the mundane world; they possess afflictions such as views and attachments, just like raw food remaining in the stomach. The fourth stage—

It is entrusted with the same transcendence. It is the antidote for purification; it is able to distance one from that arising, meaning that by departing from conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*), one attains non-arising (*anutpāda*).

This reveals the maturity of practice, as one is free from the coarseness of arising. As explained at length in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, this is now the cause for the antidote of that purification, and is therefore called the "Path" (*mārga*).
In the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, there are ten Dharma-gates of Illumination (*dharmāloka-mukha*); the first is the observation of sentient beings.
[The text] has been produced. Now, I shall only expand upon this single phrase; the rest is omitted for brevity. It concludes by stating:

"Not mixed with the Two Vehicles" means that because one practices the dual cultivation [of wisdom and compassion] as described in the subsequent phrase, it is not the same as the separation from birth [attained] through the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the Two Vehicles. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, generating prajñā (up to) not abandoning any of the bodhisattva’s vows and practices—these are the ten.
△ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation:
"O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten kinds [of practices] for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas... whereby they attain the definitive dharma of a Bodhisattva.
△ Second, clarifying its purity, in four parts. First, the heading.
Buddha-sons, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of definitive dharmas (*niyata-dharma*).
The previous section clarified that which can be abandoned; this section now reveals that which is attained, because these are the supramundane definitive dharmas. Thus, the text says:
"Attaining those internal dharmas, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata. 2. The Inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, being determined to be within the lineage of the Tathāgata... (up to) being determined to gain admission to the assembly of the Tathāgatas.
The first five constitute self-effort; the latter five constitute superior progress.
They definitively manifest the lineage of the Tathāgata (up to its point where it is non-dual with that in which all Tathāgatas abide).
△ 4. Conclusion. These constitute ten [points]. △ 3.
The Threefold Existence has three sections. It clarifies the increase of practice through antidotes. This is divided into two parts. First, two sections clarify the cultivation [of the path].
The Increase of Practice. The first section correctly clarifies the fourfold increase. First, the heading:
"O Son of the Buddha, there are ten ways in which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give birth to the path of the Buddha-dharma."
"Arising from conditions" means the sense of growth, just as exhalation increases its volume.
△ Second, the inquiry: "What are the ten?
△ Third, the explanation.
That which is called "conforming to virtuous friends" is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma (up to) because of knowing the sovereignty of the Buddhas.
The preceding two [points] involve conforming to persons and believing in the Dharma.
"Arousing great vows" is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma (up to) because of knowing that karma is never lost.
These two vows and knowledges are not in vain.
Cultivating practice throughout all kalpas without weariness is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, for the purpose of bringing sentient beings to maturity.
These two— time and place— are vast and extensive;
because they do not interrupt the bodhisattva practice and give rise to the path of the Buddha-dharma, reaching throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space,
these two are continuous and all-pervasive.
The sublime practice is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharmas (up to: because it is sustained by all wholesome dharmas.
The latter two sublime practices encompass sentient beings. △ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation.
These are the ten; if bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall obtain the title of "Great Man" (mahāpuruṣa).
△ Second, the manifestation of the establishment of this distinguished name has four parts. First, the heading.
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten titles of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa).
Because their virtuous conduct increases within, their auspicious names are established without. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, they are called *bodhisattva* (up to) because they are called supreme beings (*sattva*) due to awakening to the supreme Dharma.
The first four [categories] are named according to their objects;
they are called "Supreme Sattvas" (up to) "Superior Sattvas" because they give rise to superior diligence.
These two are named according to their essential nature. All those above pertain to self-benefit.
He is called the Unsurpassed *Sattva* (up to) being called the Powerful *Sattva* because he extensively knows the ten powers (*daśabala*).
These two [aspects] benefit others.
He is called the Unequaled *Sattva* because he is peerless in the world.

This is because it universally manifests the excellence of possessing both [self-]benefit and benefit for others. The preceding [terms] are all names for the causes of one's own nature (*svabhāva-hetu*);
they are called "inconceivable" because a *sattva* attains Buddhahood in a single thought-moment.

The final one is a designation for the fruit of supreme progress (*viśeṣa-phala*). All the preceding [terms] are provisional designations established according to their qualities; thus, it is stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 46: [text follows].
The provisional names for Bodhisattvas according to their qualities are sixteenfold. The first is named *bodhisattva*, and the sixteenth is named "Dharma Master.

This is stated identically in both the eighth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Exposition of the Noble Teachings) and the twelfth chapter of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* (Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras).

Furthermore, the *Śreṣṭhidāraka-sūtra* (Sūtra of the Merchant Prince) establishes these names based on five meanings; however, fearing that such detail would be overly prolix and difficult to comprehend, it is not elaborated here. △ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation.
These are the ten; if bodhisattvas obtain these titles, they then accomplish the bodhisattva path.
△ Second, the fourfold cultivation of remedies. First, the heading:
O Son of the Buddha, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of paths.

The *Dìjīng* (Sūtra on the Stages) relies upon provisional stations to extensively clarify the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*). Now, by relying upon the actual stations, the number is increased to ten to manifest them;
all serve as remedies and are collectively the true path. △ Second, the inquiry.
What are the ten? △ Third, the explanation:
namely, "The one path is the bodhisattva path" (up to) "...because it gives birth to wisdom and skillful means."
The first two and the last one are both in name and in meaning unique [to the Bodhisattva path].

The three paths are the path of the Bodhisattva because they practice emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and thus do not cling to the triple world (*traidhātuka*).

The first three paths share both name and meaning with [the Śrāvaka vehicle]. Next, the six [paths] share their names with the Hīnayāna, but their meanings belong exclusively to the definitive teaching.
The four practices constitute the Bodhisattva path because they are well able to discern the realm of wisdom.
The faculty of concentration knows the entry into and emergence from samādhi.

The six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) constitute the path of the bodhisattva; because [the power of knowing] the deaths and births of all sentient beings, one sees through the divine eye (divyacakṣus) their dying here and being born there.
With the divine ear, one hears the Dharma teachings of all Buddhas (up to) their universal pervasion of all beings without interruption.

Upon the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), one adds the recollection of sentient beings for the sake of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). This is also because it constitutes the single factor of mindfulness within the expanded list of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
Other cases should be understood by analogy with this.
The eightfold noble path that accords with enlightenment is the bodhisattva path.
The eight right reflections accord with omniscience;
that is to say, practicing the path of right view up to entering the nine successive meditative absorptions is the bodhisattva path.
In the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), quiescence and activity proceed in tandem.
That is to say, while remaining free from desire, ill-will, and harm, one expounds the Dharma through all vocal karma without obstruction.

Although the first dhyāna is free from desire, ill-will, and harm, one transforms sentient beings by means of contrary methods, even employing speech involving desire and the like; therefore, it is said:
All vocal karma ceases through the elimination of vitarka and vicāra, yet one employs all-knowing vitarka and vicāra to teach and transform sentient beings.
Although the second dhyāna is devoid of vitarka and vicāra, it does not destroy pure awakening (*vimala-bodhi*), which serves as the causal basis for teaching.
Having abandoned both delight and attachment, one perceives the great joy of the mind of all Buddhas.
In the third dhyāna, one is detached from joy and gives rise to the joy of the Dharma;
having left behind worldly pleasure, one accords with the supramundane bliss of the bodhisattva path.
In the fourth dhyāna, one is detached from pleasure and experiences the bliss of the path of liberation.
From this state of immovability, one enters the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) yet does not abandon the rebirths of the desire and form realms.
This clarifies the four formless attainments, which are presented here in their general characteristics to manifest their excellence.
Although one abides in the meditative attainment that extinguishes all ideation and sensation (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), one does not cease the bodhisattva practice;

therefore, it is the "attainment of extinction" (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Although this attainment exhausts and extinguishes all non-permanent mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), as well as a portion of the permanent defiled states, it is named "extinction of ideation and sensation" because it is preceded by the cultivation of revulsion toward ideation and sensation.

It is certainly because, although coarse perception (*saṃjñā*) has ceased, subtle perception still remains, as this is the state of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Now, according to the explicit teaching, it is the very nature of sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth that ceases;
therefore, one does not cease the bodhisattva practices. For this reason, the *Saptamī-bhūmi* states that one is able to "enter moment by moment and also arise moment by moment," and so forth.
The rest is as explained in the Third and Seventh Stages (*bhūmi*).
To study the ten powers of a Buddha is the path of a bodhisattva (up to) not abandoning the various practices of a bodhisattva.
[The phrase] "sixth, pervading all" below refers to the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations. The eighth is the divine eye; the ninth is the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*).
Since one now knows all three periods of time, how much more so regarding past lives? The remainder is as explained in the first assembly. △ Fourth, the conclusion.
Exhortation.
These are the ten. If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas... [up to] the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed path of skillful means.
