When the youth Sudhana heard these words, he gazed up at her with deep reverence and took his leave to depart.
△ Third, the laywoman Guṇavatī. This section consists of six parts concerning her practice of non-opposition. First, seeking according to instruction, which has two sub-sections.
First, recollecting the instructions of her former friend:
At that time, the youth Sudhana observed and reflected [until he reached] those who are able to subdue the demonic armies of rival paths.
△ Second, seeking out a future companion.
Thus reflecting, he gradually traveled on until he reached the residence within this city.
△ Second, seeing, honoring, and inquiring; third, as in the fourth [section], first seeing the external environment and its resources.
Having heard this, Sudhana went immediately to her gate; on all four sides there were gates adorned with jewels.
△ Second, the primary retribution of the friend:
Having entered, Sudhana saw the upāsikā seated upon a jeweled throne, in the prime of youth, of beautiful complexion, upright and pleasing to behold.
He is dignified and pleasing to behold because of the fruit of his patience.
He wears plain garments, has his hair hanging down, and his body is without necklaces or ornaments;
these plain garments and so forth are because he has abandoned floral adornments through his practice of patience.
The color, marks, majestic virtue, and radiance of his body were such that none but Buddhas and Bodhisattvas could equal them.
△ Third, seeing the internal environment of support:
Within that residence, ten billion seats were laid out (until) only a small vessel was placed before each one.
△ Fourth, clarifying her retinue:
She is further surrounded by ten thousand young maidens,
for the myriad practices all accord with patience.
Her majestic deportment and physical appearance were like those of a celestial maiden; (until) all who beheld her body were entirely freed from lustful defilement.
△ Second, [the section on] Reverence:
At that time, Sudhana, having seen the laywoman Guṇavatī, (until) stood with palms joined, respectfully surrounding her.

△ Third, the inquiry. He addressed [the Buddha], saying: "O Noble One, I have already previously resolved [upon enlightenment] (omitted)... You are most skilled in providing instruction; I pray that you will explain it to me.
△ Third, the formal demonstration of the Dharma-realm, in two parts. First, citing the name of the Dharma-gate and paying homage.
He then addressed him, saying: "Good son, I have attained the Bodhisattva liberation of the 'Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit.
Just as objects emerge from a vessel, merit arises inexhaustibly; therefore it is called the Dharma-realm, for it is that which is summoned by merit. [Section Two:

Discerning its Functional Activity, in three parts] First, the direct manifestation of its functional activity, in three parts. First, benefiting sentient beings, in three parts. First, a general explanation.
Within such a single small vessel, one can satisfy the various desires and inclinations of all sentient beings by means of this vessel that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

Because this single small vessel is fused with the *dharmadhātu* as an inexhaustible dependent origination, its function fails in nothing it should respond to, and its response fails in nothing that would not be beneficial;
yet, the essence of the *dharmadhātu* neither increases nor decreases. Furthermore, this represents patience (*kṣānti*).
Because it necessarily arises from self-humility, it is "small. The patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) is identical to suchness; as a single flavor, it is "one.

Because the internal is empty and the external is provisional, it is called a "vessel. Since patience can encompass all without exclusion, it emerges inexhaustibly. △ Second, a specific explanation of the emergence of flavor.
Various delicious foods and drinks are produced (up to) without end and without diminishing.
△ Third, citing one case as an example for the rest:
Just as with food and drink, so too with various superior flavors (up to) all that the heart desires, they are made fully sufficient.
△ Second, benefiting those of the Two Vehicles.
Furthermore, good son, suppose it were likewise in the eastern direction (extending to) the four intermediate directions and above and below.

Although those of the Two Vehicles do not establish the name of "patience" (*kṣānti*), they are nonetheless able to endure the principle of the exhaustion of phenomena and non-arising; only then do they achieve fruition.
Therefore. △ Third, benefiting bodhisattvas:
Furthermore, good son, from one world in the eastern direction (up to) the four intermediate directions and the zenith and nadir, it is likewise so.

In terms of the phenomenal event, it is like receiving the milk gruel; in terms of the Dharma, it is called partaking of the supreme patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*). One thereby attains Bodhi.
Because of this, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* and the *Gandavyūha* are largely identical to this. △ Second, causing them to see the same benefit:
"Good son, you see these ten thousand maidens of mine... (up to) ...sufficiently providing food for the people among humans."
△ Third, causing him to verify it with his own eyes:
"Good son, wait but a moment" (until) he provided whatever food and drink they required, making them all fully satisfied.
△ Fourth, humbling oneself and deferring to the superior.
He addressed Sudhana, saying: "Good son... how could I possibly know or speak of those meritorious practices?"
△ Fifth, pointing out a future friend:
"Good son, to the south there is a city named Mahodaya (Great Prosperity).
Because you shall arouse great diligence," [it is so called].
There is a householder there named Mingzhi (Wisdom-Light).
Because his progress depends upon being guided by the eye of wisdom, you should go to him and ask:
"How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?"
△ 6. Expressing Gratitude and Taking Leave.
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet (until) gazing up at him without weariness, then took his leave and departed.
△ Fourth, the Householder Vijñātagati. Entrusted with the practice of being unbending and unyielding. The text has six parts; first, following the instructions to seek [the teacher].
2. First, based on the preceding cultivation.
At that time, the youth Sudhana (arriving at... practiced that path of merit and cultivated those seeds of merit.
△ Second, seeking out the subsequent friend.
Gradually proceeding, he arrived at the city of Mahāsaṃbhava (Great Flourishing), where he beheld the Tathāgata Vardhamāna-daśabala-prabhāsa (The Tathāgata Increasing the Radiance of the Ten Powers).
△ Second, seeing, paying homage, and inquiring, in three parts. First, the seeing.
At that time, Sudhana saw the householder within the city at the crossroads of the marketplace.
His being at the crossroads symbolizes that, though situated in a place of clamor, he is not disturbed by it, for there is nothing he does not penetrate.
Upon the terrace of the seven precious jewels, countless beings stood in attendance, gazing upon him and awaiting his instructions.
△ Second, [the section on] Reverence:
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him immeasurable times, and stood with palms joined.
△ Third, the inquiry. He addressed [the master], saying: "O Noble One, for the sake of benefiting [all sentient beings]... until... I am able to serve as a place of reliance for all sentient beings.
△ Third, the praise and the bestowal of the Dharma, in three parts. First, extolling the excellence of his capacity to generate [the resolve].
The Elder said: "Excellent, excellent! ... [up to] ... having relied upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the mind is free from error.
2. Showing those whom he has transformed himself:
"Good son, do you see these people in my assembly? ... [up to] ... they have given rise to the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi* and are born into the family of the Tathāgata."
The retinue of those who have resolved their minds and are born into the family of the Tathāgata is identical to that of those born in the four stages of abiding.
They increase pure dharmas, dwell securely in the immeasurable [stages], and are fully able to rescue and protect all sentient beings.
△ Third, the correct demonstration of the dharma-realm has two parts. First, the presentation of the name:
"Good son, I have attained the liberation door of the treasury of merit that arises according to one's wishes.
Wealth and Dharma are inexhaustible, stored within space; they are bestowed according to one's wishes. Therefore, it is called 'the treasury of merit that arises according to one's wishes.'"
The "Treasury" (藏) also symbolizes that there is nothing incomplete in the vision of emptiness. △ Second, the manifestation of its functional activity, in two parts. First, a brief enumeration:
Whatever is required, all their vows are fulfilled... up to and including the preaching of the true and wondrous Dharma for them.
△ Second, citing events as manifest proof, in two parts. First, seeing the assembly gathered:
"Good son, wait but a moment" (until) "each according to their desire makes a request."
△ Second, the extensive giving of wealth and Dharma, in two parts. First, the giving of wealth:
At that time, the householder knew that the assembly had gathered universally (until) the entire multitude was fully satisfied.
△ Second, the giving of the Dharma.
Thereafter, he further expounds various teachings for them,
so that through this single gift of food, eight practices are brought to fulfillment.
That which is called "being fully satisfied by obtaining excellent food" (extending up to) "accumulating meritorious conduct and abandoning the conduct of poverty":
the first two practices are distinguished in terms of giving (*dāna*), while the remaining six are distinguished in terms of food. Food has five fruits.
To know the practice of all dharmas:
first, to know that all dharmas are the life of wisdom;
this is the practice of accomplishing the food of the joy of Dharma and the delight of dhyāna.
Second, those who attain joy and delight are constantly at peace and happiness;
they cultivate and fulfill the practices for the various marks and signs.
Third, being endowed with these marks and signs is their constant physical form.
Fourth is the power of constancy, which is the practice of being well-able to thoroughly comprehend the unsurpassed nutriment. This increases and accomplishes conduct that is difficult to subdue.
The fifth is the constant eloquence, which accomplishes inexhaustible great majestic power to subdue Māra and his enemies.
The sixth is also the constant power; it shares the same fruit as the aforementioned constant power.
In order to obtain excellent drink and be fully satisfied, [one attains] the mark of the supreme flavor of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
As for this mark of the supreme flavor, it is because there are springs of nectar at each of the four canine teeth.
Having obtained vehicles and being fully satisfied, [the text continues] until: "Once they had heard the Dharma, they returned to their original places.
△ Fourth, humbling oneself and extolling the excellence [of others]:
At that time, the householder [spoke] to the youth Sudhana [until] those various merits and sovereign spiritual powers.
△ Fifth, pointing out the existence of future lives:
"Good son, to the south of here there is a great city named Siṃhala (Lion Palace).
It is undisturbed by meditative concentration, like one dwelling in a deep inner palace; thus, what is spoken therein is definitive, and its activity is fearless."
Therefore, this was taken as his name.
There was an elder named Dharmaratnacūḍa (Dharma-Jewel-Crest).

Because he gathered and restrained the various disturbances and dwelt upon the crown of the mind, his concentration contained brilliant wisdom; thus, the name "Jewel" was added to it to illustrate this through metaphor.
The Dharma is named Dharmaratnaśikhin.
You should go and ask him how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
△ Sixth: Expressing Gratitude and Taking Leave.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, filled with joy and leaping for gladness, gazed upon him with earnest devotion and then took his leave and departed.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang;
recorded and annotated by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui. △ Fifth: The Elder Dharmakoṭi.
Entrusted with the practice free from delusion and confusion. The text has six parts. First: Approaching according to the teaching.
Seeking.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, having [visited] the householder Sumati, searched everywhere for the elder Ratnaśikhin.
△ Second, seeing, paying respect, and inquiring.
Seeing this elder in the midst of the marketplace,
remaining composed amidst the clamor and ever-abiding in concentration within the chaos,
[the Bodhisattva] immediately approached and prostrated at his feet, saying: "I shall follow this path to attain all-knowledge."
△ 3. Bestowing the Dharma Realm upon Oneself (4). First, taking the hand and leading [the disciple] forth is the bestowal of the skillful means of the Dharma.
At that time, the Elder took Sudhana’s hand and led him to his residence, showing him his house.

This reveals the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*), because it leads to correct realization. Second, it indicates that which is dwelt in, namely the direct bestowal of the *dharmadhātu*, by speaking these words: "Good son, look now at my house."
△ Third, the correct realization of the Dharma-realm, in two parts. First, the general overview:
At that time, Sudhana saw his residence... (extending to) that residence was vast and expansive, ten stories high with eight gates.

It is shaped like an octagonal pagoda. Regarding the two matters of the tiers and the gates, each has three meanings. These are explained in detail within the section on the distinct tiers. As for the three meanings of the gates:
first, generally speaking, they refer to the path of cultivation, taking the Eightfold Noble Path as the gate, because the Eightfold Path universally enters all stages.
Second, they refer to the path upon which one relies, taking the eight consciousnesses as the gate; specifically, within the eye-faculty...

Because one enters right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), if the faculties (*indriya*) can enter, then the objects (*viṣaya*) can be known. Third, regarding the revelation of principle through teaching, this constitutes the fourfold entry into the Dharma;
since there are four for both teaching and principle, there are eight gates. That is to say, if one loses the intended meaning, both existence and emptiness are simultaneously extinguished.

This constitutes the four types of slander. When one attains realization through the meaning, they are collectively called "gates" (mukha). Attaining understanding by following the teachings refers to the four gates of the teachings;
attaining understanding regarding the principle refers to the four gates of the principle. II. Distinctions.
Having entered, Sudhana observed them in sequence.
Regarding the ten tiers, each possessing three meanings: first, they symbolize the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Seeing that on the very bottom tier various foods and drinks were being bestowed, [he understood its significance].
First, the giving of food manifests the practice of *dāna* (generosity) on the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Second, seeing the offering of various precious robes on the second tier signifies the observance of ethical discipline (*śīla*) on the second stage;
for one who maintains precepts takes shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) as their clothing.
He saw that on the third tier all manner of precious ornaments were offered as gifts;
the practices of patience belonging to the third stage served as these ornaments.
He saw that on the fourth tier various court ladies as well as all kinds of supreme and exquisite treasures were offered as gifts.
The Chapter on the Path of the Four Grounds serves as its internal retinue; diligence is to be prized.
Upon reaching the fifth level, one perceives the radiance of wisdom and the practice of various samādhis up to the fifth ground.
The text for the fifth stage is explicit. Regarding the sixth stage, because the *prajñā* is present before one, there are three parts within the text.
First, the general [description]: seeing various bodhisattvas on the sixth level (up to) "distinctly revealing the gates of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
Next, fifteen distinct gates are revealed:
namely, the gate of the Prajñāpāramitā of the Tranquil Treasury.
Its essence is illumination, yet it is inherently quiescent; while it is quiescent, there is nothing it does not encompass.
The Prajñāpāramitā gateway of the wisdom that skillfully discriminates all sentient beings is an illumination within stillness;
there is no capacity for awakening that it does not reflect.
The Prajñāpāramitā gateway of being unshakeable and irreversible.
External conditions do not turn;
this is the light of detachment, the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Internally illuminating, it is free from seeking.
The gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "the treasury that cannot be overcome";
the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "illuminating the wheel of sentient beings" such that delusive objects are not destroyed.
It utterly destroys all delusions;
it is the ocean-treasury gateway of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
profound in its inclusion of supreme virtues.
The gate of the perfection of wisdom called "Universally Seeing and Attaining," by which one universally perceives the dharma-realm without obstruction;
and the gate of the perfection of wisdom called "Entering the Inexhaustible Treasury."
The one is itself inexhaustible;
it is the ocean of all skillful means, the gateways of Prajñāpāramitā,
which skillfully transform the infinite.
The gate of the perfection of wisdom that enters the ocean of all worlds;
the gate of the perfection of wisdom of unimpeded eloquence through internal realization of the world.
Externally, they manifest supreme eloquence,
a gateway to the Prajñāpāramitā that accords with the capacities of sentient beings,
skillfully conforming to their various desires.
The *prajñāpāramitā* gateway of unimpeded radiance;
the *prajñāpāramitā* gateway of constantly contemplating past conditions to spread the clouds of Dharma, wherein phenomena and principle interlace.
Contemplating conditions and bestowing the Dharma, he subsequently summarizes the preceding text,
stating that [these beings] are able to hear and retain the true Dharma of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas of Buddhas.
The seventh stage possesses distinguished practices; because one understands the various teachings, it is said that one attains the "patience like an echo.
One perceives the eighth level, where immeasurable bodhisattvas—headed by [the aforementioned]—expound the Dharma.
This encompasses two stages: first, attaining effortless supernatural powers (*anābhoga-abhijñā*) in the eighth stage, whereby one gains mastery over the two kinds of worlds;
second, in the ninth stage, becoming a Dharma-preacher who can expound the teaching with a single voice.
On the ninth level, one sees the assembly of bodhisattvas bound to only one more birth (ekajātipratibaddha) gathered therein;

they also comprise two ranks: first, those of the ten stages (daśabhūmi), and second, those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samābodhi). This is because both of these ranks may still have only one birth remaining.
Seeing the tenth stage, all Tathāgatas—indeed, all such things—are made clearly visible; this is the stage of the Tathāgata.
The two [preceding stages] represent the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), because the ten practices are identical to the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*). The first seven texts are manifest;

the eighth is so because it consists of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth accomplished through the eight great vows; the ninth is the supreme power of being bound to only one more birth (*eka-jāti-pratibaddha*).

Therefore, because the ten [stages] reach fulfillment only upon the wisdom of a Tathāgata, this very stage inherently encompasses all other stages. Since the preceding [stages] encompass the ten bhūmis, they thereby encompass all subsequent stages as well.
Thus, the ten layers symbolize these two meanings in tandem. This is just like Sāgaradhvaja, for whom all stages are fully contained within his own position;
it is only when the ten positions are concluded that he is said to attain Buddhahood. The preceding [discussion] was based on the sixth stage to encompass [the entire progression].

This is subsumed under the fifth stage. While the preceding [stages] were categorized according to the primary retribution (*vipāka*), this is categorized according to the secondary environment (*niśraya-vipāka*).

Both serve to demonstrate that the status of this stage is superior to the previous ones. Third, it does not indicate a distinct stage; rather, this bodhisattva, through their practice, adapts to the capacities of sentient beings and manifests as dwelling in a superior retribution that gradually increases in excellence.
Tenth, it reveals inexhaustibility: the first four involve giving material things, while each subsequent stage becomes progressively more difficult.
Next, two [verses] collect the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*); the former is shallow and the latter is profound. Next, two [verses] concern the attainment of the Dharma;

the former is narrow and the latter is vast. Finally, two [verses] manifest superior virtues; the former is the cause and the latter is the fruit. Taking these three general meanings—the dharmas of cause, fruit, practice, and stages—as the house of the elder.
△ Fourth, the causes and conditions of the question and answer, which consist of the two aspects of subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). First, the question.
At that time, having witnessed these events, Sudhana [inquired]: "...by planting what roots of goodness did he obtain such a reward?
△ Second, the answer:
The elder said, "Good son... this is called being forever free from all poverty and suffering."
Regarding the dedication toward the three places: first, one is freed from poverty and summons the retributions of the preceding four levels.
Because one constantly beholds all Buddhas and spiritual friends and perpetually hears the True Dharma, one obtains this retribution.
The two or three fruits refer to the latter six stages. Because of the power of the vow, even a minute cause such as a single pill results in a superior retribution.

Furthermore, this symbolizes the harmonious fusion of the myriad practices; when one initiates the aspiration toward Buddhahood, then through any single practice, nothing is not fully realized. What fruit would not be attained?
△ Fourth, humbling oneself and extolling the excellence [of others].
"Good son, I know only this Bodhisattva liberation door of the Treasury of Immeasurable Merit.
Because worldly treasures and the Three Jewels are all accumulated within its ten layers, it is called a 'treasury. It is used constantly without exhaustion;
therefore, it is named 'Immeasurable Merit. [Thus he] humbles himself above and defers to the superior below."
Just as all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained an inconceivable treasury of merit, so too should the excellence of the Dharma be manifested;
therefore, this treasury of merit is entirely inconceivable. The above is the general summary; the following is the detailed exposition.
Entering the ocean of the Tathāgata’s body of non-conceptualization (up to) dwelling through all kalpas without weariness or fatigue;
because one possesses all dharmas through non-conceptualization, it is inconceivable.
How could I possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct?
△ Fifth, pointing out the subsequent friend:
"Good son, to the south of here there is a land called Vamśamūla."

As for the wisteria vine: its roots penetrate deep into the earth, and above it, flowers and sprouts emerge, manifesting virtuous conduct. Prajñā realizes the profound and can give rise to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
This subsequently attained wisdom functions in accordance with sentient beings; therefore, it is compared to the vine.
In that land there is a city named Samantamukha;
just as the prajñāpāramitā of the true mark penetrates everything without obstruction,
so too is there an elder therein named Samantanetra.
Because the *prajñā* of contemplative observation sees all things, go to him and ask:
"How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
△ Sixth: Expressing devotion and taking leave.
Then the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet (and so forth), gazing up at him with earnest devotion before taking his leave and departing.

△ Sixth, the Elder Universal Eye (*Samantanetra*), who is associated with the practice of "Manifestation of Goodness" (*Sudarśana*). The text has six parts; first, following the instructions to seek [the teaching].
At that time, the youth Sudhana [from the section on] the elder Ratnacūḍa... deeply entered the immeasurable knowledge and vision of all Buddhas. There are two kinds of "immeasurable":
first, because it is manifold, it is the realm of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*); second, because it is without measure, it is the realm of ultimate wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because the object is immeasurable, the wisdom is also immeasurable. Knowledge and vision are also twofold: first, the particular, which means that knowledge is precisely...

"Knowledge" (*jñāna*). "Vision" (*darśana*) is precisely wisdom (*prajñā*; *hui*); it is the wisdom that illuminates two objects. The "two penetrations" refer to the two characters "knowledge" and "vision," as both are the Tathāgata’s ability to realize reality as it is (*yathābhūta*) by knowing those meanings;
they are thus unobstructed wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*). If this is so, why employ these redundant terms?

"Vision" is used to distinguish it from inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*), and "knowledge" is used to distinguish it from the vision of the flesh and the sleep-like [meditative] states. Therefore, it is said: [text continues].
"Knows" means to know fully and see fully, as explained in Vasubandhu’s *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. "Entry" refers to realization and penetration.
It means to abide securely in the immeasurable and supreme practices of a bodhisattva, thoroughly exerting all the faculties and remaining free from all negligence.
△ Second, seeing, paying respect, and inquiring. First, one sees the primary and secondary [receptacle worlds].
Thereafter, one is able to see the City of Universal Gate (Samantamukha-pura), surrounded on all sides by hundreds of thousands of villages;
these are the retinues of Prajñā.
The battlements are lofty and steep;

the Prajñā [walls] prevent what is non-righteous. They are high yet without surpassing them. Five boards constitute a *du*; five *du* constitute a *zhì*. The *dié* (battlements) are the same as the *nǚqiáng* (parapets).
The thoroughfare was broad and level.
This is the path of Prajñā, which all Buddhas constantly traverse; as it is not a circuitous or expedient route, it is vast and boundless.
Seeing that elder approaching his location, [the Bodhisattva] prostrated himself before him and asked: "How does one cultivate the Bodhisattva path?"
Part Two: Praising and Bestowing the Dharma.
First, the praise. The elder said: "Excellent, excellent! [up to] ... the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
△ Second, the bestowing of one’s own dharma-realm has two parts. First, the ability to cure illness, which is the downward transformation of sentient beings, has two parts.
First, the removal of physical illness, which has two parts. First, the treatment of that which is not impossible.
"Good son, I know all the various illnesses of all sentient beings (down to: I am able to rescue and treat them all through skillful means.
△ Second, "All who come are treated," while also bestowing physical ease.
"Good son, for all sentient beings in the ten directions who are afflicted by illness... (until) causing them all to be fully satisfied so that they lack nothing.
II. Treating Mental Illness. This has two parts. First, explaining the removal of delusions; this meaning applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Thereafter, he preaches the Dharma to each according to their needs (up to) manifesting for them the sublime Dharma-gate.
△ Second, causing them to achieve benefit. This pertains exclusively to the Mahāyāna and consists of sixteen phrases.
In order to cause them to generate the bodhicitta (up to) dwelling through all kalpas while cultivating the web of all practices:
the first five phrases generally reveal the great resolve, practices, and vows; the subsequent ten specifically clarify the causes of the ten perfections that bring about the fruit of the ten bodies.
In order to cause them to possess the marks and signs of a Buddha, he extols and praises the dānapāramitā;
because giving satisfies the hearts of others, the marks and signs bring joy to sentient beings.
In order to cause them to attain the pure body of a Buddha, he extols and praises the śīlapāramitā.
Since ethical discipline universally ceases all evil, it leads to the universal purity of the body;
therefore, desiring to cause them to attain the Buddha’s pure and inconceivable body, one extols and praises the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Patience encompasses both the practice of patience and its underlying principle;
therefore, it is inconceivable. This is intended to cause them to attain the Tathāgata’s [state] and to extol and praise the perfection of vigor.
Advancing through the myriad practices, none can surpass them;
desiring to cause them to attain a pure and peerless body, they extol and praise the dhyāna-pāramitā.
Dhyāna consists of the single mind; therefore, there is nothing equal to it.
It is for the purpose of causing the Tathāgata to appear [within that state] that one extols and praises the Prajñāpāramitā.
Because Prajñā illuminates the principle, it manifests the Dharmakāya;
for the purpose of causing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to appear [and so forth], up to the point of extolling and praising the *upāya-pāramitā*.
Through the manifestation of skillful means, the form-body (rūpakāya) may be beheld;
this is for the purpose of causing him to dwell through all kalpas for the sake of all sentient beings, extolling and praising the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
I vow that until the end of time, may I abide throughout infinite eons;
desiring to cause them to manifest pure bodies, [and so forth], up to praising and extolling the power of the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
His power is unshakable; he transcends all things.
This is for the purpose of manifesting his pure body (up to) extolling and praising the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*).
His wisdom exhausts all phenomena and he assumes bodies in accordance with sentient beings;
desiring to cause them to attain the ultimate [state], he has thus bestowed these gifts and now bids each of them to return.
The final phrase clarifies that, because one is universally free from all evils, it is ultimately pure and sublime.
△ Second, explaining the incense that can be blended, which corresponds to the third [section] above on making offerings to the Buddhas. First, knowing the substance of the incense.
Good son, I also well know how to compound all manner of incomparable fragrant spices and the Sindhu-pāra incense.
"Sindhu" refers to the Indus River; "pāra" means "bank. Thus, it is the incense of the further shore.
Anuttamagandha, Bodhanagandha, Aruṇavati-gandha—
Aruṇavati means "extreme redness"— Raktakālāguru-candana, and Uragasāra-candana.
Ulūka is the name of a serpent in the Western Regions; it is a venomous snake.

Because this sandalwood tree was encircled by such a snake, the agallochum incense, the immovable-rooted incense, and other such fragrances all possess the methods for their refinement and compounding, which [the Buddha] fully knows.
"Harmonious integration" refers to the unimpeded fusion of precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth. 2. Presenting Offerings and Formulating Vows:
Furthermore, son of good family, I take this incense as an offering... [up to] ...to offer to all Tathāgatas. I vow.

Furthermore, son of good family, when this incense is burned, it fills every place, serving as a magnificent adornment.
△ 4. Humility Regarding Oneself and Relegation of Superiority.
Good son, I know only this Dharma-gate for causing all sentient beings to universally behold all Buddhas and rejoice.

That is to say, by removing the illnesses of body and mind, they achieve happiness in both worlds and thus all rejoice. By universally making offerings with incense, they attain the ten bodies of a Buddha;
then, what Buddha would they not see?
Just as the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are like great medicinal kings [up to] being able to know and expound their meritorious practices.
△ Fifth, pointing out the subsequent friend.
"Good son, to the south of here there is a great city named Tāladhvaja.
*Tāla* means 'clear and pure' (*vimala*), and *dhvaja* means 'erected banner,' signifying the practice of non-attachment based upon the pure clarity of *prajñā*."
Because they establish superior practices, there is among them a king named Analaṃkṛta (Insatiable).
Through skillful means that are like an illusion, he transforms beings without attachment; therefore, his mind knows no weariness or fatigue.
"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.

he gradually travels on, passing through various lands (until) he proclaims the Dharma and transforms sentient beings.

Those who could be healed were healed; those who could be gathered were gathered. (Up to: Relying on the words of the multitude, he immediately went there.
△ Second, seeing [him] and paying respect and inquiring. This has two parts. First, seeing [him], which has four sections. First, seeing the excellence of the support and the supported.

△ Second, observing his perverse transformation:
Before him were furthermore one hundred thousand fierce soldiers (up to the point where they were) like those in the Saṃghāta Great Hell.
△ Third, doubt arises from lack of understanding.

△ Fourth, the empty deities provide instruction and exhortation in two parts. First, they cause him to recollect the reality of his previous teachings so that doubt does not arise.
While he was forming this thought, a deity appeared in the air... [leading him] to a place of safety free from all perils.
△ Second, explaining the subsequent practice of the profound mystery, causing him to enter through faith.
Noble son, the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), wisdom, and the wisdom for subduing sentient beings are inconceivable.
Nevertheless, although Sudhana constantly recalled these instructions, he gave rise to doubt because [the methods of] counteractive practice are difficult to understand.
Because greed benefits this world, he did not doubt Vasumitrā; because hatred and delusion cause manifest harm, he thus gave rise to [doubt regarding] Śūraṅgama and this king.

This is indeed strange. To speak of "profound mystery" means to penetrate that which is not the Way. Thus, it is clarified in the section on the training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*) within the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* from the Liang dynasty:
that a bodhisattva may perform "contrary actions" such as killing sentient beings, thereby generating immeasurable merit and even attaining unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Only a great Bodhisattva is capable of this matter. There are two types: first, the actual practice; second, the transformative manifestation. Regarding the actual practice:

it is when one knows for certain that the person before them will inevitably commit an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), and there is no other skillful means (*upāya*) to cause them to abandon this evil except by taking their life, so as to prevent them from doing it. Furthermore, one knows that the person before them—if...
After his life has ended, he will certainly be reborn in a favorable realm. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects to himself:

"Having committed this killing, I shall surely fall into hell and suffer there for his sake; yet although that person currently undergoes slight suffering, he will certainly attain the fruit of happiness.
This is also stated similarly in the *Śīlapaṭala* (Chapter on Ethics) of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (Yogācārabhūmi). What is referred to as "transformation" corresponds precisely to this passage.
The King himself speaks below. △ Second, the respectful inquiry:
At that time, having heard these words, the youth Sudhana said: "... [up to] ... you are well able to instruct; I pray that you will speak for me."
△ Third, the bestowing of one's own Dharma-realm, in two parts. First, the expedient means for bestowing the Dharma.
At that time, King Anala, having finished attending to the affairs of state, was about to enter his palace when he invited [the Bodhisattva] to sit together with him.

Holding hands and sitting together demonstrates the ritual of non-interruption; it signifies that by guiding their preparatory practices (*prayoga*), they are led toward the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
△ Second, the formal demonstration of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) to lead them to realization and resonance has four parts. First, raising up the fruit to cause entry.
He said, "Good son, you should observe me [until] rising first and lying down last, serving my every wish with a gentle mind.
△ Second, revealing the provisional through the real.
At that time, King Anala said to Sudhana, "[until] thus wealthy and thus sovereign."
△ Second, showing what has been attained, in two parts. First, the name:
"Good son, I have attained the Bodhisattva liberation of being like an illusion.
Because I realize that birth is like an illusion, I employ illusion to transform illusion. △ Second, clarifying the functional activity of this dharma-gate.
"Good son, all sentient beings in this land of mine [attain] the resolve for *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
△ Third, the superior benefits of the Dharma-gate:
Good son, by means of such skillful expedients, they ultimately abide on the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*)."
△ Fourth, directly manifesting actual virtues:
"Good son, my body, speech, and mind have never caused harm or affliction... (up to) ...because they are able to give rise to all wholesome dharmas."
The depth of his compassionate mindfulness is such that, from the first through the seventh stages, all are expedient means;
thus, Śūnyatā, Avalokiteśvara, and Pārijāta primarily concern themselves with compassion. △ Fourth, humbling oneself and deferring to the superior.
"Good son, I have attained only this liberation that is like an illusion (māyopama-vimokṣa), [extending] to the knowledge that all realms of existence (gati) are entirely like illusions.
It is by understanding them as being like illusions that one realizes this patience (kṣānti); furthermore, it is because this patience is realized in the subsequent stage."
The various practices of Bodhisattvas are entirely like transformations (up to: being able to know and be able to explain their meritorious conduct).

In the preceding stage, compassion increased; now, having attained the sublime wisdom of non-abiding, one carries sentient beings across.

"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.

Sentient beings—how could they be contained within a mere ten *krośas* of the world?
Therefore, all things herein should be understood as being perfectly interfused and manifesting the Dharma; reflect upon this according to principle. △ Second, the seer is unstained.

gradually traveled on until he saw King Mahāprabha at a crossroads not far from the tower where he resided.

he sits upon a lotus treasury of wish-fulfilling *maṇi* jewels, [endowed with] up to the twenty-eight marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
As for the twenty-eight marks, because the causes have not yet been fulfilled,
he adorns his body with the eighty secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana), until it is filled within with the various jewels of wisdom.
△ Third, the threefold inclusion of the primary and secondary factors in generating [benefit].
First, the items offered are enumerated: before the royal throne, there were gold, silver, and lapis lazuli (extending until) all implements for sustaining life were placed therein.
Pervading the non-substantiality of phenomena (*dharma*) is the sixty-fourth capacity, as in the fifth stage (*bhūmi*). Second, those capable of giving are the assistants;
along every path there are twenty billion bodhisattvas who bestow these various things upon sentient beings.

it is for the sake of universally gathering in all sentient beings... (up to) ...for the sake of causing sentient beings to purify all paths of karma.

At that time, King Mahāprabha immediately entered this concentration... (up to) "...all sentient beings of poisonous and evil nature are likewise so.

This reveals the functional efficacy of the concentration. That both the animate and inanimate achieve supreme benefit refers to the great compassion of the same essence (*samatā-mahāmaitrī*). Regarding "objects" (*vastu*): [text continues].

Because I am without duality. Just as when a worldly king’s virtue accords with Heaven and Earth, the qilin and phoenix come to attend him and precious jade presents its auspicious signs—how much more so for the power of the Great Compassion that transcends the world; would it not cause even grasses and trees to bend their knees in homage?

Because compassion fundamentally acts for the sake of sentient beings, it is called "accordance with the world. It rises above all other practices and is therefore termed "foremost"; this carries the meaning of a banner (*dhvaja*).
Above, one humbles oneself and knows only one's own [insufficiency]; below, one defers to the superior and acknowledges the multitude [of their virtues].
As for the various Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas... [they] are able to praise that great cloud of compassion and mercy.

There was a laywoman named Acalā (Unshakable).
Since she first resolved her mind [on enlightenment], there has been no dharma in which she has not attained meditative concentration.

Because neither afflictions nor those of the two vehicles can shake her, and because she causes the minds of sentient beings to be unshakable as well, she manifests in the form of a woman, practicing loving-kindness through wisdom.

△ Second, the benefits gained through cultivation.
A mind of joy arises, a mind of pure faith arises (up to) a mind free from turbidity arises, and a pure mind arises.
"Free from turbidity" refers to the absence of others; "pure" refers to one's own essence.

because the cultivation of compassion is about to reach fulfillment, one reflects that spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) are truly rare, [and so on] until: they cause all roots and sprouts of the bodhisattvas to grow.

In this manner, the youth Sudhana lamented... [until] he encountered the Bodhisattva-like Tathāgata-envoys (*tathāgata-dūta-deva*).
The term "deva" (天) is used in two senses here. Therefore, the Jin translation states: "The Tathāgata-envoys and the Bodhisattva-following devas.

The "Bodhisattva-following devas" are spirits manifested by the karmic actions of the bodhisattvas themselves; the "Tathāgata-envoys" are those gathered through the compassionate power of the Buddha to sustain sentient beings.
These are the deities. However, for those who have already attained the stages of cultivation, these two deities always follow them and announce from the midst of the void, saying:
"From now until you attain the stage of Buddhahood, you shall never fall back; you will be protected by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and you shall fully accomplish all goals and benefits."

△ Second, the actual bestowal of the Dharma-realm has two parts. First, showing the name and essence of the Dharma-gate.
"Good son, I have attained the bodhisattva liberation door of the treasury of wisdom that is difficult to subdue.

Although the phrasing differs from previous examples, the presentation of these five dharmas is likewise the same as in the ninth stage (*navamī bhūmi*), which corresponds to the rank of Dharma Master."

This is because one must know them extensively. Among the five, the first two represent the internal virtues they sustain. The former is wisdom that is unshackled and is specifically termed "liberation" (*vimukti*).
When there is wisdom, afflictions cannot destroy it; having shattered all grasping and attachment, nothing can overcome it, hence it is called "difficult to subdue.
Because this wisdom encompasses all, it is named a "treasury" (*kośa*).
I have attained the bodhisattva’s gate of practice for firm upholding.

Regarding these two types of firm upholding, the latter specifically receives the name "practice": namely, being able to endure when encountering evil sentient beings, and having a mind that does not become deluded even when wandering through all realms of existence; therefore, it is called "firm."
I have attained the Bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī gate of the level of equality of all dharmas.
Because one can maintain and penetrate this dharma-gate, one attains the ground of the nature of dharmas; thus, there is nothing that is not maintained.
I have attained the bodhisattva gate of eloquence that illuminates all dharmas.

This fourth [gate] pertains to external transformation. Because one clearly illuminates the distinctions [of phenomena] through correct reflection on the Buddha-dharma, one attains eloquence and is able to turn the wheel of Dharma in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings.
I have attained the Bodhisattva samādhi-door of seeking all dharmas without weariness or fatigue.

"Five" refers to the aforementioned upward-seeking; because one seeks the Dharma with a single mind, it is called *samādhi*. It is so named because one draws near to the Buddha without satiety and receives the Dharma without being satisfied.

I have already established myself in the bodhisattva practice that reaches all places."
First, the scope of transformation is universally pervasive; the name "Universal Practice" is also established from this.

Having accomplished the power of supernatural faculties that are non-reliant and non-conditioned,
one is able to reach all aforementioned places by means of these three non-conditioned supernatural faculties,
thereby accomplishing the Prajñāpāramitā of the Universal Gate.

Fourth, by virtue of universal *prajñā*, one is able to universally contemplate while in meditative concentration. If distinguished specifically, it functions without fabrication or dependence, yet remains non-abiding;
universal *prajñā* exhausts all phenomena without exception. △ Second, the manifestation of the four functional activities.
First, the function of reaching all places:
"Good son, I universally [reach] throughout the world, including all realms of existence such as humans and non-humans.
Second, the function of universally observing the world.

Whether they abide in various views or believe in the Two Vehicles (up to the point where they cannot obscure the essence of great majestic power), [the Buddha] contemplates what is appropriate for them and teaches according to their needs. △ Third, the function of being unconditioned and non-reliant.
Furthermore, good son, within this city of Tosalī... [from] "Who am I, and from where have I come?
he did not know from where he had come; it was a state of non-action and non-reliance.
It causes those who hear it to practice according to reality (up to) benefiting all in this same way.
△ Fourth, the function of the Universal Gate Prajñā:
"Good son, within Jambudvīpa, among the ninety-six [non-Buddhist] groups (up to) he preaches the Dharma for them so that they may obtain benefit."

Because all ninety-six types [of heterodox teachings] can be thoroughly exhausted [by this]. Thus far, the various categories have been assigned according to their predominant characteristics; in reality, however, the meaning applies universally.
△ Fourth, humbling oneself and deferring to the superior.
"Good son, I only know this [practice] that reaches all places; I am able to know and speak of those meritorious deeds.
△ Fifth, pointing out the subsequent friend.
"Good son, to the south of here there is a land named Vast. Because it is the initial entry into dedication,

because it is dedicated to sentient beings, and because it is a vast dedication toward Bodhi, its 'Great Dedication' (mahā-pariṇāmanā) penetrates the meaning of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) in a manner that is both vast and great."
There was an elder who sold incense.

"Sells" means to trade. Although the substance of the incense is small, its fragrance spreads far and wide; likewise, although one's roots of goodness may be slight, when dedicated, they pervade everywhere.
Whether selling or buying, both parties obtain the fragrance; similarly, the roots of goodness of both oneself and others can be dedicated.
It is named the *utpala* flower.
As for the blue lotus: though the lotus dwells in the mud, it remains unstained; likewise, it protects sentient beings while remaining detached from signs.
Among those in the water, the blue lotus is supreme; as a savior, it is the most honored among those who enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
△ Sixth, the expression of devotion and the taking of leave:
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet (until) he gazed upon him with earnest reverence and withdrew to depart.

△ Fourth, there are ten virtuous friends, corresponding to the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). Now, first is the Elder Blue Lotus (*Nīlotpala*), who corresponds to the dedication of "protecting sentient beings while being free from the notion of sentient beings. The text has six sections; the first concerns seeking according to the teaching.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, following the instructions of his spiritual friends, proceeded toward the merits of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
First, he established vows in accordance with those instructions; because this dedication is the foremost of great vows, he subsequently sought the subsequent stages.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at the country of Vaipulya.
△ Second, seeing, paying respect, and inquiring:
He went to the householder’s place, prostrated at his feet... [up to] ...and is able to give birth to the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
△ Second, the praise and the conferral of the Dharma, in two parts. First, the praise:
The Elder said, "Excellent, excellent... [you have] resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
△ Second, the bestowal of the two [empowerments]. First, the general indication of what is attained:
"Good son, I am well-versed in distinguishing all fragrances; this is the practice of differentiation.
I know the various fragrances of the world to represent the fragrance of the Dharma—that is, by means of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, compassion, and loving-kindness."
"Equal fragrance": because it perfumes and cultivates the arising of wholesome tendencies and the extinguishing of unwholesome habitual tendencies;
it also knows how to blend all methods of incense, which is the practice of universal penetration.
One crushes it with a vajra; this is the harmonization by the *prajñāpāramitā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

This causes the pure and the mixed to be unimpeded and compassion and wisdom to be perfectly integrated, thereby accomplishing the dedication [of merit]. △ Second, the specific manifestation of its functional activity has two parts.

First, the general characteristics that reveal its knowledge. This section has four parts; each of these four should be contemplated in terms of both phenomena (the particular) and principle (the universal). First, knowing the distinctness of the substance of the fragrance.
That is to say, from all perfumes and all incenses (up to) the source from which all kings of perfumes emerge.
△ Second, distinguishing differences by category:
Furthermore, he thoroughly understands all the various perfumes belonging to devas, nāgas, (up to) humans, non-humans, and so forth.
△ Third, knowing the differences in their power and function.
Furthermore, one skillfully distinguishes and knows the fragrances that treat various illnesses (up to) the fragrances of all the bodhisattva stages.
The former two concern the mundane; this concerns the supramundane. △ Fourth, thoroughly investigating the root and the branches.
I have fully realized and understood all such things as these, including the arising of the forms and characteristics of these fragrances.
△ Second, a specific explanation by citing examples: there are ten kinds of fragrance.
Good son, among humans there is a fragrance called Elephant-Treasury (*hastigarbha*).
It possesses the ten matters previously described in their entirety. First, whenever the name of this fragrance is mentioned, it must necessarily possess a physical form.
It arises from the combat of nāgas.
The combat of two nāgas serves as its origin;
if one pellet is burned, a great cloud of fragrance immediately arises.
Third, the rising clouds constitute the manifestation;
for seven days they completely cover the royal capital and rain down fine fragrant rain.
Fourth, the falling rain constitutes the fulfillment.
If it touches the body, the body becomes golden; if it touches clothing, palaces, or towers, they all likewise become golden.
These five kinds of gold are pure and radiant.
When the wind blows it into the palace, [the inhabitants] are filled with joy, and their bodies and minds experience bliss.
Sixth, joy and happiness constitute peace and security;
one is free from all illnesses, not harmed by others, and detached from all sorrow and suffering.
Seventh, being free from illness and so forth serves as the means.
Without alarm, fear, agitation, or anger, they face one another with minds of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Taking the eight [types of] loving-kindness as their object,
their resolve and intention are pure.
The purity of the nine mental states constitutes their majestic power (*vibhūti*). Their functional activity is of one kind, and their meaning extends through the preceding seven [stages].
Having understood this, I preach the Dharma for them, leading them up to the arousal of the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The ten are the root, for they are rooted in the bodhicitta. If one elucidates these ten meanings by means of the bodhicitta, it is like the fragrance of the bodhicitta being the cause of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Through the mutual interaction of good and evil, [the mind] arises;

yet, once the aspiration is generated, it inevitably raises clouds of compassion and pours down the great rain of the Dharma. All that the mind reaches is caused to return to true purity, thereby attaining the Dharma.
Joyful and at ease, free from the suffering of afflictions and karma, they successively give rise to compassion and maintain pure aspirations.
Good son, the sandalwood incense produced on Mount Malaya—even if one enters a pit of fire, the fire cannot burn it.

The remaining nine fragrances should all be designated as "endowed" (*samanvāgata*). The ten [fragrances] consisting of the dharma and its metaphors are absent here because they are abbreviated; alternatively, there may be two or three.
*Mālaya* is the name of a country; because this country abounds in this fragrance, it is the "fragrance of patience" (*kṣānti-gandha*), which cannot be burned by the fire of anger.
"Good son, in the ocean there is a fragrance named 'Invincible' (Ajeyā), [which causes] all enemy armies to retreat and disperse of their own accord.
Third is the 'Advancing' fragrance; when it is present, the demonic armies retreat and disperse."
"Good son, from the side of Lake Anavatapta (to) the abode of that Heavenly King, they go together to listen to the Dharma.
These five, in their respective order, are the fragrances of the fivefold Dharma-body."
Good son, within Tuṣita Heaven there is incense (up to) which makes offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Ninth is the Incense that Accords with the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). *Sindhu-pā* has four meanings for one name; here it should be used as salt, because this incense resembles it.
Good sons, the gods of Skillful Transformation possess fragrances (extending to) which rain down universally all manner of ornaments.
They have forgotten both subject and object; therefore they are named "Captivating the Mind. △ Fourth, humbling oneself and deferring to the superior.
"Good son, I only know this method of compounding incense (up to) discerning the conduct of body, speech, and mind that is free from defilement.
△ Fifth, pointing out the subsequent friend.
"Noble son, to the south of here there is a great city named Kūṭāgāra.
By means of this dedication, may the bodhicitta increase even further, for it excels through the mutual reliance of compassion and wisdom."
Among them was a shipmaster named Vasiṣṭha, which in this language means "Sovereign.
This means that he had already attained thorough mastery over the ocean of the Buddha’s Dharma; he was able to skillfully transport others across the ocean of birth and death;
and his profound faith in all dharmas was indestructible. For these reasons, he was called "Sovereign."
"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
△ Sixth, the expression of devotion and the taking of leave:
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet (until) he gazed upon him with earnest reverence and took his leave to depart.
△ Second, the boatman Vāsula. Entrusted with the sixth, the non-regressive dedication. First, seeking according to the teaching. 1.
Observing the path according to the teaching.
At that time, the youth Sudhana proceeded toward the city of Kūṭāgāraśālā and surveyed the road.
Regarding the path of dedication, because one first attains what is indestructible:
that is to say, observing the relative heights and depths of paths,
the Buddha-path is high, while all others are low.
Contemplating the levelness and ruggedness of the Path:
taking birth-and-death and nirvana as the level and the rugged.
Contemplating the purity and defilement of the Path.
The presence or absence of hindrances constitutes purity or defilement;

one contemplates the paths as either crooked or straight—where the two vehicles are crooked and the bodhisattvas are straight, and so forth. Second, seeking the subsequent stage, one gives rise to superior mindfulness.
Traveling by stages, he reflects in this way (up to) reaching the causal path to the city of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
This is the primary clarification; that is to say, because one attains it through the human condition of the bodhisattva path, one gains indestructible faith in the bodhisattva Dharma-preacher.
This is subsequently examined and explained.
For what reason? [He proceeded] toward the place of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), reflecting in this manner as he traveled by stages.
△ Second, seeing, paying respect, and inquiring:
Having arrived at that city, he saw the boatman standing outside the city gate on the seashore.
If one regards the ocean of the Buddha-dharma as this shore because of not abandoning birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*),

then regarding the ocean of birth-and-death as this shore by cultivating the causes through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) means abiding in great loving-kindness and compassion so as to cause [beings] to leave behind those causes.
"O Sage, who is well able to instruct hundreds of thousands of merchants and immeasurable others, please speak for me.
△ Third, the praise and the conferral of the Dharma, in two parts. First, the praise of the inquiry.
The boatman said, "Excellent, excellent! [up to] "you have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
He praised his resolution of mind and his subsequent inquiry into the Dharma; the text contains nine phrases.
Now you are further able to inquire about the causes for generating great wisdom (up to) the causes for abiding in the various whirlpools of tranquil samādhis.
The preceding five [questions] were able to inquire about the causes of the fruit. As for "whirlpool" (*āvarta*): "whirl" (*āva*) means deep; it is profound and still, submerged and not flowing.
The two vehicles are quiescent; it takes eighty thousand kalpas for them to move. Therefore, they are able to remain far removed from this bodhisattva path.
Riding the chariot of great vows, one reaches all places, reaching the cause for the pure path of the ocean of all-knowledge.

The latter four are able to inquire about the causes of causes; therefore, they are called the "causes of the Path. △ Second, the bestowal of one's own Dharma-realm has two parts. First, the designation of its name and essence:
"Good son, here in this city, along the road by the seashore, I have purely cultivated the Bodhisattva practice of the Banner of Great Compassion."
This refers to the transcendence of great compassion, for it serves as the refuge for all beings. △ Second, the analysis of its functional activity has two parts.
First, clarifying the transformation of birth on land, so that they may know there is an ocean.
"Good son, I observe within Jambudvīpa... [and so forth]... thus benefiting all sentient beings.

△ Second, "Skillfully Knowing the Characteristics of the Ocean," regarding being born by transformation in the ocean. This section has two parts: first, explaining skillful knowledge; second, illustrating the benefits of such transformation. Now, for the first part:
these "jewel islands" and so forth exist in both the ocean of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the ocean of the Dharma; however, for now, we shall discuss them in terms of birth-and-death.
The Oceanic Śakra. In this passage, the matters are briefly enumerated; knowing five types of things, they are divided into five. First is the knowledge of jewels:
"Good son, I know that within the ocean..."
The Jewel is itself wisdom. Therefore, if one does not enter the great ocean of birth and death, one cannot produce the jewel of all-knowledge (*sarvajñāna*).
Within this passage, there are twelve phrases.
It is a treasure island amidst the ocean of birth and death; it is called a treasure island because it is profoundly still and unmoving,
being the source of all treasures.
The empty and non-empty Tathāgatagarbha is the locus of jewels;
all categories of jewels— indeed,
all merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— are categories of jewels.
The seed of all jewels:
the Buddha-nature is the seed of jewels. The preceding [passage] refers entirely to what is innately present; the subsequent four [points] refer to what is accomplished through cultivation.
"I know that which purifies all jewels."
Taking pure precepts, dhūtas, and so forth as the means of purification,
one drills through all jewels;
taking the wisdom of dependent origination as the drill.
It produces all jewels;
taking the arousal of the mind of omniscience as its cause of production,
it creates all jewels.
Hearing serves as the efficient cause; the latter four serve as the functions of the jewels.
I know all jewel-vessels—the vessels of the three vehicles and so forth—to differ according to their wisdom.
The functions of all jewels—
illuminating principles, severing delusions, and their respective applications— are each distinct;
such is the realm of all jewels.
Regarding the objects of perception, there are ten thousand grades of difference;

the radiance of all jewels shatters ignorance and reveals clarity, each being distinct and unequal. △ Second, within the midst of birth and death, [there are] the three poisons of hatred, greed, and delusion.
Poison. I know all the abodes of the nāgas, all the abodes of the yakṣas, and all the abodes of the bhūtas.
*Bhūta* here means "self-born"; like the yakṣas, they are not born from parents, and for this reason they are called "many" (*bahu*).
Delusion.
[The Bodhisattva] skillfully evades all such calamities.
△ Third, knowing the characteristics of the mind and consciousness.
Furthermore, one skillfully discerns and knows the various differences such as whirlpools and rapids, shallow and deep, waves near and far, and the quality—good or bad—of the water’s color;
likewise, the realms of form and formlessness, the stability of the consciousness-mind, the duration of kalpas, the waves of the seven consciousnesses, and the proximity of defiled habits.
Depending on wholesome or unwholesome conditions, the color of the mind-water varies. △ Fourth, one is thus able to know the timing.

Furthermore, he skillfully distinguishes and knows the movements and degrees of the sun, moon, and stars, as well as the lengthening and shortening of days and nights, morning and evening, and the passage of time measured by the gnomon.

He understands the ripeness or immaturity of the faculties [of beings] and, within such times, knows what is appropriate for cultivating meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth. △ Fifth, he knows that the myriad practices are not the same.
He also knows whether the iron and wood of the ship are hard or brittle;
he knows that with skillful means it is hard, while without skillful means it is brittle;
and he knows whether its mechanisms are stiff or smooth.
That which has been cultivated is smooth; that which has not been cultivated is rough.
The "greatness" or "smallness" of water refers to whether birth and death have an end or are without end.
Regarding the favorable and adverse winds:
among the eight winds, four are favorable and four are adverse. Furthermore, it is said that this is because in spiritual practice there is both abiding and non-abiding.
Thus, one clearly understands all such signs of safety and peril; when it is appropriate to act, one acts, and when it is appropriate to cease, one ceases.
If one opens up the preceding section, there are three matters each in the third and fifth [sections], totaling ten kinds. △ Second, demonstrating the benefits of accomplishment:
"Good son, by my accomplishment of such wisdom... (up to) universally accords with the ocean of the minds of all sentient beings."

Since the ten oceans have been enumerated, one should understand that the preceding oceans should be considered according to this same principle. The first four pertain to self-benefit, while the latter six pertain to the benefit of others.
△ Fourth, humbling oneself and extolling the excellence [of others].
"Good son, I have only attained this practice of the Banner of Great Compassion (up to the point where one) is able to know and expound those meritorious practices.
△ Fifth, pointing out the subsequent spiritual friend.
"Good son, to the south of here there is a city named Ramya (Delightful).
Because of the dedication equal to that of the Buddhas, one perceives neither beauty nor ugliness; all attain purity, joy, and happiness."
Among them is an elder named Anuttarajaya (Supreme Victory).
Because he has attained supreme supernormal powers that are unsurpassed, he is equal to all Buddhas; since there is nothing superior to him, go to him and ask:
"How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?"
△ 6. Expressing Gratitude and Taking Leave.
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet (until) he departed with a heart of no satiety.
△ Third: The Elder Anupamavijaya. Entrusted with the sixth dedication, "Equal to All Buddhas. First, following the instruction.
Seeking [her].
At that time, the youth Sudhana, having aroused great compassion (up to), gradually traveled on until he arrived within that city.
△ Second, seeing, paying respect, and inquiring; this has two parts. First, seeing.
He saw the Unsurpassed Victor in the city’s eastern quarter,
within the Aśoka Grove of the Great Ornament Banner, because he was the Buddha-Sun who brings forth illumination.
They dedicate [the merit] together with the Buddha, because they are free from hatred and attachment.
They are surrounded by immeasurable merchants and hundreds of thousands of householders;
the Buddha acts as the caravan leader and the Bodhisattvas act as the merchants. This is because the external benefit of the wealth of the Dharma results in merit returning to themselves.
He resolved all the various affairs of human life (up to: he dwelt in the right mindfulness of a bodhisattva and increased his bodhisattva-aspiration.
△ Second, paying respect:
At that time, the youth Sudhana observed that elder (up to: he prostrated at his feet and remained so for a long while before rising.
△ Second, the inquiry.
He addressed him, saying: "Noble One, I am Sudhana; I am Sudhana.

By thus announcing his own name, it signifies that his reputation has long been heard, manifesting that he is a vessel for honoring the Dharma, in the hope that [the teacher] might grant him instruction.
I shall single-mindedly seek the conduct of a bodhisattva (up to) being able to attain the wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
△ Second, the praise and the conferral of the Dharma, in two parts. First, the praise.
At that time, the elder said to Sudhana: [up to] "arouse the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
△ Second, the bestowing of the Dharma has two parts. First, the indication of its name and essence.
“Good son, I have accomplished the power of the supernormal knowledge that reaches all places—reaching [all] without dependence and without effort.

Because it is without effort and without dependence, it is able to reach everywhere. Its reaching everywhere is the vastness of its function; its being without dependence is the excellence of its essence.”
"Non-reliant," because they do not rely on others; "non-acting," because they are free from deliberate effort (*prayoga*). △ Second, the interrogation and explanation of their activity, in two parts.
First, the interrogation:
"Good son, what is the bodhisattva practice-gate that reaches all places?"
△ Second, the explanation and clarification. Because he extensively teaches the Dharma wherever he goes. This section has two parts. First, citing the three thousandfold world system:
"Good son, regarding these three thousand [great thousandfold worlds]... I also teach them the transcendent and supreme Dharma."
△ Second, manifesting the ten directions.
As in this trichiliocosm... (up to) "I preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
△ Fourth, humbling oneself and deferring to the superior.
Good son, I know only this power of spiritual penetrations that reaches all places— reaching everywhere without dependence or effort—
and the gateway of the pure Dharma, which reaches everywhere for the purpose of preaching the Dharma, as previously described.
Just as all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are fully endowed with [all qualities] up to being able to know and expound those meritorious practices.
△ Fifth, pointing out the subsequent spiritual friend.
"Good son, to the south of here there is a land named Sūna, which in this language means 'Valiant.

It is called Valiant because its power enables roots of goodness to reach everywhere; furthermore, it signifies the meaning of the ten perfections (*pāramitās*), for its significance corresponds to diligence (*vīrya*)."

In that land there is a city named Kaliṅgavana, which is translated according to its meaning as "Time of Mutual Combat," because the city was established on account of victory in battle; this signifies the dedication [of merit].
May it be through the great power of faith and understanding, and through vast, unobstructed wisdom, that [the practice] be cultivated...
There is no place where roots of goodness do not reach; this meaning is the same as during battle.
There is a bhikṣuṇī whose pure compassion causes goodness to pervade everywhere.
He is named Siṃhavijṛmbhitā (Lion’s Stretch).
His stretching and unfolding are sovereign and reach everywhere;
go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
△ 6. Expressing Gratitude and Taking Leave.
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet (and so forth), gazing up at him with earnest devotion before taking his leave and departing.
*The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 103.
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Fascicle 140 (Entering the Lower Volume of the Sixty-seventh Scripture),
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang,
with Annotations on the Scripture Recorded by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.
△ Fourth: The Bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā. The sixth section: The Text on the Dedication Reaching All Places.
First, following the instructions to seek her out:
At that time, the youth Sudhana gradually traveled until he arrived at the Sunlight Garden (Sūryaprabha-udyāna), which she had relinquished as a gift.
The dhūtas of the bhikṣuṇīs, according to the Vinaya, are mostly located in royal gardens.

Because they rely on external protectors, this symbolizes the cause of the supreme light of the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), so that their roots of goodness may pervade the garden of the Dharma-realm. Since these are all identical with wisdom, they possess radiance.
He preached the Dharma to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.

△ Second, seeing, paying respect, and inquiring, in three parts. First, the sight [of the land], in two parts. First, the sight [of the land], in six parts. First, the forest trees of the untainted realm.

At that time, the youth Sudhana went to that garden... [it] universally perfumes the ten directions without obstruction, because it is established through the practice of untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma-caryā*).
Within the text there are eight sections, each of which has its own symbolic significance; reflect upon them.
△ Second, the eight streams of liberation.
Within the garden, there are further flowing springs and ponds (extending) until they spread across its entire floor with water of eight virtues.
That is to say: it is light, cool, soft, and sweet; pure and odorless; temperate and free from affliction.
It was completely filled and covered with *utpala* flowers up to *puṇḍarīka* flowers.
△ Third, the spreading of the seat of the Dharma-emptiness, which varies according to the adornments of the Dharma.
Immeasurable jewel trees stand in rows on all sides (extending to) jeweled bells that sway gently, emitting sublime sounds.
Above they are marked; below they are arranged.
Beneath some of these trees are spread lotus-treasury (extending to) lion thrones of the king of *maṇi* jewels.
The conclusion follows.
Each individual seat has one hundred thousand [features], and each is fully endowed with immeasurable adornments.
△ Fourth, a miscellaneous explanation of the various adornments.
Within this great garden, various jewels are everywhere present... (up to) its radiant light shines universally like the palace of Brahmā.
Because the myriad practices are not one. △ Fifth, revealing their underlying cause.
At that time, the youth Sudhana saw this great garden... [which was] accomplished through meritorious and virtuous karma.
△ Sixth, the explanation of mastery over the fruition and its functions.
By the power of the inconceivable majestic spiritual authority of the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings throughout the trichiliocosm...
[Section Two: Seeing the Primary Retribution, Part Four. First: A general explanation of the manifestation of the supreme virtues of sitting everywhere.]
At that time, Sudhana saw Siṃhavijṛmbhitā (up to) those who see her do not do so in vain, like Varuṇa.
"Varuṇa" here means "water. Because he can fulfill the wishes of people, the significance of the Water Deity (Varuṇa) is not empty of meaning;
however, the specific reason for this remains unclear.
It is able to cause the sprouts of all roots of goodness to grow (up to the point where) the Dharma-gates being taught are also each distinct.
△ Second, the specific explanation of the various dharmas extensively expounded. There are thirty distinct locations, divided into three parts.
First, sixteen [locations] are for the eight classes of beings, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
Alternatively, one may see [the Buddha] seated amidst a host of Śuddhāvāsa devas (up to the point where he) teaches them the dharma-gate named "Inexhaustible Liberation.
Previously, there were seven locations for these devas; the first was the Śuddhāvāsa heaven. He taught the "Inexhaustible" there to treat those *anāgāmins*.
Because they seek the exhaustion of the body and wisdom.

Or, seeing that the assembly of Brahmā devas seated there [extends] to those named the Universal Gate Differentiated Pure Wheel of Speech, the two Brahma Kings respond universally, yet only for their own retinues;
whereas [the Buddha] extensively reaches the three thousandfold world system to preach the Universal Gate, which is without limit.

It should not be so. While the Brahma-voice is pure and subtle, it is merely for the sake of teaching worldly beings. Only that which is the supreme flow from the Dharma-realm is truly pure and sublime.

Alternatively, when one sees him seated on his throne [from the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations] down to [the lower realms], preaching the Dharma-gate called "The Pure Mind of a Bodhisattva."
Third, for the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, because they give rise to supramundane pure minds and exercise mastery over the world,
[the Buddha] appears seated upon a throne as a Sunirmita deva (or up to a Paranirmita-vaśavartin deva) and preaches the Dharma-gate called "The Excellent Adornment of All Dharmas."
