His position is like the "mark of reality" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), because he realizes it through the illumination of wisdom.
It is named "Right Approach" because it approaches the universal Dharma; it is "Right Approach by Wisdom" because it approaches the characteristic of suchness.
It comes from the midst of space.
The essence of wisdom has no dependence; only then does it accord with Suchness.
Upon reaching the summit of the Cakravāḍa mountains of the Sahā world, the intention manifests that Suchness has a support, for delusive confusion is made manifest.
Pressing his foot upon the earth, this Sahā world shook in six ways;
for by the feet of meditative concentration and wisdom, he removed all fragmented wisdom.
Everything was then adorned with various jewels, after which [he] came to the abode of Avalokiteśvara.
"Meeting as before" signifies that they are not separate, for they accord with sentient beings and have attained the mark of suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, it means that wisdom unites with compassion to achieve non-abiding. △ Second, the former friend points the way.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara said to Sudhana: [omitting the section] "...study the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Because he was present in this assembly, the formal salutation and departure were omitted.

△ Third, the conferring of his own dharma-realm, in two parts. First, the designation of its name and essence.

The ten directions are boundless; therefore, it is called the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*). A single thought-moment transcends the many; therefore, it is said to be swift and rapid.

This means that [the practice] proceeds swiftly because it arises from the universal origination of the ten thousand virtues of original enlightenment, which stems from the realm of the Tathāgatagarbha, one’s own fundamental wisdom.

In each and every thought-moment, he traverses as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in an unspeakably unspeakable number of worlds.

"I enter every single Buddha-field" (up to) "teaching and transforming them without ceasing."

"Noble son, to the south of here there is a city named Dvāravatī,
which means 'Possessing Gates. This is because it possesses these subtle and wondrous dharma-gates, such as being unbound and unattached, for the sake of the Dharma-preacher."
Within it there is a spirit named Mahādeva (Great God).
Because he manifests a great body, he is without bondage and without attachment; because his wisdom is pure and sovereign, he is called a "God" (*deva*).
Because he universally responds in accordance with principle, he is called "Great" (*mahā*); because his wondrous functions are difficult to fathom, he is called a "Spirit" (*śen*).

At that time, Mahādeva extended his four hands (reaching out to) hold various golden flowers and scattered them over Sudhana.

In terms of the symbolic meaning, it refers to extending the hands of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) to take up the dharma-gates associated with the supreme stream of realization, which one must first purify within oneself.

This washes away the defilements of body and mind. Because it subsequently benefits others, it is said that "flowers are scattered," which also symbolizes the far-reaching extension of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather in the fourfold assembly.
Thus he addressed them, saying: "O sons of good family... [omitted] ...it shall always be manifest before you at all times."
The manifestation of signs praises the difficulty of encountering such a friend, thereby inspiring joy and entry [into the path]. II. The actual bestowal of what is attained has two parts.

This means that by means of the six perfections and great compassion, one covers and moistens like a cloud, and gathers and encompasses like a net. △ Second, the question and answer regarding its functional activity:
because the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) gather and guide sentient beings. Within this text there are also two parts; first, the question.

Part Two: The Response, which has two sections. First, manifesting jewels to induce giving and instructing him through the inclusion of *dāna*.
At that time, Mahādeva stood before Sudhana and [practiced] the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), being able to relinquish what is difficult to relinquish.

"Good son, just as I have manifested these things for you (up to) crossing the obstructed and perilous path to reach a place free of obstructions"—such words as these also incorporate kind speech (*priyavāditā*) and collaborative conduct (*samānārthatā*). △ Fourth, humbling oneself and extolling the superior.

The Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) entered therein is precisely the locus where awakening (bodhi) is attained; thus, awakening is the fundamental source. Previously, the south was used as a symbolic representation.
Now, moving from the source toward the south, one brings the derivative back to the fundamental Dharma-realm; therefore, it is no longer called "south.

Furthermore, the realization of Suchness (tathatā) by those on the stages (bhūmi) is likewise identical to this source. Since the dedication (pariṇāmanā) has now reached its conclusion, all is gathered and returned to this [Dharma-realm].

"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path.

A brief explanation of its function. △ Second, a detailed manifestation of its karmic activity:

This is called "Yellow. Because the Sage of the Yellow Head (Kapila) relied upon this place in the past, yellow is the central color;
it symbolizes the realization of the Middle Way. Furthermore, as this is the city where the Buddha was born, it symbolizes being born into the family of the Buddhas at the first stage (bhūmi).
There is a night goddess named Vāsantī.
*Vāsa* means "spring," and *tī* means "lord. She is so called because she presides over the crops during the spring season;
it signifies that upon first entering the stages (*bhūmi*), one is able to bring forth all practices and protect sentient beings.
"Go to her and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.

△ Fifth, there are ten virtuous friends who correspond to the ten stages (*bhūmi*). These are divided into ten sections. First is the Night Goddess Vāsantī, who corresponds to the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
The reason night goddesses appear frequently on these stages is that their realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*) is profound and subtle, as they are free from signs (*animitta*) and dispel darkness.
The nine night goddesses of the following [sections] are all female deities according to the Sanskrit original; [the first is] Gopā.
"Furthermore, she is a woman. This refers to the realization of the compassion of identical essence (*samatā-karuṇā*) upon the ground; she appears in the form of a woman. There are six sections.
First, seeking according to the teaching. Second, first, realizing based on prior cultivation.
At that time, the youth Sudhana contemplated with single-minded focus (until) he knew its boundlessness and fathomed its profound depth.
II. Seeking the Subsequent Friend:
Traveling by stages, he arrived at that city and entered through the eastern gate.
Entering through the eastern gate signifies the initial opening of illumination and the beginning of manifesting entry into realization;
thus, before long after standing there, one sees the sun set.
Seeing the sun set refers to the night deities (*rātridevatā*), which symbolizes that all discriminative perceptions of the sun have already vanished. This concludes the preceding analysis.
Upon reaching that time and place, they develop a heart of longing and aspiration;
their minds remain in accordance with the teachings of all bodhisattvas, extending universally to clearly illuminate the oceans of lands throughout the ten directions.
△ Second, seeing and respectfully inquiring of two [aspects]. First, seeing the friend’s environment and person.
While forming this thought, he sees that night goddess in the midst of space. Regarding "seeing her in space":

space represents the path of teaching (the phenomenal), while space also represents the path of realization (the noumenal). Thus, both the doctrinal exposition and its ultimate principle are fully integrated, like the sun situated in the sky.
Because it is empty.
[He dwells] within a jeweled pavilion in the fragrant lotus treasury (up to) as his adornment; he wears crimson robes.
One who wears crimson robes does so because the wisdom of realization is clearly manifest.
Wearing a Brahma-crown upon his head, all the lunar mansions and constellations shine brilliantly upon his body.
These stellar images of the Dharma-gate are inseparable from his single body, as if they were its very substance.
From every single pore of his body, there manifest the transformation and deliverance of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings in the evil realms.
The function of transformation does not depart from the nature of a single hair;
it causes beings to escape from the forms of peril and hardship, thus maturing sentient beings in these various ways.

"Noble son, I have attained the bodhisattva liberation called 'Shattering the Darkness of Ignorance of All Sentient Beings,' which immediately destroys the two types of delusion and brings forth the light of the Dharma."

This is precisely the wisdom that realizes the two kinds of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*), which is capable of destroying [delusion]. Furthermore, it destroys the darkness of sentient beings; compassion is the darkness [to be destroyed], while luminosity is wisdom.

Because it is endowed with both compassion and wisdom: [Section] Two: Clarifying the Functional Activity. This has two parts. First, the prose section. This has two parts. First, giving rise to the mind that seeks to save beings.
"Good son, regarding sentient beings of evil wisdom... [I] am always associated with such a mind.

△ Second, the explicit explanation of the ten gates of saving and gathering according to conditions. The first gate provides a general explanation that there are four kinds of rescue for those in peril at sea.
"Good son, when the night is dark and quiet, and from [the time] until all things are shrouded in gloom such that forms cannot be seen,
there is one moment of rescue. At that time,
I see sentient beings who have entered the sea, or are traveling on land through mountains, forests, wildernesses, and various perilous places."

when one encounters bandits or lacks provisions, becoming terrified, anxious, and fearful, unable to escape by oneself.

At that time, I immediately rescued them by means of various skillful expedients.

For those in maritime distress, he manifests as a shipmaster (up to) causing them to escape fear and attain complete peace and security.
First, he rescues them from worldly suffering and enables them to obtain worldly happiness.
He further forms this thought: "By means of these roots of goodness, I dedicate them to sentient beings, wishing that they may abandon all sufferings.
Subsequently, through dedication by means of great vows, he causes them to reach ultimate liberation from suffering and attain happiness.
Regarding these eight subsequent sections on liberation from suffering and attainment of happiness, there are two [types] based on the preceding pattern. △ Second, saving sentient beings on land.
To cause all sentient beings on land (up to) to completely eliminate the darkness of their various afflictions.

All sentient beings cherish their lives... [until] they reach the state of fearlessness and ultimate peace and happiness.

Good son, if there are sentient beings who are attached to their lands... [until] they abide in the realm of the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) of all Buddhas.

Good son, if there are sentient beings who delight in and are attached to villages... [up to] ultimately dwelling securely in the city of all-knowledge.

If there are sentient beings who hear [the Buddha’s] name or see his body... (up to) ...because they thereby extinguish their afflictions.

△ Second, the Night Goddess Samantāśrī-viśuddhaprabhā. She is entrusted as a spiritual friend on the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*). The meaning is as previously explained;
the text consists of six sections, which are here divided into four. First, following the instruction, she seeks [the path].
At that time, the youth Sudhana, having fully understood that night goddess’s initial arousal of the bodhicitta, first recollected the preceding dharmas.
There were eleven phrases: the first was the recollection of the arousal of the mind, and the remaining ten were the recollections of the attainment of the dharmas.
[The Bodhisattva] proceeded from the place where the Bodhisattva-piṭaka was produced and the Bodhisattva-vows were issued, until he reached the night goddess Samantaguṇaviśuddhaprabhā.
△ Second, [the section on] seeing, paying homage, and inquiring:
He prostrated at her feet and circumambulated her countless times... [asking], "How does one accomplish the bodhisattva stages?"
△ Third, the praise and the conferral of the Dharma, in two parts. First, the praise:
The night goddess replied, "Excellent, excellent... [up to] ...the cultivation, the arising, and the accomplishment."

△ Second, the bestowal [of the teaching] also has two parts. First, the prose section has three parts. First, the actual bestowal of the dharma-gate has two parts. First, a general answer to the question:
"Good son, if a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they will be able to fulfill the bodhisattva practices."
First the headings are presented, followed by the inquiry: "What are the ten?
Next follows the explanation.
First, they attain the samādhi of purity and constantly see all Buddhas;
the first [point] is general, while the remainder is specific.
Second, they attain the pure eye and constantly contemplate all Buddhas (up to) the ocean of light of the infinite dharmas of the Buddhas.
This is the light of the Dharma of wisdom.
Fifth, knowing that from every single pore of all Tathāgatas [there issues forth] light that benefits immeasurable sentient beings.
This is the benefit of emitting light.
Sixth, he saw from every single pore of all the Tathāgatas an ocean of flaming radiance in the colors of all jewels,
with their constant light emitting flames.
Seventh, in every thought-moment, he manifested inconceivable powers of mastery for the sake of taming sentient beings.
The conclusion follows.
Good son, if a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to fulfill all the practices of a bodhisattva.
Part Two: A Detailed Explanation of One’s Own Dharma has two sections. First, the designation of names and essence.
"Good son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation named 'The Universal Gait of the Joy of Tranquil Meditative Concentration.
This means that being in accord with principle and free from attachment is 'tranquility' (*śānti*); the simultaneous cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is 'meditative concentration' (*dhyāna*);

This is the meditation that contemplates reality as it is (*yathābhūta*).
It universally perceives all Buddhas of the three periods of time, seeing them all clearly without any grasping or attachment.
This is the pure meditation of the Tathāgata; it is the activity of tranquility. It is tranquil because one perceives the Buddhas without attachment.
First, the heading; second, the inquiry: "For what reason?

The ten "non-nesses" are largely identical to the eight "non-s" of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
[They range] from knowing that the Tathāgatas do not pass away into eternal extinction (up to) the non-extinction because there is no characteristic of arising.
That is to say, non-going, non-coming, non-arising, and non-ceasing constitute the four.
Because they do not truly abide, they are like illusory phenomena; because they benefit sentient beings, they are not false.
Being neither real nor false, they are thus not eternal.
It is not subject to transmigration because it transcends birth and death; it is not of a nature that perishes because it is eternally unchanging.
Thus, being neither subject to transmigration nor subject to destruction, it is uninterrupted.
It is of a single characteristic, for it is entirely free from verbal expression.
The single characteristic is not different [from no-characteristic], because the nature of no-characteristic is fundamentally empty. No-characteristic is also not one.

by not giving rise to any conceptualization or discrimination, one is immediately freed from what obstructs.
However, while worldly dhyāna merely abandons desire, evil, and unwholesome states, this One Vehicle is profound and subtle.
Being free from all conceptual constructions and providing great compassion as protection for all sentient beings constitutes the factor of benefit;
that is to say, by abandoning one's own anxiety and attending to the anxieties of sentient beings, one gives rise to joy and bliss.

this is the factor of the basis (*niśrayāṅga*), meaning that it is the support for those two. Second, the second dhyāna:
all mental activity (*manas-karman*) ceases.
That is, the cessation of applied and sustained thought,
which encompasses all sentient beings—
this is single-mindedness.
With courageous wisdom and vigor,
this is inner purity, free from directed thought and evaluation,
with a mind filled with joy and gladness.
This is the joy and bliss born of concentration;
one cultivates the second dhyāna, which likewise relies upon those two [factors]. The third and fourth dhyānas below follow this same principle. △ Third, the third dhyāna.

Contemplating the intrinsic nature of all sentient beings constitutes the two factors of equanimity and mindfulness; that is, one abandons the joy previously associated with gathering beings, for within this equanimity,
mindfulness is not lost.

Disenchantment with birth and death constitutes the two factors of wisdom and happiness; that is to say, by correctly knowing that birth and death are not to be rejoiced in, one becomes disenchanted and thereby attains the bliss of true tranquility.
They cultivate the third dhyāna.
△ Fourth, the fourth dhyāna:
they are fully able to extinguish all the suffering, heat, and afflictions of all sentient beings.
It penetrates its three branches—namely, suffering, grief, joy, and pleasure—all of which are the feverish afflictions of sentient beings.

Because one falsely conceives of pleasure within the lower forms of suffering, these four sensations are all extinguished; thus it is said that they can all be stilled, which is precisely the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
Since there is neither suffering nor pleasure, this is the sensation of the Middle Way.
One cultivates the fourth dhyāna.

Increasing and perfecting the vows for all-knowledge (up to) sporting in all supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

When pronouncing the syllable *ta*, one enters the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called the "Gate of Boundless Differentiation.

△ Second, the functional activity has two parts. First, the specific explanation.

There are ten kinds of illusions; in each case, the preceding phrase indicates "illusion," while the subsequent phrase explains it as being "produced by conditions.

Each serves as a general heading for the world produced by conditions, which encompasses both the defiled and pure oceans of lands, as these are also termed "worlds. The remaining nine [points] serve as...
They are distinct. The first five refer to the defiled aspect of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is like an illusion produced by conditions;
this is because all sentient beings abide as illusions, having arisen from karma and afflictions.

All worlds abide as illusions because they arise through the successive conditioning of ignorance, craving, and so forth.

Second, in terms of the twelve links of dependent origination, it is called "successive" (*kramika*) because they follow one another in sequence when viewed in the forward order (*anuloma*), which constitutes the world. Thus, it is said that they arise "successively."

Thirdly, within the five categories of phenomena, only unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are excluded; therefore, it says "all.

This is because unconditioned phenomena have no arising and are not produced by illusory conditions. The ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) and so forth are internally grasped as a self due to beginningless evil habits.
Because it is associated with the four afflictions, it is called "self-view" and so forth; and because it grasps external delusive objects, it is called "various illusory conditions.
Therefore, the deluded mind and its concomitants are all like illusions. The fourth and fifth lines specifically clarify the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
All things of the three periods of time are abidings in illusion, for they are produced by the inverted cognition of the view of self and so forth.
Fourth is "time": this refers to the establishment of time based on the uninterrupted stages of the continuity of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Since the formations upon which it depends are empty, what could time be established upon? To falsely conceptualize that it has a substantial essence is inverted cognition.
All sentient beings arise and perish because they are produced by false conceptualization.
Fifth is impermanence, such as birth, aging, and so forth; that is, impermanence is established based on the state of disintegration following arising.
All such things are falsely discriminated as existing;
for all lands are manifested by ignorance through the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view, which are like a magical illusion.
Sixth, regarding "all lands," the meaning applies to both defiled and pure realms. Defiled lands are mostly produced from these three perversions.

To say "ignorance" (avidyā) serves to distinguish it from the Buddha-field;
for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas abide in illusion, being produced by the illusion of the power of vows and wisdom.
The latter three kinds are explained solely in terms of the pure dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). That they arise from conditions like an illusion can be understood through reflection.
△ Second, the conclusion and praise of its profound mystery.
Good son, the self-nature of illusory phenomena is inconceivable.
Illusory dharmas are not existent, for their essence is unreal; they are not non-existent, for their appearances are not absent.

They are not one, for their nature and appearance differ; they are not different, for they lack two distinct essences. Emptiness and existence are mutually identical; oneness and difference are both transcended. Having thus departed from the two extremes, [they are inconceivable].
Furthermore, the Middle Way is not lost. Because of this mutual penetration, the many can be manifested within the one, and the many are all identical to the one;
they are layered and unimpeded, constituting the inconceivable. Therefore, its excellence is extolled as "skillfully entering the illusory net of boundless phenomena."

"Good son, a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra)... [up to] "...is able to cause one to dwell securely in all gates of the Buddha-dharma. The explanation of this intent states:
because the friend’s teaching causes one to abandon evil causes, the causes perish and the fruits are lost. Is this not the power of the friend?

By means of these forty phrases, the preceding fifteen phrases—which explicitly clarify the subject—are explained. There are both general and specific applications; the general application is as follows:
The subsequent causes of various evils correspond generally to the preceding results; specifically, however, they are each individually correlated with the preceding text.

For example, by removing various obstacles, one does not regress from the Mahāyāna; by severing various evils, one does not transgress the pure precepts; and by destroying ignorance, one does not follow evil associates.
In the following sentences, there may be two or three [causes] that correspond to a single preceding phrase; this can be understood through the context.
It is obtained. Fearing prolixity, I shall not provide a word-for-word correspondence. △ Second, the instruction on exhortation. This refers to teaching the method for befriending such a person.

The text consists of four sections, all of which clarify the meaning through metaphors; thus, it is divided into four parts. First, the instruction to contemplate the superior virtues of the friend. Second, first, praising their superiority.

△ Third, the dual conclusion of the two preceding sections on admonition and encouragement: because explaining them individually would be inexhaustible, it is necessary to conclude this extensive discussion.
Omitting the details, the text consists of two parts. First, it clarifies their multiplicity by means of enumeration:

△ Second, the general summary and conclusion:

This concludes the section. △ Sixth: Expressing Gratitude and Taking Leave.

△ This is the third major section below: Maitreya alone clarifies the characteristics of the causes for attaining Buddhahood through the integration of virtues.

Since it was previously established that by merging conditions into reality one is certainly capable of becoming a Buddha, this section now distinguishes the causes for attaining Buddhahood as a "One-Life-to-Enlightenment" (Ekajātipratibaddha) being.

Regarding the meaning: the text consists of only five sections. Because the stage of the "Successor" (Bodhisattva in his final birth) is the ultimate, the section on humility and deference is omitted. First, following the teaching, there is the seeking [of the path].
Second, first, the designation of mindfulness of what preceded and what follows.
At that time, the youth Sudhana (having arrived) reflected with right mindfulness upon the practices of all bodhisattvas and headed toward the country of Sāgaratīra.

△ Second, the specific generation of superior mindfulness: repenting the past and cultivating the future. This section has four parts; first, observing past errors and applying practice as an antidote.
Recalling that in past lives he had not cultivated respectful salutation, [and so forth], up to: reflecting in this way, he gives rise to great joy.
△ Second, observing his present suffering to spur himself on toward future goodness.
Furthermore, one contemplates that this body is the causal condition for [the attainment of] the body of the Bodhisattva’s vow and wisdom—from birth, old age, sickness, and death [up to that point].
May all practitioners examine this and emulate it. △ Third, the benefits of contemplation and mindfulness: they enhance one's superior insight (vipaśyanā).
While forming this thought, for an inconceivable length of time—extending through the equality of the three periods of time—it continues without cessation.
△ Fourth, the conclusion regarding the benefits and their attribution:
All of this is brought about solely by the acceptance of the instructions of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).

△ Second, seeing [the Buddha] and paying respect, followed by inquiry—this has two parts. First, seeing and paying respect, which has two sub-sections. First, seeing based on two factors. First, entering meditative absorption and extending respect, which has three parts.
First, concluding the previous section and indicating what follows.
The youth Sudhana, with such reverence (up to) prostrating himself before the great multi-storied pavilion, should be understood [as described].
For a moment, he collected his thoughts.
Fixing the object,
contemplation and investigation,
and the preparatory stage of concentration.
By virtue of the power of great vows and profound faith and understanding,
this is the cause of that samādhi.
One enters the gate of equality of the wisdom-body that pervades all places.

Discerning and defining names and characteristics. △ Second, specifically revealing the function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This consists of the simultaneous application of both concentration and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Within this, there are two parts. First, clarifying the wondrous function of concentration that is identical to wisdom. Within this, first: pervading the Dharma-realm with clouds of bodies.
He universally manifests his body before all Tathāgatas (up to: until the end of the future limit, without rest.
△ Second, attaining the true source of the Dharma-nature.
Because it is equal to empty space and is without limit (up to: because it has no inherent nature and transforms according to conditions).
△ Second, the profound contemplation that accords with the Dharma-realm. Within this, there are three parts: first, realizing that phenomena arise from conditions;

second, wisdom accords with the absence of inherent nature; third, returning to the Middle Way. These three are non-obstructive and constitute the three contemplations within a single mind. Now, the first [part]:
One understands that phenomena arise from conditions;
furthermore, one definitively knows that all phenomena arise from karma, as retribution corresponds to good and evil.
Therefore, it is said that they "arise from karma."
All fruits arise from causes; since the fruit is produced from its own seed, how can it be said to arise from a cause?
All karmas arise from habituation; the arising of all Buddhas arises from faith.
One attains Buddhahood through self-cultivation. Faith is the source of the Way.
All manifested acts of offering (up to) all manifested Buddhas arise from a heart of reverence.
Moved by the manifestation of his transformation body, a heart of reverence immediately arose.
All Buddha-dharmas arise from roots of goodness (up to) arising from the sphere of omniscience.
△ Second, the two wisdoms accord with the absence of intrinsic nature.
This is because one knows dedication while free from the view of nihilism (up to: because one knows the reality of things as they are while free from perverted views).
To be free from perverted views means to transcend the four or three types of perversions. A "perversion" refers to reckoning the impermanent as permanent; this is called a perversion.

When one perceives the actual reality, such inversions do not exist. To regard the impermanent as permanent is likewise not to perceive reality as it truly is, because of its nature of disintegration.
Furthermore, by being free from the view of a creator, one knows that [existence] does not depend on another.
This means that while one might claim that Īśvara can produce all things, one knows through one's own karma that it does not arise from another.
Because one understands that [phenomena] arise from conditions, one is free from the views of self and other;
to cling exclusively to self or other contradicts dependent origination.
One is free from the view of extreme adherence because one knows that the dharma-realm is boundless;
one is free from the view of coming and going because one knows that birth-and-death and so forth have no beginning or end;
and one is free from the view of existence and non-existence because one knows that there is neither arising nor ceasing.

To go from non-existence to existence is called "arising"; to go from existence to non-existence is termed "cessation. Since its essence is devoid of arising and cessation, how could there be existence or non-existence?
Because one is detached from all dharmas by seeing and knowing them as empty and unarisen;
and because, in accordance with principle, one eliminates dharmas by knowing they are not autonomous.
The dharma is negated in terms of conditions because one knows it arises from the power of vows;
the dharma is negated in terms of causes.
Because one enters the limit of signlessness by being free from all marks of perception.
△ Third, returning to the Middle Way:
because one knows that all phenomena are like seeds producing sprouts.

Nevertheless, each and every phrase is free from the aforementioned faults. For now, let us explain this generally: for example, regarding the production of a sprout from a seed, because it arises from conditions such as soil and water, it is not non-existent;
this is like the first section’s contemplation of dependent origination. Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is not existent; this is like the second section.
This state of being neither existent nor non-existent is precisely the Middle Way, and thus it is free from the extremes of nihilism and eternalism.
These points may be inferred accordingly. The horizontal analogy of the seed and sprout represents the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*), for they arise like the impression of a seal producing its mark.
The vertical analogy represents all phenomena (*sarvadharma*); as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "When this aggregate (*skandha*) ceases, another aggregate arises in succession, like a wax seal."
Sealing with clay; the seal being broken while the impression is formed, and so forth. The following phrases apply to both horizontal and vertical [analyses]:
because one knows that substance is like an image, because one knows that sound is like an echo, and so on, up to "because one realizes that the world is a manifestation of the mind."

To realize that the world is a manifestation of the mind is likewise the contemplation of Mind-only. Taking the mind as its condition, it manifests yet lacks intrinsic nature; this is the contemplation of the Middle Way.
This is because one realizes that effects arise from causes, realizes that retribution arises from the accumulation of karma, and [realizes that all things] flow forth from skillful means.
△ Third, the summary of the benefits achieved.
When the youth Sudhana entered such wisdom, [it reached] until his body and mind were cooled, refreshed, and radiant.
△ Second, Sudhana emerges from samādhi and pays homage with the three karmas. The text has three parts. First, paying homage through the body by circumambulating.
Rising from the ground, they gazed up at him with single-minded devotion, their eyes never wavering for a moment; with palms joined, they circumambulated him for immeasurable circuits.
△ Second, honoring him in mind, in ten parts: first, manifesting excellence by way of the object.
One should form this thought: "This great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who have realized emptiness, signlessness, and non-self.
However, each of these phrases individually extols the virtues of the inhabitants to praise the celestial palace in which they dwell;
because the first phrase fully manifests this, the expression "this great celestial palace" runs through all the subsequent phrases.
This is the dwelling place of those who are non-discriminative regarding all phenomena... up to ...those who have entered all paths.
△ Second, manifesting the excellence by way of qualities:
This is the dwelling place of those who enter all profound *prajñā*... up to ...the presence of all Tathāgatas.
△ Third, revealing mastery by way of function:
it is the dwelling place of one who can enter a single eon into all eons... [and so forth] ...up to all lands.
△ Fourth, revealing excellence by way of practice.
This is the dwelling place of those who, before all sentient beings, preach the Dharma that is difficult to encounter.
△ Fifth, revealing the profundity by way of contemplation:
This is the dwelling place of those who abide in the profound Dharma that is difficult to know, [up to] the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
△ Sixth, the superiority [of this dwelling] is revealed by way of its antidotes.
It is the dwelling place of those who abide in great loving-kindness and great compassion (up to: ...and who do not coexist with delusion).
△ Seventh, regarding mastery through the clarification of śamatha and vipaśyanā:
this is the dwelling place of those who, although abiding in the four dhyānas, do not take birth according to those dhyānas [but instead proceed] toward the practices and vows for bodhi.
△ 8. The superiority [of this stage] is revealed in terms of altruistic practice.
Although it is [a state] within all karma and afflictions, it is the dwelling place of one who performs deeds for the benefit of others.
△ Ninth, mastery regarding the protection of the practices of the Hīnayāna:
although he practices the nine successive meditative absorptions (up to) although he teaches all vehicles, he does not abandon the Mahāyāna.
△ Ten: The Abode of Meritorious Qualities.
This great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who abide in all such meritorious qualities as these.
Among the preceding nine [sections], excluding the first two and the fifth, the remainder all concern the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the real, and of phenomena and principle. △

Second, the praise through verbal veneration consists of fifty-five verses, which are divided into two parts. The first thirty-four verses, in heptasyllabic meter, extol his virtues while indicating the locations [of those virtues].
The latter twenty-one verses, in pentasyllabic meter, indicate the locations while clarifying his virtues. Within the former part, there are again two sections;
the first two verses provide a general praise.
At that time, the youth Sudhana spoke these verses: [up to] "the dwelling place of this peerless one.
First, there is a section concerning the stages of practice; second, a section concerning names and virtues. △ Second, the remaining verses separately concern his virtuous conduct in four parts.
First, concerning the excellence of his self-benefiting practice.
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—this is the dwelling place of those who are without dependence.
(End of section. △ Second, there are ten verses praising the excellence of altruistic conduct.
Universally beholding the various classes of beings in the evil realms... [up to] ...this dwelling place of firm resolve.

△ Four: There are seven verses praising the excellence of skillful means (*upāya*).
[They describe] the accomplishment of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and skillful wisdom, up to "the dwelling place of this compassionate one.

△ Two: Indicating the location and manifesting its excellence. Although the words rely on the physical site, the intent lies in praising the True Dharma (*saddharma*). Within this, there are six parts; first—
B. Downward Transformation.
The Buddha-sons dwell here, universally manifesting before all sentient beings... (until) filling the lands of the ten directions.

The Son of the Buddha dwells here, traveling throughout all worlds (until: his mind never grows weary or tired.

The Buddha-sons dwell here, entering samādhi in every thought-moment (up to) within all realms of existence.

The Buddha-sons dwelling here drink from the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas... (up to) ...without arising and without anything existing.

He contemplates that sentient beings are equal, dharmas are equal, Tathāgatas are equal, lands are equal, all vows are equal, and the three periods of time are entirely equal.

The Buddha-sons dwell here, transforming and teaching all living beings... (until) "I pray that you will deign to look upon me.
△ Second, seeing the primary retribution. This section has two parts. First, seeing [the primary retribution] has two parts. First, raising the mind with the wish to behold [the Buddha].
At that time, the youth Sudhana (having arrived) wished to see Maitreya Bodhisattva and to attend upon and make offerings to him.
△ Second, the actual beholding of the Compassionate Honored One:
he then saw Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva coming from another place.
Regarding the statement "coming from another place": it means that he comes to transform and guide according to the capacities of sentient beings; it means that he returns to his original source;
and it also manifests that Maitreya arrives in response to thought, yet does not cling to any location.
Immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas (up to [the rest of the list]) all came together toward the Great Tower of the Adorned Treasury.
Part Two: Establishing the Ritual of Reverence, in five sections. First: Prostration with Body and Mind.
Upon seeing this, Sudhana was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he prostrated himself on the ground with his five limbs touching the earth.
△ Second, the praise of virtues and the prediction. This section has two parts. First, the prose narrative:
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva observed Sudhana, pointed him out to the great assembly, and extolled his meritorious virtues.
The "Instruction" is so called because it causes the assembly to behold [the Buddha] together and to practice by following his example.
△ Second, the formal praise in verse consists of one hundred and thirteen stanzas, divided into three parts. First, pointing to the assembly and praising them collectively.
And he spoke in verse: "You all observe Sudhana... [and] has come to my presence. II.
Specifically praising his superior virtues, in three parts. First, twenty-two verses directly praising Sudhana;
within this, there are also three sections. First, nine verses praising him for his virtuous arrival.
"Welcome, you who have perfected loving-kindness; welcome, you who have purified compassion... [up to] "...never wearying in practice.
△ Second, there are two verses clarifying the causes and conditions for coming.
Mañjuśrī, Guṇamegha, and all other sons of the Buddha have now come to my presence.
This is because they possess virtuous friends externally and are endowed with moral conduct internally. △ Third, the purpose for which they have come.
Having sought the pure realm of all Tathāgatas, [they] have come to my presence.
△ Second, the praise for the assembly to observe, in five parts. First, four verses of general praise.
"You all observe how this person, by drawing near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), [attains] and receives various supreme fruits of retribution.
△ Second, there are four verses praising the compassion that is identical with wisdom.
Sudhana saw sentient beings suffering from birth, old age, sickness, and death (up to) and was shown the place of peace and security.
△ Third, there are seven verses praising his wisdom that is identical with compassion.
The armor of patience, the vehicle of liberation, and wisdom as a sharp sword (up to) extinguish the darkness of the three poisons.
*Jñeya* means "that which is to be known. The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states: "The stage of *jñeya* is the tenth stage (*daśamī bhūmi*).
This is because it involves the complete severance of the ten types of cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). △ Fourth, there are six verses that collectively praise all [the Buddhas].

Virtue. The awakening mind is the *kalala* (embryo), compassion is the *arbuda* (vesicle), and loving-kindness is the *peśī* (flesh). [This continues] until: "Dedicate yourself exclusively to seeking a spiritual friend.

*Kalala* is the same as *geruolán* (揭蘿藍); this is a difference in the weight of the Sanskrit vowels (*brāhmaṇa* vs. *brahman*). △ The final five verses praise the marvelous fruits that shall be realized.
"One shall extinguish all evil realms and show the path to humans and devas" (up to) "his heart is filled with great joy.
△ Section Three: Fivefold Praise of Sudhana. First, praise of his future fruit-virtue. Second, the general [praise].
"Your conduct is exceedingly gentle and your mind is profoundly pure... (until) you shall achieve great Bodhi.
△ Second, the specific [exhortation]:
"You should fulfill the ocean of all practices; you should know the ocean of all dharmas... (until) your heart gives rise to great joy."
△ Section Two consists of seven verses, which jointly praise his virtues in the present and the future:
"Regarding all dharma-gates, you have already attained [them] and shall attain [them]" (up to) "...you should give rise to great joy."
△ Section Three contains eight verses praising the virtue of encountering a spiritual friend.
[It begins with: "The faculties are untiring and the aspiration is ever-resolute... (up to: ...Excellent is the dwelling in this life."
△ Section Four consists of five verses. They praise the qualities of practice for those who have swiftly attained the stages.
[The text] from "Having been born into the family of Bodhisattvas and having already perfected the virtues of a Bodhisattva" up to "one should likewise train in this manner."
△ Section Five consists of seventeen verses. They collectively clarify all virtues and conclude with an exhortation to inspire joy.
[The text states: "All practices of merit arise from aspiration and desire... until reaching the shore of the Buddha's merits."
△ Third, one verse briefly indicates the future companion:
"You should go to the place of the Greatly Wise Mañjuśrī; he shall cause you to attain the profound and wondrous practices of Samantabhadra."
△ Section Three: A Triple Application of Reverential Manner. First, the discernment of the cause for reverence: because he heard the praise of his virtues.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... (up to) praised the great treasury of merit of Sudhana.
△ 2. Sorrowful and Reverent Response of Body and Mind.
Having heard this, Sudhana was filled with joy and leaped for gladness (until: ...), reverently gazing up at him and circumambulating him countless times.
△ 3. Offering Flowers to Express Sincerity.
By the power of Mañjuśrī’s mental recollection,
manifested through faith and wisdom,
there were various flowers and necklaces.
Because their flowers were established through virtue and their necklaces perfected through practice,
various wondrous jewels suddenly filled their hands without them even realizing it;
this was because their faith and wisdom were complete.

Sudhana, filled with joy, immediately scattered [the flowers] over Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in order to gather the causes for accomplishment and to prepare for the attainment of the future fruit. △ Fourth, the second round of praise and exposition.
Then Maitreya Bodhisattva placed his hand upon Sudhana’s head and spoke these verses for him:
"Excellent, excellent, true son of the Buddha... (as in the text)... you alone are like Mañjuśrī and myself."
△ 5. Rejoicing at the Encounter and Recalling Gratitude.
At that time, the youth Sudhana replied in verse: "I call to mind the spiritual friend... [omitted] ...may I swiftly return to behold him."

Recorded by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui. Commentary on the Sūtra. △ Second, the inquiry.
This section has two parts. First, the self-announcement of the arousal of the mind.
At that time, the youth Sudhana... [up to] ...aroused the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
△ Second, the formal inquiry into the essentials of the Dharma, in three parts. First, the statement of what is being asked:
"But I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practice, nor how one should cultivate the bodhisattva path."
△ Second, praising Maitreya for possessing the virtue of being able to answer, and taking that very virtue as the basis for the inquiry:
"The Great Sage, all the Tathāgatas, have bestowed upon the Venerable One the prediction [of future Buddhahood] up to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The former is general; the latter is specific.

From "If in one lifetime one shall attain unsurpassed bodhi" (up to) "one will already be able to swiftly tread upon the stage of omniscience," there are fifty distinct phrases, all of which are virtues of perfected causes and fulfilled fruits.
△ Third, the conclusion of the inquiry and the request for exposition, which also reveals—
The meaning of the question:
"O Great Sage Bodhisattva, how should one study the bodhisattva practices... [and so forth] up to these matters? I pray that you will explain them all for me.
△ Third, the praise and the conferral of the Dharma, in two parts. First, the praise, in two sections. The first is the praise of Sudhana for the sake of the great assembly, namely:
This is the second part of the objection. First, the person is pointed out and shown to the assembly:
"At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... [asked] whether he practiced the various merits of a bodhisattva."
△ Second, the correct praise of his virtues, in four parts. First, his diligent seeking of a friend. Within this, first, a general manifestation of his diligence:
"O virtuous ones, this son of a householder was courageous and diligent (until) he sought him everywhere, serving him and requesting the Dharma."
△ Second, a specific demonstration of the characteristics of diligent application.
"O noble ones, this son of a householder (until) never for a moment gave rise to a single thought of weariness or indolence.
This refers to diligence at a single point in time; it is not yet worthy of praise. For from beginning to end, Sudhana did not, for even a single thought-moment—
There is no deficiency; therefore, it is worthy of praise. Regarding the statement that there are one hundred and ten spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), there have been many ancient interpretations.
One says that they should logically be complete, but the text is merely missing [some names]. Master Xianshou’s interpretation states:
"The various friends before and after [the main narrative] total fifty-four positions. If one divides Deśanā and Guṇākara into two, then there are fifty-five individuals, each of whom..."
Because of their own superior progress, there are one hundred and ten. If one relies on this interpretation, it contradicts the aforementioned statement.
Since it says that one must pass through one hundred and ten before reaching Maitreya, it is clear that Maitreya and the other two are not included within the count of one hundred and ten.
Some say that "one hundred and ten" is merely a way of stating the number minus ten.
According to the actual count, there are only one hundred and eight individuals. That is to say, excluding Vidyuddeva from the aforementioned group, there remain fifty-one;
each having both a primary friend (*mukhya-mitra*) and a secondary friend (*pārṣada-mitra*), they constitute one hundred and two.
Vidyuddeva, who instructed them in various arts, although not a primary friend, is a secondary friend, thus making one hundred and three. To this, further add King Anala, Vyoman, and Gopaka.

At the wave-sites are the deity Virtue of Freedom from Sorrow, the deity Lotus Dharma-Virtue Body of Māyā, the deity Radiance of Exquisite Flowers, and the Rākṣasa Fine-Eyed Guardian of the Dharma Hall; together with the aforementioned, there are one hundred and eight persons in total.

Because he engages in dialogue regarding the characteristics of the deities of the void and so forth, he is counted among the circle of friends. It is not that he is designated as a "host-friend" by being named and pointed out as before;
therefore, he is not a host-friend, but is merely called a "companion-friend. If this were so, it would contradict the subsequent mention of "other cities. The text itself explains below:
"Previously, from the boys and girls, one hundred and ten [cities] have already been passed; now we proceed further still."
Because Mañjuśrī is already included, it is said that there are "the rest. If one were to count these as the hundred and eight, adding Maitreya would result in one hundred and nine;
including the subsequent Mañjuśrī, they would only reach one hundred and ten. How, then, could there be "the rest"? If one seeks a comprehensive reconciliation, all three interpretations are valid.
Taking the former [interpretation] and further adding the Bodhisattva Awakening at the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi-avabodha) and the Deva [makes the total complete].

The Tathāgata’s messengers bring the total number to one hundred and ten; thus, the remaining meaning is also established, as those two sages also instructed Sudhana and therefore may serve as his companions.
As for the phrase "the rest are his own [words]," this is merely the intention of the translator;
it does not appear in the Jin translation. Taking both the preceding and following contexts into account, there is no contradiction in the meaning. However—

Below, it further states "one hundred and ten cities" and again "more than one hundred and ten *yojanas*. In all these cases, the mention of "one hundred and ten" is for the sake of symbolic representation.

That is to say, excluding the stage of Buddhahood, taking the realization and entry into the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*sammyaksaṃbodhi*) constitutes the "one hundred and ten.
Within the "one," there are "ten"; thus, they form one hundred and ten. This also reveals the successive stages.
The ten and the ten are mutually fused. Even if there are the three stages of worthiness (*śaikṣa*), they likewise possess only the ten.

If one combines them with Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), it is subsumed within the "superior progress" (*viśeṣa-gāmin*) of the ten stages; thus, the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) are opened up to constitute the first [stage].

Whether one proceeds or regresses, whether in sequential arrangement (*pratipatti-vyūha*) or perfect fusion (*pariṇata-yugapat*), all accord with the statement of "one hundred and ten. Why must one insist on definitively fixing their anteriority and posteriority? △ Second.
Regarding the three points on the vastness of what he rides: first, a general challenge concerning his rarity.
"O worthy ones, this son of a householder... practices the vast dharmas that assist the path."
△ Second, the specific explanation of the difficulty of encountering [such a person], in two parts.
First, the brief enumeration: Such a person is difficult to hear of, difficult to see, and difficult to approach, dwell with, or associate with.
△ Second, the interrogation and the explanation, which are twofold. First, the interrogation: "For what reason?

△ Second, the explanation. The intent of the explanation is as follows: because it is neither saving nor vast. This immediately opens up [the section on] "protecting and rescuing all beings" from within the previous general [heading].
Birth. Within this, there are two parts. First is the general protection of all.
This son of a householder resolves his mind to rescue and protect [beings], up to severing delusion and confusion to emerge from birth and death.
△ Second, explaining by way of categories.
O virtuous ones, this son of a householder has constructed a great Dharma-ship for those who are being swept away and submerged by the four currents.
"Submerged" (*gul*) refers to the appearance of a rapid current.

For those who are submerged and drowning in the mire of views, [and so on] up to those dwelling in the city of the elements (*dhātu*), he demonstrates the various gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).

As for the "city of the elements," it refers to the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*); because within each individual faculty (*indriya*), object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), there is a distinct liberation.
Those who are in peril are led to a place of safety; those entangled by the snakes of the elements are liberated by means of the Noble Path.
The "snakes of the elements" refers to the four elements, earth and so forth.
Those who are attached to the six sense bases, which are like an empty village, are drawn out by the light of wisdom.

The six sense bases are an empty village; they are devoid of people and shrouded in the darkness of ignorance. If one does not lead them out with the light of wisdom, they will surely be plundered by the bandits of sensory dust.
Those who dwell in false salvation shall be led to enter true salvation, until they are made to enter the city of omniscience.
△ Third, the summary of what has been accomplished:
"O virtuous ones, this son of a householder... always delights in practicing in accordance [with the teachings] and never transgresses them.
△ Third, possessing virtues without deficiency.
"O virtuous ones, if there are sentient beings... (up to) "...you should know that each successive stage is increasingly more difficult to obtain.
There are thirteen phrases. To possess even one is already rare; how much more so to possess two, three, or to have them all complete.
Therefore, the Sūtra says they are "increasingly difficult to obtain. Furthermore, because each subsequent stage is more difficult than the preceding one, it is said:
Successive Progress. △ Fourth, Swift Realization Surpassing Expedient Means:
"O virtuous ones, other bodhisattvas... [until] they are then able to draw near to the Bodhi of all Buddhas.
This is based on expedient cultivation.
This son of a householder is able to purify Buddha-fields and transform sentient beings within a single lifetime;

this is because he practices in accordance with the teaching of ultimate reality (*bhūtadharmadeśanā*). That is to say, even while remaining in an ordinary body, he generates both understanding and practice within one life.
A crow that has lived for a thousand years cannot compare to a phoenix born this morning. Thus, the stages and practices of Samantabhadra are mutually integrated and encompassed.
Therefore, those who practice according to reality are all capable of this. Why not exert yourselves? The text consists of ten phrases;
the first two phrases generally clarify the possession of the practices of all stages.
Thus, one is able to penetrate deeply into the dharma-realm through wisdom.
By entering the three stages and the ten abodes,
one is able to accomplish all the pāramitās and expand and broaden all practices.
The four or five [stages] enter the ten practices (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*), whereby one is able to fulfill all great vows.

The six entries (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) are dedicated toward enlightenment. Furthermore, the aforementioned four lines also constitute the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Moreover, the meanings contained within these four preceding points encompass [the entire path].
The general and the specific:
thus one is able to transcend all demonic activities (up to) being able to fully perfect all the practices of Samantabhadra.
These four lines apply to all stages. △ Second, praising the bodhicitta for Sudhana: namely—
Praising the Dharma. The text has two parts. First, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one:
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva... having caused immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta.
△ Second, the formal praise in four parts. First, the statement praising the arousal of the mind:

The intent of this inquiry is: "Why is it that one is praised as 'excellent' and said to have 'attained excellent benefit'? △ Second, the explanation. The meaning is as follows:

Because the Great Bodhicitta possesses all virtues, the text contains two hundred and twenty-one sentences, all of which pertain to the three types of generating the mind (*cittotpāda*) and instantaneously encompass the merits of all stages (*bhūmi*). For the time being, this is divided into two parts:

the first one hundred and eighteen sentences clarify the Bodhicitta as it universally pervades all stages; the latter one hundred and three sentences clarify the Bodhicitta as it is instantaneously [perfected].

It possesses the merits of all stages. Furthermore, the preceding section primarily clarifies the accomplishment of faith-understanding and the generation of the mind through practice (*adhimukti-caryā-prasthāna-citta*), while the subsequent section primarily clarifies the generation of the mind at the stage of realization (*pramāṇa-bhūmi*). For this reason, the scriptural text frequently uses the term "attainment.

Moreover, the preceding section elucidates the extraordinary merits of the bodhicitta, which equal the fruit of Buddhahood; the subsequent section illustrates the sovereign power of the merits of the bodhicitta.
The virtues are vast, numerous, and immeasurable. Within this initial section, there are two parts. First is the specific explanation; the text applies both horizontally and vertically.

Horizontally, each and every arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) possesses the virtues of all the phrases. Vertically, they are specifically assigned to the arousal of the mind at each respective stage.

Because one proceeds from the bodhisattva lineage until reaching the ultimate state without departing from three types of arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), Master Guāngtǒng correlates these with the twelve stages (*vihāra*) and divides them into twelve sections; the first is the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi-vihāra*).
"Noble son, the bodhicitta" (up to) "is able to sustain all worlds.
Now, these first three phrases refer to the stage of abiding in the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*). Therefore, it is said: "like a seed, like a field, and also like the great earth.
All of these convey the meaning of the generation of seeds. △ Second, explaining the benefits within the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*).
The bodhicitta is like pure water... because it can emit various radiances of the Dharma.
△ Third, the Stage of Increasing Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*).
The bodhicitta is like clear eyes... because one attains mastery among all vows.

"The bodhicitta is like a great ocean" [up to] "because it is unstained by any worldly phenomena."

The bodhicitta is like the Pūrṇa wind—
here called the "swift and violent wind"—

when one personally realizes and awakens to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one enters the Dharma-realm. This is the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), which is the awakening from delusion.

Entering [the state], there is a distinction between the gate and the principle. Once realized, they are in perfect accord; subject and object both vanish. Being true within the false, there is no further place to enter;

next, with what eye does one see?

These metaphors clarify the characteristics of seeing (*darśana*). There are ten metaphors because the things they illustrate are distinct. Furthermore, there are two intended meanings:

The first [verse] provides a general analogy for both the seer and the seen, stating that all are like dream-phenomena, such as being unimpeded by size and so forth.

They are not the same. [The first] is the power of the Dragon-holder’s realization of the identity of self and others; the fifth is the power of the friend as the supporting environment (*upabhoga*); the sixth is the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

the seventh is the power of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*); the eighth is the power of mastery over the *dharmadhātu*; and the ninth is the power of the non-duality of wisdom and concentration.
Because of the Great Wisdom Sea-Seal Samādhi, there are ten powers of mastery over illusory wisdom.
