it serves as a metaphor for what is seen in accordance with the latent predispositions (*anuśaya*).
For example, it is like a person possessed by a spirit (up to: if there were someone who questioned them, there would be nothing they could not answer.
The metaphor of being possessed by a non-human being illustrates that what is perceived can be explained.
For example, it is like a person possessed by a nāga who perceives a short duration as immeasurable kalpas.
This analogy of lingering long in a nāga palace illustrates the perfect interfusion of thought-moments and kalpas.
For example, it is like the Brahma palace named *Vyūharatnakośa* (Treasury of Adornments), where various distinctions appear without being confused;
this analogy of the vast manifestation of the Brahma palace illustrates the non-obstruction between the one and the many.
For example, when a bhikṣu enters the meditative absorption of the totalities (kṛtsnāyatana), all objective spheres become entirely clear.
The object of the totalities serves as a metaphor for the clarity of what is seen.
For example, it is as if someone were in empty space [and so forth] until: they discern everything without any obstruction.
The analogy of the *gandharvanagara* (city of the gandharvas) depending upon space illustrates the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle.
For example, the palaces of yakṣas and the palaces of humans (up to) each perceive differently according to their respective karma.
This analogy of different perceptions in the same place illustrates the sovereign mastery over concealment and manifestation.
For example, within the great ocean, all forms and images of the three thousandfold world system are seen entirely.
This analogy of the ocean manifesting the three thousandfold world illustrates the simultaneous perception of both the near and the far.
It is like a master illusionist who, by the power of illusion, [creates] all manner of adornments within a realm of sovereign mastery.
The numerous metaphors of illusory manifestation illustrate that what is perceived—whether pure or mixed—is without obstruction.
*Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 118;
*Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 119 (entering the second half of the seventy-ninth scripture).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang;
recorded and annotated on the sūtra by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.
△ The four matters are concluded; now arising from meditative concentration (samādhi). First: Awakening [the assembly] to arise.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... (up to) said to Sudhana: "Good son, arise.

He also snapped his fingers. The former [instance] was attaining the essential meaning, namely, the forgetting of words; this present instance is attaining the essential meaning so as not to stagnate in quiescence.
△ Second, a brief indication of the essence and characteristics.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus.
The first phrase indicates the subject; the subsequent portion explains the characteristics perceived.
This refers to the bodhisattva’s wisdom that knows all phenomena [to be] like illusions, like dreams, like shadows, and like reflections.

They arise conditioned by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). Because they arise conditionally, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, it is said that such an intrinsic nature—like illusions, dreams, and so forth—is entirely unestablished.
This concludes the superior meaning. Because there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) apart from conditions, phenomena are not established as real entities.

Because there is no intrinsic nature apart from conditions, the underlying principle is not established as something separate. By not maintaining a fixed self-nature, it is able to follow conditions to form the aforementioned dharmas.

Although they are formed, they do not depart from the *dharmatā*; therefore, phenomena and [the principle] are identical. Such is the *dharmatā*, which is also spontaneously possessed as an inherent virtue.
Third, arising upon attaining the essential meaning.
At that time, Sudhana heard the sound of a finger-snap and arose from samādhi.
△ Second, the question and answer regarding what was seen, in two parts. First, the question.
Maitreya replied: "Good son, you abide in the bodhisattva [stage]... you know the virtues of a bodhisattva and have realized the vows of the Tathāgata.
This question concerns direct realization; yet, when traced back to its cause, it is said that he "abides in the inconceivable. △ Second, the answer.
Sudhana said: "Indeed, O Noble One! This is due to the power of the spiritual benefactor’s empowerment, mindfulness, and majestic virtue.

[The response] answers with humility and reverence, attributing the cause to external conditions and stating it is the power of the good friend. This mutual deference between teacher and disciple runs contrary to ordinary worldly sentiment.
II. Revealing the Name of the Dharma. Part 1: The Question.
"Noble One, what is the name of this gate of liberation?
△ Second, the answer:
Maitreya replied, "Good son, this gate of liberation is named 'Entering the Realms of All Three Times.'"
This very realm that is entered and perceived is the wisdom of non-forgetful mindfulness;

it is precisely this wisdom that is able to enter and manifest. Because the three periods of time are identical as one, the kalpas and moments are perfectly interfused. Accordingly, [the text continues:]

Within a single lifetime, one manifests the realms of the three periods of time. Wisdom enters the three periods, comprehending that all phenomena are empty and quiescent; thus, it accords in profound harmony with Suchness (Tathatā).
Therefore, within a single thought-moment, there is nothing that is not seen.
The "Treasury of Adornments" (Vyūha-kośa) has two meanings: first, because it is adorned by the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);

within this adornment, there is contained the production of inexhaustible ornaments, just as one sees many pavilions within a single pavilion. Second, because it accords with perfect interfusion through unimpeded wisdom.
The objective realm adorns the Tathāgatagarbha; thus, all phenomena are primordially present within it. Therefore, the preceding passage states:

"The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is such; it is not something newly produced. Consequently, within this gate, there are unspeakably many liberations. The above clarifies the primary gate; the following clarifies the gates of its retinue.
"Good son, within this gate of liberation... [it is] what can be attained by a Bodhisattva in their final birth.
△ Third, investigating the fundamental source of the causes for adornment. Within this, there are two rounds of question and answer.
In the first round, one investigates where these causes ultimately lead. Part One: The Question.
Sudhana asked, "Where has this array of adornments gone?
Because it had suddenly vanished after Sudhana beheld the power of the wondrous manifestation above, he asked for its place of departure.
△ Second, the answer.
Maitreya replied: "They go to where they came from.

They come because they flow from the root to the branches; they go because they gather the branches back into the root. Since going is not different from coming, he leads them back to where they came from.
Thus, he answered both questions simultaneously. Part Two: The Subsequent Section Clarifies Their Original Arising. 1. The Question.
He asked, "From where did you come?
Although he was led back to the place from which he had come, since the ultimate destination was not investigated, how could the original source be known? Therefore, he sought it once more.
△ Second, the answer has two parts. First, the Dharma.
It is said: They come from within the wisdom and spiritual power of the Bodhisattva;
that is to say, they come because they are produced through the conditions of the power of wisdom.
They abide by relying upon the wisdom and spiritual power of the Bodhisattva.
It abides through the power of wisdom and the addition of conditions. Its superior marks and inferior nature have no place of departure and no place of abiding.
Since it arises from conditions, there is neither coming nor going. Therefore, this adornment does not abide within the pavilion, nor...
It does not come from another place;
it is neither accumulated nor permanent.
Because it arises from conditions, it is not accumulated; because it ceases when conditions fade, it is not permanent. If it were previously fixed in a location...

If one [asserts that something] exists, one falls into the error of eternalism (*śāśvata*). If it previously existed and now does not, it constitutes annihilation; thus one falls into the error of nihilism (*uccheda*).

Being far removed from all things, and having already departed from both annihilation and permanence, how could there be characteristics such as arising and ceasing, or identity and difference? Therefore, it is said that one attains liberation from all [extremes]. △
There are two parables; the first is the parable of the dragon king raining down.
"Good son, it is like the dragon king raining down [until] such a realm is inconceivable."
This is a partial metaphor for the coming of that which has no coming.
Good son, those matters of adornment are likewise: they do not abide within, by virtue of the power of the bodhisattva.
Nor does it abide externally, due to the power of one's own virtue. When internal and external causes and conditions mutually cancel each other out, both the internal and external vanish;
yet it is not that these things are not seen—it is solely through the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva and the power of your own roots of goodness that you see such phenomena.
△ Second, the analogy of a magician manifesting illusions.
"Good son, it is like a magician... [up to] "...by the power of illusion, they are clearly visible.
This pair of analogies for coming and going shows that there is, in fact, no coming or going.
The matter of those adornments is likewise thus (up to): "By the power of great vows, they manifest in this way.
△ Fourth, examining the nature and characteristics of the primary retribution, in two parts. First, questioning the origin; second, the actual inquiry. First, the question.
The youth Sudhana said, "Great Sage, from where have you come?

Previously, he had seen Maitreya coming from another place; he immediately paid his respects and inquired about the Dharma, but had not yet had the leisure to ask from where [Maitreya] himself had come.
Therefore, because of the previous formalities of service, he now asked about the place of origin. △ Third, the answer consists of three parts.
Regarding the place from which [the Tathāgata] comes:
first, concerning the *dharmakāya*. Maitreya said: "Good son, all bodhisattvas... come in such a way as to be neither annihilated nor eternal.
This refers to the *dharmakāya* in its essential reality; it is a coming that is no-coming, and a no-coming that is coming. There are ten pairs of phrases [in this passage]. △
Second is the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Good son, the Bodhisattva comes from the realm of great compassion; because he manifests as a transformation like a reflected image, it is called the "actual reward" in terms of its characteristics.
He also comes from within the myriad practices, just as Vimalakīrti came from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of the myriad paths of practice.
...Thus. △ Third, the Transformation Body (Nirmāṇakāya).
Now, "Good son, you ask me... [up to] "...coming here from the country of Maratha.

This refers to appearing through transformation according to function, coming from wherever the faculties of beings are ready. These three are precisely the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. Furthermore—

These are essence, characteristic, and function; they also correspond to principle, phenomenon, and practice. Furthermore, the first [of these] refers exclusively to principle, the last refers exclusively to phenomena, and the middle one encompasses both principle and phenomenon.
As for *Māratī*, the full form is *Mālayatīśu*. *Mālaya* is translated here as "Garland-Giver" (*mālā-dāna*).
This is the name of the mountain. According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it is so called because that mountain is located within this country, or because the country is near that mountain.
"Good son, there is a village there named Gṛha, and in it lived a son of an elder named Gopāla."

"Gau" means earth; "pāla" means to protect. Because he protects both the land and the mind-ground, and in order to transform that person and cause them to enter the Buddha-dharma, he dwelt there and came from there.
△ Second, the question-and-answer regarding the place of birth, in two parts. First, the question:
Sudhana said, "Noble One, what is the place of birth for a bodhisattva?
This inquiry is made now because the preceding sutra stated, "coming from the place of birth. △ Second, the answer, in two parts. First, the general explanation.
There are three sections regarding the birthplaces of bodhisattvas. First is the direct answer concerning their birthplaces.
It says: "Good son, there are ten kinds of birthplaces for bodhisattvas. What are these ten?"
In these ten [analogies], the first phrase of each constitutes the practice that gives birth, while the second phrase constitutes the family into which one is born.
Good son, the bodhicitta is the place of birth for bodhisattvas, for it gives birth to them within the family of bodhisattvas.

That is to say, when one generates the bodhicitta, that bodhisattva is said to be "born into the family," because the profound mind is the place where the bodhisattva is born, being born into the family of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
If one possesses a profound resolve, one will see virtuous friends;
for the various stages (*bhūmi*) are the birthplace of Bodhisattvas and the family home of the perfections (*pāramitā*).
If one attains these stages, then one fulfills all the perfections.
The great vows are the birthplace of the bodhisattva (up to: because these are the birthplace of the bodhisattva, they give birth to the family of Buddhas).
To transform sentient beings is precisely "awakening others."
Wisdom and skillful means are the birthplace of Bodhisattvas, for they are born into the family of the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Because they possess wisdom, they comprehend that dharmas are unarisen; because they possess skillful means, they do not grasp at the mark of non-arising, nor do they stagnate in the quiescence of the two vehicles.
Thus, they are born into the family of the realization of the non-arising of dharmas. Other points may be inferred accordingly; this applies to the preceding sentence as well.
Contemplate that which is produced:
by practicing all dharmas, one is born into the family of all Tathāgatas of the past, present, and future.
△ Second, clarifying the conditions for birth and the retinue.
Good son, for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, up to [the point of] skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he takes skillful means as his father and Prajñā as his mother.

Regarding skillful means as the father, there are briefly three meanings: first, because true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) is quiescent and still, it is tranquil together with the *skandhas* (aggregates), while expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is dynamic and flowing, surging in harmony with the Yang energy; second, because it directly gives birth to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it truly arises from Prajñā.

If one lacks skillful means, one mostly shares the same path as the two vehicles; it is only by virtue of skillful means that one internally attains liberation while externally providing salvation, just like parents.
The perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) serves as the wet nurse;
through giving, one is nourished by merit.
The perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) serves as the foster mother.
The corpse serves as protection; the rest may be considered accordingly.
The perfection of patience is an ornament, up to its fulfillment of awakening, which serves to purify one's lineage.
△ Section Three: Comparing and Revealing Superiority (in two parts). First, a general exposition on the superiority of the family of birth.
"Good son, when a bodhisattva is thus [practicing], he is revered and praised by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas."
△ Second, specifically illustrating the excellence of his wisdom:
"Good son, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva... attains unimpeded penetration into all realms of existence.
△ Second, specifically revealing the birthplace of Maitreya; this section has two parts. First, it demonstrates that his true recompense and other manifestations pervade the Dharma-realm.
"Good son, my body is universally born throughout the entire dharma-realm.
This passage consists of ten phrases: the first phrase is general, while the subsequent eight are specific.
[It begins with] 'equal to the diverse physical forms of all sentient beings' (extending through) 'the vows of all bodhisattvas.'"
△ Third, the final summary.
He manifests his body filling the entire Dharma-realm.
△ Second, manifesting in accordance with the capacities of beings, which consists of two parts: first, the manifestation of birth.
"Good son, I went to the house of a brāhmaṇa in the village of Koṭṭa to transform and deliver him.
'Koṭṭa' means 'pavilion' (kūṭa) in this language; because there are many pavilions in this village, or because the Pavilion of Maitreya (Maitreyakūṭa) is located therein."
"Good son, I dwell within this great multi-storied pavilion (up to) teaching and taming [beings] through various skillful means.
△ Second, regarding what will arise hereafter, there are two parts. First, the actual manifestation of the purpose for which one will arise.
"Good son, I have followed [the path]... until my life here ended and I was reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
Regarding the 'lotus-like' [nature], there are three meanings: first, because the flower blooms where Śākyamuni planted the seed;

second, because the past cause contains the fruit—just as the flower has not yet opened, yet when the cause ceases, the fruit appears, it is like the lotus blooming; third, because it contains the permeation of hearing."
It is real. It is like a lotus that has not yet opened; when the fruit is seen, words vanish. Therefore, it is called "opening the awakening. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

"If the roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva do not encounter the sunlight of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, they will undoubtedly wither and die. This universally corroborates the preceding meaning. △ Third, the conclusion and reconciliation of the three sages.
"Good son, my vows shall be fulfilled (until) you and Mañjuśrī both behold me.
There are three reasons why we both behold me: first, because we together assist in the work of transformation;

second, because Sudhana represents practice while Mañjuśrī represents faith and wisdom, and at the time of attaining perfect enlightenment, both shall realize this together; third, because Mañjuśrī is an ancient Buddha and Sudhana is [to be] a future [Buddha]."
The Buddha. Maitreya manifests as a Buddha; the three periods of time are perfectly interfused in a vast and great equilibrium. Therefore, it is said that "both are seen.
△ Fourth, pointing out the future companion has three parts. First, the exhortation to go and the instruction to inquire.
"Good son, you should go to the spiritual friend Mañjuśrī.
Since your stage as a practitioner is nearing its culmination, he will cause you to reflect back upon the source of the mind.
Thus he spoke, saying: "How does a bodhisattva [proceed]? ... He shall analyze and explain it for you.
△ Second, the explanation of the reasons for the exhortation, in two parts.
First, the inquiry: "For what reason?
The intent of the inquiry is: Mañjuśrī has already seen [the Buddha]; why then does he exhort [others] to go? △ Second, the explanation. The intent of the explanation is: His virtue...
Profound and vast; because the conditions of past lives are weighty, there are two parts herein. First, it clarifies the breadth of his practice:
"Mañjuśrī’s great vows... [continue] until all the merits of all bodhisattvas are without rest."
Regarding the birth of the bodhisattva’s merits: he presides over the Dharma-gate of faith, for it nurtures all roots of goodness.
Good son, Mañjuśrī has constantly served as the mother of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.

As the Mother of Buddhas, she presides over the gateway of Prajñā; dwelling in profound wisdom and seeing the reality of phenomena, she is eternally the teacher of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas.
One who acts as a teacher for bodhisattvas possesses skillful wisdom, has attained mastery of liberation, and has reached the ultimate fulfillment of the practices of Samantabhadra;
thus, they teach and bring to maturity all sentient beings until they have perfected all the practices performed by Samantabhadra.
△ Second, revealing the depth of his conditions and that he has already extensively accomplished benefit for others:
"Good son Mañjuśrī... [he] was born and practiced together with you in the past."
△ Third, the summary exhortation, which is explained in three parts. First, the summary exhortation:
"Therefore, son of good family, you should go to the place where Mañjuśrī is; do not give rise to weariness."
Possessing these two aforementioned meanings, you should go without weariness.
Mañjuśrī shall explain all merits for you. △ Second, the interrogation and explanation, in two parts. First, the interrogation.
Why is this? The intent of the inquiry is:
"How do you know for certain that he possesses the two aforementioned meanings? Second, the explanation:
"The various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) whom you previously saw... [all] are due to the majestic spiritual power (vīrya-anubhāva) of Mañjuśrī."
The commentary explains: Since all benefits accomplished are due to his power, one knows that his practice is vast and his conditions are profound;
if one were to behold him directly, the benefits obtained would be even more increased. △ Third, the conclusion on the perfection of his virtues.
Mañjuśrī has attained ultimate perfection in all respects.

Seeing him at the beginning constitutes the commencement of faith; seeing him at the end constitutes the culmination of wisdom. Therefore, it is said that he has "attained ultimate perfection in all things.
△ Fifth: Expressing Gratitude and Taking Leave.
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet (and so forth), gazing up at him with earnest devotion before taking his leave and departing.
Below this, we enter the eightieth fascicle.
△ Fourth: The Wisdom of Clear Illumination Manifests Non-dual Characteristics; it reveals that while the preceding causal dharmas give rise to fruits, their essence is without discrimination.

Because the wisdom of the ultimate state and so forth are both characterized by duality; furthermore, since Sudhana’s obstacles have been exhausted and his delusions eliminated, he has never from the beginning stirred a single thought.
Therefore, his retrospective illumination is solely the initial mind, with no second [mind] at all. This is precisely the non-duality of faith and wisdom.
Although the text contains only three sections, the first concerns following the teachings to seek [the truth].

At that time, the youth Sudhana, having traveled through more than one hundred and ten cities—the meaning of "one hundred and ten" has already been seen in the preceding text—this journey through the cities further possesses two meanings:

first, from Maitreya down to Mañjuśrī, he himself traversed one hundred and ten cities independently, rather than including them in succession with the previous count; second, [the number] is augmented.
The previous one hundred and ten friends are therefore referred to as "the remaining cities," which collectively includes the aforementioned friends.

This is because all phenomena are universally gathered and returned to the single illumination. If this is so, how can the previous friends and these cities be considered the same? There are two meanings to this:
first, since a friend must rely upon a city, there is one city for each friend; second, it may be that within a single city, one encounters many friends.
Alternatively, he sought a companion, traveling through many cities until he had secured one hundred and ten, in order to symbolize the Dharma;
thus, he arrived at the kingdom of Samantamukha.

The Jin edition states: Upon reaching the country of Pumen (Universal Gate), one manifests the distinctions of dharmas and returns to the non-dual characteristic; this is precisely because it is the Universal Gate.
[This occurs at] the city of Sumana.
Sumanā, which in this [language] is translated as "Delightful," is the name of a flower. It signifies that wisdom illuminates the single nature, thereby delighting the fundamental mind;
thus, it is the City of Virtue-Born (Guṇotpatti), situated at its gateway.
Having fully perfected his understanding of the mind, and being about to enter the gate of non-duality of Prajñā,
he contemplated Mañjuśrī, observing him in accordance with his nature, searching for him everywhere, and desiring to pay him homage.
△ Second, entry through seeing, hearing, and realization. From here below is what was omitted [in the previous section]. The meaning of the text is as previously explained.
However, because it illuminates the ultimate non-duality such that both mind and object vanish, there is no abbreviated salutation or inquiry.

Because faith and understanding are both transcended, the manifested body is not seen; yet, because the reflecting awareness has not shifted from the state of faith, the right hand is extended. Furthermore, because it is not seen...
This constitutes the true vision; it is simply the realization that one's own mind is empty *prajñā*. The text has three parts. First, the bestowing of grace by touching the crown of the head:
at that time, Mañjuśrī extended his right hand from afar.
One first believes that this applies to the ultimate fruit; hence it is said, "extending afar. As the practice of compliance is accomplished, it is called the "right hand.
It passes through one hundred and ten yojanas.
Because it penetrates beyond the preceding stages. However, "passing the city" refers to transcending its boundaries, while "yojanas" clarifies the transcendence of numerical measures.

Furthermore, the former [passage] refers to transcending the various stages of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa*), while the latter refers to transcending the various stages of the ground of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*).
He places his hand upon Sudhana’s head.

Placing the hand upon the head signifies receiving and embracing him, for he has likewise placed the Universal Dharma (Pūrvavidhi) upon the crown of his mind; this is because his faith has reached its ultimate limit.

△ Second, the instruction on the Dharma-gate: this involves pointing out what is lost to reveal what is attained. That is to say, if one is separated from the root of faith and so forth, one will not understand the Dharma.

The phrase "nature, etc. serves as a counter-illustration to show that Sudhana possesses the faculty of faith and so forth, and is thus able to comprehend the nature of dharmas and so on. Within this, there are two parts:
first, a listing of the practices and dharmas that are lacking.
He spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
This passage contains nine phrases; the first seven lack the cause, for if one is separated from the faculty of faith.
First, because they lack the basis for practice, their minds are inferior and they experience sorrow and regret.
Second, because they seek only the small, their minds are inferior; dwelling within birth and death, they experience sorrow and regret.
Their meritorious practices are incomplete;
the three untimely deaths are not yet averted;
and they have fallen away from their diligent effort.
Fourth, they do not progress upward because their minds dwell with attachment to a single root of goodness.
Fifth, they stagnate in that one root of goodness.
They become satisfied with even a small amount of merit;
they do not seek extensively,
and they are unable to skillfully initiate their practices and vows.
Seventh, they do not give rise to the vow for non-abiding practice. Regarding the latter two [of the seven causes], they lack the necessary conditions:
they are not sustained by the protection of spiritual friends, nor are they remembered by the Tathāgatas.
△ Second, the inability to achieve benefit. There are fifteen phrases:
being unable to fully comprehend such a dharma-nature (up to) such conduct and such spheres of experience.
Regarding the first five [faculties], with respect to the objects and principles of what is to be known,
they are entirely incapable of either knowing them exhaustively, knowing them in their various aspects, realizing them, or attaining them.

The final ten [verses] concern the scope of the knower; reflect upon them by analogy with the preceding texts. Furthermore, among the first nine, the initial one—the faculty of faith—is the causal factor that is lacking;
without it, none of the others can accomplish benefit. If considered in terms of the Dharma, the merit accrues to faith;
if considered in terms of persons, the Dharma of the former friend is entirely due to Mañjuśrī. △ Third, concluding the benefits and attributing them [to the source].
The main text consists of ten phrases.
At this time, Mañjuśrī proclaimed this Dharma (extending to) the accomplishment of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) dharma-gates.
Of these, the first nine summarize the profound benefits; the first one is general, while the remaining eight are specific.
They are fully endowed with the immeasurable light of great wisdom—
which is the union of *prajñā* and skillful means—
thereby enabling them to attain the bodhisattva’s boundless *dhāraṇīs*, boundless supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and boundless knowledge.
This is the perfection of wisdom (jñānapāramitā).
It causes one to enter the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) of Samantabhadra’s practice;
for every lifting and placing of the feet is in accord with the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Furthermore, placing Sudhana at his own dwelling place signifies that this is the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which is the great wisdom of Mañjuśrī because it is a dwelling in non-dwelling.

Moreover, Samantabhadra’s site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is the principle of the dharma-realm, while his own dwelling place is the wisdom of Mañjuśrī; these two meanings are identical, demonstrating this for the sake of the subsequent spiritual friends.
The realm of Samantabhadra;
Mañjuśrī then withdraws and ceases to appear.

The final phrase signifies the returning of function to its source, for that which was to be accomplished is complete. Faith reaches the limit of the sphere of wisdom; thus, the characteristics of faith [are established].
They have passed away; therefore, it is said they do not appear. △ Third, encountering superior conditions, he practiced and respectfully served them.
Thereupon, Sudhana contemplated and observed (until) he received and practiced their teachings without any opposition.

However, these various friends and the subsequent Samantabhadra all lack any explicit instruction; this signifies the realization of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), as it is free from the characteristics of "this" and "that.
These three thousand friends possess many meanings: first, they fulfill the preceding [section], as they are still the benefit of Mañjuśrī;
second, they accord with what follows, serving as the skillful means for entering into principle. Furthermore, discussing these friends generally, they can be further divided into three categories.
[This is divided into] sections. The first Mañjuśrī alone represents the beginning of the arising of faith; the subsequent Mañjuśrī represents the end of the perfection of wisdom.
Thus, one sees these friends of the three thousand worlds and so forth in their entirety. The final Samantabhadra signifies the non-duality of principle and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, while the previous friends were each encountered individually, this constitutes the "Pure Gate" (*śuddha-mukha*); here, all the friends are seen simultaneously and instantaneously.

This immediately reveals the section on the intermingled gates. Subsequently, the single figure of Samantabhadra is endowed with all the aforementioned spiritual friends; this represents the non-obstruction between the pure and the intermingled.

Furthermore, the specific dharma-gates attained by these various friends and their respective practices of receiving and performing them are not fully detailed here, as the text abbreviates the extensive by concluding from the concise.
Therefore, they are collectively referred to as "three thousand. △ Fifth Major Section: Revealing the Characteristic of the Vastness of the Cause.
Because the preceding [section] shows that the illumination of principle is non-dual, it reveals its profound depth; only then is one fit to become a Buddha.
This is the vast cause, for each and every cause accords with the *dharmatā*. Thus, in the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā*, the aspects are subsumed into the essence, while in the *Samantabhadra-dharmadhātu*...
This constitutes the secret layering [of meanings]. If the two sages are contrasted with one another, Mañjuśrī is the subject who realizes;
if the two sages are contrasted with Sudhana, Mañjuśrī is likewise the object of realization, because he has now attained what had not yet been attained.
The text is divided into three parts. First, the pursuit according to the teaching, which consists of twenty-six phrases.
This increases the pursuit of all-encompassing wisdom.
The first [phrase] above indicates the seeking of the fruit of Buddhahood; the last [phrase] generally contemplates the perfected cause.

The meanings of the intermediate phrases apply to both the preceding and the following; they are all causes for attaining Buddhahood and are all objects of liberation. Therefore, they are subsumed as ten pairs.
The vast ocean of compassion increases the great cloud of loving-kindness... [up to] the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of abiding in tranquility.
The four preceding [immeasurables] are equalities; they are "universal tranquility" because they are characterized by equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Universally taking all vast objects as its focus, it studies the vast merits of all Buddhas.
These two—merit and wisdom—have no external objects as their conditions, because they are wisdom itself.
They enter into the definitive knowledge and vision of all Buddhas and increase the dharmas that assist the path to all-knowledge.
These two entries correctly increase the assistance;
they skillfully cultivate the profound resolve of all Bodhisattvas and know the sequence of the appearance of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
These two constitute the cause of cultivation and the knowledge of the fruit;
they enter the ocean of all dharmas, turn the wheel of all dharmas, and give rise to all worlds.
These three constitute the entry into the dharma and its manifestation in birth.
Entering the ocean of all bodhisattva vows and dwelling through all kalpas to cultivate bodhisattva practices—
these two constitute the realization of vows and cultivation.
They illuminate the realm of all Tathāgatas and nourish all the faculties of bodhisattvas.
These two illuminate the superior while increasing the inferior;
they attain the pure radiance of all-knowledge that universally illumines the ten directions, removing all obscurations of darkness.
These two realize the ultimate while illuminating the provisional.
Wisdom pervades the dharma-realm; throughout all buddha-fields (up to) it universally manifests its body, reaching everywhere without exception.
These two wisdoms pervade the body and reach everywhere.
They destroy all obstacles, enter the unimpeded dharma, and abide in the ground of equality within the dharma-realm.

These three destroy obstacles and enter into principle. This entry into the unimpeded dharma constitutes non-dual non-obstruction when directed upward, and constitutes the unimpeded Dharma-realm when directed downward.
Abiding in the stage of equality is precisely the dwelling place of Mañjuśrī himself mentioned in the preceding text.
He contemplates the sphere of Samantabhadra’s liberation.
The subsequent summary phrase refers back to the "place of practice" (caryā-maṇḍala) of Samantabhadra; this is because it manifests the vast characteristics of the cause.
Mañjuśrī refers generally to Sudhana’s universal contemplation, which differs from the previous text where one friend referred specifically to another friend. This is truly because...
Because Universal Observation is itself Samantabhadra. △ Second, hearing and beholding the preceding signs has two parts. First, hearing [the names] consists of thirteen phrases;
that is, hearing the name of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra.
The first line mentions the name of the person from whom one hears; the two characters "hears" (wen) then run through all the subsequent phrases.

Here, "hearing" does not mean hearing from one person or many people, but rather hearing by directly designating the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). The final twelve lines concern hearing regarding the stages of practice and realization.
Regarding the practices of the path of vows, the path of assistance, and the direct path:
the first three may be understood as before.
As for the various stages (*bhūmi*):

Within the stage of Samantabhadra, there is the stage upon which one's own practice relies, as well as the stage encompassed by perfect interfusion. The first phrase serves as the general [heading], while the following eight phrases provide the specific details.
This is the stage of skillful means (*upāya*).
The preparatory application,
the entry into the stage,
and the entry into the mind.
The stages of superior progress,
the emergence of the mind,
and the abiding in the stages.
Abiding in the mind,
one cultivates the stages and practices generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth.

The "stage of the objective realm" refers to the first [of the ten stages], the universally pervasive *tathatā* (suchness), which serves as the object to be realized; it is also the objective limit that has been attained.
The power of the stages (*bhūmi*) refers to the functions of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), such as subduing the heterodox and gathering in sentient beings;
this is the co-residence of the stages.
That is, they abide together in reliance upon the Buddha’s wisdom. △ Second, clarifying the vision [of Samantabhadra] has two parts. First, looking up to his virtue and practicing contemplation:
they thirst for and long to see the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra;
because they have heard of this person's Dharma, they give rise to such thirst and longing.
Regarding this very Vajragarbha Bodhimaṇḍa, up to the seat of the treasury of all jewel lotuses:
that which clearly elucidates the cultivation of the contemplation of the bodhimaṇḍa is the locus of contemplation.

As for "Vajragarbha," in terms of its symbolic meaning, it refers to the arising of all [phenomena] within the vajra-wisdom of the very essence of the Buddha-fruit bodhi of one's own mind, which is the object of faith.

The Indrālaṃkāra and Samantabhadra-citta-visualization: regarding the phenomena, this refers to the aforementioned vajra-ground, which is called a "treasury" (*kośa*) because it contains and is fully adorned with virtues.
However, as for the structural momentum of this sūtra, it ought to comprise ten assemblies in accordance with its inexhaustibility.
Furthermore, since the meaning of the initial awakening site should ultimately return to its source, we shall for now rely on the text.

In contrast to the two assemblies—the original and the derivative—this represents the principle of "gathering the derivative back to the original. Therefore, Sudhana does not need to seek it elsewhere;
rather, he begins his contemplative inquiry right before the Tathāgata’s seat at the very place where the first assembly was originally established.
"Generating a mind as vast as the realm of empty space" (extending to) "the ultimate mind directed toward the ten powers of the Tathāgata.
This correctly reveals the contemplation of the mind (*citta-bhāvanā*). There are eleven phrases, all of which give rise to the mind by taking the sphere of Samantabhadra as their object;
therefore, they are subsequently seen. △ Second, beholding the marvelous and rare. This has two parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent.

When the youth Sudhana gave rise to such a thought (up to the point where it says), because of the power of the common roots of goodness shared with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, this also reveals the causes for the vision.
△ Second, the actual beholding of the wonders, in two parts: first, seeing the auspicious signs.
He beholds ten kinds of auspicious signs. What are these ten?
They consist of five pairs of ten phrases. In each pair, the preceding phrase clarifies the pure land as the basis, while the succeeding phrase clarifies the sentient beings dwelling therein.
What is meant by "seeing all Buddha-fields as pure" (up to) "the mind constantly recollecting the Buddha" constitutes the ten [aspects].
△ Second, beholding the light.
Furthermore, seeing ten kinds of radiant signs (up to) "vast vows pervading the entire Dharma-realm" constitutes the ten [aspects].
The previous auspicious sign was the direct vision of a single layer of pure lands; this clarifies the vision of multiple layers. Furthermore, the former was coarse while this is subtle;

the former was the essential form (*tǐxiàng*) while this is the functional activity (*yèyòng*). Nevertheless, all are the lands of Samantabhadra’s dependent retribution (*yībào*). △ Third, the entry through seeing, hearing, and realization has three parts.
First, concluding the preceding and generating the subsequent.
At that time, the youth Sudhana saw these ten kinds of [omens], and thought: "I shall now certainly see the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
From observing these preceding signs, he developed the conviction that he would surely see him.
Increasing his roots of goodness, he beheld all Buddhas (up to) giving rise to resolute understanding and attaining all-knowledge.
△ Second, the cultivation through the arousal of contemplation:
At that time, Sudhana universally gathered all his faculties and with single-minded intent sought to see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Gathering the distracted mind to abide in meditative concentration,
they give rise to great diligence with no turning back;
they exert themselves with vigor and never retreat.
Immediately, one observes the ten directions with the Universal Eye (up to: one forms the thought of seeing Samantabhadra everywhere.
One contemplates his pervasive body, for he takes the Dharma-realm as his body.
With the eye of wisdom, one contemplates the path of Samantabhadra (up to: with great compassion as firm as a diamond.
Compassion and wisdom are vast and expansive.
May I, throughout the future, always follow [this path] (up to: enter the realm of the Tathāgata and abide in the stage of Samantabhadra.
Attaining the fruit through the perfection of the cause—this comprehensively encompasses all contemplations. If a practitioner wishes to see [the truth], they should practice according to this;
apart from this contemplative mind, even seeing it would not be superior. △ Third, the explicit clarification of seeing, hearing, realizing, and entering, in two parts.

First, the explicit seeing, hearing, realizing, and entering, in two parts. First, the perfection of the causes for attaining benefit, in four parts. First, attaining benefit by seeing the body, in two parts. First, seeing the excellence...

Regarding the four aspects of the body: first, as for the general vision of the physical marks of supreme virtue, at that time the youth Sudhana beheld Samantabhadra Bodhisattva within the assembly before the Tathāgata.
Because he previously gave rise to the sublime perception before the lion throne at the site of enlightenment,
he sat upon a precious lotus lion throne such that no bodhisattvas were able to gaze upon him.
△ Second, the specific vision of the emergence from the pores.
One sees that from each and every pore of Samantabhadra’s body [the emanations extend] until they cause all bodhisattvas to give rise to great joy.
These emerge from the pores and pervade the entire dharma-realm; in reality, they are infinitely layered and inexhaustible, though here twenty layers are briefly manifested.
Furthermore, this is also in response to the eleven types of mind arising from Sudhana’s yearning and aspiration.
Among these, the first five minds—beginning with "equal to space" and "vast as space"—pervade all these phrases; the remaining six minds give rise to the individual phrases, excluding the first one.
One sees every single pore emit all Buddha-fields (extending to) the assemblies and sites of enlightenment raining down maṇi jewels.
These five phrases arise because, through the previously mentioned path of contemplation that clarifies the mind, the emission of clouds and so forth all serve to adorn the site of enlightenment.
Seeing from each and every pore the emergence of all buddha-fields (up to) the protection and maintenance of the wheel of Dharma of all Tathāgatas—
these three phrases arise from the previously mentioned mind that enters the ocean of the Buddha-dharma.
"Seeing from every single pore, in every moment of thought, [emanations] proceeding until they provide a basis for those who are without a basis.
This single phrase, along with the first phrase, arises from the previously mentioned mind directed toward transforming the realm of sentient beings.
One sees that from every single pore, in every moment of thought, [emanations] issue forth (extending to) causing all sentient beings who are purely defiled to attain purification.
These four arise from the aforementioned mind that purifies all lands, while also concurrently incorporating the mind that transforms sentient beings.
One sees that from every single pore, in every moment of thought, [emanations] issue forth (up to) the growth of the Great Dharma and the attainment of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).
The final six phrases arise from the previous dwelling in all kalpas and the mind directed toward the ultimate ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Tathāgata;
these should both be contemplated according to the text. Thus it is known that each is seen according to the specific scope of one's own mind. △ Third: Contemplating the Substance.
The internal section contains two parts. First, connecting the preceding with the subsequent:
"At that time, the youth Sudhana (up to) his body and mind were filled with immeasurable joy and exultation.
△ Second, the main exposition of the inclusion, which also has two parts. First, seeing the three thousandfold world system.
He contemplates each and every limb of Samantabhadra again, until all such matters are clearly seen.
△ Second, the universal application to the ten directions and the three periods of time:
as when seeing this world, he sees everything in the ten directions, each distinct and not intermingled.
△ Fourth, the conclusion that [the principle] pervades everywhere.
As in this passage from "Vairocana Tathāgata" (up to) "the playful supernatural powers of all Tathāgatas," there are four layers of analogies presented.
The final phrase of the Vairocana section serves as a general conclusion for Samantabhadra within the sensory realms (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, one knows that the preceding...
Thus, within the body, one contains the *dharmadhātu*; because it is vast and boundless, this manifests its meaning of "universality" (*prabhūta*).
Now, taking this very body that contains the *dharmadhātu*, one enters imperceptibly into the midst of all particles, becoming supple and unimpeded; this clarifies its meaning of "worthy" (*bhadra*).
Pervading both internally and externally, all limitations are exhausted; therefore, he is named Samantabhadra. 2. Attaining Profound Benefit.
The youth Sudhana beholds Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... [up to] the perfection of wisdom (jñāna-pāramitā).

Having attained the perfection of wisdom, he has already manifested the fulfillment of the stages; how much more so for the ten [stages] which are inexhaustible? △ Second, receiving benefit through the touching of the crown;
this has three parts. First, the touching of the crown.
Once the youth Sudhana had attained this, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva extended his right hand and stroked the crown of his head.
△ Second, the attainment of benefits:
Having been thus stroked on the head, Sudhana immediately attained as many samādhis as there are atoms in the universe, which became his retinue.
By observing outwardly, one attains the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); by this personal realization through the touching of the crown of the head, one attains samādhi.
In each and every samādhi, one beholds that which was never seen before—right down to the pure light of omniscience (*sarvajña*) as numerous as atoms.
△ Third, the general conclusion:
Just as it is in this Sahā world, the Dharma-gates attained by Vairocana Buddha (up to the point mentioned) are likewise identical.
This is because Sudhana and others are themselves Samantabhadra.

△ Third, the profundity and vastness of the cause. Because the cause is profound, the fruit is substantial. The text is divided into three parts. First, the inquiry and response that examine the vision.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra... [up to] "...is knowable only by the Tathāgata.

△ Second, revealing the profundity and remoteness of the cause, in three parts: First, specifically clarifying the practice of seeking Bodhi; second, first, conforming to and revealing the practices undertaken.
Samantabhadra addressed him, saying: "Good son... [until] practicing the Buddha-dharma and upholding the True Teaching.
△ Second, abandoning faults and perfecting virtues:
"Good son, throughout as many oceans of kalpas as there are... [until] the factors conducive to the Path and the Great Bodhicitta."
△ Second, a general clarification of the practices of compassion and wisdom.
"Good son, my adornment of Buddha-lands... [as far as] the oceans of kalpas may be exhausted, this has no end.
△ Second, a specific clarification of the practice of seeking the Dharma, in two parts. First, a negative demonstration that there is nothing one cannot relinquish.

"Good son, within the ocean of my Dharma, regarding all that exists which one might seek to obtain, there is not even a single word that I do not relinquish, let alone an entire section. For a single word is identical to the entirety."
It is like a single drop from the ocean. △ Second, revealing the purpose for seeking [the Dharma] and concluding that it is inexhaustible:
"Good son, the Dharma I seek—from [this point] until—could not be fully expounded even in an ocean of eons equal in number to the atoms within a Buddha-field."
△ Second, the cause for binding and the fruit of accomplishment, in two parts. First, the cause for binding. The text contains ten phrases.
Therefore, son of good family, by means of such powers of the aids to the path (upakāra-mārga), up to the power of great aspiration and the power of cultivating merit...
The former four are the causal conditions;
the power of wisdom that contemplates all dharmas as they truly are and the power of the eye of wisdom are these two revealing causes.

By virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the power of great compassion, the power of pure supernormal faculties, and the power of spiritual friends, the latter four [powers] penetrate both the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the causes (*hetu*); because they possess the merit of achieving fruition, they are all termed "powers" (*bala*). △ Second, the achievement of fruition.
One attains this ultimate, pure *dharmakāya* which is equal throughout the three periods of time.
By means of the cause of realization (*vibhāva-hetu*), one attains the fruit of the *dharmakāya*,
and further attains the pure and unsurpassed *rūpakāya*.
By virtue of these causal conditions, one attains the fruit of the form body (*rūpakāya*),
which transcends all worlds and accords with all sentient beings, such that none who behold it fail to rejoice.
△ Section Three: Contemplating the Boundless Utility [of the Buddha-body]. First, exhorting contemplation by citing its benefits, which has three parts.
First, the heading: "Good son, you should first contemplate such a physical body as mine."
△ Second, the explanation has two parts. First, clarifying that it is difficult to see or hear:
"This physical body of mine [is such that] throughout oceans of boundless kalpas... even for a thousand billion nayuta kalpas, it is difficult to see and difficult to hear."
△ Second, the three benefits derived from seeing and hearing [the Buddha]. First, the benefit of not retreating from Bodhi:
"Good son, if there are sentient beings (up to) those who see or hear me, all shall likewise be so."
△ Second, the benefit of the maturation of the roots of goodness.
There may be sentient beings who, for a single day and night (up to), give rise to joy and all attain maturation.
△ Third, the general summary of many approaches: all attain maturation without falling back.
"Good son, by means of such [practices] as these, I have attained non-retrogression from *samyaksambodhi*.
Above, in all the various gates, I am non-retrogressive; below, all [beings] of every kind are brought to maturity."
"Good son, if there are sentient beings (up to) who will certainly be born within my pure body, they shall be born in a pure land.
How is this body born? There are two meanings to this. First, regarding the land of the *dharmatā-kāya*:
when it constitutes the essence of the land, it is called a 'pure land'; when it constitutes the essence of the body, it is called a 'pure body. This arises from that which is supported (*āśrita*)."
Furthermore, because he wishes to manifest that the substance upon which they rely is one, he speaks of the "body born [of karma]. Second, regarding their characteristics and functions:

the pure land is the land upon which it relies, while the pure body is the land within the body. Because he wishes to manifest the mutual fusion of the body and the land, he speaks of the "pure body born [of karma]. △ Third, the summary.
"Noble son, you should observe this pure body of mine.
△ Third, observing and seeing its wonders in three parts. First, seeing the three worlds contained within each pore.
At that time, the youth Sudhana observed Samantabhadra... (up to) ...such matters as these, each being distinct.
△ Second, seeing the body of Samantabhadra pervading all lands and manifesting great functions;
furthermore, seeing Samantabhadra within each and every ocean of worlds [until] reaching *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
△ Third, he saw himself and others as emanations of Samantabhadra.
At that time, the youth Sudhana again saw his own body (extending) throughout all worlds, teaching and transforming sentient beings.
△ Third, the comparison that reveals superiority has three parts. First, the comparison of roots of goodness:
Furthermore, even the roots of goodness of the youth Sudhana from his approach to the Buddha-fields (up to) cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
△ Second, the comparison of the oceans of lands entered.
This is from the time when the youth Sudhana first resolved his mind [until] all his pores were likewise so.
△ Second, the two aspects of the three pairs of superiorities that transcend the above. First, the specific explanation of the horizontal and vertical, the profound and the vast.
Within the pore-lands of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, the youth Sudhana [perceived].
Within this, there are three worlds;
taking a single step, one passes through worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields,
thereby manifesting their horizontal vastness.
If one were to practice in this manner throughout all kalpas until the end of the future,
even with such clear and vertical penetration,
one would still be unable to know it.
This reveals its profound depth:
within a single pore, there are successions of oceans of lands and treasuries of oceans of lands;
"treasury" refers here to that which encompasses and contains.
The distinctions of the oceans of lands and the universal entry into the oceans of lands—
the universal entry referring to their vast pervasiveness—
encompass all limits of the formation, destruction, and adornment of the oceans of lands.
Above is the world of the vessel-realm; below is the world of the wisdom of the Perfectly Awakened Ones.
Even these cannot know the sequence of the ocean of Buddhas, nor the limits of the gathering and dispersal of the ocean-like assembly of Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the world of sentient beings cannot know the limits of all such oceans, from their entry into the realm of sentient beings [up to] these [vast expanses].
△ Second, the summary of their equality and omnipresence.
When the youth Sudhana [reaches] Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, it is said that he does not vanish from this land to appear in another land;

nor does he vanish here to appear there. This is because the characteristics of vanishing and appearing are identical to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), for the characteristics of "this" and "that" are mutually identical.
In every thought-moment, they pervade the boundless oceans of lands (up to) causing [beings] to turn toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
△ The second stage: equality with the Buddhas.
At that time, the youth Sudhana (reaches) the ocean of all practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
The preceding phrase clarifies his own attainment; the remainder is equal to what has been stated above.
Equal to Samantabhadra,
they are equal in the perfection of causes; equal to all Buddhas.
The equal fruits are fulfilled. Hereafter, the specific characteristics of this equality are revealed:
first, the body fills all worlds, up to liberation and mastery, which are entirely equal.

This is precisely what is meant by "awakening" (*bodhi*). Since the stage of the cause is already fulfilled, there is nothing further to be cultivated; therefore, it is simply called "equality" (*samatā*), without distinguishing any further seeking.

This constitutes the sudden perfection in a single lifetime, wherein the sequential progression (*pratipatti*) is also complete. It is not merely that the beginning and end of the contemplation of principle (*tattva-darśana*) are perfectly integrated.
Second, hearing of the Buddha’s inconceivable supreme virtues. While the preceding prose section only manifested the fulfillment of the causes, this—

The verses now present the function of the fruition; they do not comment upon the preceding prose. However, there are two intentions: first, in relation to Samantabhadra, Samantabhadra’s intention is as follows:
"What you have perceived above regarding my inconceivable virtues still pertains to the stage of cause; I now manifest the fruition to you."
It is even more profoundly deep. Second, in contrast to Sudhana: while Sudhana is equal to the Buddha, he is merely one whose causes are perfected;

because the ocean of fruition transcends all verbal expression, his attainment of Buddhahood is not explicitly stated. Here, by relying on the manifestation of the Buddha’s virtues, the characteristics of Sudhana’s attainment of fruition are revealed;
thus, the prose and verses interweave cause and effect. Within this section, there are three parts; first, there are four verses.
He proclaims the virtues of the Buddha, exhorts them to listen, and grants permission to speak.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra spoke in verse:
"You should eliminate all defilements of delusion... (until) never giving rise to conceptual thoughts through discrimination."
△ Second, the prose section describes the assembly’s yearning desire to hear [the teaching].
At that time, having heard this exposition, the bodhisattvas (up to) formed this thought and gave rise to a profound sense of longing and veneration.

△ Third, the extensive presentation of the characteristics of virtue, which causes the assembly to seek fulfillment in two ways. First, the prose section provides a reiterated admonition and grants permission for the scope of the discourse.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... (omitted)... "I now wish to speak of a single drop from the ocean of the Buddha’s merits."
△ Second, the verses: Extensively manifesting the inconceivable virtues of the Buddha in ninety-five verses, which are divided into two parts.

First, the initial ninety-three verses separately praise the Buddha’s virtues; therein, the first eighty verses are explained through direct teaching (*dharmadeśanā*), and the latter thirteen verses clarify them through metaphors.
However, these collectively praise the twenty-one kinds of excellence of Vairocana’s ten perfected bodies.
Regarding the supreme qualities, they should actually be divided into twenty-one sections; however, for the time being, there are nineteen, because the final three are combined.
The first consists of two verses concerning the quality of proceeding with absolute unimpededness regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
He then spoke in verse: "The Buddha’s wisdom is vast and equal to space... (down to) ...manifesting boundless deeds in every thought-moment.
This refers to the Buddha’s unobstructed wisdom, which is characterized by non-attachment and non-obstruction regarding all things and their various categories and distinctions.
△ Second, there is one verse clarifying that within existence and non-existence there is no duality of characteristics. True Suchness is supremely pure;
it is able to enter into merits according to the various activities of sentient beings' minds (up to: yet the Buddha is fundamentally without movement of thought).

This means that because one realizes the non-duality of *tathatā*, there is no movement of thought. △ Third, there are three verses concerning the merit of never ceasing the effortless (*anābhoga*) buddha-activities.
There are those who see the Buddha seated in various places, yet do not hear [his teaching] because their minds are impure.
This means that he dwells in the non-abiding state of a Buddha and performs buddha-activities without rest; hence it is said, "some see," and so forth.
△ Fourth, there are fifteen verses concerning the non-differentiation of the basis, the intention, and the activity within the Dharma-body.

Regarding "virtue" (*guṇa*): it means that because the Buddhas are identical in terms of the wisdom upon which they rely, identical in their altruistic intention to benefit sentient beings, and identical in their manifesting and transformative activities, the preceding sutra states that they have "attained the equality of the Buddhas. This is also consistent with the "intention of equality" among the four intentions explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Therefore, this detailed enumeration shows that all Buddhas are mutually pervasive; this explanation is already excellent. Now, furthermore:
This is proven by the logic of the text. These various Buddhas are all the body of Vairocana. This refers to the words of the scripture:

"In this trichiliocosm, Akṣobhya is in the center. Since the Tathāgata Akṣobhya originally resided in the eastern direction, the fact that he is now said to be "here" clarifies that he is not different from this [Vairocana].
Furthermore, as for Amitāyus Buddha and Candrabuddhi Tathāgata, they both pervade the ten directions; how could it be possible for them to be separated by this [world-system]?
Furthermore, since it is said that some see [him], we know that a single Buddha appears differently according to the perceptions of those who behold him.

If one were to say that other Buddhas are praised separately while simply stating that Akṣobhya is here, how could this constitute a praise of his virtues? Moreover, the Flower Treasury Sea of Lands (*kusumatalagarbhavyūha*) is entirely the transformation realm of Vairocana;
since Amitāyus and the others have not emerged outside of these land-systems (*kṣetradhātu*), are they not indeed this very Buddha? (The Lotus Sutra...)

However, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the dharmakāya possesses five characteristics. The first phrase identifies its characteristic as pure phenomena (*śukladharma*), because it is the ultimate fruit, characterized by perfection and mastery.
The next two phrases refer to its inconceivable characteristic. The final one refers to its non-dual characteristic.

Next is the characteristic of being without dependence; next is the characteristic of eternal abiding; next, regarding the two similes: the simile of a painting in empty space and the simile of a dream without basis.
These are neither existent nor non-existent, possessing these two characteristics; other things cannot serve as similes, or they are omitted and not illustrated. △ Seventeenth:

The equality of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-samatā*) means that until the very limit of birth and death (*saṃsāra-koti*), there is the constant manifestation of the merit of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

Its equality with space means it is inexhaustible merit; its equality with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) means it is ultimate merit, for it does not end at the limit of reality but extends to the limit of the future.
